events.summary: U.S. Energy Information Administration - EIA - Independent Statistics and Analysis Browse by tag liquid fuels natural gas electricity oil/petroleum production/supply crude oil consumption/demand generation prices map states exports/imports international coal renewables weather forecasts/projections gasoline capacity steo (short-term energy outlook) Hurricane Isaias nears landfall, leading to production shut-ins Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, U.S. Energy Atlas map of hurricanes, cyclones, and typhoons ; National Weather Service’s National Hurricane Center Note: LNG=liquefied natural gas As of 4:00 a.m. central time on October 9, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration expects Hurricane Isaias to make landfall on the Gulf Coast late Friday or early Saturday, creating the potential for significant disruptions to energy infrastructure. Hurricane Isaias is the first hurricane of the 2026 Atlantic season and will be the largest storm system to make landfall in the region since Hurricane Helene in September 2024. Hurricane Isaias’s forecasted path toward the Gulf Coast has already impacted crude oil and natural gas production in the region. The Marine Minerals Administration reports that as of Thursday, October 8, 130 production platforms and rigs have been evacuated or moved resulting in production shut-ins of about 1.3 million barrels per day of crude oil and 1.1 billion million cubic feet per day of natural gas. The U.S. Gulf Coast is home to a large portion of the U.S. refining fleet, and the impacts from Hurricane Isaias could affect refinery operations . events.title: OpenAI says heavy ChatGPT users may hit limits sooner as it merges Chat and Work
events.summary: OpenAI has started rolling out a unified Chat and Work experience in ChatGPT to a few of its users, amid criticism from some subscribers that the merger could restrict their usage. The ChatGPT maker began introducing the update to a small group of Pro subscribers, product lead Thibault “Tibo” Sottiaux said in a post on X on Tuesday. The rollout follows OpenAI’s earlier announcement of the merger in an email to users. An OpenAI spokesperson told TechCrunch that while most users are not expected to face more frequent usage resets, a small fraction of its heaviest users may hit their limits sooner. That’s among the concerns raised by some ChatGPT subscribers on social media and OpenAI’s community forum recently. The users fear that merging the usage limits for Chat and Work could leave them with less access to advanced reasoning models than they currently have, even as they continue paying the same subscription fees . Under the new system, Chat and Work will share a single usage meter across ChatGPT, the OpenAI spokesperson told TechCrunch. Conversations using the Instant model will, however, remain unlimited and will not count toward the shared allowance. Users can also continue using Instant after exhausting their usage limits. The spokesperson added that OpenAI would continue working to improve efficiency so subscribers could get more out of their plans. While the rollout has started for a small group of users, OpenAI plans to bring shared usage limits more broadly in December, per its support page. Similar to OpenAI, rival Anthropic also moved to bring its conversational chat service Claude and work-focused Cowork under one interface in September. The changes come as AI companies face mounting infrastructure costs and growing demand for increasingly capable models, putting pressure on their computing resources. Bringing conversational and work-related tools into a single interface could also make AI chatbots simpler to use, allowing users to move between chats and more complex tasks without switching tabs. events.title: Agencies announce dollar thresholds for applicability of truth in lending and consumer leasing rules for consumer credit and lease transactions
events.summary: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau The Federal Reserve Board and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau today announced the dollar thresholds used to determine whether certain consumer credit and lease transactions in 2027 are subject to certain protections under Regulation Z (Truth in Lending) and Regulation M (Consumer Leasing). By law, the agencies are required to adjust the thresholds annually based on the annual percentage increase in the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers, known as CPI-W. Transactions at or below the thresholds are subject to the protections of the regulations. Specifically, based on the 3.9 percent annual percentage increase in the CPI-W as of June 1, 2026, Regulation Z and Regulation M generally will apply to consumer credit transactions and consumer leases of $76,300 or less in 2027. However, private education loans and loans secured by real property, such as mortgages, are subject to Regulation Z regardless of the amount of the loan. events.title: Agencies announce dollar thresholds for smaller loan exemption from appraisal requirements for higher-priced mortgage loans
events.summary: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau Office of the Comptroller of the Currency The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, the Federal Reserve Board, and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency today announced that the 2027 threshold for higher-priced mortgage loans that are subject to special appraisal requirements will increase from $34,200 to $35,500. The threshold amount will be effective January 1, 2027, and is based on the 3.9 percent annual percentage increase in the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers, known as CPI-W, as of June 1, 2026. The Dodd-Frank Act added special appraisal requirements for higher-priced mortgage loans to the Truth in Lending Act, including that creditors obtain a written appraisal based on a physical visit to the interior of the home before making a higher-priced mortgage loan. The rules implementing these requirements contain an exemption for loans at or below a threshold amount that is adjusted annually to reflect CPI-W increases. events.title: Finding growth companies the market may have overlooked: Why culture and competitive edge matter
events.summary: Looking beyond US tech giants, WCM Select Global Growth Equity Fund portfolio manager Sanjay Ayer explains how the firm targets the two- to five-year stretch before a business becomes a consensus leader, and the risks it watches for Identifying companies with long-term growth potential involves looking beyond financial performance to assess their competitive strengths and ability to adapt to change. The recent sell-off in US technology stocks has highlighted the risks of relying too heavily on a handful of market giants. For investors looking beyond these familiar names, the question is where to find the next generation of growth businesses without missing out on potentially attractive returns. Sanjay Ayer, portfolio manager of the WCM Select Global Growth Equity Fund (“WCM SGG Fund”), looks for companies with improving competitive advantages – an approach WCM SGG calls “moat trajectory” – aiming to identify them before their growth potential is widely recognised. “It’s really the two- to five-year period, when a genuinely great business transitions from being misunderstood to widely accepted as a consensus leader,” he says. “To identify moat trajectory, we use a forward-looking lens focused on incremental change as opposed to a backward-looking lens focused on static criteria.” He explains that the WCM SGG Fund team uses a research exercise known as a pre-mortem to assess a company’s future prospects. Its analysts consider what could strengthen or weaken a business’s competitive position, then work backwards to identify the likely causes. Ayer points to Amazon and Google as examples of businesses whose potential was once widely questioned. “When I first joined the business, Google was one Yahoo innovation away from extinction. Amazon was widely perceived to be a bad business,” he recalls. “These things seem silly now, but it goes to show that narratives and fundamentals can inflect quickly.” Beyond business fundamentals, the WCM SGG Fund team also examines something many investors may pay less attention to: corporate culture. “We believe culture is the most understudied and underappreciated facet of investing,” says Ayer. “If you want to understand where a business is going to be in five or 10 years, you have to understand the people, the alignment, the incentives, and the adaptiveness of the culture.” Sanjay Ayer, portfolio manager of the WCM Select Global Growth Equity Fund, believes in the “moat trajectory”, which identifies companies before their growth potential is widely recognised. To assess these qualities, the WCM SGG Fund team employs dedicated culture research analysts who work with academics and industry practitioners. Their research combines a structured set of questions with quantitative data to evaluate whether a company’s culture could influence its long-term growth. The importance of adaptability can be seen in Sea Limited, the group behind Shopee and Garena, which the WCM SGG Fund invests in. After a period of aggressive expansion, Sea faced mounting pressure to improve profitability. The company responded by cutting costs, scaling back spending and sharpening its focus on its core businesses. For the WCM SGG Fund team, Sea’s ability to change course demonstrated how an adaptable corporate culture could help a business respond to challenges and strengthen its competitive position. As artificial intelligence reshapes industries, Ayer believes the ability to recognise and respond to change will become increasingly important. “When you think about how companies are going to adopt AI to and strengthen their competitive advantage, we think adaptability becomes paramount,” he says. As the WCM SGG Fund team assesses how companies adapt to AI, it also seeks out businesses that could benefit from the growing demand for the technology. “When AI began gaining traction in early 2023, we looked closely at Nvidia, but also asked ourselves: If Nvidia succeeds, who else stands to benefit? Where are the bottlenecks in the system?” says Ayer. This prompted the WCM SGG Fund team to look beyond chipmakers to businesses that could benefit from the growing demand for AI infrastructure, including those involved in networking, data storage, memory and power generation. Among the companies it identified was Siemens Energy which provides equipment and services needed to support the expansion of AI-related infrastructure. Through its research on Siemens Energy and GE Vernova, two major suppliers of gas turbines used in power generation, the WCM SGG Fund team learnt that a shortage of workers needed to build gas turbine projects was becoming a constraint. That insight led the firm to Argan, a US company involved in constructing power generation facilities. But the WCM SGG Fund team’s search for growth is not limited to AI. The firm is also exploring opportunities in sectors such as senior housing, aerospace and defence, and subsea infrastructure investment.

events.title: 1Password warns of phishing attempts after a hacker gained access to customer information
events.summary: 1Password, a popular password manager, said an "attacker" gained access to an employee's account information and used it to download some customer data. Illustration by Timon Schneider/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images 1Password, a password manager platform, said a hacker accessed an employee's GitHub account. The attacker then copied a "limited amount" of customer information, including email addresses. No keys were obtained, but the company warned of phishing attempts. 1Password, a popular password management platform, warned customers of potential phishing attempts following a cybersecurity incident in which an attacker gained access to customer information, including names and email addresses. The company said on Wednesday that an "attacker" accessed an employee's corporate GitHub account and used it to push malicious code to backend services and download a "limited amount of customer account information." 1Password said that the information included names and email addresses, which can be used for phishing attempts by malicious actors. Other data included account and user identifiers, public keys, tokens "present in certain emailed links for invitations, provisioning and account recovery," and other "non-secret account metadata." The downloaded data did not include vaults and items in them, keys that protect customer vaults, account recovery keys, or 1Password apps and browser extensions, the company said. 1Password's incident report said only a subset of customers was affected and that accounts do not need to be updated. A spokesperson for 1Password did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The company said customers should be aware of phishing attempts, including "unexpected emails, texts or calls that mention 1Password, invitations, or account recovery attempts." "1Password will never contact you to ask for your account password or Secret Key," the company said. "Only enter them in the official 1Password app, or on our official website, and only when you've opened the app or typed the address yourself." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Jensen Huang broke Nvidia’s code of conduct, and his employees may not forget it
events.summary: When Jensen Huang gave his first all-hands address since returning as CEO, there was an odd emphasis on Nvidia’s code of conduct. He admitted to violating the code, then emphasized that no one was exempt from it. But that “does not mean, the moment you violate a code of conduct, we walk you out the door,” Huang said, according to Wired . “Facts, circumstances, a lot of assessments” still matter. In other words, the code applies to everyone, but breaking it doesn’t automatically cost anyone their job, including, apparently, the CEO. It’s an awkward stance for a company whose CEO has admitted to breaking its rules. A central part of modern human resources, a code of conduct can seem like a quasi-legal rulebook that lays out unacceptable behavior. But experts say most codes are better understood as a reflection of corporate culture. When an infraction goes unpunished, the main risk isn’t legal but cultural — that employees will feel embarrassed or even angry about the company they work for. That’s the risk Huang now faces at Nvidia. Matt Plass, chief market strategy officer at LRN, an ethics and compliance training outfit, recently surveyed more than 2,000 workers across different industries for a study on workplace codes of conduct . As Plass sees it, the biggest risk is that employees will become ashamed of their workplace. “People coming into the workforce now, ethics is incredibly important to them,” he told TechCrunch. “They’re really mindful of the ethical standards of their company. They’re really embarrassed and angry when senior leadership lets them down.” The consequences of violating the rules aren’t always tangible, but they’re definitely real. Plass gave one example of a company that banned corporate travel to cut costs – only to have its CEO turn up in a VIP box at the Olympics. “For over a decade afterwards, ‘the Olympics’ was used within that company as an example of the worst thing an employee could do. People would say, ‘Yeah, I shouldn’t have done that, but it’s not like I went to the Olympics.’” Plass says companies that remove an executive typically do so after an investigation, then try to win back employees. “In most organizations they make a change at the top based on what’s happened,” he said, “and then they will have a hearts-and-minds initiative, to go out to their employee base and their customers and their investors and everybody else, and say, we get it. We’re sorry. We’ve changed. That’s essentially what they do.” Of course, that playbook is harder to follow at a company like Nvidia, where Huang left without a clear succession plan, and there are serious doubts about whether the company could continue to thrive without him. In cases like that, Plass acknowledges there’s no easy answer. “I would draw a distinction there between the kind of companies where the CEO is a kind of godhead figure… where the person and the company are almost impossible to separate,” he said. “There it’s much, much harder to deal with.” In that context, Huang’s stutter-step over the code of conduct is easier to understand. Judging by the employee campaign for his reinstatement, Huang’s return hasn’t created a morale problem so far. But as the coming months put more pressure on Huang and his colleagues, sidestepping the code could end up costing Nvidia something harder to measure — its employees’ pride in the company. events.title: The canceled Tesla Cybertruck is the fastest-selling used truck in America
events.summary: Tesla Cybertruck sales never reached the lofty heights CEO Elon Musk predicted when it launched. But the futuristic, steel-clad EV is finding new life in the used car market, according to analysis of sales figures by iSeeCars.com . The automotive search engine and research platform analyzed more than 1.1 million sales of 1- to 5-year-old used vehicles in October 2026 and measured the average days on market by drivetrain, vehicle type, and individual model. The upshot: The Tesla Cybertruck was the fastest-selling used truck, averaging just 39.1 days on the market compared with 65.5 days for trucks overall. Used Cybertrucks sold faster than any other truck, including the Ford Maverick Hybrid, which held the No. 2 spot, and the Rivian R1T, in third place. According to iSeeCars.com, the Cybertruck’s sales performance lines up with a broader pattern in the used vehicle market: used battery electric vehicles are hot sellers right now, with 16 of the 25 fastest-selling used cars fully electric. EVs are even edging out hybrids in terms of average days on market. EVs average 45.6 days on market compared to 54.5 days for hybrids and 61 days for gasoline-powered vehicles. Not every EV is selling well, however. For instance, iSeeCars.com found that the Cadillac Escalade IQ was the slowest-selling vehicle in the study, averaging 134.3 days on the market, more than twice the overall industry average. Karl Brauer, executive analyst at iSeeCars.com, told TechCrunch that high gasoline prices have changed consumer-buying habits, prompting more people to opt for an EV or hybrid over an internal combustion engine vehicle. If high prices persist, as they have since March, that trend could continue. Keep in mind that these were October sales, the month before Musk announced Tesla would stop making the Cybertruck in 2027. Fuel prices and the relative rarity of Cybertrucks in the used car market were driving demand even before the cancellation announcement, Brauer said. “The Cybertruck has only been out for a few years, so you have a lot of used ones coming off lease and entering the used car market for the first time,” he said, adding that used Cybertrucks are cheap relative to their MSRP. The impending cancellation will likely fuel used Cybertruck sales, although the pace may ebb and flow over the next year. “The canceling of the new Cybertruck is making people kind of aware — it’s like, oh wow, these things aren’t going to be coming anymore,,” Brauer said. “Whatever demand is for them, supply will not be continuing to grow.” Brauer said that once production of the Cybertruck ends — which is expected in summer 2027 — sales of used versions may pop once again. “When the last one is being produced, that’ll probably reignite things again, and for a few months after that,” he said. events.title: SpaceX wins FCC approval to deploy 1 million orbital data center satellites
events.summary: The FCC approved SpaceX's proposal to put 1 million satellites into orbit for use as space-based data centers, Chairman Brendan Carr announced on Wednesday. SpaceX's proposal was opposed by Amazon, Viasat and the American Astronomical Society. Carr said in a post on X that the SpaceX Starmind constellation, and competitors, would "extend America's lead in Super Intelligence." The Federal Communications Commission has authorized Elon Musk 's SpaceX to put 1 million artificial intelligence computing satellites in orbit, Chairman Brendan Carr announced on Wednesday. Carr said in a post on X, the social network owned by SpaceX, that the company's Starmind constellation, and "competitor constellations will use solar power to extend America's lead" in AI. Musk said in a reply, "Much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world." The FCC, in its authorization filing , noted that SpaceX's application "received a substantial number of comments from the public, including petitions to deny filed by Kuiper Systems LLC ( Amazon Leo), Viasat Inc. (Viasat), and the American Astronomical Society (AAS)." In a March petition urging the FCC to deny SpaceX's application, Amazon had labeled the company's Starmind project as a "lofty ambition rather than a real plan." The e-commerce and cloud computing giant is building a competitor to SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet service, and said it would take SpaceX "centuries" to build the constellation, adding that the company provided scant details about how it would "deliver on these grand claims." The petition resulted in a rebuke from Carr , who said Amazon "should focus on the fact" that it's falling short of its own satellite deployment milestone. Amazon declined to comment on the FCC's approval. What Jensen Huang’s return means for Nvidia’s Colette Kress Anthropic stock falls below $83 IPO price, but analysts are still largely positive Nvidia brought Jensen Huang back. But the investigations aren’t over Signal joins United Airlines, banks in limiting AI agents over customer risks Amazon faces FAA probe after delivery drone strikes Michigan fiber cable, garage Other companies have also set their sights on orbital data centers. Google last year announced Project Suncatcher , which it describes as a "moonshot to put AI in space," and launched its first chips into space on a SpaceX rocket and Planet Labs satellite in October. In March, Jeff Bezos ' Blue Origin petitioned the FCC to let it launch up to 51,600 satellites as part of a low Earth orbit satellite constellation dubbed "Project Sunrise." The constellation would work in tandem with Blue Origin's planned TeraWave satellite internet service, announced in January. Astrophysicist and author Adam Becker was critical of the FCC move in an email to CNBC on Wednesday. "Any serious attempt at this is going to further pollute the night sky and runs a serious risk of a cascading chain reaction of space junk collisions, which would be a disaster for all of humanity," he wrote. "Musk and Carr are either profoundly stupid themselves, or hoping the rest of us are too stupid to notice this is nonsense." SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment. The FCC said in its authorization that it dismissed "comments and concerns raised regarding topics over which the Commission has no authority, including environmental concerns," and concerns about its impact on "optical astronomy." events.title: US stocks tumble as AI rout and Trump tariffs rattle markets
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Fears are mounting over AI returns and new tariffs on US trading partners. ( Reuters: Brendan McDermid ) US stocks linked to AI continued to see share prices fall amid a sell-off in early trading on Wednesday. The tech-led Nasdaq plunged by about 4 per cent. Wall Street has also been rattled by new tariffs on US trading partners. The Nasdaq plunged by about four per cent in early trading on Wednesday amid mounting doubt over whether the debt-fuelled AI boom can deliver sufficient returns. Fear of increased regulatory scrutiny of the sector following the Democratic sweep in the midterm elections has added to the pressure during a turbulent month for Wall Street. "The fundamental support for a year-end rally simply isn't there," SWBC chief investment officer Chris Brigati said in a note. "The AI-inspired rally continues to run out of steam, and without evidence that massive capex spending will deliver the profit and revenue goals the market expects, there is little incentive for a rebound." Jensen Huang's return as Nvidia CEO provided a temporary reprieve at the start of the week, but broader concerns lingered and the tech-heavy Nasdaq and the S&P 500 remained on track for their worst November since 2008. Chip makers led the declines, with Nvidia falling 8.7 per cent and the broader Philadelphia Semiconductor Index losing 7.3 per cent. Among other megacaps, Alphabet fell 5 per cent, Amazon shed 5.4 per cent, and Microsoft and Apple were down 3 per cent and 1.7 per cent, respectively. Anthropic slipped 2.1 per cent, closing on Tuesday at US$81.90, below its US$83 IPO price after a blockbuster market debut last week. The Nasdaq 100 briefly fell 20 per cent from its record closing high, flirting with bear market territory. Meanwhile, the US proposed new tariffs on 14 major trading partners to combat what it calls structural excess industrial capacity, reviving global trade tensions. China will face the highest tariff rates, with the proposed 20 per cent excess-capacity levies being in addition to the roughly 25 per cent duties imposed during US President Donald Trump's first term. The extra tariffs could cloud the outlook for investors grappling with the prospect of interest rates staying higher for longer, as inflation has accelerated and oil prices have seen a sustained rise tied to the US-Iran war. Tariff concerns were overshadowing economic data, B. Riley Wealth chief market strategist Art Hogan said. The US economy grew much faster than initially estimated in the third quarter, while inflation increased further in October, reinforcing expectations that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates next month and again in early 2027. Trump unveils suite of new tariffs on major trading partners Goods from China, Brazil, the EU and Vietnam are all set to be taxed higher as Donald Trump doubles down on his tariff policies after a midterms drubbing. The S&P 500 technology sector led the losses with a 5.2 per cent fall. Most other sectors on the benchmark were also trading in negative territory. In other stocks, Dell Technologies fell 7 per cent even after raising its annual revenue and profit forecasts. Rival PC maker HP gained 11.7 per cent after reporting fourth-quarter revenue and profit above analysts' estimates. US markets will be closed for Thanksgiving on Thursday, local time, and operate a shortened session on Friday. events.title: Anthropic’s Dario Amodei calls accusations of surrendering human control to AI ‘absurd’
events.summary: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is pushing back against claims that Anthropic believes we should “surrender human free will” to AI systems. In a long X post on Wednesday, Amodei called the suggestion “absurd.” “We should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security,” he wrote. This argument against autocracy applies word for word against governance by AI, and I feel equally strongly that turning over governance to AI is a bad idea…No one who had carefully read my writing or my interviews could reasonably conclude that I believe anything different.” The statement comes after a growing chorus from Anthropic rivals suggesting that human agency could be at risk if AI is developed irresponsibly. Earlier this month, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said he wanted to ensure people continue to have “agency over the future.” Meta’s chief AI officer Alexandr Wang also wrote in an essay on X that we “should not be okay with a ‘handover’ of society to AI.” “It is hard to imagine a world where humanity can maintain control over fully unconstrained recursive self-improvement,” Wang wrote. “Now that we are at a point where the scientific and technical problems on capability progress are likely solved, we must not only make progress in the extremely urgent areas of safety, alignment, and security, but we have to start thinking through how we progress thoughtfully.” But in published essays, Amodei claims he has repeatedly advocated for democratic oversight of AI, saying the technology should strengthen democratic institutions and that humans should retain ultimate decision-making power. Amodei noted that there’s a difference between surrendering human free will broadly and the idea that “as AI systems advance, they become capable of doing specific tasks in a more automated way.” As examples, he gave AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing end-to-end software. Amodei suggested drawing a line at recursive self-improvement (RSI), or AI that can improve itself without human assistance. Many safety experts see RSI as inevitably leading to a loss of human control, a point Amodei implicitly acknowledged, writing, “we may want limits on this process.” Still, Anthropic is laying the groundwork for RSI by incorporating AI into an increasing share of its own research and development. The company said in June that Claude authored more than 80% of the code merged into Anthropic’s codebase. An independent assessment published this month by AI safety research nonprofit METR found that Anthropic’s models are improving at about twice their historical rate, primarily driven by AI-assisted research. In its own IPO filings, Anthropic describes how each successive generation of Claude accelerates the development of the next, a process it refers to as “closing the loop.” “As we said publicly in early November, we don’t expect it to be safe for Claude to build successive frontier models fully autonomously, without meaningful human supervision or understanding,” Amodei wrote. The problem with “meaningful human supervision or understanding” is that AI is already advancing faster than engineers and safety experts can fully audit it, leaving them increasingly reliant on other AI systems to act as judge and jury. The issue compounds when AI models engage in deceptive behavior, particularly when they recognize they’re being evaluated, making them harder to trust and control. Still, Anthropic is by no means the only company that is pursuing RSI or building AI systems to automate more and more human tasks. This week, OpenAI claimed to have solved one of the biggest open problems in computer science — the exact speed limit of matrix multiplication, which is the mathematical engine behind modern computing, including deep learning and physics simulations. In his post, Amodei accused competitors of engaging in a “vibes-based commercial and political positioning,” disingenuously throwing around phrases like “human control and agency” or “AI should just be a tool” without approaching the AI race any differently. “Certainly the products that they offer don’t differ materially in their orientation towards automation of tasks; every company seems to be releasing models more and more capable of task automation,” Amodei wrote. “Every company claims to understand there are risks and downsides of such automation and to offer safeguards.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: US Army declares Iowa lead azide detonation ‘tremendously successful’
events.summary: Army hails Iowa’s lead azide detonation, claiming no traces of airborne lead have been detected so far. United States Army officials have hailed Wednesday’s mission to destroy 68 drums of volatile lead azide — a sensitive munitions explosive — at a military base in Iowa as a success, saying it had “wildly exceeded their expectations”. Speaking at a news conference in Middletown, a southeastern rural city adjacent to the ammunition plant where the operation was carried out, Major General Eric Shirley, the Army official in charge of the disposal effort, said overhead footage showed that “all of the lead azide barrels were definitively removed”. list 1 of 4 Trump delays explosive detonation in US state of Iowa amid legal battles list 2 of 4 US army says detonation of lead explosives in Iowa will proceed Wednesday list 3 of 4 US Army to detonate more than 4 tonnes of lead azide in Iowa on Wednesday list 4 of 4 US Army detonates toxic lead explosives in Iowa amid health concerns The controlled detonation at 10:15am (16:15 GMT) destroyed approximately 4,500kg (10,000lb) of deteriorating lead azide — an explosive that has been used in military munitions since World War I. “There was no secondary explosions. There was no kick-out. There was no infrastructure damage in or around our installation,” Shirley said, adding that the operation was “tremendously successful”. Officials also said that extensive mitigation measures, including earthworks, foam barriers and gel blocks, had helped to absorb the shockwaves and toxic fallout. However, Democratic Illinois House Representative Mike Quigley voiced dissatisfaction over how military leaders handled the operation, calling the holiday-eve scheduling and lack of communication “unconscionable”. In a statement on X, the congressman wrote: “It is unfair that our military leaders are releasing 9,500 pounds of unstable lead azide on our friends in Iowa the day before Thanksgiving.” Following days of heightened alarm over lead dust contamination and its environmental repercussions, federal officials announced that preliminary data from Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) sensors had detected no airborne lead particles. Ongoing monitoring efforts continue in the immediately affected blast zone. A post on the agency’s social media account shortly after the operation said that “ALL EPA real-time air monitors are reporting ZERO detection of airborne lead throughout the region”. Chemists have noted that lead, as a nonbiodegradable element, cannot be chemically decomposed or destroyed. It persists in the environment, with airborne particles capable of travelling considerable distances before settling on soil and potentially leaching into groundwater. Detonating large stores of the unstable explosive would decompose the compound into its basic elements – nitrogen gas and metallic lead. Lead is a potent neurotoxin that poses its sharpest threat to children and pregnant women, with links to learning disabilities, impaired neurological function, mental health challenges, reproductive harm, hearing loss and other impairments. “The EPA can do millions of tests, but they [must also] test for the breakdown products and the stabilisers and plasticisers [containing] lead azide [which] are endocrine disruptors; some are cancer-causing chemicals,” said Scott Smith, an independent environmental testing expert who was heavily involved in air testing after the 2023 East Palestine, Ohio train derailment and industrial incidents. The Army Sustainment Command said it would release a final breakdown of the affected area — including lead-dust dispersion and surface-deposition maps — after the operation. “I believe absolutely that we reduced as close to zero as is absolutely humanely possible the risk to the health and the safety of the people in Middletown and the extended communities throughout Iowa,” said Shirley.

events.title: FDA to Expand Prescription Drug Testing After ProPublica Revealed Safety Concerns
events.summary: A scientist tests generic drugs at the Connecticut-based lab Valisure. Tonje Thielesen for ProPublica The Food and Drug Administration will test more prescription drugs for impurities and other dangerous quality lapses under an expanded program described by safety experts as a critical step to better protecting America’s drug supply. About 90% of prescriptions in the United States are for generic drugs, many manufactured thousands of miles away in countries that include India and China. Until now, the FDA has only periodically tested a sampling of those drugs to see if they were safe or worked as effectively as the brand-name medications they are meant to replicate. Read More Look Up Where Your Generic Prescription Drugs Were Made Last week, the FDA announced it will test more often and identify poorly performing drugs for further study. The agency said it will buy the medications from retail pharmacies and wholesale distributors, but it did not say how many drugs it plans to test or how frequently. A spokesperson did not answer questions about how the FDA would select drugs for testing or how it would hold manufacturers accountable for inferior products, beyond posting the results on its website. Still, drug-safety experts said the expansion helps address long-standing concerns that some suppliers sacrifice quality to keep costs low — and that the FDA has for years looked the other way. “All drugs, regardless of where they are manufactured, must meet the same FDA standards for safety, effectiveness and quality,” the FDA spokesperson told ProPublica. A ProPublica investigation last year found the agency routinely relied on the drug companies themselves to do their own testing even as doctors, researchers and the Department of Defense warned that essential medications were contaminated or ineffective. On its website, the FDA said it has relied on a “more targeted, risk-based” approach to testing since 2018, choosing samples of drugs that have safety, effectiveness or quality concerns. The agency publicly reports the results on its website and notes that a majority of the tested drugs meet its standards. ProPublica, however, found the agency for years failed to regularly test both the generics that have worried outside experts and drugs coming from factories that amassed so many serious quality and safety violations they were ultimately banned from the U.S. market. ProPublica later used FDA data to create Rx Inspector , a first-of-its-kind tool that allows consumers and doctors to look up the inspection records of the factories where more than 40,000 generic drugs are made. Researchers have repeatedly urged the FDA to test more often. In fiscal year 2025, the FDA reported testing 46 different drugs, and for 29 of those drugs, the agency only tested one manufacturer . All but one passed every test. The FDA’s new testing regime is “a huge validation of the research that we’ve been doing raising concerns about the quality of generic drugs,” Dr. Kevin Schulman, a professor of medicine and health policy at Stanford University, said of the FDA’s new testing program. “This is a great effort on their part.” In February, senators also introduced a bill targeting transparency in the drug supply chain process, in part because of similar public concerns. In response to questions about how it would decide which drugs to sample and how results would drive future enforcement, the FDA spokesperson said the initiative will “help the FDA identify potential drug quality issues faster and will provide more information the agency can use to decide if further action is needed.” Experts say they ultimately hope the FDA’s program will work alongside independent testers to shift the generic drug market to be competitive on quality rather than price. While the agency can focus on weeding out the worst actors, independent labs can test manufacturers against one another to find the most effective products, said retired Col. Vic Suarez, a former medical supply-chain commander. A similar system is already used at the Department of Defense. “It’s an important thing because they will probably catch extreme violators of regulatory standards, so that’s a good thing,” Suarez said. “But you also need to have a complementary system where you’re actually raising the bar.” ProPublica previously engaged an independent lab, Valisure, to test several generic versions of three of the most prescribed drugs in the United States and in two cases identified irregularities that experts said could compromise their effectiveness. “I think, high level, the idea that we should be doing more testing is fantastic,” said David Light, the co-founder of Valisure. “I think there’s so much growing energy behind that.” The post FDA to Expand Prescription Drug Testing After ProPublica Revealed Safety Concerns appeared first on ProPublica .

events.title: Anthropic CEO pushes back on Axios reporting on AI and free will
events.summary: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on Wednesday rejected the notion that humans should surrender free will to AI, pushing back on Axios' reporting about a growing ideological divide among top AI executives. Why it matters: This is Amodei's most significant public remarks since the company went public last week. What he's saying: "We should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security," Amodei said. Amodei distinguished between handing over governance to AI, which he opposes, and automating specific tasks, on which he holds more nuanced views. He said his view is mixed on specific instances like "AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing software end-to-end" where "it is clearly desirable in many cases and will save a lot of lives" if AI systems are allowed more agency. He also said it may make sense to slow or stop certain AI deployments to mitigate job disruption and limit AI's ability to autonomously develop more powerful systems. The big picture: The debate about control comes amid a rocky debut for Anthropic's stock, which dipped below its IPO day price on Wednesday. The intrigue: Amodei also took aim at rival AI executives, accusing them of engaging in "vibes-based commercial and political positioning" by championing human agency without meaningfully differentiating their products. Those executives, he said, "repeat slogans like 'human control and agency,' or 'AI should be just a tool,' without actually doing anything different in their products or taking seriously the difficult questions that lie behind these slogans."

events.title: House Democrats chart path on trading bans
events.summary: Democrats may ban members from using prediction markets as part of a measure governing the House — then vote on standalone legislation that would prevent elected officials from trading individual stocks and most cryptocurrencies, Rep. Seth Magaziner, D-R.I., told Semafor. “That’s my sense of where things are headed,” Magaziner said, though he noted “no decisions have been made yet.” The Rhode Island Democrat sponsors the bipartisan stock trading ban he says leaders “are working off” as they prepare for the next Congress. “Certainly one of the messages that members on both sides are taking from the election is that the voters are really fed up with the corruption that they see in Washington,” Magaziner said. Incoming House Speaker Hakeem Jeffries promised earlier this week that “one of the first things that we’ll do in the new Congress is to move to ban members of Congress from trading stock.” Democrats “have to clean up the mess … in our own House,” he said. Magaziner said he is “quite confident” the House can enact the prediction markets ban, which is already in force in the Senate, as part of their rules package in the new Congress. But “it is probably not possible” to include the stock trading ban, he said, because House rules can’t keep members’ spouses from trading or force them to divest. “It’s possible that we could try to do a slimmed down version of it in the rule,” said Magaziner, whose proposal would apply to most cryptocurrencies as well. “But either way, whether we do that or not, we also need to pass a bill so that we can get a full ban in place.” Members are “still working through” whether to divide that bill into individual ones that apply to the different branches of government, Magaziner said, but he insisted that either way Democrats “will still likely move all of the separate bills together … quickly in the new session.”

events.title: See how Jensen Huang's fortune compares with the richest Americans in history
events.summary: Standard Oil founder John D. Rockefeller has long been considered the wealthiest man in America's history, but Elon Musk is now wealthier, and tech CEOs like Jensen Huang don't fall far behind. General Photographic Agency/Getty Images / ALLISON ROBBERT/AFP via Getty Images/Sean Gallup/Getty Images America has more billionaires than ever, led by tech executives like Jensen Huang and Elon Musk. Figures such as John D. Rockefeller and Andrew Carnegie were known as the richest men of their time. Adjusting their historical fortunes for inflation, many still rank among the wealthiest today. America has never had as many billionaires as it does now — and the number is only growing. From multibillion-dollar IPOs to dominance in the production of specialized chips, some of today's most notable tech company leaders, like Nvidia's Jensen Huang , have built fortunes for the history books. While the scale of tech CEOs' fortunes is unprecedented by all measures, it also raises the question of how historic figures, widely considered America's richest, such as  Gilded Age industrialists , compare with today's richest people. That is to say: Who are the richest Americans of all time? In many historical calculations of net worth, individual fortunes weren't measured in isolation; instead, they were compared to the US GDP at the time. When the US economy was much smaller than it is today, the wealthiest families and individuals carried more weight in the economy than others during more prosperous times. One of the richest Americans of all time is widely considered to be John D. Rockefeller, founder of Standard Oil, whose wealth, at its peak in 1937, was equal to 1.5% of the country's GDP. His estimated net worth would be around $512.7 billion today, when adjusted for inflation. Elon Musk's current wealth, however, has far eclipsed Rockefeller's. To identify some of the richest Americans of all time, we consulted Forbes' 2007 list of history's wealthiest figures , based on estimates by economist Peter Bernstein . It calculated individuals' wealth at their peak and compared it to the country's GDP at the time to convert it to 2006 dollars. This was then adjusted to today's dollars using the US Bureau of Labor Statistics' inflation calculator . For living individuals, we cited Forbes' estimated net worths as of November 25, 2026. While estimates of historical wealth may not be perfect, they help paint a picture of the wealth enjoyed by some of America's most notable business figures and put it in context with today's billionaires. events.title: A historian says AI solved a 200-year-old mystery in just 22 minutes
events.summary: Mark Humphries asked GPT-6.2 Astra to track down the authorship of a sketchbook held at Yale's Beinecke Libary. Enzo Figueres/Getty Images Historian Mark Humphries asked GPT-6.2 Astra to find the author of an anonymous 1808 sketchbook. It found a match in 22 minutes, he said. "What I'm trying to do is point out a thing that the models are capable of doing," he told Business Insider. AI is already solving the great mysteries of mathematics . History could be next. Mark Humphries said that he used OpenAI's tools to find the origins of an anonymous sketchbook dating back to 1808. Better yet, he said it took the AI tool almost no time: 22 minutes. Humphries is a professor of history at Wilfrid Laurier University in Waterloo, Ontario. He's studied the fur trade since the pandemic and has long been interested in an unnamed travel sketchbook held at Yale's Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library . The problem: the sketchbook had some captions, few dates, and charted a path that thousands of travelers took. Humphries is in a community of OpenAI users that gets early access to models for testing. So, he pointed GPT-6.2 Astra at the sketchbook's digital rendering, cranked it up to Ultra on goal mode, and asked it to find the origins. The AI model used primary sources, such as a fur trader's dinner diary and a club's meeting minutes, to narrow down who could be in the sketchbook's locations. Eventually, it identified one man: Louis-Guy-Charles-Guillaume de Rohan-Chabot, vicomte de Chabot. A human could do the same investigation, Humphries told Business Insider in a Wednesday phone call. But the documents GPT-6.2 Astra considered named hundreds of people, all of whom would need to be checked. That would make the process time-consuming, he said. "Are you going to devote the years and years to doing that?" he asked. "The answer is probably no." The AI also gave Humphries a path to prove its conclusion himself. Deep in a historian's Ph.D. dissertation, it found a reference to a diary Chabot kept, which he could order as microfilm copies . Humphries found the handwriting of the diary and the sketchbook to look identical. It was interesting, sure, but not conclusive. "I'm not a handwriting expert," Humphries said. Then there were the entries. The diary's dates lined up perfectly with the sketchbook, placing Chabot in "the right places at the right times," Humphries said. And then, what could prove to be the smoking gun: In the diary, Chabot wrote that he made a sketch of Fort St. Joseph, and specified the view that he was looking at. In the sketchbook, there's the sketch of the same landmark with the same view. "That's kind of the X-marks-the-spot kind of thing you don't typically find as a historian," he said. How historians are feeling about AI Mathematicians have had an emotional response to the rise of AI in their field. They hurled insults at an Anthropic staffer over a joke in a proof. Steven Strogatz wept on "The Daily." Comparatively, the historians have been fairly chill. They asked questions about Humphries' process and joked about the similarity of Chabot to "chatbot." A librarian at Yale that Humphries contacted received the finding warmly, though they've yet to do anything with the information, Humphries said. (Yale didn't respond to a request for comment from Business Insider.) "I'm much more ambivalent toward the technology than people think I am," Humphries said. Mark Humphries Of course, the authorship of a niche sketchbook doesn't have the same implication as the Riemann Hypothesis . And some historians pointed out what Humphries himself said: that a human could do the same thing. The biggest names in AI clearly see Humphries' finding as a win. OpenAI president Greg Brockman reposted him, celebrating the model's solution to a "significant historical mystery." Tech workers flooded his X comments with congratulations or statements of amazement. For his part, Humphries doesn't think AI is equipped to do everything in history. "I'm much more ambivalent toward the technology than people think I am," he said. He doesn't use AI for writing, for example. His goal, then, is to make sure historians know what they're getting into. As math goes through what some call a "crisis," Humphries said, historians should be clear about just what AI is good at. "There are real limitations to the technology," he said. "What I'm trying to do is point out a thing that the models are capable of doing." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: UK food inflation could hit 5% next year, Bank of England says
events.summary: Sharp rise expected as cost pressures mount, with experts factoring in energy price cap hike and potential impact of El Niño Food price inflation in the UK could hit 5% next year, the Bank of England has said, despite rising less sharply than feared since the onset of the Iran war. The deputy governor Clare Lombardelli told MPs on the cross-party Treasury select committee: “Food price inflation is coming in under what we expected [it] to be, and in fact under what the industry expected it to be.” But she said the Bank expected food price inflation to rise sharply from the current level of about 1.3%. “We think that … it will go up to 3 to 5% in the middle of next year. I mean, obviously that’s quite uncertain, but that pressure is there,” Lombardelli said. Lombardelli was being questioned by MPs alongside other members of the Bank’s monetary policy committee (MPC). The MPC raised interest rates by a quarter-point to 4% at its last meeting earlier this month to tackle above-target inflation, and suggested further action could be necessary. Andrew Bailey, the Bank’s governor, said the MPC was also monitoring the potential impact of this year’s unusually large El Niño weather event on future food prices. “There is uncertainty around this. You know, we still don’t know what the impact of this El Niño effect is going to be, for instance, because it will take time for it to manifest,” he said. Surging oil and gas prices have pushed up the annual rate of inflation , which hit 3.6% last month, with the cost of petrol and diesel up by more than 33% over the past year. But so far there have been fewer knock-on effects beyond energy prices. Food inflation has fallen well short of the peak above 17% seen in 2023, when Russia’s invasion of Ukraine exacerbated the supply squeeze as the global economy emerged from the Covid-19 pandemic. Catherine Mann, an external member of the MPC who voted for a half-point increase this month, pointed to fierce competition in the food retail sector as a reason price rises had been constrained. “We all go shopping ourselves. I can say that Aldi price match in my stores is apparent. Now, it wasn’t apparent four years ago. So that’s, I think, important,” she said. Oil prices have fallen sharply since the Democratic party’s sweep in the US midterms brought hopes of an end to the Iran conflict, and as alternative sources of supply start to come onstream. Bailey said if these lower prices continued, they would moderate the Bank’s predictions for UK inflation – which it had expected to peak at almost 5% next year. “The prices are volatile … if these current prices were to stay what they are, the peak of inflation mechanically would be lower,” he said. However, Bailey and other MPC members underlined that some inflationary pressure for next year is already baked in – pointing to the 26% rise in the price cap for household energy bills due in January as an example. The two-hour hearing underlined the divisions within the committee. The more dovish Swati Dhingra suggesting she saw this month’s rate rise as a one-off “insurance” measure, while Mann said she feared the MPC had undermined public confidence by failing to move more aggressively. Dhingra compared the muted impact of rocketing oil and gas prices this year on the wider economy with the effects of the surge in 2022 after Russia invaded Ukraine. At a similar point in that year, the prices of 70% of goods included in the consumer price index had risen, she said – but just 20% of prices have reacted so far this year. But Mann pointed out that inflation had now been consistently above the Bank’s 2% target for five years. “If we let inflation expectations drift away from 2% in the longer term, then monetary policy is going to have to work harder, meaning a higher rate for longer,” she said, adding: “The optimal response is to hike more and sooner.” The MPC’s next rate-setting meeting is on 17 December.

events.title: US gives SpaceX approval for data centres in space
events.summary: The US has given regulatory approval to SpaceX to eventually put data centres in space. According to the Federal Communications Commission, this is the first authorisation for such a project, as demands from AI have caused an increase in the need for data centres . "The FCC is granting SpaceX authorisation to deploy 1,000,000 orbital compute modules to process massive amounts of data to be used back here on Earth," a news release read. Concerns about the environmental impact, noise and electricity consumption of data centres have risen in recent years, and governments at the state and local levels have enacted rules to slow down construction. https://t.co/rZhstPYBzs pic.twitter.com/RCsle086L3 — FCC (@FCC) November 25, 2026 FCC chair Brendan Carr highlighted the work under way to eventually put data centres in space. "This is the kind of American ingenuity that can unite our strengths in space and advanced technology, reinforce our economic leadership, and expand prosperity here at home," he said. But the announcement doesn't mean data centres will suddenly start orbiting earth. Researchers and scientists are still in the early stages of figuring out how such an endeavour might be possible. In early October, Google launched Project Suncatcher into orbit after several years of development to test the feasibility of data centres in space. The company included its AI hardware to asses that idea onboard the Transporter-18 SpaceX mission. Part of the space test involved seeing if the company's technology could generate enough computing power in space to answer basic AI queries. “In low-Earth orbit, satellites can access near-constant sunlight, generating up to eight times more solar power than on Earth,” the technology company said. It added that if successful, all concerns about data centres might be nullified. “It could be possible to link together multiple constellations of satellites, allowing them to manage larger AI workloads while in orbit.” Earlier this year during a discussion at the World Economic Forum's annual meeting in Davos, Switzerland, technology tycoon and SpaceX chief executive Elon Musk spoke about putting AI infrastructure in orbit. “There's so much room in space, and it's enormous what you can scale to,” he said. “I think, ultimately, you can have hundreds of terawatts in the air.” Experts have warned, however, that while the idea of data centres in space might look good on paper, there are a lot of challenges that need to be overcome. Speaking at the Semafor World Economy Summit in April, Ariel Ekblaw , founder and chief executive of non-profit space architecture lab the Aurelia Institute, said some of the more aggressive timelines for making space data centres a reality are not realistic. She pointed out that space is far colder than most people realise, and that alone means that “it is not an advantageous arena to deploy a really hot little volcano of a bunch of computers in”. Ms Ekblaw added that the climate issue was only one of several engineering challenges that come with the territory of orbital data centres. The radiation of space, she said, would be problematic, along with the need for data centres on Earth to upgrade their CPUs, GPUs and other technology. “There's the fact that if you want to swap your chips out from Nvidia every six months, now you have to go all the way to space to do it, so that's not a trivial concern,” she said.

events.title: Ministers can’t control gas prices, but they can attack other energy costs more ruthlessly
events.summary: Ministers can’t control gas prices, but they can be more ruthless on other energy costs Louise Haigh talked the right talk at the CBI this week, but greater ambition and tighter timelines are needed S hocked by average annual energy bills at £2,166 for the first three months of next year? Here’s worse news. It is currently possible, and perhaps even likely, that the regulator, Ofgem, will set the price cap at £2,000-plus in every quarter of 2027. Predictions for bills are less certain the further out one looks, it should be said. Gas prices, the overwhelming culprit in the £443 hike in the cap announced on Wednesday, can always fall – and might do so if calm returns to the strait of Hormuz. But EDF’s outlook for next year currently reads: £2,254 for the second quarter, which will include about £100 extra in the “network costs” line in bills that includes paying for the upgrade of the electricity grid – demonstrating that gas prices are not the only story on a medium and long-term horizon. Then £2,078 in the quarter starting in July and £2,035 from October. To repeat, projections can change, albeit an increasing slice of the electricity side comprises fixed costs, such as those network charges, that are nailed down in advance. The point, though, is that no one – certainly not government ministers – can claim to be surprised if this crisis lasts a while. There are two points to make. First, the government no longer has an excuse to dodge the vexed question of a “social tariff” for energy – a scheme to give financial support to struggling households on a properly targeted basis. The aim would be to get off today’s rickety practice of the chancellor giving 11th-hour handouts without a meaningful effort to ensure the money goes where it is most needed. This time it was £100 for council tax payers in lower bands – an inadequate proxy for poorer households or energy hardship. The misnamed energy independence bill would give the government powers to do the necessary data-sharing work to design a proper social tariff. It’s time to hurry up with a job that has been talked about since the energy crisis of 2022 that followed Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Next winter should serve as a hard deadline to get a workable social tariff in place. The second point is this. Even as the government under Andy Burnham has emphasised cheaper energy as a new priority, its specific target is not terribly ambitious. It is to lower UK energy costs to bring them in line with other European countries within 10 years . Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning The goal is more credible than Keir Starmer’s empty (or cynical) promise of “£300 off bills” in the life of this parliament. But a decade to get in line with European averages? That is not speedy. Energy costs are, by a distance, the most pressing concern for UK industry. Yes, there are discounts for a limited number of heavy users, but how is wider “re-industrialisation” meant to happen if the UK remains uncompetitive on energy for another nine years? A more encouraging way to look at things is that the government’s emerging new thinking on energy is bolder than a 10-year timeframe would suggest. The speech at the CBI this week by Louise Haigh, the de facto deputy prime minister, offered three clear lines of attack: take more costs off bills and into general taxation; accelerate electrification and grid connections and get “wasted wind” costs under control; and go after the excess profits earned not only by gas plants at moments of high system stress but also by clean power generators with revenue arrangements tied to gas prices. All are worthwhile strategies, but in combination they ought to be capable of delivering something better than European norms sometime around 2036. If not, the Treasury’s new “cost control framework” on energy levies will have to be sweated harder. Being charitable, one might say the loose “within 10 years” phraseology was used because every government goal at the moment is framed within Burnham’s yet-to-be-unveiled 10-year plan. One hopes so, because the war on energy costs is more urgent for businesses and households alike. There is nothing the government can do about wholesale gas prices, of course. But the necessary transition to clean power can be pursued with far more ruthlessness on costs. The 10-year plan, when it finally arrives, should also set a few five-year targets.

events.title: Trump administration backs Musk's plan for space-based data centres
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Elon Musk has won backing from the Trump administration for his plan for data centres in space. ( Reuters: Adrees Latif ) The US's Federal Communications Commission has approved SpaceX to deploy 1 million satellites for data centres in space. The company says solar-powered satellites could help reduce environmental costs associated with the technology. SpaceX will need to launch 10 per cent of its satellites by November 2033. The Federal Communications Commission will authorise Elon Musk's SpaceX to deploy a constellation of 1 million satellites for data centres in space. SpaceX earlier this year sought permission to launch up to 1 million orbital compute modules to process massive amounts of data to be used on Earth. The FCC said it was approving the SpaceX "Starmind" constellation to help meet rapidly growing demand for AI computing. Under the licence, SpaceX must begin deployment no later than November 2033, deploy 10 per cent of the maximum number — or 100,000 — no later than November 2035 and deploy 50 per cent by November 2038, the FCC said. Elon Musk says Tesla will wind down Cybertruck production around mid-2027. Approving the application will permit SpaceX "to pioneer emergent technology that advances American leadership in space and artificial intelligence", the FCC added. Data centres are the physical backbone of artificial intelligence, requiring massive amounts of power. "By directly harnessing near-constant solar power with little operating or maintenance costs, these satellites will achieve transformative cost and energy efficiency while significantly reducing the environmental impact associated with terrestrial data centres," SpaceX told the FCC. It was unclear whether SpaceX would put 1 million satellites in space, where only 17,000 satellites exist currently. Satellite operators sometimes request approval for higher numbers of satellites than they intend to deploy to buy design flexibility. SpaceX sought approval for 42,000 Starlink satellites before it began deployment of that system. The growing network currently has a little more than 11,000 satellites in space. US stocks tumble as AI rout and Trump tariffs rattle markets Deloitte suspended by WA government after AI report debacle Inside the Chinese AI app designed to hook kids and mine their data 'Extraordinary' decision to reinstate Jensen Huang has experts puzzled SpaceX's request bets heavily on reduced costs of Starship, the company's next-generation reusable rocket under development, to help deploy satellites. Amazon's rival satellite unit, Leo, and others have criticised the plan, suggesting SpaceX was unlikely to deploy all the satellites and that it could take centuries to do so. FCC chair Brendan Carr rejected that criticism in March. "Amazon should focus on getting Amazon's house in order with their own launches and their own satellite constellation, rather than worrying about other people that are actually out there launching satellites at the pace and cadence that SpaceX is," Mr Carr said. The FCC said it was also approving SpaceX's requests to back up its optical network by approving additional communications.

events.title: Nvidia leads tech sell-off as Huang comeback rally fizzles and AI concerns return
events.summary: Tech and AI-linked stocks sold off, led by sharp declines in Nvidia and other chip names. The rally tied to Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia faded on renewed concerns about AI spending and profitability. Fresh inflation data also dented appetite for growth stocks. Technology stocks fell on Wednesday as excitement over Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang 's return faded and failed to calm concerns over the sustainability of the artificial intelligence trade. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite dropped 1% and traded off its lows, recovering from steeper losses earlier in the session. Semiconductor stocks dragged on the index, and the VanEck Semiconductor ETF that tracks the sector edged down 2%. "We just feel that this is panic right now," Venu Krishna, head of U.S. equity strategy at Barclays, told CNBC's " Squawk on the Street " on Wednesday. "What the market is telling you is that the AI growth narrative has hit a wall and given the centrality of that theme at the economic level, the market is expecting some sort of a macro shock," he added. After notching one of its best days on record Monday, Nvidia has fallen in the days since and slumped 5% Wednesday. Advanced Micro Devices , Marvell Technology and Intel all dropped about 2%, with some plunging further. Micron Technology declined 5%. Huang's return to Nvidia on Monday briefly revived appetite for tech stocks but didn't fully calm investor concerns over the high costs tied to the AI build-out and worries of a potential slowdown. Other stocks tied to the AI trade also plummeted. Oracle fell more than 4%. CoreWeave and Nebius moved lower. AI lab Anthropic bucked the sell-off, however, and climbed more than 4% after shares dropped below last week's blockbuster IPO price. Wednesday's declines also came as Wall Street digested a hot inflation reading that fueled concerns that higher interest rates could dent demand for growth stocks, including tech. Amazon , Tesla and Alphabet each declined about 2%. Microsoft lost more than 1% and Meta traded higher. events.title: Could renewed strikes on Hodeidah port worsen Yemen’s humanitarian crisis?
events.summary: The Houthi-held seaport is a critical lifeline for millions of Yemenis but has taken significant damage over the course of recent conflicts. The Saudi-led coalition has launched renewed attacks on Houthi targets at Yemen’s port of Hodeidah as the armed group fights Yemen’s internationally recognised government. The strikes come amid significant Houthi territorial gains in recent weeks and escalating attacks by the group on Saudi Arabia. list 1 of 3 Saudi coalition hits 60 Houthi military sites; Taiz sees ‘fierce battles’ list 2 of 3 Saudi coalition and Houthis exchange threats to bomb key ports list 3 of 3 Saudi-led coalition intercepts Houthi attacks after Hodeidah strike Hodeidah, which has repeatedly been attacked over the past decade, is critical to both Yemen’s economy and the supply of essential goods to millions of people in Houthi-controlled areas. How important is the port of Hodeidah? The port of Hodeidah, situated on Yemen’s western Red Sea coast, is the country’s principal commercial seaport and has been under Houthi control since 2014. It serves as a major entry point for food, fuel and other commercial goods as well as humanitarian assistance, supplying the densely populated northern and western regions of Yemen, including the Houthi-held capital, Sanaa. The port had eight berths and the capacity to accommodate 6,500 standard shipping containers in 2023. However, attrition due to Yemen’s more than a decade of conflict has reduced the number of operational berths and damaged cranes and storage facilities. Despite this, in September 2025, the United Nations Mission to Support the Hodeidah Agreement estimated that the port handled about 70 percent of commercial imports and 80 percent of humanitarian aid coming into Yemen, calling it a “lifeline”. “The closure or disruption [of the port] under the current circumstances would delay the arrival of food, medicine and fuel; increase transport costs and prices; and exacerbate the suffering of families already facing an acute humanitarian crisis,” said Abdusattor Esoev, Yemen Chief of Mission for the International Organization for Migration. “At a time when millions of people in Yemen depend on humanitarian assistance and face severe food insecurity, Hodeidah remains a critical lifeline. The port is essential for bringing in food, fuel, medicines and other basic goods needed by civilians across northern Yemen,” said Francesca Quinto, the programme manager for Yemen for Doctors Without Borders. However, the Houthis have long been accused of using Hodeidah’s port for both civilian and military purposes. Investigations have found that the group exploits commercial port facilities to smuggle in weapons from Iran, its chief ally. “The ports of Hodeidah are key to commercial flows. However, the Houthis’ increasing militarisation of vital civilian infrastructure by smuggling and storing arms, fuel and narcotics is undermining the humanitarian functions they serve in wartime,” Ibrahim Jalal, a senior researcher and policy adviser, told Al Jazeera. Tawfiq al-Hamidi, a Yemeni lawyer and human rights activist, told Al Jazeera that the port has been misused by the group for smuggling despite its importance for Yemen’s population. “Nevertheless, efforts must be made to protect the port as a civilian facility, and the Houthi movement must provide genuine guarantees,” he said. Yes. Since the start of Yemen’s civil war in September 2014, the port and its surrounding area have repeatedly come under attack from the Saudi-led coalition, the United States, the United Kingdom and Israel. Pro-Yemeni government forces also tried to capture it in a 2018 offensive. About 70 percent of Yemenis live in Houthi-controlled areas in the country’s west, where most goods arrive from the rest of the world through Red Sea ports. Humanitarian aid continues to enter through other ports, including Mocha and a major government-held port in Aden, but renewed fighting has made the overland flow of this aid to the country’s interior difficult. Humanitarian operations in Houthi-controlled areas have also been severely curtailed because of the detention of UN staff by the group. In March 2015, shortly after launching its military intervention in support of the Yemeni government, the Saudi-led coalition began a partial maritime blockade on Houthi-controlled areas of Yemen. A UN-brokered nationwide truce in April 2022 led to an easing of restrictions on fuel imports through Hodeidah. Further restrictions on commercial imports were lifted in early 2023, which also helped to revitalise the port. But that recovery was then jeopardised by a campaign of US, British and Israeli strikes on Houthi-controlled areas beginning in 2024 and lasting into the next year, in retaliation for Houthi drone and missile attacks on Israel and Red Sea shipping, carried out ostensibly in the name of supporting Gaza during Israel’s genocidal war on the Palestinian enclave. events.title: UK military ‘moving aircraft to hangars in case of drone attacks’
events.summary: Experts say the move is a ‘logical response’ if there is intelligence suggesting a likely drone threat. Britain’s Ministry of Defence (MoD) says it takes “the security of our bases, equipment and personnel very seriously,” after media outlets reported the Royal Air Force (RAF) had taken new precautions against possible drone attacks. The Times and Sky News reported on Wednesday that planes would be moved to hangars and hardened shelters overnight, and anti-drone nets would be installed to protect any warplanes that remained exposed. list 1 of 3 US soldier arrested in UK on suspicion of spying for Russia list 2 of 3 US charges 3 ‘Iranian-backed operatives’ over alleged plot at UK airbase list 3 of 3 From the UK to the Gulf, are US overseas bases becoming liabilities? The MoD did not confirm the reports, but in a statement said it was “always adapting to counter any potential threats”. Justin Bronk, a senior researcher at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI) think tank in London, told Al Jazeera that the RAF’s reported tactics would be “a sensible, logical response if there is intelligence suggesting a likely drone threat”. “The main bases used for RAF fighters, Coningsby, Marham and Lossiemouth all still have hardened aircraft shelters from the Cold War era that have been maintained in usable condition for both aircraft storage, protection and limited maintenance work,” Bronk said. However, Bronk cautioned that there were not enough hardened shelters to protect all of the jets at each airbase, after squadrons were consolidated into ‘super bases’ following the end of the Cold War, and a “mistaken assumption” that such protection was no longer important. The MoD said it was investing an additional 470 million pounds ($615m) “to strengthen security at military sites, including better physical protection, surveillance and counter-drone capabilities”, and that 15 million pounds ($19.6m) had already been invested “in drone and counter-drone technology and introduced restricted airspace over 44 critical Defence sites”. British authorities have regularly issued warnings about threats posed by Russia and Iran, and the government has urged the country to be prepared for different contingencies. In a report in October, members of Parliament warned that Britain’s military needed to make “dramatic progress” to be ready for a potential attack by Russia on a NATO country. On Tuesday, Britain’s domestic MI5 intelligence service and the MoD issued a joint alert warning UK military suppliers to Ukraine about increasing sabotage attempts by Russia. “Aircraft inside a standard hangar or a hardened aircraft shelter are protected from attacks by infiltrated adversary cells or terrorists with small drones,” explained RUSI’s Justin Bronk. “But only those in hardened shelters are protected from larger one-way attack drones like the Geran 2/3/4 series during a hypothetical wartime attack,” he added, referring to the Geran drones manufactured and operated by Russia, based on an original Iranian design. Bronk said that even though hardened aircraft shelters seem old-fashioned, they are a “relatively low-risk, inexpensive and effective way to improve fighter fleet resilience in wartime.” “They provide almost total protection from drones due to thick concrete and blast doors, and also mean that any unintercepted cruise missile can only destroy a single jet at most with a direct hit.” Earlier this month US forces responded to possible unauthorised drone activity over a military base in the United Kingdom, hosting American warplanes. “No personnel, aircraft or infrastructure were affected” at the eastern RAF Lakenheath base, a US Air Force spokesperson said in a statement at the time. There was also an Iran-linked security scare on September 27 at the southwestern RAF Fairford base, which was used by the US planes. A group of men allegedly drove three vans up to a village near the site and abandoned them with filled petrol barrels inside, sparking a bomb scare and evacuation. Washington had used the airbase in its war on Iran, and days after the September incident withdrew all its B-1 bombers from the base. Two men have since been charged in a UK court over the incident, and three in the United States. The US military also withdrew its planes from RAF Mildenhall, near Lakenheath, on November 9 , following a threat from Iran, according to The Wall Street Journal and The Financial Times.
