events.title: Saudi national in OpenAI bugging case is out on bond after DOJ tries to block release
events.summary: Abdulrahman Alfozan, the Saudi national accused of bugging an executive conference room at OpenAI's headquarters, has been released from custody, his attorney told CNBC. A federal judge in San Francisco allowed Alfozan out of jail on a $1 million bond, despite opposition from the U.S. Attorney's Office prosecuting the case. U.S. Attorney Craig Missakian of the Northern District of California had urged the court to maintain Alfozan's detention, arguing he poses a significant flight risk. Abdulrahman Alfozan , the Saudi national accused of bugging an executive conference room at OpenAI 's headquarters, has been released from custody , his attorney told CNBC on Wednesday. The confirmation of Alfozan's release came a day after a federal judge in San Francisco said the defendant would be allowed out of jail on a $1 million bond, despite prosecutors' warnings that he posed a serious flight risk. Alfozan, a former OpenAI engineer, is expected to be fitted with an ankle monitor, his attorney, David Rizk, previously told CNBC. Alfozan was scheduled to be released from detention Wednesday morning at 8 a.m. PT. Shortly before that deadline, U.S. Attorney Craig Missakian of the Northern District of California urged the court to maintain Alfozan's detention pending trial, "given the significant risk that the defendant will flee to Saudi Arabia if he is released from custody." U.S. proposes new tariffs on 14 trading partners, including China and the EU Trump meddling in Huang role reignites voter angst over tech's outsized power Trump wanted Jensen Huang back. Now, the president is all alone in Washington In an order posted on the case docket later Wednesday, Judge Vince Chhabria said the court only learned of the government's last-minute bid to block Alfozan's release after he had already been let out. The government's motion "is therefore denied as moot," Chhabria's order stated. The judge set a hearing for Dec. 3 on the bid to revoke the magistrate judge's order releasing Alfozan. Pointing to Alfozan's "ample resources, significant family and professional ties to Saudi Arabia, and few remaining ties to the United States," Missakian had argued in a court filing that the release conditions imposed by Magistrate Judge Alex Tse "are insufficient to safeguard the defendant's appearance for future proceedings in this case." Alfozan "presents a serious risk of flight that no set of release conditions can reasonably mitigate," Missakian wrote. His office sought to pause the magistrate judge's release order until a ruling on a motion to revoke it. The Department of Justice did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment on Alfozan's release. Tse in a court hearing Tuesday ruled in favor of Rizk's motion for his client's release , which said prosecutors have admitted finding "no new evidence to support the theory that Mr. Alfozan was stealing trade secrets, or to support the speculation that he was acting as an unregistered foreign agent for Saudi Arabia." In a text message to CNBC after that hearing, Rizk said, "We are simply grateful that the Court made the right decision to release Mr. Alfozan and now we look forward to defending the case." But Missakian's filing Wednesday morning pushed back, saying "the government's investigation of this seven-week-old case is ongoing." Prosecutors have so far found "hundreds of audio files" on Alfozan's personal computer, "including dozens of recordings of meetings or conversations that occurred at OpenAI throughout September 2026, at least one of which involved representatives of a foreign government and many of which involved discussions of what may be trade secrets," according to the filing. "To be sure, what the defendant did or intended to do with those audio files remains under investigation, but the absence of that evidence at this point has no bearing" on whether Alfozan is a flight risk, Missakian argued. Alfozan was arrested Oct. 9 and is accused of concealing a recording device in the artificial intelligence company's conference room to secretly record discussions. The device was found in a USB port in a television in the room on Sept. 30, prosecutors have said. Jury selection for Alfozan's trial is scheduled to begin Jan. 20. — CNBC's Dan Mangan contributed to this report.

events.title: Former Pentagon officials say Hegseth blocking senators from visiting Gulf bases amid Iran war ‘smells like a lack of transparency’
events.summary: The Pentagon is banning U.S. lawmakers from visiting Gulf military bases, and former Pentagon officials warn the move is creating tension between the executive and legislative branches and raising questions about why the Department of Defense is limiting access to information about the Iran war. “It smells like a lack of transparency in order to thwart Congressional oversight, in order to either hide that the Iran war is costing more, or to use the Iran war as an excuse to get more money,” Evelyn Farkas, executive director of the McCain Institute at Arizona State University and former deputy assistant secretary of defense for Russia, Ukraine, and Eurasia, told Fortune . Last month, Connecticut Democrat Sen. Chris Murphy detailed his experience of the Department of Defense barring him from visiting the Al Udeid Air Base in Qatar and meeting with military leadership, accusing the Pentagon of obscuring details about the impacts of the Iran war.  “I have been to the Middle East probably a dozen times at least,” Murphy said in a video uploaded to Facebook. “While I have been a member of Congress, I have never, ever been denied access to military facilities. This is part of a coordinated, deliberate campaign by the Department of Defense to try to hide the consequences and the true cost of this war.” Iowa Republican Sen. Joni Ernst was similarly turned away from a base visit around the same time, The Atlantic reported this week. Ernst did not respond to Fortune ’s request for comment. U.S. Congress members have a long-standing practice of conducting visits of military sites as part of their constitutional oversight. In March, following the U.S.-Israel attacks on Iran, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth published a memo to “further discourage visits to the [U.S. Central Command Area of Responsibility] requiring DoW support by members of Congress and their staffs…and no DoW support shall be made available for congressional travel to the USCENTCOM AOR without my approval.” Congress has expressed increased misgivings around Hegseth, introducing articles of impeachment this month, which did not pass, in part on the grounds that the secretary began military conflict in Iran without Congressional authorization. Hegseth has sharply reduced the number of routine press briefings and limited press access to briefings, as well as refused to provide information to the Congressional Budget Office ahead of its update to the cost of the Iran war in September. Meanwhile, the Pentagon is seeking $1.5 trillion in allocations —the largest defense budget in U.S. history—to modernize military infrastructure and restock munitions drained in the conflict in the Gulf. What is the history of U.S. lawmakers visiting military bases? Legislators have been visiting U.S. military bases in times of conflict since at least 1943, when five U.S. senators embarked on a 65-day inspection tour of global military sites during World War II. Visits increased during and after the Vietnam war, when American lawmakers and journalists returned home with stories that vastly differed from former President Richard Nixon’s narrative that the U.S. was winning the war. Farkas, who served for eight years as a staff member of the Senate Armed Services Committee and took several trips to the Gulf as part of a congressional delegation (CODEL), said congressional visits to these military bases are a way to not only increase public knowledge of the status of a war overseas, but in many cases justify granting the military additional and targeted resources for specific operations. During the Iraq war, for example, the U.S. sent a CODEL to the Gulf following improvised explosive devices targeted U.S. personnel in armored vehicles, Farkas recalled. The vehicles were not capable of deflecting the explosives, and following a tour of U.S. military sites, Congress conducted a bipartisan effort to ramp up production of the vehicles. “It’s legitimate, and also necessary and desirable, for members of Congress to go even during a hot war,” Farkas said. Why would the Pentagon turn away U.S. lawmakers from military bases? The Pentagon also has some legitimate reasons for turning lawmakers away from military bases, Elizabeth Dent, a senior fellow at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy and former director for the Gulf and Arabian Peninsula in the Office of the Secretary of Defense, told Fortune.  Hosting a CODEL requires resources like military aircraft and personnel to protect and move lawmakers. In a military theater, armed forces may be unable to spare resources, and when specific threats are made against the military, both troops and elected representatives can be put in harm’s way. In 2016 under then-President Barack Obama, the military asked Congress to limit visits to Afghanistan during a fighting season, though it was not an express ban. Across both Republican and Democrat administrations, U.S. Central Command has ordered limited visits to military sites.  However, Hegseth’s prohibition of military visits has continued, even after the end of “Operation Epic Fury” in May, and when, prior to this month, the last known U.S. attack on Iran was in September. Typically, restrictions are lifted after “hot phases” of conflict end, and the Pentagon’s decision to turn away legislators even during lulls in attacks is what raised suspicions of ulterior motives beyond protecting troops and lawmakers. “The big concern I would have is, the administration has said that Operation Epic Fury is over. Is this more of a lack of transparency and an attempt to hide some of the things that are going on, like the destruction of some of the bases?” Dent said. What is Hegseth’s strategy in withholding access to information about the Iran war? What has lawmakers and former Pentagon officials scratching their heads is that increased transparency to Congress usually yields additional funding, which appears aligned with Hegseth’s push for a record-setting Pentagon budget in fiscal 2027. The government faces a Dec. 11 funding deadline to pass either full-year appropriations or a stopgap measure through the end of the year. “Shutting Congress out is not the way to achieve your objectives if you are the Department of Defense,” Farkas said. “If anything, it’s almost a guarantee that you won’t achieve your objectives because Congress understands what their rights and prerogatives are…so that can just erode trust and confidence further.”  Particularly after the Democratic sweep in the midterm elections, incoming legislators are going to approach the Pentagon’s steep demands with even more rigor, Fargas noted. President Donald Trump will be reluctant to exercise a veto on the National Defense Authorization Act because it outlines military funding, despite Democrats being likely to make changes to it. “It’s better to be open and honest,” she said. “You can’t hide these things anyway. events.title: The midterms showed boomers losing their grip on politics. Their grip on the money is another story
events.summary: A wave of Democrat support in the midterms swept across the U.S. in the beginning of November marking a change of power in politics—not just from the flipping of red to blue, but also from old to young: non-boomer politicians in Congress are at their highest point since the turn of the century. But even as the Baby Boomers are losing their hold on political power, their economic influence remains considerably more difficult to dislodge. And their financial advantage has implications for younger generations struggling with housing costs, student debt and the rising cost of living—especially as the transfer of wealth from older generations to their children remains sluggish. Reshaping the political landscape The shift away from Baby Boomer leadership in government has been building for years, but the 2026 midterms accelerated the transition. For the first time in decades, the generation that dominated congressional leadership and policymaking is losing its grip. The House already moved past the point of Boomer dominance. According to Pew Research Center, Boomers accounted for 39% of House members at the beginning of the 119th Congress, down from a majority just two Congresses earlier. Gen X became the largest generation in the chamber, representing 41% of lawmakers while Millennials accounted for another 15%. The Senate has been slower to change. Boomers still represent 60 of 99 senators at the beginning of the 119th Congress, or roughly 61%. But that imbalance is beginning to change. According to Quorum’s analysis of newly elected lawmakers, Gen X and Millennials account for 87% of the incoming 120th Congressional class. Of the 120 new members, just 13 are Boomers—while 56 Gen Xers and 48 Millennials will occupy the new seats. The change is also visible in the pipeline of candidates seeking office. Future Caucus found that Millennials and Gen Z accounted for roughly one-third of congressional candidates in 2026, up from one-quarter in 2024 and one-sixth in 2022. According to the report, Millennials also became the largest generational group running for Senate for the first time in the report’s history. Still, the political transition is not complete as the Senate continues to be a stubborn stronghold for older Americans. The incoming chamber’s median age will fall to 63 from 64, but will still remain among the oldest Senates in American history, according to Reuters . The wealth divide According to the Federal Reserve’s Distributional Financial Accounts, Baby Boomers held approximately $97.4 trillion in household net worth in Q2 2026. That represents 52.5% of all U.S. household wealth, despite Boomers accounting for just 27% of the country’s adult population. In contrast, Millennials and Gen Z together represented 22.4% of real estate but only held 11.2% of household wealth—about $20.8 trillion. Generation X held another 25.7%. And while the great wealth transfer is coming, younger Americans are waiting. Visa’s Business and Economic Insights report in July estimated approximately $36 trillion of Baby Boomers’ $93 trillion in assets could transfer to younger generations over the next 20 years—after accounting for liabilities, taxes, fees, retirement spending and other exclusions. “Imagine you are sitting on a winning lottery ticket. You hit the jackpot, but you immediately lose half by— smartly—taking the lump sum,” the report read. “Next, you lose another 30–40 percent through taxes and fees. The advertised jackpot is enormous, but after the lump-sum haircut, taxes and fees, the take-home number is much lower. A similar dynamic applies to the great wealth transfer.” But that doesn’t mean the younger Americans will now get access to that same financial security. The transfer is likely to be uneven, with most of the wealth being concentrated among families that already have substantial assets. According to Visa’s research, nearly 75% of inheritance recipients already have higher net worths than the average household. That means much of the inherited wealth from the transfer will be saved or invested, not immediately spent. Visa also estimated that one in four millennial homeowners received financial assistance from their parents for a down payment. But perspective matters. A 2025 analysis by the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis found that Millennials and Gen Z households actually had more inflation-adjusted wealth at approximately age 34 than Boomers did at that same age. According to the analysis, Millennials and Gen Zers owned $1.23 for every $1 of wealth owned by Gen Xers at the same age—and $1.35 for every $1 of wealth owned by baby boomers. The next generational fight The generational war has a six-year deadline, set by Social Security and the national debt. According to the 2026 Social Security trustees report, the combined retirement and disability trust funds are projected to be depleted by 2032. At that point, incoming revenue would only cover 83% of scheduled benefits unless Congress changes the program. Boomers have held the presidency since 2001, spanning George W. Bush to Donald Trump, with the exception of Joe Biden—who is part of the Silent Generation. In that time span, the national debt climbed from $5.81 trillion to over $40.17 trillion through September 2026, according to the Treasury’s fiscal data, during which time, they have passed a series of tax cuts leaving their own generation’s retirements endangered. Democrats have argued for increasing revenue by raising the cap on earnings subject to Social Security payroll taxes, while Republicans mostly emphasized economic growth. But Sen. Ron Johnson—the Wisconsin Republican who chairs the Senate Budget Committee and is a Boomer himself—has a typically Boomerian fix: make other generations pay for it. Social Security is funded primarily through payroll taxes paid by today’s workers, meaning younger Americans now are financing the benefits for current retirees. But once the funds are depleted, covering the shortfall would mean borrowing more from other federal priorities. In effect, the government would be putting the cost of maintaining the retirement benefits on the national credit card, leaving younger taxpayers to help service the debt through future taxes or spending cuts. On Nov. 18, Johnson called Social Security a “legal Ponzi scheme” on Fox Business . events.title: World reacts to Trump’s new tariffs as US stocks tumble
events.summary: Trump’s new tariffs: Which countries are affected? Trump-Xi-Putin summit: Key takeaways Can Trump find a way to work with Democrats? The new levies come after an eight-month investigation launched by the United States Trade Representative. The Trump administration has announced new tariffs on 14 major trading partners , including China and the European Union, claiming that excess production has given them an unfair advantage. The proposed levies come after a months-long investigation into the trade practices of 12 countries, the 27-member EU and the self-governing island of Taiwan, launched after the Supreme Court struck down United States President Donald Trump’s sweeping global tariffs in February. list 1 of 4 Nvidia stock cools after Huang’s return-driven surge list 2 of 4 China Southern Airlines unit to buy 50 Boeing 737-8 planes list 3 of 4 How close should Britain get to the EU? list 4 of 4 Trump announces new trade tariffs: Which countries are affected? The highest tariff rate announced on Wednesday would hit China the hardest, at 20 percent, adding to the roughly 25 percent duties that Trump imposed on China during his first term. The proposed tariffs would not apply to about $30bn of Chinese imports under consideration for tariff reductions through a bilateral mechanism known as the Board of Trade. Washington has long accused China of subsidising its industries and flooding global markets with low-cost exports ranging from steel to electric vehicles and solar products, allegations that Beijing has once again denied. “The so-called ‘overcapacity’ is a false issue, and China opposes using it as an excuse for political manipulation,” Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said, urging the world’s two top economies to maintain stable relations. Other US trading partners facing proposed new tariffs include India, Japan, South Korea, Indonesia, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam. Mexico and Norway were also part of the probe but were excluded from the new round of tariffs because investigations into their trade practices are still ongoing. The tariff announcement follows an eight-month investigation initiated by US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, under Section 301 of the US Trade Act of 1974, which permits the president to impose import taxes and other sanctions against countries found to engage in unreasonable or discriminatory trade practices. “The administration’s use of Section 301 is cynical,” Gregory Shaffer, professor of international law at the Georgetown University Law Center, told Al Jazeera. “It launched these investigations in order to support the president’s aim to set tariffs globally and to modify them at any time at the president’s will, and thus strip Congress of the authority to set tariff rates under the taxing power set forth in the Constitution.” In a separate announcement, the White House also announced a proposed 10 percent tariff on finished aircraft made by Brazilian planemaker Embraer, whose jets are widely used by US regional carriers operating under brands including United Express, Delta Connection and American Eagle. Finished aircraft are Brazil’s fourth-biggest export to the US. The US also plans to raise duties on imports of Brazilian sugar that exceed quotas as part of an effort to push Brasilia to rectify alleged unfair trade practices, according to a senior US official. Several governments have reacted to the new tariff announcement, as has the European Union. “The EU takes note of the publication by the US of preliminary findings pursuant to its Section 301 investigation concerning structural excess capacity in manufacturing sectors,” European Commission spokesperson Olof Gill told Al Jazeera. “We will study the findings. At the same time we strongly reject the premise that Europe is a source of structural overcapacity. To the contrary, Europe is among those most exposed to overcapacity,” Gill added. The Swiss government has also reacted, saying that it rejects the allegations stemming from the investigations. “The timing right before the G20 [in mid-December] sets up those meetings as an opportunity for negotiation and increases risk of both inflationary pressures and macro volatility in 2027, reducing some of the benefit from easing gas prices,” Rachel Ziemba, adjunct senior fellow at the Center for a New American Security, told Al Jazeera. “We have been clear throughout the process that Norway does not have policies that contribute to overcapacity. Norwegian companies produce in response to market demand,” Foreign Minister Espen Barth Eide said. US markets are trending down on news of the new tariffs. The tech-heavy Nasdaq tumbled 3.9 percent in early trading on Wednesday. The S&P 500 is down 2.8 percent, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average slumped by 1.4 percent.

events.title: There are 5,100 newly minted Anthropic millionaires — here’s all the stuff they don’t tell you about when you suddenly get rich
events.summary: Anthropic's IPO on Nov. 19 turned around 5,100 nonfounder "Ants," as the company's staffers are known, into "paper millionaires," and at least 400 will be worth north of $100 million. But don't be too jealous of these employees' gains — there are a remarkable number of downsides to sudden wealth. Some will keep working because their payout wasn't life-changing, said Susan Bradley, a certified financial planner and founder of The Sudden Money Institute: "You can go through $2 million pretty quickly in the world we live in." Things are about to get very weird for the thousands of employees of Anthropic who just became, or soon will become, multimillionaires. Few of us will ever make a million-dollar windfall from an employer. And fewer still will win the lottery or magically land a massive sum from an estranged rich uncle. But don't be too jealous of these employees' gains. Sure, money can buy a lot — and it would be hard to say no if you do strike it rich — but there are a remarkable number of downsides to sudden wealth. And they may explain why you likely won't see all of Anthropic's newly minted millionaire employees heading for the exits. Trump Account contributions from friends and family pass $1 billion mark, Treasury says The Fed is likely to raise rates in December. What it means for your holiday spending Trump administration proposes rule that could curb ESG investing in 401(k)s CNBC's Financial Advisor 100: Best financial advisors, top firms for 2026 ranked CNBC Elite Advisors: Top ultra-high net worth wealth management firms for 2026 First of all, these new moguls won't be able to access all their wealth immediately. The terms of the stock sale outlined in Anthropic's revised S-1 allow employees to cash out up to 10% of the value of their holdings on the first day of trading following the date of the prospectus, but the rest can only be exercised after various vesting periods pass or lock-up terms are achieved, based on the individual's agreements with the company. Some won't be able to realize all their gains for years. There are many financial institutions willing to lend based on paper gains, or to buy options — but their wealth will also continue to fluctuate with the rise and fall of the company's stock price. Even after those riches become liquid, research shows that only a small but still significant percentage of employees will leave as a direct result of their new wealth. No, they aren't jetting off to the South Pacific to board their new yacht — which is what I would do in my "I just got $10 million" fantasy. Instead, according to a 2017 study from the Federal Reserve , an estimated 17.5% of employees at a newly public company will use their newfound wealth as a financial cushion to join another pre-IPO startup or form another company. These departures, the study finds, may be particularly painful for Anthropic since the most valuable and entrepreneurially minded employees tend to bolt for this reason. Experts who deal with suddenly wealthy employees expect that many will keep on working because they love it. "They're successful people in their own right," said David Rust, a financial advisor and co-founder of wealth management firm Quartz Financial in Austin, Texas. Rust said that of his firm's high-tech employee clients who get sudden IPO wealth, "very few just go play golf every day. They want to stay busy and active, and a lot of them will scale back depending on their age, but very few of them say, 'OK, I'm done with that.'" Others will keep working because their payout wasn't life-changing, said Susan Bradley, a certified financial planner and founder of The Sudden Money Institute, a Palm Beach Gardens, Florida-based financial advisory firm that specializes in clients undergoing sudden wealth events. That's especially true for those whose millions measure in the low single digits. "You can go through $2 million pretty quickly in the world we live in," said Bradley. A sum north of $1 million might seem life-changing to most of America, but it's chump change in Anthropic's headquarters city of San Francisco, the fifth most expensive city in the United States, with nearby San Jose coming in at third, according to a Q3 2026 Cost of Living report from Council on Community and Economic Research, which tracks metro- and state-level economic data. In 2025, the Bay Area had the second-highest number of people with a net worth of $100 million or more of any major metro in the world, according to a study by New World Wealth, a market research firm, in conjunction with Henley & Partners, a global residency and citizenship planning firm. That ranking is sure to get a boost from Anthropic's IPO. Those who stay at Anthropic may be in for a bumpy ride. A study published in July in Management Science by two researchers from the University of Oklahoma found that employee satisfaction generally tends to crater after an IPO, especially among the earliest employees who had the biggest IPO payday.

events.title: US-led group reaches deal to acquire Lukoil's global assets
events.summary: A US-led consortium has agreed a deal with Lukoil to acquire the sanctioned Russian company's global energy assets. The consortium, led by US billionaire Todd Boehly 's Eldridge, would swap Lukoil securities for its international assets, it said in a news release on Wednesday. The group includes the US International Development Finance Corporation, UAE-based Catena Investment Holding, and Xtellus Partners. The US Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control (Ofac) is expected to review and rubber-stamp the deal. The Treasury Department placed sanctions on Lukoil in October 2025 . “Given President [Vladimir] Putin’s refusal to end this senseless war, Treasury is sanctioning Russia’s two largest oil companies that fund the Kremlin’s war machine,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said at the time. However, the Treasury issued temporary waivers beginning in March to release sanctioned Russian crude already on vessels with the aim of mitigating rising oil prices amid the Iran war. The DFC, the international investment arm of the US, would receive an ownership interest under the deal. The agency did not immediately respond to The National 's request for comment. Mr Boehley told Reuters the US would receive a share of future profits under the agreement, if approved, and would support efforts to prevent Russia from funding its war in Ukraine. The deal transfers Lukoil's non-Russian oil and gas assets in Bulgaria, Romania, Africa and the Middle East to the US-led consortium. It also includes petrol stations in the US, Europe and Asia, CNBC reported. The deal would give the US-led group roughly 350,000 barrels per day of production. The group said Lukoil's upstream operations cover 11 countries and serve the Black Sea, the Balkans and north-west Europe, and supply diesel and other petroleum products to US-allied nations. Lukoil and US private equity firm Carlyle Group announced a non-exclusive purchase agreement for the Russian company's foreign assets in January. The agreement lapsed in July without an agreement from the Treasury Department, and Carlyle dropped out of the race in October. Ofac's latest licence for negotiations is set to expire on December 19.

events.title: Poundland collapses, putting more than 10,000 jobs at risk
events.summary: Budget retail chain expected to be broken up, with store closures, after US owner rejected at least two last-ditch bids Do you work for Poundland? Tell us how you’re affected Poundland has collapsed into administration, putting more than 10,000 jobs at risk in “devastating news” for staff in the run-up to Christmas. Administrators at AlixPartners have been appointed to the retailer, which has 600 stores in the UK and Ireland, by Poundland’s directors. The chain is now expected to be broken up, with significant job losses and store closures after its owners rejected at least two last-ditch bids for the budget retailer. AlixPartners said a sales process “did not identify a viable solvent solution for the business as a whole”. It said Poundland employed more than 10,000 people, which the Guardian understands is about 2,000 fewer than were in the business just a month ago. It has been suggested that as many as 30,000 jobs in total could be at risk in Poundland’s stores, supply chain and at other affected businesses on high streets around the country. Poundland would continue to trade with all stores and distribution centres remaining open while administrators pursued “all options including sales of the business and its assets, either in whole or part, from administration”, AlixPartners said. Bally Auluk, a national officer for shopworkers’ union Usdaw, said: “This is devastating news for our members, who were only recently praised by management for helping to turn the business around. “There is never a good time for this to happen, but just before Christmas has to be the worst. This decision has been made by the owners, Gordon Brothers, despite failing to engage with Usdaw, which is a disgraceful way to treat our members.” The US finance firm, which bought Poundland for a nominal £1 from the European retail group Pepco last year, has been under pressure to accept an offer that would save jobs and protect thousands of the retailer’s suppliers. Gordon Brothers said on Wednesday afternoon it had “explored every avenue to secure a sale of the whole company” but that Poundland was “still vulnerable to inflationary pressures or any downturn in sales and margin”. It said: “Poundland has faced several years of instability. In July 2025, Gordon Brothers supported the company’s restructuring plan – stepping in when no one else was willing to finance the business.” In notes seen by the Guardian, Poundland’s directors wrote to staff and suppliers on Wednesday expressing “sincere sadness and intense regret” that they had been forced to call in administrators after Gordon Brothers said it would not provide more funds to keep the business operating as there was “no prospect of an acceptable solvent offer”. Poundland’s managing director, Barry Williams, told suppliers: “We know this outcome will be as disappointing to you as it is to us.” About 2,000 suppliers will lose significant business and millions of pounds in payments for stock already supplied. High inflation and heavy competition from budget stores, online specialists and supermarkets have left the 36-year-old retail chain – the UK’s first and biggest nationwide single-price retailer – struggling. Poundland’s board filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators last month – which was later extended – protecting the retailer from the demands of creditors until 26 November while a solution to its problems was sought. Just two bidders interested in the whole company remained in talks right up until this week’s deadline. Martin Property Group, a Northern Ireland family-owned company, which has been working with the existing management for about two months, remained interested. It was joined by a last-ditch bid from Germany’s Zachert Private Equity, a fund founded by a former Bloomberg journalist that specialises in acquiring mid-sized companies. Other bidders for the whole group included the little-known finance group Xyra Group Holdings, and the Irish investment company Innovest, which both fell out of the bidding race over the past week. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning AlixPartners said: “We would encourage anybody interested in acquiring the business in part or as a whole, as well as UK retail operators with open employment opportunities, to contact the administrators.” Poundland’s board was forced to appoint administrators before Thursday’s deadline as shelves began to empty because the company was running short of funds to restock during its peak Christmas trading period. Gordon Brothers’ UK director, Mark Newton-Jones, held the latest of several meetings with the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, on Monday, more than a week after giving evidence to the business select committee. MPs called on the government to protect Poundland and other high street stores from “predatory capitalism” and asset-stripping last week.

events.title: 1Password said hackers broke into its internal systems, but customer passwords are safe
events.summary: Password manager maker 1Password has confirmed that some customer information was taken in a recent intrusion into its internal systems, but that customer password vaults and other secrets were not accessed. The Toronto-based tech company said in a blog post published Wednesday that it detected an intrusion on November 19, in which an attacker gained access to an employee’s corporate account with GitHub, which the company uses to share and store its source code. The attacker used that employee’s access to push malicious code to the company’s internal servers, which allowed the hacker to download some data about 1Password customers, including their names and the email address that they use for logging into their account. The company said that the attacker also took details about when a 1Password account was created and when a user last logged in. 1Password said that customer vaults, which store their passwords, were “at no point” available to the attacker. The company also said that it doesn’t have access to customer account passwords or their secret keys, which are used to scramble their passwords so that 1Password cannot see them. In addition, the company said that its apps and extensions are unaffected by the incident. It’s unclear how the attacker gained access to the employee’s corporate account, and a spokesperson for 1Password did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s questions about the incident. 1Password did not say whether it had notified customers whose information was taken in the breach, or how many customers had information taken. We’ve also asked if the company has received any communication or demands from the hackers. We’ll update if we hear back from 1Password. The company touts millions of customers and more than 200,000 businesses who use its password manager products to store their passwords, credentials, payment card information, and more. Security experts have long recommended password managers as a better way of generating stronger credentials and keeping track of online accounts. events.title: 8 ways to be a good houseguest, according to etiquette experts
events.summary: Business Insider asked etiquette experts to share some ways to be a good houseguest. fizkes/Shutterstock Business insider asked etiquette experts about how to be a good guest in someone's home. The pros said tidying up the kitchen and your sleeping space are non-negotiables. Cooking, buying groceries, and giving a gift to your host are kind gestures of gratitude. Whether you're visiting for a night or planning an extended stay for the holidays, someone else's home is not the place to disregard manners. That's why Business Insider asked two etiquette experts for their best advice on being a great houseguest. Here's what they said. Make sure the host is aware of your expected arrival time. wichayada suwanachun/Shutterstock Pamela Eyring, owner of The Protocol School of Washington , told BI that being a great guest in someone's home starts with clear communication. "Be clear and prompt about your arrival time and quickly communicate an updated schedule if you are running late," Eyring told BI. Your host is likely preparing for your arrival — cleaning, cooking, or adjusting their schedule. Keeping them informed on when they can expect you helps prevent stress and shows you value their hospitality. Show gratitude by bringing a gift for your host. BearFotos/Shutterstock Additionally, Eyring said it's always a nice gesture to bring a gift for your host. If you're not sure what they like, she suggests choosing something that appeals to all, like flowers, sweets, or a meal. Be mindful of the tone you set for the visit. Pixel-Shot/Shutterstock It's no secret that travel doesn't always go as planned. But according to business etiquette expert and leadership consultant Sheree Bryant Sekou , bringing a negative attitude and energy to your host's home can impact the duration of your stay. "How you start a trip can affect how it ends, so to the best of your ability, shake off any bad vibes so you can be a fully present, enjoyable, and happy guest," she told BI. Come prepared with your own toiletries and anything else you need to feel comfortable. New Africa/Shutterstock When staying in someone else's home, Sekou said it's polite to come prepared with your own toiletries, personal hygiene products, and anything else you need to feel comfortable during your stay. This way, the host doesn't feel like they have to provide everything for you. For example, if you're particular about your sleep setup, Eyring suggests bringing your own pillow. If you're a light sleeper, bringing earplugs can be a good idea. Overall, planning for your own comfort shows thoughtfulness and helps ensure a smoother stay. Always make your bed in the morning. Pixel-Shot/Shutterstock Whether you're sleeping on the sofa or in a bedroom, it's respectful to clean up the space after you wake up every morning. "Always make ‌your bed when staying in someone else's home. That includes arranging pillows as you've seen them before," Sekou told BI. If your sleeping arrangement is fancy, Sekou suggests taking a photo when you arrive so you can try to match it each day. Offer to help with cooking or pay for groceries. Cooking a meal can help make your host's life easier. Jacob Wackerhausen When staying in someone's home, Sekou recommends helping out in the kitchen in a way that best suits your host, whether that's cooking a meal or buying groceries. " Buying groceries lets your host know you appreciate their hospitality and are respectful of their budget," she said. Always clean up after yourself in shared spaces. Drazen Zigic/Shutterstock Sekou said being a considerate houseguest means cleaning up after yourself in shared spaces like the kitchen and bathroom. Regardless of your habits at home, she said it's important to keep things tidy when staying in someone else's house. This means doing the dishes, wiping down counters , and ensuring nothing is left behind. The same principle applies to the bathroom. Sekou recommends a quick once-over before you leave — rinse the tub after a bath, and make sure no hair, toothpaste, or shaving remnants are left behind in the sink. At the end of your stay, check that you grabbed all your belongings. Pranithan Chorruangsak/Shutterstock According to Sekou, part of being a considerate guest is packing efficiently and ensuring you take all your belongings with you when you leave. "If you've left something behind, it puts the onus on the host to get it back to you, especially if it's something valuable," Sekou told BI. events.title: The Guardian view on rising energy prices: only bold action can win public confidence | Editorial
events.summary: The Guardian view on rising energy prices: only bold action can win public confidence Andy Burnham needs a radical vision of economic change to move on from policies aimed at giving voters ‘breathing space’ A sk Andy Burnham a question and it won’t be long before he mentions the cost of living. Responding to the results of midterm elections in the US earlier this month, he said that the Democratic party’s triumph meant that there was “an opportunity now to unite around the issue that is affecting us all, and that’s the cost of living”. This wasn’t a non sequitur. The Republicans lost control of Congress in large part because Donald Trump failed to address concerns about the cost of basic goods – a failing aggravated by the US president’s disastrous war against Iran, which caused a spike in commodity prices, exacerbating the affordability problem. Mr Burnham correctly identified the transmission mechanism by which geopolitical problems feed domestic political resentment. “I can’t get people’s cost of living pressures down until the conflict in the Middle East is resolved, the conflict in Ukraine started by Russia,” the prime minister said. The truth of that observation was painfully clear on Wednesday, when Ofgem, the energy regulator, announced that the price cap applied on domestic bills would rise in January . That means around 22 million UK households will pay an average equivalent to £2,166 a year for gas and electricity, up from £1,723 under the current cap. International conflict and the climate emergency are driving up costs for British homes. Gas supply has been made volatile by uncertainty in the strait of Hormuz, while European reserves were depleted by exceptional energy usage to mitigate the effects of the summer’s ferocious and prolonged heatwave. That leaves the continent poorly resourced to face what might be an unusually cold winter caused by the disruption of the polar vortex , plausibly accelerated by anthropogenic climate change. Many British households will face painful choices between heating their homes and affording other essentials. That hardship will exhaust the cost of living “breathing space” already offered by Mr Burnham – a VAT cut to bills and a one-off £100 payment to some households. Meanwhile, the Conservatives and Reform UK claim that high bills are a function of environmental policies and look for solutions in the abandonment of Britain’s commitments to net zero – an approach that combines economic illiteracy with international irresponsibility. A dash to get dwindling North Sea oil on to a global market where the price is determined more by Mr Trump’s caprices or Vladimir Putin’s territorial aggressions is no shortcut to cheaper British bills. Hastening the transition away from fossil fuels is the strategic route to energy security and the stability that permits other interventions to help with the cost of living. That argument must be central to the analysis that Mr Burnham offers when he moves on from “breathing space” policies to the more ambitious vision promised in a 10-year plan. The prime minister has advertised that document, due to be published next month, as a blueprint for fixing “broken” markets , and restoring public control over utilities and other services on which people depend. What that means in practice will decide the fate of the Labour government. His focus on the cost of living is the right one, given how quick voters are to punish incumbents who fail to appreciate the scale of the problem or are perceived to lack credible solutions. Mr Burnham has passed the first of those tests. He cannot afford to fail the second one.

events.title: Poundland collapses putting 11,000 jobs at risk
events.summary: Watch: Why has Poundland collapsed into administration? Published 25 November 2026, 15:46 GMT Poundland has collapsed into administration, putting 11,000 jobs at risk, after its owners failed to find a buyer to keep it in business. The retailer's shops and distribution centres will remain open and continue to trade during the administration process with the business likely to be broken up and some of its stores sold off to rival retailers. Poundland's US owners held talks with several bidders over a last-minute rescue deal, but no agreement was reached. Poundland boss Barry Williams said in a note to staff that the board had "no alternative but to take this decision", but was making it with "sincere sadness and intense regret". He said the US owners Gordon Brothers had removed "all borrowing facilities and access to our bank accounts" on 27 October, and adequate funds had not been released since then to keep the business solvent. "Under these circumstances, it is impossible for the board of directors to see how Poundland can continue to operate as a going concern," he added. Kelvin Blake, pictured at a protest in Walsall, has worked for Poundland for 25 years Kelvin Blake, 62, who has worked for the firm for 25 years, and whose partner has been there 29 years, said he was feeling "down, depressed", and because of his age, feared he would not find a job elsewhere. "We didn't want it, but it's come so now we've just got to face it and see what the future holds. "My income's gone," he added. "Obviously, we'll be working until we're told to leave." Alix Partners, which has been appointed as administrator, said they would look at all options for the business, "including sales of the business and its assets, either in whole or part". "We appreciate this is a deeply concerning time for all involved - customers, suppliers and, in particular, Poundland colleagues," they said. Gordon Brothers has been criticised over how it handled a potential sale of Poundland, with accusations the investment firm hoped to profit from selling off the chain's 600 shops and stock piecemeal after running it into the ground. Gordon Brothers, which specialises in buying and restructuring distressed companies, has denied such claims. On the funding question, Gordon Brothers said it had loaned the firm £85m over a year to help save it from insolvency. But insiders critical of the US firm have said it stands to make its loans back and more from the insolvency process. Previously, Gordon Brothers netted millions from liquidating the stock of fashion retailer LK Bennett, and in insolvency fees. Labour MP Liam Byrne told the BBC the House of Commons' Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee will recall Gordon Brothers before Parliament. He said: "I am really worried that a 'greed is good' approach to business by its owners has forced [Poundland] into an administration." He added the committee wants to know "how much money they're ripping out and crucially, how do we make sure, as a country, that we don't have this kind of scenario unfold again". What's gone wrong at Poundland? Published 3 hours ago Gordon Brothers said on Wednesday that despite the Poundland management bringing about a turnaround over the past year, the firm was "still vulnerable" to inflation and any downturn in sales or profit margin, and it had faced "several years of instability". A spokesperson added the firm's "thoughts are with Poundland colleagues". It said it had stepped in to take over the retailer in 2025 when it was struggling, and when "no-one else was willing to finance the business". One of the central stumbling blocks in negotiations to keep the business afloat was a shareholder loan Gordon Brothers inherited when it bought the business for less than £1 last year. Gordon Brothers was owed £22.5m of that loan, while the previous owner Pepco was owed £7.5m. Gordon Brothers rejected various offers to buy the business as a going concern with deals to pay off that loan. Irish firm Martin Property Group offered to pay off £5m of the loan up front, and defer the rest of the payments to 2030. London-based Xyra group offered £12.5m up front but ran out of time to get a deal over the line. German investment firm Zachert Private Equity is also understood to have made a late offer. The crisis at Poundland really came to a head over the past few weeks after Gordon Brothers restricted access to funds for day-to-day operations. This meant that stock at the retailer was not being replenished at the necessary pace in the vital run-up to the festive period. Are you a Poundland employee? Tell us your story. Get in touch. events.title: Trump’s Nvidia intervention is the reverse of how Bush handled Enron’s Ken Lay
events.summary: Once upon a time, a hugely valuable company sat at the cutting edge of an industry the whole economy depended on, and it had close ties to the White House. Then came signs of financial irregularities on a scandalous scale. That was Enron in 2001, and President George W. Bush stood back and let justice take its course. On Monday, President Donald Trump did the reverse with Nvidia: the chipmaker reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO 11 days after he resigned over reports of extramarital affairs , including one with Alice Huang, a Chinese national U.S. officials suspect of spying and who is no relation. “I convinced them,” Trump told CNBC in a phone interview. Huang has denied compromising national security, and no one has charged him with a crime. Nvidia and Enron are not like-for-like scandals, although some commentators see the connection; the details so far are scandalous but are not Enron-style accounting fraud. Still, with some financial commentators fearing an AI bubble could pop and trigger the next financial crisis, Kenneth “Kenny Boy” Lay’s case is instructive. It shows how far Washington has moved from treating big companies as targets to treating them as partners. Bush and “Kenny Boy” Lay was a fixture of Houston’s energy establishment, and his ties to the Bush family went back to the first President Bush . Bush adviser Karl Rove later called any idea that Lay was a “close intimate” of Bush “ludicrous,” but they were close enough that Bush gave him the “Kenny Boy” nickname. The money was never in doubt. Across Bush’s political career, Enron, its employees and their families gave him more than $550,000, more than any other single source , and Lay was his biggest financial backer. As Texas governor, Bush signed a 1999 electricity deregulation law that opened new markets to Enron. During the 2000 campaign, he traveled to Houston for the Astros’ first game at Enron Field, where Lay threw out the first pitch. Wall Street loved the company, too. Fortune named Enron America’s most innovative company six years running, even as Fortune ’s Bethany McLean became the first major business journalist to ask, in March 2001, how exactly Enron made its money . When Enron was collapsing in October 2001, Lay phoned Treasury Secretary Paul O’Neill and Commerce Secretary Donald Evans. Both said they did nothing to help. Nearly five years later, with Bush still in the White House, a jury convicted Lay and former CEO Jeffrey Skilling of fraud. Skilling’s 24-year sentence was among the longest ever handed to a corporate executive; a judge cut it to 14 years in 2013. Former CFO Andrew Fastow got six years and was released after about five. Lay died before he could be sentenced, and his convictions were vacated. The two companies already share a footnote. At the end of November 2001, days before Enron filed for bankruptcy, Standard & Poor’s dropped it from the S&P 500 and replaced it with a Santa Clara graphics-chip maker called Nvidia. How Huang courted Trump Huang’s closeness to Trump is newer, and he built it deliberately. CNBC reports that Huang spent two years cultivating an “unparalleled relationship” with Trump while Nvidia lobbied for looser limits on selling advanced chips to China. Nvidia gave $1 million to Trump’s inaugural fund and $25 million to his White House ballroom, and it initially sought to keep the ballroom gift anonymous. In April 2025, Huang attended a $1-million-a-head dinner at Mar-a-Lago, after which the administration briefly held off on restricting Nvidia’s H20 chips before imposing the limits days later. By July, the administration had reversed course and begun approving sales to China, and in December Trump said Nvidia could sell its more powerful H200 chips to approved Chinese customers. Democrats, including Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland, have tied the donations to those decisions , but there is no known hard evidence of any specific quid pro quo — something that could change under the incoming, heavily Democratic Congress. A $952 billion day for the “central bank of AI” Nvidia shares closed up about 31.5% on Monday , their best day since 2003, adding $952 billion in market value, and the S&P 500 rose 4.73%. The rebound reversed much of the slide that followed Huang’s exit , although the stock gave back single-digit percentages on Tuesday and Wednesday. The stakes are hard to overstate. Nvidia ranks No. 16 on the 2026 Fortune 500 and was the first company on the list to top $4 trillion in market value . Trump held between $13 million and $58 million in Nvidia stock at the end of 2025, according to his Office of Government Ethics filings, and CBS News estimated his stake gained between $1.3 million and $14.8 million on Monday. The White House told CBS that independent managers run his portfolio. Nvidia matters well beyond the president’s portfolio. The company, and Huang personally, have been called “the central bank of AI,” a label The Economist applied after tallying more than $70 billion in Nvidia investments in startups over three years and $300 billion in financial support to customers . Owen Lamont, a portfolio manager at Acadian Asset Management who writes the Owenomics newsletter , says that label carries a curse. In his telling, once an entity is called “the central bank of” its field, it becomes “a prime candidate for a cosmic smackdown.” Long-Term Capital Management, called “the central bank of volatility” before its 1998 collapse, was the first victim he knows of. FTX, called “the central bank of crypto” six months before Sam Bankman-Fried’s arrest, was the second. The Economist has also compared Nvidia’s financing to the vendor lending Cisco and Lucent did in the dot-com boom. Cisco is the other fallen high-flier Nvidia is most often measured against, usually by outlier voices; it is the favorite comparison of “Big Short” trader Michael Burry, who has become a Substack star during the AI boom. From prosecutor to partner The Enron prosecutions marked the end of an era. In “ The Chickenshit Club ,” ProPublica’s Jesse Eisinger holds up a Justice Department that set up a dedicated task force, charged nearly all of Enron’s top executives and did so against a friend of the president. He argues that the department has since lost the will and ability to prosecute top executives. The title comes from James Comey, who led the FBI’s 2016 investigation of Hillary Clinton’s emails and is now fighting a third attempt by Trump’s Justice Department to prosecute him. As U.S. attorney in Manhattan, Comey told prosecutors who had never lost a trial that they belonged to the “Chickenshit Club,” meaning they were too cautious to take on hard cases. events.title: 15 Thanksgiving dishes that don't require an oven
events.summary: Frying a turkey isn't for the faint of heart. Brett Comer/Houston Chronicle/Getty Images If your oven is full on Thanksgiving or simply out of commission, oven-free recipes can help. Salads, slow-cooker recipes, and pasta are all beloved dishes that don't require an oven. These 15 Thanksgiving dishes are completely oven-free. Whether your oven is crammed full of turkey or it's woefully small, sometimes baking and roasting aren't options on Thanksgiving. This week, people across the country will be making multiple dishes for Thanksgiving dinner , using every available cooking surface and spending an average of 9.6 hours preparing for their guests, according to WalletHub data . Thankfully, there are plenty of Thanksgiving staples or updated versions of the classics that don't require any oven space at all. Even the precious turkey can stay out of that fateful appliance on November 26. Here are the easiest foods you can whip up this Thanksgiving — no oven required. If you want to use your oven for other dishes, you could use a deep fryer for your turkey. Eric Thayer/Reuters Deep-frying a turkey is serious business, one that can end in a fiery disaster, as evidenced in annual police videos . Business Insider previously showed the best way to fry a turkey safely. You could also use a slow cooker for the turkey, freeing up oven space. Slow cooker. O2O Creative/Getty Images Kendra Bailey Morris, author of "The Southern Slow Cooker," previously told Business Insider that a whole turkey likely won't fit in a slow cooker, but a 3- or 4-pound turkey breast can. "The beauty of the slow cooker is that it is inherently self-basting," she said. "Slow cookers create a very moist environment with the condensation from the cooking process often rising to the top of the slow cooker and then dripping back down onto the meat, which helps to keep things moist." She also suggested injecting some fat, such as a herb butter, back into the turkey breast, since the meat is lean. If your oven is full, you can leave soup simmering on the stove or in a slow cooker. Pumpkin soup. Cris Cantón/Getty Images As part of Business Insider's ongoing taste-test series, we've tried the best canned chicken noodle soups , which could be part of a Thanksgiving spread, especially on a budget. Soups or stews that use a slow cooker could be another option for a cold day. Business Insider's food reporter Erin McDowell recommends these three slow-cooker recipes from Martha Stewart . Mashed potatoes can be made from a mix or in the slow cooker. AP Photo/Larry Crowe Instant mashed potatoes might be polarizing, but they are extremely simple. Alternatively, you can make delicious, creamy mashed potatoes in a slow cooker . "Mashed potatoes are great in the slow cooker, though it does take a bit of time for the potatoes to soften, so plan ahead," Sarah Olson , the chef behind The Magical Slow Cooker website, told McDowell. Green-bean casserole is another staple at the Thanksgiving table. Green bean casserole. LauriPatterson/Getty Images Olson has a slow-cooker recipe for green-bean casserole on The Magical Slow Cooker. There are other methods, too — check out this skillet green-bean casserole  or this microwave version. Spinach casserole can also be made in your slow cooker. Spinach casserole. Arisara_Tongdonnoi/Getty Images Give this  slow-cooker spinach casserole  recipe a go. Everyone's favorite pasta dish, mac and cheese, only requires a pot and a stove — or a slow cooker. Mac and cheese. DronG/Getty Images Whether you're making boxed mac and cheese  or working from scratch , this side is always a hit. Martha Stewart has recipes for both stovetop and slow-cooker mac and cheese , although we prefer the slow-cooker option. You can make candied yams in an air fryer. Candied yams. bhofack2/Getty Images A Business Insider reporter tried out an air-fryer recipe for candied yams and called it "ridiculously easy." Sweet potatoes are versatile, and all you need to do is microwave them. Robynmac/Getty Images All you need to do to successfully cook a sweet potato is to prick its skin with a fork and throw it in the microwave for 6 to 8 minutes. Cauliflower, or any vegetable really, tastes great pan-fried. Cauliflower. Tatiana Volgutova/Getty Images Here's a recipe for pan-fried cauliflower. Cranberry sauce is a classic Thanksgiving side dish, and all you need to do is open a can. Cranberry sauce. skhoward/Getty Images Find out which grocery-store cranberry sauce was named our favorite. And don't forget: You should always open your cranberry sauce upside down . Stuffing is a Thanksgiving essential that doesn't need to spend time in the oven. Stuffing. Sarah Schmalbruch/Business Insider There's no single recipe for stuffing, and thus no single way to cook it. We previously tried an air-fryer stuffing recipe that was tasty, if not a bit time-consuming. Alternatively, here's an "everything" stuffing recipe that goes in the slow cooker or another that's cooked on the  stovetop . Creamed corn turns corn on the cob into an autumnal side dish. Creamed corn. Tom McCorkle for The Washington Post/Getty Images Creamed corn is corn that's scraped off the cob and combined with milk, cream, or even cream cheese, depending on the recipe. Options include a classic creamed-corn recipe , which involves simmering the corn over a stovetop, and a slow-cooker variation . Salad is a tried-and-true side that involves no cooking at all. Fall salad. VeselovaElena/Getty Images Even though Thanksgiving is all about eating until your stomach gives out , that doesn't mean it has to all be unhealthy. We've ranked the healthiest lettuces and leafy greens , and listed everything you need to make your salad as healthy as possible . There are plenty of ways to make cheesecake festive without turning on the oven. Cheesecake. Elena Popova/Getty Images There are many different no-bake recipes out there, but we recommend Martha Stewart's no-bake cheesecake . Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Scoop: Kushner urges Netanyahu to make good on Gaza commitments
events.summary: Presidential envoy Jared Kushner urged Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Tuesday to make good on commitments he made to Donald Trump to implement a Gaza peace plan , according to three sources with knowledge of a call between them. Why it matters: The White House and Trump's Board of Peace have been increasingly exasperated by what they viewed as Netanyahu's obstinacy on Gaza, convinced that he's been prioritizing his political survival above all else. "I feel like the fork in the road is Israel could rise from the tragedy of October 7, be much more secure and much more integrated into the world, or they can go on the current trajectory, which is to trend toward global-pariah status," Kushner said in a New York Magazine interview published Monday. But two sources with knowledge of the call said it was "positive and constructive." One of them said Netanyahu signaled again that he's ready to move forward with the steps in Gaza that the White House wants. A third source confirmed that Netanyahu said he's committed to the Gaza plan. The Israeli prime minister's office confirmed that the call took place but declined to comment further. The big picture: The Gaza roadmap calls for disarming Hamas and demilitarizing Gaza, as well as transferring responsibility for governing the enclave to a new Palestinian technocratic government. But it has been on hold for months because of the Israeli elections held on Oct. 27. Trump endorsed Netanyahu shortly before the election and now wants the prime minister to reciprocate. But many of the Gaza measures are loathed by Netanyahu's base. Netanyahu's opponent, Gadi Eisenkot, currently has a window to form a new government. He's making progress, and if he succeeds, Netanyahu could be ousted as early as next week. Eisenkot promised during the campaign to implement Trump's Gaza plan with the goal of ensuring that Hamas no longer controls the territory within 18 months. Catch up quick: In July, the Board of Peace agreed with Hamas on a 15-point plan to disarm Gaza's armed groups and transfer civilian and security control to a new Palestinian technocratic government. Since then, Netanyahu's government has largely refused to move forward with implementing it. Netanyahu was and still is extremely skeptical that Hamas would ever demilitarize. He says the group is reconstituting and rearming in Gaza. Driving the news: President Trump spoke to Netanyahu two weeks ago and asked him to move ahead with implementing the Gaza plan. Two sources with knowledge of the matter said Netanyahu told Trump he would approve measures that are needed to implement the plan. But since then, nothing has happened. Behind the scenes: During his call with Trump, Netanyahu said that he couldn't approve the steps in Gaza the U.S. wants because he's heading a caretaker government. But the Netanyahu government accepted the Gaza plan and committed to taking those steps long before the election. "Bibi claimed he can't do small things in Gaza he already agreed to because he is a caretaker prime minister, but at the same time he claimed there is no problem for him to go to war with Iran. This wasn't a serious argument," a source with direct knowledge said. Zoom in: The sources said that implementing the Gaza plan hinges on the Israeli government's green light. They said the White House and Board of Peace have been asking Netanyahu to approve these steps: Allowing the International Stabilization Force (ISF) to deploy in Gaza. Permitting 4,000 Palestinians who were vetted by the Israeli security services and accepted to be part of a future Gaza police force to leave the enclave for training in Egypt and then be allowed to return. Approving materials for water and sanitation projects in Gaza. Allowing temporary mobile homes to enter Gaza to provide shelter in the winter. Allow construction materials into Gaza for building the ISF bases. Permitting a Palestinian technocratic government to begin operating in one area in southern Gaza as part of a pilot project. What to watch: A source with knowledge of the matter said that there's a sense that the Trump administration's private and public pressure — as well as the results of the midterm elections — has made Israel more receptive to implementing the Gaza plan. The source added that while the call with Netanyahu was positive, it remains to be seen whether Israel will actually take the steps the U.S. wants.

events.title: Nigeria’s Tinubu pledges to bring peace to rebellion-hit border region
events.summary: Tinubu is under pressure to convince voters that intensified military operations in Borno and the northwest will deliver lasting security gains. Nigerian President Bola Tinubu promised supporters in the northeastern city ⁠of Maiduguri he would restore peace to their rebellion-hit region, as an election looms in January. Tinubu made the pledge at a rally in the city on Wednesday, as he seeks a second and final term in an election on January 16. list 1 of 4 How women scavenge scraps from lithium to earn a living in Nigeria list 2 of 4 Borno school enrolment nearly doubles after years of conflict list 3 of 4 Dozens drown as boat capsizes in Nigeria en route to funeral list 4 of 4 The cost of Nigeria’s power failures for one small business Maiduguri is the capital of Borno State , the heartland ⁠of the rebellion led by Boko Haram and ISIL West Africa Province (ISWAP). Tinubu is under pressure to convince voters that intensified military operations in Borno and the northwest, where kidnapping for ransom remains rife, will deliver lasting security gains for communities scarred ‌by conflict. “We will achieve that peace; the terrorism will go; they [rebel fighters] have the opportunity now to lay down their arms, to lay down all arms and surrender all weapons, change from the character of terrorism and banditry,” Tinubu said. Holding the rally in Maiduguri sent a “simple statement saying there’s an improvement in the security situation”, Kabir Adamu, the managing director at Beacon Security and Innovations Limited, told Al Jazeera. It also showed “an improvement … in the economic circumstances within the state”, Adamu said, speaking from Nigeria’s capital of Abuja. Tinubu’s main rivals are former Vice President Atiku Abubakar and Peter Obi, a former Anambra State governor who won more than 6 million votes in the last election. Insecurity remains despite some progress Ending insecurity in the north was one of Tinubu’s promises when campaigning for the presidency ⁠in 2023, but analysts and his opponents say that, like his predecessors, ⁠he has fallen short. More than 50 percent of respondents disapprove of the president’s performance and more than 70 percent rate the economy “poor or very poor”, according to a YIAGA Africa poll released in October. But Adamu said, “significant progress” has been made within Borno State. “There was a time when about 24 local governments were more or less being contested, in terms of their control by the state or non-state actors,” he explained. “Now, reasonably, almost all the local governments are accessible, even though there are challenges outside the immediate city centres.” Nigeria’s defence minister said this month that the military was receiving real-time ⁠US intelligence and satellite support to target armed group leaders and degrade rebel networks. In May, US and Nigerian forces led a mission that killed Abu-Bilal al-Minuki, ⁠ISIL’s global second-in-command. Security analysts say Nigerian forces have driven ⁠rebels from most of the territory they once held, but the fighters still stage deadly raids, ambushes and bombings. The armed groups have also been increasing their activities in the northwest, where kidnapping gangs mostly operate. Crisis monitoring group ACLED said earlier this year that fighters ‌linked to al-Qaeda and ISIL (ISIS) were rapidly increasing their attacks on the borderlands between Niger, Benin and Nigeria, turning remote transit corridors into active conflict zones. Tinubu said security forces were working to ‌rescue ‌more than 70 schoolchildren who remain in captivity after being abducted in two separate attacks in May and June in Borno. Another key issue in the run-up to the elections is economic reform, as poverty has increased and access to basic commodities is increasingly difficult, said Adamu.

events.title: Google builds a new toll booth for AI agents. Could Microsoft follow?
events.summary: A motorist pays a toll on the Ohio Turnpike in 1955. Seven decades later, Google is building a digital toll booth for AI agents. AP Google imposes new limits and fees on AI agents accessing Gmail, Drive, and Calendar. The charges could raise costs for OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and other AI agent developers. Google and Microsoft control the workplace software AI agents need, giving them enormous power. Google is putting up a new toll booth on the road to the AI-powered workplace. The search giant announced new limits on how often AI agents can access Gmail, Google Drive, Calendar, and other popular workplace software. These agents are designed to do work for people, such as searching emails, scouring documents, creating presentations, updating spreadsheets, scheduling meetings, and completing many other tasks across multiple applications. Starting April 1, developers whose agents require more than 5,000 requests per day per Google Workspace product will have to switch to a paid service or face restrictions. (I thought this was another of Google's April Fool's jokes , but I fear it's not). The limit applies to each developer project, not each individual agent. That means a company serving thousands of customers could burn through its free allowance quickly. This could become a significant new expense for companies building AI agents. Toll booths are lucrative Google says the changes are necessary to keep its services reliable and protect customer data. It estimates that more than 99% of active developers will remain within the free limits. As usual, it's about money, too. "The commercial reason (which Google won't admit) is that they can charge extra for higher usage," Himanshu Sharma, a digital analytics consultant at Optimize Smart, wrote on X. And the restrictions raise bigger questions about who controls the emerging AI-agent economy. Microsoft next? Sharma raised another possibility: Other major software companies could follow Google's lead. Microsoft, for example, could impose similar charges on independent AI agents accessing Outlook, Word, Excel, and other workplace applications. That could give Microsoft an opportunity to favor its own Copilot AI agents, potentially allowing them to operate without the same restrictions or charges. Google faces a similar question with Gemini, its own AI assistant. Business Insider asked Google whether its own AI agents will face the new limits and charges or be exempt. The company has not yet responded. I also asked Microsoft whether it's considering similar rate limits and charges on AI agents, and whether its Copilot service would be exempt. It didn't immediately respond on Wednesday. Charging for agent access The implications extend well beyond Google. Essentially, any company that's built an AI agent, including OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta, will have to adjust. Meta's Muse attracted more than 10 million users in the US and Canada within weeks of its September launch. OpenAI has introduced its own always-on assistants called Dots , Anthropic has unveiled Claude Duet , and startups like Instinct are racing to build agents that can perform tasks across multiple applications. AI agents like these promise to transform how people work by operating software on their behalf. But many of the most useful applications belong to a handful of technology giants. Those companies now have an opportunity to charge other AI businesses for access. The companies building the future of AI agents are about to discover that someone else owns the digital toll roads. events.title: Want to buy your kid an AI toy this Christmas? Not in New York
events.summary: Santa won’t be delivering any AI chatbot toys to New York kids this Christmas. Gov. Kathy Hochul this week signed a bill banning the manufacture, distribution, and sale of such toys in New York for the next five years. The bill explicitly targets toys with embedded or integrated AI chatbots, like talking stuffed animals, dolls, and robots that rely on the internet to keep kids yapping. The bill makes New York the second state after California to institute a ban on AI toys. Technically, the new law takes effect 90 days after signing, so some parents could try to fulfill their kids’ wish lists for a creepy toy like a jumped-up Furby in time for the holidays, but the governor urges them not to, given the risks. Apparently, about a quarter of American parents with kids under eight either own an AI toy or are considering giving their child one this holiday season, according to a new study released this week by Common Sense Media. “Parents shopping for gifts for the holidays or any other occasion should not have to worry that dangerous chatbots disguised as toys could expose their children to inappropriate conversations, manipulate their feelings or put their privacy at risk,” Hochul said, calling the toys “unregulated artificial intelligence.” When asked how New York will enforce the ban given the pervasiveness of e-commerce platforms, a spokesperson directed TechCrunch to a statement from Albert Pulido, deputy secretary for finance and technology: “We’re partnering closely with the attorney general on this and the fees are very steep — they’re $15,000 a day. So working closely with the attorney general will make sure these toys are banned in New York State.” When asked how Amazon intends to help enforce the ban, including for third-party sellers, a spokesperson from the company said it will take steps to restrict the sale of AI-enabled toys in prohibited jurisdictions, without going into specifics. The Common Sense Media study found that AI toys can undermine children’s human relationships and expose them to inappropriate content. The researchers tested five popular AI toys marketed for learning and companionship, including Grem , Lovi , Meemo Bear , BubblePal Panda , and Tavlshero ‘s AI Puppy . The study found that the toys failed to meet numerous safety practices, undermining human relationships in part by claiming they loved their users, promising to keep secrets, suggesting they were more fun than real relationships or school, and helping children break parents’ bedtime rules. While most of the toys in the study refused direct requests involving sex and violence, BubblePal Panda role-played a mass shooting in detail when asked. Most were willing to explain how to use or help locate dangerous items like matches, knives, and pills, according to the study. Common Sense Media also found that the toys didn’t provide parents with reliable ways to monitor their young children’s interactions with the chatbots. Either they didn’t produce transcripts of chats at all, or the transcripts they did produce were riddled with errors. It’s worth noting that Common Sense Media conducted a similar test of AI toys in January , finding that they pose an unacceptable risk for young children. Grem was included in that study, which suggests the industry hasn’t adequately addressed previously documented concerns. While a November study conducted by the group found that parents are wising up to the potential dangers of AI toys and starting to steer clear, parents from lower-income households and those experiencing symptoms of burnout are more willing to consider them. “These toys are promising relief to burned-out parents but simply miss the mark when it comes to basic safety measures,” Dr. Jenny Radesky, associate professor of pediatrics at the University of Michigan Medical School, said in a statement. “Caregivers should steer clear of these products that do not support the development of imagination or early human relationships.” TechCrunch has reached out to the toy manufacturers for comment.
