events.title: 10-year Treasury yield slides despite sticky inflation data as investors buy bonds for protection
events.summary: U.S. Treasury yields fell on Wednesday, with investors fleeing to bonds for protection after October's personal consumption expenditures price index showed that inflation continued to accelerate. The 10-year Treasury note yield — the main benchmark for mortgages, auto loans and credit card debt — was more than 6 basis points lower at 4.836%. The yield on the 2-year Treasury note, which typically moves in line with short-term Federal Reserve interest rate decisions, was down more than 4 basis points at 4.623%. The longer-dated 30-year Treasury yield, which tends to track geopolitical events, was more than 5 basis points lower at 5.236%. One basis point equals 0.01%, or 1/100th of 1%, and yields and prices move inversely to one another. The personal consumption expenditures price index — the Federal Reserve's preferred gauge of underlying inflation — rose 3.8% year over year for October, in line with the Dow Jones consensus estimate. Separately, economic growth came in much stronger for the third quarter. Gross domestic product rose at a 4.3% annualized rate, according to a revised Commerce Department estimate. The data reinforced expectations for another Fed rate hike in December. "[I]t is more urgent than ever that Fed officials step up the pace of interest rate hikes to cool off economic demand," said Chris Rupkey, chief economist at FWDBONDS. "Rate hikes are coming. Lots of them. Bet on it. The economy and inflation are literally on fire." Wednesday's drop comes after yields steadied on Tuesday , with traders digesting softer demand for a 5-year Treasury auction. Trading is shortened this week due to the Thanksgiving holiday. Bond markets will be closed all day Thursday for Thanksgiving, and will close at 2 p.m. E.T. on Friday. — CNBC's Jeff Cox contributed reporting.

events.title: I went to Miss Universe for the first time and found a fandom that won't quit, no matter the number of scandals
events.summary: Contestants at the Miss Universe 2026 pageant in San Juan, Puerto Rico, on Tuesday. Jaydee Lee/Getty Images After covering pageants since 2019, I finally went to my first Miss Universe pageant. I wanted to see what the atmosphere would be like after last year's scandal-plagued pageant. The fans — who lined up every morning and night to see the pageant queens — are as loyal as ever. It was just after midnight when the pain of my 4.5-inch high heels had become too much to bear. I was standing alongside hundreds of fans who had lined up just to catch a glimpse of the 116 women competing for the title of Miss Universe 2026 . Two hours had passed without a beauty queen in sight. I stole a glance at the shoes of the pageant bloggers next to me. Flat, sensible, arch support — these were veterans. The Miss Universe pageant has been consumed with controversy over the last few years, but its fandom's fierce devotion was still on full display in San Juan, Puerto Rico, where the 75th annual competition took place this month. I spoke to dozens of people while attending the pageant's three main competitions and found that many were unfazed by its scandals. And after the new winner made history by becoming the first mother to take the crown , it seems the organization is hoping to move on as well. Here's what my very first Miss Universe pageant was like. My Miss Universe journey began at the organization's official museum. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider After dropping my bags off following a red-eye flight, I dragged myself to Plaza Las Américas to pick up my press pass and check out the official Miss Universe Experience Museum. The museum wasn't in the mall's directory, and there weren't any signs advertising it. The shopkeepers I asked for help had no idea what I was talking about! After nearly an hour of searching — did I mention this is the largest mall in the Caribbean? — I finally found the pop-up museum. Standing at the entrance was the dress Fátima Bosch wore when she won Miss Universe 2025 after a scandal-plagued competition that included a viral shouting match, multiple judges dropping out, and rigging allegations. I was almost surprised the museum would want to remind people of last year's pageant. But after a few days in Puerto Rico, it was clear that Miss Universe's biggest fans were happy to forget about it. Then it was time for the national costume competition, my first Miss Universe event. I was shocked to see so many empty seats. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider Of the four rounds of the Miss Universe competition, the national costume contest is always my favorite. Most of the contestants celebrate their countries with over-the-top ensembles that would fit right in at Carnival or a show in Las Vegas. It's pure camp. So I was really surprised that the Coliseo de Puerto Rico felt so empty. Most of the middle section of the stadium — which can fit up to 18,500 people total — was vacant, as were the nosebleeds. But the official stage was really impressive. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider This year's Miss Universe stage was designed as a large "X" framed by shimmering steps. Purple, blue, and gold lights flickered as a projection of the pageant's logo slowly twirled in the middle. It was showtime. The announcers fully committed to the tradition of creating a little rhyme for each costume as the contestants walked across the stage. They seemed to get more unhinged as the show went on. "Doesn't get much hotter than the mother of water!" "You will get your wish if you love fish!" "Life sure is great when you look like a gate!" The unsung hero of the night was the man standing behind the judges, cueing the woman. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider This man must have logged 10,000 steps as he ran back and forth on the platform, dramatically waving his hands to direct the contestants. His big white gloves and frantic hand movements reminded me of Mickey Mouse in "Fantasia." The contestants managed to navigate their dramatic backpieces and feather headdresses without a single collision, although Miss Turks and Caicos lost one of her lobster antennae. A stagehand quickly jumped up and grabbed it before the next contestant walked by. After the national costume contest, I headed to the official pageant hotel. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider Watching the Miss Universe contestants' arrivals and departures at their hotel has become a tradition of the competition, and hundreds turned out for them every night at the San Juan Marriott Resort & Stellaris Casino. Security at the hotel was strict — everyone who entered needed to get a new wristband every morning and night. If the lobby was at capacity and you weren't a guest, you had to wait and watch outside, even if you were a family member. The pageant bloggers knew the drill and were always the first people there, setting up shop behind the barricade with their ring lights and selfie sticks. The first ones to arrive and the last to leave, these pageant superfans were working on almost the exact same schedule as the contestants. Many of them were livestreaming the entire time. I peeked at one man's camera and saw that 2,000 people were tuning in. "I'm barely eating, I'm barely sleeping, but I know it's worth it," one blogger said. He planned to get to the hotel at 6:45 a.m. the next day in case the women left early. After about an hour, the contestants began to arrive. Some contestants hammed it up for the camera as the bloggers begged them to twirl, others walked by with a quick wave. None of the women were allowed to stop and say hi to their family or give interviews. A security guard stopped Miss Cabo Verde from giving her man a kiss, while Miss Ukraine's family climbed on chairs to wave their flags and catch a glimpse. I returned to the hotel the next morning, where I had a chance to chat with some of the contestants' family members. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider I've now covered five different pageants. Speaking to the contestants' relatives is always my favorite part of the gig. You only get to see the women onstage for a few minutes. When you talk to their family members, you learn the whole story behind them. Clarine and Morena Gomberts and Shanoulle Biker are the aunts and godmother of Miss Curaçao Bianty Rojer-Gomperts. They told me how Rojer-Gomperts had put her career on hold to become the sole caregiver for her mother, who is now bedridden with severe Alzheimer's. One aunt had traveled 21 hours across three flights to see her compete. "It's very emotional," they told me. "She did it all for her mother." Many family members were being introduced to the culture of pageantry for the first time. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider "This world is really crazy, I had no idea," Miss Ireland's sister told me. "It's so intense how many fans come here. Even yesterday, we couldn't get in. We had to wait outside." There were also pageant veterans waiting to see the contestant

EDA is an umbrella term for software, hardware, and services essential to the planning, design, and production of modern chips. Today, Cadence Design Systems, Synopsys, and Siemens dominate the industry, but US export controls have restricted Huawei and other blacklisted Chinese businesses' access to their tools. The US blacklisted Huawei back in 2019 over concerns the telecommunications equipment giant could be forced to inject backdoors into its gear. Unable to access top EDA tools, Huawei’s chip division, HiSilicon, was forced to develop its own with the help of Phlexing Technology. This week, Phlexing chairman Qing He detailed the company’s efforts to bring new EDA tools to support Huawei’s so-called Tau Scaling Law design philosophy. “Tau EDA is the domestic EDA tool chain for Tau chips. It comes from a long, close partnership with Huawei,” he said. We discussed the tech earlier this year, but in a nutshell, it involves using advanced packaging, specifically 3D hybrid bonding, to achieve higher transistor density for a given area. The TSMC of China, Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corporation (SMIC), is still years behind Taiwan, South Korea, and the US on process technology. It currently has the ability to mass-produce chips on the equivalent of a 7 nm process. For comparison, TSMC began producing 5 nm-class products in 2020 and commenced mass production of 2 nm-class chips in late 2025. So, Huawei aims to use 3D packaging to close the gap, but for this to happen, it first needs tools capable of designing such chips, and that’s just what Phlexing claims to have done with its GloryBolt and GloryEX platforms. “Traditional EDA has long handled only single processes. Tau EDA needs to integrate and decompose multiple processes,” He said. “Coupling multi-scale, multi-structure, and multi-physics issues called for new analysis tools.” This, He says, culminated in the co-development of a process design kit (PDK) with Huawei beginning in 2024. These technologies have now gone live. The development comes as Huawei looks to bring larger, more capable processors to market. We previously discussed the company’s latest developments around AI accelerators, near packaged optics, networking, and rack systems. events.title: Kmart sued over 'dupes' three times in 18 months
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Kmart has been sued three times in the past 18 months for alleged IP infringements. ( ABC News ) Kmart has been sued three times in the past 18 months over dupe products companies say infringe their intellectual property (IP). Luxury jewellery brand Richemont and hair care company Amika are among the complainants. Two open cases return to court in December. One of Australia's biggest retailers has been sued three times over its "dupe" products in the past two years. The Wesfarmers-owned Kmart and connected chain Target have been taken to court by aggrieved Australian and global companies with claims they ripped off jewellery designs of a luxury brand and accusations it and other retailers copied the designs of a Queensland fashion label. The cases highlight how endemic duping has become in retail culture, and highlight the legal tightrope that discount chains like Kmart are walking to get customers buying their version of well-known products. "Dupes" is short for duplicate, and the goods, sometimes known as super-fakes, are products made to look and feel like another company's original product without the same trademarks or logos. They differ from counterfeits, which are deceptive imitations of authentic products. Where counterfeits are clearly illegal, dupes push the boundaries. Hair care brand Amika accused Kmart of copying its designs. ( Supplied ) US Hair care brand Amika sued Kmart and Target in May this year, describing the alleged conduct as "flagrant". In Federal Court documents, it accused the retail giants of infringing on its intellectual property (IP) over a range of hair care products being sold under Kmart's OXX brand. It featured "plain black sans serif text over a coloured background featuring a bright, multi-coloured artwork" on "distinctive bottle and container shapes" with matching bright colours, which Amika says are the same as or very similar to its own products. In its defence, Kmart claimed the design features in question were common features of hair care packaging and by selling its products under its OXX branding, it did not require permission from Amika to use them. Both parties agreed to dismiss the case and the products in question are no longer being sold. Richemont noted in its statement of claim that the likes of Queen Camilla were known to wear Van Cleef jewellery. ( Getty: Mark Cuthbert ) Richemont International, the owners of popular jewellery brand Van Cleef & Arpels, has sued Kmart and Target Australia for allegedly infringing on its trademark clover design. It claims Target and Kmart had sold numerous pieces of jewellery that were "deceptively similar" to its designs. In court documents, the Swiss company said it had suffered substantial loss and damage by means of "misappropriation of goodwill of Van Cleef & Aprels", damage to reputation and loss of sales. Four trademarks registered by Richemont. ( Supplied ) Target has defended the claim, arguing that consumers would know the items with the clover design were not from Van Cleef if they did not include a device mark, a certificate of authenticity and were not sold at similar prices to Van Cleef jewellery. It further argues there are key differences in its designs to Van Cleef's. Target has also launched a counterclaim, arguing the clover was not distinctive and cannot be trademarked, which Richemont is defending. The case has been ongoing since September 2025. Items sold by Kmart that Richemont says infringe on its trademark. ( Supplied ) Intellectual Property lawyer Georgina O'Farrell said Richemont had likely sued Kmart and Target to send a message to other retailers. Earlier this year Kmart was one of 16 businesses Queensland clothing company Sabo Skirt had sued for IP infringement. Australian company Sabo Skirt alleged Kmart had copied a print featuring aquatic items, including lobsters, shells, and leaves, portrayed in different orientations scattered across a white background. A registered print by Sabo Skirt which it alleges Kmart copied. ( Supplied ) Kmart filed a counterclaim earlier this year, alleging Sabo Skirts designs were not distinct, but has since withdrawn that suit. A Kmart spokesperson said it offered a wide range of products while "operating with due regard to legal and compliance requirements". "Our customers love our great products at affordable prices," the spokesperson said. "Our design teams create curated ranges that align back to global trends." Ms O'Farrell said dupes had become more accepted in the mainstream.

events.title: In country Victoria, a divided electorate sums up the mood of a nation
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Exhaustion breaks in country Victoria as divided electorate sums up mood of a nation Topic: State and Territory Elections The seat of Ripon has become a microcosm of Australian political disaffection. ( ABC News: Jeremy Story Carter ) On the eve of a transformative state election, the vast regional seat of Ripon has become a microcosm of Australian disaffection. Midway through a recent candidates debate in a country shed, a rooster named Luke let out a panicked squawk and tried to break free. The man holding Luke as a feathered political mascot was one of 12 candidates vying for the ultra-marginal seat of Ripon. "Luke and I both believe in free speech, as he just demonstrated," said Bernard Quince, an independent who advocates the self-sufficiency benefits of owning a few chooks and a fruit tree. For voters in this weekend's Victorian election, and perhaps all Australians, it was an unneeded reminder of how deeply unserious politics can appear, even in the face of its deeply serious consequences. As Australians become "more pessimistic" and "more divided," trust in politicians has sagged to new lows , according to the Scanlon Foundation's social cohesion survey. Candidates in the 14,444-square-kilometre electorate have been earnestly selling the idea they can be the change the public craves. "I don't think we can assume that our politicians have our best interests at heart," said Samantha Rickinson, a caravan park owner in Ararat, 200km out of Melbourne on the seat's western border. Like so many segments of the country, exhaustion, distrust and outright anger are easily found. Motorists have become adept at dodging potholes; ratepayers are locked in years-long battles with council for basic improvements; households are squeezed by cost-of-living pressures and infuriated by ballooning government debt. "You could pick this electorate [of Ripon] up and plonk it into regional New South Wales or Queensland and get very similar responses from punters," said Kos Samaras from political polling firm Redbridge Group. In the picturesque town of Beaufort, local mechanic Chris Johnstone is a staunch advocate for his community, but he can gesture around at any number of issues that rile him up. Trucks rumbling through the otherwise quiet main street are a reminder of an unbuilt and as-yet unfunded bypass. A solar-powered bin a few metres away had, to his bewilderment, been installed in near-permanent shade. For the president of the local business group, it amounts to a general sense that things are not working as they should, even if he's not sure what the answer is. "It'll take a lot longer to bring it back under control." No political ad or AI social media video will override the potholes on a voter's street. Damaged and dangerous roads have long plagued regional communities , but durable solutions from politicians are harder to find. "A politician likes to cut a ribbon on a new road, but you can't cut a ribbon on a repaired pothole," said Rob Pelletier, a horticulturist on the outskirts of Beaufort. "It's now caught up with them after so many years of neglect." In September, a motorcyclist died after reportedly hitting a pothole on a stretch of the much-maligned Western Highway, not far from Mr Pelletier's home. The tragedy occurred in a state where roads are crumbling faster than the government can repair them . Experts have bemoaned the "old techniques" used for maintenance . Former VicRoads staff have blamed privatisation . Even those paid to fix them say the current system is failing local communities. "I drive on these roads every day. I'm so pissed off about it too," said Greg*, a contractor in the area who didn't want to risk losing work by using his name. Greg sees angry Facebook comments from his community, and understands why people are lashing out at politicians, or even contractors like him. The pothole problem has loomed especially large over the election, with costly promises for change coming from all directions . Greg is unconvinced any of the parties have a meaningful answer. "The biggest cost of it is bureaucracy," he said. "We'll spend an excessive amount of money fixing a small patch because they can't make their mind up about where the budget's going to go." The town of Maryborough is nestled in the north-east of Ripon, where temperatures can reach 45 degrees Celsius. Locals like Rowena Butler are staring down a fifth summer without a public pool. The heritage-listed complex was closed in 2022 after an independent assessment found cracking and leaking in the 50-metre outdoor pool spelled its "end of life".

events.title: Ecuador and US review joint military operations, official says
events.summary: Joint military efforts have been paused as the US investigates a lethal operation carried out by Ecuador. The United States and Ecuador have held talks on reviewing operations in the South American country, which the US paused pending an investigation into one carried out by Ecuadoran forces. That operation is believed to have been linked to a campaign against drug trafficking and illegal mining and has raised questions over whether the Ecuadoran military committed human rights abuses. list 1 of 4 ‘On the same page’: Hegseth hails US ties with Colombia’s de la Espriella list 2 of 4 Secret votes and vetoes: How will the next UN chief be picked? list 3 of 4 Ecuador’s president denies existence of US military base list 4 of 4 Ecuadorian fishermen sue Trump administration over drone strike Ecuador’s interior minister, John Reimberg, said on Wednesday that last week’s talks between US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Ecuadoran President Daniel Noboa in Quito, Ecuador, were ‌‌productive and resulted in Ecuador having an “established action plan” with the US. “Some would like to see these relationships, which have yielded so many positive results, damaged,” Reimberg said in a radio interview. The pause in joint operations was prompted by concerns over possible crimes ‌or human-rights violations committed by Ecuadoran forces during an operation on September 23 that killed Carlos German Munoz Jara, who officials say was a high-ranking gang member, The New York Times reported. In March, Noboa announced joint operations with the US and other allies, describing the effort as “a new phase” in the ‌fight against ‌drug trafficking and illegal mining. Later, the Taura Air Base in Ecuador reportedly witnessed an unusual deployment of US soldiers and aircraft. Noboa said US personnel were at the airbase solely for “temporary activities” as part of cooperation between the two countries . He denied the US has a military base in his country. “We work together. It’s not an American base,” he said. Noboa has adopted hardline anti-gang policies. Under his administration, Ecuador has been constructing mega-prisons as it attempts to deal with a wave of drug violence. The first facility, which opened in November 2025, was modelled on El Salvador’s Terrorism Confinement Center (CECOT) and has the capacity for 800 prisoners.

events.title: Peter Thiel bought a historic Bel Air mansion at auction for nearly $100 million less than its original asking price. See inside.
events.summary: The mansion, nicknamed Casa Encantada, has 60 rooms over 40,000 square feet and overlooks the golf course at the Bel-Air Country Club. Nils Timm Peter Thiel bought the historic Bel Air mansion Casa Encantada at auction for a steep discount. Casa Encantada traded for record-breaking numbers multiple times to magnates like Conrad Hilton. The 40,000-square-foot home is now a part of Peter Thiel's intercontinental real estate portfolio. Billionaire Peter Thiel snapped up a 40,000-square-foot mansion in Bel Air for a steep discount at an auction, but he still paid nine figures for it. Casa Encantada, a mansion once owned by Hilton Hotels magnate Conrad Hilton, has been on the market since 2019; it first debuted with a hefty asking price of $225 million. At that price, it would have been one of the most expensive properties sold in the US — a record currently held by Ken Griffin . The home had suitors like Jeff Bezos , who ultimately bought a place elsewhere . The home's asking price has fluctuated over the years, reaching as high as $250 million in 2023, but the final ask was $170 million in April, according to the property's listing history. The former owner of the home was Karen Winnick, the widow of Gary Winnick, a financier who founded the telecommunications company Global Crossing and died in 2023. Gary used the Bel Air home, as well as a different home in Malibu, as collateral for loans he took out starting in 2020, according to The Wall Street Journal, which also first identified Thiel as the buyer. After the Winnicks defaulted on payments, the home eventually went to auction, where Thiel outbid others and purchased it for $130 million. Casa Encantada is one of many properties in Thiel's US real estate portfolio, which includes a compound in Miami , a mansion in Washington, DC , and a property in Maui. But Casa Encantada might be the most historic. See inside Thiel's latest purchase. Casa Encantada was built in 1938, according to Los Angeles County property records. Nils Timm Hilda Boldt Weber, the widow of a glass manufacturer, commissioned architect James E. Dolena to build the estate. Weber was a nurse who married a Midwestern glass bottle manufacturer after nursing him back to health. The death of her husband left her very wealthy, and she spared no expense in building this massive estate. Hotelier Conrad Hilton purchased the home from Weber for $225,000 in 1950. The Huntington Library Hilton lived in Casa Encantada until he died in 1979. The Hilton family then sold the property to Dole Foods CEO and Chairman, billionaire David Murdock, for $12.4 million. The Huntington Library At the time, the deal was a record for the US market. Murdock then sold the home to financier Gary Winnick for $94 million. picture of the home from 1939 The Huntington Library The $94 million price in 2000 was another record. Winnick commissioned architect Peter Marino to help restore the property. The Huntington Library The project took nearly two years and millions of dollars to complete. Today, the mansion spans 40,000 square feet and has 60 rooms, including seven bedrooms and 20 bathrooms. Nils Timm While the Winnicks updated the home for modern living, they kept a classic feel. The main entrance greets guests with a spiral staircase and a grand entry hall with 14-foot ceilings. Nils Timm The basement was once used to house walk-in vaults for silver, fur, and wine. A third of the rooms were once used as dedicated servants' quarters, according to an old listing. Nils Timm Also included in the 60 rooms are multiple living, sitting, and dining rooms. Some are meant for entertaining, but there's also a junior dining room for dinners with fewer guests. Almost every room has a view of the Pacific Ocean and nearby mountains. Nils Timm The property also overlooks the golf course at the Bel-Air Country Club. Casa Encantada's exterior is just as elaborate as its interior. Nils Timm The grounds were designed by landscape architect Benjamin Purdy. The grounds feature formal rose gardens, a vegetable and herb garden, and a tropical botanical garden. Nils Timm There's also a tennis court with a viewing pavilion. The backyard has a tiled, 60-foot pool and views of Bel Air below. Nils Timm There is also an outdoor kitchen near the pool. Thiel bought the historic home at a reasonable price. Nils Timm The Journal reported that the auction started with bids at $125 million, increasing in $1 million increments before it was sold to Thiel for $130 million. Open-air auctions have previously resulted in anticlimactic outcomes; for example, in 2019, a lot in Beverly Hills once listed at $1 billion, sold for $100,000. Thiel is buying property in all corners of the world. Nils Timm In addition to his domestic purchases, Thiel recently bought property in Argentina and New Zealand . events.title: Former Tesla engineer says AI will create more 'fake jobs' — not mass unemployment
events.summary: Employees are worried that AI could replace their jobs. This startup founder thinks it'll create more pointless ones. Matthew Chattle/Future Publishing via Getty Images An AI founder and former Tesla engineer says AI is about to make our paperwork morass worse. Tejas Bhakta said a large part of the internet's jobs are a form of universal basic income. His take on AI's impact on jobs differs from the up-and-down warnings of other Silicon Valley execs. Worried that AI could replace your job ? Tejas Bhakta says he thinks the tech will do the opposite — and add to our pile of useless work. "Some people have this take that we're going to have mass unemployment as a result of this," he said during an interview with MTS Live. "I almost feel the opposite. Like, I think we're going to have more bullshit jobs. Just way more." Bhakta, a former Tesla machine-learning engineer, is now the founder of Morph, an AI-infrastructure startup that was in Y Combinator's Summer 2023 batch. "Basically most jobs are UBI right now." Morph founder @tejasybhakta argues that AI could create even more bullshit jobs rather than lead to mass unemployment: "Most people are in jobs that don't need to exist. These procurement officers that are putting out this paperwork that doesn't need to be done to sign this doc that no one cares about or will ever read. "Basically most jobs are UBI right now. That's sort of the hottest take in there." "Some people have this take that we're gonna have more mass unemployment as a result of this. I almost feel the opposite. I think we're gonna have more bullshit jobs, just way more." "Pre-AGI, 40% of jobs were just not really actually doing anything. In order for that organism to keep surviving, it needs these people to have UBI, otherwise the economy falls apart." "So we'll just have more jobs that are fake jobs while AGI does all the work." @morphllm — MTS (@MTSlive) November 24, 2026 Bhakta's take is different from the roller-coaster warnings coming from other Silicon Valley-based executives. In May 2025, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei cautioned that AI could wipe out 50% of all entry-level white-collar jobs. AI's top bosses have adjusted their tone in 2026, saying the technology could create a new hiring boom cycle. Bhakta is closer to that boom cycle camp — but with a less rosy tint. His view: Our current economy is filled with "jobs that don't need to exist," including procurement workers generating paperwork "that no one cares about or will ever read." "Basically most jobs are UBI right now," he said, referring to universal basic income. He estimated that 40% of internet jobs are "not actually doing anything." Bhakta predicted that AI will add to that paperwork morass — but those jobs will continue to serve as an unofficial safety net. "It's almost like the organism of the US, like, in order for that organism to keep surviving, it needs these people to have UBI," he said. "Otherwise, the economy falls apart. And so, we'll just have more jobs that are fake jobs while AGI does all of the work." He didn't immediately respond to a request for comment from Business Insider. events.title: ASML's CEO makes the case for selling chips to China
events.summary: Export controls on chips and other technology shouldn’t aim to cut China off completely — a strategy that will only backfire, warns Christophe Fouquet, CEO of ASML, the sole maker of the lithography machines needed to produce the world’s most advanced AI chips. “You need [export controls] to protect very advanced technology, but you also have to use export control in such a way that you don’t completely frustrate a country and invite that country to basically double down or triple down on development,” Fouquet said on Semafor’s Future Proof . The debate over Chinese access to Western technology has intensified in Washington after revelations of Jensen Huang’s affair with a suspected Chinese spy left lawmakers divided on how aggressively to tighten curbs. As a $520 billion de facto monopoly in chipmaking equipment, ASML sits at the center of that fight. Fouquet argued that continuing to sell China older equipment — ASML’s shipments there are more than a decade behind the cutting edge — maintains a strategic “generation gap” that keeps Beijing hooked on Western hardware rather than racing to build its own. “For almost 30 years, we have been able to keep an extremely high market share in China — very high means close to 100% — which means that they have accepted to rely on our technology with the idea that they had access to it,” Fouquet said. — Reed Albergotti

events.title: US stocks fall further as fears over AI intensify
events.summary: Published 25 November 2026, 15:05 GMT Big technology firms connected to AI continued to see share prices fall on Wednesday, with stock in Nvidia and Anthropic dropping sharply in early trading. The surge in Nvidia shares after boss Jensen Huang was reinstated was temporary, and the general stock sell-off continued, with all three main US stock market indices down. The tech-dominated Nasdaq has shed over 2%. The declines come amid concerns over the level and sustainability of AI investment which has rattled investors in recent weeks. Nvidia's share price was down 8% in early trading on Wednesday, extending Tuesday's slide as the boost from Huang's return eased. The resignation and subsequent reinstatement of Nvidia boss Jensen Huang after revelations of his extra marital affairs has seen the market value of the world's premier AI chipmaker fluctuate wildly. Given Nvidia's position as both supplier and financier of many other firms involved in the AI rollout, its rocky fortnight has had a wider impact. The US government also announced a raft of new tariffs on countries and trading partners on Wednesday as part of President Donald Trump's flagship trade policy. The value of big tech companies have sheltered the US economy from global economic shocks, including tariffs, but share prices in recent weeks have been volatile in response to the US midterm elections and other events in the AI industry. Faisal Islam: Fears over the AI boom haven't gone away Published 1 day ago Investors have taken fright at Democrat gains in the US midterm elections, with many having campaigned for tougher regulation of AI firms and even a moratorium on the development of new data centres. Questions also remain about whether the huge sums being invested in AI will eventually pay off. "It seems that these companies are trying to one-up each other on the amount of money that they're spending but you have to show that it's worth it, and that's where Wall Street is saying I don't know," said Todd Schoenberger, chief investment officer at CrossCheck Management. Despite concerns, investment in AI is expected to exceed $1 trillion in 2026, according to investment bank Goldman Sachs, which said the technology will remain the "dominant driver of business investment growth" next year. The declines come ahead of the US stock market closing for Thanksgiving on Thursday before opening for a shortened session on Friday. events.title: Average US 30-year mortgage rate eases to 7.21%, not far from 2026 high
events.summary: The average long-term U.S. mortgage rate eased this week, though it remains above 7% and near the 2026 high it reached last month The average long-term U.S. mortgage rate eased this week, though it remains above 7% and near the 2026 high it reached last month. The average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage in the U.S. fell to 7.21% from 7.28% last week, mortgage buyer Freddie Mac said Wednesday. One year ago, it was at 6.23%. The weekly average rate has been above 7% since late September. As recently as Oct. 15, it was at 7.4%, its highest level in nearly three years. Elevated mortgage rates can add hundreds of dollars a month in costs for borrowers, limiting homebuyers’ purchasing power at a time when affordability challenges continue to sideline many aspiring homeowners. Borrowing costs on 15-year fixed-rate mortgages, often sought by borrowers refinancing a home loan, also eased this week. That average rate fell to 6.54% from 6.66% last week. A year ago, it was at 5.51%. Rates on home loans are influenced by inflation, Federal Reserve policy and bond-market investors’ expectations for the economy, among other factors. They generally follow the trajectory of the 10-year Treasury yield, which lenders use as a guide to pricing home loans. That yield was at 4.81% at midday on the bond market Wednesday. 'The threat is finally real': Judge rips White House 'weaponization' Teen fatally struck by gunfire while camping near Florida river: Authorities Pennsylvania teen who died in 2020 could become first Gen Z saint Mortgage rates have been marching higher overall since late February, when the U.S. war with Iran began , pushing up the price of oil and driving inflation higher . The upward march in mortgage rates this year has weighed on home sales, deepening a national housing slump that dates back to 2022, when mortgage rates began to climb from pandemic-era lows. Sales of previously occupied U.S. homes were essentially flat last year, stuck at a 30-year low. They declined last month to their slowest annual pace in more than 16 years as mortgage rates surged. Data pointing to accelerating inflation have raised the odds that the Federal Reserve will hike its key interest rate at its next meeting in December. The central bank kept rates unchanged late last month , after raising them in September. While the Fed doesn’t set mortgage rates, its decisions to raise or lower its short-term rate are watched closely by bond investors and can ultimately influence rates on home loans. events.title: Student-loan borrowers are being notified they’re ineligible for their income-based payments
events.summary: New notices are going out to student-loan borrowers telling them they're ineligible for their income-based repayment plan. Robyn Beck / AFP via Getty Images The Education Department said it "discovered" some student-loan borrowers are ineligible for an income-based repayment plan. Borrowers received a notice giving them 90 days to transition to a new plan or be placed in a standard plan. Some borrowers said they're concerned the switch could jeopardize their loan forgiveness progress. Some student-loan borrowers got a surprise notice days before Thanksgiving: they may no longer pay off their balances under a more generous version of the income-based repayment plan. An Education Department spokesperson confirmed to Business Insider that a group of student-loan borrowers was enrolled in its newer income-based repayment plan when they were only eligible for an older version. Borrowers with loans disbursed before July 2014 qualify for plans paying 15% of their discretionary income, with loan forgiveness after 25 years. The department said an error led to fewer than 0.1% of borrowers being mistakenly enrolled in a newer, more generous IBR plan, which carries payments of 10% of their discretionary income and forgiveness after 20 years. Only borrowers with loan disbursements on or after July 1, 2014, are eligible for that plan. The department did not comment on the cause of the error and said that affected borrowers can apply for an eligible plan at studentaid.gov. The notice, viewed by Business Insider, said that the Education Department "has discovered that some borrowers were enrolled in the Income-Based Repayment (IBR) Plan for which they were not eligible." MOHELA, a student-loan servicer, said in the notice that the department directed it to remove all ineligible borrowers from the IBR plan. The notice gave borrowers 90 days to select a new plan. If they do not select a plan within that timeframe, MOHELA said it would place borrowers in the standard or tiered repayment plans, which typically give borrowers the most expensive monthly payments. Borrowers who received the notice said they hoped it was an error, given they had been making payments on the plan for months or years. One borrower said she has a few payments to go on the Public Service Loan Forgiveness program, which forgives student debt for government and nonprofit workers after 10 years. The payments she was making under IBR were affordable and allowed her to make progress on her PSLF timeline, and she's worried that switching off the plan would jeopardize that. The department spokesperson said that switching plans should not directly affect PSLF progress. These notices are similar to the ones borrowers enrolled in the Biden-era SAVE plan have received. The Trump administration eliminated SAVE, which allowed for cheaper payments and a shorter timeline to debt relief. Beginning in July, enrolled borrowers received notices with a 90-day timeframe to transition off SAVE or be placed in a standard plan. However, borrowers who reached their 90 days then received an additional 30-day "final notice" to switch plans, and those who have surpassed the extra month are still waiting to be switched. The department has not commented on its timeline for transferring borrowers to the standard plan, and it's unclear if borrowers who received the IBR notice will receive a similar extension. events.title: LA Lakers announce deal with Kalshi, signaling sports leagues’ growing embrace of prediction markets
events.summary: The Los Angeles Lakers have announced a tie-up with Kalshi, becoming the latest sports team to partner with a prediction market—and leaving little doubt about where the National Basketball Association has placed its chips in the ongoing debate about the role of the controversial wagering platforms in the world of pro sports. The team announced the news on Tuesday in a brief announcement that hailed the partnership, but offered few details on what it will entail.  “We’re excited… to explore innovative ways to engage fans and strengthen their connection to the game,” said Los Angeles Lakers President and Chief Business Officer Lon Rosen in a statement.  The announcement also solidified a broader alliance between the NBA and prediction markets. The league only officially embraced the platforms a month ago, when it named Kalshi and Polymarket its preferred exchanges. Kalshi has since moved quickly to turn that opening into team-level agreements, signing the Philadelphia 76ers in October before adding the Lakers this week.  The NBA’s overall positioning came as something of a surprise, given that it and the National Football League had largely held back while other major sports leagues signed agreements with prediction markets. Some of these platforms let users as young as 18 wager on event contracts, with sports making up the bulk of trading. Other major sports organizations have mostly taken a welcoming approach. The National Hockey League became the first major North American professional sports league to strike prediction market deals in October 2025, signing multiyear agreements with Kalshi and Polymarket that included rights to league data, branding and broadcast advertising. That push expanded to more teams last week, when seven NHL teams announced their own marketing deals with Novig . Others, including Major League Soccer, Major League Baseball, UFC and LIV Golf, have also struck deals with prediction markets. The NFL, meanwhile, has remained as the odd one out. In early October, the league filed a 24-page brief urging the Supreme Court to back state gambling regulators, who argue that sports prediction contracts should follow the same rules as traditional sports bets. At the heart of that dispute is whether the contracts are financial products governed by federal regulators or bets subject to state gambling laws.The league also raised concerns about cheating, insider trading , consumer protection, and risks to younger users. The legal fight also hangs over the Lakers’ new partnership. California allows tribal casinos and a state lottery, but it has kept traditional sports betting off the table, with a bookmaking ban dating back more than a century. The state kept that prohibition in place after the Supreme Court cleared the way for states to legalize sports betting in 2018, and voters rejected two legalization measures in 2022. If the Supreme Court takes up the case and sides with state regulators, Kalshi could face new limits on offering sports contracts in California—complicating its push to reach fans in the Lakers’ home market. events.title: DOJ accuses former cyber executive of defrauding ransomware victims by secretly paying hackers
events.summary: The U.S. Department of Justice has indicted a former executive of a ransomware recovery firm after he allegedly defrauded victims of cyberattacks by claiming the company could get their encrypted files back. According to federal prosecutors , Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar, 52, was the chief technology officer at RansomwareHelp, which purported to offer data recovery services to victims of ransomware. The company’s website, which currently reads as “under maintenance,” claimed it could decrypt hacked data by using its proprietary technology, according to an archived copy of the site from earlier this year. RansomwareHelp touted a success rate of “over 99%.” But the company allegedly had no technical ability to unscramble data and instead “negotiated with and paid a ransom to the ransomware actors to decrypt the victim data,” while charging the ransomware victim more and keeping the difference,” per the Justice Department’s statement. Palacio Escobar then allegedly used the funds to buy several properties in Florida. The DOJ said the FBI carried out an undercover operation in June, in part posing as a company that claimed it had been hit by ransomware. The company claimed to the undercover agents that it never negotiated with hackers or paid a ransom. But then Palacio Escobar paid the apparent hackers some $6,000 in cryptocurrency, without the knowledge that FBI agents were also posing as the ransomware hackers. 404 Media first reported the indictment last week against Palacio Escobar. He faces three charges of wire fraud, and could receive 20 years in prison on each count. Palacio Escobar is the latest, albeit rare, example of cybersecurity professionals going rogue. Earlier this year, two ransomware negotiators working for cybersecurity companies were jailed on hacking and extortion charges, after being caught moonlighting with the ransomware gangs that they were ostensibly investigating. A third ransomware negotiator was also convicted of helping hackers deploy ransomware against several companies. Last month, independent cybersecurity journalist Brian Krebs reported that FBI agents arrested a Canadian cybersecurity executive in Philadelphia on allegations that he was involved with the theft of FBI personnel records by the hacking and extortion gang ShinyHunters. The hacking group told TechCrunch that they took credit for the theft of FBI data in September, which they said they would not publicly release, a departure from its earlier extortion-based cyberattacks. The federal charges against the Canadian cybersecurity executive relate to conspiracy to commit extortion, though much of the court docket — and his alleged links to the hacking group — remains under seal. events.title: Character.AI’s plan to auction off users’ private chats challenged by state AGs
events.summary: What happens to your private conversations when an AI company goes bankrupt ? If it’s Character.ai, apparently, the plan is to auction them off to the highest bidder. Now, a coalition of 42 state attorneys general is intervening in Character.ai’s bankruptcy proceedings in an effort to stop the chatbot maker from selling off sensitive user data, which includes the private conversations of millions of users. The attorneys general involved in the matter have put out individual press releases , claiming that Character.ai’s dataset includes chat histories from more than 21 million U.S. accounts, more than 2.1 million of which belong to minors. In addition, the sale would involve other personal data, like IP addresses, the statements said. Character.ai, which filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in October, previously told consumers that their personal information would not be sold, the statements also noted. ( In a blog post , Character.ai assured its users that their information would still be protected under its privacy policy.) Only one anonymous bidder for the chat data has been disclosed so far: Smirks and Pangs Acquisition LLC (Smirks), which was set up as a Delaware company on November 13, 2026. The following day, Character.ai picked it as the base bid for the auction, scheduled for December 1, California Attorney General Rob Bonta noted . It is unclear what the buyer’s plans are for the chats. The AGs are opposing this sale on the grounds that there are no protections for users — whoever buys the data can do as they like, including reselling the data without disclosure, they said. Buyers also won’t have to honor Character.ai’s privacy policy. Plus, Character.ai hasn’t provided the court with as much information as the bidders have been given about any potential safety or legal issues following the sale, the AGs claim. In addition, some states, including California, Colorado, New York, and Connecticut, have enacted chatbot safety legislation that will go into effect on January 1, 2027, which could trigger further violations if the sale goes through. “Character.AI promised consumers that their data would not be sold. This kind of behavior is illegal under federal and California law and bankruptcy should not be used to sidestep these consumer protections,” Bonta said in a statement. Connecticut Attorney General William Tong also criticized Character.ai’s business model. “Their chatbots drove vulnerable youth down a rabbit hole of emotionally volatile and sexually inappropriate chats,” Tong said . “Their reckless misconduct and broken business model drove their company into the ground. Now they want to abuse the bankruptcy process to do exactly what they said they wouldn’t do — auction off those private chat records and personal details to a shady buyer.” Tong added: “We objected to the Disney sale, and we’re calling on the bankruptcy court to reject this sale too as yet another guise to eviscerate legal liability and consumer protection.” The opposition to the Disney sale was led by a similar but not identical coalition of state AGs. They fought against a proposed $20 million licensing deal that would give Disney access to Character.ai’s intellectual property, but not to users’ chats. The deal has not yet received final court approval. (Disney also agreed to hire most of Character.ai’s remaining staff .) Character.ai suffered after its co-founders, Noam Shazeer and Daniel De Freitas, returned to Google , when the tech giant signed a non-exclusive license to use the AI startup’s tech. The company also faced lawsuits related to child safety — one involved the suicide of a 14-year-old Florida boy whose mother claimed he had become obsessed with a chatbot on the platform. California AG Bonta is joined in the effort to oppose the sale of Character.ai user data by attorneys general from Alaska, Arkansas, Colorado, Connecticut, the District of Columbia, Delaware, Florida, Georgia, Hawaii, Idaho, Illinois, Indiana, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maine, Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, Mississippi, Missouri, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New York, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Utah, Virginia, Vermont, Washington, Wisconsin, and West Virginia. events.title: Powerful but unpredictable AI is a product no one will buy
events.summary: Reed’s view A new ripple of consternation recently made its way out of AI labs to Axios, which reported internal concern that models have become too unsafe to release publicly. But “safety” can mean different things in different contexts. What this concern really means is that AI labs are having trouble creating ever more capable models that they can both understand control. These models are not actually a threat — so long as nobody uses them to do any important work, or gives them access to important things. The industry has internalized this framework. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella treats AI as an “ insider risk. ” This is bad news for AI labs. They wanted to build AI models that were so good they could take over all knowledge work. At closed-door conferences in Silicon Valley, people talked about Anthropic being nationalized because it became the entire economy. But the failure to build anything remotely like that is good news for the rest of society. An AI model that is powerful but completely unpredictable is a very expensive and very useless tool. The company that builds such a thing would have no customers. Notable Anthropic’s share price has dropped below its $83 IPO price, as investors rethink the AI trade.

AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Next step is to move in for a closer look at the carnage The European Space Agency's Hera probe has revealed a stadium-sized crater on Dimorphos, the asteroid NASA struck with its DART spacecraft in 2022. The Double Asteroid Redirection Test was deliberately crashed into the asteroid on September 26, 2022. The original plan called for a European spacecraft – Asteroid Impact Mission (AIM) – to launch first and observe the before and after effects of DART. AIM was canceled, and the Hera mission launched in 2024. DART was a success. Scientists were able to determine that the impact had indeed changed the orbit of Dimorphos. The question was what else had happened to the asteroid. Scientists spotted ejecta and debris following the DART impact, but the close-up observations by Hera have revealed the full extent of the collision. Hera principal investigator Patrick Michel, Director of Research at CNRS / Observatoire de la Côte d'Azur, said: "Scientists debated whether Dimorphos had sustained an impact crater, changed its shape or stayed the same. "Much to our surprise the answer turns out to be all three at once! The face struck by DART has been flattened into an impact crater the size of a sports stadium, which extends across the asteroid's entire width." Scientists also noted that the asteroid is now tumbling in its orbit. Hera is surveying the 151-meter-wide Dimorphos and its larger companion, the 730-meter-wide Didymos, from about 25 to 30 km away. It moves around the pair at roughly 12 cm/s, using thruster firings to trace rectangular paths rather than conventional circular orbits. The plan is to approach closer, to about 13 km, to get higher-resolution snaps. A complicating factor is the discovery that hundreds of orbiting boulders surround the asteroids. Michael Kueppers, ESA's Hera mission scientist, said: "The team will have to take account of these objects in the coming weeks as the mission moves in closer." Hera will deploy two CubeSats, Juventas and Milani, in early 2027. The Italian-led Milani will study surface composition and surrounding dust, while the Luxembourg-led Juventas will use radar to probe Dimorphos's interior before attempting a landing. Scientists also want to measure Dimorphos's mass. Combined with the observed change in its orbit, that will help them assess how effectively DART transferred momentum to the asteroid and improve predictions for future deflection attempts. Hera mission manager Ian Carnelli said: "NASA's DART mission demonstrated that we can change an asteroid's orbit. Hera is now revealing what happened to the asteroid itself. events.title: Iraq’s top court rules government can take over Kurdish borders, oil fields
events.summary: The Kurdish region had denounced Baghdad’s ‘unconstitutional’ attempts to take over its borders and oil fields. Iraq’s top court has ruled that the federal government can deploy troops to the country’s international borders, including in the semi-autonomous Kurdish region. Wednesday’s ruling comes a day after Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi ordered federal forces to take over Kurdish-run border crossings and demanded authority over oil fields controlled by Kurdish security forces, in an effort to curb oil smuggling. list 1 of 4 Iraq reaches compromise with Kataib Hezbollah over armed group’s stronghold list 2 of 4 Iraq PM targets militia stronghold in bid to assert state control list 3 of 4 What next for Iraq’s push against militias following Jurf al-Sakhar deal? list 4 of 4 Iraq orders takeover of oilfields in areas under Kurdish control Kurdish authorities denounced the move, with the regional government calling it “an assault” on the region’s “constitutional rights”. The Federal ⁠⁠⁠⁠Supreme Court also ruled that federal authorities could oversee agencies operating at all border crossings, including those in northern Iraq’s Kurdish region, though they must coordinate with regional and provincial governments on customs administration, state television reported. The court said the federal oil ministry can also oversee and audit oil and gas fields, while Baghdad shares responsibility for managing the oil and gas they produce with regional governments and producing provinces, according to state TV. The Iraqi government did not specify how or when the takeover would be implemented. The move comes just a week after al-Zaidi also took on Kataib Hezbollah – a powerful Shia militia aligned with Iran – following oil smuggling allegations. He ordered troops to prepare to enter the city of Jurf al-Sakhar, a Kataib stronghold south of Baghdad. The group initially responded with defiance but allowed soldiers into the city, following a compromise brokered by Shia politicians. The court’s decision appears to be a victory for al-Zaidi, but analysts say it will be challenging to implement moves against the Kurds and the heavily armed Shia militias loyal to Iran. Renad Mansour, deputy director of the Middle East and ‌‌‌‌North Africa programme and director of the Iraq Initiative at Chatham House, said Iraq’s judiciary was “very much supportive” of the government’s campaign to establish a centralised political order. “The Iraqi government [is] trying to reclaim some sovereignty … because it’s such a fragmented state where there isn’t a centre,” he said. A senior Shia politician close to Zaidi told the Reuters news agency that the prime minister was trying to dismantle the model of a “state within a state”. He added that al-Zaidi was trying to restrain armed factions operating above state authority, as well as draw clearer limits on the semi-autonomous Kurdish region’s exercise of authority over strategic economic and security matters. The Kurdistan Regional Government on Wednesday rejected what it called “military ⁠⁠⁠⁠language and threats” in a statement from the Iraqi military announcing the new measures. It said ⁠⁠⁠⁠it was working with federal authorities to combat corruption and called for an end to oil smuggling across Iraq. Iraq’s state news agency, citing what it said was a federal government intelligence report, said oil belonging to the state-owned North Oil Company was being diverted and smuggled from Kirkuk, as well as from Sulaimaniyah inside Iraq’s Kurdish region, to Iran and onward to Afghanistan. Also on Wednesday, the Syrian and Iraqi defence ministers discussed “several issues of mutual interest” over the phone, according to Syria’s Ministry of Defence.

The tools are designed to help creators make professional-quality vertical videos, share original content more easily, and earn more. They also give creators more ways to record, edit, and publish content directly on the platform without relying on third-party apps. A key addition is an upgraded media editor that lets creators produce polished vertical videos without leaving X. Recording features include the ability to capture video in segments and use green-screen effects, the company said. The editor also offers a range of postproduction tools. Creators can convert horizontal videos to vertical format, automatically generate captions, trim footage, add text overlays, choose custom thumbnails, and adjust photos before publishing. Thanks to a recently announced update , users can now add up to 20 photos and videos to a single post, which audiences can swipe through horizontally. X says the feature is intended for sharing event recaps, behind-the-scenes moments, and product launches. Availability of the new features varies by region, X said. Earlier this month, the company introduced a clipping feature that lets users take snippets from longer videos, add their own commentary, and post the clips without leaving X. Clips credit and link to the original video, plus the person who creates a clip and the original poster can earn from its views. Another feature, “React with Video,” launched earlier this year . Similar to TikTok’s “stitch” feature, this lets creators respond to posts with video commentary while displaying the original post in the background. X has also introduced new earning opportunities and updates to its creator monetization programs in recent months. These include the “ Video Kickstart Bonus ,” an invitation-only pilot that rewards selected creators for publishing original vertical videos under three minutes long and without watermarks. The platform has also launched “ Subscriber-only Group Chats ,” which let creators host private, real-time conversations with paying subscribers. The feature is currently open to creators with 800 or fewer subscribers, and each group chat can accommodate up to 1,000 members. events.title: Energy price increase 'could put me in hospital'
events.summary: Kathleen Simms said she relies on food banks because her energy bills are so high Published 25 November 2026, 16:06 GMT A hike in energy costs in the new year has prompted concerns many families will see a hard winter. Energy bills are expected to increase by 26% from January after a surge in gas prices sparked by the Iran war, with the government saying it will pay millions of households £100 from 4 January to help cover winter costs on top of an existing VAT cut on electricity. However, residents in Stockton-on-Tees and Darlington said that was not enough to mitigate the rise of about £440 annually. Kathleen Simms, from Stockton, said: "If I can't have the heating on, I'm going to end up in hospital." Simms, who is in remission from cancer and has a lung condition, said: "It's hard to live now, if they put the bills any higher, we don't know what we can live on. "We rely on food banks and stuff which we don't really like doing, but if it comes to that crunch, we have to." Alice Smith Burns said energy price rises might be harder for young parents In Darlington town centre, Alice Smith Burns said she was fortunate she could "suck up" the extra charges as she lived with her parents, but knew that option was not available to everyone. "I have my daughter with me, and I'd rather she's not just sat there with blanket on her," Smith Burns said. "I'd rather she just had that heat source. "I think especially as a young parent, if there are other young parents out there, it might be harder for those kinds of people. "For low income households, it's a massive toll on everyone." Alexandra Blowers said solar panels had brought her electricity bills down Alexandra Blowers said she was fortunate to have solar panels on her home as they had brought her electricity bills down. However, she still predicts she will limit her heating use. "The gas price is obviously not the cheapest right now," she said. "We do tend to not put the heading on as much as we might like to, I layer up because I do tend to get quite cold." Tim Robinson is worried the increase in energy costs will affect vulnerable people Tim Robinson said he also felt fortunate as he would not be hit by the 26% rise immediately due to being on a fixed rate. However, he said he did not know how others would cope. "I think the vulnerable always have to be protected no matter what circumstance they're in, whether it's in relation to heating, energy or food," he said. "If you don't look after the vulnerable in society, then you're a very poor society." Staff at Stockton Citizens' Advice said they expected to see a wave of people already in debt accessing services in the coming months. "We know our clients are struggling enough as it is anyway," said CEO Sarah McPhie. "We know that in the Tees Valley, 70% of those children who are growing up in poverty are coming from a working household and unfortunately those working households are not going to see the increase in their wages compared to the increase in their energy prices." events.title: Prediction markets push OpenAI IPO expectations later into 2027
events.summary: Prediction market traders on Kalshi now think it's unlikely that OpenAI goes to the public markets by June 2027, after placing about 50-50 odds on the event earlier this month. This comes after chief rival Anthropic's debut last week has been met with a falling stock, amid a broader sell-off among names in the AI buildout. A perpetual futures contract on Hyperliquid tied to OpenAI has declined 30% since early October. Anthropic's shaky performance on the public markets since its debut last week and a continuing tech sell-off may be changing the outlook for when prediction markets think OpenAI will go public. Speculators on prediction market platform Kalshi think there's a roughly 28% chance the ChatGPT developer officially announces an IPO by June 2027. That figure was most recently above 50% earlier this month. Even by October 2027, odds are still only 50-50 that the private company — most recently conducting a funding round at a $1.25 trillion valuation — will make its move to the public markets. Kalshi defines officially announcing an IPO as either the Securities and Exchange Commission declaring an S-1 form as effective, the IPO being priced or an exchange has assigned a ticker to the company. Contracts are resolved using reports from media outlets. OpenAI confidentially filed for an IPO in June, but then in an interview with Fortune published in September CEO Sam Altman ruled out a 2026 public markets debut as questions over artificial intelligence safety grew. The company's chief rival, Anthropic, debuted on the public markets last week. However, the stock has declined nearly 30% from its peak during its first trading session, and on Tuesday it closed below its IPO price of $83 . Meanwhile, a perpetual futures contract for OpenAI on Hyperliquid has tumbled more than 30% since highs in early October. In late October, OpenAI pared back its goal for its recent funding round to $20 billion from $30 billion. events.title: How Gap is using AI agents to prevent costly website glitches during the holiday season
events.summary: When millions of shoppers scour the internet in the coming days for Black Friday and Cyber Monday deals, lurking just underneath the surface at retailers like Gap are artificial intelligence tools that help engineers troubleshoot e-commerce site issues to prevent lost sales.  For roughly half a year, the apparel retailer has relied on Devin, an AI software engineering agent developed by the AI lab Cognition, to hunt for online technical issues, identify the root causes of any issues, and develop tested code fixes that human engineers review, validate, and publish. Sven Gerjets, Gap’s chief technology officer, says that when a TikTok Shop landing page erroneously blocked users from the site, or when a similar technical failure that involved a PayPal site recently occurred, Devin has been able to accelerate the team’s ability to solve these issues that can add up to become “multi-million-dollar problems.” “Every e-commerce company is constantly focused on how you get the paper cuts out of your website so that everybody has a great experience,” says Gerjets, who joined the Fortune 500 company ( No. 293 ) in June 2024 to reunite with President and CEO Richard Dickson after the pair worked together at toy maker Mattel . “It’s just a lot of work on these large, complex sites, and having an agent that’s watching your site 24/7 and is able to do the coding work, so that when the engineer gets engaged, they’re just making sure the fix is valid.” Gerjets is heading into his third holiday season with Gap, which processes more than 1,500 orders every minute during peak demand spikes. Getting Devin up and running involved a proof of concept test with a small cohort of workers that later convinced skeptical colleagues that the tool’s autonomous features were actually helpful. Across Gap, Gerjets has prioritized giving employees broad access to AI tools, but has also invested in upskilling that’s more recently focused on agentic AI. Last year, Gap conducted a study with Microsoft that involved 400 employees split into two groups. One got only prompt training, while the other also received more mindset-focused training. The latter group was two times more likely to successfully adopt AI in their workflows and this finding has helped influence Gap’s upskilling approach. Workers across the company, including designers who tend to be especially protective of their creative process, are now leaning more on AI. “All of these places where we start getting that mindset shift to happen, adoption happens much more rapidly,” explains Gerjets. “But, we have to make sure the capabilities are good enough where people aren’t disillusioned by it and get an AI hangover.” Gerjets adds that Gap is now prioritizing more transformative changes to workflows with autonomous agentic AI, with a priority on three key parts of the business: marketing, technology, and the product-to-market life cycle, the latter involving Gap employees who identify a style trend and all the work that goes into getting those fashionable garments on the shelf. “We’re redefining what gets done by people and what gets done by agents and resetting what a role looks like and what a function looks like,” says Gerjets. “It’s heavy organizational change management and heavy process reengineering.” Eight years after a Black Friday crash, Lowe’s turns to “chaos testing” At Lowe’s, appliances, holiday decorations, and tools are all big sellers during the holiday season. But, the home-improvement retailer’s IT team had a particularly rough Black Friday in 2018, when the company’s e-commerce site crashed. Since then, Chief Information & AI Officer Seemantini Godbole says the retailer has “done tremendous work in terms of our technology stack and stability.” These efforts include a centralized human-run “command center” that monitors all of its online properties, including the retailer’s own desktop website, mobile app, and links that populate social channels including Instagram and TikTok. Lowe’s, which ranks 52nd on the Fortune 500, also conducts “chaos testing,” simulations in which the retailer purposely puts synthetic pressure on its ecosystem to ensure it can handle a spike in sales that mirrors Black Friday. Lowe’s will even take down a service—say, an inventory software system—to not only keep an eye on the redundancy layers it has invested in to pick up the slack, but also to observe how adeptly IT workers are able to bring the service back online. “We also try to figure out how long it took for the teams to detect that the service was down, and whether they are using AI tools, looking at it themselves, and how long did it take for them to bring the service back up,” says Godbole. The team then dedicates some time to discuss what went well and what processes could be improved upon. “There is a little bit of an introspection after the incident is over,” adds Godbole. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters It's not our fault if you've implemented it wrong Microsoft fixes Office dialog that had nothing to say and wouldn't go away 3 hours ago Microsoft 365 Backup stretches recovery window to ten years 5 hours ago Microsoft refreshes Copilot app search for users without an AI subscription 1 day ago Microsoft mega outage: Report reveals testing gaps and emails that never arrived 2 days ago Everything going down at once wasn't evidence of a conspiracy – but the truth may be scarier 2 days ago Microsoft's November security updates can break authentication in some third-party applications and devices following changes to NTLM message signing. Affected systems include authentication proxy servers, single sign-on (SSO) products, and application packaging tools, the company's support notice says. The failures stem from products that claim to supply required information during NTLM authentication but return incomplete or empty data, Microsoft said: "An affected device might set the NTLMSSP_NEGOTIATE_TARGET_INFO flag in its CHALLENGE_MESSAGE but provide an empty or incomplete TargetInfo field." Administrators can use the notice's network trace and event log examples to identify affected products. For confirmed cases, the temporary workaround is to set the ClientAllowUnsignedNtlm Registry value to 1 on affected clients. This stops the client offering signing, backing out the new default rather than fixing the incompatible product. The recommended long-term options are a vendor update or Kerberos authentication, where supported. The value sits under HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\MSV1_0 and defaults to 0, enabling clients to offer signing on non-anonymous connections. The NTLM changes arrived in the November 10 update as phase 1 in a 2-phase process. In phase 1, "Windows client devices begin offering NTLM signing on all connections by default. Servers accept both signed and unsigned clients. Auditing events identify clients not using signing." Phase 2, scheduled for May 2027, will make Windows servers require NTLM signing by default. "Clients that do not offer signing will be rejected by secure servers," Microsoft stated. Ominously, Microsoft warned that it "might remove the registry keys at a future date," so the company is not kidding about the temporary workaround thing. The additional protections were added to address CVE-2026-118737 , a vulnerability in which "improper verification of cryptographic signature in Windows Remote Procedure Call Runtime allows an unauthorized attacker to execute code over a network." NTLM is on Microsoft's hit list, having joined the Deprecated Features list in 2024. It dates back to the era of Windows NT, and Microsoft has made clear that it wants customers to move to Kerberos, which became the default in 2000. Even so, NTLM lingers on. Deprecation doesn't remove Microsoft's obligation to secure NTLM while it remains in supported Windows releases. events.title: What's gone wrong at Poundland?
events.summary: Watch: Why has Poundland collapsed into administration? The future of Poundland hangs in the balance after the discount retailer's collapse into administration. Its owner, US investment firm Gordon Brothers, put it up for sale in September, but then rejected offers to keep the business afloat. Poundland has a major presence on the High Street, with 600 stores in the UK and Ireland, where it trades under the Dealz brand. Its collapse puts the jobs of its 11,000 employees at risk, as well as potentially thousands of others at firms that supply the retailer. Have people stopped shopping at Poundland? People have not stopped shopping at Poundland - quite the opposite. Although the chain was struggling when it was sold by Pepco last year for £1, the business turned a corner over the year to September, going from a £68m loss to an £18.1m profit before interest, tax and certain accounting charges. Going into the vital Christmas period, first-quarter like-for-like sales were up 7% and operational profits of £1.9m were up £1.2m on last year. According to Julie Palmer, managing partner at insolvency specialist Begbies Traynor, "this isn't a story about shoppers abandoning Poundland". She told the BBC the tills were "busier than they were a year ago", adding that on the face of it a turnaround seemed "well under way". However, Gordon Brothers had been restricting Poundland's access to cash needed to restock stores and meet day-to-day expenses. So why is it now in administration? Poundland faced "a funding and ownership problem rather than a trading collapse", according to Palmer. However, while Poundland boss Barry Williams claimed the business was making a "strong recovery", Gordon Brothers painted a different picture, saying the chain remained "challenged and vulnerable to any potential downturn in future trading". It said it had provided significant funding to support the company's ability to trade since it acquired the business. Poundland collapses putting 11,000 jobs at risk Published 1 hour ago Poundland workers 'in limbo' over firm's future Published 1 day ago It has also made about £18m from a combination of debt interest payments and other fees and charges. As well as being Poundland's owner, it is one of its lenders, and is owed loans, including a £22.5m shareholder loan it inherited when it bought the business for £1. As the main creditor, Gordon Brothers would be first in line to get paid back if the business goes under - but its suppliers are not. "When the owner is also the main lender, its first priority is recovering [loans]," says Palmer. "Sometimes the route that best protects the lender is different from the one that saves the most jobs, and that tension is why this has become such a political story." Irish firm Martin Property Group, London-based holding company Xyra Group and German investment firm Zachert Private Equity are all also understood to have made offers for Poundland. Gordon Brothers had also been weighing options to break Poundland up. Its view was that ultimately breaking the retailer up would provide more security for employees in the long term, because any buyers of its store estate would also have to agree to keep the employees on. Insiders who are critical of how Gordon Brothers has handled the Poundland sale accuse it of driving the business into the ground to make money through the insolvency process. But the investment firm, which specialises in buying and restructuring distressed companies, has denied the claim. Now that the company has entered administration, consultants at Alix Partners have been appointed to pursue a sale of the business and its assets. There are various options on the table, which include securing a buyer for the business either in whole or piecemeal. The prime minister has said he wants "every effort made to secure a deal that protects jobs and keeps as many shops open as possible". In the immediate future, Poundland stores and distribution centres will continue operating as normal.
