events.title: How data centers are driving a US natural-gas boom
events.summary: In May 2025, my colleague David Rotman wrote a feature story describing how AI could keep us dependent on natural gas. Just 18 months later, I’ve lost count of how many times he’s already been proved right. Sure, it’s technically possible to meet the world’s rising electricity demand with other power sources, including renewables like wind and solar supported by batteries. But the reality in the US so far is that the data center boom is helping to fuel a massive natural-gas resurgence. Just one example: Plans for the Meta data center in Louisiana that David focused on in his story have expanded, and its power needs have too. The local utility went from three planned natural-gas plants to 10 . And as I wrote in a new story this week, data center developers are now looking beyond the grid and planning to build their own off-grid gas power plants . How did we get here? If you want to understand the future of the grid, one way to do it is by looking at interconnection queues—lists of power plants that have requested a connection to the system. In recent years these queues have been dominated by renewables like wind and solar power, which are generally the cheapest way to build new energy capacity today. But there’s been a shift in some places, particularly for PJM, the country’s largest power grid operator, which covers parts of 13 states in an area stretching from Illinois to Washington, DC. PJM has seen a major uptick in natural-gas proposals. In August, the operator announced that it had accepted proposals for 715 total projects with a capacity of over 200 gigawatts to join its queue. Nearly half that total capacity represented natural-gas plants. If all the projects in the queue were built, it would increase the fossil-fuel share on PJM’s grid from 61% to 67%, according to an analysis by Kevin Kircher , an energy modeler and assistant professor of mechanical engineering at Purdue. PJM’s queue is reflective of a bigger trend across the US. Natural gas is already the single biggest source of electricity in the country, and it has basically become the default to meet exploding power demand.  This AI-driven rush is already affecting greenhouse-gas emissions for tech companies. Meta’s emissions are up 45% over last year’s, according to the company’s recently released 2026 Sustainability Report . That’s even higher than the jumps from fellow hyperscalers Google ( 18% ), Amazon ( 16% ), and Microsoft ( 25% ). The company is also “reevaluating” its 2030 goal to reach net-zero emissions, according to the report, though there aren’t details about how or when it might reach a decision there. And there’s another tidbit in that Meta report worth noting: The company said that when the grid can’t deliver power “on the necessary timeline,” it will look to other methods, including building its own on-site power generation. This fits into a related and growing trend that I’ve been tracking recently: Data center developers are looking to bypass long wait times to hook up to the grid by building their own power plants instead. It’s not new for large industrial facilities to supply their own power. Chemical plants often have natural-gas infrastructure on-site to generate electricity and heat, for example (though they’re generally connected to the grid as well). Mining operations are often remote, requiring an off-grid power source. But the desire to come online quickly means there could be a massive boom in off-grid power plants for data centers. Over 100 such facilities have been proposed in the US, with a total capacity of 115 gigawatts (that’s more than double the entire peak power demand of California). The vast majority of these sites have been proposed since the beginning of 2025. There are alternative ways to help meet growing electricity demand: Wind and solar are inexpensive options, and pairing them with batteries could improve their reliability, for example. I’ve also written before about demand flexibility —efforts to limit power drawn from the grid when demand is high. Right now, though, the evidence continues to stack up that the AI boom in the US is basically synonymous with a natural-gas boom.  This article is from The Spark, MIT Technology Review ’s weekly climate newsletter. events.title: Djibouti: The Man Who Dared
events.summary: War hero turned nationalist, Mahmoud Harbi defied colonial rule to fight for independence in today’s Djibouti, until his death in a mysterious 1960 plane crash. World War Two hero, firebrand nationalist – and the man who dared to defy France in the Horn of Africa. Born in 1921, Mahmoud Harbi fought with the Free French Navy in the Second World War, winning the Croix de Guerre, before returning home to French Somaliland determined to end colonial rule. He founded the Democratic Union Party in 1947, giving voice to demands for independence and Pan-Somalism. By 1956, Harbi was vice president of the local Government Council – inside the system, but increasingly against it. He broke with France, backing full independence as Paris pushed a 1958 referendum that nationalists condemned as rigged and poisoned by ethnic division. Forced into exile, Harbi died in a mysterious 1960 plane crash off the Italian island of Elba, amid unproven rumours of sabotage. Djibouti would not gain independence until 1977. This film tells the story of the visionary who tried to get there first. Interim CEO Bruce Broussard said HP would do this "by capitalizing on the growing shift of AI workloads to the edge and leveraging our industry-leading portfolio designed to meet the needs of users with more demanding workloads." The pitch echoes the previous quarter's earnings call . "Our focus is on helping customers implement and manage AI across their environments. We believe that the future of AI is hybrid with workloads running both in the cloud and closer to where people work and data is created," he added. Broussard cited IDC estimates that half of enterprise AI inference workloads will run on endpoints or edge nodes by 2030, and claimed that with half a billion devices shipped, HP has "deep expertise in how devices perform, how they're secured and how they're managed at scale." HP fourth quarter revenue - for the three months ended October 31 - was $16 billion, up 9.3 percent year-on-year. Full-year fiscal 2026 revenue was up 9.5 percent to $60 billion. Personal Systems drove the growth, as its printer business slipped slightly. Personal Systems revenue grew 14 percent on commercial and advanced compute sales, and AI PCs represented nearly 60 percent of HP’s shipments in the quarter. "That said, higher component costs and challenging pricing environment, particularly in consumer, pressured profitability," said Broussard. Like its rivals, HP is leaning on higher-margin premium models and signing long-term deals with the memory chip makers to secure supplies. Nikkei Asia named HP among the firms buying a limited amount of memory from China’s ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT). Asked whether it planned to procure more Chinese chippery, HP’s CFO Karen Parkhill sidestepped the question: "We don't expect any material changes in our suppliers right now. We're confident in the suppliers that we have, and we are confident in the supply that we have what we need to fulfil the demand this year." She conceded that "We are using suppliers from all over the world." Parkhill said HP expects memory and storage costs to continue rising, but at a slower rate than during this last fiscal year. "We also expect CPU costs to increase, but not as much as what we've seen with memory and storage. And all of that is baked into our outlook." Broussard expects Q4 to prove the low point for Personal Systems margins, with improvement coming from further optimization of its product design and component configurations. In Ferbruary, HP said memory and storage costs had grown from 15 to 18 percent of the PC bill of materials at the start of the year to a figure closer to 40 percent. Parkhill declined to update the figure, saying the moderating cost curves and fast-changing production mix make the BOM percentage "less useful." HP’s newly hired CEO , former GSK boss Emma Walmsley, will start work at the company on January 4, leading it through what continues to be uncertain times for the PC industry.

events.title: Switzerland forced to close office in North Korea over sanctions feud
events.summary: The closure came after North Korea condemned Switzerland for adding a children’s camp to its sanctions list. The Swiss government has said it regretted North Korea’s decision to close Switzerland’s diplomatic office in Pyongyang in a spat over sanctions just weeks after Bern reopened its office in the North Korean capital. Switzerland’s Federal Department of Foreign Affairs said it was officially informed earlier on Wednesday of the North Korean authorities’ decision to close the Swiss diplomatic office. list 1 of 4 Russia and North Korea deepen relations with symbolic road bridge list 2 of 4 Zelenskyy says Ukraine sent two North Korean POWs to South Korea list 3 of 4 Trump calls Kim Jong Un a ‘friend’ and plays down N Korea’s nuclear arsenal list 4 of 4 North Koreans being recruited into forced labour in Russia, report says On Tuesday, North Korea condemned Switzerland for adding a children’s camp to its sanctions list over Western allegations that it was involved in transferring children from Russian-occupied areas of Ukraine and said it would consider shutting down the diplomatic office in Pyongyang. “The [foreign ministry] regrets this decision and is arranging for the Head of the Office to return to the Embassy of Switzerland in Beijing,” the Swiss ministry said in a statement. North Korea ordered the envoy to leave within 48 hours, its Foreign Ministry said. In a statement carried by the state-run Korean Central News Agency (KCNA), the ministry said the move was in response to Switzerland’s decision to impose sanctions on North Korea’s Songdowon International Children’s Camp, calling it an overtly hostile act. Pyongyang’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs summoned the head of the diplomatic office, Sylvain Astier, and handed him a memorandum urging him to close the office, KCNA said. “The Foreign Ministry of the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea [DPRK] declared the head of the Swiss Diplomatic Office in the DPRK persona non grata and urged him to leave the country within 48 hours,” KCNA said, using the country’s official name. “Any act of violating the sovereign rights of the DPRK and the interests of its citizens can never be welcomed by us,” it said. The expulsion comes less than a month after Swiss Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis formally reopened the diplomatic office in Pyongyang. The sanctions infringed on North Korea’s sovereignty by denying what was its obligation to provide children with opportunities for culture and recreation, North Korean leader Kim Jong Un’s influential sister, Kim Yo Jong, said. Switzerland’s Federal Department of Foreign Affairs defended its sanctions policy on Tuesday, saying it was independent of the reopening of the diplomatic office, which it said was carried out “in line with our universalist foreign policy”. “Its aim is to maintain channels of dialogue, including with states with which we have differences on certain issues,” it told the Reuters news agency. Over the weekend, Kim Jong Un personally received credentials from the new ambassadors of 10 countries, including Russia and Sweden, in a rare diplomatic ceremony in Pyongyang. Kim said North Korea sought to expand foreign relations with countries that respected its sovereignty, but would oppose attempts to restrict the independent rights and right to development of sovereign states. Switzerland established diplomatic relations with North Korea in 1974 and is one of the few Western countries to maintain dialogue with the country. Both Kim Jong Un and Kim Yo Jong reportedly attended school in Switzerland as teenagers in the 1990s. Meanwhile, North Korea has closely aligned with Russia over the war in Ukraine, sending thousands of troops and large shipments of weapons in recent years to support Russian President Vladimir Putin’s full-scale invasion, possibly in exchange for aid and military technology transfers.

events.title: WhatsApp now lets you schedule messages in group and individual chats
events.summary: WhatsApp on Wednesday started rolling out a much-sought-after feature: the ability to schedule messages in both individual and group chats. The feature is rolling out globally to all users across iOS and Android. Once it becomes available, you can type a message and long-press the send button to schedule it. You can choose to send a message anywhere between 10 minutes and 14 days later. Users will be able to see all their scheduled messages and delete them if needed. It’s not clear if there is a way to edit the schedule of a message. Notably, scheduled messages will be sent even if your phone is off or outside network coverage. You can schedule messages containing text, photos, and videos. The feature could prove useful for wishing someone a happy birthday on time or chatting with people across time zones. Businesses may also find it easier to schedule texts and updates to their customers, and people who use the app to coordinate work will likely find themselves using scheduled texts to update their teams. WhatsApp rivals like Telegram and Signal have had the ability to schedule messages for a while now, so the Meta-owned chat app is late in rolling it out. events.title: Terence Tao calls for a transition to ‘math 2.0’ in the wake of AI bombshells
events.summary: UCLA math professor Terence Tao says math needs to undergo a transition. Richard Hartog/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images Terence Tao is going scorched-earth as AI unsettles mathematics. The UCLA professor said incentive structures and academic journals need to change — and quickly. Tao laid out his vision before an Anthropic researcher solved math's most famous problem using AI. Terence Tao is calling for radical change. The UCLA math phenom, viewed by many as a thought leader in the field, recently said mathematicians are living in the past if they think they can maintain their old values and stay relevant in the age of AI . "Math 1.0 is going to have to transition into what I call math 2.0," Tao said at Harvard University last week. To start with, Tao said that solving problems should no longer be the lodestar of mathematical research . Now that AI can tackle dense conjectures more efficiently than humans can, dying on that hill would be foolish, he said. "Further blind optimization of problem-solving alone is now actively harmful to the long-term health of mathematics," his slideshow presentation read. Instead, Tao said mathematicians should focus on subjects that humans already excel at, like explaining what AI-generated solutions actually mean and extrapolating new problems from them. And getting work published in academic journals, once a prestigious accolade for mathematicians, is rapidly losing its value, he said. As submission inboxes become flooded with AI-generated research by less and less capable mathematicians, who in many cases don't even understand what they're submitting, Tao said journals need to rethink their values or lose their importance. "We can't go by just how many papers you have in the top journals anymore," he said, adding that mathematicians should earn clout only if they can explain their research before human inquisitors. Tao laid out his vision to a room full of Harvard mathematicians shortly before the math community was once again rocked by a bombshell AI solution — this time for the most famous open question in all of mathematics. On Friday, a mathematician employed by Anthropic said he cracked the Riemann Hypothesis using Claude. Mathematicians told Business Insider that the breakthrough is a huge deal. Steven Strogatz, a professor at Cornell, called the problem the "white whale" of the field. In an interview on the "Numberphile" podcast last month, Tao said humans working with AI models wouldn't "make progress" on the Riemann Hypothesis before 2050. Still, Tao didn't say that young mathematicians should drop out of their Ph.D. programs and join AI startups. He pointed to Caltech's mathathon , an event organized by students in which participants use AI to find new ways to solve old problems, as a possible way forward for the field. "Despite all the tumult that we have today, the future of math actually is quite bright," he said. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: The U.S. economy is ripping
events.summary: Wall Street has been reeling amid fears about the future of the AI boom. But in the here and now, the U.S. economy is experiencing an outright boom. The big picture: Growth was even stronger this summer than it appeared, and the robust expansion is continuing this fall, according to a range of data released Wednesday morning. That is pushing Americans' incomes up and the pace of layoffs down. The strong data helps explain why the Federal Reserve is prepared to raise interest rates two weeks from now even in the face of financial market turbulence. Driving the news: The U.S. economy grew at a 4.3% annual rate in the July-through-September quarter, according to the second revision to GDP data — well above the 3.4% originally reported. The strong results have continued into Q4. The Commerce Department separately said that personal income rose 0.7% in October, well ahead of analysts' expectations. Overall orders for durable goods came in below forecasts for October, but core capital goods orders — a forward-looking measure of investment spending — climbed 1.2%, also well ahead of projections. The Labor Department said that only 189,000 people filed new claims for jobless benefits last week, matching the lowest of 2026 and among the lowest readings on record (claims go back to 1967). Zoom out: The Q3 GDP reading was powered by business investment, especially for software, showing that the AI buildout remains a powerful driver of overall economic growth. It wasn't driven by volatile components of GDP like inventory and trade swings; real final sales to private domestic purchasers surged at a whopping 5.8% pace, and gross domestic income — conceptually similar to GDP — rose at a 4.4% rate. Translation: This isn't some fluky reading, but rather a sign of underlying robustness. Rapid growth looks set to continue in Q4; the Atlanta Fed's GDPNow tool estimates current-quarter growth at 2.9%. Zoom in: Nonresidential fixed investment — the GDP subcategory that covers capital spending — contributed 2.2 percentage points to overall growth in Q3. That was the highest since the bounce back following the 2020 pandemic. Excluding that episode, it was the highest since 2011. Yes, but: Personal consumption expenditures rose a moderate 0.3% in October, below analysts' forecasts (+0.4%) and September readings (+0.6%). That implies some softness in consumer spending, which, along with AI investment, has been powering the economy forward. The silver lining, however, is that strong income growth paired with modest consumption growth is good news for American household balance sheets: The personal savings rate rose to 4.1%, from 3.6% in September. Data: Bureau of Economic Analysis; Chart: Neil Irwin/Axios The strong growth readings affirm the Fed's all-but-certain plans to raise interest rates at a meeting concluding Dec. 9. Inflation data also released in the report shows why. By the numbers: The Personal Consumption Expenditures Price Index, which the Fed targets, was up 3.8% over the last 12 months, or 3.3% excluding volatile food and energy. In month-on-month terms, both total and core PCE inflation came in at 0.3% for October, implying no meaningful deceleration is underway. The core number annualizes to 3.5% inflation. State of play: While those readings were right in line with forecasts, they underscore that inflation remains far above the Fed's 2% target — as it has been for nearly six consecutive years. The combination of rapid growth and elevated inflation looks more like a classic overheating economy — one in which the central bank needs to tighten policy to bring inflation into line. Between the lines: The market turbulence of the last few weeks — the S&P 500 was down 2.8% as of 11:45am ET — points to risks that the AI investment boom may deflate in the quarters ahead. But the Fed is unlikely to react to what might happen when growth numbers are coming in so hot and it has been missing its inflation target for so long. What they're saying: "The economy isn't merely hanging in there," Jim Baird, chief investment officer at Plante Moran Financial Advisors, wrote in a note. "It continues to demonstrate considerable resilience, with consumers spending, businesses investing, and few signs that restrictive monetary policy is creating significant cracks in the broader expansion," he added. "Boil it all down, and [Wednesday's] report reinforces an increasingly familiar tension: the economy is performing quite well, but its resilience also gives the Fed an even stronger case for further rate hikes."

events.title: Democrats’ long 2016 primary is finally over — and Sanders won
events.summary: David’s view I don’t want to sound hasty, but Democrats’ 2016 presidential primary finally ended this week. Bernie Sanders won. The Democratic National Committee’s mandate that candidates reject super PACs or forfeit the 2028 debate stage surprised some likely candidates for the nomination. It didn’t surprise the Vermont independent senator, who had been asking as much for years from a party that he never joined. “I believe the Party should make a public statement about our values and simultaneously consider actions that punish candidates who refuse to adhere to this principle,” Sanders wrote in a letter to then-DNC Chair Jaime Harrison in 2022. Sanders did not have a close relationship with Harrison, who was picked to lead the party by Joe Biden. He has a friendly relationship with current DNC Chair Ken Martin — who, in a twist few Democrats might have called this summer , faces fewer post-midterm challenges for his job than Hakeem Jeffries or Chuck Schumer. Now Martin has signed off on an idea that many Democrats considered well-meaning but unenforceable. The party can’t prevent super PACs or “dark money” groups (not always the same thing) from spending on behalf of candidates. Its new Fair Campaign Practices Pledge asks candidates to tell the DNC if an outside group is spending in the primary and allows the DNC to punish those who don’t denounce that spending. This hasn’t been universally welcomed by Democrats, who would rather be talking about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang right now. But the story of Democratic politics since Sanders lost the 2016 primary to Hillary Clinton has been, eventually, the party giving Sanders what he wants. If Donald Trump led the most successful raid of a major party in modern history, Sanders is the unquestioned runner-up. He’s succeeded for two basic reasons. One: Everything he’s asked for is both populist and popular. Two: Democrats would rather keep Sanders inside the tent than risk him rallying anti-establishment voters from outside. He gets to put up stumbling blocks for the sort of party lifers, donors, and strategists who don’t want the left to win a Democratic nomination. They get party rules and priorities that prevent the left wing’s potential standard-bearer in 2028 (be it Ocasio-Cortez, Khanna, or another) from making sharp contrasts with a candidate more appealing to insiders. It wasn’t inevitable, but Democrats were definitely heading in this direction. The mollification of Sanders started right before the 2016 party convention, when he declined to release his delegates before they could influence the party platform. While Clinton’s allies had more seats on key committees, they agreed to create a Unity Reform Commission to change party rules after the election — which, at that point, they assumed Clinton would win. She didn’t, and the commission actually went to work, changing the primary process largely in line with what Sanders wanted. Had the change occurred in 2008, Clinton would have likely defeated Barack Obama; in 2016, Clinton would have padded her delegate count over Sanders. I don’t think that Sanders out-smarted himself, but the rules-making Democrats definitely saw a win-win in opening primaries to more “normie” voters. This week’s Fair Campaign Practices Pledge is more beneficial to the Sanders wing. It only commits candidates to shaming and shunning super PACs in the primaries; it’s understood that Democratic super PACs will wind up again for a 2028 general election. “It creates a free rider problem where socialists can decry mainstream Dems for outside spending but still get the benefit of it if they ever win,” said Democratic strategist Caitlin Legacki, who opposes the change, and worked for Rep. Haley Stevens in the party’s Michigan Senate primary. For the next year, a wet blanket will be thrown on Democrats who could get support from super PACs. If any governor wanted to follow Ron DeSantis, and divert his state election funds into a federal PAC — well, GOP commissioners on the FEC might let him, but the party wouldn’t. Some Democrats believe that the super PAC shaming policy will be toothless, but the Sanders wing clearly sees it as a win. “A lot of progress [is] being made on getting dark money out of the Democratic primaries,” said Sen. Jeff Merkley, D-Ore., the only senator who endorsed Sanders over Clinton in 2016, on a Monday call organized to support Sanders-endorsed Senate majority leader candidate Chris Van Hollen. “Thank you, everybody who’s working on that!” Sanders and his wing won this, again, without ever winning a presidential primary. The credit he’s gotten for changing the Democratic Party’s rhetoric and priorities this cycle has rankled some Democrats. But this is the best of all possible post-2016 worlds for them. Sanders rebuffed supporters who wanted him to lead a third party, which would have split the anti-Trump opposition. He demanded that the party neuter “superdelegates” and then super PACs, which most Democrats basically agreed were big perception problems for their party. Progressives are betting that these changes will help Democrats characterize Republicans as corrupt, at a moment when voters believe it. In 2016, Trump initially benefited from the fact that large GOP donors were horrified by him, and that he didn’t have a super PAC at all. Who was defined as the candidate of big money and closed-door fundraisers? When the 2016 primaries were over, clearly, Hillary Clinton was — even though Trump will leave office as the most successful super PAC fundraiser of all time. He’s piled up seven- and eight-figure donations, often from donors with business before his administration. Trump pulled Elon Musk into frontline politics, where the CEO became the biggest single super PAC donor in the country. Democrats picked this moment to heighten the contrasts, ostentatiously opposing super PACs, bidding for the roving anti-establishment vote that seems to like this sort of thing. The 2016 primary is over, and the 2028 primary can begin. Notable In The Washington Sun, Elena Schneider and Daniella Diaz heard from frustrated political staffers who think their candidates are going to be asked to abide by an enforceable rule. In The Washington Post, Dylan Wells talked to some of the social media creators and influencers who are now thinking about their role in the next Democratic debates — shaping the discourse in a way that used to be up to corporate media.

events.title: China Securities opens first overseas office in Dubai to boost Middle East ties
events.summary: China Securities, the investment bank controlled by Citic Group, has opened its first overseas office in Dubai as it seeks to play a larger role in relations between the Middle East and the world’s second-largest economy . The office of China Securities International at the Dubai International Financial Centre is intended to meet clients’ cross-border needs and grow its portfolio of nearly $75 billion in assets under management, the DIFC said in a statement on Wednesday. China Securities, which received a licence in September to set up its regional presence at the DIFC, served more than 17.1 million securities brokerage clients in the first half of 2026. China Securities International will provide cross-border investment banking services. It will support Chinese companies expanding into the Middle East and help the region’s investors to tap into China’s market, while continuing to contribute to the Belt and Road Initiative, the DIFC said. Liu Cheng, chairman of China Securities, said the Dubai office “marks a key milestone in the company’s international expansion and a practical response to the growing cross-border needs of its clients”. “The company will leverage Dubai’s institutional framework and strategic location as a new platform to strengthen two-way connectivity between the China and Middle East capital markets,” he added. China is the Emirates’ biggest trading partner, according to the UAE Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The two countries established a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership in 2018 , which provides a structured platform for co-operation in trade, investment, technology and energy. Earlier this year, they signed an agreement to boost investment and mobilise more capital between them, adding to a string of recent deals. China Securities is the latest to join a cluster of major Chinese financial institutions at the DIFC. They include Agricultural Bank of China, Bank of China, Bank of Communications, China Construction Bank, China International Capital Corporation, China Merchants Bank International and Industrial and Commercial Bank of China. China’s five largest banks together account for more than 30 per cent of total assets in the DIFC’s banking and capital markets sector, state news agency Wam previously reported. “China Securities’ presence adds further depth to the DIFC’s financial ecosystem and creates new opportunities to connect Chinese businesses and investors with regional and international capital markets,” said Arif Amiri, chief executive of the DIFC Authority.

events.title: Trump's accounts traded Nvidia shares 44 times this year, records show
events.summary: Donald Trump's investment portfolios have bought or sold shares in chipmaker Nvidia at least 44 times this year, a review of the US president's financial disclosures shows. Trump's most recent public declarations of his investment trading show that between January and September the portfolios purchased between $5.2m and $17m (£4m and £13m) in Nvidia stock - and sold between $4.4m and $12m. His portfolios held between $12.5m and $58m of Nvidia shares at the end of 2025. Financial disclosures to the Office of Government Ethics report a low and high range of transaction values, so a more precise analysis of how much Nvidia stock was traded is not possible. The period of recent turmoil at Nvidia and volatility in its share price is not covered by the disclosures. In the last two weeks, co-founder and chief executive Jensen Huang resigned and then Trump played a significant part in his reinstatement. The White House has said that Trump's stock and bond portfolio is independently managed by third parties and neither he nor his family "has any ability to direct, influence or provide input regarding how the portfolio is invested or when investments are bought or sold". Huang resigned on 12 November after reports of extramarital affairs, including with one woman who has alleged ties to Chinese intelligence. Nvidia's share price dived following news of his resignation. But on Monday Nvidia's board announced the 63-year-old was being reinstated as CEO. Trump told US media he had "made the deal" to "convince" the tech giant's board to bring Huang back. The board said it had "received input from senior levels of the United States government" that he posed "no national security risk". Nvidia's share price surged 31% on Monday following Huang's return. About $1tn (£763bn) was added to Nvidia's market value, but the company's shares are still trading below their value before reports of Huang's alleged affairs began to circulate. However, concerns remain among both Republican and Democratic politicians about Huang's actions and Nvidia's compliance with US controls over the export of advanced computer chips to China, as well as Trump's involvement in getting him reappointed as CEO. Nvidia's chip technology and investments have been critical to the growth of the artificial intelligence (AI) industry , leading to it becoming one of the world's most valuable companies. The firm now represents more than 6% of the S&P 500 share index, according to State Street financial services. This makes it the second most valuable company on the index after Apple, whose shares Trump's accounts also frequently trade. Nvidia also ranks highly in many global indices, meaning that investment accounts held around the world, including pensions, are likely to include its shares. Our analysis of Trump's Nvidia trades does not include other investment products held by him which may include its shares. Trump made at least $2.2bn (£1.7bn) from a variety of investments and commercial activities, according to the financial disclosure report for the first year of Trump's second term. Barbara Perry, a presidential historian at the University of Virginia's Miller Center, told the BBC there is "no precedent for this," adding: "It's beyond anything we've ever seen in the presidency." events.title: Why are school shootings continuing to shake the Balkans?
events.summary: A shooting in Serbia has renewed concerns over firearm access, online warning signs and failures to prevent violence. A school shooting in central Serbia has renewed concerns about the availability of firearms, social media warning signs, and systemic failures, following a wave of similar violence across the Balkans. On Tuesday, a 17-year-old suspect shot and wounded two school staff members at the First Technical School in Kragujevac, a city about 145km (90 miles) south of Belgrade. list 1 of 4 Turkiye school shooting leaves 11 pupils wounded list 2 of 4 Could AI firms be held responsible for mass shootings? list 3 of 4 Teenager shoots headmaster, teacher at French school list 4 of 4 What to know about the Logan Circle shooting in Washington, DC Local media reported that the suspect, a student at the school, posted a photo posing with a rifle on social media hours before the attack. The shooting began at about 8am (07:00 GMT) during the first class of the day. According to the Kragujevac Police Department, a 17-year-old fourth-year student, identified by his initials V.M., brought a small-caliber rifle into the building and fired a shot towards the security reception desk. A 50-year-old maintenance worker was struck in the leg, while another employee sustained leg injuries from shattered glass. Both victims were women and sustained lower limb injuries. After being treated in intensive care, they are now in a stable condition and out of danger. A police patrol stationed nearby responded immediately, disarming and arresting the teenager while students and teachers were safely evacuated. A juvenile judge at the Higher Court in Kragujevac ordered a 30-day detention for the suspect. The Higher Public Prosecutor’s Office has charged him with attempted aggravated murder and illegal possession and carrying of firearms. His father was also arrested on suspicion of keeping the rifle at home without a permit. The school’s head teacher Nemanja Joksimovic and graduating students described the suspect as quiet, with no history of disciplinary issues. Following the event, the school shortened class schedules and deployed counsellors and psychologists. What do we know about the suspect’s social media activity? The photo of the suspect holding a rifle posted hours prior to the shooting has raised questions about online vigilance. Nedzad Korajlic, a professor of criminology and safety studies at CEPS Kiseljak, said if other students see posts like this, they should immediately inform a parent, teacher, or trusted adult. In cases of a specific threat or immediate danger, the post should be saved and reported to the police and school leadership immediately, rather than forwarded across group chats, he said. Korajlic added that adolescents often dismiss such posts as posturing or simply do not know who to contact. For that reason, schools must establish clear, confidential reporting protocols so students know exactly where to turn and what will happen next, he said. What measures can be taken to prevent further attacks? In response to previous attacks, governments across the Western Balkans have introduced school police officers, tightened entry controls, and installed security cameras. However, Korajlic said prevention is key. Schools should assign a designated safety officer and staff to evaluate reports. Law enforcement should be notified immediately if firearms or explicit threats are involved, with social and health services joining efforts as needed, he said. The Kragujevac attack highlights the broader issue of widespread civilian firearm ownership in the region due to the availability of legal weapons and unregistered arms remaining from the 1990s Yugoslav wars. Korajlic stressed that weapon storage regulations must be strictly enforced, meaning firearms must be locked away, ammunition kept separately, and keys or codes strictly inaccessible to minors. Psychologist Goran Tomin told Serbia’s Beta news agency that shootings traumatise school communities, noting that institutional responses and sentencing policies are often too lenient. There is a high tolerance for violence in public discourse and the media, he said, while school counsellors are frequently overburdened with administrative work. Following the attack, public officials pointed to digital content. Zarko Micin, a mayor and politician, promised heightened security in local schools while singling out video games, as he urged parents to monitor media consumption. But Korajlic cautioned against reducing complex incidents to cases of media consumption, noting that simply playing a violent video game tells us very little about a person’s real-world behaviour without analysing specific motives, context, and explicit threats. Where else have shootings taken place in the Balkans? Several shootings have shaken schools in Serbia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Croatia over the past three years.

events.title: US announces new tariffs on host of countries including China
events.summary: Watch: What we know about Trump's Thanksgiving tariffs Published 25 November 2026, 00:38 GMT The US has announced a fresh raft of tariffs as President Donald Trump pushes ahead with his signature trade policy. The new taxes charged on imports to America are set to hit many of the country's biggest trading partners - China, the European Union and 12 other jurisdictions. The move follows the White House's investigation into the trade practices of other countries in March after the US Supreme Court ruled Trump's previously announced Liberation Day tariffs were illegal . China is facing the highest rate of up to 40%, followed by Vietnam at up to 35% and then others facing either 20% or 25%. The new duties are not expected to take effect until next year. Tariffs are taxes levied on imported goods. The amount is typically calculated as a percentage of the good's value and paid to the government by businesses importing the products from abroad. Some of these rates will be effectively reduced because of caps on tariffs Trump has agreed to. Individual countries also face different levies. The proposed tariffs will affect China, the European Union, Singapore, Switzerland, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia, Thailand, Korea, Vietnam, Taiwan, Bangladesh, Japan, and India. US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the latest tariffs issued would "level the playing field for American workers and chart a new, more sustainable course for the world economy". He claimed that many of America's trading partners had "for decades" adopted industrial strategies which included "targeting manufacturing, wage and labor suppression" as well as "other market distorting practices that tilt the trade balance in their favor while eroding America's manufacturing base". But economists have warned tariffs can fuel inflation and push prices up for consumers if businesses pass on higher costs, as well as dampen global trade. Trump has repeatedly threatened or imposed tariffs during his second term, arguing they will boost US manufacturing and create jobs. Despite a poor result for the Republican party in the midterm elections, the president has continued to press on with his flagship trade policy. Trump is also seeking to cut the US trade deficit - the gap between the value of goods it buys from other countries and those it sells to them. Trump's so-called Liberation Day tariffs were struck down by the Supreme Court earlier this year However, Stephen Brown, chief North America economist for Capital Economics, said the latest tariff announcement was "not as alarming as it looks", due to the taxes "essentially replacing" previously announced tariffs made in the summer. "The increase in the effective tariff rate looks set to be a touch lower than we've been assuming for our forecasts, although the new tariffs will still provide a marginal boost to prices," he said in a note. "The key message is that the additional tariff burden is likely to be small, especially as various goods... are also not subject to these new tariffs." The announcement is likely to increase tensions between the US and China, the world's two biggest economies, who remain locked in a trade dispute and the AI race. The two countries have also been embroiled in a tit-for-tat tariffs war, which is currently on hold. Despite last week's meeting between Trump and China's President Xi Jinping, the two sides made no announcement on the trade war truce, which is set to expire on 10 January. The European Commission rejected the new US tariffs, saying it would investigate the US's reasons for bringing them in. It pointed out that tariffs are limited to the 15% previously agreed. What tariffs has Trump introduced and why? events.title: Even the price of toys is on the rise. How Americans are scaling back holiday plans
events.summary: U.S. households face higher food, travel, heating and gift costs during the 2026 holiday season. Energy costs have surged since the Iran conflict began, while food and other consumer prices remain elevated. While some are expecting record retail spending during the holidays, there's signs that families are buckling under the pressure of higher prices. As Amanda Brecht planned how her family would spend Thanksgiving this year, she had to make some difficult decisions. Because of high gas prices , the 30-year-old decided she wouldn't drive across her home state of Michigan to celebrate with extended family. Instead, Brecht and her husband will spend the holiday with just their three kids. And with food prices rising, they'll be skipping appetizers and serving turkey breast instead of a whole bird. "Thanksgiving is definitely going to look different this year," Brecht said. "Money doesn't grow on trees. You can only do so much." With inflation accelerating, Americans like Brecht will see higher prices almost everywhere they look this holiday season . At a time of year synonymous with food, gifts and big spending, many consumers are instead pinching pennies, paring back their plans and making tough choices about how they'll celebrate. Some are raiding their savings accounts and running up debt on credit cards. They're reporting downbeat outlooks about the economy in surveys. And they've become more selective with spending as inflationary pressures mount. "Families are facing some tough choices this year," said Alexander Smith, an associate professor who researches behavioral economics at the Worcester Polytechnic Institute. "They might have to cut back on holiday spending in whatever way that they can." A classic Thanksgiving feast will be harder to pull off as grocery prices rise. The price of a 10-person Thanksgiving dinner increased 6% to $58.63 in 2026, according to an annual survey from the American Farm Bureau Federation. Faith Parum, the organization's deputy chief economist, said the price increase was a result of higher costs for labor and transportation. Grocers including Walmart and Aldi have gained traction on social media by offering Thanksgiving meal bundles as a value-focused workaround to higher prices. Walmart's offering promises to feed 10 for $35, and includes a turkey and ingredients to make mashed potatoes, green bean casserole, cranberries, marshmallow-topped sweet potatoes and a pumpkin pie. Still, some consumers will feel disappointed by having less choice in their menus due to higher prices, according to Joe Bruseulas, chief economist at tax firm RSM. "We're missing the point here if all we're doing is focusing on the fact that Walmart will sell you a homogeneous dinner meal" at a discount, Bruseulas said. "People feel horrible that they have to go to that because the price of everything has just risen so significantly over the past five years." Peterson: Here’s what Bessent’s about-face on Jensen Huang reveals about Trump and China Consumer confidence shoots up after Democrats’ midterm victories — though inflation worries persist Warsh wants Fed officials to talk less. Instead, they're talking more Tech outages are fueling a new doomsday economy Inflation is affecting more than Thanksgiving staples like turkey or stuffing. Food prices on average have jumped around 24% over the last five years, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Some items have seen even sharper increases: Coffee and ground beef, for example, have each climbed by more than 40% in the same period despite pulling back from recent highs. At the same time, millions of Americans lost SNAP benefits under policy changes included in President Donald Trump 's "big beautiful bill." Food banks across the U.S. have seen foot traffic skyrocket this year as the reduction in federal nutrition aid coincides with rising prices in grocery aisles. The Salvation Army said some of its food pantries in October provided double or triple the amount of groceries than they did in the same month a year ago. Demand is now so high that some food banks in Feeding America's national network are worried about running out of supplies. "We want to make sure that our food banks are as full as they possibly can be going into the holiday season," said Linda Nageotte, Feeding America's president and operations chief. "Far too many of them have empty shelves." High energy prices as a result of the war with Iran are also affecting Americans' holiday plans. Slightly fewer Americans will travel at least 50 miles around the Thanksgiving holiday in 2026, marking the first year-over-year decline since the country was in lockdown from the pandemic in 2020, according to AAA. Stacey Barber, a vice president at the auto association, attributed this year's pullback in part to higher fuel costs. AAA said that about nine out of every 10 Thanksgiving travelers will do so by car.

events.title: Army detonates Iowa explosives amid toxic lead fears
events.summary: The Army detonated 68 drums of unstable lead azide on an Iowa plant Wednesday after multiple delays, a court challenge and presidential intervention . The big picture: Elected officials slammed the military over communication shortfalls ahead of the detonation, which triggered evacuations, closures and fears about exposure to toxic lead dust in surrounding communities and states . Federal officials have repeatedly stressed that detonating the unstable lead is safer than risking it exploding spontaneously. What they're saying: "Early reports from Iowa are that the Army's mitigation efforts have far exceeded expectations," President Trump said on Truth Social . Missouri Gov. Mike Kehoe also said early analysis from federal partners indicates the detonation was "well-contained." The Army has not yet released a statement on the status of the operation. Reporters near the plant witnessed large clouds of smoke rising following the detonation. Context: The evacuation zone is a 5-mile cone extending southwest of the ammunition plant, per the Army's public safety notice . Evacuees are set to receive notice by phone when it's safe to return. Those outside of the evacuation zone should still shelter in place by closing all windows and doors, recirculating heating and turning off fans that pull in outside air, among other protective measures for children and livestock, per the Army. State of play: President Trump ordered the Army to pause plans to detonate the explosives on Monday, saying the blast couldn't proceed without approval from a court and Democratic Gov.-elect Rob Sand . But Trump warned he would hold Sand responsible for "any and all death or destruction" if the governor-elect refuses to approve the detonation. The court initially granted an administrative stay but lifted it Monday, allowing the plan to proceed. Sand said in a statement that the administration should decide "based on the information they have from the people they brought in to do the job months ago and have been on the ground in Middletown for weeks," adding, "Everyday Iowans are entitled to know how Middletown came to this situation." What they're saying: "We are mindful of the very real risks presented by the Army's planned detonation of the stores of degraded lead azide," a panel of judges concluded . "However, we must acknowledge the realities of the situation: the degraded explosives present a risk of an uncontrolled and unplanned explosion, which would occur without the benefit of the safety measures that the Permit puts in place." Catch up quick: The Army announced Sunday night that the controlled detonation plan would be pushed to Wednesday "to allow for optimal weather conditions and all mitigation measures to be emplaced" after initially planning the blast for Friday, and then Monday. But on Monday, Trump halted those plans — though only momentarily. Editor's note: This is a breaking news story and has been updated.

events.title: Biden’s enduring win
events.summary: Democrats can be thankful for at least one decision by the Trump administration this year: Health officials continued to empower Medicare to negotiate prescription drug prices, a signature achievement of former President Joe Biden. CMS announced this week that if newly negotiated prices had been in effect last year, they would’ve reduced the cost of the 13 drugs included in the program by $9.2 billion, a 45% savings. The new prices take effect in 2028 and cover high-cost drugs with no generic competitors, like Gilead Sciences’ HIV drug Biktarvy and Janssen’s prostate cancer drug Erleada. As Democrats debate their healthcare agenda, the drug negotiation program offers a contemporary example of how a Democratic health policy can endure, even under a Republican administration. During the legislative battle over Medicare drug price negotiations, Democrats were more insulated from outside pressure because of the COVID-19 pandemic. Reporters who cover turn-of-the-screw developments were mostly cloistered at home in the spring of 2021. Lobbyists, who had previously used terms like “ nuclear winter ” to describe the proposal’s impact on the pharmaceutical industry, could not apply face-to-face pressure on lawmakers. While no Republicans publicly backed the proposal, even pro-market conservatives have said to me in private that it makes sense to allow Medicare to haggle with drugmakers on drugs with no competition. The idea was also popular with voters across party lines. Unlike the Biden era, Democrats, obviously, do not control the White House. But health policy wonks perked up when President Donald Trump posted a screenshot on Truth Social of Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, D-Mich., directly pitching guaranteed “cradle-to-grave” healthcare for Americans. They hope it signals there’s room for a deal between the president and Democrats in Congress. “The devil is in the details and if the president is serious about working on this, let’s think about how we can get the broadest number of people guaranteed health insurance from cradle-to-grave without the out-of-pocket costs that are driving people into bankruptcy,” El-Sayed said this past weekend on Meet the Press . Whatever healthcare agenda Democrats end up pursuing, if they can get it signed into law, it may follow in the footsteps of Medicare drug price negotiations. The lesson: Even if healthcare legislation is initially unpopular in certain corners, it can quickly become politically durable.

events.title: Patent expiration cliffs spur drugmaker M&A
events.summary: The looming expiration of a blockbuster drug patent pushed Sanofi into its biggest M&A deal in two decades this week (and the largest pharma deal in three years). It won’t be the last. The French giant’s $41 billion takeover of respiratory drugmaker Insmed is in part a bid to replenish its pipeline ahead of the patent cliff facing Dupixent, the eczema drug whose $20-plus billion in annual sales will face generic competition starting in 2031. Across the industry, more than $500 billion of prescription-drug sales face patent expirations in the next six years, which could usher in a takeover wave. The biggest of those is Merck’s Keytruda, the world’s best-selling drug, which loses US patent in 2028. But all the big drugmakers are facing a similar crisis: Nearly half of Bristol’s sales are at risk by 2030 (which might help explain its merger flirtations with AstraZeneca earlier this year). Ozempic maker Novo Nordisk is regrouping after losing a bidding war over a new weight-loss drug last year to Pfizer. Hoovering up promising molecules doesn’t always pay off. Merck’s $12 billion purchase of Acceleron in 2021 brought it a new blockbuster blood-pressure drug whose sales have outperformed , but the jury is still out on Bristol’s $14 billion deal for schizophrenia drug Cobenfy. — David Lim

events.title: Iraq's National Security Service reports two more oil smuggling operations
events.summary: Iraq's domestic intelligence agency says it has uncovered more syndicates diverting the country's oil and crude derivatives amid a wider government campaign against theft and smuggling. The National Security Service on Wednesday said it discovered a tapped oil pipeline in Al Luhais, south of Baghdad, with three hoses connected to it by valves. “The hoses were being used to siphon oil and load it into tankers for smuggling, and they were shut down in co-ordination with technical authorities,” the service said. In the northern city of Kirkuk, officers seized a vehicle prepared for smuggling oil derivatives, the agency said. The vehicle was modified with openings on its sides to unload the product and "white oil" was found in its tank. The suspect was arrested. The service did not say when the operations were carried out, but its announcement comes after Prime Minister Ali Al Zaidi launched a crackdown on oil theft and smuggling last week. The campaign began in Jurf Al Sakhar , about 60km south of Baghdad. An intelligence agency report documented oil theft there between 2021 and 2026, with sites suspected of storing oil hidden underground and under steel structures. Investigators later said they found evidence that smugglers had punctured a pipeline passing through the area, hidden pumping equipment inside hangars to avoid aerial surveillance and built a small concealed refinery. The area has long been closed to federal institutions and residents, after the influential Iran-backed Kataib Hezbollah militia took control in 2014 following the fight against ISIS . The government ordered federal troops into the area, and dismissed nine senior security and oil officials, including the police chief and the director of the Oil Pipelines Company. Kataib Hezbollah has denied the allegations. The crackdown then widened to Najaf, where investigators discovered a similar pattern: a tap on a strategic pipeline, hidden pipes running to private land, and alleged collusion by those meant to guard the network. The Supreme Judicial Council said an investigative judge had inspected an encroachment on land belonging to a Najaf Provincial Council member who heads its Energy Committee and his brother, a member of parliament, and that initial findings indicated oil had been illegally diverted. The court ordered the detention of five officers and three Energy Police personnel pending investigation. It issued arrest warrants for the two brothers, one of whom later surrendered while the other was reported to have left for Iran. In the north, the campaign has taken on a constitutional dimension after Mr Al Zaidi on Tuesday ordered federal authorities to take over border crossings run by the semi-autonomous Kurdistan Region and directed the Oil Ministry to manage oilfields under Kurdish security control in Kirkuk, Nineveh, Diyala and Salahuddin provinces. The move followed an investigation into alleged smuggling at the state-run North Oil Company. The Kurdistan Regional Government rejected Baghdad's orders as unconstitutional and said it was working with federal authorities to combat corruption. It called for an end to oil smuggling across Iraq.

events.title: U.S. proposes new tariffs on 14 trading partners, including China and the EU
events.summary: The Trump administration is proposing new Section 301 tariffs on China, the EU, Japan and India, following investigations into alleged structural excess capacity in manufacturing sectors. The new tariffs are "targeted," not blanket rates, and will vary for each economy, and many will not exceed the rates established in previously reached trade deals, a senior U.S. official told reporters. U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC the new tariffs likely will not take effect for months. The U.S. is preparing new tariffs on 14 economies , including China, the EU, Japan and India, following investigations into what the Trump administration says are excess manufacturing practices that disadvantage U.S. commerce. The administration launched those and other trade investigations in March , weeks after the Supreme Court unraveled a major piece of President Donald Trump 's tariff-heavy economic policy by striking down his "liberation day" duties. Trump has since been accused by critics of his tariffs of trying to revive the canceled duties using other legal authorities. The latest action targets foreign economies that create, sustain or contribute to structural excess capacity and production in manufacturing sectors that the U.S. finds unreasonable and burdensome or restrictive to its commerce, a senior U.S. official told reporters Tuesday evening. The new tariffs are "targeted," not blanket rates, and will vary for each economy, and many will not exceed the rates established in previously reached trade deals, said the official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the forthcoming duties. Trump meddling in Huang role reignites voter angst over tech's outsized power Trump wanted Jensen Huang back. Now, the president is all alone in Washington The rates, which mostly range from 15% to 20%, are "not really additive" and generally will not stack on top of existing duties, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC's "Squawk Box" Wednesday morning. "In effect, it'll look more like a top up," Greer said. "When it all nets out, it really will just top up a few percentage points." An exception is China, which faces a 20% rate under the new tariff policy, "so it will go up some," Greer said. But at the same time, both countries are moving to remove tariffs on some of each other's goods in what Greer called "stability-generating activity through this action." The senior U.S. official said Tuesday that the 20% rate will come on top of the so-called forced technology transfer-related tariffs of roughly 25%, which were implemented during Trump's first presidential term. U.S. tariffs on Chinese goods will therefore reach about 45%, give or take for different goods, the official said. Average U.S. tariffs rates on Chinese goods stood at about 36.5% as of July, according to the Congressional Research Service . Greer also said on CNBC that the new policy likely will not take effect for months. "We've talked to our trading partners about this. They know what we're proposing," he said. "I think a lot of this is baked in, and I don't think any of these would actually take effect earlier than a couple months from now." The administration says the tariffs target what it calls "overcapacity" — excess industrial production, often supported by government subsidies, that allows cheaper goods to flood global markets and undercut U.S. producers. China has disputed the allegations. "The so-called 'overcapacity' does not really exist," China's foreign ministry said Wednesday before the official reports were released by the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative, according to Reuters. The overcapacity levies are being imposed under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. The Trump administration invoked the same statute to launch investigations into 60 economies over alleged forced-labor issues. Those investigations, which also began in March, led to broad tariffs of 10% to 12.5% on goods from dozens of countries covering 99.4% of U.S. imports. The Section 301 actions came weeks after the Supreme Court struck down the near-global tariffs that Trump had enacted under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act. Shortly after the court's ruling, Trump invoked Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974 to impose a 10% global tariff. That tariff expired after 150 days, and was immediately replaced with the forced-labor-related duties. An ongoing lawsuit accuses the Trump administration of citing forced-labor issues as a "pretext" in pursuit of reviving Trump's worldwide tariff regime.

events.title: How Qualcomm’s CMO is reshaping his team for its post-Apple era
events.summary: The iPhone 18, released in September, was the first of Apple’s flagship models to use its in-house C2 cellular modem. It marked the end of a 15-year arrangement with U.S. chipmaker Qualcomm , whose chips had been used in every iPhone since the iPhone 4, excluding some of Apple’s budget ‘e’ series, to connect the devices to a mobile network.  “You take us out and your iPhone becomes an iPod, basically,” Don McGuire, Qualcomm’s chief marketing officer, says, explaining how its chips work.  While he adds that the company knew that the end of Apple’s reliance on Qualcomm’s chips was coming, chief executive Cristiano Amon reported that revenue from Apple products would decline faster than expected, because of supply constraints.   In the year to September, Qualcomm’s total revenue fell 3% to $43.1 billion. Chip sales were down 26%, in the final three months to September.  McGuire argues the loss of Apple leaves Qualcomm less exposed to a single customer. “It’s actually very freeing when you can rebalance your customer ecosystem,” he says. In his view, Qualcomm’s success does not hinge on whether its chips end up in one phone maker’s handsets. “Are we in the iPhone? Are we not in the iPhone? I don’t care.”  The company now expects that loss of its chip sales to come from outside of the smartphone category and has recently been expanding into the laptop, car, smart-home device, wearables, and data center markets. Revenue outside of Qualcomm’s mobile chip business is anticipated to grow by more than 60% in 2027.  Data centers remain a lucrative market for chipmakers but it is currently dominated by Nvidia . Nvidia’s data center business accounted for 92% of its revenues in its latest quarter ly results.   In June, Qualcomm unveiled a new line of data center chips, and it is targeting $5 billion in data center revenue in 2027.  Qualcomm’s marketing challenge   As CMO, McGuire has to persuade carmakers, computer manufacturers, and cloud companies to buy chips from a business best known for making phone modems. “We’ve diversified so much and expanded our portfolio of where we play in markets that historically we may not have been used to,” he says. “It’s given us a really great opportunity, but it’s also obviously presented some challenges.”  To manage that, he split Qualcomm into three brands, each covering a different chip depending on the buyer. Snapdragon is the firm’s consumer brand, covering the processors inside phones, laptops, and cars. Dragonwing is Qualcomm’s industrial and robotics brand, and Dragonfly, launched in June, covers Qualcomm’s data center products, including server processors and AI chips.    Qualcomm sells to device makers, rather than consumers. However, there is still an advantage to marketing to the broader public. The more people look for a Snapdragon laptop, the more chips Dell, Samsung , and others order, McGuire explains.   “Are we in the iPhone? Are we not in the iPhone? I don’t care.”  don mcguire, cmo, qualcomm This is why the brand has focused on building partnerships with sports teams, including a sponsorship deal with Manchester United, which McGuire says delivers exposure equal to 42 Super Bowl ads a season, and its partnership with the Mercedes Formula 1 team. McGuire says the aim is to make technology “visible and emotionally resonant.”   This year’s Christmas, which sees a father build a time machine using Qualcomm’s chips so his impatient son can travel forward through time to Christmas morning, takes a similar approach.  “People don’t care about specs, speeds or feeds,” McGuire says. “They care about what technology can do for them and they care about their passions.”  Data center customers are a different audience, however. The people signing off on Qualcomm’s server chips are cloud companies and finance chiefs, for whom cost matters most. Here, Qualcomm competes with Nvidia on price and power use, a growing concern as data centers’ electricity demands rise. “Nobody does performance per watt better than we do,” McGuire says. Qualcomm has already signed Meta and AWS. Rebuilding the marketing team   Running separate brands across so many markets has also stretched McGuire’s team, which he says has not grown as fast as the company’s ambitions.   McGuire wants his team to spend 75% of its time on planned work and 25% on what he calls “dive and catch,” meaning urgent, last-minute requests. By last year, those figures had flipped, and most of the team’s time was spent firefighting. “I knew this wasn’t going to be sustainable,” he adds.  McGuire believes AI will be crucial in enabling his small marketing team to keep pace with the growing list of demands. In January, McGuire tore up the department’s structure and rebuilt it around AI. “CMOs have a new role now, and that’s chief architect,” he says.  “Roles we thought were going to be important three to five years ago are less important today,” McGuire adds, such as production design and copywriting that is now handled by AI agents. Meanwhile, data, strategy, and creative direction have become more important.  According to McGuire, fewer than 5% of the marketing department was affected. Most of those people moved into new roles, and a smaller number whose skills no longer matched what the team needed left. He calls it “more of a redeployment.”  McGuire says the new structure is already paying off, helping to lower the company’s reliance on agencies and reduce cycle times by two-thirds.   Despite all the changes, McGuire expects further upheaval in the near future. “It’s probably only going to last us 24 months. Technology is changing so fast, I’m not so naive as to think we’ve got another five years,” he adds.  His previous structure, designed in 2021, was meant to last five years but only lasted three and a half years. “The department has gone from a single AI writing tool to several AI systems in three years and McGuire sees no sign of that slowing. “Every day there’s a new tool,” he says. “Every day they’re becoming more agentic.”  McGuire says he has pushed back on demands for AI-driven cost cuts. “I don’t believe we’re at a stage right now where anyone could demand a reduction in cost because of AI,” he says. “It’s too early for that. We’re experimenting and learning.”  Many CMOs face similar pressures. A third of marketing leaders surveyed by executive-search firm Spencer Stuart said they expected to cut headcount within two years, through AI or by eliminating redundancies.  For Qualcomm, the challenge will be whether it can make the jump from phones to data centers, and whether its marketing can keep up. “If we believe we can disrupt, if we believe we have a better solution, we’re going to tak

events.title: Share your most outrageous experience when trying to rent a room in the UK?
events.summary: We’d like to hear your stories of trying to find flatmates in the private rental market in the UK. Have you had to audition? What demands or restrictive rules have you encountered? Finding a room to rent in the UK has become intensely competitive, with prices rising and the number of rooms available shrinking. In big cities, prospective tenants often find they are competing with dozens of applicants for a single room - with potential housemates imposing increasingly specific and unusual demands. We would like to hear your experiences of trying to find flatmates in the private rental market. Have you sent dozens of applications without success? Have you had to go through lenghty interviews or flatmate “auditions” to secure a space? Have you encountered bizarre or restrictive rules, such as bans on working from home, or strict requirements around profession and lifestyle? What is the most outrageous experience you’ve had while looking for somewhere to live, and how has the process affected your finances and wellbeing? events.title: Investors led by U.S. billionaire Todd Boehly to buy Lukoil's oil and gas assets outside Russia, sources say
events.summary: The deal transfers Lukoil's international refineries and other production assets to a U.S.-led group of investors. The agreement would allow Europe to buy fuel such as diesel previously produced by Lukoil through the U.S.-led group rather than Russia. Investors led by U.S. billionaire Todd Boehly's asset management company Eldridge have struck a deal to buy Lukoil's assets outside of Russia, sources confirmed to CNBC. The U.S. International Development Finance Corporation and Catena Investments, based in the United Arab Emirates, are also parties to the deal, the sources said. The deal transfers Lukoil's international refineries and other production assets in Bulgaria, Romania, Africa and the Middle East to the U.S.-led group, the sources said. It also includes retail gas stations in the U.S., Europe and Asia, they said. The U.S. Office of Foreign Assets Control is expected to sign off on the deal but final approval is still needed, the sources said. The deal would give the U.S.-led group about 350,000 barrels per day of production.

events.title: Saudi national charged in OpenAI bugging to be released on $1 million bond
events.summary: Abdulrahman Alfozan, the Saudi national accused of bugging an OpenAI executive conference room, will be allowed to be released from jail on a $1 million bond, a San Francisco federal court judge ruled. Alfozan, 35, is expected to be released Wednesday and be fitted with an ankle monitor, according to his attorney. The San Francisco U.S. Attorney's Office opposed the former OpenAI engineer's release, saying in its response that he remains a flight risk due to his "considerable resources and ties to Saudi Arabia." Abdulrahman Alfozan , the Saudi national accused of bugging an OpenAI executive conference room, will be allowed to be released from jail on a $1 million bond , a San Francisco federal court judge ruled Tuesday. Alfozan, 35, is expected to be released on Wednesday and be fitted with an ankle monitor, according to his attorney, David Rizk. "We are simply grateful that the Court made the right decision to release Mr. Alfozan and now we look forward to defending the case," Rizk said in a text message after a hearing before U.S. District Court Magistrate Judge Alex Tse. Tse ruled in favor of a release motion by Rizk filed last week that said prosecutors had admitted they had "found no new evidence to support the theory that Mr. Alfozan was stealing trade secrets, or to support the speculation that he was acting as an unregistered foreign agent for Saudi Arabia." U.S. proposes new tariffs on 14 trading partners, including China and the EU Trump meddling in Huang role reignites voter angst over tech's outsized power Trump wanted Jensen Huang back. Now, the president is all alone in Washington Alfozan's release request "blithely dismisses the seriousness" of the charge he faces, and "appears to presume, without support, that the government's investigation is complete," prosecutors wrote. Alfozan, who was arrested Oct. 9, is accused of concealing a recording device in the artificial intelligence company's conference room to secretly record discussions. The device was found in a USB port in a television in the room on Sept. 30, prosecutors have said. Prosecutors said they have found hundreds of audio files on Alfozan's personal computer, "including dozens of recordings of meetings or conversations that occurred at OpenAI throughout September 2026, many of which involve discussions of what may be trade secrets." Jury selection for Alfozan's trial is scheduled to begin Jan. 20. Alfozan is a venture partner in a Saudi Arabian venture capital firm that lists Prince Khalid Bin Bader Al Saud , a member of that nation's ruling royal family, as a fellow partner. OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Alfozan's planned release. — CNBC's Ashley Capoot contributed to this article.

events.title: Dubai Islamic Bank to acquire Emirates Islamic to form Dh585bn company
events.summary: Dubai Islamic Bank has agreed to acquire Emirates Islamic Bank in an all-share deal that would create a Sharia-compliant lender with Dh585 billion ($159.2 billion) in assets. DIB will acquire 100 per cent of the issued share capital of Emirates Islamic and will strengthen its position as the UAE's largest Islamic lender, DIB and Emirates Islamic said on Wednesday in a joint statement posted on the Dubai Financial Market. Emirates Islamic is a unit of Dubai's biggest bank, Emirates NBD . The deal would also create the world's second-largest Islamic lender by assets, trailing only Saudi Arabia's Al Rajhi Bank. The takeover is subject to approval from authorities, including the UAE Central Bank and the Capital Markets Authority. “This transaction represents an important opportunity for Dubai to … further strengthen the emirate’s position as a global centre for Islamic finance,” said Sheikh Ahmed bin Saeed, chairman of Emirates NBD. Dubai Islamic Bank (DIB) and Emirates NBD announce that they have signed a share purchase agreement for DIB to acquire 100% of the issued share capital of Emirates Islamic Bank, a wholly owned subsidiary of Emirates NBD. DIB will pay the consideration entirely by issuing new… pic.twitter.com/wopIJr4me3 — Dubai Media Office (@DXBMediaOffice) November 25, 2026 "By bringing together two highly complementary Islamic banking franchises, the combination will create a stronger institution to serve customers, support the UAE’s economic ambitions and contribute to Dubai’s continued growth," he said. The acquisition is one of the biggest mergers in UAE banking following the merger of Abu Dhabi Commercial Bank with Union National Bank and Al Hilal Bank in 2019. In 2017, National Bank of Abu Dhabi was combined with First Gulf Bank to create First Abu Dhabi Bank, the UAE's biggest lender. DIB, established in 1975, is the largest Islamic bank in the UAE by assets. With group assets exceeding Dh427 billion by the end of September, the bank has about 12,000 employees and more than 540 branches in the Middle East, Asia and Africa. Emirates Islamic was previously listed, before Emirates NBD bought out minority shareholders and delisted the business in June last year. DIB's takeover of Emirates Islamic "also reinforces Dubai’s position as the global capital for Islamic finance and places the full weight of a stronger DIB behind the emirate's future", DIB chairman Fadhel Al Ali said. The bank's shares - which surged 11 per cent on Monday amid initial reports on the takeover of Emirates Islamic - settled 1.6 per cent higher at Dh8.92 on Wednesday.
