events.title: The 10 best movies and TV shows to stream this Thanksgiving weekend
events.summary: The women of "The Hunting Wives" practice shooting in season two of the Netflix drama. Netflix Netflix's "The Hunting Wives" returns for its second season this week. "The Mosquito Bowl" brings the story of college football players during World War II to the screen. Peacock's "Dig" and Prime Video's "Blade Runner 2099" are among this week's new releases. Whether you're looking for something to watch with the family after Thanksgiving dinner or need to sneak away for some time on your own, streaming services have you covered. Netflix released " The Altruists ," a series about former FTX executives Sam Bankman-Fried and Caroline Ellison and the collapse of the cryptocurrency exchange. The streamer is also bringing back its drama series "The Hunting Wives," and it just added "The Mosquito Bowl," a film based on the true story of college football players who joined the Marines during World War II. Other platforms have plenty to offer, too. Peacock is premiering "Dig," a new comedy starring Amy Poehler and Hugh Laurie, while Prime Video is taking viewers back to the world of "Blade Runner" with "Blade Runner 2099," starring Michelle Yeoh and Hunter Schafer. From comedies and animated adventures to true-crime stories, fantasy, and drama, here are 10 movies and TV shows to stream this Thanksgiving weekend. Netflix's hit drama "The Hunting Wives" returns for season 2 on Thanksgiving Day. Netflix Brittany Snow and Malin Akerman return as Sophie and Margo in the second season of Netflix's drama. Their complicated friendship continues to unravel amid secrets, scandal, and murder in an affluent Texas community. At the start of the new season, the two women are on the outs, but old secrets and new enemies bring them back together. Streaming on: Netflix, November 26 Peter Berg's World War II drama "The Mosquito Bowl" arrived on Netflix just before Thanksgiving. Netflix "The Mosquito Bowl" brings together football and wartime history. Directed by Peter Berg, the movie follows four college football stars who enlist in the US Marines after the attack on Pearl Harbor. The men eventually take part in a football game that becomes a memorable moment in military history. The cast includes Nicholas Galitzine, Bill Skarsgård, Ray Nicholson, and Tom Francis. Streaming on: Netflix, November 25 Michelle Yeoh and Hunter Schafer enter a futuristic world in "Blade Runner 2099." Prime Video The "Blade Runner" universe gets another chapter with this science-fiction series set 50 years after the events of "Blade Runner 2049." Michelle Yeoh stars as Olwen, a dying Replicant, while Hunter Schafer plays Cora, a fugitive who becomes a Blade Runner. The two form an unlikely partnership while searching for a runaway whose secrets could threaten their city. All eight episodes arrive together, giving viewers plenty of time to explore the series over Thanksgiving weekend. Streaming on: Prime Video, November 25 Amy Poehler and Hugh Laurie lead Peacock's new comedy series "Dig." Peacock The comedy follows four women archaeologists working at an excavation site in Greece, where they uncover a rare artifact. Poehler stars as Elise, an ambitious archaeologist hoping to take over the dig from her longtime boss, Neville, played by Laurie. The series also reunites Poehler with Mike Schur, her former "Parks and Recreation" collaborator. All 10 episodes are available to stream now. Streaming on: Peacock (now streaming) Netflix's "The Altruists" follows the scandal that shook the cryptocurrency world. Netflix "The Altruists" tells the story of former cryptocurrency executives Sam Bankman-Fried and Caroline Ellison , whose ambitions to reshape the financial world unraveled amid an $8 billion fraud scandal. The eight-episode series stars Anthony Boyle and Julia Garner and follows the couple's rise in the cryptocurrency industry and the scandal that brought their business empire crashing down. Streaming on: Netflix (now streaming) "Yellowjackets" returns for its fourth and final season on Paramount+. Paramount+ "Yellowjackets" follows the survivors of a plane crash as they try to rebuild their lives after being stranded in the wilderness. "Yellowjackets'" fourth season brings the Emmy-nominated drama to an end, following the women as they face the secrets and consequences of their time in the woods. Streaming on: Paramount+ Premium (season 4 premiered November 20) "Percy Jackson and the Olympians" returns for season 3 on Disney+. Disney+ Walker Scobell stars as Percy Jackson in the third season of the fantasy adventure series. This time, Percy and his friends set out to rescue Annabeth after she's captured by the forces of Kronos. The new season adapts " The Titan's Curse ," the third book in Rick Riordan's bestselling series. Two episodes premiered November 20, with two new episodes arriving each week. Streaming on: Disney+ and Hulu (new episodes weekly) "Steps" puts a different spin on the Cinderella story. Netflix If you've seen enough traditional Cinderella adaptations, Netflix's animated movie "Steps" offers a different perspective on the familiar fairy tale. Ali Wong voices Lilith, Cinderella's so-called evil stepsister, who steals the Fairy Godmother's wand and accidentally turns the kingdom's story upside down. Amanda Seyfried voices Cinderella, and Stephanie Hsu plays her younger stepsister, Margot. Bette Midler plays the Fairy Godmother, while Peter Dinklage also lends his voice. Streaming on: Netflix (now streaming) "Way of the Warrior Kid" stars Chris Pratt as a Navy SEAL helping his nephew find confidence. Apple TV Pratt stars in " Way of the Warrior Kid ," a family adventure about Marc (Jude Hill), a middle schooler struggling with bullying and fitting in. His summer takes a turn when his injured uncle Jake (Pratt), a decorated Navy SEAL, comes to stay with him and his mother. Jake creates a training program to help Marc build confidence. Linda Cardellini also stars as Marc's mother. Streaming on: Apple TV, November 25 "The Magic Faraway Tree" brings a fantasy adventure to the screen. Vertical Entertainment Andrew Garfield and Claire Foy star in "The Magic Faraway Tree," a fantasy adventure about a family that moves to the English countryside and discovers a magical tree near their new home. Their children soon meet the tree's unusual residents and are transported to fantastical lands. The film is based on Enid Blyton's popular children's book series and also stars Nicola Coughlan and Rebecca Ferguson. events.title: Canadian Finance Minister says his country and the UAE are 'open for business'
events.summary: There is growing momentum on the UAE’s pledge to invest $50 billion in Canada , with the two countries working together to “bring projects to the table”, as economic ties strengthen, according to Canada’s Minister of Finance and National Revenue. Partnerships in the fields of critical minerals, energy and artificial intelligence are being worked on, Francois-Philippe Champagne told The National in an interview in Abu Dhabi. “That’s the reason why I'm here. It's to translate the vision of the President [Sheikh Mohamed] and the Prime Minister [Mark Carney] into action,” Mr Champagne said. The UAE announced the investment commitment during Mr Carney’s visit to the country last year, with a focus on energy, AI, logistics, mining and other strategic sectors. Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed, Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi, visited Canada last month and held talks with Mr Carney. “This is a long-term strategic partnership. My presence at a time when we have seen the security situation in the region sent a very strong signal to my partners here and to the world that Canada is open for business, UAE is open for business, and we're working together,” Mr Champagne said. A Canadian bank and an insurance firm will open offices in the UAE as part of the strengthening of ties, he confirmed. Canada is also looking to bolster defence partnerships, with a possible joint venture with UAE conglomerate Edge. Mr Champagne held a meeting with the Edge leadership during his current visit. “The meeting with Edge was very important because that's the kind of capabilities that we want to build. Looking at joint ventures, looking at investments that can come also with the partnership we're creating,” Mr Champagne said. Energy also remains a key area of focus with the official visiting Masdar's office in Abu Dhabi. “Masdar is another example; there are projects in Canada that could further our ambition to double the electricity generation. We’ve been looking at how we can bring … Masdar to build with us the grid of the 21st century.” Last month, Masdar signed an energy pact with Natural Resources Canada to lay the groundwork for co-operation across renewable energy, battery storage, grid infrastructure and clean power solutions to support growing demand from AI and data centres. Owned jointly by Abu Dhabi's Taqa, Adnoc and Mubadala, Masdar is aiming for a portfolio capacity of 100 gigawatts by 2030 as it continues to develop renewable projects as part of its global expansion plans. Cepa to double trade In July, the UAE finalised a Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement with Canada , with the pact signed during Sheikh Khaled's visit to the country last month. The pact gives Canadian companies better access to the UAE, which remains the largest Middle East market for Canadian exports, and could help attract capital into different sectors. The deal needs to be ratified by the Canadian parliament before it goes into effect, Mr Champagne said, without providing a timeline. “[The] Parliament has its own dynamic, but I would think we're going to put everything that we need to do on our side to have it ratified as quickly as possible.” There was a lot of enthusiasm behind that partnership, he said, with a target to double bilateral trade to $7 billion within 10 years, with energy, food security, defence, AI, and quantum technology to play a prominent role. The pact comes as Canada looks to diversify its partnerships with different countries amid trade tension with the US. “Historically, we have been doing a lot north-south, but now we have a diversification agenda. The Middle East, the GCC countries, here in the UAE where we have long established relationships, those are going to be key in our vision to increase our exports to the world,” Mr Champagne said. “And the fact that we were able to negotiate a comprehensive economic partnership in 47 days is showing the level of ambition and urgency that we're bringing to that, which I think is a very positive sign for businesses on both sides.” Canadian companies will continue to invest in the region despite the Iran war, he added. The Iran war, in its ninth month, has affected a number of sectors across the region, including energy, aviation, tourism and hospitality. Despite the disruption, the UAE is expected to expand by 0.2 per cent this year, according to International Monetary Fund estimates, amid a recovery in the oil and non-oil sectors. There are also big opportunities for UAE-based sovereign wealth funds to invest in Canada, Mr Champagne added. “I’ve been meeting with the CEO of Mubadala, Khaldoon [Al Mubarak], whom I've known for a long time. I know there's a lot of interest in Canada,” he said. “Canada provides unique opportunities: stability, predictability, the rule of law, the level of trust you want for the long term. You're looking at the megatrend. This is a country which, when you look at critical minerals, it's not only the exploration and extraction; it's the processing, it's the refining. So big opportunities there.” Abu Dhabi sovereign investor Mubadala Investment Company already has interests in Canada, in logistics firm Canada Cartage and CoolIT Systems, a liquid cooling provider for AI infrastructure. Energy advantage Canada, one of the top oil producers globally with about six million barrels a day of output, is boosting international exports amid the disruption to supplies due to the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz due to the Iran war. “Because of what's happening, the world energy architecture is being redesigned,” Mr Champagne said. “One way to mitigate the impact is to partner with countries like Canada, which can export to allies and partners. “If you export from the west coast, you gain about eight days to go to the Pacific because you don't need to go to the Panama Canal. So we are doubling our capacity to be able to serve our partners there.” There is also opportunity on the east coast to support countries in Europe with gas supply. “We’re working on both sides; we can bring more natural resources to the Pacific. At the same time, there's a number of opportunities to support our European colleagues."

events.title: Saudi Arabia’s PIF looking to sell 25% of Newcastle through share issue
events.summary: PIF seeking investment to fund infrastructure projects JP Morgan appointed to handle the sale Newcastle United’s owner, Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF), is looking to sell up to 25% of the club by issuing new shares. The New York-based bank JP Morgan, whose most recent involvement in a major football deal was Fifa’s aborted attempt to sell off 20% of its commercial rights last summer, has been appointed to handle the sale, as first reported by the Athletic . PIF is seeking investment partners to help fund major infrastructure projects, such as building a new stadium or redeveloping St James’ Park, and would dilute its shareholding rather than profiting from the proceeds of the share issue. The state-owned fund owns 84% of Newcastle after the departure of the minority shareholder Amanda Staveley two years ago, with the remaining 16% owned by the London-based Reuben brothers. How do I sign up for sport breaking news alerts? In the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications. If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version. If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from the iOS App Store on iPhone or the Google Play store on Android by searching for 'The Guardian'. Newcastle are the second Premier League club to formally seek investment this season, after Everton’s owners appointed the US bank Moelis & Company to handle their sale process last month. Last summer Liverpool’s owner, Fenway Sports Group, sold 38% of the club to a consortium which includes the Amazon founder Jeff Bezos. PIF sources insist they retain a long-term commitment to Newcastle, whose value has soared since they bought the club from Mike Ashley for £305m four years ago in a deal that has not proved as transformative for their fortunes as many expected. Newcastle qualified for the Champions League twice under Eddie Howe, who also led the club to their first domestic trophy for 70 years by winning the Carabao Cup in 2025 , but the Premier League’s spending rules have prevented the owners from investing as heavily as the competition’s other state-owned club, Manchester City. PIF has also cut back its spending on sport generally, with the Newcastle share issue coming months after the fund withdrew its support for LIV Golf , which filed for bankruptcy this month . PIF has also sold a stake in the Saudi Pro League club Al-Hilal, is open to selling other clubs, and has withdrawn from a three-year deal to host the Women’s Tennis Association finals 12 months early. Newcastle has been wrestling for several years with the issue of whether to expand St James’ Park or build a new stadium on an adjacent site, but have made clear a project on that scale would require external funding.

events.title: Bill Ackman poked at Carl Icahn's wealth plunge and stoked one of Wall Street's most iconic feuds
events.summary: Bill Ackman poured a little fuel on his mostly dormant feud with Carl Icahn. Kimberly White/Getty Images for Semafor; Victor J. Blue/Bloomberg via Getty Images It appears that Bill Ackman can't resist basking in Carl Icahn's misfortune. Ackman shared an article on X about Icahn's wealth falling to its lowest level in at least 14 years. The two billionaire investors famously feuded over Herbalife in the mid-2010s. By the looks of it, Bill Ackman still has beef with Carl Icahn. On Tuesday, hedge-fund billionaire Ackman clicked X's repost button to share a Bloomberg article about the legendary corporate raider's net worth sinking to $1.2 billion on Friday. That was down sharply from its $26 billion peak in 2013, and marked the lowest estimate since the Bloomberg Billionaires Index began tracking Icahn's wealth in 2012. This guy can’t be serious man 😭🙏 https://t.co/nPK9ryxhGj — Equity Cats (@EquityCats) November 24, 2026 The Pershing Square chief and the Icahn Enterprises chairman famously locked horns over Herbalife, a nutrition-supplement company, in the mid-2010s. Ackman began shorting Herbalife in late 2012, betting $1 billion that the stock would go to zero . He also launched a campaign to convince regulators and investors that the multi-level marketer was a pyramid scheme. Icahn took the other side of that trade and went on to become Herbalife's largest shareholder. The two Wall Street titans memorably clashed on live television in 2013, trading a barrage of insults, with Icahn labeling Ackman a "crybaby," and Ackman calling him a "bully." The pair cooled things down , hugging onstage at a conference in 2014. Icahn said in 2016 that he and Ackman were on "friendly terms," but when it came to Herbalife, they had "agreed to disagree (vehemently) on this subject." However, the two men have butted heads in recent years. Ackman wrote in an X post in 2023: "Over his storied career, Icahn has made many enemies. I don't know that he has any real friends." Icahn fired back in a comment to CNBC's Scott Wapner: "Taking advice from Ackman concerning short selling is like taking advice from Napoleon or the German General Staff on how to invade Russia." Neither Icahn nor Ackman immediately responded to requests for comment from Business Insider on Wednesday. Called @Carl_C_Icahn regarding @BillAckman’s tweet from earlier. Carl told me quote: “Taking advice from Ackman concerning short selling is like taking advice from Napoleon or the German General Staff on how to invade Russia.” Mr. Icahn wouldn’t comment further. — Scott Wapner (@TheJudgeCNBC) May 24, 2023 Icahn's fortune has shrunk due to the plunging value of his stake in Icahn Enterprises, fueled by mounting concerns about its debt and liquidity. The price of its depositary units has tumbled 65% over the past year alone. Icahn Enterprises has also been targeted by short-seller Hindenburg Research and investigated by the Securities and Exchange Commission over disclosure failures. Icahn and his company settled with the SEC in 2024, paying a combined $2 million in civil penalties without admitting or denying the findings. Read the original article on Business Insider

Targeting launch in late 2028, SR-1 would be the first fission-powered spacecraft to travel beyond Earth orbit. It is designed to demonstrate nuclear electric propulsion and deliver a capsule carrying three helicopters to Mars. There have been some changes since NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman showed off the concept [PDF] at the agency's Ignition event in March. Improved shielding and spacecraft design will allow a shorter boom between the reactor and the spacecraft's main body, protecting its electronics and the SkyFall payload. The shorter boom will, according to NASA, "reduce weight, simplify assembly, and help streamline the spacecraft’s design." The revised design also includes larger X-band antenna dishes to transmit data to Earth. Decisions are still pending on how many radiator panels the vehicle needs, the output power levels of the nuclear power module, and how long the reactor will operate. Currently, the mission calls for the spacecraft to start its reactor once it has left Earth orbit and gradually ramp up power. After a period during which performance data will be sent back to Earth, the reactor will be shut down until after the SkyFall capsule, containing a trio of Mars Ingenuity-class helicopters, is delivered to Martian orbit. Solar arrays will power the spacecraft during its cruise to Mars. The fission reactor will then be reactivated to let engineers collect more data on its performance in deep space. NASA also awarded a $39.3 million contract to Johns Hopkins University's Applied Physics Laboratory to develop the heat rejection system for the nuclear power module. "Further maturation of the spacecraft plans will focus on reducing risk, simplifying the design, and staying on schedule," the agency said. The latter part regarding the schedule is certainly a challenge . Meeting the late-2028 launch target leaves roughly two years to finish designing, building, and testing the spacecraft. ESA is also targeting late 2028 for its long-delayed Rosalind Franklin rover. events.title: Stick or switch? UK billpayers weigh up how to beat January energy jump
events.summary: Despite dozens of fixed deals lower than next Ofgem price cap, many customers argue savings do not justify the risk Energy bills in Great Britain to rise 26% in January “I’m looking at the off-peak rate more than doubling, peak increasing considerably as well as the standing charge,” says Andy, who lives on Scotland’s west coast. “I have an electric vehicle and an air-source heat pump and use a lot of off-peak energy. I’d like to stay with Octopus Energy … but there are better-looking deals out there.” The retired woodworker is among the millions facing a jump in energy bills when the price cap in Great Britain rises by 26% in January. He says he “got lucky” last time with a “very good” 12-month deal, but it ends next month. The new cap, set by the regulator Ofgem , works out at £2,166 for a typical annual gas and electricity bill – up £443 on the October to December equivalent. Yet, even though there are dozens of deals available to fix for less, two-thirds of households remain on the default tariff that tracks the cap. So what is stopping people from switching? We asked for people’s views on why they plan to change provider or stick with a variable account. For Andy, a big concern is locking in at the top of the market. He has switched numerous times to save money but with variable tracker rates “eye-wateringly high”, he says he worries “that if I fix now at an increased rate, prices could start to come down”. The cheapest current fix is Fuse Energy’s 18-month deal at £1,754, according to the price comparison service Uswitch. That is £412 a year below the new cap, while the 10 cheapest deals are all at least £317 below it, according to Sabrina Hoque of Uswitch. Its data shows 41 deals are priced below the Ofgem rate. Opting for a fixed deal is a “way to take control”, Hoque argues. “With only a 1% fall [in the cap] forecast for April, waiting is unlikely to bring much relief, and a fix also protects you from any further rise.” However, if you are already on a fixed tariff contract with 50 or more days left until it ends you may have to pay an exit fee if you want to switch. The size of this charge varies by supplier and length of deal. They can be as much as £100 per fuel - so if you’re on a gas and electricity deal, it could cost you £200 to leave early. Hailey, who is a London-based university administrator, has trawled price comparison sites but found that “all the notably cheaper tariffs came from providers I’d never heard of with terrible customer satisfaction ratings”. “Ultimately, the savings on offer weren’t enough to justify the risk,” says the 36-year-old, who also has an account with Octopus, the UK’s largest supplier with more than 8 million customers. “My provider is reliable, and energy is too important to chase a great offer that might turn out to be too good to be true. “The prices are getting all but impossible to manage, especially as someone living and paying for bills alone. But I really don’t see what I can do except cut back in other areas, because you’ve got to have light, heat, and electricity for appliances.” Steve from Merseyside feels there is little point shopping around for a different deal because there “really isn’t much competition any more. They pretty much all charge whatever the cap is.” The father of two, who works in education, says: “I don’t see that the government has customers’ needs first and foremost with these price increases. They are looking after the energy giants’ profits. ” There are certainly fewer energy providers – and deals – to choose from than a couple of years ago. The rise in global gas prices caused about 30 small energy suppliers to go bust during late 2021 and early 2022, including Bulb. The number of suppliers in the domestic gas and electricity retail market has fallen from about 70 before the crisis to just 17 today. Annette, who is in her 40s and lives in Edinburgh, is “stuck” on a variable tariff. “I can’t switch because I’m in a precarious job where I can’t commit to a two-year contract as is usually required. I will likely have to move.” She says that “paying sky-high rent” is crippling her ability to save: “I already don’t turn the heating on – in Edinburgh. It’s a miserable way to live.” To help households cope with their energy bills this winter, the government will make a one-off payment of £100 in January to 20m households in council tax bands A to D. The 5% VAT levy has also been taken off electricity bills until July next year. Rich from Gloucestershire thinks this is not enough. He says: “I remain hugely disappointed that the regulator seems not to be working on behalf of consumers, and that the government is tweaking rather than making the changes necessary to decouple electricity prices from gas , and challenge the profits of the suppliers.” Rather than fix at a time when wholesale costs are high, Plymouth-based Nick plans to stay on his “no frills” variable tariff with Home Energy, having switched from Octopus.

events.title: Everyone said traveling with little kids was a waste. I'm glad I didn't listen.
events.summary: The author said traveling with young kids wasn't always easy, but knows there are many benefits. Courtesy of Christina Valhouli. We've traveled internationally with our kids since they were babies. Everyone thought we were crazy. We took them to France, New Zealand, and the Caribbean when they were young. While they may not have loved everything we did, they became flexible and confident travelers. When my sons were babies, and I'd tell friends about an upcoming trip, I'd always get the same reaction. "What's the point of taking kids on vacations they'll never remember? Why not wait until they're old enough to appreciate it?" I was a travel writer before I had kids and was determined to keep exploring the world as my family expanded. Instead of choosing kid-centric resorts, my husband and I took our boys where we wanted to go. This meant museums, unfamiliar foods, long flights, and plenty of mishaps. My boys are now 14 and 18, and while I can't say they always appreciated the cultural aspects of our travels, they've become confident, easy-going travelers who aren't fazed by change. Early travel wasn't always easy Some of that early travel was out of necessity. When my oldest was born, I was living in London and wanted to bring him home to Boston to meet my family. I applied for his passport shortly after he was born. At four months old and teething, he made his first transatlantic flight — and screamed nearly the entire way. I arrived exhausted and ready to cry, too. Do you have a hot take on a common parenting belief? Email Jennifer Beck Goldblatt at jgoldblatt@insider.com to share your experience with Business Insider. Undeterred, we kept traveling and took our boys to Edinburgh, Antigua, Amsterdam, the French Alps, Ireland, and New Zealand over the next decade. My older son tried his first piece of cake at a fancy resort in the Turks and Caicos. My younger son tried edamame for the first time in London because I needed to grab something quickly to stave off a hangry meltdown — and loved it. He also learned how to nap anywhere, even sleeping through an off-roading adventure in Utah. The author said her kids learned adaptability while traveling as babies and toddlers. Courtesy of Christina Valhouli. We accepted the mishaps and meltdowns This is not to say that everything went smoothly. It's a genuine pain to lug around car seats, strollers, and diapers. There were meltdowns and diaper blowouts at the most inconvenient times. But mishaps happen at every age. When my kids were 4 and 7, I was excited to show them the Greek antiquities at the British Museum. They giggled at all the nudity, and I almost had a heart attack when they casually tried to touch a priceless statue. We survived the encounter and carried on, as we always did. It was a learning experience . They learned a lot, but not what you'll find in a guidebook While my kids were marginally interested in things like Scottish castles (sometimes the tea room was the bigger draw), travel taught them subtle lessons. Sometimes their only takeaway was a small observation. "Why does the milk taste different in France?" or "Why aren't the eggs refrigerated in Scotland?" They also learned to make friends in playgrounds abroad, because swing sets and sandboxes don't require a shared language. I believe all those experiences added up. Travel exposed them to different ways of living that simply felt normal in the moment. Today, they're easygoing travelers who have even flown alone. The author said trips to far-away places like New Zealand (shown) and Caribbean islands exposed her children to different ways of living. Courtesy of Christina Valhouli. Traveling isn't necessarily easier when kids are older Looking back, I'm glad we didn't put off traveling with our kids. If we had waited for an "ideal" age, we would have missed years of seeing the world together — and milestones like my older son taking his first steps on a Caribbean beach. Ironically, travel isn't necessarily easier now that they're older. At 4, I could push a kid through a museum in a stroller. As teens, they can simply refuse to go, as I discovered when they pulled out their phones in silent protest at the Picasso Museum in Barcelona. While they may roll their eyes at Picasso, I feel good knowing they can navigate an airport solo. I'll take that as a win. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Allstate suffers multi-day tech outage ahead of Thanksgiving
events.summary: U.S. insurer Allstate has been experiencing a tech outage since Monday morning, leaving customers nationwide unable to access their accounts, review their policy information, file claims, pay their bills, and more, just ahead of the U.S. Thanksgiving holidays. The outage has been impacting both the company’s website and mobile app, TechCrunch confirmed. The breakdown follows a report from earlier this month that Allstate was planning to lay off up to 10% of its staff as part of an AI-driven efficiency push. (The company had not confirmed the report, which was attributed to unnamed sources.) Allstate’s outage is the latest in a series of disruptions to services such as Microsoft Outlook and Teams , the airlines , Apple Pay, and several banks. Trump administration officials have said the outages are not being caused by cyberattacks, but are rather being caused by a recent set of upgrades to systems, many of which run on older technology. Those systems are now in need of more frequent security and bug fixes as AI makes it easier and faster to discover vulnerabilities. At present, a message on Allstate’s website advises customers trying to log in that its services aren’t available, and that the company is “working to restore access as soon as possible.” On X, Allstate is employing what appear to be automated replies to customer complaints , asking them to DM the Allstate account with more information. Downdetector , a crowdsourced outage-reporting website, shows users began reporting Allstate’s outage from Monday morning. However, the company hasn’t yet issued a formal statement about the disruption, what’s causing it, or when it may be resolved. In the meantime, local insurance agents have been fielding calls and emails from customers who aren’t able to use the company’s online services. The timing of the outage is particularly bad given that Thanksgiving is a big travel holiday in the U.S., which means there will be car accidents. Customers will be left without a way to get in touch with their auto insurer to file claims and get roadside assistance through Allstate’s app. Allstate did not immediately return a request for comment. events.title: I tried 8 different types of store-bought biscuits, and the best melted in my mouth
events.summary: I compared biscuits from Annie's, Red Lobster, Trader Joe's, Immaculate Baking, Amazon Fresh, and Pillsbury. Gabbi Shaw/Business Insider Biscuits are a beloved side at many Thanksgiving meals. I tried eight different biscuit mixes and doughs to see which was the tastiest. The original Pillsbury Biscuits and the Red Lobster Cheddar Bay Biscuits came out on top. Thanksgiving is upon us, which means families around the country are preparing their kitchens for a long day of cooking. Not every dish needs to be made from scratch, though. I decided to test eight store-bought biscuit brands to see which might make it to my Thanksgiving table. A couple of years ago, I tried Annie's Organic Flaky Biscuits, Red Lobster Cheddar Bay Biscuits, Trader Joe's Organic Biscuits, Immaculate Organic Biscuits, Happy Belly Jumbo Buttermilk Biscuits, and three different kinds from Pillsbury: its Original Flaky Layers, Grands! Southern Homestyle Southern Recipe, and Grands! Southern Homestyle Butter Tastin'. The brands are still available this year, although Amazon has since consolidated its Happy Belly and Amazon Fresh brands under the Amazon Grocery name. All were delicious, though some were slightly tastier — and better value — than others. Here's how I ranked them, from my least favorite to my favorite. For me, biscuits are one of the most beloved parts of Thanksgiving dinner. I put eight types of store-bought biscuits (from six different brands) to the test. Karen Warren/Houston Chronicle via Getty Images There are a lot of options in grocery stores, so I decided to try all the biscuit mixes and doughs I could find — both in my local store and online — ahead of my Thanksgiving feast. I was looking for biscuits that were light, flaky, and buttery, with a hint of sweetness. I'm put off by biscuits that are thick and cakey, and seem more like dinner rolls. In my opinion, a good biscuit tastes delicious without butter, so I didn't add any to the ones I bought, except when they came with butter. I ended up with seven tubes of dough and one boxed mix. All the biscuit mixes I used. Gabbi Shaw/Business Insider I bought bake-at-home biscuits from Annie's, Red Lobster, Trader Joe's, Immaculate Organic Biscuits, Pillsbury, and Happy Belly, which is now under the Amazon Grocery name. The Red Lobster biscuits were the only ones to come in a box, and its recipe yielded six to 10 biscuits. The other types, which were all canned, each contained eight. For each tube, I had to peel off the wrapper and use a spoon to pop the seam of the packaging. A popped biscuit can. Gabbi Shaw/Business Insider I did this seven times, and it scared me every time. In terms of preparation, the brands were almost exactly the same. Biscuit dough. Gabbi Shaw/Business Insider The oven temperatures ranged from 350 to 375 degrees, but that was essentially the only difference between recipes. I appreciated that the Pillsbury options included directions for using an air fryer, too. The only baking experience that differed significantly was the Red Lobster biscuits. Gabbi Shaw/Business Insider The recipe required combining the dry mix, water, and cheese. I then had to portion out the biscuits, leaving me with sticky, messy hands. The biscuits also mostly looked the same before baking, apart from one. Gabbi Shaw/Business Insider Pillsbury's Butter Tastin' flavor, pictured, looked slightly different — it had butter flecks that were visible in the dough. After a day of baking, I ended up with a platter of golden biscuits, and I was ready to compare them. All of my biscuits. Gabbi Shaw/Business Insider It took a few hours of swapping out baking sheets in my oven, but eventually it was time to taste them. My least favorite were the Pillsbury Southern Homestyle Southern Recipe biscuits. Pillsbury Southern Homestyle Grands Southern Recipe. Gabbi Shaw/Business Insider The biscuits, which cost $2.99 for eight, emerged from the oven looking golden and smelling delicious, but unfortunately they tasted dry and cakey to me. I had a similar experience with the Happy Belly biscuits. Happy Belly Jumbo Buttermilk Biscuits. Gabbi Shaw/Business Insider I thought they were more like thick dinner rolls than light biscuits. At $1.96, these were cheaper than the Pillsbury Southern Homestyle Southern Recipe. The next three brands in my ranking were all virtually indistinguishable from each other. Annie's, Trader Joe's, and Immaculate biscuits. Gabbi Shaw/Business Insider I thought Annie's Organic Flaky Biscuits ($7.69), Trader Joe's Organic Biscuits ($4.49), and Immaculate Organic Biscuits ($6.49) ranked equally. All three had layers, a similar golden-brown crust, and weren't too heavy. Trader Joe's biscuits. Gabbi Shaw/Business Insider Since the Trader Joe's biscuits were the cheapest, I'd recommend them first, but you can't go wrong with any of these three options if they are the brands available to you. My third favorite biscuits were the Butter Tastin' Pillsbury biscuits. Gabbi Shaw/Business Insider These cost $3.39 for eight, putting them in the middle of the pack in terms of price. I was impressed with the subtle flavor. Gabbi Shaw/Business Insider I was apprehensive that the butter flavoring would be overwhelmingly artificial, but instead I found it had more of a hint of butter. My second favorite biscuit was the Pillsbury Original Flaky Layers. Gabbi Shaw/Business Insider These also cost $3.39 for eight. The Flaky Layers were, indeed, as flaky as any tasty biscuit could hope to be. Gabbi Shaw/Business Insider During the tasting, I described these as the "platonic ideal of a biscuit." But by far, my favorite biscuits were the Red Lobster Cheddar Bay Biscuits, which came with a garlic-herb butter. The Red Lobster biscuits. Gabbi Shaw/Business Insider At $4.49, they also cost less than some of the others I tried. They had the perfect crunchy outer layer and a melt-in-your-mouth interior. Gabbi Shaw/Business Insider Plus, the garlic butter complemented the sweetness of the biscuit. Ultimately, I had to declare this brand as the winner. A biscuit selfie. Gabbi Shaw/Business Insider If you're short on time and are looking for a more classic biscuit, you can't go wrong with the Pillsbury Original Flaky Layers. But if you have any extra time and counter space this Thanksgiving, I'd recommend the Red Lobster biscuits. events.title: Wealthy investors seek tax savings from municipal bonds as yields remain elevated
events.summary: Thanks to rising rates, top bracket investors can use municipal bonds to earn high tax-equivalent yields and offset gains elsewhere in their portfolio. Done right, bonds can even be used to reduce taxes rather than defer them. Investment advisors told CNBC how this "stay rich" strategy works. The business of tax-loss harvesting is booming with wealthy investors pouring billions of dollars into products like tax-aware long-short strategies. As 10-year Treasury yields have climbed to levels not seen since 2007, tax-savvy clients are also turning to municipal bonds to keep more of what they earn. "High-net-worth investors, because of all the noise in direct indexing and tax-aware long-short strategies, have begun to expect tax management from all of their investments, including their fixed income," said Gavin Romm, senior vice president and head of separately managed accounts at AllianceBernstein. While tax-loss harvesting can be done with other types of fixed income, high-income investors typically gravitate to municipal bonds for their tax-exempt income. Separately managed accounts, known as SMAs, held about $1.6 trillion in municipal bonds at the end of 2025, a 44% jump since 2017, per JPMorgan's estimate. For top-bracket investors, municipal bonds can offer a twofold benefit: tax-equivalent yields that approach long-run stock-market returns, and losses that may offset gains elsewhere in a portfolio, according to Ran Leshem, BlackRock's head of SMA solutions. BlackRock, which manages $42 billion in muni SMAs, estimates that assets across muni SMAs have grown by 10% industry-wide over the past three years. "You can get a tax-equivalent yield of over 7% that is becoming quite compelling for a lot of clients," said Leshem. "We are seeing yields that haven't been around for quite a few years, so it's a good opportunity for clients to lock in yields at these higher rates." Rising yields earlier this fall pushed bond prices down, leaving some investors with paper losses, Leshem said. However, tax-loss harvesting can be harder with bonds than with stock, particularly municipal bonds, he noted. The municipal bond market is highly fragmented with more than 50,000 issuers, and it costs more and takes longer to transact, he said. "There might not always be liquidity or someone willing to buy it for a fair price," Leshem said. That said, bonds can offer a distinct tax advantage from equities, according to Romm. By selling a stock at a loss, an investor can reduce the current tax bill by offsetting gains elsewhere. In exchange, the investor faces a potentially larger taxable gain if they later sell the replacement stock. However, if an investor sells a bond at a loss and buys a replacement bond for more than its par value (or face value) the replacement bond's tax basis is generally adjusted down over time as it approaches maturity, Romm said. If the investor holds it to maturity, the amount repaid may match that adjusted basis, leaving no capital gain or loss on the replacement bond, he added. "Tax-loss harvesting with equities, by definition, is tax deferral," he said. "With bonds, when done thoughtfully, it is actually tax avoidance." That said, investors must be careful not to violate the IRS wash-sale rule by buying a "substantially identical asset" within 30 days before or after the sale. That tax benefit gives fixed income another job beyond providing income and stability, Romm said. "These aren't really positioned as get-rich strategies. They're more of stay-rich strategies," he said. events.title: Democrats Vow to Shield Smithsonian From Any Trump Overhaul
events.summary: A D.C.-area train commuter photographed a White House staffer’s laptop and notes, which showed a draft plan for the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History. Photo illustration by Jovelle Tamayo/ProPublica. Source images: obtained by ProPublica, Elizabeth Frantz for ProPublica. A top congressional Democrat announced she will investigate the Trump White House’s potential overhaul of the leadership and curatorial decisions at the Smithsonian Institution, the independent agency that oversees 21 national museums. In a letter sent on Tuesday to the Smithsonian’s Board of Regents, Rep. Chellie Pingree, D-Maine, cited ProPublica’s recent story on the draft plans by a White House staffer targeting one of the Smithsonian’s most prominent museums, calling the reporting “extremely concerning.” Read More Spotted on the D.C. Metro: Trump Staffer Accidentally Reveals Plan for Smithsonian Overhaul Pingree, who is slated to lead the subcommittee that controls the Smithsonian’s funding in the next Congress, said the plans revealed in the ProPublica story align with the administration’s broader efforts to interfere with the Smithsonian, which receives federal funding but is governed by a 17-person Board of Regents whose members include the chief justice of the United States, members of Congress, the vice president and private citizens. In an interview with ProPublica, Pingree said that she intended her letter to put the Smithsonian governing board on notice that the incoming Democratic majority in Congress is monitoring the institution to make sure the board upholds its responsibility to keep the agency independent from political pressure. “No White House employee riding on the Metro gets to design a plan for what future exhibits look like or gets to veto staffers or exhibits at the Smithsonian,” Pingree said. “That’s not how it works.” Pingree told ProPublica that she plans to use her powers as chair in the next Congress to aggressively look into what she called the Trump administration’s meddling with the Smithsonian and to expose those efforts to the broader American public. “We fully intend to dig deeper than has been done in the past,” she said. Pingree’s letter comes in response to ProPublica reporting on a 25-item list of possible changes that, taken together, would amount to an unprecedented attempt by the White House to control the content and personnel of the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History, which attracts nearly 2 million people a year. Those reforms include firing many of the museum’s top officials; rolling out a new permanent exhibit called “The Riches of Our Western Civilization Inheritance”; introducing new K-12 learning materials such as a “Founders-focused curriculum titled something like Architects of Liberty: The Heroic Journey of America’s Founders OR Profiles in Liberty: Washington and America’s Heroic Men of Courage”; and unveiling a new “Colossus Statue” of George Washington for the museum’s entrance. The draft plans were visible on the laptop and in handwritten notes of a White House staffer who was riding a D.C.-area Metro train in late October. A nearby commuter took pictures of the materials and sent them to ProPublica reporters, who in turn verified the information. It’s unclear what kind of reception the plans have received inside the Trump White House. The staffer and White House did not respond to requests for comment for the story. Also on Tuesday, Lonnie Bunch, the Smithsonian Institution’s outgoing leader, responded to ProPublica’s reporting in a message sent to employees. “The intended use of this list is unclear,” Bunch wrote in his letter . “What remains clear is that the Smithsonian is an independent institution with the responsibility and privilege to present accurate information to millions of visitors through our scholarship and educational programs.” Pingree was not the only member of Congress who responded to ProPublica’s reporting with a pledge to defend the Smithsonian’s independence. Sen. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., said on social media that if he becomes chair of the Senate Rules Committee — which has jurisdiction over the Smithsonian — in the next Congress, “we will protect it from Trump’s interference and overreach.” “The Smithsonian is NOT a federal agency, it is an independent, nonpartisan organization overseen by Congress – not the White House,” Padilla wrote . Incoming Congressman Fred Wellman, a Democrat elected this month to represent the suburbs of St. Louis, responded even more forcefully to ProPublica’s reporting on social media. “Over my dead body,” he wrote . The post Democrats Vow to Shield Smithsonian From Any Trump Overhaul appeared first on ProPublica .

events.title: Trump proposing new tariffs on 14 partners including China and EU
events.summary: Administration is suggesting an added 20% tax on Chinese imports, which would bring the total to about 40% Donald Trump is proposing new tariffs on 14 trading partners, including China and the European Union, that would go into effect early next year, the office of the US trade representative said on Wednesday. The administration is proposing an additional 20% tax on Chinese imports, which would bring the total tax to about 40%. Other countries affected by the new tariffs include Bangladesh, ‌Cambodia, the European Union, India, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam. In February, the supreme court ruled Trump’s so-called Liberation Day tariffs illegal. The court issued a narrow decision saying the administration had improperly used a specific emergency powers law to implement the tariffs, but did not broadly curb the president’s power to introduce new tariffs. The administration is now using section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 as the legal basis for the new rounds of tariffs. The law gives the executive branch power to respond to unfair foreign trade practices after conducting formal investigations. Though the White House did not give a timeline for the new tariffs, it said they could go into effect in January at the earliest. The US trade office said it would hold hearings on the new tariffs and its investigation into the unfair trade practices on 25 January. This is the second major batch of section 301 tariffs, after the White House announced a broad slate of tariffs on more than 80 countries in July, including the UK, Mexico and Canada, saying the countries had failed to enforce bans on forced labor. A lawsuit fighting those tariffs is currently awaiting a decision in the court of international trade. “For decades, many of our trading partners have adopted industrial strategies built on targeting manufacturing, wage and labor suppression, financial and other support, non-market economy inputs, and other market distorting practices that tilt the trade balance in their favor while eroding America’s manufacturing base,” the US trade representative, Jamieson Greer, said in a statement on Wednesday. “President Trump is proposing to take action to bring about the elimination of these unfair acts, policies, and practices. In doing so, we can level the playing field for American workers and chart a new, more sustainable course for the world economy.” Tariffs have proven unpopular with US voters, who handed Democrats a decisive victory in the midterm elections that will give the party control of Congress. The Yale Budget Lab estimates that tariffs currently in effect have added an additional $900 in costs for each US household. The rising cost of living was the number one issue for voters ahead of November’s midterm elections, according to a Harris Poll survey for the Guardian. An earlier Harris poll found seven in 10 Americans blamed tariffs for higher prices. Consumer prices rose an annualized 3.8% in October, the Bureau of Economic Analysis announced on Wednesday, the highest rate since May and well above the Federal Reserve’s 2% annual target.

events.title: My best friend and I live on opposite sides of the country. We stay connected by taking joint birthday trips.
events.summary: My best friend and I stay connected through annual trips. Laura Grace Tarpley My best friend, Heather, and I live on opposite sides of the country. To stay connected, we take annual joint birthday trips together. Our trips have changed over the years, and sometimes, our spouses or families join us. I met my best friend Heather when we were both 6 years old. We attended the same small school from first grade through high school, and as teenagers, we bonded over a shared urge to see the world beyond our little bubble. Our first trip together was a school-sponsored tour of Europe the summer before senior year, where we explored major tourist hubs like London and Paris but really fell in love with under-the-radar spots we found in Lyon, France. We bonded over our love of trying new foods, from escargot to fancy cheeses, and exploring tiny boutiques instead of touristy gift shops. Now, in our mid-30s, our lives look very different from what they did back in high school. My husband and I settled down in Olympia, Washington, and Heather and her family live in Wilmington, North Carolina. Although we live on opposite sides of the country, we've found a way to stay close through our shared love of travel with annual birthday trips . We've kept the tradition alive for 8 years now One year, we backpacked through Great Smoky Mountains National Park. Laura Grace Tarpley The tradition began in July 2018, when Heather wanted to take a long-weekend trip for her 26th birthday. Since I was in Baltimore for the summer while my husband was interning in Washington, DC , we decided she should come visit, and I could show her around both cities. When you live far away from a friend and finally reunite, it's easy to spend time just catching up on what's happening in the other person's life rather than making new memories together. But that wasn't the case this time. We had so much fun trying new things on this trip — from touring landmarks in DC to spending a rainy day in a brewery and tasting seafood dishes we never would've considered when we were kids — that we ended up making it an annual tradition to celebrate both of our birthdays. During our first trip, I showed Heather around Baltimore and DC. Laura Grace Tarpley Heather and I have each changed over the years, in big and small ways. We might be in different phases of life, and we may switch up our travel destinations, but one thing stays the same — we always find ways to spend time together in ways we both enjoy. And that usually involves two things: eating at new restaurants and exploring the outdoors. For example, Heather visited me in Nashville for our annual birthday trip right after I moved to the city in 2019. Because it's a major foodie destination, we filled the itinerary with restaurants I loved and wanted Heather to try. However, when many restaurants closed down for the COVID-19 pandemic the next year, we decided to pivot and go backpacking in Great Smoky Mountains National Park . We have a lot of great memories from that trip, but we'd both tell you that in hindsight, planning a backpacking trip in the Tennessee heat and humidity probably wasn't our best idea. There was a lot of sweat and nausea on that excursion, but we still enjoyed our time together. When she visited me in Washington for our 31st birthday, I took her to the famous Hoh Rainforest in Olympic National Park. Her favorite part of the hike was the Hall of Mosses, since she creates custom moss art as part of her job. She was mesmerized. We may have different careers and hobbies, but we've built trips around activities we both enjoy to make each one special. Our birthday trips have changed as we've gotten older This year, I went to Wilmington to visit Heather and her family. Laura Grace Tarpley Over the years, our trips have started to look a little different, and sometimes, they even include our loved ones. The year that Heather became a mom, her husband and baby came on the trip with her. Our husbands are friends, and mine wanted to meet her child, so they joined us on most of our activities. Some years, our trips are more about seeing each other's lives than going on adventures. This year, I visited her in Wilmington, where we attended a comedy show and took the ferry to spend time in a quaint beach town. But I also read bedtime stories to her daughter, and we spent evenings completing a jigsaw puzzle while rewatching " When Harry Met Sally ." These aren't bad changes. In fact, I'm grateful that even though our lives look vastly different from what they did eight, 15, or 20 years ago, we still prioritize seeing each other every year. events.title: I tried 5 kinds of store-bought instant mashed potatoes. The best tasted nearly homemade.
events.summary: I tried instant mashed potatoes to determine which one is the best for Thanksgiving. Erin McDowell/Business Insider I tried instant mashed potatoes from Idahoan in various flavors. Idahoan nailed it with buttery, flavorful mashed potatoes that were perfectly light and creamy. I liked the brand's Baby Bliss mashed potatoes best. With a mountain of dishes to make for Thanksgiving, sometimes it's necessary to take a shortcut or two. Despite usually swearing by homemade mashed potatoes , I decided to try out a variety of instant mashed-potato brands and flavors to determine the best option at the grocery store, and to see if any were good enough to earn a spot on my Thanksgiving table. I tried five flavors of Idahoan instant mashed potatoes, one of the biggest mashed-potato brands in the US — it reported in January 2026 that it accounts for 80% of the US packaged potato market. It was also the only brand available at my local grocery stores in the Northeast. The flavors included classic butter, roasted garlic, sour cream and chives, baby bliss, and cheddar broccoli. For the comparison, I followed the instructions on each package. Almost every kind of instant mashed potatoes I tried required only a kettle to boil water, a measuring cup, and a bowl. Here's how they compared, from my least favorite to my favorite. Idahoan's classic mashed potatoes required just the mashed potato packets and water. Idahoan classic mashed potatoes. Erin McDowell/Business Insider A 4-ounce bag of Idahoan instant mashed potatoes costs $1.67 and makes 4 servings. I appreciated the ease and not having to take up precious stove space, and I imagine I would appreciate that even more if I were actually cooking these for Thanksgiving. To make each flavor of potatoes, I boiled two cups of water and added it to a large measuring cup. I then added the entire packet of potatoes, covered it with tin foil for five minutes, and then mixed the potatoes before serving in a separate bowl. The potatoes had a good, fluffy consistency. Idahoan classic mashed potatoes. Erin McDowell/Business Insider Despite being made from a powder, they weren't grainy or thick.  The classic version of Idahoan instant mashed potatoes looked and tasted like homemade mashed potatoes. Idahoan classic mashed potatoes. Erin McDowell/Business Insider If someone had told me they had come from a packet, I probably wouldn't have believed them. The butter flavor was prominent, in a good way. My only criticism of the classic mashed potatoes was that they were slightly salty for my liking. I also tried Idahoan's sour cream-and-chive flavor. Idahoan sour cream and chive mashed potatoes. Erin McDowell/Business Insider A 4-ounce bag cost me $1.67 and contained 4 servings. Idahoan's sour cream-and-chive mashed potatoes had a light and fluffy texture. Idahoan sour cream and chive mashed potatoes. Erin McDowell/Business Insider I could also spot specks of chives mixed into the potatoes, which gave them an authentic appearance. The sour cream-and-chive flavor really came through. Idahoan sour cream and chive mashed potatoes. Erin McDowell/Business Insider I was again impressed by both the texture and flavor of the mashed potatoes. Unlike the classic flavor, I didn't find this flavor too salty at all. Rather, they were creamy and seasoned perfectly. I also tried Idahoan's cheddar broccoli mashed potatoes, which ranked as my third-favorite option overall. Erin McDowell/Business Insider The 4.1-ounce packet cost $1.67 at my local Big Y grocery store. The potatoes had a pronounced cheese flavor that made them feel more indulgent than a classic buttery mash. Erin McDowell/Business Insider I especially liked the savory cheddar notes, which came through clearly without being overwhelming. However, I didn't get much broccoli flavor in my serving, so that element felt a little underwhelming. Erin McDowell/Business Insider The texture was also thicker and stodgier than the smoother varieties I tried. Still, it would be a convenient choice for anyone craving a cheesy, comfort-food-style side dish. My second-favorite flavor of instant mashed potatoes was the Idahoan roasted garlic. Idahoan roasted garlic mashed potatoes. Erin McDowell/Business Insider Just like the brand's other flavors, a 4-ounce bag cost me $1.79 and contained 4 servings. Right away after mixing, I could smell the garlic — I even saw flecks of it in the mashed potatoes. Idahoan roasted garlic mashed potatoes. Erin McDowell/Business Insider The potatoes also had a light, fluffy texture while still holding their shape. These mashed potatoes were buttery and extremely flavorful. Idahoan roasted garlic mashed potatoes. Erin McDowell/Business Insider Even for someone who can be a little sensitive to garlic, the garlic flavor was strong but not overpowering. I thought this kind would pair well with gravy and other Thanksgiving foods. Think garlic bread meets mashed potatoes — what more could you want on the holidays? Idahoan's Baby Bliss red mashed potatoes tasted practically homemade. Erin McDowell/Business Insider It cost $1.67 for a packet at my local Big Y grocery store. The potatoes turned out shockingly smooth, and I could see flecks of red potato. Erin McDowell/Business Insider The mix had a pleasantly rustic texture that made it feel more substantial than standard instant mashed potatoes. I would make these potatoes again — with a few simple additions to really make them the star of the show. Erin McDowell/Business Insider The potatoes' mild, buttery flavor was comforting without tasting overly salty or artificial, but they would probably taste even better if I added in melted butter or a dollop or two of sour cream — simple additions I always have in my kitchen. I also liked that the red-potato flecks gave the side dish some visual interest straight from the packet. The potatoes would be an easy addition to a weeknight dinner, but they also tasted good enough to serve alongside a holiday meal. For the price, I would totally make these potatoes again. events.title: Nationwide unveils 1% deposit mortgage deal for first-time buyers
events.summary: People can borrow up to six times their income, but brokers sound alarm over risks of negative equity if house prices fall A mortgage deal that lets first-time buyers borrow 99% of a property’s value has prompted warnings that even a small dip in house prices could result in borrowers falling into negative equity. On Wednesday, Nationwide unveiled a mortgage enabling people to buy a home with just a 1% deposit and potentially borrow up to six times their income. Britain’s biggest building society said it was putting £1bn a year behind the new product, which it believes will open up home ownership to more than 5,000 additional first-time buyers each year. During the last couple of years, a number of mortgages have gone on sale that require only a small deposit, or no deposit at all. Nationwide said its 99% home loan would “combine meaningful support with responsible lending” – but the mortgage’s launch coincided with data suggesting UK house prices were falling amid the continuing challenging economic conditions. Lloyds bank said UK house prices dropped by 0.6% in October and were down 1.2% year on year, while the property firm Savills said this month that average prices were expected to drift lower during the rest of 2026 and fall by 1.5% in 2027 . The Nationwide product is a five-year fixed-rate deal with an interest rate of 5.99%. While many commentators have welcomed it as a lifeline to struggling first-time buyers, some brokers cautioned borrowers could be pushed into negative equity if prices did fall. Negative equity is when someone is living in a property worth less than their mortgage. Negative equity can leave homeowners trapped, unable to climb the housing ladder as their homes reduce in value. Riz Malik, an independent financial adviser at the firm R3 Wealth, said: “Nationwide is sticking its neck out with a 1% deposit deal, as even a small slip in prices could leave borrowers in negative equity.” Darryl Dhoffer, the founder of the brokerage firm The Mortgage Geezer, said those signing up “must tread carefully”. He added: “Borrowing up to six times income at a 5.99% rate creates massive monthly commitments and leaves almost zero equity buffer – meaning even a slight market dip could trigger negative equity.” Negative equity mainly becomes a problem when homeowners intend to sell their property. As a result, the Nationwide deal was probably most suitable for those buyers “planning to stay put well beyond five years”, said Craig Fish, the managing director of the broker Lodestone Mortgages . He added: “This is a genuine step forward for first-time buyers who can afford the monthly payments but can’t save a deposit while paying rent.” Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Henry Jordan, Nationwide’s group director of mortgages, said “a range of controls” were built into the product to reduce the risk of negative equity. The deal is only available as a five-year fix, providing certainty over monthly payments, and is restricted to “used” houses only meaning it will not be available to those buying a flat or a newbuild home. In addition, every applicant must receive mortgage advice and “robust” affordability checks will be carried out, with minimum income requirements imposed and the exclusion of self-employed people. Jordan added: “I don’t think anyone is forecasting a fall in house prices over the next five years.” Savills said it expected UK house prices to rise by 15.8% – or £56,500 on average – over the five years to 2031, adding that price growth was expected to accelerate during the second half of 2028.

events.title: How should investors evaluate performance?
events.summary: Why fund performance needs a detailed review in concentrated marketsA fund’s headline return tells only part of the story. Before selling a fund that has underperformed its benchmark, investors should ask why and whether it still meets their needs.This matters when a small group of companies dominate stock market returns. A fund that spreads its investments more widely may underperform a concentrated index. That does not necessarily mean its manager has made poor decisions. Equally, diversification should not become an excuse for weak stock picking.There could also be a big impact on pensions, which play a vital role in people’s financial futures. We want pension schemes to deliver long-term value for savers. Firms and asset owners should look at the bigger picture, including a fund manager’s stated investment objective, strategy and style.How market concentration makes a real difference to returnsWhen a handful of stocks drive market performance, a manager’s decision on how much to invest in them can have a significant effect on returns.The ‘Magnificent Seven’ (Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, Meta, Microsoft, NVIDIA and Tesla) illustrate the point. Together, they made up about 34% of the S&P 500 Index on 11 November 2026, according to Bloomberg. They also accounted for around 25% of the MSCI World Index in October 2026.Managers seeking a more diversified portfolio may hold less of these companies than the index does. If those stocks continue to outperform, the fund may deliver lower returns than the index. For investors, the challenge is to work out whether a fund has underperformed because of the investment approach or by poor decisions. Looking only at the headline return number can’t answer that question.Start with the fund’s purposeMost investors hold a fund as part of a wider portfolio. They may have chosen it for exposure to a particular region, smaller companies, an investment style or a sustainability goal. Others may want it to generate income.So, the first question isn’t simply: ‘Did this fund beat the market?’Instead, investors should ask: ‘Is this fund fulfilling its intended role?’That means looking at its stated objective, strategy and style (for example, whether it invests in particular countries or sectors, or favours value or growth companies). Investors should also consider the portfolio’s overall balance of risk and return and the timeframe for assessing results.A fund chosen to bring a different investment approach to a portfolio should be assessed with that purpose in mind. Its contribution cannot always be judged by comparing it with a broad market index alone.Understand the benchmark and the risksA market index can be a useful benchmark, but investors need to understand how the fund uses it.Fund documents should clearly explain the investment strategy, the benchmark’s role and any important investment styles or biases. Before buying a fund, investors should understand why and when it might perform differently from its benchmark.If a fund underperforms because of an investment approach that was clearly disclosed to investors, they may have good reason to stay invested. The fund may be behaving as expected and still serving its purpose within the wider portfolio.But clear disclosure is not a free pass. Investors should also examine whether the manager has made good investment decisions when putting that approach into practice.Separate investment style from stock-picking skillConsider a fund with a disclosed ‘value’ style. Investors may have chosen it to help balance the risks and potential returns of their overall portfolio.That fund could underperform a broad market benchmark when other investment styles are doing better. This alone would not mean it offers poor value.The next step is to examine what drove its returns. Looking at the reasons behind a fund’s performance and comparing it with an appropriate value-focused benchmark can help investors assess how well the manager is picking stocks.The aim is to check that the fund’s style is not masking poor investment decisions. If the investment approach was not clearly explained, or stock picking has been weak despite taking that approach into account, investors may reconsider whether to stay invested.Before switching, they should apply the same scrutiny to any new fund: how might it perform in different market conditions, what will drive its returns, and how will it fit into their portfolio?Look at value in the roundOur Assessment of Value rules require authorised fund managers to assess their funds’ value annually. This means considering performance alongside factors such as costs and service quality.We expect managers to account for disclosed style biases when assessing performance. In our industry feedback in 2021 and 2023, we highlighted the need to clearly explain these biases and the associated risk of underperforming market benchmarks in fund documents.The proposed Value for Money framework for workplace pensions also considers performance, costs and service quality. This should encourage pension schemes to assess how different investments contribute to their objectives over time.Ask better questions before sellingThe message is not to ignore underperformance. It’s to understand it before acting.Investors should ask whether the fund is delivering what they were led to expect, whether the manager’s investment decisions stand up to scrutiny, and whether it still belongs in the wider portfolio.Those using consultants should ask how their analysis answers these questions. A considered decision starts with the bigger picture – not just the headline return.

events.title: High prices force many across the US to scale back for Thanksgiving: ‘We can’t afford the food’
events.summary: Americans are opting for smaller gatherings, reconsidering travel or swapping expensive ingredients for cheaper alternatives Thanksgiving is just one day away, but for some Americans, the holiday may look a little different this year as higher costs for food, drinks , household goods, air travel and gasoline have prompted some families to rethink their plans and spending. The Guardian recently asked readers across the United States how they were marking the holiday this year and whether higher prices had affected their plans or made them rethink their usual traditions. While some said their plans remained unchanged, many said that they were scaling back and cutting costs. Some said that they were opting for smaller gatherings, reconsidering travel or choosing not to host at all. Others said they were swapping more expensive ingredients for cheaper alternatives or cooking less than they normally would. In Florida, one man in his 60s said that he and his girlfriend were “scaling way back” this year. “The expense has made it impossible for us to have what we usually do,” he said, adding that “food is horribly expensive”. Instead of doing three different pies, they are preparing just one this year, along with a single side dish. Cindy Van Vreede, 66, in Wisconsin, told the Guardian that the senior center where she goes for “free meals several times a week, is offering to bring a free Thanksgiving dinner to me at my home”. “By not traveling or expected to bring a dish, I am saving money staying at home,” she said. “I’m also saving money on gas because I’m not driving my car two hours each way.” A recent report from the American Farm Bureau Federation estimated that Americans preparing a Thanksgiving meal will face “higher prices overall this year”, with the average cost of a 10-person dinner up 6% from last year. It marks the first time since 2022 that American shoppers will see an increase “in the price of goods for Thanksgiving dinner”, according to the report. The increase for this year is “largely driven by increased prices for Thanksgiving staples such as turkey, milk, rolls and cranberries”, the report says, noting the increases “aren’t a complete surprise as the effects of significant spikes in prices for critical inputs throughout the supply chain, like fuel for processing and transportation, have made their way to consumers”. America’s farmers and ranchers, the report states, are also facing “significant challenges, with record diesel costs, elevated fertilizer prices, increased labor expenses, and a bigger bill for items like rent and electricity – all of which hurt their ability to break even at the end of the year”. In Texas, 55-year-old Cheryl said that she was “probably not going to celebrate this year”. “I’ll miss it, just getting together with my family,” she said, “but we can’t afford the food, and going to a friend’s house is unlikely, too.” Cheryl said that she had watched as her “regular weekly groceries have gone up so much it’s getting harder to afford them”. Others are finding ways to preserve some of their traditions while spending less. In Virginia, 39-year-old Hannah told the Guardian: “We’re going low-key.” “This year, I’m sticking with a few essential dishes – turkey, gravy, potatoes, cranberries, and mac and cheese,” she said. “I’m using recipes that use cheaper ingredients. I’m having my 10-year-old make Kraft mac and cheese from the box rather than using a homemade recipe with more expensive cheeses.” Hannah said that she was spending “more time than ever looking at prices at different stores, and I’ve been using store loyalty programs to squeeze extra savings”. A recent survey by Lending Tree found that, among those planning to celebrate Thanksgiving, more than half said that inflation was affecting their plans or budget, with 25% saying that they were changing their food choices as a result, 22% saying they were using more coupons and 14% saying they were cutting back on guests. The survey also found that nearly two-thirds of respondents said that they may need to borrow to host Thanksgiving, including 38% who said they planned to use credit cards to cover the costs. In Seattle, Liliya said that she was trying to persuade her partner “not to order the whole turkey but to buy a few cuts instead”. Their Thanksgiving, she said, “will be a very small family gathering, no different from other years outside of me trying to scale down on the turkey”. For others, the expense of traveling for the holiday has prompted a change of plans. A woman in North Carolina said that she had decided not to travel this year, partly due to the cost of “fuel and lodging”. Instead, she said, they will be treating themselves to a restaurant meal.
