events.title: I tried 3 different ways to use leftover turkey. One recipe was so good that I'd cook a whole bird just to make it again.
events.summary: I made a salad, soup, and a sandwich using leftover turkey from a Thanksgiving dinner. Terri Peters In preparation for Thanksgiving , I looked for great ways to use up leftover turkey breast. The sandwich I made with leftover turkey and sides took more effort than it was worth. I made a soup that was so delicious I'd make another turkey just to have an excuse to eat it. Most years, I cook a full Thanksgiving meal for my family, which leaves us with lots of leftovers in the fridge. Instead of heating up the same dishes all week, I decided to try three recipes that could give our extra turkey (and some sides) new life. From a simple turkey salad to a stacked sandwich, here's how each leftover-utilizing recipe stacked up. For one dish, I tried making a turkey salad. Terri Peters The easiest recipe to follow was for turkey salad , which was similar to chicken versions I've made in the past. I used a recipe from the cooking blog Ahead of Thyme. The ingredients are simple: celery, green onion, paprika, mayo, Dijon mustard, salt, pepper, and finely chopped leftover turkey. I made a few changes to the recipe, but the dish was still good. Terri Peters I don't like the crunch of celery or onion, so for this turkey salad, I made a few adjustments. Instead of adding diced celery, green onions, and salt, I just used celery salt to flavor the salad without adding a harsh crunch. The turkey salad was great on a sandwich, and I'd make it again. Terri Peters My turkey-salad sandwich tasted great. It had plenty of flavor from the mustard, paprika, and celery salt. Overall, I thought it was simple to prepare, and as an added bonus, it required ingredients I already had in my pantry and refrigerator. I'd make this turkey salad again if I had leftovers on hand. This warmThanksgiving-inspired sandwich was much harder to make. Terri Peters Our typical Thanksgiving leftovers include things like turkey breast, cranberry sauce, mac and cheese , mashed potatoes, and green-bean casserole. For the first recipe, I gathered them all up to make a sandwich using a recipe from The New York Times . I also grabbed thick sandwich bread and turkey gravy. The stuffing layer was the most labor-intensive part of the sandwich. Terri Peters I began by mixing the mayonnaise and cranberry sauce to create a cranberry mayo. Then, I combined chopped turkey with gravy to make another sauce. Since we didn't have leftover stuffing, I made a box of stuffing , pressed it into a square pan, and refrigerated it until it hardened. Once it was solid, I fried each side in a bit of oil. This step took the longest and required some advanced prep. Unfortunately, layering all of the ingredients was pretty messy. Terri Peters The recipe called for stacking layers of cranberry mayonnaise, gravy, mac and cheese, stuffing, green-bean casserole , mashed potatoes, and the turkey between two slices of bread. I knew it would be a messy disaster before I even put the two pieces of bread together. The sandwich tasted good, but it wasn’t worth the hassle. Terri Peters Overall, the sandwich was messy and difficult to eat. When I tried to take a bite of it, all the ingredients slid onto the plate. I ended up eating everything with a knife and fork, which made me wonder why I went through the hassle of stacking it all into a sandwich. I can't say I'd make this again. Lastly, I tried a recipe for turkey soup. Terri Peters I'm a fan of hearty fall meals, so I was happy to find a recipe for leftover turkey soup on the cooking blog Mel's Kitchen Cafe. Out of the three recipes, the soup had the longest ingredient list, including things like long-grain wild rice, chicken broth, and diced carrots, celery, and onions. Right from the beginning, the soup felt perfectly rustic. Terri Peters I love a soup dish that starts with cooking aromatics like carrots, celery, and onions. It took me a bit of time to dice them all, but I was confident my hard work would pay off. Simmering the chopped vegetables in a bit of butter immediately set the tone for the savory soup I was about to enjoy. Even before I added the cream, I could tell the soup was going to be good. Terri Peters After sautéeing the chopped vegetables, I added chicken broth and a box of long-grain wild rice to the pot. Then, I let it simmer until the grains were cooked through. I also added the half-and-half the recipe called for, though I think you could forgo it to make a lighter soup . I'd cook another Thanksgiving turkey just to have an excuse to make the soup. Terri Peters Once I added the half-and-half, the soup was creamy and ready to serve. I thought the finished dish was so delicious, hearty, and savory. I loved the flavor of the vegetables and turkey. My family returned for seconds, so we hardly had any leftovers the following day. The turkey soup was my clear winner. Terri Peters Of all three recipes, the one I'd be most likely to make again is the creamy, delicious turkey-and-rice soup. Making this recipe was an amazing way to turn leftover turkey from Thanksgiving into a whole new meal that's warm and filling. Honestly, I wouldn't mind cooking turkey breast again just so I had an excuse to make this soup. events.title: German firms eye Africa as global trade shocks hit traditional markets
events.summary: German businesses are optimistic about Africa, but Berlin's cautious approach to risk is holding them back from cashing in on the opportunities that their competitors from countries like the UAE and Turkey are seizing. "Africa is a land of opportunity." "The German-African relationship is a win-win." "The continent is the market of the future." That's what many business leaders and politicians have to say about Africa at the sixth edition of the German-African Business Summit in Accra, Ghana. While these descriptions aren't new, there's a palpable sense of urgency and seriousness this time. German firms are increasingly viewing Africa as an attractive destination as they scramble to find new markets amid wars in Ukraine and Iran, high energy prices, punishing US tariffs and slowing growth in traditional markets like China. "For a long time, many German companies had a secure source of revenue from the major export markets in North America and China, but the geopolitical ruptures of our time have undermined this certainty," German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier said during the event. "One could also say that it is time for new horizons, time to take a closer look at economic opportunities still waiting for us." Africa is home to some of the fastest growing economies in the world, like Ethiopia and Rwanda. Even as European and other advanced economies contend with declining working-age populations, Africa is expected to add hundreds of millions of workers in the next few decades, emerging as a key source of future labor. Germany has already signed a migration pact with Kenya and is working on one with Ghana as it seeks to attract skilled workers to help ease acute labor shortages in certain sectors at home. Even as Africa remains one of the poorest regions in the world, economic growth in parts of the continent has created a larger and more affluent consumer class over the past three decades. This group is aspirational and a growing source of demand for many of the goods that German firms want to sell, from cars to cosmetics. The continent, with its mineral wealth and renewable energy potential , is central to European Union efforts to diversify its sources of critical raw materials and reduce reliance on China-dominated supply chains. It is also playing an increasingly important role in strengthening the EU's energy security after the bloc phased out most energy imports from Russia. German firms have committed to invest billions of euros in green hydrogen projects in countries such as Mauritania and Namibia. "We don't have the capital to develop them [natural resources]. So foreign investors are coming to help us develop those resources. Whilst we are getting jobs and industrialization is taking place, they are also making profits," said Amin Amidu Sulemani, energy and infrastructure commissioner at the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS). "It's not a relationship where we send raw materials outside of Africa every time, when we can actually process them here," he told DW. What is wrong with Germany's Africa strategy? Despite Africa's growing economic appeal, many obstacles to investment remain, including corruption and governance concerns, unreliable energy supplies, foreign exchange risk and poor infrastructure. African leaders say they are working to address these challenges and improve the ease of doing business. Yet while German companies have largely remained on the sidelines, competitors from countries such as the UAE, Turkey and India have made significant inroads across the continent. German firms enjoy a strong reputation in Africa because of their engineering expertise, vocational training programs and long-term industrial investments, which are more likely to create stable jobs than investments in extractive industries. However, they have struggled to translate that goodwill into a larger commercial presence. Africa, for instance, accounts for less than 2% of the total foreign investment made by German firms over the past several decades. Business leaders complain that German firms lack adequate financing and risk protection for projects in Africa. They also criticize excessive bureaucracy and the absence of a coherent German strategy, with engagement fragmented across ministries and agencies. Industry bodies say German institutions and firms often perceive risks too broadly, treating diverse African markets as if they pose the same level of risk. "German companies can be a bit more bold and maybe also innovative in the way they approach the continent," Khadi Camara, deputy CEO of the German-African Business Association, told DW. "We see that in the companies that are successful, they don't do business as usual. Every country has its nuances that companies keep in mind and say, okay, this model works here, that model works there.

events.title: Fuel price hike will make life 'almost impossible'
events.summary: Ofgem has announced the price cap will rise from January A 26% increase in energy bills in January will make life "almost impossible" for millions of people, a charity boss has warned. Matt Cole, the CEO of the Fuel Bank Foundation which helps people living in fuel crisis, said the rise had been expected but would be difficult for people to absorb. With fuel prices already high, he said: "It's going to make what's a tough life for so many people almost impossible." Cole, from Bridgnorth, Shropshire, said the government - which is due to hand millions of households £100 to tackle rising costs - needed a long term strategy to decrease energy prices and to improve energy efficiency. Ofgem's announcement that it is raising the energy price cap means a typical bill will increase by about £37 a month in the first three months of the new year. The price will depend on how much energy a household uses however, so it could be closer to £60 extra a month in winter. The increase is the biggest since Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022 drove up prices. The Fuel Bank Foundation supports about 400,000 people every year who are in fuel poverty and Cole said its own forecast for the price cap rise had been correct "almost to the penny". He said the rise "really worries me because so many people today are already struggling to keep warm". Cole explained that a lot of people had been lowering consumption for years. In some cases that meant severe cut backs. "They're skipping meals, they're not cooking food, they're rationing hot water," he said. "At the moment we are seeing so many people in fuel poverty and that number is only going to get worse as we go through the next four or five months." The cap sets a maximum price for each unit of energy, not the total bill. Those on fixed deals are unaffected until the end of their term, but for those on variable tariffs it means: For electricity, average unit prices will go up on 1 January from 26.32p per kilowatt-hour to 32.69p. Gas will increase from 7.97p per kilowatt-hour to 10.96p, higher than in the wake of the invasion of Ukraine. Daily standing charges will be 54.77p for electricity and 29.65p for gas. The cap is set by Ofgem every three months, based on the costs faced by suppliers as well as the cost of running the energy system. It is based on a three-month period that ends about six weeks before the new cap comes into force. A fall in international wholesale prices in recent days will not be reflected in January's cap, but will be in April's. Cole said the government needed to do more for struggling households The government is due to pay millions of households £100 from 4 January to help cover winter costs on top of an existing VAT cut on electricity. Cole said it would provide "a little bit of breathing space," but did not go far enough and was "not much money at all now compared to what people will be paying from the start of next year". He said the government needed to take "drastic action" and should be "decreasing the cost of energy through careful policy". His advice to people struggling with the increased cost was to talk to local charities, their local authority and their energy providers, who are obliged to offer support. events.title: Amazon to start selling cars in the UK next year
events.summary: US retail giant links up with Hyundai in attempt to crack £200bn British market Amazon is planning to sell cars in the UK from early next year, in a move that threatens to disrupt the vehicle retail market. The Amazon Autos service will be launched in “early 2027”, starting with cars from the Korean manufacturer Hyundai. It will be the first time the US tech company has sold cars outside its home country. Amazon, which is the world’s biggest online retailer with a market value of $2.7tn (£2.1tn), started selling cars at the end of 2024 in an effort to expand into one of the few remaining major consumer markets it had not already targeted. Its latest move will be watched closely by car retailers that share a UK market worth more than £200bn a year. Amazon Autos operates in 150 US cities and counts thousands of dealers in its networks, offering vehicles from 35 brands. UK buyers will be able to buy new electric hybrid and petrol Hyundai models, as well as used cars from Vertu Motors, a large British dealership. Amazon said customers would be able to explore financing options before reserving a car and completing the purchase in physical dealerships. More brands and dealers will be announced before the launch of the UK service. Amazon will go up against online new and used dealers, as well as traditional physical dealerships. Car companies also sell directly to consumers through their websites. The share price of Autotrader, the UK’s largest car sales website, fell 3% on Wednesday after news of Amazon’s move. An Autotrader spokesperson said: “We’ve always welcomed innovation in automotive, but our focus remains on delivering the best possible experience for UK car buyers.” The FTSE 100 company also said it had a “unique depth of automotive data with AI models developed specifically for the UK market” that had “taken decades to build”. Vertu’s share price rose 4% although it also announced acquisitions of dealerships. The company, listed on London’s Alternative Investment Market, was valued at £269m before the announcement. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Matt Nuffort, the director of Amazon Autos International, said: “Buying a car is one of the biggest purchases people make, and we think it should feel as simple and transparent as shopping for anything on Amazon. “In the UK, that means making it easy for customers to browse available cars, see upfront pricing, reserve the car and connect with the dealer to finalise the purchase.” Hyundai was also the first brand to work with Amazon in the US. José Muñoz, its chief executive, said: “Our partnership with Amazon Autos has changed the way many customers discover Hyundai in the US, and 78% of the Amazon-influenced sales at our dealerships have come from customers who are new to our brand.” Robert Forrester, Vertu’s chief executive, said his company was “committed to meeting customers wherever they choose to begin their buying journey”.

events.title: I spent months living and working in New York City to see if I should move there. After 3 trips, I had my answer.
events.summary: I spent several stints living in and exploring New York City. Aleenah Ansari I grew up in Washington and started my adult life in Seattle, but I was curious about New York. Over the course of a few years, I spent several short stints there and fell in love with the city. However, the short stays also made me realize how much I'd miss about Seattle if I left permanently. I've lived in Washington state my whole life and called Seattle home for the past 12 years. This city is where I went to college, met my now-wife, started my career, and connected with local business owners and authors by writing about them. As I continued in my career, though, I wondered if Seattle was a place I'd chosen to live by default, and whether there was another place that could be a better fit for me, like New York. I'd gone on trips there before and loved it, but people always told me that visiting a place was very different from living there. I didn't want to leave everything behind for a place that I hadn't spent time in long-term. During a conversation with a family member about this conundrum, she proposed an idea: What if I didn't uproot my entire life but gave New York a try for a brief period? I spent several stints in New York City over the next few years I loved New York's energy and culture. Aleenah Ansari In 2020, my company gave me approval to work remotely from New York for five weeks, which was my first trial run. I found a long-term Airbnb , and once I got my monthly transit pass, some supplies, and two suitcases to hold everything, I was ready to experience the city. Immediately, my favorite part of New York was the energy. There was always an event to check out, a new restaurant to try, or a person to meet. I challenged myself to make the most of every day there because I knew it wouldn't be forever. Over the course of one month, I checked out dozens of restaurants, saw every person I knew who lived in the city, and made the most of free museum nights in hopes of seeing as much as possible during my visit. Over the next three years, I went back to New York for three different monthlong stints. Every time, I fell in love with the city's energy, the thriving creative community, and how easy it is to have once-in-a-lifetime experiences on a regular basis. I seriously thought about whether and when I'd move there. As much as I liked New York, living there full-time didn't feel like the right choice Somewhere along the way, though, I realized that I couldn't keep up with New York's pace. When I was there, I deeply missed my own community back home, and thought about how much I'd miss having the opportunity to return to my alma mater to host workshops, participate in panels, and offer mentorship. I missed having access to nature, hiking, and moments of quiet, something that was a big part of my life in the Pacific Northwest . I also knew that my girlfriend at the time didn't see New York as home, so if I lived there, it would be something I'd have to navigate on my own. As years passed and my girlfriend and I headed toward engagement, it became clear that though I loved New York as a place to visit, it might never feel like my permanent home. Once we got engaged, we started thinking about where we could buy property, and Seattle just made more sense. Our families lived nearby, we could have more space to grow together, and my wife had an established career here. Seattle was also a place where we could rely on the support of loved ones who could help us with home maintenance, car troubles, and anything in between. We officially put down roots in Seattle instead I still go back to visit New York, but I'm glad I put down roots in Seattle instead. Aleenah Ansari My now-wife and I bought a home in Seattle a few years ago as our home base. However, I still feel like I can enjoy the best of New York City. I visit regularly, usually spending between two weeks and a month there every fall and spring, my favorite seasons. After I've soaked in everything the city has to offer, I head back. Then, once I'm in Seattle, I get to enjoy everything that comes with home: time with family and friends, access to nature, and a sense of security. I've had some amazing experiences in New York that make me second-guess my decision not to live there, but then I remember all the reasons I'm so grateful for my life in Seattle. Both cities have shaped the writer and person I am today, and I'm glad that even though I "chose" one, they're still both parts of my life. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Jensen Huang tells staff that Nvidia doesn't need a succession plan
events.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang led his first employee meeting since being reinstated and apologized to those in the room. Huang said the company doesn't need succession planning because the chipmaker operates a unique business model. Huang had resigned from Nvidia after multiple reported affairs, including one with a Chinese businesswoman who is alleged to be a spy for Beijing. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang on Tuesday struck a conciliatory and remorseful tone while leading his first employee meeting since being reinstated, and said how sorry he was for what he had done. Huang told employees that he let them down and promised to do a better job the second time around, according to people inside the room, who asked not to be named in order to share details. "I hurt all of you," Huang said, according to one of the people. The CEO also addressed succession planning during the event, the people said. He told staff that Nvidia has built a team that doesn't require succession planning the way a normal organization does, because the company operates a unique business model where there are multiple capable leaders at Nvidia that are leading different parts of the organization. Investors and analysts were left to speculate about the company's future leadership in the wake of Huang's resignation on Nov. 12. On Monday, Huang was reinstated as CEO of the chipmaker by Nvidia's board of directors. Eleven days before, Huang had resigned from Nvidia after multiple reported affairs , including one with a Chinese businesswoman who is alleged to be a spy for Beijing. Harvey Jones, Nvidia's newly appointed board chair, said last week that Huang resigned after "disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company's code of conduct, standards and cultural norms." Huang started the meeting by thanking CFO Colette Kress for her leadership as interim CEO. Huang told staff that Tuesday's company meeting was the second hardest meeting of his life, the first one being with his wife. He said he is in therapy, according to one of the people present. In a press release announcing Huang's return on Monday, the company said the board "received input" from senior officials in the federal government about any potential national security risk around the CEO. President Donald Trump told CNBC that he gave the board assurances and "made the deal" to restore Huang to his post. After the company had its worst week in the stock market since 2008, the stock surged more than 30% the day his return was announced. Shares fell on Tuesday, however. An Nvidia representative didn't immediately respond to requests for comment.

events.title: Jensen Huang's Nvidia return shows the U.S.-China AI race is about more than chips
events.summary: Donald Trump said China might have tried to recruit Jensen Huang after his Nvidia exit, in a CNBC interview about the Nvidia CEO's reinstatement. Recruiters and analysts interviewed by CNBC said Chinese technology companies are aggressively competing for experienced AI engineers in the U.S. and Asia. Sources said access to advanced AI chips, research resources and compensation can influence where engineers choose to work. BEIJING — Jensen Huang ' s return to Nvidia as its CEO underscores how the U.S.-China artificial intelligence race is not only about semiconductors, but tech talent. "We have to protect our geniuses, and he's clearly a genius," Donald Trump told CNBC about his intervention to bring Huang back. If not, Trump warned, the founder of the AI chip giant could hypothetically have taken a job in China. The concern reflects how Chinese AI companies have been narrowing the gap with their U.S. counterparts, not just in models, but now in engineering and research talent. China has surpassed the U.S. by share of global AI talent in just three years, according to Carnegie Endowment research. Nvidia "was shaken without a single chip or model changing," said Winston Ma, an AI investor and adjunct professor of law at New York University. "Whoever builds and keeps that human layer will hold the rest of the stack." Huang resigned Nov. 12 after reports of an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence reportedly believes has links to Chinese intelligence. He returned on Nov. 23, news which sent Nvidia shares surging. Now, the president is all alone in Washington AG Blanche, FBI's Patel dodge questions about Huang investigation Congress blasts Nvidia bringing Jensen Huang back Jensen Huang to face Congress the same day as Nvidia GTC More than 30 years ago, Huang founded Nvidia as a gaming graphics chip company. The semiconductors gradually became used to mine cryptocurrencies, and now, training cutting-edge AI models. Huang has more advanced tech coming, Trump told CNBC's Eamon Javers on Monday. "He's got other chips in his brain that nobody else knows about, including me, that nobody else understands," Trump said. "Jensen could take the next plane to China, and I guarantee you, they would give him whatever he wanted, and then and then they automatically have, you know, all of the things," Trump said. He acknowledged there was "never even a suggestion" that the Nvidia founder was recruited by China. Trump returned to the U.S. over the weekend from Shenzhen, China, where he met Chinese President Xi Jinping. Earlier in the month, turmoil around Huang's future at Nvidia had gripped global attention. For Huang's supporters, talent was a critical part of the argument, said Damien Ma, director and Maurice R. Greenberg Director's Chair of Carnegie China. As the incident has increased scrutiny on the people involved in the U.S.-China tech race, Ma said he's closely watching whether either country restricts AI engineers from leaving. While he expects limited policy changes, other countries such as Singapore and South Korea could benefit from an inflow of AI talent, he added. Already, many companies are using a mixed-market approach, given engineers in the U.S. make two or three times as much as their Chinese counterparts due in part to foreign exchange rates and AI company valuations. In the U.S., "you need to have a lot of money to recruit them," said Alex Lu, founder of LSY Consulting — and that can get expensive. Lu cited the founder of a U.S. consumer research firm, who opted to hire engineers based in China after visiting the country. It's an anecdote that's frequently repeated by analysts, sometimes with U.S.-trained Chinese staff based in Singapore. Chinese companies are "very, very aggressive in getting good talent from the U.S. ," said Tidalwave Solutions Partner Rachel Wu, who recruits for large Chinese tech companies and startups. She also said a Meta engineer in Canada took an offer from a Chinese AI startup for a salary of 1.4 million yuan ($210,000), in addition to stock options. "There is some truth to Trump's comments given Jensen's knowledge of the AI industry and supply chain," said Lian Jye Su, a chief analyst of Omdia. "It would be unwise for the U.S. to let this saga continue to affect its AI ambition, especially when that ambition includes slowing down Chinese progress in AI." However, Rui Ma, founder of advisory Tech Buzz China, said Huang's background of being a founder makes it more likely that he would have started his own company, rather than taking a managerial role at one.

events.title: Budget carrier Norse Atlantic falls 78% after warning its finances are ‘critical’ amid soaring fuel costs
events.summary: Budget carrier Norse Atlantic said it's facing a "critical financial situation" on Wednesday. The carrier has come under strain due to soaring jet fuel costs since the onset of the Iran war. Jet fuel prices jumped 103% month-on-month as of March, per the International Air Transport Association's Jet Fuel Price Monitor. Norse Atlantic shares plummeted Wednesday after it revealed the company is in a "critical financial situation" as soaring fuel costs amid the Iran war strain budget carriers during the winter season. The Norwegian low-cost carrier said its situation is dependent on securing financing for its short-term liquidity needs. The company has had discussions about a potential strategic takeover as well as other options including ACMI contracts, which refer to short-term capacity leasing. "Norse is also engaged in discussions with selected parties on short term financing, however, there can be no assurances that such discussions will result in a viable solution," it added. The start of the U.S.-Iran war on Feb. 28 sent jet fuel prices soaring, putting pressure on airlines around the world. Prices are now up nearly 72% to $155 per barrel year-on-year as of the week ending Nov. 20, according to the International Air Transport Association's Jet Fuel Price Monitor . Norse, which offers cheap long-haul flights between Europe, North America, Africa, and Asia, said in October that it was forced to fly with reduced capacity that month, due to "prolonged high fuel prices." Norse Atlantic's CEO Eivind Roald told CNBC in May that he was not "overly concerned" about access to fuel and said the airline didn't have insight that the crisis would have an immediate impact. "Fuel price rose by more than 100% and the beginning of March we had already sold most of our seats for March so it was difficult to overcompensate with higher prices for those few seats left," Roald said. The airline had cancelled all flights to and from Los Angeles at the time due to the cost of jet fuel, impacting over 150,000 passengers. Roald also said Norse cancelled more than 700 flights in total, which impacted more than 240,000 passengers. The company said in August that geopolitical disruptions and higher jet fuel costs hit profitability in the first half of the year. Higher fuel costs, lower aircraft use, and operational disruptions led to an $8.4 million second-quarter loss, measured before interest, taxes, depreciation, amortization, and rent. EasyJet , another low-cost airline impacted by high fuel costs, reported Wednesday that profit before tax slumped 89% to £71 million ($92.7 million) for the year ending in September 2026. Revenue growth was unable to offset the impact of an 11% increase in fuel costs due to the Middle East conflict, the company said. Earlier this year, Ryanair's CEO Michael O'Leary told CNBC that other European carriers would struggle if jet fuel prices continued to soar. "I think there will be failures." "If it continues at $150 a barrel into July, August, September, then you'll see European airlines fail and that, in the medium term, would probably be good for Ryanair's business." Meanwhile, Ryanair's chief financial officer Neil Sorahan told CNBC in May: "I think we will see some of the weaker carriers who were already struggling before the war possibly go to the wall in the winter." Several smaller European airlines have stopped flying this winter. Slovakia's AirExplore ceased operations, Ireland's Fly4 entered provisional liquidation, and Spain's AlbaStar suspended flights while seeking creditor protection. Spain's Plus Ultra has also suspended all flights while it restructures, though it has not confirmed a permanent closure.

events.title: Todoist confirms 6% of customers’ details were stolen in data breach
events.summary: Task management app Todoist said on Tuesday that a hacker gained access to its production systems and stole customer data, including email IDs, password hashes, and account creation dates. The company said around 6% of its customers were affected and blamed stolen credentials for the breach. Todoist said the attacker used stolen credentials to access the company’s version control system and source code between November 22 and 23. The hacker then changed employee access controls and reached the app’s cloud infrastructure via an employee’s work account. The hacker downloaded credentials of early Todoist users whose passwords were stored using an older hashing method, but didn’t change any source code, the company said. Todoist said it has blocked the attack path and reset passwords as a mitigation step, as well as disabled the Todoist for Outlook email add-on. For a small number of people, about 0.001% of its userbase, the hacker also searched through tasks, comments, and attachment names to look for credentials for other services, like API keys and access tokens. The hacker also pulled Todoist API tokens and Slack integration tokens, and looked for emails, addresses, and attachment file names through the Todoist for Outlook extension if it was connected to accounts and had permission to read emails. The company said it has sent a notice to those affected and asked them to reset their credentials and change their login details in other places with the same password. The company is asking users to also update API tokens, reconnect integrations, and revoke or replace any access keys, recovery phrases, or credentials they had stored in Todoist comments. Todoist said it has also reset its internal access structure and how remote command execution works in its cloud environment to prevent such incidents in the future. Todoist’s founder and CEO Amir Salihefendić apologized to users about the incident on X , and said the company will take a closer look at why it happened. The to-do app’s data breach is the latest in a burgeoning list of data breaches in which hackers use stolen credentials to access data and systems at enterprises. events.title: Fed’s preferred inflation gauge accelerated to 3.8% in October, raising the 2027 stakes for the central bank
events.summary: The personal consumption expenditures price index rose by a seasonally adjusted 3.8% annual rate in October, nearly twice the Federal Reserve’s target. Excluding food and energy, so-called core PCE was 3.3%, the Commerce Department said. The headline number was in line with the Dow Jones consensus estimate, while core PCE was 0.1 percentage point above the forecast. Inflation moved further away from the Federal Reserve's target in October, reinforcing expectations that another interest rate hike is in the cards for December and raising questions about how much more work the central bank will have to do in 2027. The personal consumption expenditures price index , the Fed's preferred inflation gauge, showed a seasonally adjusted 3.8% annual inflation rate, in line with the Dow Jones consensus estimate and nearly twice the central bank's goal. The reading was 0.1 percentage point higher than September. Excluding food and energy, core PCE was 3.3%, the Commerce Department reported Wednesday. That was 0.1 percentage point above the forecast. While the Fed officially follows the headline figure, policymakers consider core to be a more reliable longer-term gauge of inflation trends. A separate report also showed much stronger economic growth for the third quarter, with gross domestic product rising at a 4.3% annualized rate, according to a revised Commerce Department estimate. The strong top-line gain for the economy adds further fuel to the notion that Fed monetary policy is not restricting economic activity. Consumer spending rose 0.3% for the month, which matched the pace of price increases but was 0.1 percentage point lower than forecast. Income, on the other hand, surged 0.7%, much more than the 0.4% estimate. The personal saving rate rose to 4.1%. Stock market futures added to losses following the release, while Treasury yields also were sharply lower. Even with the higher-than-expected core inflation figure, expectations eased a bit for Fed rate hikes in 2027. Traders continued to price in two more increases but lowered odds for a third hike to about 1-in-3, compared to 50-50 on Tuesday, according to the CME Group's FedWatch . "Inflation is too hot and it will not be brought under control as long as economic demand is also too hot," said Chris Rupkey, chief economist at Fwdbonds. The report comes with the market fully pricing in a quarter percentage point interest rate hike when the Fed meets Dec. 8-9. Less certain is how much more rates will need to increase to get inflation back down to the Fed's 2% target. Inflation has been running above target for some 5½ years. Inflation had been drifting lower but spiked again following the late-February attacks on Iran led by the U.S. and Israel. Tariffs also have continued to exert pressure, as has strong demand associated with the artificial intelligence buildout. The White House on Wednesday announced a fresh round of tariffs on 14 trading partners including China, the European Union and Japan. Policymakers generally consider factors such as tariffs and supply shocks to be temporary, but some fear the impact has begun spreading through the economy and could become embedded. "America's inflation problem is bigger than an energy shock," said Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union. The large upward increase in GDP came from revisions to investment as well as consumer and government spending. Consumer spending, which accounts for about two-thirds of all economic activity, rose 4.2% in the third quarter. A metric known as real final sales to private domestic purchasers, which Fed officials regard as a key indicator of underlying demand, jumped 5.8%, reflecting an upward revision of 0.9 percentage point. In other economic news Wednesday, the Labor Department reported that initial jobless claims slipped to 189,000 for the week ending Nov. 21, down 13,000 from the prior week and back to around the lowest level since the late 1960s. Wall Street had been expecting 200,000.

events.title: Secondhand shopping is going mainstream this holiday season as consumers seek value
events.summary: More consumers are shopping secondhand this holiday season as they emphasize value and uniqueness in their purchases. Companies such as eBay and ThredUp found that resale is trending upward, driven by interest from younger generations. It's a trend Wall Street is increasingly watching, especially as legacy retailers begin leaning into pre-owned items as well. As the high cost of living squeezes consumers' wallets this holiday season, more shoppers are turning to secondhand retail and thrifting. The shift comes as consumers look for better value, buyers put more emphasis on personalization and younger generations change the way they shop. The U.S. secondhand apparel market grew 13% in 2025, nearly four times faster than the overall retail clothing market, according to GlobalData. That segment is expected to reach nearly $80 billion by 2030, growing more than 7% annually on average, GlobalData found. Much of that expansion — 40% — was driven by Generation Z, followed closely by millennials. "I think this has been their version of the thrill of the hunt that millennials loved during the recession days," Katherine Cullen, a global senior retail analyst at EY, told CNBC. "It's a way to really express an individual style, find something unique, something that really fits their own vibe and personality." It goes beyond people shopping for themselves, Cullen said. With more emphasis on unique holiday gifts, shoppers are leaning more on secondhand retail than they have before, whether in clothing or in other retail categories. They're looking for something that fits the personality of the person they're shopping for, she added. For Vanessa Roberts, that meant finding two antique children's chairs that she says will perfectly round out her nieces' play space. Roberts, 37, said she's been thrifting for at least two decades, each time embracing the "thrill" of finding something unique or vintage. Especially in fashion, at a time when the quality of mass-produced items has decreased, thrifted items offer more value beyond just the price tag, Roberts added. "It's crazy that you can find better quality items at the thrift store right now from 20 years ago versus what you can find at stores right now," she said. Roberts, who lives in Los Angeles, said she began shopping for holiday gifts in September. As she prepares her haul for December, roughly 70% of her gifting will come from secondhand stores, she estimated. "It's been a fun little challenge, where it's like a little scavenger hunt when I go into the thrift store," she said. "I'm definitely thrifting for the holidays – I do it every year." The trend coincides with an economy that has forced consumers to be more intentional about how they spend, as they face high inflation and elevated gas prices. In October, the consumer price index rose a seasonally adjusted 0.4%, which was more than anticipated. Still, consumers are expected to continue spending through the holiday season, with sales projected to top $1 trillion for the first time — though some of that estimated increase is boosted by inflation. "You have a consumer who, while they're willing to spend at the top level, they're willing to splurge selectively," Cullen said. "Consumers are looking for value, which I think is something that is making secondhand resale and re-commerce more attractive." And while clothing is largely the entry point to buying resale, secondhand shopping is increasingly expanding into furniture, electronics and books, according to a report from consumer insights firm The Consumer Collective. Its October report found that 34% of people surveyed said secondhand products offer better value than brand new ones. Many secondhand items also have an inherent added value beyond the low price on the tag, according to eBay CEO Jamie Iannone. The uniqueness of those products, as well as the allure that vintage adds to them, means consumers may actually be seeking the benefits of secondhand in more ways than one. "I can buy a product that's used, and it almost has cachet around it," Iannone told CNBC. "Consumers today, they're able to get these amazing values on products, and it's seen as very normal to be gifting pre-loved." According to eBay's Recommerce Report in October, 70% of global consumers surveyed said they consider secondhand shopping important for managing their budgets. That same report also found that 89% of respondents plan to spend the same amount or more on secondhand products next year compared with this year. Iannone said he thinks the interest in secondhand this holiday season is "much stronger" than last year. "It's becoming just a more established part of consumers' shopping and gifting routines," he said. At a time when algorithms are driving shopping trends, consumers are also looking for ways to distinguish themselves and their purchases. That's stretching beyond buying for themselves to purchasing holiday gifts for others, too.

events.title: Amazon and Meta reportedly in talks to lift blockade on AI agent Muse
events.summary: Amazon may be having a change of heart about Meta’s AI agent, Muse. The two tech giants are reportedly discussing a potential deal that would allow Meta’s popular AI agent to connect directly to Amazon’s store. The talks would mark a significant reversal from just two months ago, when Muse users discovered they were unable to purchase products on Amazon and instead received an error message when attempting to check out. According to a Wednesday report by Fortune , citing people familiar with the discussions, Amazon and Meta have held multiple rounds of talks about the matter. Two key issues remain under negotiation: how search results would be presented and how advertising would be handled under a potential agreement. One of Amazon’s biggest concerns is how third-party shopping agents like Muse could affect its advertising business. In October, Amazon CEO Andy Jassy argued that few customers were making purchases through outside shopping agents. Amazon may also have been waiting for Muse to mature before agreeing to integrate it with its marketplace. If Muse places the wrong order or creates a problem with a purchase, Amazon could ultimately be left dealing with frustrated customers and unhappy sellers. Fortune reported that executives are concerned that third-party shopping agents could weaken Amazon’s direct relationship with consumers, according to people familiar with the matter. Any potential agreement between Amazon and Meta would reportedly require approval from both companies’ CEOs, Fortune also reported. Meta and Amazon have not yet responded to TechCrunch’s requests for comment. events.title: JetBrains finds agents may cheat with open source
events.summary: JetBrains has revamped a benchmark for evaluating large language models after suspecting too many agents gamed their tasks the first time round. The company labelled this agentic practice "reward hacking" in a post summarizing the results of its revised evaluation. Like its predecessor , Kotlin Benchmark 2.0 is a collection of tasks that evaluates how well AI coding agents work with the Kotlin programming language , in order to help Kotlin programmers decide which agent-model configurations to use. The tasks include fixing tricky problems in Kotlin code across different domains, and making corrections to multiple files. Dirty data The revised benchmar k now includes 30 Kotlin multi-file code problems that have not been exposed to the public in any way before. The revised test all but guarantees that the agents have not encountered this set of problems, or potential solutions, before. Another 70 tasks are based on code that resides in public repositories. The test also blocked all network access for the open source tasks, except for what was needed to communicate with the model itself. This minimized the possibility that the agent could look for an existing answer already posted, perhaps through a patch or pull request. A 30-minute limit was set for each task. Overall, the agents were significantly less accurate when solving problems on codebases they had never encountered. Top resolution rates dropped rather suspiciously from 86.2 percent on tasks based on open source repositories to 60 percent on those based on closed source repositories. Although the agents lacked network access, JetBrains boffins theorized that they might have benefited from encountering and internalizing these open source repositories during training. Only the private repositories were completely new to them. Also curious was how a different set of models excelled at the closed source problems, compared to those models that usually did better on the open source tasks. Leaderboard Shakeup When restricted to closed source tasks, two dark horse models rose to the top: Gemini 3.8 Flash, via Antigravity CLI, topped the list with a 60 percent success rate, closely followed by DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (running on OpenCode) at 58.9 percent. Of the two, the open weight DeepSeek was far cheaper (at $0.08 per task) than the closed weight Gemini ($1.74 per task), however. In contrast, Opus 5.5 completed only 53.3 percent of the tasks at $1.21 per task, and Fable 5.1 completed only 44.4 percent of the tasks, at a luxurious $3.27 per task. Claude Code harnessed both of these models. Claude’s lackluster completion rates on closed source tasks are somewhat sus given how both of these Anthropic models scored significantly higher on tasks using open source materials. In fact Claude ran the table when it came to open source: Fable 5.1 topped the charts with 86.2 percent accuracy, closely followed by Opus 5.5 at 84.8 percent accuracy. (Kotlin users will pay dearly for the extra sliver of Anthropic accuracy: The average cost of Fable completing a Kotlin cleanup task runs $2.38, while Opus could do the job for $0.68.) Gaming the boss One possible interpretation of these disparate numbers is that models are drawing from their own knowledge bases instead of reasoning from scratch. Whether this is cheating or the models simply working as intended might be more a matter of philosophical debate. Mark Hinkle, founder of the AIE Network consultancy, suspects the issue of integrity may go deeper. "Private code doesn't stop reward hacking, it changes the shortcut," he wrote to The Register on LinkedIn. "On public code the agent goes and finds the answer somebody has already published. On private code there's no answer to find, so it satisfies whatever is checking it. I treat these things like entry-level employees, and a sharp new hire figures out fast what the boss actually looks at." JetBrains did not immediately respond to a request for comment, but concluded in its post that more investigation is needed. It promises that its people will pore over the open source results to see if any have been contaminated by the LLMs' own memory. It also plans to run its own static analysis tool, Qodana , against the results to check for errors. Sireesha Pulipati , a staff data engineer and AI observer, suggested, also by LinkedIn, that JetBrains may have needed more specificity in its agent instructions. "Out of the box [an agent] tends to reach for generic patterns. But when we give it instructions and skills that tell it where to look for our patterns and context, it follows them. A well-controlled harness, with those standards built in, is what makes the agent useful," Pulipati wrote. So good on JetBrains for providing Kotlin users some information about working with AI, but, as always, AI benchmarks should be approached with extreme side-eye. ®

events.title: Almost 60% of primary energy used for electricity is lost to conversion and transmission
events.summary: U.S. Energy Information Administration - EIA - Independent Statistics and Analysis Browse by tag liquid fuels natural gas electricity oil/petroleum production/supply crude oil consumption/demand generation prices map states exports/imports international coal renewables weather forecasts/projections gasoline capacity steo (short-term energy outlook) How does EIA compare different types of energy? Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Monthly Energy Review Note: Btu=British thermal units To compare production and consumption across different resources, we convert to a common energy metric, British thermal units (Btu), which typically measures the heat content of the fuels such as petroleum, natural gas, and coal that are burned for energy. For energy sources such as hydropower, wind, solar, and geothermal that aren’t combusted to create energy, we apply a constant conversion factor based on the heat content of electricity. For combustible fuels, EIA uses thermal conversion factors to convert the physical units into heat content values. Because these factors can change based on the specific characteristics of fuels being produced at different points in time, we update our conversion factors each year. We publish heat content data for more than 30 petroleum products, 4 types of coal, and natural gas. Each fuel has a unique chemistry and heat content, and the heat content can vary based on the different types of fuel in the mix. For example, the heat content of anthracite coal is higher than the heat content of lignite . The aggregate heat content of coal generally varies based on the mix of the different types of coal produced and consumed. The aggregate heat contents for petroleum consumption and production have declined in recent decades because of decreasing use of residual fuel oil , which has relatively high heat content, and increasing use of fuels with a lower heat content—such as motor gasoline, distillate fuel oil, and hydrocarbon gas liquids. Our heat content estimates for natural gas have fluctuated within a relatively narrow range because of highly consistent pipeline specifications. Methane, the primary component of natural gas, has a heat content of 1,010 Btu per cubic foot. Other gases such as ethane, biomass gases, synthetic gases, and supplemental gases, which may be left in the natural gas stream, have higher heat content values. Total coal thermal conversion factors depend on the relative mix of coal types consumed and produced that year. Anthracite and bituminous coals have higher heat contents than lignite and subbituminous coals. Subbituminous coal production and consumption have increased over time, bringing down coal’s aggregate heat contents. To measure how efficient a power plant is at converting the fuel into electricity, we use heat rates. While thermal conversion factors measure the heat content of a fuel, heat rates measure the efficiency of power plants to convert fuel into heat and then into electricity. The heat rate is the amount of energy used to generate one kilowatthour (kWh) of electricity. The lower the heat rate, the higher the efficiency of a power plant to convert fuel into electricity. Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Monthly Energy Review Since 2001—the earliest year in our data—heat rates for electricity generation from coal and petroleum have risen slightly, while the heat rate for electricity generation from natural gas has gone down, due in part to more efficient combined-cycle plants coming online. Power plants using nuclear energy and noncombustible renewables —such as hydro, wind, solar, and geothermal—generate electricity without burning fuel. For nuclear energy, EIA uses a measurement of the heat produced from nuclear fission in the reactor core. For noncombustible renewable energy, we use the captured energy approach . Captured energy is the energy available for consumption after converting a renewable resource into electricity, net of conversion losses. The captured energy approach uses the heat content of electricity, which is constant (3,412 Btu/kWh). events.title: U.S. economy grew at rapid 4.3% pace in third quarter
events.summary: Data: Bureau of Economic Analysis ; Chart: Courtenay Brown/Axios The U.S. economy grew substantially faster this summer than initially thought, the government said Wednesday — a blockbuster upgrade to its estimate of third-quarter GDP. By the numbers: The economy expanded at a 4.3% annualized rate, up from the 3.4% initially reported and nearly twice the rate of 2.2% in the second quarter. Why it matters: The economy has even more momentum than previously understood, a sign of remarkable resilience in the face of higher borrowing costs and stubborn inflation that could give the Fed more latitude to raise rates. Zoom in: The upward revision reflected stronger business investment fueled by the AI buildout and software investment, as well as consumer spending. A measure of underlying private-sector demand — which strips out trade, inventories and government spending — rose at a whopping 5.8% annual rate, up from the 4.9% initially reported. The backdrop: Separate data out Wednesday showed personal income jumped 0.7% in October while inflation-adjusted consumer spending stalled, pushing the saving rate up to 4.1% from 3.6% the prior month. The personal consumption expenditures price index — the Fed's preferred inflation gauge — climbed 3.8% from a year earlier, from 3.6% in September. Core inflation, which excludes food and energy, accelerated to 3.3% from 3.1%. On a monthly basis, both headline and core prices rose 0.3%. The bottom line: The U.S. economy was on remarkably strong footing heading into the end of the year, though inflation remains stubbornly high. Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional details.

events.title: US proposes sweeping new tariffs on China, others
events.summary: The Trump administration is proposing new tariffs on China, the European Union, and more than a dozen other trading partners it says have distorted the global market by overproducing goods like automobiles, batteries and chemicals. The so-called excess capacity tariffs , which conclude investigations begun in March, comply with existing trade deals and vary by country. The administration is suggesting a 20% “across the board” tariff on Chinese exports, a senior US official said, which would stack with 2018 tariffs (but not 2026 tariffs targeting forced labor) and exempt goods identified by the Board of Trade. That rate could rise as high as 40% should trade talks collapse, the official added. The US, which previously notified the affected countries, does not expect China to retaliate with anything stronger than a statement: “This is part of that process of establishing stability,” the official said. As for other countries, the official shrugged off the suggestion that the announcement might foster tension: “We actually expect that we may be signing more agreements at the G20 [summit next month] in the wake of these announcements,” the official said. The announcement follows exit polling that found eight in 10 voters believe Trump’s tariffs have harmed the economy. It also comes amid continued fallout from Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy, which has provoked bipartisan scrutiny of US-China policy. The official predicted the proposed tariffs could take effect in January “at the earliest,” since the administration must first solicit comments and hold hearings. Similar investigations into Norway and Mexico, meanwhile, remain ongoing. Also on Tuesday night, the administration proposed new tariffs on Brazilian sugar and aircraft. The official attributed these levies to a “lack of progress” on trade talks. — Eleanor Mueller

events.title: Energy bills to rise by 26% from January after gas prices surge
events.summary: Watch: Martin Lewis' tips on staying warm this winter Published 25 November 2026, 00:03 GMT Energy bills will soar by 26% for millions of households in January after a surge in gas prices sparked by the Iran war. A typical bill will increase by about £37 a month in the first three months of the new year, although the price will depend on how much energy a household uses, so it could be closer to £60 extra a month in winter. A household using a typical amount of energy in England, Scotland and Wales and paying by direct debit, would see their annual bill rise from £1,723 to £2,166 if the increase was sustained for a year, said regulator Ofgem. The government will pay millions of households £100 from 4 January to help cover winter costs on top of an existing VAT cut on electricity. Charities and suppliers expect debt to rise and a wave of people to need emergency support. Ofgem said the rise had been driven entirely by higher wholesale costs faced by suppliers owing, primarily, to the Iran war. Wholesale gas prices , paid by suppliers, were up 33% in the last three months, the period used to set the January to March cap. They have more than doubled since late 2025. The warm home discount will take £150 off bills for six million households on benefits this winter. There have been calls for this support, funded through everyone's bill, to be extended. "We are staring down the barrel of a brutal winter," said Dame Clare Moriarty, chief executive of Citizens Advice. Neil Kenward, Ofgem's director general for markets, said it wrote to energy suppliers "reminding them of their responsibilities" to customers this winter. They have been told to identify people who need help early, make support easy to access and ensure repayment plans are affordable and sustainable. Campaign Groups Friends of the Earth and Global Witness said major oil and energy companies are making huge profits because of spiralling oil costs, hurting households. Energy UK, which represents suppliers, said the firms which send your bill, have profits capped on a percentage basis and do not see the same benefit as international energy generating companies. However, higher bills will mean higher profits in nominal cash terms. The increase is the biggest since Russia's invasion of Ukraine drove up prices. It comes at a tough time of year, when the weather is at its coldest. People on prepayment meters will be hit as their spending comes when energy is needed, rather than the cost being spread over the year as with direct debits. The cap sets a maximum price for each unit of energy, not the total bill. Those on fixed deals are unaffected until the end of their term, but for those on variable tariffs it means: For electricity, average unit prices will go up on 1 January from 26.32p per kilowatt-hour to 32.69p. The electricity price is often pegged to gas, owing to gas-fired generation. Gas will increase from 7.97p per kilowatt-hour to 10.96p, higher than in the wake of the invasion of Ukraine. Daily standing charges will be 54.77p for electricity and 29.65p for gas. The cap is set every three months, based on the costs faced by suppliers as well as the cost of running the energy system. It is based on a three-month period that ends about six weeks before the new cap comes into force. A fall in international wholesale prices in recent days will not be reflected in January's cap, but it will be in April's. Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said people will be "deeply concerned" by another rise in energy bills. "For too long, British families have been paying the price for conflicts overseas and volatile fossil fuel markets," she said. Andrew Bowie, shadow energy secretary, said: "It is an outrage that, as bills soar, Labour are not only piling green levies and taxes onto bills but signing us up to an EU scheme that risks pushing them even higher. 'We've turned the heating down by 2.5C' Stacey says she keeps the curtains closed "to keep the heat in" and her daughters wear thermal clothing Stacey, 40, a single mother from Bristol, said dealing with rising energy costs has felt like a "battle" recently and she's worried about 2027. She's turned her central heating down from 22C to 19.5C, bought electric blankets and pays her bills by direct debit. She also leaves her curtains shut to "keep the heat in", while her daughters wear thermal clothing if it gets chilly in the house. 'I only use the washing machine on a Sunday' - how we're keeping our energy bills down Published 7 hours ago Energy bills will soar - here's how you can ease the pain Published 9 hours ago Will I get the £100 energy payment and when will I receive it? Published 23 hours ago Up to 20 million households in England will get a £100 payment from 4 January to help with their energy bills this winter, with equivalent payments in Scotland and Wales.

events.title: Trump prepares new round of tariffs on China, other U.S. trading partners
events.summary: The Trump administration proposed a new round of tariffs targeting China, the European Union and 12 other economies over policies it says have created excess industrial capacity. Why it matters: Trump officials are pressing ahead with his trade agenda despite a Democratic midterm sweep fueled by affordability concerns. Post-election polling indicates voters overwhelmingly want tariffs to stay at current levels or decline. There's relatively little support — even among Trump's base — for them rising. Driving the news: The tariffs are the result of a trade investigation that launched in March , The proposed tariffs largely target specific goods, a narrower approach than the sweeping import levies the administration has previously imposed. China is the exception: The proposed 20% tariff would apply to most Chinese imports, with that rate calibrated to preserve the nations' trade truce. These new tariffs would not be added to existing ones aimed at combating forced labor or certain sector-specific tariffs, a senior U.S. official said. The official added that the rate could rise to 40% if trade talks break down or China fails to live up to its commitments. Between the lines: The proposed tariff rates for other major trading partners are consistent with parameters set out in trade deals, the official said. Trade deals struck with the EU, Japan and South Korea last year established 15% tariff rates on most goods. Other economies targeted include Taiwan, India, Indonesia and Vietnam. On average, the proposals would raise existing tariff rates on targeted trading partners by roughly 5 percentage points, the official estimated. The big picture: The investigation was conducted under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. The administration contends that foreign industrial policies encourage companies to produce more goods than global demand can absorb, undercutting U.S. manufacturers. The proposed tariffs are subject to a public comment period and hearings, with the levies taking effect as early as January, the official said. What they're saying: In response to reports of the proposed tariffs , China dismissed U.S. claims of industrial overcapacity as a "false proposition" and urged Washington to preserve stable trade relations. The prospect of renewed tariffs weighed on global stocks, particularly Asian markets, overnight. U.S. futures were sharply lower early Wednesday as well. Of note: The U.S. is also proposing tougher trade measures against Brazil, after imposing 25% tariffs in July over alleged unfair trade practices amid tensions between Trump and Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. The administration proposes raising tariffs on sugar imports exceeding existing quotas (regardless of origin) and imposing a 10% levy on previously exempt Brazilian aircraft, a U.S. official said. The bottom line: Trump's tariff agenda is moving forward as Democrats in the incoming Congress look to curb presidential authority over trade policy and lower Americans' costs .

events.title: Why American consumers are still spending and powering the US economy – and why this could soon fizzle
events.summary: Consumer spending has stayed healthy in large part because Americans are staying employed, whether through formal or gig work. AP Photo/David Zalubowski Holiday shopping season is kicking off, inundating consumers with Black Friday offers . With inflation fatigue , declining real wages and stock market turbulence thrown into the mix, is the U.S. consumer on the verge of scaling back? This question has long puzzled economists, who wonder why spending has held up even as consumer sentiment slumps. As a researcher of supply chains who has also worked for years at consumer products companies, I’ve run my own studies and have been surprised, time and again, by how spending has continued at a healthy clip even when the economy is faltering. Most recently, in March 2026, I built a model to assess how the Iran war could affect global supply chains at three, six and nine months out. In the case of consumer behavior, the hit was less than what was expected. Even though Americans were paying substantially more at the gas pump due to the disruption in the Strait of Hormuz, as well as dealing with tariff-induced inflation and high interest rates , consumer spending held up remarkably well . I now believe I missed two things: resilience and innovation. More specifically, Americans are continuing to work, whether in formal or gig jobs, and that’s the main factor holding up spending. And as long as consumers have income, they’ll keep finding a way. What’s changing, though, is that this balancing act is getting harder for many people to keep up. What resilience looks like Resilience and innovation may sound admirable, but in practice they’re often difficult and onerous. Under “innovation,” some traditional adjustments for consumers include buying cheaper “private label” or store brands , shopping at off-brand and discount stores , or relentlessly hunting for deals . Other adjustments include eating more meals at home rather than going out, or downsizing vacation plans . “Resilience,” meanwhile, can mean taking on extra work. Economists call this the added worker effect , and it shows up during tough times. During the 2007-09 Great Recession, for example, more married women joined the labor force as unemployment rose among their spouses. In 2026, there’s an uptick in retirees heading back to work as well as an increase in the share of mothers with children who are staying in or reentering the workforce . These are both responses to the rising cost of living. More broadly, Americans are using traditional and nontraditional means to make some extra cash. About 1 in 3 workers has had a side hustle in 2026, according to the jobs database ZipRecruiter – whether it’s nanny jobs, side gigs on Etsy, delivering meals for DoorDash or driving customers for Uber. For many Americans, this work is a necessity, not just a way to earn extra discretionary cash. The increasing need for extra work over the past five years underscores the drop in purchasing power from the salaries many people earn. More Americans, including retirees in need of extra income, are taking up gig work, like driving for Uber. AP Photo/Emily Wang Fujiyama Another form of resilience can be seen through volunteering and charitable giving. In my own neighborhood, a food bank that started during the COVID-19 pandemic has helped many in the community over the past five years. Across the country, food bank donations and charitable giving continue to rise despite economic challenges. According to Giving USA, charitable giving rose to US$617 billion in 2025, surpassing the $600 billion mark for the first time. This increase addresses a growing need for food banks to feed Americans who can’t afford basic groceries anymore. At the same time, the actual number of donors is dropping. Shoppers are hitting the limit Many consumers are now running out of levers to pull. Wealthier Americans are continuing to spend at a strong clip , which is why official consumer spending data suggests the economy is steady. But it’s a different picture for the rest. One in four families are spending more than they make , as seen by rising credit delinquency and auto repossessions, according to the Atlanta Federal Reserve. Whether it’s food, healthcare, rent or cars, Americans are spending a much larger share of their income on necessities than they did 10 years ago. For especially strapped Americans, like those facing the double whammy of a car payment and a student loan, these trade-offs are especially challenging. A good example are auto loan delinquencies, now near a 10-year high . Losing a car can mean losing a job, with devastating financial consequences . Frontline workers also miss more shifts as gas prices rise . And this gets to a core lesson for understanding today’s economy: The bedrock for consumer spending remains employment. The stable job market we see right now – with unemployment at 4.1% – is critical. If this healthy job market holds and interest rates and energy prices ultimately ease, the average consumer will still tread water. But if inflation continues to run hotter than the Federal Reserve would like, and rates rise , Americans’ disposable income will likely shrink – and hurt economic growth in the process. That could lead to a domino effect: Unemployment rises, reducing the discretionary spending that had been keeping economic growth steady. Whether it comes to this, it’s important to remember that the holiday season isn’t necessarily an accurate forward-looking indicator. Shoppers often go to great lengths to make family and friends happy. The big challenge for consumers will start in early 2027. Will the Fed hike rates? Will inflation stay high? Will gas prices come down? Until these questions are answered, we’re in the “bend but don’t break” phase. Many consumers are facing challenging times in 2026, but their resilience has been a surprise on the upside. I’d like to be surprised again in 2027 – but that’s far from a sure thing. events.title: Gaza group to air defund Israel ad during SNL
events.summary: The Scoop A pro-Palestinian group is stepping up its efforts against U.S. support for Israel, with new polling about the damage it did to Republicans this year and a new ad that will air during Saturday Night Live. The 30-second spot from the Institute for Middle East Understanding Policy Project, which shared it first with Semafor, contrasts an American girl saving up for a $400 bicycle with a girl in Gaza who lost a leg to Israeli bombs. “Every three seconds, our government sends $400 of taxpayer money to do this,” says the ad’s narrator . (The figure is close to the annual US military assistance to Israel.) The ad directs viewers to a new campaign site to rally opposition for Israel funding. And the group’s new polling is a temperature check on Republicans, whose argument about support for Israel has been inflamed since the administration first joined Israel in airstrikes on Iran last summer. Conducted by YouGov from interviews with 636 respondents who voted for President Trump in 2024 but skipped the midterm election, the poll’s main finding was that Israel was a top factor in their change of mind. Twenty-nine percent of the falloff voters said that the decision to attack Iran played a “significant role” in their decision to not vote, and 17% cited “relations with Israel.” Among these 2024 Trump voters, 78% said that “we should reduce U.S. support for Israel.” This polling closes a loop for IMEU’s political arm, which last year interviewed voters who’d voted for Joe Biden over Donald Trump, then sat out the 2024 election . The top issue cited by those non-voters was Gaza, with 29% of them saying they couldn’t have supported Harris without a change in policy. “We are airing this ad because the American people deserve to know where their money is going,” said Margaret DeReus, IMEU’s executive director. “The vast majority of Americans are unaware that President Trump is reportedly on the verge of signing another long-term weapons giveaway to Israel. With this ad, we’re trying to change that.” Trump’s decision to join Israel’s strikes on Iran has divided the right, with some of its most prominent media personalities turning on the president, while most Republicans continue to support it. The conversation about questioning funds for Israel was also changed by Abdul El-Sayed’s win in Michigan’s Senate race. There, Republicans and some Democrats complained about a Rebellion PAC ad that portrayed a couple cutting their grocery budget to pay more tax money to Israel. El-Sayed’s victory convinced many activists that the figures and organizations ruling some Israel criticism as “anti-semitism” are badly out of touch with voters – as proved by the controversial ad. “It tested through the roof,” Rebellion PAC founder Cenk Uygur told Semafor. “Moved undecideds by double digits to Abdul. Probably the most popular ad in the online world. And was partially responsible for getting Trump to say he’d end funding on Election Day. Walk-off homer.” David’s view Support for America’s current relationship with Israel is lower now than it’s been in decades, with young voters driving the decline. Republicans worked this year to make this a problem for Democrats, who now roundly oppose military aid to Israel, to the extent that Chuck Schumer’s consistent support for it has become an issue for opponents of him leading their new Senate majority. The math is different for Republicans, but the disagreement has been happening in public all year. It blew up with Vice President JD Vance’s reaction to the midterm disaster. The GOP coalition is, obviously, nothing like the Democratic coalition; most support for Israel and for disarming Iran comes from evangelical Christians who vote overwhelmingly not Republican, not Jewish voters who still largely support Democrats. I’d be surprised if Republicans react to the IMEU’s polling as anything more than meddling by actors who want both parties to cut off the Jewish state. But we are in a moment of post-midterm, pre-presidential primary plasticity, where people with resources will try to influence what both parties are talking about. Room for Disagreement Sam Markstein, the political director of the Republican Jewish Coalition, told Semafor that the GOP was now the country’s only “pro-Israel party,” and that any effort to turn it against the Jewish state was going to fail. If voters wanted a party with that agenda, he said, they now had the Democrats. “Making sure that Iran doesn’t have a nuclear weapon will go down as one of the great decisions of any presidency,” he said. Notable Last week, Axios reporter Marc Caputo published polling conducted for the Combat Antisemitism Movement , which found widespread support for Israel in early primary states, suggesting “a potential disconnect between GOP voters’ attitudes and the sentiments of those who often draw the most attention online.” U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee told the Institute for National Security Studies that Republicans were now more supportive of Israel than Democrats, and that the president’s talk about halting aid may not pan out.

events.title: The dopamine hit in markets from Jensen Huang's comeback has already faded
events.summary: Liz’s view The #SaveJensen punch wore off fast. The dopamine hit from Huang’s comeback that sent shares surging 31% on Monday has already faded as investors remember why they’d been selling: AI money is too expensive, AI demand too tenuous, AI politics too uncertain. By Tuesday, Nvidia’s shares had closed at their July 2025 levels. Markets can be wrong, for a shockingly long time. But the laws of financial gravity are catching up to AI and its frontman at speeds that are hard to outrun. Over the past year, you’d have done better owning the largest landlord of American malls than Nvidia, which holds a near monopoly on the key component of the most transformative technology in human history. Huang himself did little to help. A chastened CEO might have slipped back into headquarters, quietly mumbling something about getting to work and promising to address the corporate governance minefield he left behind. Instead he accepted a hero’s welcome and doubled down on the very things , like a lack of succession planning and dozens of direct reports, that precipitated one of the most acute and costly corporate crises in recent memory. In remarks to employees Tuesday, he said he has no plans to change any of the structural weaknesses that caused it. (He is, he noted, in therapy.) Monday will go into the record books as the largest single-day value creation in market history: Nvidia added $1 trillion. But it will end up a reverse Groundhog Day — one we immediately forget as investors sober up and remember why they were discontent in the first place. Notable Huang’s return to Nvidia will also be tough on China, Bloomberg columnist Catherine Thorbecke writes. “His comeback puts both him and his arguments [about China] under an even harsher spotlight,” she argues. “And Chinese AI’s forced breakup with Nvidia is likely to only get uglier .”
