In the second quarter, real GDP increased 2.2 percent. The contributors to the increase in real GDP in the third quarter were increases in investment, consumer spending, and government spending that were partly offset by a decrease in exports. Imports, which are a subtraction in the calculation of GDP, increased. Real GDP was revised up 0.9 percentage point from the advance estimate, primarily reflecting upward revisions to investment and consumer spending. For more information, refer to the " Technical Notes " below. Compared to the second quarter, the acceleration in real GDP in the third quarter primarily reflected an acceleration in investment and an upturn in government spending that were partly offset by a downturn in exports. Imports increased more in the third quarter than in the second quarter. Real final sales to private domestic purchasers , the sum of consumer spending and gross private fixed investment, increased 5.8 percent in the third quarter, revised up 0.9 percentage point from the previous estimate. The price index for gross domestic purchases increased 2.7 percent in the third quarter, revised down 0.3 percentage point from the previous estimate. The personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index increased 2.1 percent, and the PCE price index, excluding food and energy increased 2.5 percent, both the same as previously estimated. Real gross domestic income (GDI) increased 4.4 percent in the third quarter, compared with an increase of 2.3 percent (revised) in the second quarter. The average of real GDP and real GDI also increased 4.4 percent, compared with an increase of 2.2 percent (revised). Profits from current production (corporate profits with inventory valuation and capital consumption adjustments) increased $206.0 billion in the third quarter, compared with an increase of $384.0 billion in the second quarter. events.title: Anthropic stock tumble shows IPO gamesmanship
events.summary: IPO allocation gamesmanship strikes again, this time at Anthropic. Anthropic shares fell below their $83-a-share IPO price on Tuesday, careening toward the original target of $78 a share. The listing was reportedly six times oversubscribed, so where did those buyers go? Investors in anticipated deals ask for more shares than they actually want, assuming they’ll be cut back. “If it sounds oversubscribed, they inflate their orders, and then it gets more oversubscribed, and so on,” said Jay Ritter, academia’s godfather of IPO research. “It’s not the same as actual desire to own the stock.” He notes that pension funds, the classic buy-and-hold investors, tend to be cut out entirely of IPO allocations. Investment banks tend to steer shares to favored hedge-fund clients likely to sell into an IPO pop (Anthropic shares opened last week above $111, a first-trade gain of 34%). Supply and demand are now fighting it out, which is harder for a $1 trillion-plus company with a murky path to profitability — just ask SpaceX, whose shares are down 22% since its IPO. And Ritter? He put in an order in his Schwab account for 3,000 shares. He got 51. — Liz Hoffman

events.title: South Africa baobab trees replanted after smuggling attempt
events.summary: Five baobabs have been replanted in a South African nature reserve after being uprooted and trucked to Durban’s port, where they were going to be illegally exported. A landscaping company had sold the two-century-old trees, revered in many parts of Africa, to a customer in the Caucasus country of Georgia without seeking permission from the authorities, the South Africa-based conservation charity Baobab Foundation — instrumental in saving the trees — told Semafor. After a three-day, 900 kilometer-journey on huge flatbed vehicles, the 7 meter to 9 meter high baobabs were returned to the soil. There is no systematic data collection on baobab smuggling, but others across the continent have told the Foundation of similar incidents targeting the trees, which for some serve as shrines and a connection with the spirit world, while also providing food, shade, and a meeting place. — Damian Zane

AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Win4Wine runs the genuine Explorer shell atop Linux Microsoft fixes Office dialog that had nothing to say and wouldn't go away 3 hours ago 9/UX brings a classic Mac feel to 9front 1 day ago Old-school Linux desktops find fresh routes to Wayland 2 days ago Palo Alto Networks opens wallet for open-weight training biz 5 days ago XXRI-OS explores the lowest end of the Linux desktop 5 days ago Win4Wine is one of the more remarkable and creative hacks we've read about in recent years. It runs Windows XP's genuine Explorer shell through patched Wine on Debian 13, with a custom window manager integrating Linux applications into the desktop. As its GitHub repository explains: "The taskbar, Start menu, desktop and folder windows are XP's real ones, and Linux applications get XP's frames and taskbar buttons." This impressive, possibly demented project has English installation instructions and a README, although its design documents are in Japanese. We found Mozilla's built-in translation handled those pretty well. Its developer goes by miKuta0407 on GitHub, their homepage , and X . Also note, you're going to need some Windows installation media for the full experience. The README says: "No Microsoft files are included. Only the files that are needed are extracted locally from your own ISO." It supports Windows XP Professional SP3 installation images in 32-bit Japanese or English editions, with an experimental option for Windows 7 SP1 x64. Without either Windows image, it can download and use ReactOS's free software shell instead, for what it terms "a Windows 2000-like classic look." In our view, that sounds much better anyway. Before any former Windows users cry hurray and reach for an optical drive, this is not some ready-to-run project. The top of the README warns: "This is a personal, experimental project, not a finished product for daily use." The developer has tested it only on a fresh Debian 13 installation and recommends a VM or spare machine, rather than an existing working desktop, which sounds like an excellent precaution to us. Also, before you ask, yes, it was vibe-coded with Claude. We found ourselves reminded of another crazy-but-is-it project that we wrote about back in January: What if Linux ran Windows... and meant it? Meet Loss32 . The Loss32 proposal was even more extreme. It suggested replacing essentially the entire Linux userland, so it would be a Linux kernel running Wine with a Windows desktop and Windows apps. However, Mikuta-san was way ahead of us – lower down, the README mentions and even links to Loss32. Saying that, since it launched at the end of 2025, the bottom of the Loss32 web page shows a couple of updates, reporting on delays in getting it working. That, to be honest, did not shock us, but we still admire the let's-do-this spirit. The developer also seems to have got slightly distracted by a previous project, touchHLE: high-level emulator for early iOS apps . Loss32, in turn, reminded us of Neptune OS, an attempt to give seL4 a Windows personality transplant . We wrote about that back in 2022, and work on it has continued: the project page shows updates in recent months. The team has also pushed out preview releases in 2022, 2024, 2025, and most recently in September. This OS face transplant also reminded us of our article, Classic 7 is Windows 10 LTSC cosplaying as Windows 7 . Some people really miss the look and feel of vintage Windows. Can someone do Windows NT 4 next, please?

events.title: Senegal restored as AFCON champions
events.summary: Senegal were reinstated as the winners of Africa’s top football competition, after a court in Switzerland overturned a decision by the sport’s continental governing body that had declared Morocco the champions. January’s Africa Cup of Nations final in Rabat descended into chaos after Senegalese players walked off the pitch to protest refereeing decisions, only to return after some 15 minutes and go on to win the game. Eight weeks later, the Confederation of African Football annulled their victory over the walkout, handing Morocco the title. But the Lausanne-based Court of Arbitration for Sport disagreed, respecting the decision of the referee to continue the match. The extraordinary episode threatened to question the integrity of the CAF under the leadership of South African billionaire Patrice Motsepe. Senegal’s football federation celebrated, declaring on Instagram: “ Again and always African champions.” But Morocco said it will look for ways to challenge the ruling. — Alexander Onukwue

events.title: Trump’s meddling in Huang scandal reignites voter angst over tech’s outsized political power
events.summary: Voters this year called out the tech industry's outsized power in Washington and close ties to the president, flipping control of Congress in part as a result of their outrage. Nvidia's reinstatement of CEO Jensen Huang after President Donald Trump pressed the company’s board to bring him back may add fuel to voters' fire. Lawmakers from both parties are questioning Huang's return as the CEO faces scrutiny over national security, export controls and corporate governance and they prepare for a new Congress with voter expectations to address rising costs. When voters headed to the polls and flipped Congress this month, they sent a clear message to Washington: They wanted change. Voters wanted curbs on the technology industry's outsized power in Washington and CEOs cozying up to President Donald Trump to sway politics in their favor. The Monday reinstatement of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang at Trump's urging may be exactly the opposite of what voters voiced with their ballots. "This whole ordeal only reinforces what Americans already believe about a broken political system that stands up for Big Tech CEOs and not the American people," Sacha Haworth, founder and CEO of The Tech Oversight Project, told CNBC. Huang reinstatement reignites voter angst over tech's outsized power Jensen Huang's Nvidia return highlights U.S.-China AI talent race Nvidia whiplash tests Kevin Warsh's push to read market signals: Liesman AI debt worries grow as Nvidia rebound masks Big Tech spending squeeze Jensen Huang tells staff that Nvidia doesn't need a succession plan Trump wanted Jensen Huang back. Now, the president is all alone in Washington AG Blanche, FBI's Patel dodge questions about Huang investigation Congress blasts Nvidia bringing Jensen Huang back Jensen Huang to face Congress the same day as Nvidia GTC Republicans are warning that Trump's unwavering support for the embattled artificial intelligence chip kingpin could further alienate voters. "The data were so clear in the election that people don't trust big tech. The corruption message, I think, resonated a lot for Democrats in the election, and I think this sort of thing isn't helpful to Republicans in Congress who are going to be running again in two years," said Brendan Steinhauser, a GOP strategist and CEO of The Alliance for Secure AI Action , who had warned that AI data centers could be a "sleeper issue" in the lead-up to the 2026 midterms. Before and after Election Day, voters were clear about their concern, which centered on data centers. A Pew Research Center survey published in October found that 44% of voters considered AI very important to their vote. An NBC News exit poll found that 56% of voters said AI and data centers were crucial or a major factor in their vote for Congress. And in states including Texas, data center opposition forced GOP lawmakers who once welcomed development to change their positions. Wins for tech companies under Trump There's a lot for tech CEOs to cheer under Trump, who was welcomed with open arms following a period of tough enforcement under President Joe Biden , and many reasons to align with the administration, said Sarah Kreps, a political scientist and professor at Cornell University who studies the intersection of technology and national security. Chief among the reasons for celebration are the market's AI-driven gains since Trump's 2025 inauguration and his light-touch approach to tech regulation . The Nasdaq has gained nearly 21% from Jan. 17, 2025, the last trading day before the inauguration, and Tuesday's close. "In the end, this looks like a calculated risk that the people and interests Trump prioritizes benefit more from a stable, rising market than the administration loses from the optics," Kreps said of Huang's reinstatement, adding that the Republican Party will be left to "bear the consequences" in 2028. Outside the rarefied air of Silicon Valley and the White House, there is scant support for Huang's comeback after a series of extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy that critics say could have jeopardized national security and undermined the U.S.'s advantage in the AI race. Trump sought to allay those fears this week when he told CNBC that he assured the board that Huang posed no national security threat. Instead, Trump used concerns over the CEO giving his talents to China as a major rationale behind the reinstatement push. "The bigger threat would be losing the brain power of somebody like Jensen," Trump told CNBC this week. "That would be a threat to me. That would be a far bigger threat than anything we're talking about." Haworth said the reinstatement raises concerns over how Huang's access to Trump benefits the company's business interests, especially as the U.S. investigates chip smuggling into China.

events.title: Nigeria holds interest rate before January elections
events.summary: Nigeria’s central bank held its benchmark interest rate at 23%, with its governor expressing confidence that West Africa’s largest economy was stable ahead of crunch elections in January. The bank’s rate-setting committee pointed to slowing inflation, which has eased for five consecutive months, but noted that continued tensions in the Middle East “could sustain pressure on energy prices .” Fuel prices have surged this year in Nigeria due to supply shortfalls connected to the Iran war, despite the country being Africa’s largest crude oil producer and exporter. Higher prices are driving cost-of-living concerns that have become a central campaign issue between the leading candidates in the presidential poll, re-igniting a debate around the wisdom of President Bola Tinubu’s removal of a yearslong fuel subsidy. — Alexander Onukwue

events.title: The Download: AI swamping open records, and firefighting for permafrost
events.summary: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. AI is straining America’s open records systems AI has intensified investors’ interest in public records. Over the last few years, venture-backed startups have raised upwards of $100 million to collect data from thousands of agencies and turn it into AI-powered “signals” that help businesses sell to governments. At the same time, chatbots are making it easier for individuals to file requests. As agencies struggle to tell whether they’re dealing with a citizen, a chatbot, or a sales pipeline, some states are passing legislation that makes it easier to deny requests. That could potentially make public offices less transparent. Find out how AI is testing the limits of America’s right to know . —Matthew King MIT Technology Review Narrated: Inside the quest to combat Arctic fires and save the planet’s frozen carbon In July 2021, a wildfire burned through a forest on the University of Alaska, Fairbanks campus, stripping away the moss and soil insulating the permafrost below. Five years later, we followed researchers into the forest to investigate how fighting fires could help keep that carbon locked in the ground. Their probe revealed an escalating problem: As climate change fuels more frequent and severe fires, they’re accelerating permafrost thaw and releasing greenhouse gases. Now, researchers are trying to break that cycle. But how much should we spend, and what risks are worth taking? This is our latest story to become an MIT Technology Review Narrated podcast, which we publish each week on Spotify and Apple Podcasts . Just navigate to MIT Technology Review Narrated on either platform, and follow us to get all our new content as it’s released. The must-reads I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology. 1 Hackers reportedly used an AI tool to breach US spy agencies The tool, Artex, was originally designed for cyber defense. ( NYT $) + Sources suggested that China may be behind the attack. ( CNN ) + Officials say it exposed non-classified data. ( Gizmodo ) + A US financial crimes bureau has also disclosed a breach. ( Verge ) + AI is making online crimes easier. ( MIT Technology Review ) 2 Firms tied to Alice Huang financed $270 million of AI servers in China It’s unclear whether they contained chips restricted by the US. ( Reuters $)  + Chuck Schumer has accused Jensen Huang of export violations. ( Guardian ) 3 A powerful HIV vaccine may finally be within reach “Super antibodies” blocked diverse strains in monkeys. ( Nature ) + Yet vaccine hesitancy is on the rise. ( MIT Technology Review ) 4 China’s Huawei has been convicted of stealing US trade secrets It was found guilty on 10 of 12 counts, including bank fraud. ( BBC ) + The DoJ says it also helped Iran surveil protesters. ( Guardian ) + But it was cleared of the more serious racketeering charge. ( CNBC ) 5 Data centers have been linked to hundreds of premature deaths The culprit is pollution from connected power plants. ( Newsweek ) + Data centers are getting their own gas plants. ( MIT Technology Review ) 6 Meta insiders warn its AI moderation is causing dangerous mistakes They say the errors could have sweeping political consequences. ( Guardian ) 7 The ex-OpenAI engineer accused of spying has been freed He’ll wear an ankle monitor after posting a $1 million bond. ( CNBC ) 8 An immune-calming pill has healed severe eczema in a clinical trial Over a third of patients saw their symptoms improve. ( Bloomberg $) 9 AI is forcing researchers to reconsider artificial minds Some now think minds may not need bodies after all. ( New Scientist $) + AI consciousness debates are a trap. ( MIT Technology Review ) 10 The US Army is about to blow up 10,000 pounds of unstable explosives The old stockpile has become too dangerous to move or neutralize. ( Verge ) Quote of the day “All this guy did was cheat on his wife with two employees and a Chinese spy. Who hasn’t done that?” —Late-night host Jimmy Kimmel skewers Jensen Huang’s swift reinstatement as Nvidia’s CEO. One more thing SELMAN DESIGN Kids outlearn AI—and we still don’t know why Teaching a computer to use human language requires an inhuman amount of data. An LLM can easily churn through a hundred thousand times more words than a person will experience in the process of mastering their mother tongue. This yawning divide between children and machines is called the data efficiency gap. It raises a tantalizing question for researchers: How can children learn so much with so little? By reverse-engineering how they learn, scientists hope to create more efficient AI models—and perhaps settle enduring questions about language and children’s developing minds. Here’s how they’re trying to close the data gap . —Elise Cutts We can still have nice things A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? events.title: Flipkart CEO Kalyan Krishnamurthy to step down next week amid IPO uncertainty
events.summary: Kalyan Krishnamurthy (pictured above), who steered Flipkart through Walmart’s acquisition in 2018 and helped build it into one of India’s biggest e-commerce companies, is stepping down as chief executive next week after more than 11 years with the company. On Wednesday, Flipkart said it would announce Krishnamurthy’s successor in the coming weeks, and Chief Product and Technology Officer Balaji Thiagarajan will lead the company until a replacement is found. A Walmart spokesperson told TechCrunch that Krishnamurthy’s last day at Flipkart will be December 4. Krishnamurthy joined Flipkart in 2015 from Tiger Global, one of the company’s early investors, and became its CEO in 2017. He remained at the helm after Walmart acquired a controlling stake in the company for $16 billion in 2018. Under Krishnamurthy, Flipkart said its business grew more than five-fold. The company has more than 500 million registered users and over 1.4 million sellers, including those on Shopsy, its low-cost shopping platform. The company’s marketplace offers over 150 million products across more than 80 categories. Flipkart has of late moved into newer segments, including quick-commerce through Flipkart Minutes and, more recently, food delivery through a venture called Eat-in by Minutes . The expansion is targeted at Indian consumers who are increasingly turning to quick-delivery services for everything from groceries to electronics. Thiagarajan joined Flipkart in September last year to lead its product and technology teams. Before that, he had founded Kasu.ai , a Bay Area startup working on AI assistants for corporate finance. He also previously worked at Google, Microsoft, and Uber in senior engineering positions, per his LinkedIn profile . Krishnamurthy’s exit comes amid uncertainty around Flipkart’s IPO. In March, the company moved its headquarters from Singapore to India as part of its preparations to go public, but in May, Walmart reportedly told Flipkart to delay its IPO and focus on becoming profitable first . Walmart declined to comment beyond its announcement when asked what prompted Krishnamurthy’s departure, and whether the leadership change would affect Flipkart’s IPO plans. Flipkart did not respond to a request for comment. Founded in 2007 by Sachin and Binny Bansal as an online bookstore, much like its bigger rival Amazon, Flipkart eventually expanded into other categories. Under Krishnamurthy, it has grown into India’s largest online retailer by gross merchandise value, ahead of Amazon. “Both Flipkart and Walmart are better because of Kalyan. We are grateful for his leadership, the governance he instilled and his many contributions to the company,” Chris Nicholas, president and CEO, Walmart International, said in a statement. events.title: How datacentres are driving an illegal mining rush in the Amazon ‘more devastating than gold’
events.summary: As demand for tin ores pushes up prices, criminal gangs are exploiting Indigenous lands and weak regulation to profit from Brazil’s abundant cassiterite W hile searching for documents tied to an illegal cassiterite export network last September, Brazilian federal police officers were surprised to find a link between an illegal mining and money-laundering scheme and an address connected to one of Brazil ’s biggest showbusiness stars from the 90s. Alexandre Pires, a popular pagode singer-songwriter, is now under investigation as part of Operation Disco de Ouro (Gold Disc) for his alleged involvement in a scheme to illegally ship cassiterite worth millions of dollars abroad. During the investigation, police uncovered a message in which he allegedly admitted to his participation and said that he failed to deliver the illegal ore he had promised his associates. “This time, I sent crushed rock,” Pires said, “because I had no cassiterite.” While the involvement of a celebrity may come as a surprise, illegal ore mining in the Amazon is not. Rising demand for cassiterite, a tin-bearing ore abundant in Brazil, mirrors the 3% increase in global refined tin consumption last year as countries scramble to secure supplies for datacentres and the AI industry , electric vehicles and electrification projects linked to the energy transition. As demand increases, rising global prices have drawn illegal miners to the Amazon, where criminal groups have been exploiting the land without regard for the environment – including on protected Indigenous lands such as the Yanomami territory, which has historically suffered from illegal gold mining . To make tin extraction profitable, cassiterite must be mined in large quantities, with significant environmental impact . Illegal cassiterite mining was seldom an issue in Brazil when global prices were low. Now, criminal organisations have become increasingly involved, threatening local communities and the environment. Brazilian gangs, such as the Primeiro Comando da Capital (PCC) and Comando Vermelho (CV), have transformed illegal mining into a lucrative venture, often seen as less complicated than drug trafficking and capable of garnering political support. Jair Bolsonaro, the far-right former president of Brazil now in prison for attempting a coup , was an advocate for mining , including on Indigenous lands . “Interest in mining on Yanomami lands dates back to the 1970s, fuelled by limited regulation and support from local elites. The rise in metal prices has further incentivised this activity,” says Rodrigo Pereira Chagas, an expert in socio-environmental conflicts at the Federal University of Roraima. D emand for tin has risen, while supply disruptions have increased across the main producers. Global supply is concentrated in a few countries, and leading producers such as the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Indonesia, Bolivia and Myanmar faced disruptions last year. These production declines led the International Tin Association to predict a 13,000-tonne deficit by 2030 , further driving price increases. On the London Metal Exchange, the price per tonne surged from a 2023 low of $22,000 (£16,800) to a record $58,000 this year . “From artificial intelligence to datacentres, everything relies on tin-based solder joints,” says Natalie Scott-Gray, senior metals demand analyst at financial services network StoneX. “Tin is price-inelastic; its low melting point and excellent conductivity make it hard to replace.” Although silver could serve as an alternative, it is significantly more expensive. Scott-Gray notes that because more than 50% of tin is used in soldering applications, and demand is driven by fast-growing sectors such as digitalisation, electric vehicles and renewable energy, the demand outlook for tin is structural rather than cyclical. A supply shortfall may not halt industries but could cause delays and drive up costs. As demand for tin continues to rise, the Amazon is attracting increasing interest. Traditional artisanal mining methods – while illegal – were less environmentally damaging and are no longer feasible. According to police and prosecutors, criminal groups are now taking control: seizing public lands, displacing Indigenous communities, financing equipment purchases, and managing production and logistics. Previously, cassiterite was transported in bulk by road, but now it is often transported by air, as with gold. “Air transport is being used more frequently, even for large volumes. In some cases, such as in Yanomami territory, the same aeroplane that transports gold may also carry cassiterite,” says Pedro Duarte, head of the environmental division of the federal police in Roraima. Between 2020 and 2023, the federal police seized about 400 tonnes of cassiterite, with estimated seizures for 2025 totalling about 188 tonnes .

events.title: The questions Jensen Huang and Nvidia will still have to answer about Megaspeed
events.summary: Jensen Huang’s return as CEO to Nvidia hasn’t eased the scrutiny the company faces. The chipmaker still needs to address multiple inquiries into allegations that its advanced GPUs were smuggled into China by a customer, the Singapore-based data center operator Megaspeed, in violation of U.S. export rules designed to slow China’s development of frontier AI models. The central question for investigators is what Nvidia knew about where those chips ended up and whether Huang’s affair with a Megaspeed executive gave the company reason to doubt Megaspeed’s assurances. Huang’s return doesn’t settle that. U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche has suggested Nvidia isn’t a target of an investigation, but California’s attorney general and Congress are pressing ahead, and the Securities and Exchange Commission is reportedly investigating, too. The U.S. government opened an investigation into Megaspeed in 2024 and requested information from Nvidia about its billions of dollars in sales to the company, concerned that some of the chips Megaspeed bought for data center projects in Malaysia were in fact being diverted to China. Singapore also began investigating similar allegations in 2025. Megaspeed has denied any wrongdoing. Diversion of this kind would be a fairly routine issue for a company like Nvidia, whose in-demand chips are the targets of smugglers and resellers. When it comes to compliance and liability for export-control violations, Nvidia and other chip sellers need assurances that the end users of their chips are obeying the rules. However, they also cannot ignore other information that might call the reliability of those assurances into question, export-control attorneys told TechCrunch. And that’s why Jensen Huang’s affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang was such a problem for Nvidia, likely even more so than her alleged role as a source for Chinese intelligence agencies. If Nvidia personnel, from lower-level employees up to the CEO, had reason to believe that statements from Megaspeed weren’t reliable, the attorneys said, that would increase the company’s legal risk. “Government investigators likely would want to know, notwithstanding whatever formal assurances were exchanged between the parties, what anyone at Nvidia actually knew about the end use and end users of the chips,” Dan Fisher-Owens, an attorney at the firm Berliner Corcoran & Rowe, told TechCrunch last week. The concern Nvidia’s board faced when it decided to oust Huang is that he knew more about what Megaspeed was doing with Nvidia’s products than was reflected in any of the compliance statements. The Wall Street Journal reported that Alice Huang and her husband, Kang Wei, were part of a network of businesses that funneled chips to a company in Shanghai. Kang also reportedly introduced his wife to Jensen Huang, whom he had known for a decade. On Monday, the U.S. government added Megaspeed and its affiliates to a list of companies restricted from U.S. trade due to national security concerns. The U.S. also issued new rules last week barring large data centers that purchase U.S. chips from serving customers in China and other nations seen as problematic by the U.S. government. Nvidia, meanwhile, said it would stop selling licensed chips to China and laid out plans to hire its first compliance officer and create a new board committee focused on export controls. Nvidia’s board said it reinstated Huang on Monday after receiving “input from senior levels of the United States government” that left it confident his return posed no national security risk. President Donald Trump later said he called into the meeting to give them that assurance. In a news conference Tuesday, Blanche said that Nvidia was “a good corporate citizen” and suggested it is not the target of an investigation, but Blanche declined to answer questions about the government’s investigation into Megaspeed, which the Justice Department said was ongoing as recently as last week. “When you say the export investigation is still ongoing, I don’t know what you’re talking about,” Blanche said. Other authorities may be more demanding. Nvidia faces investigations by California Attorney General Rob Bonta and, reportedly , the SEC, both tied to its corporate disclosures. While many details of the investigation still aren’t known, short sellers complained about the company’s decision to stop breaking out its exports to Singapore in financial filings after journalists raised concerns about chip diversion. Members of Congress from both parties say they want answers from Nvidia, with many citing alarm about China and some questioning the White House’s role in Huang’s return. Three committees in the House of Representatives will privately interview Huang and Nvidia’s top lawyer, Tim Teter, next week. Teter reportedly intervened in the Department of Commerce’s investigation of Megaspeed last year.

events.title: Africa’s cashless revolution faces AI challenge
events.summary: Alexis’s view The phrase “cash is king” remains true across Africa in a way that it doesn’t in other parts of the world. In many African countries, the informal economy dominates and the flow of cash unites millions of entrepreneurs. But it’s also true that the continent has for years been at the vanguard of digital payments: That provides policymakers with more visibility into economic activity, expands the tax base, and improves the efficiency of revenue collection. The small businesses that drive African economies are increasingly making use of cheaper mobile phone handsets to swap cash for digital payments, a new report suggests. Overall transactions using mobile phones in Africa last year were more than double the figure of 2021, according to digital payment research group AfricaNenda Foundation. The average amount spent on each mobile transfer nearly halved over the same period, suggesting digital systems are increasingly being used for everyday purchases , rather than larger one-off transactions. These changing habits have far-reaching consequences. At an individual level, a digital transaction history can help to build a credit history. Some countries are even going further, linking payment systems to national digital IDs. But at the same time, AI poses a raft of new challenges by making it easier, cheaper, and faster for criminals to set up scams, such as deepfakes, to trick people into authorizing payments. A recent Interpol report found AI was linked to more than half of cybercrime in Africa , with losses across 26 nations more than doubling in 2025 compared with the previous year. Cash has remained popular because people trust money they can hold. Now that so many people in Africa have learned to trust digital payments, the next big challenge for policymakers and financial institutions is to protect users against the evolution of fraud. Notable AXIAN Digibank & Fintech, which operates across Madagascar, Tanzania, Senegal, Togo, and the Comoros Islands , signed an agreement with Huawei to upgrade mobile money platforms.

The change took effect on October 31, though Exchange remains capped at two years. Administrators can select recovery windows of three months, six months, or any whole number of years from one to ten. Microsoft's list price is $0.15 per GiB per month of protected content. Extended windows can increase costs by keeping deleted data billable for longer. Switching to a longer recovery window will also not make backups for that period magically available. So no nostalgic trips back to 2016. Wider recovery windows may appeal to organizations that need access to older data, but backups are not a substitute for compliance retention and archiving. Recovery after a breach or ransomware attack is also critical, particularly getting back to a healthy state before any malware seeped into files. Microsoft says backups are physically redundant and geographically replicated while respecting the tenant's data residency requirements. Full OneDrive account and SharePoint site restores offer recovery points every ten minutes for the most recent two weeks, then weekly points through the configured window, up to ten years. Individual file and folder recovery is limited to recovery points from the most recent 14 days, regardless of the configured window. Restore remains free, which is handy since regular testing is a vital part of any disaster recovery plan. The arrival of a ten-year recovery window is good for enterprises that need it and have deep enough pockets. However, it is important to keep in mind that being able to configure a longer recovery window doesn't constitute a disaster recovery plan in itself and may be overkill in many instances. Microsoft notes: "The existing one-year default recovery window remains unchanged. Longer recovery windows must be configured on the applicable backup policies." The company also recommends that users "review your organization's SharePoint and OneDrive backup requirements to determine whether longer recovery windows are needed." A decade of recovery history could be valuable. events.title: Saudi Arabia can fund a ‘prolonged’ war, Finance Minister says
events.summary: The News Saudi Arabia can withstand the regional war without derailing its finances, Finance Minister Mohammed Al Jadaan said, warning adversaries that missile attacks on civilian targets won’t force the kingdom’s hand. The idea that Saudi Arabia “can be blackmailed” by missile attacks on civilian targets “is a total mistake,” Al Jadaan told reporters in Riyadh. “We’re resilient enough to stand a prolonged conflict.” The kingdom has only modestly increased its defense budget after nine months of war and can significantly boost military spending if required, the minister said. “We have no price tag, we have no cap in terms of how much we can provide to our military if they need supplies.” Saudi Arabia’s finances have stood up to almost a year of unprecedented challenges from conflict in the region and disruptions to oil exports without dipping into reserves, Al Jadaan said. Higher oil prices have offset lower export volumes this year, helping total government revenue beat earlier expectations. The non-oil economy is growing despite supply chain disruptions and strains on efforts to attract tourists. But higher oil prices haven’t been enough to keep the economy running, and the government boosted spending to soften the impact, widening the deficit to 4.9% of GDP compared to forecast of a 3.3% deficit before the war. The kingdom plans to cut spending next year as some investment projects are completed and the government seeks to contain the deficit, which it expects to narrow to 3.6% of GDP. No ‘good time to reform’ Over the past year, Saudi Arabia has dropped some of its most expensive projects , including the 170-kilometer twin skyscrapers at NEOM, as it reins in runaway spending. Al Jadaan drew a distinction between projects used to achieve longer term economic goals and the overall vision for the kingdom’s economic development. “If some of the tools are not right for the moment, we’ll change them,” Jadaan said. “If some need to be warehoused, we’ll warehouse them … Vision 2030 is way beyond just one program or one project.” The economy is expected to contract 3.3% this year before bouncing back with 7.9% growth in 2027. Much of that is down to lower oil output. Corporate profits for listed companies rose around 15% in the first nine months of 2026, Al Jadaan said, indicating that the private sector growth is robust. The government expects to keep running a deficit. Debt-to-GDP is forecast to hit 39% by 2029, with some economists expecting it could breach a self-imposed 40% ceiling sooner. Al Jadaan sees no reason to increase the limit in the next few years, saying it “serves us well, it brings more discipline.” The kingdom is also pressing ahead with subsidy reforms such as measures to increase power prices from next year. The moves are unpopular and have received rare criticism of the government from Saudi citizens. “There will never be a good time to reform,” Al Jadaan said. “You go with the plan.” Notable Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman is planning to travel to the US in December for the G20 Leaders’ summit, Semafor reported. Nine months into the Iran war, Generation MBS are rallying behind the Crown Prince , who they credit for an era of new-found freedoms .

events.title: 'I only use the washing machine on a Sunday' - how we're keeping our energy bills down
events.summary: Published 25 November 2026, 00:30 GMT Domestic energy prices will soar by 26% in January under the regulator Ofgem's new price cap, pushing up bills for millions of households across England, Scotland and Wales. With household budgets already under pressure, finding ways to reduce gas and electricity costs has become increasingly important. But how much difference can simple changes really make? The BBC spoke to three people about what they're doing to keep their energy costs down. Kelly Anne Harvey uses electric blankets and portable oil radiators in some rooms to save on the central heating Like many people, Kelly Anne Harvey, a building surveyor from Cleveleys near Blackpool, is worried about her energy bill going up next year. The 44-year-old, who is married with a five-year-old son, has a combined household income of £60,000. She currently pays about £154 a month for gas and electricity on a standard variable rate with Octopus, but is looking for a fixed-rate deal to offset the rise. The family fell into arrears on their energy bills a few years ago and Kelly says she won't let it happen again. To control her costs she pays by direct debit, which spreads her payments and is typically £138 cheaper a year than paying on receipt of a bill . The family uses electric blankets and portable oil radiators in some rooms so they don't have to turn the central heating on as often. They also take part in Octopus's energy saving scheme, which rewards customers who use less electricity at peak times, such as early evenings, with a free hour of energy at the weekend. "On Sunday we'll turn on the dishwasher, tumble drier, washing machine and maybe even charge our electric cars," says Kelly. 'We've turned the heating down by 2.5C' Stacey says she keeps the curtains closed "to keep the heat in" and her daughters wear thermal clothing Stacey, 40, a single mother from Bristol, says dealing with rising energy costs has felt like a "battle" recently and she's worried about 2027. The office worker, whose daughters are aged 10 and 12, is on a fixed-term tracker tariff with E.On Next, which charges rates set below the quarterly Ofgem price cap. She expects to pay £1,800 for energy this year, up £400 on last year. Stacey, who is part of the Changing Realities project at Glasgow University, which documents life for people on low incomes, has tried a number of things to control her energy costs. She's turned her central heating down from 22C to 19.5C, bought electric blankets and pays her bills by direct debit. She also leaves her curtains shut to "keep the heat in", while her daughters wear thermal clothing if it gets chilly in the house. The family is also using less hot water. "I've got girls and they're growing up and they want to spend loads of time in the shower [but] it's just not possible." Energy bills to rise by 26% from January after gas prices surge Published 6 hours ago Three reasons why your energy bill is so high Published 10 hours ago Will I get the £100 energy payment and when will I receive it? Published 23 hours ago Around 1.5 million households in the UK rely on heating oil for heating and hot water, and their costs have already soared in the past year due to disruption in global oil markets. "When I first moved here two years ago you could get a litre of heating oil for 50-60p," says Bradley Knowles, 32, who lives in a barn conversion with his husband, mother and sister in rural Lincolnshire. "At the height of the Iran war it went up to £1.20 or £1.30 and now it's stabilised at around £1." To cut costs, the finance worker orders oil in bulk, buying 1,000-1,500 litres, preferably in the summer months when prices are lower. He also tries to order a few weeks in advance to avoid expensive next-day deliveries. Bradley uses comparison sites to see which local suppliers offer the cheapest oil and puts money aside each month so he can always afford his orders. Oil-powered boilers may take time to heat up, but Bradley advises against leaving them on all day as that can be very expensive. Instead, he uses an electric tank to store his warm water and tops up the heating in parts of the property with electric radiators. Additional reporting by Kris Bramwell & Bernadette McCague. events.title: Solomon Islands drops China pact, turns to Australia
events.summary: The Solomon Islands scrapped a security pact with China in favor of one with Australia , a reversal that dealt a major blow to Beijing’s efforts to expand its influence in the Pacific. The 2022 agreement allowed China to rotate police training teams through the Solomon Islands, sparking alarm in Washington and Canberra, which feared China was deepening a foothold in the region. Australia has in recent years contested that effort, strengthening ties with Pacific nations including Fiji, Papua New Guinea, Tuvalu, and Vanuatu with its own deals. “From China’s closest friend in the Pacific to one of Australia’s,” The Economist’s Asia diplomatic editor posted on X of the Solomon Islands’ decision, “ a big shift and an impressive piece of diplomacy .” — Prashant Rao

events.title: US court finds Chinese tech giant Huawei guilty of fraud
events.summary: A US court found Chinese tech giant Huawei guilty of fraud, deepening antagonism between the superpowers as tech and trade tensions mount. The countries’ leaders have built a strong rapport, but their policies are another matter. The US is clamping down on chip sales to China, and is reportedly weighing imposing new tariffs on the world’s second-biggest economy. The court ruling — which elicited an angry reaction from Beijing — found Huawei guilty of 10 out of 12 counts, though not the most serious charge of racketeering. The verdict crystallizes many concerns: Western firms have long accused Huawei of stealing their intellectual property, and Western capitals accuse China of unfairly supporting its firms in a bid to outcompete their overseas rivals. — Prashant Rao

events.title: Saudi defences destroy drones in Ras Tanura as footage shows smoke from refinery
events.summary: The Saudi-led coalition on Wednesday said air defences had intercepted and destroyed four drones in Ras Tanura, in the kingdom's Eastern Province, where its largest refinery is located. It did not say the refinery had been struck. However, footage circulating online appeared to show smoke rising from the energy site, which has a capacity of 550,000 barrels per day. Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis said that they had attacked the Ras Tanura oil refinery. Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the strike had caused fires at the site. The claim could not be independently verified immediately. The Houthis have been targeting Saudi airports, oil infrastructure and buildings since Yemen's frozen civil war reignited in July in the spillover from the US-Iran conflict. Previous attacks have temporarily disrupted some of Saudi Aramco's operations and led to the cancellation of most international flights to Riyadh. The refinery is part of a complex on Saudi Arabia's Gulf coast that served as the kingdom's main oil export terminal until the US-Iran war increased the importance of Yanbu on the Red Sea coast, which receives crude through the East-West pipeline . Ras Tanura is also the kingdom's oldest refinery, accounting for about 16 per cent of its refining capacity. The adjoining terminal, one of the world's largest crude export facilities, can load about 6.5 million bpd. Crude shipped from Saudi Arabia's Gulf coast goes mainly to Asian buyers, including China, Japan, South Korea and India. The complex has been attacked repeatedly this year. Aramco shut the refinery after Iranian drones targeted it on March 2, two days after the US-Iran war began, with debris causing a limited fire. The refinery restarted in mid-March, but oil loadings at the terminal resumed only in late June . On October 27, the Houthis claimed a ballistic missile strike on the complex, and a fire broke out near the export terminal. The Houthis, who control much of western Yemen, including the capital Sanaa, have also targeted the East-West pipeline. After an attack on November 9 sparked a fire, the group claimed strikes on a pumping station and a Yanbu oil facility three days later. A fire broke out at Aramco's Jizan refinery in August after it was targeted. In April, attacks cut Saudi production capacity by about 600,000 bpd and East-West pipeline throughput by about 700,000 bpd, the Energy Ministry said. The attacks recall September 2019, when drones and missiles launched by the Houthis hit Aramco's Abqaiq processing plant and the Khurais oilfield, briefly knocking out 5.7 million bpd, about half the kingdom's output. The Houthis claimed that attack, but the US and Saudi Arabia blamed Iran, which denied involvement. In March 2021, a Houthi drone targeted a storage area at Ras Tanura's port. Mr Saree also said the Houthis had attacked Riyadh's financial district in three phases, claiming the operation caused “significant damage”. Saudi civil defence said 11 people were wounded on Tuesday in a strike on a tower in Riyadh's financial district, the capital's tallest building, which houses the headquarters of the Public Investment Fund, the kingdom's sovereign wealth fund. It was the second strike on the tower in less than a week. The first, on November 19 , damaged the building but caused no injuries. Saudi civil defence released an image on Tuesday showing damage around halfway up the tower's facade, in a section similar to that affected in last week's attack.

events.title: EasyJet boss unable to rule out further job losses after profits collapse by 96%
events.summary: Kenton Jarvis says rival airlines could go bust after Iran war drives sharp rises in fuel prices and hits travel demand The boss of easyJet has said he cannot rule out further job cuts and predicted some rival airlines could go bust, after soaring fuel prices this year triggered a collapse in profits. EasyJet’s pre-tax profit dropped 96% to £24m in its financial year ending in September, compared with £658m in the previous 12 months. The airline, which has agreed to a £5.7bn takeover by the US private equity firm Apollo , said in July it had lost more money than expected during the spring, as the Iran war pushed up fuel prices and hit travel demand . Kenton Jarvis, the chief executive of easyJet, said on Wednesday that the year was “challenging for airlines due to the Middle East conflict and its effect on demand and fuel prices, which materially impacted our financial performance”. This month, it emerged that the airline was consulting on cutting up to 50 roles at its head office in Luton. EasyJet employs about 16,000 people around the world. Jarvis said: “Will I rule out future [job cuts]? Of course not. This is a commercial business, so we will always look to optimise our cost base.” He said the group continued to “look for ways to be more efficient” in its head office, adding that he had no plans for cuts to frontline staff such as cabin crew and pilots. Jarvis said weaker airlines in Europe could face an existential threat from elevated fuel prices. EasyJet’s fuel bill rose by 11% – or £244m – to £2.5bn this year alone. Surging fuel bills have pushed several airlines to collapse, such as Spirit in the US. “There could be airline failures. It would not surprise me,” Jarvis said. “This will put a lot of pressure on airlines because the fuel increase is still stubbornly high and not all airlines are hedged. “We could see some consolidation both from the flag carriers continuing on their acquisition trail, but also potentially with some market failures.” Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning While the company said it had hedged 70% of its fuel costs at just over $800 a metric tonne for the winter, and 54% hedged for the summer period at about $890, prolonged higher costs could feed into higher ticket prices. “Clearly these fuel costs will put a lot of pressure on fares,” Jarvis said, although he added that it was unlikely they would rise by as much as 20% next year, as predicted by Ryanair’s chief executive, Michael O’Leary . “It will always be dependent on demand,” Jarvis said. “EasyJet will always look to have greater value fares.” Many airlines have already reduced their flight schedules this winter to offset the impact of higher fuel prices. This month, the chief executive of Virgin Atlantic, Corneel Koster, said the airline would fly less than planned by “probably about 8% because of the cost of fuel” and “because of the drop in demand in the winter schedule”.

events.title: Energy bills jump: how to switch providers and is it worth it?
events.summary: It is possible to switch to a better tariff and save money despite the 26% price rise in January Average energy bill in Great Britain predicted to rise to £2,166 The energy price cap in Great Britain will go up by 26% in January to the equivalent of £2,166 a year. However, your bills might not have to rise by the same amount. If you are paying a tariff that matches the price cap you could save by switching to something lower. And if you do it now, you could make a substantial saving. On Wednesday, the cheapest fixed tariff on the market, an 18-month fix from Fuse Energy, was priced at £1,754 for an average home – £412 below the new January cap. It’s worth noting that it’s the price of the energy you use that is fixed, not your bill – so you will still be charged according to what you use. The easiest way is to use a price comparison website such as Uswitch , GoCompare and The Energy Shop . They typically obtain a lot of information from suppliers so you need to provide very little to get a quote (you might be alarmed by how much data is on there). Once your usage details are in and you have selected which energy you want to compare – probably gas and electricity – and how you pay, you will be presented with a list of tariffs. You will see the price for using the same amount of energy as you do now, what type of deal it is – fixed or variable – and how long it lasts. You will also be shown if there are exit fees. You will have to pay these if you want to move again before the end of the deal, and there is usually one for gas and one for electricity. Some are just £25 each, although some are £100. As a default, comparison sites typically show only the deals from providers that pay them commission when you switch, but a list of all offers should be available; look out for filters that let you see the whole of the market. The cheapest tariffs are often with providers that do not operate via switching sites, so you will only see them if you opt for all deals. If you want to move to one of them, you need to go direct. If you would prefer not to move, call your provider and ask if you are on the best tariff for your usage. If you are not, then it should also be able to help you move to a better deal. Should I move my gas and electricity? It’s up to you, and comparison sites will let you compare dual-fuel deals and separate accounts for each, letting you decide which is cheapest. What if I owe my energy supplier money? You will not be allowed to switch if you are more than 28 days behind with payments to your current supplier. If you’re on a prepayment meter you cannot move if you have a debt of £500 or more. What if the supplier owes me money? Your old provider should give you a final bill within six weeks of your switch and it then has 10 working days to refund you anything it owes. For each milestone it misses it has to pay you £40 in compensation. Can I switch if I am on a prepayment meter? Yes. You can switch as long as you do not have a debt of £500 or more on your account so it is worth checking if there are better deals available. Ben Gallizzi, energy expert at Uswitch.com, says if you’re comparing tariffs, “look at the unit rate and standing charge together rather than the headline rate alone, and think about how you’ll top up. Smart prepayment meters make topping up easier, as you can usually do it online or by app, and many suppliers now offer that for other prepayment meters too.” If you want to switch away from a prepayment meter to a standard credit one that should be possible if there is no debt. The new provider may do a credit check or ask you for a deposit. I’m a tenant – does that mean I’m stuck? No. Unless you pay the landlord for your gas and electricity and they manage the accounts, you should be able to switch. Citizens Advice says if your landlord pays your energy provider and you want to switch, you should find a tariff you want and then explain to the landlord why it’s a good deal – but it says they do not have to switch. How long does it take to switch providers? The new supplier must take over your account within five working days, unless you specify a later date for the move – for example if you are switching from an existing contract with exit fees. If there are delays, your new supplier must give you £40 in compensation. Switchers who have problems should complain to the provider in the first instance, but can then approach the energy ombudsman .

events.title: Radiant World creditor Incomlend files to withdraw lawsuit
events.summary: Incomlend is among several creditors that launched legal action against Radiant World. SINGAPORE – Singapore trade finance firm Incomlend has applied to withdraw its suit against iron ore trader Radiant World, according to a hearing schedule on the city-state’s court website. Incomlend is among several creditors that launched legal action against Radiant World after some banks and counterparties stopped doing business with it amid allegations it falsified invoices to secure financing. The summons for withdrawal or discontinuance is listed for hearing on Nov 30. It does not give a reason for the withdrawal, and Incomlend did not immediately respond to an e-mailed request to comment. A Radiant World spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The trader has denied wrongdoing, and said it conducts business “to the highest commercial and legal standards”. Incomlend provided Radiant World with over US$30 million (S$38.76 million) in credit earlier in 2026 underpinned by two invoices purportedly for sales to commodity giant Glencore, which the larger trader later told it were not genuine, according to Incomlend’s Singapore court filings. In September, a Singapore High Court judge appointed KPMG as interim judicial managers of Radiant World’s Singapore operating entity in a case brought by creditor Mizuho Bank. Judge Kristy Tan wrote there was enough initial evidence that Radiant World “is or is likely to become unable to pay its debts” to support the appointment. Radiant World’s interim judicial managers did not immediately respond to an e-mailed request to comment. REUTERS

events.title: Generation MBS has closed ranks
events.summary: Raised on reform Countries such as France, India, and Serbia may have increasingly disaffected and volatile Gen Z populations … Saudi Arabia has Gen MBS. Here, nine months into the Iran war — and roughly nine weeks into an intensifying conflict with the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen — the kingdom’s young people have been rallying behind Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, their loyalty a result of growing up in an era of new-found freedoms. There was a time before MBS — before cinemas, concerts, and women being allowed to get behind the wheel of a car — but under-25s (around half the population) either can’t remember, or don’t care to remember, what things were like a decade ago, prior to his reformist Vision 2030. Gen MBS is not bothered if the prince’s megaprojects or futuristic cities in the desert flop, they attend music festivals and watch the world’s top artists perform in Saudi — hi Travis Scott, Metallica, Eminem, Cardi B, Bruno Mars, and friends — events that, if you had told me about growing up, would’ve seemed far fetched. They go out in mixed groups of men and women, and live the way he said they would — in newly opened beach fronts in Jeddah and Six Flags in Riyadh. They came of age as the changes were bedding in and credit him entirely. Over the coming decades of his rule, the stakes will remain immense: The crown prince needs to deliver jobs and growing prosperity to keep this generation on his side. The first signs of strain are already showing, with grumblings about the recent increase in energy prices , the rising cost of living , and the number of jobs going to foreigners . But since the US-Israel war on Iran began in February, and especially since Houthi strikes intensified here from September, this cohort has become the most vocal constituency defending the country. Free lattes for loyalty The question I often get from people not from Saudi Arabia is whether these conspicuous demonstrations of loyalty are coerced. While there is no reliable polling on the subject, and no other way to survey the country writ large, in daily conversations and posts on socials the sentiment is palpable: The answer, as far as I can tell, is no. Social media feeds are filled with Saudi flag waving and the slogan “my homeland is a red line,” implying that it will be defended without compromise. Coffee chains and businesses have run promotions for members of the armed forces and those who have donated blood. Influencers have posted what amount to loyalty pledges: Among them, Saudi food blogger Yousef Hinnawi, who goes by Bo3omarEats, made a viral TikTok explainer making clear that “all Saudi nationals are the country’s first line of defense.” Influencers who have not taken a stance have been harangued by comments demanding they make their position clear. Saudis, like me, who came of age during the 2015 Yemen war, have always measured their lives against the West, questioned a government they nevertheless did not expect to change, and thought first of fellow Muslims when the Saudi-backed coalition went in. It was uncomfortable to be at war with Yemenis seen by many as less-affluent kin. For those just a bit younger, things were different. The religious police lost their arrest powers in 2016; women began driving for the first time in 2018, the same year Riyadh’s first movie theater in decades opened with . This generation is more satisfied with the standard of living, less inclined to look abroad, or question a government it sees as having delivered on a promise of bringing about reform, and is more unabashedly Saudi. With regular strikes on the capital, the prince faces a defining chapter of his rule, and he is grappling with the same restless generation confronting leaders around the world. The difference is that his people are loyal to him, and have conjured more virality around backing the prince than criticizing him. Notable Elsewhere, the kids fly pirate flags: Bloomberg charted a Gen Z protest wave — 53 mass demonstrations across 33 economies — that toppled leaders in Nepal, Madagascar, and Bulgaria. Riyadh Season opened its seventh edition on schedule in October, with sold-out concerts, a 2,760-drone show, and new zones still opening through November.

events.title: LLMs are so last year: Why Jack Hidary says AI's future runs on numbers not words
events.summary: Hours before Nvidia brought back Jensen Huang, SandboxAQ founder Jack Hidary described the sell-off as a healthy correction and said the next wave of AI would be built on physics, chemistry and finance, not the internet. He is not panicking. On a Monday morning in Abu Dhabi, with Nvidia nearly 50 per cent off its high and the Nasdaq edging towards a bear market, the SandboxAQ founder called the rout what he believes it is. “It's a healthy correction,” he said. “You need corrections like this to reassess where things are at.” Within hours, Nvidia's board would reinstate Jensen Huang as chief executive , 11 days after his resignation. By then, Mr Hidary had already addressed the question hanging over the market: what happens to AI without its central banker? The central bank of AI Mr Huang had been likened to the Ben Bernanke of AI, effectively running quantitative easing for the entire industry. With Colette Kress then in charge as interim chief executive of Nvidia, would a change at the top usher in an era of quantitative tightening for an industry increasingly reliant on circular financing? “I don't think we as an economy are going to go through that,” Mr Hidary says. “I do think some neoclouds are going to go through that.” With Mr Huang back in the chair by nightfall, the question of who runs AI's central bank has been answered. The neoclouds' problem has not. The wider sell-off , Mr Hidary says, reflects market nerves, year-end positioning and rising interest rates drawing money out of equities. “When [Federal Reserve chairman] Kevin Warsh and his colleagues around the world at central banks are offering you good rates, you're going to see some money move over to the other side,” he says. “That's natural.” His test for any correction is simple. “Was there anything fundamentally different in the economy from one day to the other? Or is it just market sentiment?” In this instance, he believes it is the latter. Enterprises remain committed to AI. 2027: The year of convergence Mr Hidary calls 2027 “the year of convergence”, when the focus of AI shifts from the commodity data of the internet to “verticalised, domain-specific data sets in energy, in bio, in quantitative finance”. “People have now ticked the box when it comes to LLMs [large language models], he says. “Every CEO had to go to their boards and say, 'we've checked the box.'” The next wave, he argues, will be driven by large quantitative models (LQMs). Trained on scientific and numerical data rather than the open internet, they are built to design products rather than draft emails. “A model trained on cat pictures and Reddit isn't the model we need to actually make these new batteries,” he says. He is not dismissing chatbots. SandboxAQ's models can now be accessed through Claude under a partnership with Anthropic. The former neuroscientist draws a parallel with the human brain, where language is only part of the equation. “But 95 per cent of the brain is not about language. It's about the real world.” Enterprise AI has so far “only penetrated documents, slides and basic research”, he says. This correspondent, whose interview preparation leans on precisely those tools, conceded he needed to up his game. The real economy For Mr Hidary, the bigger opportunity lies in energy, commodities, agriculture and industry. “This is the real economy,” he says. “That's 80 per cent of the GDP.” Batteries are perhaps his clearest example. Less than 2 per cent of electricity on the US grid can be stored, he says, leaving the grid vulnerable. He points to Egypt, which he says has secured $127 million from the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development and Germany's DEG to install batteries at the Benban Solar Park in the Western Desert region. His argument is that the pursuit of AI independence starts well before the first chip is switched on. “To get AI sovereignty, you must first start with the basics of energy sovereignty,” he says. A real-estate play For all the billions being poured into AI infrastructure, Mr Hidary is more interested in what happens beyond the data centre. “The data centre focus, I think, is a red herring,” he says, revisiting a call he made two years ago. “Data centres is a real-estate play, not an AI play.” Strip away the AI narrative and they are, in his words, “buildings and warehouses, essentially, with electricity”. The investment opportunity, he argues, lies instead in companies across pharmaceuticals, aerospace and industry that are “embracing AI faster than their peers”. He singles out Eli Lilly and Roche. Numbers not words Finance is where Mr Hidary expects quantitative AI to cut deepest. “Ultimately, it's numbers and equations, not words, that drive banks, hedge funds, investment funds,” he says. “Language models, fantastic for content, but not great on numbers.” The lessons of the 2008 financial crisis and the US bank failures of recent years, he argues, should push the industry towards more sophisticated risk management, taking it “beyond Monte Carlo”. Abu Dhabi's classroom The talent needed to build these models, Mr Hidary says, is already being trained just down the road. The Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence has grown from 200 students to 900 in three years, he says. The university welcomed its first undergraduate cohort last year. “That is a very good sign for the health of AI over the next three to five years.” For all the volatility on Wall Street, Mr Hidary's conviction about where AI goes next appears undiminished. The future, in his telling, is less about what machines can say and more about what they can do.

events.title: Africa's clothing industry opportunity is bigger than AGOA
events.summary: Eve’s view The world’s top clothing brands have been looking to diversify their supply chains beyond China and are starting to create an opening for African manufacturers. But while preferential trade access to the US has helped improve their prospects, the ability of African economies to capture a lasting share of global manufacturing will depend on a lot more than trade preferences. It’s worth noting that while China continues to dominate global clothing manufacturing, its position has gradually weakened over the past 15 years as international brands look elsewhere for sourcing. Several African countries have emerged as promising alternatives, that’s partly thanks to the African Growth and Opportunity Act, which gives eligible sub-Saharan African countries duty-free access to the US market for qualifying products, including clothing. In the latest ranking by global trade insurer Coface of the countries well positioned to expand their role in global apparel and footwear manufacturing amid changes in US trade policy, Lesotho and Madagascar climbed to fourth and sixth place respectively, having previously ranked outside the top 20. Their improved positions largely reflect the restoration of duty-free access under AGOA, following announcements of additional US tariffs of 50% and 47% in April 2025. Mauritius, another AGOA beneficiary, also features in the top 20. The benefits should not be underestimated because most competing suppliers remain subject to standard US tariffs, with some also facing new US measures targeting forced labor as well as China being subject to further country-specific duties. These are particularly significant for Lesotho and Madagascar, as the US market accounts for approximately half and nearly 30% of their respective clothing and footwear export volumes. However, that dependence exposes the limits of building a manufacturing strategy around preferential trade access. Unlike a typical free trade agreement, AGOA is a unilateral US program that allows Washington to withdraw benefits from individual countries who might fail its annual reviews to meet certain economic, governance and foreign policy criteria. That means AGOA’s recent extension until December 2028 offered no guarantee that all current beneficiaries will retain access. On Nov. 2 — just two months after the extension was agreed — Washington announced plans to terminate South Africa’s and Rwanda’s eligibility from January 2027. Ultimately this means African manufacturers need to diversify their export markets. One particularly attractive option would be to strengthen trade ties with the European Union, the world’s largest clothing consumer market, to help mitigate exposure to unpredictable US trade policy. More importantly, Africa’s manufacturing prospects extend beyond AGOA. Morocco and Tunisia, which have never benefited from the program, also feature among Coface’s top 20 countries. Rwanda remains in the ranking despite losing preferential treatment for clothing exports under AGOA in 2018. These countries’ respective approaches point to a broader set of factors that determine where international brands choose to manufacture. Labor costs, logistics, social stability, and production capacity all matter but so does the ability to deliver reliable supplies at scale. AGOA will continue to help African countries attract manufacturers, but it can’t guarantee that they stay. The real longer-term opportunity will lie in building industries that international brands choose for their commercial competitiveness, rather than simply the tariff advantages they enjoy. Notable South Africa’s exclusion from AGOA is an opportunity to find new markets says President Cyril Ramaphosa.

events.title: Huawei convicted on 10 counts in U.S. trial, but verdict is unlikely to slow China’s ‘national champion’
events.summary: A federal jury in New York convicted Huawei on 10 of 12 counts Tuesday, including bank fraud, wire fraud, and conspiracy to steal trade secrets. Yet Huawei was acquitted of racketeering conspiracy and conspiracy to obstruct justice. The verdict caps a U.S. case launched in 2018 that accused the Chinese telecommunications giant of misleading banks about its business in Iran while stealing trade secrets from U.S. companies. Sentencing is scheduled for September 2027. “Few crimes are as serious as Huawei’s decades-long pattern of endangering U.S. national security, violating the sanctity of U.S. commerce, and impeding the enforcement of U.S. laws,” U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella Jr. said in a statement . “Today’s verdict is a step towards accountability for Huawei’s criminal activities, which includes yearslong collaboration with sanctioned entities in Iran, repeated lies to banks, and blatant thefts from U.S. technology companies,” he added. Brian Heberlig, a lawyer for Huawei, told reporters that the acquittal on the racketeering charge reflected the company’s “good-faith compliance culture.” “We fully expect to appeal,” Heberlig told reporters, according to Reuters . In a statement, Huawei argued that the acquittal on the racketeering charge “confirms that these allegations lack factual basis.” The company also said it believed the other charges “are equally without legal or factual merit,” and that it would “take all necessary legal actions to defend our rights and interests.” The Chinese embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment.  Meng Wanzhou, Huawei’s chief financial officer and the daughter of founder Ren Zhengfei, was arrested in Canada in December 2018 at the request of U.S. authorities. Prosecutors accused her of misleading banks about Huawei’s relationship with Skycom, a subsidiary operating in Iran. After nearly three years fighting extradition, she was released in September 2021 under a deferred prosecution agreement with U.S. prosecutors; the charges were later dismissed. Separately, the U.S. Commerce Department placed Huawei on its Entity List in 2019, restricting its access to American goods, software, and technology. Washington tightened those controls in 2020 to cover certain foreign-made products manufactured using U.S. technology or software. Tuesday’s verdict is unlikely to slow Huawei, says Dexter Tiff Roberts, a nonresident senior fellow at the Atlantic Council’s Global China Hub. “Huawei has already weathered years of sanctions and still been able to grow and develop remarkably, even with limited access to a number of developed country markets and in particular the U.S.” Beijing may double down on Huawei instead, he adds. “In some ways, the adversity it’s already faced with sanctions [has] made Beijing double down on supporting it as a national champion, and if anything, the latest court ruling will only strengthen Beijing’s resolve to support Huawei to ensure it does not stumble.” Huawei’s role in China’s AI ambitions  The verdict comes as Huawei takes on a growing role in China’s push to build a domestic AI-computing industry, amid U.S. export controls blocking the country’s access to Nvidia’s most advanced chips. The company’s Ascend semiconductors are China’s best hope for the AI processors needed to train and run models. Chinese models are increasingly being designed to run on Huawei chips, even if Nvidia’s are better for training. Huawei rotating chair Eric Xu said the company cannot produce enough AI chips and servers to meet demand in mainland China. “Since we don’t have enough capacity to even satisfy the demand in China, we don’t have a plan to expand into the international market in a fully fledged way,” Xu told reporters at Huawei Connect in Shanghai in September, according to Reuters . Huawei reported 880.9 billion yuan ($126 billion) in revenue last year, according to its annual report.  This story was originally featured on Fortune.com
