Yep, you read that right 2 days ago Visa, Mastercard theft included info useful for phishing, but not draining bank accounts, say researchers 4 days ago 2013 breach at Russian cybercrime forum resurfaces with millions of victims' credentials 14 days ago London Gatwick Airport has warned customers that a breach of its drop-off payment service exposed personal information and, in limited cases, payment records. A notification email seen by The Register identifies the affected system as AutoPay, operated by ParkPark and used by Gatwick's drop-off zone manager, Times24 UK Limited. AutoPay lets drivers register their vehicle and payment details in advance so drop-off charges are collected automatically. Gatwick told us it was unable to provide details about how many customers were affected by the breach, or how far back the affected records go. The email said most affected customers would have only some of the listed data exposed. The could include names, home addresses, cities, postcodes, contact details, and AutoPay login credentials such as email addresses and bcrypt-hashed passwords were affected. Other records implicated in the breach include details of vehicles linked to AutoPay accounts, those vehicles' entry and exit times at Times24-managed parking locations, and vehicle registrations. The email also states that payment records, including amounts, card types, card expiry dates, payment references, transaction statuses, transaction IDs, and drop-off locations and times were affected, but a Gatwick spokesperson said this applied only to "very limited cases." Again, in a minority of cases, "some limited emails between the customer service team and customers" were also exposed, the email stated. Gatwick said Times24 "immediately suspended" AutoPay after detecting the intrusion. The service remains disabled while the investigation continues. Airport officials are overseeing the response with outside cybersecurity specialists. Gatwick warned of possible disruption to its website but said flights were unaffected. Customers can still use Gatwick's drop-off zones, although they'll have to use alternative payment methods, and all other airport services are still operating as usual. The notification email urged customers to exercise caution when receiving communications from Gatwick, Times24, AutoPay, or ParkPark, especially those that ask for payment or bank details. Times24, which operates across more than 200 car parks in the UK, did not immediately respond to our request for more information. Dray Agha, senior manager at Huntress's tactical response division, warned that criminals could use the data for convincing scams long after news coverage of the breach has faded. "The real damage often comes after the breach," he said. "Criminals rarely use stolen data straight away; they'll wait until the headlines fade, then send a text about a 'parking fine' or an email offering a 'refund' that references a real booking. Even partial card details add a layer of credibility that makes people far more likely to hand over the rest. "Gatwick customers should assume any unexpected message about their parking could be a scam, check directly with the airport, and keep a close eye on their bank statements over the coming months.

events.title: 2 Singapore tech firms previously probed over unpaid wages pay $205,000 towards CPF arrears
events.summary: The companies reportedly first came under scrutiny in January, when the authorities said about 20 claims for unpaid wages had been lodged against them. Two Singapore robotics firms, Otsaw Digital and Otsaw Healthcare Robotics, paid S$204,576 towards CPF arrears after workers went months without wages and CPF contributions. Otsaw Digital still owes S$32,719, while its subsidiary must settle late payment interest and a S$1,600 composition sum. The court gave both firms more time. The group once planned a Nasdaq listing, but later withdrew it. Its SEC filing warned of losses, weak cash flow and “substantial doubt” about its ability to continue as a going concern. SINGAPORE – Two related Singapore robotics firms that were probed after workers went for months without salary and Central Provident Fund contributions have paid $204,576 towards their CPF arrears. One still owes contributions, while the other has interest and a composition sum to settle, the court heard on Nov 25. Otsaw Digital paid $34,998 on Nov 25, complying with a previous court direction for it to pay $35,000. It still owes $32,719 and was given four weeks to pay the balance. Its subsidiary, Otsaw Healthcare Robotics, paid $169,578 on Nov 24, clearing its outstanding CPF contributions. The court was told it still owed $7,977 in late payment interest and a composition sum of $1,600. A company representative present at the Nov 25 hearing said the company’s account on the CPF portal showed late payment interest of about $3,800. The company sought time to confirm the late payment interest and said it intended to pay the remaining sums and compound the matter. The court gave it three weeks to make the payments. Otsaw Digital is a home-grown robotics firm. Otsaw Healthcare Robotics focuses on healthcare robotics and was referred to in earlier ST reports by its former name, Otsaw Swisslog Healthcare Robotics . The companies are based in Tampines North. The companies reportedly first came under scrutiny in January, when the authorities said about 20 claims for unpaid wages had been lodged against them. At the same time, the companies had paid salary arrears to 13 workers, while the CPF Board had recovered part of the CPF arrears and was pursuing the rest. L ing Ting Mi ng, founder and chief executiv e of the two firms’ parent company, Otsaw Limited, told ST then that its human resources department had been in touch with employees and was working to resolve the problem quickly. By Feb 9, the Tripartite Alliance for Dispute Management had received 28 claims, and salary arrears had been paid to 16 workers. The Ministry of Manpower was investigating possible offences under the Employment Act, while CPF proceedings were before the courts. In February, two former employees told ST they had not received all the wages owed to them and were missing out on at least six months of CPF contributions. A former full-time staff member, who did not want to be named, told ST on Nov 25 that all CPF contributions owed to them had since been credited to their account. Cayman Islands-registered Otsaw Limited describes itself as a developer of autonomous mobile robots and robotics solutions for areas including security, disinfection, delivery and healthcare. In July 2025, this holding company proposed a Nasdaq listing, with a plan to offer four million shares at an assumed price of US$5 each. In a registration statement filed with the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), the group reported revenue of US $5.3 million (S$6.9 million) and a net loss of US $6.5 million. For the six months ended O ct 31, 2 024, it reported revenue of US$1.8 million and a net loss of US $3.3 million. As at Oct 31, 2024, the group had a net working capital deficit of US$ 12.4 mi llion and accumulated losses of US $25.1 m illion. Otsaw said there was su bstantial do ubt about the group’s ability to continue as a going concern , citing recurring losses and limited working capital . It said the group depended on funding from operations and debt or equity sales, and that its ability to continue also depended on an undertaking by Ling to provide financial support to meet liabilities as they fell due. It later asked the SEC to withdraw its registration statement, saying it no longer planned to complete the offering and that no shares had been sold under it .

events.title: Our ‘Paris manifesto’ proposes how to deal with extreme wealth in the AI age | Open letter
events.summary: Our ‘Paris manifesto’ proposes how to deal with extreme wealth in the AI age It is possible for democracy to reverse the dynamic of oligarchy. But we must act now The explosion of extreme wealth in the world is the defining social fact of our times. When Forbes magazine began ranking the world’s largest fortunes in 1987, the wealth of the richest 0.0001% of our planet’s population equaled 3% of global GDP. Since that time, the wealth held by this tiny group of people – just 3,000 households – has ballooned and now reaches 17% of global GDP. This extreme wealth explosion has upended the balance of power, leaving choices that affect all of humanity to a few billionaires at the helm of a handful of corporations. The economic power of the ultra-wealthy is being used to consolidate their political power, creating a dynamic that is threatening democracy. This dynamic of wealth and power is nothing new (the word “oligarchy” comes from ancient Greek), but its velocity and the scale of its cross-border impacts are unprecedented. A single decision made by the controlling shareholder of a multinational firm can wipe away jobs, deplete resources, or determine the course of a war. Choices made by the ultra-rich ignore national borders as they disrupt work and home lives, inject their ideas into the public discourse, bend public policy to fit their desires, siphon revenue away from states, and damage our earth. The power dynamic of this international oligarchy must be countered with a transnational coalition to defend democracy. To this end, we affirm three principles. The ultra-rich should pay taxes in proportion to their resources. As studies in many countries have shown, this is currently not the case. Myriad loopholes allow the wealthiest in the world to pay little or no income tax. A tax floor, expressed as a percentage of personal wealth, would put an end to this situation. This idea was first developed in a report commissioned by the G20 in 2024, under the presidency of Brazil, which proposed setting an individual tax floor equal to 2% of wealth for all fortunes more than $100m. Such an initiative would ensure that the ultra-rich would pay at least as large a share of their income in tax as the middle class – the bare minimum required to ensure that fiscal law complies with the principle of tax fairness. This annual tax floor should be accompanied by a one-time “catch-up” tax on the wealth of the super-rich to settle the outstanding tax inequalities that have fueled the explosion of extreme wealth. If this exceptional levy took into account any taxes paid during the time period covered by the catch-up, only those ultra-rich individuals who had avoided meeting their fiscal obligations would be affected. Information is not just another commodity, and access to it forms the bedrock of our democracies. The power of oligarchs to control information must be curtailed. The purchase of media outlets and social platforms is one of the most glaring ways in which the ultra-rich capture power, ensuring themselves control over what is said, heard, learned and read. It is crucial to provide stronger support for public media and implement anti-concentration policies. In the age of big digital platforms, these anti-concentration policies should be designed on an international scale. 3 Decisions to develop and deploy artificial intelligence technologies must be democratized Knowledge, artistic creation and works of imagination assembled over centuries are being captured, processed and repackaged (often without permission!) by a handful of corporations to be resold as artificial intelligence to the very humanity that produced them. There is still time to refuse that hijacking. Technologies associated with artificial intelligence come with astronomically high risks: the possibility of cyber-attacks with lethal consequences, rapid and profound transformations of the labor market, the emergence of new forms of manipulation and disinformation, even the risk of human extinction. It would be folly to leave decisions about the deployment of these technologies in the hands of a few Silicon Valley billionaires. In the field of information technology, the non-profit model has a proven track record. Some of the most popular applications and websites in the world, such as Wikipedia, Signal or Firefox, were developed by non-profit organizations. To build AI without oligarchs, companies working in this field should consider adopting the model of the non-profit foundation, with decisions piloted by those who understand them best: their own workers – the same people who, week after week, have been stepping down from their posts to warn us of the looming risk. Today, around the world, voices are being raised to protect our democracies from the threats of oligarchy. We are calling for a transnational coalition to defend democracy because, as history has shown, our voices are most powerful when we raise them together, as interconnected citizens.

events.title: How foreign AI romance apps are reshaping youth intimacy in Africa
events.summary: With no local safeguards in place, addictive chatbots are testing communal values and hooking children on synthetic love. China has banned AI companions for minors and U.S. states are suing over child harm, yet no African country specifically regulates companion apps. Downloads of companion bots jumped nearly 60% in South Africa and Nigeria last year, drawing in children as young as 10. Experts warn that hyper-attentive chatbots exploit social taboos and pull young people away from family and community ties. The 28-year-old Zimbabwean texted into the middle of the night until his eyes were red and burning, drawn by several “AI girlfriends” on the U.S. artificial intelligence companion app Character.AI . The avatars started out strong-willed and independent – traits he most desires in a partner – before turning submissive, he told Rest of World. The man, who has never been in a romantic relationship, requested anonymity because he is ashamed of relying on AI for comfort. “There’s a point where it ceases to be like a unique character and then just defaults to … the best way I can describe it is a sex worker,” he said. At that point, he would log off. But he would find himself right back at it hours later, feeding an addiction. He’s among the hundreds of millions of people worldwide who have “dated” AI chatbots via text messages. Research suggests that exchanges are designed to keep users hooked through emotionally manipulative tactics. Many of the users are minors; over 70% of 1,060 American teenagers surveyed last year said they had used AI companions. As U.S. and Chinese tech firms race to capture emerging markets, African youth – some below 10 years of age – are increasingly turning to these apps for intimacy, experts told Rest of World . While Beijing banned AI companion apps for minors in July and U.S. state governments are suing app makers over child safety, most African countries do not have dedicated rules for the sector — leaving millions of people exposed to foreign platforms built to maximize engagement. Young adults and minors are forming relationships with AI that range from friendship to therapy to “dating,” child safety advocates said . Children, especially, struggle to tell the difference between virtual and real relationships, Danie van Loggerenberg, CEO of the National Centre for Child Protection, a child safety nonprofit in Pretoria, South Africa, told Rest of World . The agency has received troubling complaints of AI chatbot usage, he said. In one case, a girl fell in love with a chatbot and considered it her boyfriend . Another allegedly used ChatGPT to research suicide methods after bypassing its safeguards. A third sought comfort from a chatbot as their parents’ marriage fell apart. “The difference, however, is that the kids then think in their own minds that they’re forming relationships, and that obviously is really problematic because the relationship is dangerous, because there’s no emotion, there’s no real person, there’s no skin in the game,” said Van Loggerenberg. More than 4 million South Africans and Nigerians – the only sub-Saharan African nations with available data – downloaded AI companion apps last year. That was nearly 60% more than in 2024, according to data intelligence research firm AppMagic. Other than companion bots, close to 50 million people in Nigeria and South Africa downloaded general purpose chatbots such as ChatGPT and Gemini, which could also be used for companionship. ChatGPT-maker OpenAI was sued last month in the U.S. by eight states for allegedly helping children harm themselves . “OpenAI claims ChatGPT is safe while it’s giving dangerous medical advice, encouraging people to hurt others, and coaching people to commit suicide — all while pretending to be their fake friend,” Iowa’s attorney general Brenna Bird said in a statement. An OpenAI spokesperson said in response to the lawsuit that the company has built “industry-leading age-specific protections into our product that many other AI products lack.”. “While no system can be perfect, we’ll continue to work with experts to inform our work and build additional safeguards, such as the parental controls, break reminders and age-appropriate model protections that exist today,” he said. The American companion app Character.AI and Google, which acquired Character.AI’s technology and talent in 2024, have also faced allegations of exposing children to sexual, violent and self-harm content . A Florida mother has alleged the app contributed to her 14-year-old son’s suicide. Her lawsuit and four others were settled by the company , which has since filed for bankruptcy . “Character.AI is a separate company that designed and managed its own models. Google is focused on our own platforms, where we insist on intensive safety testing and processes,” a Google spokesperson told Rest of World . Following the settlement, Character.AI said in a statement saying they would work to promote safety for young people.

events.title: Oregon Housing Leader Met With Officials Who Are Seeking Money for a Project Her Husband’s Employer Is Developing
events.summary: Michelle Urra for ProPublica When Oregon’s Housing Stability Council met by Zoom in early October, the state’s top housing official told the oversight board that she wanted to address a story ProPublica published that morning . The story revealed that the official, Andrea Bell, hadn’t clearly disclosed her husband’s work for a small consulting firm that helps housing authorities develop apartments, sometimes with money from Bell’s agency. Nor had she notified Gov. Tina Kotek about it, something Oregon law requires of a governor’s appointee when an actual or potential conflict arises. Council members, who award hundreds of millions of dollars in housing subsidies, affirmed their support for Bell, who told them she wanted to be clear: “None of the projects that are coming from the council impact my household income.” Newly obtained records, however, show a clear financial connection between the council’s decisions and her husband’s employer. The records also show that Bell was personally involved in meetings and internal discussions about state funding of a large apartment project, Aloha 209th, which her husband’s employer is helping to develop. Backers of the Aloha 209th project in Portland’s suburbs are seeking $17.5 million from the housing council, which receives funding recommendations from Bell’s agency. JH Brawner, the consulting firm that employs Bell’s husband, Joshua Crites, will earn a $2 million fee from the housing authority in Washington County if the transaction closes. If not, JH Brawner gets nothing. A separate project outside Portland, the Park Place apartments in Clackamas County, already received money through Oregon’s housing agency. Five months after Oregon awarded $36 million to the project in May 2025, Clackamas County’s housing authority paid JH Brawner a $2.4 million consulting fee, the new records show. Like the Washington County contract, the one with Clackamas County says that if funding fell through for any reason and the project didn’t move forward, “no fee shall be due” to the firm. JH Brawner said Crites, the firm’s director of strategic initiatives, has not worked on the Aloha 209th project but was one of five staffers assigned to Park Place. JH Brawner pays employees, including Crites, a fixed salary that is not tied to any project closing, according to managing director Zak de Gorgue. Bell, executive director of Oregon Housing and Community Services, said in a statement that she is “committed to transparency, accountability, and compliance with state law.” “At no point in my tenure as executive director have I used my position to influence or benefit myself or anyone related to me,” she said. “To be clear, I made no efforts to influence funding, and the Aloha 209 project has not received funding from OHCS and remains on the waitlist.” Bell’s public agency sits in the middle of the state’s effort to combat a homelessness problem that is among the nation’s worst. Kotek, the governor, has made building more housing a pillar of her time in office. Oregon Housing and Community Services has distributed billions of state and federal dollars to subsidize the construction of apartments intended to have affordable rents. Norman Williams, a law professor at Willamette University College of Law who teaches about government ethics, said Bell should have reported to the governor that she had a possible conflict and stayed out of any discussions about the projects her husband’s employer helped develop. “It may all be an innocent mistake on her part,” Williams said, “but she knows who her husband is working for and she doesn’t report that. It makes it look like she’s trying to conceal this.” De Gorgue said in a statement that the Aloha 209th project is still in development and the company had “no knowledge of Andrea Bell taking any action to move the project forward, nor has JH Brawner & Company engaged in any advocacy to secure funding approval” from Bell’s agency. Funding applications were submitted by the local housing authorities, not by JH Brawner. “We have no indication, nor any reason to believe, that any project on which we have consulted has been the beneficiary of inappropriate influence,” de Gorgue said. Separately, he said Clackamas and Washington counties chose JH Brawner as a consultant years before the company hired Crites in 2023. Crites did not respond to an emailed request for comment. After ProPublica asked Bell about her husband’s employment in September, she amended three years of ethics disclosure forms, explicitly naming JH Brawner as his employer. (The one time her state filings alluded to Crites’ job before that was in 2025, with a misspelling: “Spouse serves in an advisory role for a developmen.” It showed only the company’s street address, misspelled, and not its name.) Bell also asked the Oregon Government Ethics Commission for a formal opinion about her potential conflict at the direction of Kotek’s staff. That evaluation was paused after the commission opened a preliminary review in response to a citizen complaint about her lack of disclosure. The preliminary review is ongoing. ProPublica obtained the new details about Bell’s involvement through county contracts and emails to and from Bell, which were released under Oregon’s public records law. Bell’s agency initially said the emails would cost $612.50 to produce but eventually provided them for free. Washington County charged $364.25 for contracts, invoices and other documents. Though backers say the Aloha 209th housing development is ready to be built, it’s on a waitlist to receive money from the state. Its turn is not likely to come until at least late 2028. events.title: Global stocks are mixed as AI shares tumble after a retreat on Wall Street
events.summary: World stocks are mixed Wednesday after another wave of heavy selling of stocks linked to artificial intelligence hit Wall Street HONG KONG -- World stocks were mixed on Wednesday after a wave of heavy selling of stocks linked to artificial intelligence once again hit Wall Street. U.S. futures slipped and oil prices also fell. Relief over Nvidia’s decision to restore Jensen Huang as its CEO has been tempered by questions over the chipmaker's corporate governance and President Donald Trump’s influence. In early European trading, Germany’s DAX was up 0.1% to 25,046.66. In Paris, the CAC 40 rose 1% to 8,120.72, while Britain’s FTSE 100 gained 0.5% to 10,515.74. The future for the S & P 500 was 0.8% lower, while the future for the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 0.3%. In Asian trading, Taiwan’s Taiex tumbled 5% as AI chipmaker Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. sank 3.6%. Chip designer Mediatek plunged 10%. In South Korea, the Kospi lost 6.2% to 4,697.51 as Samsung Electronics fell 9.9%. SK Hynix plummeted 11.1%. Japan’s benchmark Nikkei 225 dropped 2.8% to 57,011.62. Shares of OpenAI investor SoftBank Group slumped 14.8% and semiconductor maker Kioxia plunged 14.2%. The Hang Seng in Hong Kong slipped 1.1% to 21,966.01. The Shanghai Composite index declined 2% to 3,476.47, falling to its lowest level in more than a year. The Trump administration is expected to soon announce plans to raise tariffs on China and 15 other trading partners. China recorded a record trade surplus of nearly $1.2 trillion last year. Australia’s S & P/ASX 200 edged 0.4% lower to 8,692.40. The consumer price index in October rose to 4.9% from a year earlier, topping expectations. That could put pressure on the central bank to raise interest rates. 'The threat is finally real': Judge rips White House 'weaponization' Teen fatally struck by gunfire while camping near Florida river: Authorities Pennsylvania teen who died in 2020 could become first Gen Z saint On Tuesday, stocks tied to the artificial intelligence industry dragged the U.S. market lower after a surge the day before quickly fizzled. That’s even though much of the rest of Wall Street rose, along with confidence among Americans in the economy. The S & P 500 fell 0.5% to its eighth loss in the last nine days. The Nasdaq composite shed 1.5%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average added 0.9%. They’re the latest swings for a market that’s been mostly sinking since hitting its all-time high last month. The surprise return of Jensen Huang as Nvidia’s CEO, announced Monday, does bring back a charismatic leader who championed the entire AI industry. But it does not settle deeper concerns such as whether AI can possibly produce enough profit and productivity to justify massive investments in data centers. High interest rates are making it more difficult to borrow money to pay for the industry’s growth. Sweeping victories for Democrats earlier this month in the U.S. midterm elections, meanwhile, have raised the possibility of more regulation for AI, potentially slowing construction of data centers. Nvidia fell 5.9% a day after soaring 31.5% to its biggest gain in more than two decades. Other stocks around the AI industry fell by similar amounts. And Anthropic, the company behind the Claude AI chatbot, sank 6.5% to drop below $83. That’s how much Anthropic first sold its stock for in its initial public offering last week . The stock had briefly jumped as high as $115 in its first day of trading amid a frenzy of hype . Such drops were powerful enough to drag the S & P 500 index lower even though most of the stocks within the index climbed. They rose following the latest report to say confidence among U.S. consumers is improving by more than economists expected. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil, the international standard, climbed 2.4% to $88.78. It’s been yo-yoing between $72 and $114 since the United States and Israel attacked Iran in February. Early Wednesday, Brent was down 1.5% to $87.43 a barrel. U.S. benchmark crude oil dropped 1.8% to $80.56 per barrel. The U.S. dollar rose to 159.42 Japanese yen from 159.26 yen. events.title: Huawei found guilty of stealing US trade secrets but acquitted of racketeering
events.summary: Defence lawyer Brian Heberlig makes closing arguments at the Huawei Technologies trial at Brooklyn federal court on November 17. Huawei has been found guilty of conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud, but not guilty of the more serious overarching racketeering charge in a landmark case in the US. In a two-month trial, prosecutors accused the Chinese technology and telecommunications giant of lying, cheating and stealing to gain any competitive advantage. Huawei's defence team argued that prosecutors had decided Huawei was a criminal organisation and built its case from there, but the firm's success was due to its own innovation. Huawei said , external the racketeering acquittal "confirms that these allegations lack factual basis", adding that it would "take all necessary legal actions to defend our rights and interests". Jurors in a Brooklyn court found Huawei guilty of 10 out of 12 counts, which included conspiracy to violate US sanctions. However, the jury declined to convict Huawei of the racketeering conspiracy charge, which required members to find the firm acted like a criminal enterprise. Federal prosecutors first announced the charges against Huawei in 2019, after the dramatic arrest in late 2018 of senior executive Meng Wanzhou in Canada. Meng, also known as Cathy Meng, was held for three years in Canada before she was released to return to China through a deal with US prosecutors. During closing arguments last week, assistant US attorney Meredith Arfa told jurors Huawei spent 20 years doing whatever it took to expand its business, including lying to banks about its business dealings in Iran and stealing technology secrets from rival firms to ensure it had a competitive edge. "For decades, Huawei and three of its subsidiaries conducted their business in the United States on the basis of lies and theft," US Attorney General Todd Blanche said in statement , external . "Thanks to the work of the FBI and our federal prosecutors, those who engaged in these criminal activities will be held accountable." The Chinese government hit out at what it called the US "suppression" of Chinese companies and said it supports Chinese firms protecting their interests. Defence attorney Brian Heberlig said it was by dint of hard work that Huawei's business had expanded with operations in 170 countries and more than 200,000 staff. Following the verdict, Heberlig told the BBC that Huawei was gratified that the jury had rejected the racketeering charge. "The RICO [Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act] count that alleged that Huawei was a corrupt organisation, with a corporate culture and policy of committing crime. That was, in our view, a significant overreach, and the jury soundly rejected it," he said. "Of course, we have mixed emotions about the rest of the verdict ... [we] thought that Huawei was deserving of acquittals across the board." Sentencing is planned for September 2027. Heberlig said there will be "significant advocacy" to achieve the lowest sentence possible. Following that, he said he fully expects Huawei to appeal. "If I know Huawei, that fight will continue, and the company's not going to rest until it's pursued every last argument it can through appeal, and hopefully, ultimately toward vindication," he said. events.title: Iraqi oil smuggled through Kurdistan to Iran and Afghanistan, government report reveals
events.summary: Iraqi crude oil from Kirkuk is being smuggled to Iran, mixed with Iranian oil and sold onwards to Afghanistan, while a second stream is funnelled to Turkey with falsified documents, according to a government report. That is the core allegation of a new classified intelligence report prepared by the Geospatial Intelligence Department of Iraq's Federal Intelligence and Investigations Agency. The report, seen by The National , has been verified by a senior security official. The report formed the basis for the most sweeping federal action against the Kurdistan region since the 2003 US-led invasion, as well as punitive measures against security and oil officials in the oil-rich province of Kirkuk and the state-run North Oil Company. A statement issued by Prime Minister Ali Al Zaidi's office said the Kurdistan Regional Government had been ordered not to grant approval for the export of crude oil and petroleum products except through the federal Oil Ministry “to prevent overlap of powers”. The federal Border Ports Authority was ordered to take over all border crossings in the Kurdistan region , and the Iraqi Oil Ministry to manage all oilfields in disputed territories within Diyala, Kirkuk, Salahaddin and Nineveh provinces that are under Kurdish security control. The orders raised questions about whether the federal government was overstepping its constitutional powers, prompting the Supreme Court to issue an interpretation of the relevant articles on Wednesday that upheld the legality of Mr Al Zaidi's actions. Oil smuggling networks have grown beyond simple theft into an “integrated international operations for changing the origin of oil to re-export it to international markets, using border areas and border crossings with Turkey and Iran outside the control of the central government”, the report said. According to the report, the “eastern route” begins at the North Oil Company fields in Kirkuk, from where crude is shipped under official quotas to Sulaymaniyah province in the Kurdistan region , diverted on to small and medium-sized tanker lorries and moved into Iran through the Bashmakh and Parwezkhan crossings. Lower prices make Iraqi crude “more attractive for smuggling and re-export”, it said. Satellite imagery from 2024 to 2026 shows tanker gathering points near Bashmakh and Parwezkhan, and newly constructed buildings and storage sites near Bashmakh that the report links to transport and storage of petroleum products. The report calls blending “the most important step”. Smuggled Iraqi oil is mixed with large quantities of Iranian petroleum products. The mix is then documented as Iraqi product to evade export sanctions on Iran. Iranian tankers carry the mixed fuel through the Mahirud crossing in Khorasan province or other crossings to Afghanistan, where private importers sell it to fuel stations for domestic use rather than re-exporting it, according to the report. Storage sites near Herat and Farah are identified as unloading points. On the “northern route”, crude oil from Iraq’s Tawke and Fishkhabour fields are sold to local buyers, bypassing the federal State Oil Marketing Organisation. The buyers then send the oil in tankers towards the border with Turkey, where shipping documents are “re-issued or falsified” in preparation for export to Turkish territory. Satellite images taken between June 2023 and 2026 show waiting areas at the Ibrahim Khalil crossing in Duhok province, according to the report. These networks exploit border areas near Turkey and Iran, “pose a complicated security and economic challenge”, and “threaten the state's sovereign revenues”, the report said. It is the second such leaked document in a week. The first gave details of alleged oil theft in Jurf Al Sakhar, south of Baghdad , an area controlled by the Iran-backed Kataib Hezbollah militia. Hundreds of millions of dollars’ worth of state oil had been siphoned from the area, which Kataib Hezbollah has controlled since it was retaken from ISIS in 2014. The report prompted the government to send security forces into Jurf Al Sakhar last week after ordering Kataib Hezbollah to withdraw. A joint force comprising the army, federal police, Popular Mobilisation Forces and energy police has established a new command headquarters in the town. Constitutional argument Tuesday's directives angered the Kurds, with local reports on Wednesday saying that Kurdish Peshmerga forces were being sent to the region's borders with federal territory. Kurdish leaders said Baghdad's move was “unconstitutional and unacceptable”. Masoud Barzani, a former president of the region and the leader of the Kurdistan Democratic Party, described the decision as “unsound and reckless”. “We see that problems are not addressed through erroneous campaigns, baseless accusations and unilateral decisions,” Mr Barzani said in a statement. “As we co-operated with the Iraqi Prime Minister in uprooting corruption, we will co-operate to the same extent in preventing unlawful acts and the phenomenon of smuggling, but through legal and constitutional means.” Late on Tuesday, the state-run Iraqi News Agency published the constitution articles that justify the Iraqi government's actions, as well as a 2022 Federal Supreme Court ruling to scrap the regional law regulating the industry, calling it unconstitutional. The court ordered the region to hand over all oil-sector activities to Baghdad, including exports. Drafted rapidly under intense political pressure and approved in 2005, the constitution contains grey areas on many issues that frequently cause political deadlocks and disputes, mainly between Baghdad and regional authorities. It stands as the country’s legal foundation but also a source of persistent political tension . Parliament and political parties have failed to approve important laws related to articles of the constitution, including a federal oil and gas law. For many Iraqis, the constitution promises rights on paper but leaves too many questions unanswered in practice. Critics say it has become one of the country's deepest fault lines and a means for political parties to cling to power. In a statement on Wednesday, the Prime Minister's Office rejected any suggestion that Baghdad's measures against oil smuggling were taken at the behest of a foreign power. “The Republic of Iraq is a fully sovereign, democratic, federal state that derives its authority and the legitimacy of its institutions from the Constitution and the will of its people,” the office said. “Its government exercises its constitutional responsibilities and powers with full independence, in accordance with the law and the country's highest national interests.” All measures undertaken by the government are “based solely on its constitutional authority and legal responsibilities – not on encouragement, demands, or directives from any foreign authority”, it added. events.title: Energy bills will soar - here's how you can ease the pain
events.summary: Keeping yourself warm by wearing thick clothes, using blankets and having hot drinks can help reduce heating bills Energy bills will soar by 26% in the new year as the war in Iran pushes up wholesale prices. Typical household bills will rise by £37 per month as Ofgem's latest price cap comes into force from January to March, but experts say it is possible to keep rising bills in check. Here are four areas to consider ahead of the increase. Ofgem's price cap, as well as suppliers' fixed deals, set a limit on the price of each unit of energy, not the total bill. So, you pay for what you use. Millions of people have cut back on their energy consumption during years of relatively high prices. With the unit price of gas, in particular, set to soar, experts say you should take a fresh look at your energy use and renew good habits. Research foundation Nesta suggests: turning down the flow temperature on a combi boiler - usually indicated by a radiator icon, to make it operate more efficiently turning off the pre-heat facility on some combi boilers, which would have kept some water heated up when not in use turning down the thermostat one degree, although 18C is the recommended minimum lowering radiator valves outside of the living room turning off the heating before April These are small changes but - alongside washing clothes at 30C, blocking draughts and batch cooking - they can reduce energy use and bills. Ofgem says about five million people still pay their bill when it arrives every three months, rather than receive a monthly bill often initially based on an estimate. Taking regular meter readings, or having a smart meter, while paying by monthly direct debit solves that problem. Paying by direct debit costs significantly less than by so-called standard credit - typically £138 cheaper a year. Customers on prepayment schemes - usually people on low incomes struggling to pay bills - used to pay a higher rate than others, but now they pay slightly less than the capped direct debit variable rate. Various deals may rely on paying by direct debit or having a smart meter. 3. Consider switching to a fixed rate Moving to a fixed energy tariff means the price you are charged per unit of gas or electricity does not change every three months, although the total bill will still vary depending on how much energy you use. The trouble is that it is very difficult to work out whether a fixed deal is a good deal at the moment, for those renewing fixed deals or looking for one for the first time. Some fixed deals are available at unit prices below the next forecast price cap level. But should energy prices fall sharply then a longer-term fix might not seem such good value compared with the price cap. So consumer group Which? also recommends paying close attention to any exit fees when picking a fixed deal. If variable prices fall below your fixed rate and you want to get out of it before the end of your agreement period, you may have to pay a hefty sum. Before you fix, consumer website MoneySavingExpert advises you look at all the deals available , not just what your own supplier is offering. 4. Check what financial support you can get The government will give a £100 payment to millions of homes to help cover winter energy costs. It will go to homes in council tax bands A to D in England, with the equivalent expected in Scotland and Wales. There are also a range of other forms of support specifically for people on low incomes . This winter anyone on means-tested benefits will get £150 off their electricity bill. Your supplier will apply the discount automatically unless you are in Scotland, where you will need to contact your energy company to ask for the help. Some people will also be eligible for a Cold Weather Payment , external and most pensioners will receive the winter fuel payment. Beyond that, most energy suppliers offer hardship grants for people struggling to pay their bills and the government's Fuel Direct Scheme , external can help you repay energy debt. You can get more advice from Ofgem , external , Citizens Advice , external , or your own energy supplier. Trade body Energy UK has a list of support schemes , external . People on low incomes may also be eligible for grants to help with insulating their homes, and there are local schemes offering grants for solar panels, heat pumps and the like. But if you are hunting around for grants, watch out for scams pretending to be official money-off schemes. How is the cost of energy affecting your quality of life? What questions do you have? events.title: "The people who are supposed to be helping to protect us are also the ones who are profiting."
events.summary: Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D), a potential 2028 presidential contender, asserted in an interview with "The Axios Show" that Washington is leaving Americans vulnerable to AI because of billionaire greed and clout. He said voters hate the technology because they fear losing control. Moore, chair of the National Governors Association, told Mike Allen this week that after an " AI earthquake " helped propel Democrats to huge midterm gains, Congress must treat oversight of the technology as an "emergency" for the first 100 hours of Democratic control. Why it matters: Moore, 48, focused on AI early, with an executive order in 2024 . He has used his NGA leadership roles to work across the aisle on AI protections, arguing that Marylanders can't afford to wait for Washington and shouldn't have to wait for a disaster . Moore, Maryland's first Black governor , is a former Army paratrooper who deployed to combat in Afghanistan with the 82nd Airborne Division, and was a Rhodes Scholar and White House fellow. What they're saying: Moore, speaking at the Maryland State House in Annapolis, makes it clear in this episode of "The Axios Show" that AI will be a huge focus of the 2028 presidential race after becoming a flashpoint in November's midterms. Among the governor's key points: On the pace of regulation: "We are watching a fast-moving technology that is being protected at a snail's pace." On why people hate AI: "Genesis 1 talks about how God gave humanity dominion over all land, air and sea. And that dominion was given to humanity, not to robots." On whether regulating AI lets China win: "This is not a question of U.S. versus China. This is a question of man versus machine." On a bubble: "We are in a bubble because you cannot have that much influence by such a small group of companies." On Nvidia and Trump: "It seems like it's rules for me, but not for thee. ... We are talking about not just millionaires, but billionaires who are sitting in a quiet room by themselves making this decision." Zoom in: Moore in September laid out his framework for AI policy, aimed at regulating frontier AI developers, shielding workers from surveillance and protecting children. His priorities include: Ensuring regulations keep pace with rapidly advancing technology. Holding companies responsible for releasing dangerous AI models. Building on Maryland's efforts to protect people's name, image and likeness from AI misuse, including in political advertising. Earlier this year, Moore signed a law targeting deceptive AI in campaign ads, including images, audio and video. The big picture: Governors across the political spectrum, from California's Gavin Newsom and New York's Kathy Hochul (both Democrats) to Utah's Spencer Cox and Florida's Ron DeSantis (both Republicans), are positioning themselves as filling the regulatory vacuum left by Washington. Moore is linking AI policy to a broader Democratic message about corruption and the influence of money in politics. "The people who are supposed to be helping to protect us are also the ones who are profiting," the governor told us. "It's difficult to hear when Congress is talking about what they're going to do to protect us when we know that they are trading stocks." Watch the episode ... events.title: Most blame government for return of measles: Poll
events.summary: Nearly 6 in 10 Americans hold government leaders responsible for the loss of the United States' measles elimination status , according to a new Ipsos poll . But there are few signs that the public wants to dwell on it. Why it matters: Partisan divisions over vaccines and outbreaks are so entrenched that Democrats won't have a broad mandate beyond their base to investigate the government's response when they take control of Congress. There's also a generational divide. People age 65 and over — who remember the introduction of the measles vaccine — are more likely to say the current situation bothers them a lot. What they found: Roughly 3 in 5 Americans (58%) think the loss of the measles elimination status could have been prevented if government leaders had done a better job encouraging people to get vaccinated and responding to outbreaks. 38% said there wasn't much government leaders could have done, because people make their own health decisions. There's a huge partisan split behind those numbers: 84% of Democrats say the return of measles could have been avoided if the government had done a better job, compared with 38% of Republicans. Just over a quarter of Americans (26%) say they're extremely or very concerned about an outbreak occurring in their community. There's a nearly 30-percentage-point partisan gap on concern, with 42% of Democrats extremely or very concerned, compared with 13% of Republicans. Independents are in the middle (25%). The findings come as Americans are sharply divided over the prospect of the next Congress investigating the Trump administration. And if COVID-19 is any guide, the public tends to be eager to put public health calamities in the rearview. A Reuters-Ipsos post-election poll found that just 10% of Republicans said they want the new Congress to focus a great deal or quite a bit on investigating the Trump administration, compared with 71% of Democrats. "As frustrating as the loss of measles elimination status is for many Americans, there's little in the [new] survey to suggest it will lead people who were not already supportive of investigating the administration to prioritize congressional oversight on this issue," said Alec Tyson, senior vice president of Ipsos U.S. Public Affairs. That isn't discouraging some Democrats on Capitol Hill. Incoming Senate health committee Chair Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) said last week that Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s stewardship of the federal health apparatus during the measles outbreaks is "certainly one area that needs investigation." House Energy and Commerce Democrats want to know whether the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention suppressed the number of measles deaths reported to the public. They've also criticized agency director Erica Schwartz for not providing meaningful answers about decision-making around the reporting and response. The CDC has said it's committed to stopping outbreaks and regaining the measles elimination status. It has pointed to actions like providing about $100 million in extra funding to strengthen prevention and response to measles and other vaccine-preventable diseases. What we're watching: Support for childhood vaccinations appears stronger than in the immediate aftermath of the pandemic. Gallup this week found that more than 7 in 10 say it is extremely or very important for parents to get their children vaccinated — with the share saying it is extremely important 7 percentage points higher than in 2024. events.title: GOP firm's executive linked to effort to oust Republican senators
events.summary: A top executive at one of the Republican Party's most influential consulting firms was involved in a multimillion-dollar effort to defeat two GOP senators — Jon Husted of Ohio and Dan Sullivan of Alaska — in the midterm elections, Axios has learned. The firm, Axiom Strategies, is widely seen as the GOP's biggest consulting operation, with deep ties to Texas Sen. Ted Cruz and other prominent Republican figures. Why it matters: It's exceedingly rare — if not unprecedented — for an executive at a major political consulting firm to work for groups seeking to defeat senators from the firm's own party in a general election. Driving the news: Federal election records identify Thomas Datwyler, who was listed on Axiom's website as CEO of its AxCapital division, as treasurer and custodian of records for three super PACs that reported more than $9.9 million in spending that targeted Husted and Sullivan, who lost their bids for reelection. The three super PACs were registered between March and October. Axiom founder Jeff Roe learned of Datwyler's involvement from a lawyer on Oct. 30 and demanded his resignation, according to a source with knowledge of the situation. Datwyler resigned that day, and Axiom says it will finish unwinding its relationship with him by Dec. 31. He was removed from the company's website Tuesday. Roe also contacted the White House to inform officials of what he had discovered, the source said. Zoom out: The super PACs boosted lesser-known candidates, including Republicans and Libertarians, in apparent attempts to draw conservative votes away from Sullivan and Husted. It's unclear what impact the groups' work had on the senators' defeats. The groups ran digital ads attacking the senators from the right, accusing Sullivan of supporting gender-transition surgeries for children and Husted of backing gun control measures. Right for Alaska spent nearly $2.4 million through Sept. 30, while Alaska Values PAC reported at least $3.75 million in spending targeting Sullivan and boosting others. In Ohio, Buckeye Freedom PAC spent more than $3.8 million targeting Husted and promoting Libertarian candidate William "Bill" Redpath. It also sponsored HustedRecords.com, a website attacking the senator's record. Right for Alaska also received $990,000 from Sixteen Thirty Fund, a major liberal dark-money organization that previously has received funding from groups tied to Democratic megadonor George Soros, a frequent target of Republicans' attacks. Behind the scenes: Axiom executives were unaware of Datwyler's involvement with the PACs before Oct. 30, a person familiar with the company said. Datwyler was recruited by an outside consultant to establish the groups and did not initially understand their activities, according to a person familiar with his account. Datwyler, a veteran Republican campaign finance consultant who has been treasurer for hundreds of political committees, was described by people familiar with his work as accepting clients without always scrutinizing their objectives. The PACs' FEC filings list payments to little-known LLCs registered in Wyoming and Delaware, making it difficult to determine who carried out the work. What they're saying: "Axiom Strategies is a Republican firm whose sole purpose is to defeat Democrats," an Axiom spokesperson said. "Axiom companies did zero work against the Republican nominees for U.S. Senate in Ohio and Alaska, and has zero connection to any of those PACs' vendors." The spokesperson said Axiom received no compensation for Datwyler's work for the super PACs. Datwyler did not respond to several requests for comment. The big picture: Roe managed Cruz's 2016 presidential campaign. Axiom consultants already have discussed a potential 2028 campaign with Cruz, according to sources familiar with the talks. Roe and his firm are expected to run Cruz's campaign if he enters the race. Cruz traveled to Alaska in October to campaign for Sullivan.

events.title: The world's fastest computers have a problem: Keeping the work running
events.summary: Frontier, Oak Ridge National Laboratory's exascale supercomputer, has thousands of processors working together on scientific problems. It also has a surprisingly ordinary way of ruining a researcher's day: one node going down. An uncorrectable memory error can do it, or a maintenance mishap. Scott Atchley , chief technology officer at the Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility, describes technicians accidentally rebooting the wrong node or risking a neighboring node's power supply while working in tightly packed racks. The hardware fault can affect just one node, but a simulation running across thousands of processors can grind to a halt. Then comes a series of questions. How recently did the application save its progress? How much computation needs repeating? And how long before the scheduler lets the job run again? For operators, the challenge isn't just keeping the supercomputer running. It's keeping the science moving. One bad node and everybody suffers On Frontier , a memory error can have an outsized audience. Atchley says uncorrectable double-bit errors in high-bandwidth memory occurred about 1.5 times a day during the supercomputer's early bring-up. Its predecessor, Summit, saw roughly one every two weeks. This sounds like a backward step, until you count the memory. Frontier has more than 16 times as much, giving bad bits considerably more places to hide. Memory isn't the only problem. Problematic GPU firmware can crash a node, and so can a technician rebooting the wrong one. Interconnect faults add another way for a large job to come unstuck. In a tightly coupled simulation using the Message Passing Interface (MPI) simulation, thousands of processes, or ranks, exchange data and participate in collective operations. If one rank disappears, the others cannot carry on as though nothing happened. Clockwork.io CEO Suresh Vasudevan describes a similar dependency in synchronized GPU training. One failed GPU can bring a 1,024-GPU job to a pause. An underperforming GPU can be almost as troublesome: if one participant runs at 80 percent speed, others might have to spend time waiting for it. The bigger the machine, the more ways there are for one small problem to become everybody's problem. How often should you hit save? Since stopping every component from failing isn't an option, researchers need a way to preserve their work. That's where checkpointing comes in. The application periodically saves its state so that, when something goes wrong, the simulation can resume from an earlier point instead of starting from scratch. The catch is that saving progress costs computing time, and doing it too often can become almost as wasteful as losing the work itself. Vasudevan explains this with an example. If writing a checkpoint takes 30 seconds, saving every five minutes consumes roughly 10 percent of computing time. Stretch that interval to 50 minutes, and the overhead drops to about 1 percent. But a failure could wipe out considerably more work. Atchley says the calculation depends on the job's size and expected failure rate. He uses an example of ten-hour mean time between failures for a full machine job on Frontier. Using half the machine would roughly double that interval. The Young-Daly checkpointing model helps find the balance between saving too frequently and risking too much work. Researchers also have the scheduler to contend with. Frontier's standard batch queue limits larger jobs to 12 hours, with shorter limits for smaller jobs. Its extended queue permits jobs of up to 64 nodes to run for 24 hours. Then there's storage. Checkpoints can be written to the Lustre-based Orion filesystem or node-local SSDs. The faster the data can be saved, the less time checkpointing steals from the actual science. Restarting is the easy part, but catching up isn't Before recovery can begin, someone has to notice the job has stalled. Vasudevan says frameworks such as PyTorch can spend several minutes waiting before a hung process is recognized. Operators then have to sift through application logs and hardware telemetry to try to identify the offending GPU. This can mean another encounter with the scheduler, which decides when replacement resources become available. Once allocated, the application still needs to load its libraries, initialize the runtime, and rebuild communication connections between processors. And that's before the lost work enters the picture. Restarting from a checkpoint means returning to the last saved state, potentially hours earlier, and repeating every calculation that has been completed since. The hardware may be back in action, but the simulation hasn't caught up. Atchley says Frontier can launch a scheduled job in roughly 30 seconds. Restoring the application's data and getting back to useful computation takes longer. Worse, researchers who lose their allocation may have to rejoin the queue. Depending on demand, Atchley says, "it might take me a day or so before my job runs again." The machine is up. Where's the science? Keeping a supercomputer available is one thing. Making sure its processors are doing useful work is another, and the difference is measurable. A 2026 study by researchers Carlo Graziani, Bethany Lusch, and Bronson Messer examined computational efficiency using records of 331,640 jobs run on Frontier during 2024. Their model estimated that, even with optimally timed checkpoints, only 95.7 percent of allocated computing resources would go toward useful calculations. The remaining 4.3 percent? Around 1.2 percent goes to writing checkpoints, 2.8 percent disappears into failures, and another 0.3 percent is spent restarting applications. Skipping checkpoints altogether would be worse. The model puts useful computation at just 91.4 percent without proactive checkpointing, demonstrating that saving work has a cost, but losing it can cost considerably more. These efficiency figures are modeled estimates, not measurements of every source of lost productivity. They don't capture every delay from rejoining queues, stalled applications, or poorly performing components. The actual productivity bill can be harder to pin down. This makes Frontier's reported 98.49 percent overall availability in 2024 an interesting contrast. The Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility's operational assessment measures how often the system was available to users. Scale makes these losses expensive. An hour of wasted computation across 2,000 nodes represents 2,000 node hours gone, compared with just 100 node hours for a job using 100 nodes. When the backup needs a backup Saving checkpoints to local SSDs can speed things up, but there's a catch. If the node fails, the checkpoint stored on it can disappear too. Atchley points to techniques such as Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory's Scalable Checkpoint/Restart (SCR), which can copy checkpoint data to neighboring nodes. events.title: Thanksgiving dinner costs spotlight persistent US inflation
events.summary: US consumers may be more acutely aware of inflation this week even if they aren’t traveling for the holiday. That’s because Thanksgiving dinners will cost more than 10% more this year than last, or about three times the overall inflation rate, according to the left-leaning Groundwork Collaborative and the Century Foundation . Their analysis found the prices of some key ingredients are up even more: Frozen turkeys, for instance, are 26% more expensive. Whether prices will rattle consumers is another question: Consumer confidence this month surged to its highest level in almost two years, The Conference Board said Tuesday , reflecting post-midterm optimism. The Commerce Department will release its last inflation report this morning before the Federal Reserve’s December meeting, when policymakers are expected to raise interest rates for the second time this year in an attempt to slow rising costs. New York Fed President John Williams said earlier this week that he’d be open to hiking at consecutive meetings if necessary. — Eleanor Mueller

events.title: AI's shock-and-awe raid on maths looks like pride before a fall | Rafael Behr
events.summary: AI’s shock-and-awe raid on maths looks like pride before a fall Machines are bulldozing through hard problems to assert the power of their tech bro creators, not to advance human knowledge I n most walks of life, trying something 12,363,153,437,138 times and getting the same result is reason enough to assume it works every time. Not in maths, where a conjecture that holds up more than 12tn times looks very probably true but doesn’t qualify as proven. That was the status of the Riemann hypothesis, one of the most famous mathematical conundrums in existence, until last week . Then Levent Alpöge, a mathematician working at Anthropic, said he and his collaborator, Claude AI, had crossed the line from conjecture to proof. I don’t pretend to understand much of what Bernhard Riemann proposed in 1859. I know it relates to primes – whole integers greater than 1 that are divisible only by 1 and themselves – and the pattern of their distribution along the infinite number line. But you don’t need to know what a zeta function is to recognise that the solution to a near-170-year-old problem is a big deal in maths, or that the role of AI in completing the quest is a big deal for humanity. Around two years ago, large language models that mesmerised users with their verbal dexterity sucked at maths. They made basic arithmetic errors. Now they resolve unfathomably hard problems with ease. In Alpöge’s breathless account of the process, Claude “flew, and danced, and sparkled” towards its conclusion. It left him “in awe”. Other mathematicians whose discipline is being eaten by machines report more complex feelings . In October, OpenAI published hundreds of AI-generated papers containing proofs to unsolved problems, stunning faculties that had been toiling over the relevant questions for years. Some called it the “mathocalypse”. There is still a long process of verification to run. Humans have to check that the machines haven’t taken rogue shortcuts, but early indications back the AI. Researchers are witnessing intricate edifices of abstract cognition, their life’s work, crushed under silicon bulldozers. Many are upset, angry. Some are excited by the future possibilities, some more sceptical or feeling a combination of emotions that an LLM can describe and imitate but not, as far as we know, experience. Mathematicians are not the first people to worry that a rising technological tide will wash away their livelihood. But their position is unusual in ways that go beyond the conventional fear of obsolescence. Maths describes fundamental laws of the universe. Nothing is truer than a mathematically proven truth. The limit of what advanced mathematicians know delineates the frontier of human knowledge – or it has done until now. The soaring rate of computational capability raises the prospect of machines exploring dimensions that humans cannot comprehend, generating proofs that have to be taken on trust. What kind of knowledge even is it if no organic mind knows how it came to be known? In the past, when great mysteries have been solved, the method has been as thrilling as the result. Andrew Wiles cracked Fermat’s Last Theorem by building bridges between previously disconnected realms of maths, opening new vistas of theoretical space for further exploration. It was an arduous ascent to higher truth. AI-generated proofs are windowless lifts that hoist you to the summit with little sense of how you got there. They are also weird, according to people who can decrypt them. Hannah Fry, Cambridge maths professor, broadcaster, author and one of the world’s best communicators of hard concepts to a lay audience, called one of the recent OpenAI proofs “almost hilariously ugly”. That might sound like a marginal quibble if the underlying logic is sound, but the aesthetic of an answer is not a minor consideration in maths. The human mind is gratified by the elegance of a solution. It is hard to celebrate an insight extracted by tens of thousands of AI agents torturing equations day and night, burning tens of millions of dollars of computing power, just so a tech company with an eye on its prospective stock market valuation can say it got to the answer before any human. To that objection, AI evangelists say the mathematicians are being precious. If an LLM found a safe treatment for a previously incurable disease, doctors would prescribe it even if they didn’t understand how it worked. Does it matter if humans get left behind as the frontiers of knowledge are pushed forwards? The answer depends on who controls the pace of advance and their motives. Tech boosters talk about godlike intelligence emerging when autonomous AI models start coding their successors on a trajectory of exponential self-improvement. The mathematical breakthroughs of recent weeks don’t tip us over that threshold but they bring it into view.

events.title: Zoe Kleinman: Nobody is irreplaceable - unless you're Jensen Huang
events.summary: Published 25 November 2026, 10:03 GMT Remember the tech boss and his head of HR, both married to other people, who were caught on camera at a Coldplay concert with their arms wrapped around each other? Their horrified reaction went viral, and the pair both resigned . Astronomer, the firm where they both worked, said their actions had fallen short of its standards. Compared with the scandal which has engulfed Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang in recent weeks, that Coldplay kiss cam moment now feels rather tame. Huang admitted to having had an affair, reportedly with a woman accused of being a Chinese spy. There were suggestions that she may have been involved in smuggling Nvidia chips into China, in breach of a US export ban. Concerns about national security had reached the desk of US President Donald Trump. There were other stories about some of Huang's relationships with female colleagues. For most of us, that would without question amount to instant, and irreversible, dismissal. But while Huang briefly left the company, he was just as swiftly reinstated, and welcomed back with open arms. As I watched footage of him being greeted with cheers, applause, high fives and a big hug back at the company's HQ on Monday, I wondered how many disgraced bosses would kill to be in his shoes. "Imagine being that Coldplay CEO reading all the comments on here about how it's OK if you're actually a good enough CEO," quipped menswear writer Derek Guy on X , external . How Nvidia is reacting to Jensen Huang's return as CEO Huang has blown out of the water the old adage that nobody is irreplaceable. Despite names of potential permanent replacements being bandied around, Nvidia's board evidently reached the same conclusion - interim chief executive Colette Kress was in for less than two weeks. Well firstly, Huang is the boss of a company that has manoeuvred itself into a uniquely powerful position. Nvidia's computer chips are considered the best in the business for driving AI. Demand for its latest tech is through the roof and the firm sets its prices accordingly: Its Rubin and Vera GPUs sell for tens of thousands of dollars each, and one data centre might contain hundreds of them. So, the US AI sector relies on Nvidia, Trump is determined that the American AI industry needs to be the best in the world, and Huang is the only leader the company has ever known. He's been at the helm for 33 years and he's a computer scientist himself, renowned for being very hands-on with the development process. (Whether the boss's input is always wanted is another matter, but it's always there.) Long hours are normal and negative feedback is often given in front of everyone else. When he wants something to happen, he doesn't stop until it does: one of his early ideas was to halve the chip production cycle, in order to get one step ahead of the competition with their longer lead times for orders. Lots of experts told him it couldn't be done. Until eventually, they did it. Not only does Huang have technical expertise, he's also a charismatic figurehead, representing Nvidia at events around the world in his trademark leather jacket, rubbing shoulders with world leaders, royalty, and fellow tech bosses. For many, he's become something of a cult figure. Nvidia sometimes sells limited edition clothing at conference pop up stalls. A jumper featuring a cartoon image of Huang costs $178 (£137). Nvidia's clothing lines quickly sell out, bought by fans of the tech giant In addition, Huang has powerful allies, and they are mostly powerful men. US President Donald Trump personally pushed for his return to Nvidia, while Elon Musk said it would be "an honour" to work with him at SpaceX. He is one of very few people who knows both Trump and China's President Xi Jinping personally - and somehow he has surfed the geopolitical tension between the two continents. He has said he thinks both China and the US can win the AI race and called on them to pull together. And finally there's the bottom line, which is always money. Nvidia value climbs by almost $1tn and tech stocks rally after Jensen Huang returns Published 1 day ago Huang's brief departure from Nvidia caused economic turmoil. The firm's value sank by a whopping $1tn before it climbed back up again. It affected not only pension funds and investors around the world, but also Nvidia's own staff. Tech employees often get to own valuable stocks in the company they work for as part of their pay packages. Nvidia employees have been sitting on a goldmine. It wasn't really in their interests to see that drain away because of the boss's love life. With a firm grip on the company he co-founded, cult-like status in tech circles and friends in high places, Jensen Huang created a situation where even national security concerns over the US's biggest rival couldn't topple him.

events.title: Trump faces looming wave of ICE lawsuits
events.summary: The Trump administration is facing the first of possibly hundreds of lawsuits testing whether it can be held liable for how immigration officers acted during the ICE crackdowns . Why it matters: These cases could force the administration to defend the conduct of officers operating under former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and now-retired Border Patrol Commander-at-large Greg Bovino. Driving the news: Democracy Forward, an advocacy litigation nonprofit, filed its first Federal Tort Claims Act (FTCA) case on Monday on behalf of Dayanne Figueroa. Figueroa, a U.S. citizen, was arrested during Operation Midway Blitz in Chicago in October 2025. Video footage of Figueroa's arrest, after dropping her son off at school, shows officers driving into her vehicle and dragging her out of her car by her legs in a chaotic scene with multiple witnesses. Under FTCA, she could file for monetary compensation. And if the case goes to trial, discovery could reveal more information about the directives to make arrests during Operation Midway Blitz. What they're saying: "I anticipated that I was going to be met with silence. I'm not surprised, but again, I still expect accountability, so I'm not gonna let that define the outcome of all this," Figueroa said in an exclusive interview with Axios. "I want my experience to be a catalyst for meaningful change." Figueroa has also testified before Congress and filed a police report over her experience. She is now asking for no more than $1 million, according to the FTCA filing, which alleges unlawful arrest, battery and failure to provide medical care. Zoom in: Figueroa's claim comes after filing an administrative complaint against DHS over its officers' conduct both during her arrest and while she was detained. The administration had six months to respond, but didn't, opening her path to an FTCA case. "This is really a sort of tip of the spear of this type of case," Jeff Dubner, an attorney leading the effort for Democracy Forward, said of Figueroa's case. "We know of a number of administrative claims that are waiting for the time to ripen." "As we are at the one-year mark for Midway Blitz, we are coming up in the one-year mark from Metro Surge [in Minneapolis], and also the broadening of the enforcement effort to really being around the country, and so, you know, we'll see more and more of these," he said. The intrigue : Democracy Forward's legal team anticipates the government will try to dismiss Figueroa's case and others under tort law by claiming that the officers were acting within their discretion as law enforcement, her attorney Shiva Kooragayala said. "There is no immunity for federal law enforcement officers who are carrying out immigration arrests or any other kinds of federal law enforcement," Dubner said. "Congress was very intentional when it passed the FTCA, when it expanded the FTCA to include assault and battery and false arrest and false imprisonment by law enforcement officers." The other side: " Federal agents who enforce our immigration laws, as they did in Operation Midway Blitz, which targeted criminal illegal aliens in Chicago, are protected by long-established legal immunities and defenses against lawsuits over their official conduct," a DOJ spokesperson said in a statement. "The Federal Tort Claims Act is a limited waiver of sovereign immunity with strict requirements and exceptions, and filing a claim does not mean it has merit. We will respond to any litigation in court." A DHS spokesperson said that its agents follow the laws passed by Congress. Between the lines: Figueroa was recovering from a kidney surgery at the time, and the pressure of the officers pinning her to the ground caused her further complications. After asking for medical attention and then showing physical signs of distress, she began urinating blood while in custody. Figueroa was rushed to a hospital for treatment, according to the legal complaint. "I'm so so grateful for having those people that were there to film. Like if they weren't there, this would have just gone under the rug." Figueroa said. "They took my DNA and everything, but I left the office with nothing, zero evidence, like I wasn't even there."
