events.title: Rival AI leaders push back against Anthropic vision of surrendering human agency to AI
events.summary: Top AI executives are increasingly pushing back against a common view inside Anthropic: that humanity should surrender some decision-making power to superintelligent AI systems, sources told Axios. That would put us on a slippery slope to forfeiting free will, critics say. Why it matters : The debate has picked up steam as top AI companies develop models certain employees consider too powerful to ever release . Many see Anthropic as the first company that will confront these questions due to its lead at the frontier of AI development. While critics have yet to call out the company by name, their public defenses of human agency and control take direct aim at what some have come to see as the worldview of Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei. When AI systems far surpass human intelligence, Amodei has said repeatedly that it will be preferable to turn over decision-making for "life-critical" cases to AI, and also said AI should oversee research and potentially distribute economic resources. Flashback: A product vision slide from several years ago that was revealed during litigation described Anthropic's "vision for a better world" as a "utopia ruled by god in a box." The big picture: The thinking for Amodei and others is that once AI can demonstrably cure diseases, safeguard humans from harming themselves or prevent disasters better than any person, refusing to hand over control becomes irrational — or even unethical. Proponents point to self-driving cars to make their case: Once statistical evidence points to autonomous vehicles being safer than human drivers, it is logical for humans to drive far less, if at all, they say. Inside Anthropic, a broad consensus has developed among some employees that humanity will—and in many cases should — safely hand over authority to superintelligent systems rather than fighting to retain control, according to people familiar with internal discussions. An Anthropic spokesperson said Amodei has advocated for human control of AI in many public remarks and that Anthropic trains Claude not to undermine human oversight. Driving the news: Rival executives are increasingly rebuking the notion that humans will surrender agency, even as major math and reasoning breakthroughs convince insiders that superintelligence is imminent. "We should not be okay with a 'handover' of society to AI," Meta's top AI leader Alexandr Wang wrote on X, reflecting on the importance of a coming superintelligence moment after an Anthropic breakthrough on a "Holy Grail" mathematics problem. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman rebuked this view earlier this month: "I want people to have the agency over the future... I think it's really important that we advocate for this." Dean Ball, OpenAI's head of strategic futures, calls this phenomenon the " silent consensus. " He told Axios this is "an extraordinarily common view in AI safety circles," adding that "People don't always think it's good. Some people do." Zoom in: Across podcasts, public interviews and in his writing, Amodei has for years pointed to specific arenas where he believes the best choice will be for humans to step back, although he has also said there will be "many cases where we do want to stay in charge" even if humans make worse decisions: Safety: In a February New York Times interview, Amodei said that in " life-critical, safety-critical cases , we really want to turn it over" to AI, noting society will simply need time to adapt. Defense: In a CBS discussion that month, he argued that fully autonomous weapons may eventually be "needed for the defense of democracy " if adversaries deploy them first. Education: In November of 2024, Amodei noted that the traditional system of a professor supervising graduate students could be reversed, as "the AI systems will be the PIs, will be the leaders, and they'll be ordering humans or other AI systems around." Writing: In his 2024 essay "Machines of Loving Grace," Amodei suggested one possible future economy in which superintelligent AI systems distribute resources based on "what the AI systems think makes sense to reward in humans." He notes that it could the distribution could be "derived from human values." Between the lines: Some AI leaders are privately frustrated by rhetoric about turning over decision-making because they fear it is pouring fuel on a growing public and political backlash against the technology. That's exactly what Maryland Gov. Wes Moore — a potential 2028 Democratic presidential contender — said this week in an interview on "The Axios Show." Invoking the Book of Genesis, Moore argued that God gave humanity dominion over the earth, "not to robots, not to agents." Friction point: Outside of Anthropic, AI executives have appeared divided in their public views on free will in the superintelligence era. Elon Musk recently reiterated his decade-plus-long view that when we hit superintelligence, the human race will become "like pet labradors," although he's also backed technology to amplify the human brain with machine computation capabilities in order to give humans a continued advantage. The bottom line: The debate over superintelligence is no longer just about how to keep rogue machines from destroying humanity — it's about whether humans should be willing to voluntarily step aside.

events.title: This Thanksgiving won't be stuffed with politics, Americans say: Poll
events.summary: Data: YouGov; Chart: Avery Lotz/Axios. Note: Data for this question among 929 adults who say they're celebrating Thanksgiving After November's midterm blue wave , Democrats are more likely to say political discussions will be on the table this Thanksgiving than Republicans, per recent polling . Why it matters: The volatility and vitriol of modern politics often threatens to infiltrate our social dynamics. Still, most Americans doubt the holiday will bring political arguments. By the numbers: In YouGov's survey, 37% of respondents planning to celebrate Thanksgiving said they were at least somewhat likely to discuss politics during dinner. More than half (56%) say politics is not likely to come up during their gathering. Yes, but: The share who expect to talk politics this year varies by party affiliation. Forty-five percent of Democrats celebrating Thanksgiving say they expect political conversations, compared to 28% of Independents and 39% of Republicans in YouGov's trend. Zoom in: And more than eight in ten think politics won't start turkey day tiffs: Just 12% expect arguments over politics at the celebration. Those numbers are relatively stable among political ideologies: 83% of Democrats, 82% of Independents and 85% of Republicans aren't prepping for a political food fight this year. Last year, among all respondents in YouGov's poll , 11% expected arguments, compared to 72% who didn't. Zoom out: Data for Progress, a progressive polling and research organization, similarly found that 11% of likely voters said they'd definitely discuss politics at Thanksgiving, and 26% said they probably would. Another 59% said they probably or definitely would not. However, 65% said they plan to talk at least some about the cost of living. Friction point: Even if political arguments don't fuel Thanksgiving stress, pocketbook strain is another story. This year, the average Thanksgiving dinner is up 6%, ending three straight years of price declines, according to the American Farm Bureau Federation . But as Axios' Brad Jennings notes, the survey's price checks were done earlier in the month, possibly before deeper discounts or promotions kicked off. The bottom line: We can't promise the turkey won't be dry or that your nosy aunt won't pry. But if your dinner goes how most Americans expect, politics won't be the root of this year's family drama. Methodology: The YouGov poll was conducted online on November 8 - 10, 2026 among 1,081 U.S. adult citizens. The margin of error for the overall sample is approximately 4 percentage points. events.title: ‘Half price!’ ‘Only two left!’ How to resist the bargains you just don’t need – this Black Friday and beyond
events.summary: Everywhere you look, there’s another unrepeatable deal at an unmissable price. What’s on offer will make you happier, smarter and sexier. Except, of course, it won’t. Let us help you ignore the ‘consumption noise’ T he other morning a parcel arrived and I was momentarily mystified by its contents. Peering at what appeared to be a shiny maroon and pink cushion cover, the penny eventually dropped. It was the fancy “Sweat Bag” I had bought on impulse when it popped up on Instagram after a particularly trying day. The blurb had convinced me it was the perfect solution for storing sweaty gym gear, ensuring that everything else in my bag remained pristine. “Whether it’s a 6am class before work or squeezing in lunchtime workouts, the Sweat Bag moves with you, wherever your day takes you.” I liked the idea of being this busy, efficient human, but in reality, I generally head straight home after my workouts and collapse beside the nearest biscuit tin. I had no business spending, ahem, £39 on it. If you’ve ever fallen into a similar retail trance only to experience buyer’s remorse, chances are that you, too, have been ambushed by “consumption noise”. Since the rise in popularity of weight-loss drugs we’ve heard quite the cacophony about “food noise”, with users celebrating the welcome absence of cravings. In a similar vein, consumption noise can best be described as the low-level but relentless triggering of a hunger to buy stuff just for the sake of it. “Consumption noise is everywhere. It’s online, it’s outdoors. If you look at the amount of advertising we constantly receive, when we’re on public transport, on the streets, especially in big cities, it’s a lot,” says Emilie Bellet, a former private equity analyst and the founder of the financial education platform Vestpod . This constant exposure is best summed up, she says, by the phrase “‘visual pollution’, a term invented by Marine Tanguy, the author of The Visual Detox. Then, of course, there’s online pollution as well. You buy from a brand one time and you’re on their mailing list, bombarding you with offers, which creates more temptation.” I like to think that I’m good with money. I’m a thrifty Scot who agonises over whether to buy the posh butter or the Aldi dupe. And yet when it comes to marketing tricks, I’m pretty gullible. When I see a tempting offer online flagged with “only two left in stock”, I can feel my heart-rate speed up. Recently, this drove me to buy the world’s most useless slow cooker – it doesn’t have a timer. “I mean, even if it is true that the stock is about to run out, don’t worry. Chances are good that the item will come back,” says Bellet. “For me, the feeling of just putting an item in the basket makes me happy. I get a little hit of dopamine. And then after two days, I realise actually, I don’t really want it, or I’m busy with something else and decide not to buy.” Bellet goes as far as using a Brick blocking device to remove social media from her phone in the early morning and in the evening. The gadget contains a Near Field Communication chip and works with a companion mobile phone app. You choose which apps and websites to block and tap your phone against the Brick to activate. The device is magnetic, the idea being that you stick it on the fridge so you can’t turn your apps back on until you return to the kitchen to tap it. “It creates more clarity, more space for something other than always looking at people trying to sell you stuff,” says Bellet. Another option is to pay £3.99 a month to go ad-free on, say, Instagram. “It sounds like a lot to pay but it’s a gamechanger,” reports a colleague. “Weirdly, now I’m free from falling down rabbit holes into fashion brands I can’t afford, I am drawn to look at the app a lot less.” But the special-occasion buzz around Black Friday and its manufactured sense of urgency can destabilise the best of intentions. “We’re bombarded with these time-limited discounts; perhaps there’s even a countdown timer or warnings about how many other customers are viewing the same item,” says Aarron Atkinson-Toal, the author of a new book, Influenced: The Science of Why We Buy. “Suddenly not buying something can feel like missing out on an opportunity rather than choosing not to spend our money. It’s easy to feel overwhelmed by all that information, all the different offers, and so we start to respond to these quick prompts to ‘buy it now’ instead of carefully considering what we actually need.” Atkinson-Toal identifies an interesting paradox. “Humans are generally risk-averse. We don’t like missing out on something. So with Black Friday-style offers we are forced to decide which is worse for us as an individual – the pain of missing out on the deal or the pain of buying something that you later realise you don’t need. More often than not, we make the purchase.” This explains why even the most mindful among us can sometimes make unwise impulse buys.

The Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA) and Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) have today published revised rules designed to support securitisation’s contribution to economic growth. Securitisation allows a firm to divide loans into 'tranches' which have different risk profiles. Investors may buy some or all tranches, providing the firm with funding for further lending, while the interest from the loans pays the investors, who also absorb some of the losses when borrowers do not repay their loans. Securitisation can help firms manage their funding and risk, supporting further lending to businesses and households. Today’s changes are designed to make the regulators’ requirements more proportionate and less prescriptive, helping reduce unnecessary costs for firms, while maintaining financial stability. They include: Simplifying due diligence and transparency requirements, holding investors and issuers to the same standards of understanding and disclosing risks without being overly prescriptive; Introducing more flexible risk retention options, while ensuring firms keep at least 5% of a securitisation's value at risk; Allowing some simple and prudent re-securitisations to support firms' funding and liquidity needs, while continuing the ban on the wider practice. The reforms are also estimated to reduce industry costs by around £168 million over the next decade while maintaining important safeguards and high standards. Phil Evans, Director of Prudential Policy at the Prudential Regulation Authority, said: 'Securitisation is an important part of a modern financial system. It is obvious that we must never go back to the dangerous practices in place before the great financial crisis, but we shouldn’t go too far the other way either and stifle lending. Today’s final rules strike that balance and should encourage firms to lend more to households and businesses.' Jon Relleen, Director of Infrastructure and Exchanges at the Financial Conduct Authority, said: 'Strong capital markets are vital to support economic growth. By simplifying the UK's securitisation regime, we’re reducing unnecessary costs, giving firms and investors greater flexibility, and better reflecting market practice. The changes support more effective markets but crucially also maintain high standards to mitigate potential risks.' The FCA has published near-final rules as part of its reforms to the UK securitisation framework. This policy statement follows a number of recent PRA and FCA measures aimed at supporting growth, competitiveness and innovation in UK financial services while maintaining financial stability, including, exploring ideas to support the growth of credit unions; simplifying the Senior Managers & Certification regime; and automatically increasing over 100 PRA regulatory thresholds to provide certainty for firms. The FCA has published near-final rules as part of its reforms to the UK securitisation framework. The rules are near-final because the related statutory instrument has been laid by HM Treasury but has not yet been made. The FCA intends to make the final rules shortly after the statutory instrument has been made and does not expect any significant changes to them. The PRA has published final rules at the same time. For further details of estimated costs saving, please refer to the cost benefit analyses set out in FCA Consultation Paper CP26/6 . Regulators implement growth-friendly securitisation... events.title: Not Just Nvidia: Inside Team Trump’s Takeover of Intel
events.summary: ‘Rejection Will Have Consequences’: Inside Team Trump’s Takeover of a Chips Giant The message from the Trump administration to one of the world’s leading semiconductor companies was clear: Give the US government a chunk of your company. Right now. Or else. Do not make the “mistake of thinking that this is a negotiation,” Commerce Department lawyer David Shapiro told the chief financial officer of the Intel Corporation in August 2025, according to internal notes from a company call contained in a federal lawsuit. “The President is expecting to announce a deal on these terms on Friday.” Shapiro acknowledged that “the Board could choose not to accept the offer,” according to a summary of his remarks prepared for Intel’s directors. But the Trump administration official “noted that rejection will have consequences that [Shapiro] cannot predict.” Days later, the board gave the administration what it wanted . “It is my Great Honor to report that the United States of America now fully owns and controls 10% of INTEL,” Donald Trump posted to his social platform . “The United States paid nothing for these Shares, and the Shares are now valued at approximately $11 Billion Dollars. This is a great Deal for America.” President Trump was similarly jubilant on Monday, announcing that he had “ convinced ” Nvidia’s board of directors to rehire chief executive Jensen Huang. The proclamation was a shock. But it wasn’t entirely without precedent. Fifteen months earlier, the Trump administration had interfered with the leadership decisions at another major chipmaker, court documents allege. Then, as now, allegations swirled that the company’s CEO was too close to China. Then, as now, the Trump administration dealt itself into the company’s financial future. It’s part of a broader shift within the government in general and the Commerce Department in particular, a former member of that department tells WIRED. Out are old metrics “like creating jobs or the US being more competitive or owning more of the market share,” this ex-Trump administration official says. When dealing with private companies, a single overriding concern is: “Are you going to give back to the government in cash?” Documents unredacted as part of a shareholder’s lawsuit against Intel’s board show how far the administration has been willing to go to get what it wants. The lawsuit’s allegations were previously reported by WP Intelligence. “The Board, operating under the shadow of the President’s threats,” the lawsuit alleges, “caved to the government’s extortion.” A second case, asking for internal records, was filed in April by the same shareholder, Richard Paisner, against Nvidia. “It's just straight-up coercion,” says Scott Lincicome, a vice president at the libertarian Cato Institute. “The company starts making decisions not based on what's best for the company in the short or long term, what's best for shareholders, but what's best for politics and what the government is demanding.” “That's not what you want from any company,” he adds. “When you're talking about the world's most innovative companies and these kinds of bleeding-edge technologies that have not only huge economic implications but national security ones, then that's a huge problem.” Representatives for Intel declined to comment for this story. The White House, Commerce Department, and Nvidia did not respond to requests for comment. The parallels between Nvidia’s government-assisted autogolpe and Intel’s alleged forced sale aren’t exact. In the Intel case, Trump all but accused the company’s boss of being compromised by Beijing; in the Nvidia situation, the president reportedly dismissed concerns from his own intelligence agencies about the executive’s connections to China. But both instances show a growing fusion of private enterprise and public office . During the Biden administration, Intel won awards for up to $11 billion in government grants and contracts, much of it under the CHIPS Act, which was meant to help build semiconductor manufacturing and assembly plants in America and bolster domestic research. At the time, there was some grumbling inside the Commerce Department, which administered the CHIPS and Science Act grants, about funding what was seen as a “failing incumbent” in the semiconductor space, says the former official. (Intel had, in recent years, fallen on hard times .) But by March 2025, Intel had received about $2.2 billion of the grants. That’s when President Trump told Congress that the CHIPS Act was “ a horrible, horrible thing .” The rest of Intel’s money was put on hold, tied to hitting certain milestones, while the administration said it was renegotiating the deals. The same month Lip-Bu Tan was hired as Intel’s new CEO. Soon after, his ties to China made him a Trump target, when Reuters reported that Tan had invested in “hundreds of Chinese tech firms,” some with connections to Beijing's military.

events.title: AI is straining America’s open records systems
events.summary: In Panton, Vermont, population 660, town clerk Kyle Rowe did it all. He crafted budgets, paid vendors, handled property tax disputes, and served as the town’s zoning supervisor and presiding elections officer. During morning office hours at the town hall—a wood-frame structure built as a church in 1858—he also fielded public records requests. Recently, he got rather busy. Panton used to get a request every year or so from a company called SmartProcure for “all purchasing records,” covering everything from road salt to computers to toilet paper. Last year, those requests started coming quarterly. Then different companies began making more specific requests, like records of every purchase related to emergency road flares. These targeted inquiries started coming monthly or more. “I’m happy to answer public records requests from people,” says Rowe, who recently moved into a position at a nearby town. “But answering it for these purposes—it feels like I’m doing unpaid opposition research on the taxpayers’ time.”  Rowe’s experiences are being repeated across the US. While data brokers have mined public records for decades, AI has intensified investors’ interest. Over the last few years, venture-backed startups have raised upwards of $100 million to collect data from thousands of agencies and turn it into AI-powered “signals” that help businesses sell to governments. At the same time, AI tools have made it easier for individuals to draft public records requests. Many places have seen double-digit annual increases in recent years. While more activity is good for democracy, AI-drafted requests tend to be longer, and broader in scope—and the offices answering them haven’t always grown in head count or budget.  As agencies struggle to tell whether they’re dealing with a citizen, a chatbot, or a sales pipeline, some states are passing legislation that makes it easier to deny requests, possibly making public offices less transparent.  Transparency, monetized The US Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) of 1966 established citizens’ right to know what their government is doing, and by now every state has written its own version into law. Greater transparency has led to cleaner drinking water, lower taxes, and better schools. But the system is far from perfect: Many requests linger for months, the process is often frustratingly bureaucratic, and rules and guidelines vary by state, county, and even town.  This is why businesses, with the time and resources to navigate this labyrinth, have often dominated FOIA since its early days. Margaret Kwoka, a law professor at Ohio State University and a recent member of the FOIA Advisory Committee, documented the trend in her 2016 study “ FOIA, Inc .” Her analysis found that commercial requesters of all kinds—regulated companies, government contractors, information resellers—have accounted for 79% to 96% of public records requests at federal agencies like the Environmental Protection Agency and the Food and Drug Administration. What Kwoka once described as a cottage industry of small shops reselling public records has become a lucrative market for “much more sophisticated and integrated database products,” she says. SmartProcure (which does business as GovSpend) pioneered the model 15 years ago, with a standardized approach for collecting government purchasing data. Its requests are “handled by real people with long-standing relationships,” says Trip Colden, GovSpend’s chief operating officer, and the company has preferential pricing for agencies. The newer AI startups promise to make selling to government faster and fairer. Starbridge has raised $52 million, including a Series A led by Craft Ventures (the firm of David Sacks, the former White House AI and crypto czar), to build the equivalent of a “Bloomberg Terminal for public sector data,” a reference to the pricey data consoles that are a fixture on Wall Street trading desks. The company describes its mission as getting “the best technology into the hands of public leaders,” with public records as one input that helps match agencies with vendors. Pursuit, backed by investors including Bill Gurley and Jack Altman, has raised $25.5 million to help companies identify likely government buyers, drawing on board minutes, budgets, and what it calls “an industrial-scale FOIA operation.” CEO and cofounder Mike Vichich says Pursuit’s data will benefit the public, noting that many towns are seeing costs rise faster than revenues and “competition is what saves taxpayers money.”  While incumbents employ account teams to build a rapport with agencies, several clerks and county attorneys say newer startups often send many requests as they scramble to catch up on historical data. For example, PinPoint Analytics, which analyzes construction bid data, sent as many as 2,000 requests per day while building its dataset before settling closer to 500 today, says chief operating officer Mark Zurada. That mirrors the activity of SmartProcure and Pursuit, which send roughly 180,000 requests per year, according to their websites. But the numbers can be much higher. NationGraph, which serves midsize vendors such as janitorial service providers, claims to send about 10,000 requests per day on behalf of clients; the company did not respond to requests for comment. The requests that companies send are typically written with templates, not AI. But AI helps standardize what comes back—spreadsheets, PDFs, mailed packets—and analyze it all to create branded sales “signals,” or benchmarks to help the business clients set their prices. In small towns, this activity can be an annoyance; in cities and counties, which get many times the volume, handling it is becoming a full-time job. Chautauqua County, New York, hired a paralegal this summer after seeing requests double—an increase its county attorney blamed on people using ChatGPT to generate requests and on others seeking records to resell. In Ann Arbor, Michigan, chief deputy clerk Sarah Alanis has seen the number of requests climb from 581 in 2021 to 937 last year—“our new normal is high,” she says. A growing share comes from requesters harvesting data at scale, sometimes asking for purchases from “vendors that don’t have much to do with one another,” or ones the city has never used. FOIA used to take a few hours of her week; now it’s often half her day , she told the Michigan Advance earlier this year. The AI detection problem It’s not just sales tech—AI tools have made it easy for anyone to fire off requests. Federal agencies received a record 1.7 million last year, which a New York Times report attributed partly to AI, as well as to mass filings by the Heritage Foundation and a rise in the number of immigrants seeking their own records for legal protection. events.title: An Alarming Spike in Ectopic Pregnancy Deaths Was Hiding in Plain Sight in a Federal Dataset
events.summary: Ectopic pregnancy deaths have nearly doubled in the United States in recent years. Shawn Patrick Ouellette/Portland Portland Press Herald/Getty Images For years, ProPublica has examined maternal health and the ongoing impacts of abortion bans since the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade. Data analysis has been central to that effort, offering a quantitative view into an area that has long been underresearched, especially as studying the impact of abortion bans has become politicized and federal agencies have been gutted under the Trump administration. For example, last year my colleagues uncovered a dramatic rise in sepsis rates since Texas instituted its abortion ban, which carries the strictest penalties for healthcare providers. The number of blood transfusions during emergency room visits for first-trimester miscarriage spiked in the state as well.  Most recently, my colleagues Andrea Suozzo, Sophie Chou, Kavitha Surana and I examined pregnancy-related deaths on a national level . We turned our attention to Centers for Disease Control and Prevention data. The agency collects information from death certificates and publishes totals based on variables like location, demographics and cause of death. It’s a commonly used resource for journalists and academics who want to learn more about trends in mortality. Deaths involving an ectopic pregnancy are presented as a rate within three-year intervals to meet data suppression thresholds. Source: ProPublica analysis of CDC WONDER multiple cause of death and natality data. Lucas Waldron/ProPublica The increase was particularly stark in states that had banned abortion. Deaths involving an ectopic pregnancy are grouped into three-year periods to meet data suppression thresholds. States with abortion bans that begin at six weeks of pregnancy or earlier are considered to have a strict ban. Source: ProPublica analysis of CDC WONDER multiple cause of death and natality data. Lucas Waldron/ProPublica This was a significant and serious finding. And as far as we could tell, the fact that the number of women who died from ectopic pregnancies nearly doubled after abortion bans came into effect hadn’t been reported before.  A death from an ectopic pregnancy should be a “never event,” according to Dr. Alice Abernathy, an OB-GYN in Philadelphia. And yet, as we later confirmed, more than a dozen leaders in the field of maternal health were unaware of the spike. Neither state governments nor the federal government, whose own dataset we were using, had publicly identified this trend.  How could it be that seemingly no one was aware of this but us? The answer, as it turns out, is multifold and begins with the nature of the condition itself. Ectopic pregnancies occur when an embryo fails to properly implant in the uterus and begins to develop elsewhere, most commonly inside a fallopian tube. The pregnancy grows until it causes the organ to rupture, triggering catastrophic bleeding. It is a rare condition, estimated to impact up to 2% of pregnancies, but it is incredibly dangerous.  “I genuinely thought I was going to die,” said Kyleigh Thurman, whose right fallopian tube ruptured after she struggled to get ectopic care in Texas in 2023. “There were a few times I asked my husband if I was going to die,” Leitaea Lowrimore of Oklahoma said in an ongoing lawsuit challenging an abortion ban, after being denied treatment for an ectopic pregnancy at multiple hospitals in February. “I kept thinking about our kids.” Even before ectopic pregnancy deaths began rising, the condition was noted as the leading cause of death in the first trimester of pregnancy. The most recent nationwide study we could find examined data only through 2013. Instead, in our country, much of the work of investigating pregnancy-related deaths is left to state committees. This creates a large potential knowledge gap. In individual states, the number of ectopic deaths is small and subject to a lot of variation, making it harder to spot a trend. After our story was published, we reached out to maternal mortality review committees in states with abortions bans; many of them responded that they didn’t identify an increase in ectopic deaths and that, despite the findings of our reporting, they had no plans to examine this issue further. We realized the fact that nearly double the number of women are dying from ectopic pregnancies is visible at only the national level. It is unclear why the CDC and other federal agencies across two administrations have failed to publicly respond to the increase in deaths despite having access to the same information ProPublica analyzed. We reached out to the CDC to ask what the agency has done to investigate or address this trend. It has epidemiologists who review death and birth records and has in the past done its own investigations and analyses. A spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services, which oversees the CDC, didn’t provide a direct answer to that question but said the agency continues to track maternal mortality trends, investigate their causes and provide funding for research. The CDC’s Division of Reproductive Health, for example, lost most of its 100 employees, according to a lawsuit filed by more than a dozen states’ attorneys general last year. This lack of awareness surrounding ectopic pregnancy deaths is imperiling women’s lives.  Read More Ectopic Pregnancy Deaths Have Nearly Doubled. It’s Worse in States With Abortion Bans. events.title: Gatwick Airport hacked: Cyber-attack may have exposed customers’ bank details
events.summary: Travellers using Gatwick Airport have been warned their personal details may have been compromised after its parking system was hacked. Attackers breached AutoPay, the automated drop-off payment system, possibly accessing some customer card details. Gatwick, the UK’s second-largest airport with 43 million passengers annually, told customers on Monday of the risk to their personal information. Drivers are charged £10 for staying up to 10 minutes in terminal drop-off zones. Although the payment system was switched off after the breach, customers were told they must still pay the charge through its website. The airport did not reveal when the hack occurred or how many people were affected. In an email sent to customers, the airport apologised and said it had been informed by its third-party provider Times24 UK Limited, there had been “unauthorised access” to the payments system. It said the data that had potentially been stolen included names, postcodes, contact details, vehicle details, payment records and some card details, including in “some isolated cases” the card brand, last four digits and expiry date. It told customers it was trying to determine the “nature and scope of the incident”, while relevant authorities had been informed. “We have been informed by Times24 UK Limited, the company which manages drop-off zones on behalf of London Gatwick that they experienced unauthorised access to AutoPay, a third-party system that automatically processes the payment of drop-off charges," Gatwick said. “As a precaution and to help protect affected accounts, the AutoPay system has been disabled. Passengers can still continue to use the drop-off zones and pay using one of the alternative payment methods available on our London Gatwick website.” The breach is the latest attack on the UK’s data systems. In August, the data of almost nine million passengers using three airports was accessed by hackers, who demanded a ransom. The attack on Manchester Airports Group, which owns Manchester, East Midlands and London Stansted airports, breached similar data to the Gatwick incident. Last year, European airports including Heathrow were hit by delays after a cyber attack hit the check-in and baggage systems. Earlier this month, UK businesses were told they must urgently strengthen their cyber defences or face major disruption . Britain’s head of cyber security issued the warning after supermarkets across Europe were victims of hacking. Richard Horne, head of the UK's National Cyber Security Centre , said organisations were relying on outdated technology that was increasingly vulnerable to cyber attacks, while artificial intelligence was giving hostile states and criminals new ways to identify and exploit weaknesses.

events.title: What will the energy cap changes mean for my bills?
events.summary: Energy bills are to soar in January, as prices governed by regulator Ofgem's cap rise at the coldest time of the year. The cap affects millions of people in England, Scotland and Wales, and reflects higher wholesale gas costs which have been pushed up by the US-Israel war with Iran. It means people on variable tariffs should give an accurate meter reading, ensure they are receiving all the support to which they are entitled, and take care over energy use. What is the energy cap and how is it changing? The energy cap fixes the maximum amount which customers on standard variable tariffs can be charged for each unit of gas and electricity used. It covers more than 20 million households in England, Wales and Scotland and is set by the regulator Ofgem every three months , external . It affects those paying by direct debit, by standard credit (they pay when they get a bill), or prepayment meters in slightly different ways. Most of the increase in the energy price cap has, and will be, driven by higher gas prices. The government's decision to temporarily remove VAT from domestic electricity bills has cut about £45 a year from a typical bill. Meanwhile, millions of households will receive a £100 automatic payment to help cover winter costs. Customers' actual bills depend on the amount of energy they use and how they pay for it. From January, for those on variable tariffs: For electricity, average unit prices will go up on 1 January from 26.32p per kilowatt-hour to 32.69p Gas will increase from 7.97p per kilowatt-hour to 10.96p, higher than in the wake of the invasion of Ukraine Daily standing charges will be 54.77p for electricity and 29.65p for gas The roughly 11 million households on fixed tariffs will not see their prices change until the end of their fixed term. Ofgem regulates the energy market in England, Scotland and Wales. Northern Ireland has a separate system. As well as how much energy you use and how you pay for it, where you live, the type of property you have, how energy efficient it is, how many people live there, and the weather all make a difference. The Ofgem cap is illustrated using "typical" household energy use in a year with a single bill for gas and electricity settled by direct debit. The vast majority of people pay their bill this way to help spread payments across the year. In July, Ofgem reduced what it believes to be a "typical" level of energy use, because many homes have cut back due to high prices in recent years while energy efficiency has improved. Its new estimate is 9,500 kWh of gas and 2,500 kWh of electricity a year. Should I take a meter reading when the energy cap changes? Submitting a meter reading when the cap changes means you are not charged for estimated usage at the wrong rate. This is especially important when prices go up. Customers with working smart meters do not need to submit a reading as their bill is calculated automatically. Energy bills will soar - here's how you can ease the pain Published 9 hours ago What are standing charges and how are they changing? Ofgem also controls standing charges, which are a fixed daily fee to cover the costs of connecting households to gas and electricity supplies. These vary slightly by region , external and payment method. Between 1 October and 31 December 2026, average standing charges for direct debit customers are 54.83p a day for electricity and 29.68p a day for gas. From January, daily standing charges will be 54.77p for electricity and 29.65p for gas. The electricity standing charge is lower than the amount charged over the previous three months, while the gas charge is largely unchanged. Campaigners have long argued that standing charges are unfair because they make up a bigger proportion of the bill for low-energy households. Others say it just shifts the cost from one part of the bill to another rather than cutting it. The government has announced plans to remove gas standing charges, although no details have been published on how that will happen Fixed deals provide certainty for a set period – often a year, or longer – but if energy prices drop while you are on the deal, you could be stuck at a higher price. You may also have to pay a penalty to leave a fixed deal early if you change your mind. Experts recommend checking whole-of-market energy price comparison sites to help find the best deal and studying the details of exit fees. What else has changed about the way energy bills are calculated? Since 1 April, energy bill charges related to the low-income household insulation scheme - called the Energy Company Obligation - have been scrapped, and for three years, renewable energy projects will be 75%-funded by general taxation instead of a levy on energy bills. Nearly everyone in England, Wales and Scotland will benefit from this cut, although the amounts will vary between households. However, the cost of maintaining and strengthening energy network infrastructure like power lines, cables and gas pipes is rising.

events.title: Spain's economy has grown under Sánchez, but many voters aren't feeling it. 5 charts explain why
events.summary: Spain's economy is growing faster than most of Europe, but many Spaniards are struggling with high living costs MADRID -- Spain's economy has been growing faster than most of its European peers, but many Spaniards haven't felt the benefits. Discontent, particularly around soaring housing costs, is widespread and bound to be a decisive force in Sunday's national election . On the campaign trail, incumbent Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has had to tread a careful line between boasting about Spain's enviable growth rates while acknowledging voters' frustration over the rising cost of living. The progressive Spanish leader called an early election for Nov. 29 after weeks of nationwide protests over living conditions , hoping to capitalize on their anger. While Sánchez has warned voters that a right-wing government would not make their lives more affordable, his conservative opponents have slammed his government for doing too little. These five charts illustrate the disconnect between Spain's economic growth under Sánchez and the financial pressures many voters face. House prices in Spain rose 43% between 2015 and 2025 when adjusted for inflation, according to Eurostat’s house price index. Across the European Union, prices rose an average of 25% during the same period. Market pressures and insufficient construction have driven prices even higher in Spain's largest cities and popular tourist destinations, putting homeownership beyond the reach of many young Spaniards. Spain has a strong tradition of homeownership, but the Bank of Spain estimates the country of 50 million people has a shortage of 750,000 houses based on demand and the pace of new construction. Academics and policymakers trace the origins of the problem to the 2008 financial crash. Home construction plummeted following a building boom that helped fuel the country's housing bubble. Large-scale investors began buying property in the aftermath, contributing to speculation years later. Both Sánchez and his main opponent, conservative Popular Party leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo , have promised to enact measures if elected to financially help first-time home buyers. That's the share of Spaniards aged 18 to 34 who were still living with their parents in 2025, according to Spain’s National Statistics Institute. Almost half of those between 26 and 34 cited an inability to pay rent or buy a home as the reason why. Rents across Spain have also risen by 43% over the past decade, with the largest increases in cities and coastal areas. Analysts say the rental supply in these areas has diminished due to a combination of factors, including population growth driven by immigration and tourism. In cities and holiday hot spots, short-term and tourist accommodations on platforms like Airbnb and Booking.com have proliferated, reducing the available rental stock. That’s roughly the share of renters in Spain who spend more than 40% of their income on housing, excluding those who receive government-subsidized or free housing. Spain has a higher proportion of overburdened renters than other major European Union economies, including Germany, France, and Italy. In cities like Madrid and Barcelona, many renters fork over an even larger share of their income every month. “You have a big chunk of the population that essentially has seen their income in real terms go down because prices have gone up more than their wages," said Ángel Talavera, an economist who studies Europe at Oxford Economics. “Housing has gone, well, bananas.” 'The threat is finally real': Judge rips White House 'weaponization' Teen fatally struck by gunfire while camping near Florida river: Authorities Pennsylvania teen who died in 2020 could become first Gen Z saint That was the last time Spanish real wages peaked when adjusted for inflation. Spain’s economy has substantially outgrown the eurozone average since Sánchez took office in 2018 , particularly since the COVID-19 pandemic. The Spanish economy is expected to expand by an estimated 2.6% this year, more than double the eurozone's projected growth of 1.2%, according to the EU. Even so, real wages have barely budged. Economists say much of Spain's growth in recent years has been driven by immigration, with new arrivals expanding the labor force. Sánchez has defended his immigration-friendly policies as a way to maintain Spain's large social welfare system. Many immigrants fill critical jobs in agriculture, tourism and other industries, but often in low-paying positions. “What’s happening is that we have more people working,” said Pedro Aznar, an economist at the Barcelona-based Esade Business School. "We have a larger working population contributing to GDP, but our growth is driven more by volume rather than by generating more output per worker.” Minimum-wage earners are an exception. Their wages have grown 66% since Sánchez took office in 2018, leaving them better off even after inflation. That's how much the cost of food increased between 2015 and 2025.

events.title: Chinese manufacturers are making bigger bets on Africa
events.summary: Yinka’s view African governments have spent decades promising to turn their countries from exporters of raw materials into manufacturing economies. But concrete progress has been limited. Now, after years in which Chinese companies appeared mostly focused on extracting African resources, a new report shows they are pivoting to building a manufacturing presence across the continent. At least $19 billion in Chinese manufacturing investment was made across 113 projects in 19 African countries between Sep. 2024 and June 2026, according to Development Reimagined, a consultancy. That’s nearly double the $10 billion pledged by Chinese companies at a 2024 China-Africa summit in Beijing, and is separate from $41.2 billion in mining and mineral processing investments identified in a companion study. “We last saw a big government push on Chinese FDI into Africa around 2015/2016, it seems now, post-COVID, that push is back, and it seems with more gusto than ever,” said Hannah Ryder, chief executive of Development Reimagined. The renewed interest comes as Chinese manufacturers deal with excess capacity and intense price competition at home, while trade barriers in the US and Europe make these export markets harder to access. But it’s also clear Africa offers growing consumer markets, lower-cost production opportunities and, since May, duty-free access to China for 53 of 54 countries. A bigger Chinese manufacturing footprint does not mean Africa is about to become the world’s next industrial hub. The continent’s share of global manufacturing output has actually fallen to less than 2% today from about 3% in the 1970s, according to the UN Industrial Development Organization. Familiar obstacles still give investors pause including unreliable electricity, poor transport links, and limited access to finance. But the opportunity remains significant: Global supply chains are shifting just as demand grows for locally made construction materials and clean-energy equipment. Chinese companies that already operate on the continent are expanding, Ryder said, suggesting the trend has commercial momentum. The question to consider is whether African governments can turn that interest into something more durable with local suppliers, skilled jobs, and technology transfer. Attracting manufacturers is a start but ensuring more of the value stays in Africa is the harder test. Notable Private Chinese companies are investing in African manufacturing after years of state-led infrastructure projects on the continent , with China’s total investment at almost $8 billion in 2025 .

Turn it on its head June 29, 2026 A study suggests extending the TV license to cover streaming services such as YouTube and Netflix could solve the BBC’s funding problems, netting it an extra £1.6 billion ($2 billion) per year by 2032. The British government is due to publish a white paper by the end of this year outlining its plans for the BBC's license fee and Royal Charter, which expires at the end of 2027. One of the options is to extend the license so that it is needed to access streaming platforms like Netflix, Disney+, or Amazon Prime Video. This is unlikely to prove popular, but if the fee was held at the current level (£180, $236 per year) it would generate up to £1.6 billion extra a year for the corporation and would better reflect how audiences watch television, according to entertainment industry research biz Ampere Analysis . As any Brit knows, the BBC is funded primarily through the TV license, which is charged on a per household basis. A license is required to watch or record live TV on any broadcast channel, or access the BBC iPlayer for on-demand content. A license is not currently needed for on-demand streaming platforms. The government is understood to believe the current license scheme is “outdated and no longer fit for purpose,” and is weighing several options to reform it. Scrapping it entirely looks unlikely for now: a committee found that other European countries that did so ended up with less stable funding for their public service broadcasters, and weaker independence from political interference. TV licensing is controversial, with some people resenting having to pay the BBC just for the right to watch television. In response, the government has tried to limit fee increases, and made the license free for some elderly people. Together, these moved have reduced the BBC's funding, leading to service cuts and further. dissatisfaction. Responding to a report by the National Audit Office (NAO) that found the BBC will remain under financial pressure despite widespread cuts, the National Union of Journalists (NUJ) urged the government to secure the broadcaster's future in the next charter renewal. "The BBC shouldn't be in this position. These cuts are the result of a decade of underfunding, with NAO identifying a 26 percent real-terms reduction in license fee income in the last nine years alone," said NUJ general secretary Laura Davison. Many Brits no longer pay the license fee, preferring to watch only streamed content, or claiming that they do. Ampere says more than 90 percent of UK households watch live television, but only 84 percent of eligible households pay the fee, meaning a sizable number are freeloading. Extending the fee to cover on-demand and streaming services would close the loophole, it says. Another option could see the license fee reduced to £150 ($196) in 2028, assuming perfect enforcement, analysts at Ampere say. They neglect to detail what this "perfect enforcement" mechanism consists of. "Widening the remit of the license fee at current prices would significantly increase the BBC’s funding, strengthening its long-term financial position and ability to compete with local and global rivals," said Ampere Senior Analyst Sam Khoury. events.title: M&G boss urges UK to stem flood of firms leaving London Stock Exchange after Compass exit
events.summary: Warning comes after £46bn school and NHS caterer decides to moves main listing to New York, the latest in a long line of departures The boss of the British investment group M&G has called on the government to “take a stand” against the long line of companies leaving the London Stock Exchange, after the FTSE 100 caterer Compass announced plans to switch its primary listing to New York. Andrea Rossi, chief executive of M&G, said his fund managers would vote against the Compass’s proposed move. In a letter to the Financial Times , Rossi warned that its decision to switch away from London was a “warning about the health of the UK stock market”. Rossi wrote that “when one of the largest members of the FTSE 100 concludes that its interests are better served elsewhere, policymakers cannot regard it as an isolated corporate decision.” “ The continued departure of major companies from London’s stock market should concern anyone who cares about Britain’s economic future,” he said. Compass, which is the 18th biggest company on the FTSE 100 by market capitalisation at £45.9bn, said it had become a “predominantly North American business” and that a move would give it better access to “the world’s largest and deepest pool of capital”. The group, which is the largest caterer in the world, makes about two-thirds of its profit in North America, while about two-fifths of its shareholders are based in the US. There are concerns that other big firms could make the same argument, given that across the FTSE 100 only about a third of reported revenue is derived from the UK . The M&G boss added that the government should introduce “targeted” interventions to help reduce the number of companies leaving the UK stock market, such as reducing or removing stamp duty on UK shares. The government would lose about £40m in stamp duty revenue when Compass moves its primary listing, according to analysis by the Financial Times. Rossi also argued that pension providers could allocate more of their default funds to British stocks. He wrote: “Where taxpayer support is provided to private companies, a future UK listing should form part of the bargain.” Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning M&G Investment Management owns 0.75% of Compass’s shares, according to LSEG data, making it the 18th largest shareholder Compass’s departure would mark the latest in a string of exits by companies seeking deeper pools of capital and higher valuations in the US. In recent years, the equipment rental company Ashtead , the building material supplier CRH , and the owner of Paddy Power, Flutter Entertainment , have all moved their primary listings to the US. The UK’s biggest drugmaker, AstraZeneca, listed its shares directly on the New York Stock Exchange this year , putting its US shares on an even footing with its London-listed stock. Meanwhile, three FTSE 100 companies – the fund manager Schroders, the insurer Beazley, and the product testing group Intertek – have left the stock market after being acquired by overseas groups this year. The UK government was approached for comment.

events.title: Indonesian company taking over tycoon’s seized forest land is Danantara unit, document shows
events.summary: The awarding of the concession is the latest sign of Danantara’s growing clout across Indonesia’s economy following its launch early in 2025. JAKARTA – A new Indonesian company appointed to manage concessions seized from a subsidiary of a Singapore-based conglomerate is a unit of sovereign wealth fund Danantara, a document seen by Reuters showed, making it the largest single state seizure of land linked to the 2026 forest fires. The awarding of the concession is the latest sign of Danantara’s growing clout across Indonesia’s economy following its launch early in 2025 , with hundreds of state firms worth more than US$1 trillion (S$1.29 trillion) now under its control. The move comes amid President Prabowo Subianto’s drive to increase state control over the country’s vast natural resources. The government last week revoked the forest usage permits of Riau Andalan Pulp and Paper (RAPP) , a unit of Singapore-headquartered Royal Golden Eagle, which cover 338,536ha of concessions in Riau province, citing fires and other violations. On Nov 24, it was announced the area would be managed by a previously unknown company called Garuda Adidaya Nusantara. According to a Law Ministry document about the company reviewed by Reuters, Garuda Adidaya is 99% controlled by Danantara Asset Management and was established to engage in a wide range of forestry and plantation businesses as well as the processing of forest commodities. It was established on Nov 19, the document shows, the same day the government issued the decree to revoke RAPP’s permits. Neither the company’s status as a unit of Danantara nor the time when it was established has been previously reported. It is one of the highest-profile state takeovers ever, with the land previously used by a company belonging to one of Indonesia’s best-known billionaire tycoons, Sukanto Tanoto. “We respect the government’s authority and will continue to engage constructively with the relevant authorities,” a RAPP spokesperson said on Nov 25 , without responding to queries about the concession being run by Garuda Adidaya. “RAPP firmly believes that it has operated in compliance with all applicable government regulatory requirements in the management of its forestry concessions.” A call to Garuda Adidaya’s listed phone number was unanswered. Danantara did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The local government in Riau, where the concession is located, urged Garuda Adidaya and the central government’s forestry task force to provide clarity regarding the continuation of operations on the concession and the fate of its workers. The task force has previously pledged that no RAPP employees would be laid off. REUTERS

events.title: German auto workers on back foot as costs, competition bite
events.summary: German auto workers profited during the industry's boom years, but are now increasingly being asked to trade past gains for future job security. For decades, German auto bosses and labor representatives touted their ability to work through their disagreements in a uniquely cooperative process. Those days appear to be gone. A series of crises across the industry and abrupt moves by management to slash costs are testing the limits of the German power-sharing agreement. As negotiations between union representatives and Germany's largest carmaker, Volkswagen, began on Tuesday, the balance of power appeared increasingly one-sided. Volkswagen wants to freeze wages for the next two years while cutting several allowances and bonuses. Alongside Mercedes , it's demanding longer hours under the same pay, with both companies threatening to withhold investment from German factories. Unions have responded with warning strikes and the threat of larger walkouts. Yet workers are aware of the grim outlook, with Germany's auto industry losing more than 123,000 jobs between 2019 and 2025, according to the Ifo Institute. "I think that the labor representatives are in a very difficult situation," said Thomas Haipeter, a labor researcher at the University of Duisburg-Essen. "On the one hand, they have to make concessions in order to safeguard jobs. And despite these massive employment reductions to safeguard the rest of the jobs and locations, what is missing for them is a kind of more offensive strategy." Can 'legacy' bring Volkswagen back from the brink? Labor's outsized role in German auto companies goes back decades and includes a 1945 deal at Volkswagen promising a hot shower a day. That year marks the start of "co-determination" at the company, in which workers are represented internally by employee-led workers' councils, as well as by outside labor unions. Berlin then anchored labor's strong say in Volkswagen in 1960, before the firm issued public shares, ensuring government officials retained extra votes in the supervisory board. Those seats, belonging to the Lower Saxony government, tend to be sympathetic to workers. Workers' councils, meanwhile, became a fixture across the German auto industry, with representation extending across multiple production sites within the same companies. Pay and benefits for auto workers have risen over the years. During the last German industry boom, between 2011 and 2019, pay for auto workers clearly outpaced the average German wage. In early 2025, auto workers were earning nearly a third more per hour than the typical German worker, when bonuses and allowances are factored in, according to Germany's Federal Statistical Office (Destatis). That same year, Volkswagen CEO Oliver Blume praised cooperation with the unions as one of the company's "great strengths" during the 80th anniversary of the 1945 agreement. Cracks were long in the making, according to case studies by Haipeter and others. Labor was increasingly forced to protect plants and jobs as companies chased cheaper workers abroad. Workers' councils turned their attention to saving their own production lines. They focused on business strategy and even hired business consultants in an effort to sway strategy. When combustion engines dominated , autoworkers could argue German production was the most technologically advanced, according to Haipeter. That changed with the shift to electric vehicles. "This line of compromise is canceled now by management," he said. "They say it doesn't matter for us where we produce. We have to produce at the locations or in countries which are best-cost countries and not in countries which have higher wages." Slow sales of electric autos and competition from Chinese manufacturers have, meanwhile, exposed the cost difference. In 2024, Volkswagen abruptly canceled a series of labor agreements and threatened factory closures. After tough negotiations, labor agreed to significant cuts — €1.5 billion yearly in abandoned wage hikes and the elimination of 50,000 positions through attrition — in exchange for job security for current employees through 2030. Management returned this summer with a restructuring plan that included the closures of four German plants. It delayed that decision following negotiations, but slated another 50,000 positions for attrition. Volkswagen declined to comment for this article. The most sensitive issue for unions may be the demand that employees work more for the same amount of pay, or even receive less for less work. The union IG Metall won the concession for a 35-hour workweek in 1984 after seven weeks of strikes. It's now standard in every labor contract in the auto industry , although it's not uncommon for worksites to deviate from the employee agreement, according to Haipeter. Mercedes has called for employees to agree to an exception across the company. The company acknowledged that the 35-hour workweek was "hard-won" and "means a great deal" to its workers.

events.title: Aramco opens $7bn Shaheen chemicals project in Seoul
events.summary: Saudi Arabia's Aramco and its Seoul-based subsidiary S-oil have inaugurated the $7 billion Shaheen project in South Korea, aimed at growing petrochemicals demand in Asia. The project is the world's largest oil-producing company’s biggest investment in the country. Shaheen is expected to add about 3.2 million tonnes of annual petrochemical production capacity for S-Oil, making it a key player in the global supply of high-value polymers and advanced materials, Aramco said on Wednesday. The deal was first announced in November 2022 during visit to South Korea by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman . “Economic headwinds and rising geopolitical risks do not alter our long-term view on strategic investments,” said Amin Nasser, Aramco president and chief executive. “Investments like Shaheen build the resilience that markets need in uncertain times.” Aramco, Opec’s biggest oil producer and the main driver of Saudi Arabia's industrial sector, has faced waves of missile and drone attacks from Yemen’s Houthi militants. This month, an administrative building in Riyadh belonging to Aramco was damaged by falling shrapnel during an attempted attack, the Saudi Ministry of Energy said. The building sustained minor damage, with no injuries or deaths reported. In October, a Houthi missile attack damaged Saudi Aramco’s headquarters in Dhahran. The attack caused a fire in an administrative building in the complex. Several crude refining sites, including those in Jazan in the west and Riyadh, have also been attacked in recent weeks. However, the company will continue to invest in expanding its projects, both domestically and internationally, Aramco said this month, as it reported a 34 per cent annual increase in its third-quarter net income. Technology boost Located in Ulsan, the Shaheen project combines refining capabilities with the first major commercial deployment of Aramco’s thermal crude to chemicals technology. The use of the technology is expected to increase the share of crude oil converted into high-value chemicals. The project features the “world’s largest single steam cracker, a propylene fractionator, crude-to-chemicals conversion facilities, and polymer production units”, Aramco said. Expanded production from the facility is projected to increase the share of petrochemicals in S-Oil's overall business portfolio from 12 per cent to 25 per cent, Aramco said. It will be integrated with S-Oil’s existing refining and petrochemical facilities in Ulsan. Through pipeline networks, the facility is expected to provide a domestic supply of basic petrochemical feedstocks to nearby downstream companies, reducing their reliance on imports and logistics. Commercial operations are scheduled to begin in 2027 following the completion of commissioning. The project will help “meet the rising demand for materials essential to Asia’s key industries, from electric vehicles to semiconductors”, Mr Nasser said. The global petrochemicals market is expected to grow from $702.9 billion in 2026 to $977.80 billion by 2034, according to data from Fortune Business Insights. Asia Pacific dominates with a market share of more than 50 per cent in 2025, data shows. Aramco, which made an initial investment in S-Oil in 1991, is currently its majority shareholder, holding more than 63 per cent of the Korean company’s shares. “Petrochemicals are critical to overall industrial competitiveness,” Mohammed Al Qahtani, Aramco Downstream president, said. The focus on advanced manufacturing is “expected to support product diversification and industrial growth and help meet rising demand for petrochemical feedstock in the years to come”, he added.

events.title: Walmart’s shopper base is shifting: High earners lead its gains as low-income shoppers turn to Amazon
events.summary: Walmart is known for its bargains, but its growth increasingly comes from shoppers who don’t strictly need them. Six-figure households like a good deal, too. Upper-income households led Walmart’s U.S. market-share gains, the company said Nov. 19 as it reported fiscal third-quarter results . Revenue rose 5.2% to $188.8 billion from $179.5 billion a year earlier and topped Wall Street’s forecasts for both sales and profit. E-commerce did the heavy lifting. U.S. online sales rose 23%, the 11th straight quarter up more than 20%, while global e-commerce grew 17%. “We delivered strong results, growing our core business and gaining market share,” CEO John Furner said in the release. Walmart raised its full-year outlook for the third time this year and now expects net sales growth of 4.9% to 5.2% and adjusted earnings per share of $2.84 to $2.89, up from $2.80 to $2.87. Not everything accelerated. U.S. comparable sales rose 2.9%, well below the 4.5% gain a year earlier, and the new outlook came in more conservative than analysts expected, the Associated Press reported . The split matters well beyond Bentonville. With more than 150 million customers shopping its stores or website each week, Walmart is one of the clearest windows into American spending heading into the holidays, and right now that window shows higher earners stepping up while others pull back. Higher earners, younger members Furner said in February that most of Walmart’s share gains came from households earning more than $100,000 , and in June he told reporters that higher-income customers were visiting more often and buying more . The new customers also skew young. At Sam’s Club, Gen Z and millennials made up more than half of new sign-ups in the quarter, and more than half of that group chose the pricier Plus tier. Convenience is a big part of the pitch. Mobile ordering, free pickup, and fast delivery let customers fill a grocery cart, pick up prescriptions, and stock the garden in one stop, and Walmart said its biggest market-share gains in three years came in food, CNBC reported . Membership is the next lever. In October, Walmart launched a $120-a-year bundle of Walmart+ and Sam’s Club Plus , nearly $100 less than buying both separately. “It does help at a time when we do see some customers showing some signs of pressure,” Furner told Fox News Digital at the launch, pointing to higher energy costs. Stores do double duty Walmart’s stores power its online business. The company said more than 80% of U.S. e-commerce orders, including third-party marketplace orders, are fulfilled from stores, letting it deliver a wide assortment faster. Fuel costs have tested that network this year. Diesel hit a record national average of $6.53 a gallon on Sept. 22, according to AAA, a surge CBS News reported was especially painful for farmers and small businesses. Prices have since eased, with diesel falling below $6 in mid-November for the first time in two months as President Trump signaled he wouldn’t escalate the war in Iran. Furner told CNBC the retailer aims to keep prices low despite fuel costs, and Walmart ended the quarter with about 7,700 rollbacks. Advertising is padding the margins. Walmart U.S. ad sales rose 37% in the quarter, and WARC platform benchmarks put Walmart’s average return on ad spend about 25% above Amazon’s. Walmart’s global ad business brought in roughly $6.4 billion last fiscal year, per WARC. That’s far behind Amazon’s roughly $68 billion but well ahead of Target’s Roundel and of Instacart and DoorDash combined. The shoppers slipping away Not every customer is on board. Numerator data released days before the earnings report showed Walmart stores lost 5.6% of their low-income purchasing households, and the ones who stayed made fewer trips. Among low-income shoppers cutting back on Walmart store visits, 51% named Amazon as an alternative, ahead of local grocery stores and dollar stores. That rivalry has already cost Walmart a crown. Amazon ended Walmart’s 13-year run atop the Fortune 500 this year, and Walmart now ranks No. 2 on the 2026 Fortune 500 , with $713.2 billion in revenue. Furner’s answer is to pull every part of the business into the fight. “From membership and agentic shopping to new ways of using our stores and delivery network, we’re bringing the best of Walmart together to serve customers better and create new opportunities for growth,” he said. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Cape York residents swelter through heatwaves and nightly water outages
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Seisia resident Kawia Akinsola says the rolling water outages are adversely affecting elderly and disabled residents. ( Supplied ) Lengthy water outages during ongoing heatwaves are causing discomfort for residents on Cape York Peninsula. "Abnormal" water use and power outages have been blamed for low reservoir levels. The $10 million joint federal-state Northern Peninsula Area Water Supply Project is underway, and further unfunded measures have been identified. Remote communities at the tip of Cape York are having their water turned off overnight as reservoirs run critically low during a prolonged heatwave. Mains water has been cut, often with only a few hours' notice, across the five communities of Queensland's Northern Peninsula Area (NPA) since early September. The Bureau of Meteorology has issued heatwave warnings for the peninsula district for several weeks, the most recent forecasting temperatures in the low 40s and overnight minimums in the mid-20s until Friday. Residents in the coastal NPA town of Seisia, near the northernmost point of the Cape, say the rolling restrictions are having a significant impact on their lives. Kawia Akinsola, 45, said the outages, from 9pm to 6am on allocated days, were disrupting activities including cooking, cleaning and taking medication. A new backup generator has ben installed at the Bamaga Water Treatment Plant to assist during power outages. ( Facebook: NPARC ) The Northern Peninsula Area Regional Council (NPARC) uses its Facebook page to provide updates, but Ms Akinsola said not everyone in the communities was receiving the messages. "Some of us, especially older people or people with disabilities, are not on social media, so they don't get told until the last minute most of the time," she said. The raw water pond near Bamaga Water Treatment plant was 50 per cent full earlier this month. ( Supplied ) "Our elders and people with disabilities don't know the water's turned off and go to the toilet and we have to wait for the next day to flush it or clean it." She said many households were also overcrowded, and stored water could run out quickly. According to the 2021 Census, the Peninsula region is home to about 2,800 people living in 1,090 dwellings, with residents in New Mapoon, Injinoo, Umagico, Bamaga and Seisia impacted. The Jardine River provides the NPA's mains water. ( ABC Far North: Brendan Mounter ) Veolia, the council's water contractor, warned in early November that storage levels at the region's reservoirs were at critically low levels after power outages disrupted pumping from the Jardine River. The council has since installed an emergency backup generator to allow reservoirs to recharge, but it has been switching off water supplies to alternating communities overnight. Premier David Crisafulli described the restrictions as "completely unacceptable" and said his government had invested in water pumps and pipes in New Mapoon and Bamaga. David Crisafulli, in the Far North this week, said his government had invested in NPA water infrastructure. ( ABC Far North: Brendan Mounter ) The $10 million joint federal-state Northern Peninsula Area Water Supply Project includes upgrades to the Bamaga Water Treatment Plant, increasing capacity to a proposed nine megalitres a day, replacing asbestos-cement water pipes and connecting a new water main in New Mapoon. A spokesperson for Federal Water Minister Murray Watt said the investment would support long-term improvements to water supply infrastructure in the region. But Cook MP David Kempton said it remained unclear whether the planned works would resolve the council's ongoing supply issues. David Kempton says water security will be an ongoing issue for the NPA. ( ABC Far North: Christopher Testa ) "That's the plan, but we don't know what the state of some of those other asbestos pipes are, but as things fail, of course, we'll fix them," he said. The ABC has contacted Veolia and NPARC for comment. In March, the council's Local Resilience Action Plan identified securing a second pipeline from the Jardine River as a critical infrastructure priority. The project remains unfunded. The council has also said it is considering a second raw water pond, estimated to cost $4 million, to increase storage capacity. NPARC Mayor Robert Poipoi (right) inspects a new backup generator at the Bamaga Water Treatment Plant.
