events.title: Martha Ford, former Lions owner with link to auto giants, dies at 101
events.summary: Former Detroit Lions owner Martha Firestone Ford has died Martha Firestone Ford, the tire heiress who became a link between two of the automotive industry's most iconic families and later took over the NFL's Detroit Lions, has died. She was 101. The Lions say she died Tuesday at her home in Grosse Pointe, Michigan, surrounded by family. No cause of death was given. Ford was a granddaughter of tire magnate Harvey Firestone, and her husband, William Clay Ford Sr., was Henry Ford's grandson. He also owned the Lions for a half-century before his death in 2014. Martha Ford then took over his controlling interest in the team, keeping it within the family. Although she seldom spoke to reporters or commented publicly on the direction of the franchise, her influence was felt. She was in charge of the team from 2014 until 2020, when she turned the Lions over to her daughter, Sheila Ford Hamp. The Lions made the playoffs in 2014, but lost seven of their first eight games the following season. In November 2015, the team fired its president and general manager in a midseason shakeup. When she announced the changes, Ford told fans the franchise intended to “identify and hire the very best leadership in order to produce a consistently, winning football team.” The Lions played better down the stretch that season, and after hiring Bob Quinn as their new general manager, they returned to the playoffs a year later. “Martha was special," NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell said in a statement. "She cared so deeply about her family, the players, their fans, and the city of Detroit. She was committed to making the Lions - and the game of football - better. Martha and her husband, William Clay Ford, led the franchise with dignity and integrity. We will miss her kindness and sweet sense of humor. We extend our deepest condolences to her children, the entire Ford family, and the Lions’ organization.” Born Sept. 16, 1925, in Akron, Ohio, Martha Parke Firestone graduated from Vassar College in 1946 and married William Clay Ford the next year. Their wedding received a huge amount of coverage — looking back in 2014, the Akron Beacon Journal described it as “Akron’s royal wedding” — and the marriage joined two families that already had a long history. Harvey Firestone, the founder of the Firestone Tire and Rubber Co., was a close friend of Ford Motor Co. founder Henry Ford. Ford chose Firestone to supply the tires for the first Model T in 1906. The two men often went on long camping trips together, sometimes accompanied by their friend Thomas Edison. Martha and William Clay Ford had three daughters and a son. Their son, William Clay Ford Jr., is the current executive chairman of Ford Motor Co.. In 2001, Bridgestone/Firestone and Ford severed their nearly 100-year relationship because of a dispute over a series of deadly tire failures on the Ford Explorer. 'The threat is finally real': Judge rips White House 'weaponization' Teen fatally struck by gunfire while camping near Florida river: Authorities Pennsylvania teen who died in 2020 could become first Gen Z saint Sheila Ford Hamp is the Lions’ principal owner and chairman. William Clay Ford’s first full season leading the Lions was in 1964, seven years after they won an NFL title. Since that 1957 championship, the franchise has won playoff games in 1992 and 2023 and has not played in the Super Bowl. Although Martha Ford kept a low profile, the shakeup in the middle of the 2015 season was a sign that she was more than willing to bring about change in an effort to reverse the team’s fortunes. Then-coach Jim Caldwell said she was very much a presence within the organization. “I think visible ownership is great, and Mrs. Ford does it extremely well,” Caldwell said in 2015. “She’s there before games and she’s there after games, and I think guys enjoy that part of it. She comes to practice and things of that nature, so it’s been fun.” Even at 101, she attended games, including a win over the Minnesota Vikings earlier this month. Martha Ford also made an impact in the Detroit community. She was an officer on the board for Detroit Lions Charities and on the board of the Henry Ford Health System. Martha and William Clay Ford were credited with helping establish the Maplegrove Center, a substance abuse treatment facility in West Bloomfield. In 2017, Forbes estimated Martha Ford’s net worth at more than $1.4 billion. She survived by her four children, 14 grandchildren, and 17 great-grandchildren. events.title: GTA VI’s $3.79 billion debut has Zuckerberg joking and Musk laughing, but Take-Two investors still want more
events.summary: Mark Zuckerberg wanted to know which version of Grand Theft Auto VI he’d bought. On Nov. 20, the Meta CEO posted an edited screenshot on X of one of the game’s in-game prompts: a mission to “pick up groceries” with a pink heart and the line, “Priscilla will appreciate this.” His caption: “Wait which version did I get?” Elon Musk, the CEO of Tesla and SpaceX, replied with a laughing emoji. The exchange capped the first full day of what is now the biggest entertainment launch on record. Rockstar Games, the Take-Two Interactive label behind the franchise, said GTA VI generated $3.79 billion in worldwide retail sales on its Nov. 19 release day , based on company estimates. That is more than four times the roughly $800 million GTA V took in on its first day in 2013. The game also sold 32.5 million units before it went on sale. For scale, the day-one retail figure is more than half of the $6.66 billion in net revenue Take-Two reported for its entire fiscal year ended March 2026 . Retail sales account for what consumers spent, not what Take-Two keeps after platform holders and retailers take their cut. Still, the opening validates a bet CEO Strauss Zelnick described to Fortune only as “expensive,” and that one former Take-Two CEO Ben Feder called the last pre-AI blockbuster of its kind . Wall Street wants more than a record opening The sales kept coming after launch day. Research firm Alinea Analytics estimates 44.9 million copies were sold by the end of its opening weekend , grossing more than $4 billion. Take-Two has not confirmed those figures. Investors were less euphoric. Take-Two shares fell almost 4% on launch day , even as the game earned a 99 on Metacritic. TD Cowen analyst Doug Creutz wrote that the timing and size of the next GTA Online matter more to the stock than GTA VI unit sales. Take-Two has reiterated its outlook of $8 billion to $8.2 billion in net bookings for fiscal 2027 . It has guided to $3.35 billion to $3.5 billion in net bookings for the October–December quarter, the first that will show how much of the launch reaches its books. Rockstar bet its biggest launch on a love story Zuckerberg’s joke riffs on a mechanic at the center of GTA VI . Players can build up, or neglect, the relationship between protagonists Jason and Lucia through everyday gestures such as running errands, holding hands, and spending time together. Rockstar North co–studio head Rob Nelson has said the romance is optional, but how players nurture it shapes how the couple’s story unfolds. That is a departure from the more strictly violence-focused themes of earlier GTA games. Despite complaints from some longtime fans, many players have posted warmly about the pair. Rupert Humphries, Rockstar Games’ senior vice president of narrative, told Game Informer that the realistic domestic dynamic between the Bonnie-and-Clyde-esque leads was meant to immerse players and anchor the story in something positive. “We wanted to create a world that held up a mirror to that—showed that fever pitch of craziness that we are all maybe a couple of bad decisions away from. But we wanted the story we were going to tell to have something positive at its core and the message that human connection is better than division,” he said. Emphasizing the couple, rather than violence alone, may also help Rockstar reach players beyond the franchise’s traditionally male-heavy core. Silicon Valley’s ‘last wife guy’ Musk’s reply carried some history. He and Zuckerberg once came close to a cage match. Both later attended President Donald Trump’s second inauguration, and Zuckerberg texted Musk offering to help with his Department of Government Efficiency effort , according to court documents. Some users answered with their own GTA -style notifications, including one with a mission to “fight Elon Musk.” The post also landed during a rough stretch for tech leaders’ personal lives. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned on Nov. 12 after admitting to an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. Nvidia’s board reinstated him 11 days later , after Trump pressed for his return. Against that backdrop, and after other tech billionaires, including Jeff Bezos and Bill Gates, faced public reckonings over infidelity, a commenter on his post dubbed him Silicon Valley’s “last wife guy.” It’s an unexpected image for Zuckerberg, who said on Joe Rogan’s podcast in January 2025 that corporate America needed more “masculine energy.” Zuckerberg met Priscilla Chan, a pediatrician with whom he has three children, in a bathroom line at a Harvard fraternity party. The couple married the day after Facebook went public in 2012. Since then, Zuckerberg has made grand gestures a habit. He recorded a cover of “Get Low,” the song playing when they met, with T-Pain. He also commissioned a 7-foot statue of Chan and posted it on Instagram with the caption, “bringing back the Roman tradition of making sculptures of your wife.” A grocery run, even a virtual one, is a smaller ask. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Exclusive: Meta and Amazon discuss ending Muse shopping bot blockade, as ads, search emerge as key issues
events.summary: Amazon and Meta Platforms are in ongoing discussions over a potential deal to connect Meta’s popular Muse AI agent to the e-commerce giant’s online store and end a blockade of the shopping bot imposed by Amazon two months ago. The two tech giants have held talks on multiple occasions, and two major factors being negotiated are how the companies will handle search results and advertising in any deal, according to people familiar with the matter. Discussions are fluid, and it’s unclear if or how soon an agreement will be struck. There are numerous issues, ranging from Amazon’s own AI shopping ambitions to how, exactly, Muse would connect to Amazon. A major threat Muse poses to Amazon is that, in theory, it would bypass advertisements on Amazon’s website, which are a large source of revenue for the retailer. Amazon is worried about losing advertising revenue and about the quality of the product search results Muse would surface, and executives are also concerned that shopping agents like Muse will weaken the relationship Amazon has with consumers, people familiar with the matter said. Any deal between Amazon and Meta is expected to require sign-off from the CEOs of both companies, they noted. Meta and Amazon declined to comment. The negotiations are being closely followed because they have major implications for the future of online shopping and represent an important test case for how large corporations respond to the advent of AI agents. As agents like Muse become more widely used, companies like Amazon are scrambling to understand how the bots alter typical shopping patterns as well as the valued connections that brands and retailers have with consumers. The talks are ongoing as Amazon prepares for another Black Friday and Cyber Monday, one of its most critical shopping periods of the year. This year, roughly half of holiday shoppers plan to use AI in some way to help make purchases, a National Retail Federation survey this month showed. AI agents promise to bring major changes to many industries. Agentic shopping could total $190 billion to $385 billion in U.S. e-commerce spending by 2030, representing 10% to 20% of the total market, according to a 2025 report by Morgan Stanley . Analysts at JPMorgan have praised Muse as a powerful agent, recently writing that tens of millions of businesses could eventually use the tool. Amazon blocked Meta’s Muse app from accessing its store in September, saying at the time that Muse’s access would violate its user agreements. Muse, which Meta released in the U.S. that month, is a personalized AI agent that users can name and direct to autonomously carry out tasks on their behalf, such as checking email, managing calendars, and booking reservations. As of October, more than 10 million people in the U.S. and Canada had set up the app, making it Meta’s biggest consumer AI hit to date. Chief executive Mark Zuckerberg has said shopping is Muse’s top use case. “We think that billions of Muses in a network at scale will be able to get more done for people and businesses by working together,” Zuckerberg said last month on a call with analysts. “We’d like to create a large-scale Muse network as quickly as possible.” One of Amazon’s main concerns is how shopping agents such as Muse will affect its advertising business. Advertising has become a $68.6 billion business for Amazon, representing nearly 10% of its total yearly revenue. In October, Amazon chief executive Andy Jassy, while not naming Muse, tried to quell investor concern by saying few customers are buying with outside shopping agents because the experience is “still not great, nor more convenient than coming to a retailer directly.” Still, Jassy said this month at a Semafor conference that Amazon hadn’t ruled out letting outside shopping agents into its store, but that they would have to provide a “fair exchange of value.” Aside from Meta, OpenAI launched its Dots personal AI agents in September, and startup Instinct’s personal assistant has also become a mainstream AI agent. Amazon has its own shopping agent for its website, dubbed “Alexa for shopping,” which Jassy said has been used by more than 400 million customers in the past year. Meta and Amazon have partnered on e-commerce before. In 2023, the companies struck a deal that allowed Facebook and Instagram users to purchase Amazon products without leaving the apps. Meta makes money from ads it serves users on its apps, including for Amazon products, and Amazon earns revenue through the actual purchases. The partnership was made as TikTok expanded into U.S. e-commerce. Meta signed on other partners early in its Muse efforts, including Amazon rivals such as Shopify, Walmart , and Best Buy . Thus, retailers have gained another channel for selling products as Meta tries to grow Muse, and according to Zuckerberg, the company eventually plans to profit by taking a “small fee from transactions.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: NSW regional and interstate trains could be offline for a week from Friday
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Planned strike means NSW regional and interstate trains could be offline for a week from Friday Passenger services are expected to be disrupted on Friday due to an ongoing dispute with workers. ( ABC News: Liam Patrick ) Protected industrial action is being taken by rail workers over an enterprise bargaining agreement dispute. NSW regional and interstate passenger services will be suspended for a week, with major disruptions to freight trains also expected. The Australian Rail Track Corporation is seeking to block the industrial action at an urgent hearing tomorrow. Regional and interstate passenger train services across NSW will be suspended for a week from Friday unless a last-ditch effort to stave off proposed industrial action is successful. Rail workers plan to walk off the job following six months of enterprise bargaining negotiations between the Australian Rail Track Corporation (ARTC) and the Rail, Tram and Bus Union (RTBU) and Australian Services Union (ASU). Impacted train services include regional routes, interstate XPT services between Sydney, Melbourne and Brisbane, and Sydney Trains services on the Hunter Line and Southern Highlands Line. Freight movements leading into Christmas are set to be impacted. ( Supplied: Australasian Railway Association ) ARTC said the work bans would mean the safe passage of passenger trains could not be guaranteed, forcing the suspension of passenger services across its network . "Without work-on-track authorities, ARTC cannot be assured that its people can safely access the live rail corridor to undertake essential inspections, maintenance and repairs or respond to potentially dangerous track defects," an ARTC spokesperson said in a statement. "The restrictions arising from the notified industrial action could also compromise ARTC’s ability to respond to a safety-related incident involving a passenger service. As part of the industrial action, coal and freight trains would alternate days of operation over the seven-day period. "Significant disruption to freight services is also expected, with national consequences for supply chains and the movement of essential goods at one of the busiest times of the year," the spokesperson said. "ARTC is implementing contingency arrangements and working closely with customers to minimise disruption." ARTC has lodged an application with the Fair Work Commission seeking a three-month suspension of protected industrial action on safety and economic grounds, with an urgent hearing requested for Thursday. NSW RTBU Secretary Toby Warnes said members "deeply regret the impact this will have on the public". "The people who keep trains moving safely across NSW have been denied a fair say over their own pay and conditions for more than a decade," he said. "ARTC has rigged the vote by lumping network controllers and signal electricians in with a much larger group of office staff, so it can ignore frontline workers and still get its deal through. NSW TrainLink, which is not involved with the enterprise agreement dispute, said it would contact passengers with bookings with us to "secure bookings on next available services or provide refunds". "All our regional lines, like out to Dubbo, Griffith, Moree for example, will not be able to operate and as a consequence we are now working to secure coaches for those passengers that have current bookings for that week," NSW TrainLink chief executive Roger Weeks said. "We'll make our best effort to still get them where they need to go.

events.title: Australian regulator finds more suspected audit misconduct at Big Four firms
events.summary: KPMG is under regulatory and political investigation after the firm was accused of sharing confidential audit client information to bid for more work with other companies. ASIC found 35 of 558 audit complaints at KPMG, PwC, Deloitte and EY involved suspected misconduct, including falsified work and misuse of client information. The regulator criticised the firms for legalistic delays and weak internal responses, while saying some complaints may lead to enforcement action. Senators called the scale of misconduct “alarming”, and the government is considering tougher rules, including firm break-ups, size caps and mandatory audit rotation. SYDNEY – Australia’s corporate regulator said on Nov 25 it has discovered dozens of additional cases of suspected audit misconduct among the Big Four accounting firms, ranging from misuse of client information to falsified work. The Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) said it was now considering its enforcement and regulatory options following its review of 558 audit complaints at KPMG, PwC, Deloitte and EY. The Big Four have been beset by a number of scandals in recent years. KPMG is currently under regulatory and political investigation after whistleblower allegations came to light in 2026 , accusing the firm of sharing confidential audit client information to bid for more work with other companies. The Australian government is considering breaking up the Big ​Four firms and imposing partnership size caps as well as stipulating a mandatory rotation of audit firms in a bid to clean up the sector. ASIC’s review, announced in July, required the firms to hand over internal documents dating back to July 2023. The Big Four recorded 3,215 internal complaints during the three-year period. Of the 558 audit complaints ASIC examined, 35 raised questions about “the conduct of a statutory audit, or the misuse of statutory audit client information”, the review found. The most common concerns involved audit work that had been falsified, inaccurately documented or recorded without adequate evidence, ASIC said. A number of complaints alleged employees were directed to disregard, conceal or not escalate issues identified during an audit or that, when escalated, the issues were not investigated appropriately. There was also misuse and sharing of confidential statutory audit client information, including during an audit tender process, ASIC said. “Some of the complaints included serious allegations of misconduct that are under consideration for enforcement action,” ASIC’s report said. Other issues related to matters currently being investigated by ASIC, including its existing KPMG probe. ASIC criticised the firms’ internal responses to the complaints, finding they had investigated a number of concerns as workplace matters instead of audit quality issues. It also said the majority of firms initially engaged with its inquiries in a “protracted and legalistic” way, withholding or redacting documents, making extensive legal privilege claims and missing deadlines. KPMG said in a statement it was considering ASIC’s report and how it could help the firm improve its processes. “We are also progressing a number of measures to further strengthen our speak-up culture,” KPMG said. PwC also said it was considering the report, and that audit quality was its highest priority. “We take complaints raised seriously and are continuously improving our processes and practices,” a spokesperson said. Deloitte said it welcomed ASIC’s ongoing work to maintain trust in the profession. EY welcomed the review and said it would consider its observations. “What a shameful list of failures,” Deborah O’Neill, a senator from the ruling Labour Party who made the whistleblower allegations against KPMG public in March, said in a statement. “It’s clearer than ever that the barrel contains more than just a few bad apples.” Greens Senator Barbara Pocock said the “sheer scale of misconduct within the Big Four is alarming”, calling for ASIC to be given more powers to police the firms. “The evidence points to a culture of misconduct running right across the Big Four,” she said. “The Big Four cannot be allowed to continue operating like corporate cowboys, effectively policing themselves while misconduct goes unchecked. We need proper regulation, real oversight and a watchdog with teeth.” The firms are treated as partnerships rather than companies in Australia. That means they are not subject to supervision by ASIC, which has strict reporting requirements, and are instead regulated by state-based ‌laws. ASIC’s powers only extend to individual company auditors. Commissioner Kate O’Rourke said ASIC would continue to engage with the government on the regulation of audit firms. “The issues identified through this review reinforce the case for audit firm licensing and stronger enforcement and disciplinary powers,” she said.

events.title: Indonesia central bank expects to keep benchmark rate at 6% in 2027, governor says
events.summary: Bank Indonesia’s governor told a parliamentary hearing the rupiah exchange rate is expected to average between 17,800 to 18,200 per US dollar in 2027. Indonesia’s central bank expects its benchmark rate to stay at 6% in 2027, the same as at the end of 2026, Destry Damayanti told Parliament. Bank Indonesia expects the rupiah to average 17,800 to 18,200 per US dollar in 2027, after hitting a record low of 18,290 this week. The bank has raised rates by 125 basis points since May to support the rupiah, while concerns remain over policy independence and pressure to back growth. JAKARTA – Indonesia’s central bank in its 2027 budget proposal to Parliament assumes its benchmark rate to be at 6% in 2027 , unchanged from now, its governor said on Nov 25 . Destry Damayanti told a parliamentary hearing the rupiah exchange rate is expected to average between 17,800 to 18,200 per US dollar in 2027.b “BI’s (Bank Indonesia) rate in 2027 we expect at 6%, same as our expectation for the end of 2026,” Destry said, reading a list of economic and policy assumptions the central bank uses to come up with its 2027 budget proposal. BI has raised interest rates by 125 basis points since May in a bid to put a floor under the falling rupiah. Its last rate hike was in November , after which Destry said future rate moves would depend on data. The rupiah hit a record low of 18,290 per US dollar again on Nov 25 , a level it touched for the first time on Nov 23 . Analysts have flagged concerns about the potential for interference in the central bank’s policymaking after President Prabowo Subianto appointed his nephew to a senior BI role and parliament passed a law in 2026 that widened its mandate to emphasise the central bank’s role in promoting economic growth. Prabowo has expressed his determination to meet his target of 8% growth during his five-year term. Destry told Reuters in an interview in October that the central bank has full autonomy on interest rate policy. It will still pursue its dual goal of maintaining market stability and supporting economic growth using its policy mix in 2027, Destry said, noting the economy was still growing below its capacity. events.title: Construction underway on temporary transmission towers for Eyre Peninsula
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Topic: Electricity Production and Distribution ElectraNet transmission towers downed on the Eyre Peninsula. ( ABC News: Stephen Opie ) Construction on four temporary transmission towers is underway on the Eyre Peninsula, to replace those damaged by storm activity last week. The temporary towers are expected to be online by Friday. Construction of permanent replacement towers is expected to take up to a year. The southern Eyre Peninsula is expected to be reconnected to the national electricity grid by Friday morning, after storm activity last week downed two transmission towers and severely damaged a third. More than 20,000 properties on the peninsula and West Coast lost power on Thursday during the severe weather, and while construction has begun on temporary towers, operators say it could take a year for permanent structures to be installed. The damaged towers were located on a farm at Wharminda, which sits along a 270-kilometre transmission line between Port Lincoln and Cultana. Construction of four temporary transmission towers has began. ( ABC Eyre Peninsula: Jodie Hamilton ) Electricity transmission operator ElectraNet said local generation restored power for Port Lincoln and surrounding areas on Thursday night, and the network had to be reconfigured to allow services to return to some other parts of the Eyre Peninsula. Following their installation, the four temporary towers would need to be tested before being re-energised, which would restore transmission services from Cultana to Port Lincoln. ElectraNet chief executive Simon Emms said he was hoping services would be operational by early Friday. ElectraNet's Alex Trento and Simon Emms spoke from the Eyre Peninsula on Wednesday. ( ABC Eyre Peninsula: Jodie Hamilton ) "We're actually going to put up temporary towers each side of the existing line route, and then route the existing conductors around that," he said. SA Power Networks had advised residents in and around Port Lincoln of a planned power outage occurring on Thursday night while the region is reconnected to the transmission network. Mr Emms said the temporary towers have been built to the same standard as the current line. ElectraNet confident in tower design Mr Emms said on Wednesday the three transmission towers were damaged by a "localised, very severe wind event", and he was confident they had been built to the right strength. "We know the towers are designed to the appropriate Australian standard. That design has been checked, independently checked, and we also built a test tower and tested it to destruction," he said. Mr Emms said ElectraNet would undertake a "thorough and complete" investigation into the incident. Following the storms last week, ElectraNet had suggested the towers were likely brought down by a "one-in-2,000-year weather event", something the SA government said would form part of investigations into the incident. Damage to ElectraNet's transmission towers on the Eyre Peninsula. ( ABC News: Steve Opie ) Mr Emms said new permanent transmission towers would need to be built in place of the three damaged structures, which he estimated could take up to a year. events.title: Energy bills in Great Britain to rise 26% in January, lifting annual bills over £2,000
events.summary: Ofgem’s price cap will increase for third quarter in a row after rise in wholesale cost of gas Stick or switch? Billpayers weigh up how to beat energy jump Millions of British households will face annual energy bills of more than £2,000 a year for the first time since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, as the cap on energy bills climbs for a third straight quarter. Gas and electricity prices will rise by 26% from January under the government’s new price cap after an increase in wholesale prices not experienced since the first winter after the invasion. The regulator for Great Britain, Ofgem , said about 22 million households covered by the price cap would need to pay an average equivalent to £2,166 a year for gas and electricity from the new year, up from £1,723 under the current quarterly cap. The increase means that the average household will be forced to pay almost £600 a year more on their dual-fuel bill than before the start of the Middle East crisis. There was a 4% rise at the start of October and a 13% increase at the start of July. About a third of households that pay for their gas and electricity on fixed tariffs will not be affected by the latest price cap rise. However, the highest energy price cap since early 2023 is still expected to reignite calls for the government to help struggling families and reduce reliance on fossil fuels. The cap is a limit on how much energy suppliers can charge for a unit of electricity or gas, not a ceiling for how high bills can rise. Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, said: “I know people are deeply concerned by another rise in energy bills. For too long, British families have been paying the price for conflicts overseas and volatile fossil fuel markets.” The government has promised to give “breathing space” to struggling households this winter through a one-off payment of £100 in January for 20 million households in council tax bands A to D. The payment will be in addition to the warm home discount, which offers about 6 million means-tested households in England, Wales and Scotland £150 off winter fuel bills. “But there is more to do to take the pressure off families and bring bills down for good,” Fahnbulleh said. “That means more cheap, clean, homegrown power so we’re less reliant on expensive fossil fuels, and reforming our broken energy system so it’s fairer for British people.” The government help remains well below the surging prices for gas, electricity and road fuels, which have forced up living costs in the nine months since the US-Israeli strikes on Iran. Energy bills are expected to only fall slightly in April, when the price cap is next set, according to a new forecast from Cornwall Insight on Wednesday. The energy consultancy said market volatility caused by disruption to the strait of Hormuz meant its predictions could change “several times” in the coming months. Europe’s benchmark gas price has tripled in response to a global supply squeeze, that meant the continent entered the cooler months with gas stores at some of the lowest levels ever recorded . Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning The price could climb even higher, according to Goldman Sachs, if disruption to Gulf gas exports causes storage facilities to empty before the end of the heating season. Craig Lowrey, a principal at Cornwall Insight, warned that if the Middle East conflict continues, current forecasts suggest bills could remain about £2,000 a year for the typical household until the end of 2027. Lorwey said the forecast fall of 1% in April was “so small that many households will barely notice it, and by then the £100 payment, for those who are eligible, will be a distant memory”. Ministers have sought to cushion the blow by moving electricity levies into general taxation over the past year, which has shaved about £150 a year off costs. The Treasury also promised to keep the 5% VAT levy off electricity bills for 29 million households until July next year, which should extend the tax relief to £50 a year. Danny Gross, a climate campaigner at Friends of the Earth, called on the government to accelerate the shift to “cheap, homegrown renewable energy” to cushion energy bills from the volatility of the fossil fuel markets. “This will cut bills, create long-term jobs, strengthen our energy security and tackle the climate crisis at the same time,” Gross said. “But people need relief now, not just promises. Ministers must introduce a social tariff to protect low-income households and move the hidden levies piled onto electricity bills into general taxation,” he added.

events.title: ‘Nature’s Ozempic’: oat sales soar as shoppers seek out foods that mimic effect of GLP-1s
events.summary: Porridge emerges as trend’s poster child with consumers looking to foods that help them feel full for longer, says Waitrose Sales of filling foods such as porridge oats that mimic the effect of taking weight-loss medication are booming on the back of social media hype billing them as “nature’s Ozempic” or “oatzempic”. Sales of Waitrose Scottish Oats are up 124% this year, according to the retailer’s annual food and drink report, which dissects the biggest trends sweeping the grocery aisles. A poll conducted for the report revealed that 64% of shoppers are “actively choosing to eat foods like oats that keep us feeling fuller for longer”. “GLP-1s are reshaping the entire food and drink landscape, even for people who aren’t on the medication,” said Dr Joanne Lunn, Waitrose’s head of health and nutrition. “As appetite patterns change, customers’ baskets are shifting towards smaller portions, nutrient density and high-satiety (feeling full) foods.” There are now more homes with GLP-1 users than contain vegetarians and pescatarians combined in Great Britain, according to a recent survey by Worldpanel by Numerator. About 2.6 million adults were using weight-loss medication in August, a rise of about 700,000 people since February, it said. But those taking the medication have a big influence on what is bought in the supermarket as nearly eight in 10 GLP-1 users are also the main grocery shopper for their household, according to the report. Just over 4,000 customers were polled for the report. Of the respondents who were taking weight-loss medication, 88% said they were shopping differently as a result. More than half were eating more protein while a third were drinking less alcohol. One in five had started taking more supplements while a similar number ate more fish. The terms “nature’s Ozempic” and “Oatzempic” refer to a wave of social media trends promoting everyday alternatives to prescription weight-loss jabs. Foods on this list include pulses, seeds, nuts, and tinned fish, the retailer said, but are also good options for those taking the appetite-suppressing medications and who want to eat a balanced diet. As part of this, Waitrose says it is seeing “fibre-maths” enter everyday home cooking, with people using salad toppers, seeds, and cereal stir-ins to stack extra nutrients on to ordinary meals. Porridge is the unlikely poster child for the trend, with the budget-friendly cereal billed as a “standout wellness staple” in the report. Recipe creators are experimenting with everything from miso versions to sour cherry and pistachio butter toppings. “We’re seeing a growing shift towards savoury porridge,” said Lunn, who suggests swapping sweet toppings for chilli oil, bone broth and roasted veg is the “ultimate hack for a low-sugar, high-satiety boost”. The report also highlights the food trends that will shape what appears on supermarket shelves in the future. You may already have heard about switter (sweet-bitter) and fricy (spicy fruit), but the flavour mashup of 2027 is set to be “smugar” which is sugar with a burnt makeover. Waitrose says you can expect to see this smoky-sweet portmanteau flavour turn up in bakeries, barbecue ranges and as bitter-caramel finishes on desserts.

events.title: Door not closed on capital gains carve-out for businesses as inquiry confirmed
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Capital gains startup exemptions heads for Senate inquiry, leaving open possibility of wider carve-out Treasurer Jim Chalmers says it is possible an inquiry could be held into capital gains tax carve-outs, an issue raised by independent MP Allegra Spender. ( ABC News: Ian Cutmore/Luke Stephenson ) Labor's capital gains tax carve-out for startups is headed to a Senate inquiry, where Allegra Spender's alternative proposal could be probed. Treasury has concerns with her proposal, including that it is too complex and could be gamed. The inquiry would push the matter into next year. A push to exempt every active business from Labor's new capital gains tax regime is headed for a Senate inquiry, despite Treasury's strong reservations about the idea. The proposal by independent MP Allegra Spender would apply a flat 40 per cent capital gains tax discount to all active assets, a term that captures anything used, or ready to use, to operate a business. Mr Chalmers wrote a letter to Ms Spender last week saying her idea would not be "simpler, fairer, or enhance productivity" compared to his proposal, which applies a discount tied to inflation, with a narrower carve-out for "innovative" businesses. But while he repeated those concerns in Question Time on Wednesday, Mr Chalmers said an inquiry was "a possible outcome". A senior government source went further and said it was all but certain and would soon be confirmed. The government struck a deal with the Greens on Wednesday to pass the 30 per cent minimum tax on discretionary trusts, another key budget measure. Multiple sources with knowledge of Senate negotiations said that was the government's main priority. While Mr Chalmers has given no direct indication that he is open to amending his innovation carve-out along the lines of Ms Spender's proposal, an inquiry would push the matter into next year and make that a distinct possibility. The debate stems from the anger of the startup sector about the May budget decision to apply the new inflation discount to businesses and shares, not just to housing. Startups said an inflation discount would leave them worse off than the existing 50 per cent discount, because an inflation discount is calculated based on the starting cost of an asset. Startups without physical assets often begin near zero, meaning no discount. The minor party's support will be critical to pass a minimum tax on trusts and a carve-out for start-ups in the capital gains tax regime. The government acknowledged these concerns in budget week and promised to consult on an alternative. The innovative business carve-out was the result, giving any eligible business younger than 15 years the choice between the new discount and the old one. But Ms Spender and some business groups said this was too narrow and that deciding which businesses were "innovative" would be too subjective. Ms Spender said a flat 40 per cent discount for active assets would be simpler and raise similar revenue. In his letter, Mr Chalmers outlined three main concerns, informed by Treasury analysis. The first was that a flat 40 per cent discount would see business pay more tax in some circumstances than under an inflation discount. The second was an integrity concern that a business would be deemed "active" as long as 80 per cent of its assets are active, creating a loophole for people to put large passive assets such as properties into otherwise-active businesses to escape the tax. The third was a complexity concern that businesses and their shareholders would need to maintain an ongoing list of which assets were active and which were not, adding a layer of red tape to the tax system that does not currently exist. Ms Spender has discussed the idea in private with Mr Chalmers, as both have publicly indicated, and also with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese. Ms Spender has indicated that she is receptive to modifying her proposal to address the integrity concerns. The concern that some businesses could pay more tax could be addressed by simply allowing them to choose between the old discount and a 40 per cent discount, similar to Labor's current proposal. It's unclear how the complexity issue could be solved. Ms Spender has emphasised the support from many business groups for her proposal, including the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry. She has argued that the government could repair its troubled relationship with businesses and their advocates.

events.title: Bitcoin funds headed for worst month as outflows near US$5 billion
events.summary: Bitcoin is facing numerous headwinds, from high-profile hacks to the prospect of higher interest rates and greater regulatory scrutiny following recent US midterm elections. Bitcoin ETFs are having their worst month since launch, with US$4.71 billion withdrawn in November and BlackRock’s fund losing about US$4 billion. Bitcoin fell below US$60,000, down about 23% this month, and is heading for its worst monthly performance since June 2022. Analysts say weak demand, hacks, higher rates and more regulation are hurting Bitcoin, and the industry may need a new catalyst to recover. US-listed exchange-traded funds (ETFs) investing in Bitcoin are heading for the worst month of outflows since their 2024 debut, as a persistent sell-off in the world’s largest cryptocurrency drives investors away. A net US$4.71 billion (S$6 billion) has been withdrawn from the funds in November so far, according to data compiled by Bloomberg through Nov 23. BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust, the largest fund holding the token, has suffered about US$4 billion of redemptions in November , also putting it on course for its worst monthly outflow. The exodus comes as Bitcoin tumbles below US$60,000 and heads for its worst monthly performance since June 2022, when a string of corporate failures triggered a broader crypto market meltdown. The token has dropped about 23% in November and was trading around US$59,200 as at 1pm on Nov 25 in Singapore, down about 1% in the Asia session. The losses underscore a sharp reversal for a group of ETFs that helped propel Bitcoin higher after their US debut in January 2024. The funds opened the cryptocurrency to a wider pool of institutional and retail investors and became an important source of demand during the bull market. Their record redemptions are now reinforcing the current downturn as that source of buying dries up. Bitcoin briefly recovered alongside other risk assets on Nov 23 after Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive, but has since surrendered all of those gains, a sign that investors are using rallies to reduce exposure. “When a market cannot hold a rally on good news, it usually means that investors are using any strength to sell,” data analytics firm Glassnode said in a note. “Bitcoin trades round the clock and tends to be one of the first assets sold when investors want less risk.” Bitcoin is facing numerous headwinds, from high-profile hacks that have undermined confidence in its security to the prospect of higher interest rates and greater regulatory scrutiny following the recent US midterm elections . The absence of US demand is adding to the pressure, according to Glassnode. “The ETFs and other institutions were an important source of demand on the way up, and there is little interest from them at these prices,” the firm said. “A return to ETF inflows, together with net buying on Coinbase, would be the first sign that this is changing.” Bitcoin is also facing greater competition for investor capital as money gravitates towards equities and assets offering income, according to Ayesha Kiani, chief operating officer of Monarq Asset Management. Bitcoin is “competing for the same risk capital that is going into equities right now”, Kiani told Bloomberg Television, describing the ETF exodus as “concerning”. The cryptocurrency industry may need a fresh catalyst to revive demand after the forces that drove the previous rally have faded, she said. “I think we do need to find a new narrative, a new catalyst, a new market, something new for the entire industry for us to become that emerging asset class again,” Kiani said. “There are better yield-bearing assets out there at this point. So, like, why Bitcoin?” BLOOMBERG

AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Criminal masterminds claimed to work for ‘Weihua’ or to have source code from ‘oscic’ instead of Cisco Huawei and crew tout homegrown EDA tools to overcome China’s fab deficit now Huawei says it’s made a 100 percent Chinese PC 16 days ago Google says Asian advertisers spending less due to Europe's customs changes 23 days ago openEuler brings China's enterprise Linux ambitions to the desktop October 20, 2026 EU’s hodgepodge tech policy exposes members to Chinese vendor risks, says think tank October 1, 2026 A US jury has found Chinese tech giant Huawei stole tech from American companies, laundered money, and violated sanctions by building major internet infrastructure for Iran, but didn’t operate an illegal racket to get that done. This case kicked off in 2020, when the US Department of Justice claimed entities Huawei operated in America violated federal law. The indictment led to a trial on a dozen criminal matters that has played out over the last three months in the Eastern District Court of New York. The trial ended on Tuesday when a jury found Huawei and three subsidiary companies guilty of conspiracy to steal trade secrets, conspiracy to commit wire and bank fraud, wire fraud, bank fraud, conspiracy to defraud the United States, conspiracy to violate the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) and substantive violations of that law, plus money laundering conspiracy. The Department of Justice’s celebration of the decision says Huawei was found to have stolen Cisco’s source code, after prosecutors showed evidence that “Huawei engineers left Cisco’s notes about the Cisco code, referred to Cisco using its name backwards ‘ocsic’ and described that portions of the code remained as they existed in the ‘ocsic’ code.” Another item of evidence apparently showed a Huawei staffer photographing Fujitsu equipment while wearing a fake employee badge for a company called “Weihua” – cunningly reversing the two syllables of “Huawei.” Another allegation the jury accepted involved Huawei staffers signing a non-disclosure agreement (NDA) ahead of a visit to T-Mobile to inspect a robot the telco created to test mobile devices. Huawei staff ignored that NDA so thoroughly that they “sent photographs and technical details of the robot back to China” so the Chinese company could make its own robot. “When that data was not sufficient, a Huawei employee stole a part of the robot in his backpack and carried it out of T-Mobile’s controlled laboratory,” the DoJ says. The feds say the Chinese company also “lied about its activities in Iran to banks to obtain billions of U.S. dollars and access to U.S.-dollar clearing services, which enabled Huawei to be a sophisticated participant in a global marketplace for telecommunications services — in part because of its lies.” Huawei has issued a statement noting that the jury found it not guilty of racketeering and insisting the charges on which it was found guilty are “without legal or factual merit.” “The five trade secret-related disputes cited by the government were all civil matters that were resolved over the past two decades,” the statement adds. Sentencing will take place in September 2027. The presiding judge will likely consider the fact that in 2017, US authorities fined Chinese telco equipment maker ZTE $900 million just for selling to Iran, then added an additional $1.4 billion penalty to lift a ban on doing business in the USA. Washington has already banned Huawei from selling its telco products and personal devices in the USA. Lawmakers have little appetite to let the Chinese company return to the American market after spending billions to help American telcos replace the Huawei kit with locally made alternatives.

events.title: Compass exit leaves London seeking next generation of defining businesses
events.summary: Now and again, there is a piece of news that brings you up short. So it is with the decision of Compass to move its primary listing from London to New York. That may seem anodyne and relatively obscure, small feed in the order of things. But not if you live and work in London, and take delight and comfort in the UK capital being a world business centre. It’s a hegemony that has been long in the making, nurtured and honed over centuries, based on the City of London's reputation and traditions making it a magnet for companies and investors from all over. At its heart is the London Stock Exchange , once a historic, mighty market for shares, the place that businesses were proud to call home. Compass is off. We’ve seen stocks defect before, of course, and in increasing numbers in recent years. Wise, Flutter, Ferguson, Indivior, Diversified Energy and Sunbelt are just some of those to switch. Another major one was building materials supplier CRH. They’re not moving their operations but where they list their shares. So, it’s not as if they are taking thousands of jobs, although their use of professional services and advisers will be affected. But it says much about where they see themselves, where they wish to be and inevitably, over time, they loosen the chains of their origins and America’s influence becomes pervasive. Compass began after the Second World War, when legislation was introduced obliging manufacturing and armaments firms that employed 250 people or more to provide hot meals for their workers. Today, this contract caterer is all over the UK and abroad, employing 600,000 people in 25 countries under brands such as Levy, which handles hospitality at sports stadiums including Allianz in Twickenham, Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, Old Trafford and Edgbaston. Other leading Compass-owned brands include Bon Appetit, Eurest, Morrison Healthcare and Chartwells. It likes to call itself “possibly the biggest business you’ve never heard of”. Except the investment community is aware of Compass. Revenue last year was $46.1 billion. That should be clue enough as to what it was planning – reporting its performance in dollars, not pounds. Even so, while that was noted, Compass remained a definably British story and a hugely successful one to boot. Who's next? There is palpable shock at the announcement. Invariably too, attention focuses to who might follow – with Shell, a fixture of the London market, and pharma colossus AstraZeneca tipped to be next. Companies jumping ship is not new either. Previously there was no shortage of replacements – from the UK and overseas. Just as there have been exits, so too has the flow of entrants dried up. Last year, London hosted 23 initial public offerings (IPOs), which together raised £2.1 billion. In the US, there were 354, raising $44 billion. This year, IPOs in London have reduced to a trickle – Dealogic reckons the UK is down to 14th globally, behind Malaysia, Turkey and Norway. Fourteenth! Meanwhile, the disappearing is continuing in another direction. So far this year, $133 billion of UK-listed companies have been bought, the highest tally since 2018. They include familiar names such as easyJet and Schroders. It’s a three-pronged onslaught: companies listing elsewhere, usually New York; few rushing to take their place; and still more being acquired. Not for nothing does Dame Julia Hoggett, beleaguered boss of the LSE, say: “If we want Britain to back Britain, which is what I hear the Chancellor and the Prime Minister saying, then let’s make sure that we’re creating structural incentives to do so. We need to take the handbrake off.” Hoggett is correct, John Healey and Andy Burnham are saying that. She would not be wrong either if she thought they were rocked by the Compass decision. “Genuinely frustrating”, was how the mood was described by a government official. As soon as Labour returned to power, it announced new rules for company listings in a step designed to boost London’s appeal. That was more than two years ago and it has not worked. In his recent Budget , Healey fell back on that old get out – stamp duty, and how he was holding a review (another one) into the charge – and how he would also introduce a three-year window for trading in newly listed shares. Ministers, not least City Minister Lucy Rigby, maintain stamp duty is what holds companies back from listing their shares in London. To which the riposte is “if you say so, minister”. The truth is that it does not help but to argue it is the main factor is nonsense. The issue goes much deeper. Replacements required It’s not so much Compass opting for New York but that lack of substitutes that is the worry. Compass is a global concern; the US is the dominant capital market, offering liquidity on a vast, accessible scale. To tap into that, the caterer is heading to Manhattan. Fair enough. London has never taken business from New York; rather they have existed side by side, the one broadly feeding the Americas and the other the rest. That was and is, London’s place, and it did and still can thrive as a result. To restore London’s lustre is about encouraging talent, giving it the tools to prosper (of which tax breaks form a part). It’s about creating the mood, setting a direction of travel that is positive for business, domestic and foreign, for wealth creation. That means stripping away the regulations, reducing red tape – not reviewing and pondering. Not taxing. In the very week Compass dropped its grenade, Burnham and business secretary Jonathan Reynolds had breakfast with a select group of CEOs on the fringe of the CBI annual conference. They heard about the PM’s intentions towards the European Union and his “10-year plan” to change Britain. It was excitable. But all talk and no action, and looking beyond the next election. What it wasn’t was of the present. Compass should serve as a red flag; stop talking and start doing.

events.title: Mandatory lead testing of childcare centres in Broken Hill
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Lead testing to be mandatory at Broken Hill early learning facilities Soil is tested for lead contamination in Broken Hill. ( ABC News: Bill Ormonde ) A new multi-agency committee will oversee mandatory lead-contamination testing at all Broken Hill early learning centres. Earlier this year it was found that many centres were over the national health investigation thresholds. While the new committee is expected to be up and running from early 2027, testing will begin this month. Early learning centres in Broken Hill will undergo mandatory testing for lead contamination following the announcement of a new multi-agency committee. The testing will apply to all childcare services for 0-5-year-olds in the remote mining city, with remediation provided where needed. Testing was previously an opt-in service for early learning services, which could then choose to have remediation work carried out. Remediation is a process of making buildings and spaces lead-free through methods such as sealing windows and doors, and laying grass to trap dirt. Testing will begin this month and continue into next year, with services to be contacted to make individual arrangements. A new expert panel will decide when remediation is funded, based on how exposed children are to areas with elevated lead levels. Lead contamination spreads across Broken Hill via windblown dust from the slag heap of the original mine. ( ABC Broken Hill: Rhys Carman ) Broken Hill faces a historical lead pollution problem, sitting around one of the world's largest ore bodies of lead, silver and zinc. It has been mined continuously for almost 140 years, resulting in the widespread distribution of lead in soil and dust throughout Broken Hill and surrounding areas. Exposure to lead can cause learning disabilities, behavioural problems, slow or abnormal growth, poor coordination and hearing problems. Children under five are particularly vulnerable because their brains are still developing. Lead testing will now be mandatory at all early learning centres. ( ABC News: Bill Ormonde ) Broken Hill mother Alisha McInerney has three-year-old twins and said the decision to conduct mandatory testing was important. Ms McInerney said there was a lack of information after her son Hendrix had recorded above-normal blood lead levels. "I was a little bit concerned, but we weren't really given anything, any tools to help lower them besides washing hands thoroughly." Alisha McInerney with her twins Hendrix and Niya. ( ABC Broken Hill: Em Jensen ) She said she is worried about the impact of the lead, such as developmental delays, as her children grow older. "It is becoming such a normal thing here in Broken Hill to just accept that lead levels and regular lead testing is normal. "I don't know any different as a parent." Three-year-old Hendrix McInerney recorded above-average blood lead levels. ( ABC Broken Hill: Em Jensen ) Interim chief executive of the NSW Environment Protection Authority (EPA) Nancy Chang said in a statement that despite a drop in Broken Hill blood lead levels by more than 75 per cent in children under 5, they are still too high. "We know that children under 5 years of age are more likely to be at risk of harm from lead because of their hand-to-mouth behaviour, touching and crawling on dusty surfaces and their young bodies absorbing a higher proportion of lead than adults as they grow," Ms Chang said. According to the latest Annual Lead Program Report from NSW Ministry of Health, 35 per cent of children aged one to five, and 56 per cent of Aboriginal children, have blood lead levels above the national health investigative guideline of 5 micrograms per decilitre (5 µg/dL). Testing of childcare centres conducted by the NSW EPA between 2015 and 2025 found high lead contamination levels at 10 facilities, but parents were not informed . The new mandatory testing and clean-up will be conducted under a new Broken Hill Lead Coordination Committee, coordinated by the NSW EPA and including NSW Health and the Department of Education, expected to be running by early 2027. Cartoon character Lead Ted advises children to wash their hands after playing on equipment at a public park in Broken Hill. ( ABC Broken Hill: Em Jensen ) In January, a report from the Office of the Chief Scientist and Engineer (OCSE) made four main recommendations around coordination, data and program evaluation, public health initiatives, remediation, and emissions control to address lead contamination in the city. The NSW government has now accepted all recommendations.

AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Four more critical vulns, including another unauthorized access flaw in vCenter The security of US water systems is even leakier than we thought now Microsoft's NTLM security changes trip up third-party logins 2 hours ago US Treasury financial crimes unit becomes latest fed breach victim 3 hours ago Gatwick drop-off customers' personal data exposed in supplier breach 8 hours ago 'We are not ShinyHunters,' says criminal hacking crew that looks and acts just like ShinyHunters 23 hours ago VMware has issued its third critical security advisory in a week, this time to warn of four critical flaws and address a total of 23 issues. VMSA-2026-0011 landed on November 24, just five days after two other advisories. VMware’s FAQ for the new advisory includes the following remarks: Because of coordinated disclosure and release pipeline timing this VMSA comes on the heels of VMSA-2026-0009, and atop a major holiday in the United States. The security vulnerability landscape is more dynamic than ever; please know that while we acknowledge this timing is not optimal, your ability to operate and maintain a secure environment amidst modern, AI-assisted threats is paramount to us. REG AD Make of that what you will as you ponder how and when to patch the four critical flaws, including the 9.8-rated CVE-2026-123903, which allows a malicious actor to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to vCenter, the management tool VMware users rely on to manage hosts and VMs. REG AD This is the third 9.8-rated authentication issue VMware has fixed in vCenter since July. Two of the other critical flaws in this new advisory allow an attacker to run code on an ESX host, earning the bugs a 9.8 rating. CVE-2026-123910 makes that possible thanks to a heap out-of-bounds write vulnerability in the I/O filter service, while CVE-2026-123911 is a use-after-free vulnerability. The other critical flaw, CVE-2026-123912, can result in a guest escape from VMware’s desktop Workstation and Fusion desktop hypervisors. It’s also present in VMware’s ESX hypervisor, but attackers thankfully can’t escape that product’s sandbox. This one’s easy to mitigate because the problem is in a USB controller that users can turn off. Most of the other flaws require installation of updated software. There’s a little good news in that some of the software updates VMware issued last week include fixes for the newly disclosed flaws. But there are still plenty of fresh fixes to apply, across ten products: ESX, vCenter, Workstation, Fusion, VMware tools, Cloud Foundation, vSphere Foundation, the Telco Cloud Platform, Telco Cloud Infrastructure, and the VMware Avi Load Balancer. VMware’s advisory thanks external researchers for finding and reporting most of the flaws. The Broadcom business unit is known to be a member of Project Glasswing, the Anthropic-run effort to use the Mythos model to find flaws that has seen many vendors dramatically increase the number of patches they produce. In past years, VMware has often published considerably more than this year’s 11 security advisories. events.title: Huawei found guilty of money laundering and conspiracy to steal trade secrets in US case
events.summary: Huawei, China’s largest technology company, has been found guilty of charges in the US, including money laundering, conspiracy to steal trade secrets and defrauding banks over its business in Iran and North Korea. A federal jury in Brooklyn, New York, deliberated for about four days before reaching a verdict Tuesday in a rare US prosecution of a foreign corporation. The panel found the company guilty of 10 of 12 counts following an 11-week trial. Huawei was cleared of two conspiracy charges related to racketeering and obstruction of justice. The verdict against one of China’s biggest and best-known tech giants lands at a delicate time for relations between the world’s largest economies, with the administration of President Donald Trump tightening curbs on China’s ability to access American chips after revelations that Nvidia's Jensen Huang had an affair with a woman suspected of links to Chinese intelligence. Even so, the years-old case is unlikely to affect the broader trade truce between Mr Trump and President Xi Jinping, who affirmed a commitment to keep ties stable at a summit last week. While that deal is set to expire in January, both sides have an incentive to prevent a deterioration that could lead to much higher tariffs and bans on essential items like rare earths, aeroplane parts and chip design software. “Few crimes are as serious as Huawei’s decades-long pattern of endangering US national security, violating the sanctity of US commerce, and impeding the enforcement of US laws,” said Brooklyn US Attorney Joseph Nocella. “Today’s verdict is a step towards accountability for Huawei’s criminal activities, which include years-long collaboration with sanctioned entities in Iran, repeated lies to banks, and blatant thefts from US technology companies.” Brian Heberlig, Huawei’s lead lawyer, focused on the company’s acquittal on two charges, including the so-called RICO racketeering count, which he called the government’s lead charge. The company said in a separate statement that the remaining charges have no merit and it will review its legal options. Mixed emotions “It’s hard not to have profoundly mixed emotions from the verdict we just heard,” Mr Heberlig said. The RICO charge “alleged that the company was corrupt from top to bottom, that it had a corporate culture and policy of cheating, stealing, and lying, and the jury found the company not guilty on that charge”. The decision comes years after the Justice Department first filed charges against the world’s largest maker of telecoms equipment. For most of that time, the company has been largely excluded from the American market under trade measures imposed by the Trump and Biden administrations in the name of national security. The telecom titan has emerged as China’s de facto national chipmaking champion and is one of a handful of firms central to Beijing’s goal of dominating artificial intelligence and replacing American software and circuitry with local equivalents. The case was publicly unveiled in early 2019 under the first Trump administration’s so-called China Initiative, a Justice Department programme to combat Chinese espionage and influence in the US. Prosecutors have since won numerous convictions against Chinese nationals, but have struggled in trials against large Chinese companies on American soil. 60 witnesses The jury of nine women and three men heard testimony from more than 60 witnesses during the 11-week trial. Huawei was convicted of a scheme to steal trade secrets from rival tech competitors over 20 years, including source code from Cisco Systems, semiconductor equipment from CNEX Labs, robotic phone testing equipment from T-Mobile as well as proprietary information from Fujitsu Network Communications. “Today’s verdict makes clear that fraud, sanctions evasion, and the theft of intellectual property are not business strategies, they are serious crimes,” said James Barnacle, head of the FBI’s New York office. “Huawei’s success was built on deception and theft, and the FBI will never hesitate to pursue those who profit by breaking the law.” In their verdict on Tuesday, however, the panel rejected the government’s theory that Huawei had engaged in a racketeering scheme for more than two decades to “grow its global brand” into one of the biggest telecoms in the world. The panel also rejected a US charge that Huawei obstructed a federal grand jury investigation. Jurors left the courthouse and declined to speak to the press. The conviction is a vindication for the Justice Department, which overcame attempts by Huawei to derail the case before trial and had to navigate years of delays because of the Covid pandemic, which made it difficult for lawyers and witnesses to travel. Along the way, two Chinese intelligence officers were accused in 2022 of trying to bribe a US law enforcement official with $61,000 in Bitcoin to steal evidence and get inside information about the case. Huawei now faces fines, forfeiture and restitution but the US has not specified the scope of financial penalties it will seek at sentencing, which is scheduled for September 2027. From the beginning, the Huawei case heightened tensions between Washington and Beijing while the world’s two largest economies were mired in a trade war. Months later, officials in Donald Trump’s administration labelled the company a national security threat, alleging that it sold telecoms equipment that could be used by China’s Communist Party for spying. The initial criminal indictment set off a diplomatic crisis when Huawei chief financial officer Meng Wanzhou, whose father founded the company, was arrested at the behest of the US on financial fraud charges while travelling through Canada. Almost three years after Meng was held under house arrest in Vancouver, she reached a deferred prosecution agreement in 2021 that allowed her to return to China, but after she admitted that the company violated US sanctions by illegally conducting business in Iran.

events.title: ADGM's Iliad Partners closes start-up fund with more backing from Greek entities
events.summary: Abu Dhabi's Iliad Partners has raised funds for the final close of its Gulf-focused investment fund backed by Greek banks, as it looks to boost its portfolio in the region's start-up scene. The $33.4 million Iliad Partners Tech Ventures Fund I will primarily focus on opportunities in the UAE and Saudi Arabia , with selective investments in Europe, particularly in Greece, ADGM-based Iliad Partners said in a statement on Wednesday. Among the new major institutional investors are the Hellenic Development Bank of Investments, Greece's $2.5 billion sovereign fund of funds, and Alpha Bank, one of the country's four systemic lenders. Three of Greece's other major banks, National Bank of Greece, Eurobank and Piraeus Bank, joined the fund last year, marking their first foray into venture capital investment in the wider Middle East and North Africa region. The fund, which originally had a target of $50 million, announced its first close in December 2024, followed by a second close in September last year that nearly doubled its assets under management. The fund aims to support early-stage companies in artificial intelligence and business-to-business software in sectors such as finance, property, logistics and enterprise. Iliad's current portfolio includes Balio, Comfi, OTO, Penny and Qashio; its previous investments include Fetchr, OSeven and Trukker. Additional investments are in progress under a three-year strategy. The focus on the Gulf mirrors its emergence as a region offering "significant" opportunities for start-ups to grow, with Europe serving as a source for talent and expertise, said Christos Mastoras, founder and managing partner of Iliad Partners. "We see tremendous potential in building bridges between these complementary ecosystems, unlocking new opportunities for entrepreneurs and businesses across both regions," he said. The close of the fund is a "new chapter, focused on translating this vision into tangible opportunities for the founders we back and supporting them in building enduring, globally competitive businesses". Start-ups remain vital players in economies as they continue to develop tech solutions in the digital era. The business environment and regulations in the UAE are making it easier for start-ups to access funding. AI in particular has drawn significant attention. The Emirates is pursuing its National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence 2031, aimed at establishing the Emirates as a global leader in AI by integrating advanced technology into government, business and daily life. The participation of Greece's institutions in Iliad Partners' funding vehicle also reflects the growing ties between Greece and the Middle East, said Lazaros Papagaryfallou, deputy chief executive of Athens' Alpha Bank. "We see growing opportunities for our clients and the wider business community ... at the same time, the investment contributes to the broader effort to foster commercial and cross-border business opportunities in the broader region," he added. Iliad Partners Tech Ventures Fund I's other investors include Jada Fund of Funds, a wholly owned subsidiary of Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, Alpha Bank's peers Eurobank, National Bank of Greece and Piraeus Bank, and family groups and family offices from Saudi Arabia, the Gulf and Europe.

events.title: Starbucks to engage banks for sale of Japan business
events.summary: Starbucks has about 2,000 coffeehouses in Japan, making it one of the company’s biggest markets. TOKYO – Starbucks has tapped advisers to prepare for a potential sale of its Japan business for several billion dollars, according to sources familiar with the matter. The US coffee chain is working with banks including Citigroup and Morgan Stanley and has started sounding out interest from some strategic and financial investors, the sources said, asking not to be identified because the information is not public. A formal process might start as soon as 2026, they said. Deliberations about the business are ongoing and might not result in a sale, the people said. A Starbucks spokesperson said the company continually assesses the best structure for its customers and creating value for shareholders. The chain has a strong business in Japan, where it has been for more than 30 years, the spokesperson said. Citi and Morgan Stanley declined to comment. Bloomberg News reported in June that Starbucks was considering options for the Japanese business and had held preliminary talks with banks. Starbucks does not break out standalone revenue for Japan, but combined with Canada and Britain, the three accounted for about 72% of net revenues generated outside the US and China in fiscal 2026. events.title: Companies linked to restaurant chain Komala’s settle 20 CPF charges after paying dues
events.summary: There are five Komala’s outlets, in Race Course Road, Fernvale Link, Anson Road, Yishun Central and Jurong East. Komala’s Pte Ltd and Komala’s F&B Enterprises settled 20 CPF charges after all required payments were made. The State Courts gave both firms a discharge amounting to an acquittal. Director Rajoo Thanasekaran attended for both companies. Komala’s was set up in 1997 and Komala’s F&B Enterprises in 2001, with restaurants as their main business. The hearing adds to uncertainty over former Komala Vilas in Little India. The 1947 vegetarian restaurant is closed for renovations, and Ishtara Jewellery plans to take over the unit. SINGAPORE – Two companies linked to restaurant chain Komala’s had their CPF cases compounded after all required payments were made, the State Courts heard on Nov 25. Komala’s Pte Ltd and Komala’s F&B Enterprises each faced 10 charges. The court granted both companies a discharge amounting to an acquittal for all 20 charges. Both matters were compounded after all payments had been made. According to charge sheets seen by The Straits Times, Komala’s failed to pay Central Provident Fund contributions for 10 employees in December 2025, while Komala’s F&B Enterprises failed to pay CPF contributions for 10 employees for the same month. Rajoo Thanasekaran, director of Komala’s, attended court as a representative of both companies. The cases were listed separately. Business profiles of both companies, retrieved on Nov 25, list them as live companies. According to records, Komala’s was incorporated in 1997, and lists restaurants as its primary business activity and the manufacture of prepared meals and dishes as its secondary activity. Komala’s F&B Enterprises was incorporated in 2001 and its registered activities are restaurants and cafes. The restaurant chain’s official website lists Komala’s outlets in Race Course Road, Fernvale Link, International Plaza in Anson Road, Yishun Central and Jurong East. The International Plaza restaurant is identified as a franchise outlet. The hearing comes as the future of the former Komala Vilas flagship in Little India remains uncertain. Komala’s and Komala Vilas operate separately The beloved vegetarian restaurant was established in 1947 and its outlet at 76 to 78 Serangoon Road had hosted then Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong and India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi in 2015. The restaurant is listed under the National Heritage Board’s SG Heritage Business Scheme. Both Komala’s and Komala Vilas trace back to Murugiah Rajoo, who founded the original Komala Vilas. While the Indian fast-food hybrid Komala’s came from the Komala Vilas family business, the two chains operate under separate websites, menus and family branches – with Komala Vilas most recently run by Rajoo’s grandson, Rajakumar Gunasekaran, and Komala’s headed by his son, Rajoo Thanasekaran. The 76 to 78 Serangoon Road outlet has been closed for renovations since Jan 19, with no reopening date announced. When ST visited the premises in March, no renovation work was visible. Google Maps now marks the outlet as permanently closed. In October, Ishtara Jewellery secured the former restaurant unit and planned to open a second outlet there during the Deepavali season. Its existing flagship is across the road at 111 Serangoon Road and specialises in 22K gold and diamond jewellery. The planned takeover makes it unlikely that Komala Vilas will return to its former flagship premises.
