events.title: Dubai sees early signs of tourism recovery with October visitor figures
events.summary: Dubai welcomed 1.15 million international overnight visitors in October, its highest monthly total since February, when the Iran war began. Total visitor numbers for the first 10 months of the year reached 9.68 million, the Dubai Department of Economy and Tourism said, attributing the figures to the city's diversified strategy. The city welcomed 15.7 million overnight visitors during the same period last year. “Challenging times are not new to us in Dubai, and through them we have always come together, adapted, learnt and emerged even stronger,” said Issam Kazim, chief executive of Dubai Corporation for Tourism and Commerce Marketing. “The fundamentals that have driven Dubai’s success remain robust, and we are seeing encouraging signs of momentum across our markets.” The Iran war, now in its ninth month, has severely disrupted travel and tourism this year, driving up fuel prices and causing flight delays, cancellations and diversions across the Middle East and beyond. International airlines have been forced to adjust schedules for Middle East flights in the aftermath of the war, which broke out on February 28, as airspace restrictions persist. Dubai International Airport handled 50.4 million passengers in the first nine months of 2026, with traffic down 28.1 per cent year on year. Third-quarter volumes declined 22.1 per cent to 18.8 million passengers, operator Dubai Airports said this month. August was the busiest month of the quarter, with 6.6 million passengers. Airlines have gradually begun to restart flights to the region. This month, British Airways resumed flights between London Heathrow and Dubai after an eight-month suspension caused by the conflict. Lufthansa Group is also due to resume Dubai services on November 25, joining Royal Air Maroc, SunExpress and Cebu Pacific. The Dubai airport expects to welcome more than 70 million passengers this year, Dubai Airports’ chief executive Paul Griffiths said. That is down from 95.2 million passengers last year . DET said public-private partnerships have helped boost tourism in the city. Its recent “A Dubai Invite” initiative, which encouraged residents to invite friends and family, saw more than 73,000 visitors arrive into the city, the authority said. Meanwhile, Dubai Access Club, a new invitation-only tourism membership programme, combines a five-year membership with exclusive destination benefits and a multiple-entry tourist visa, subject to eligibility and visa approval. The initiative aims to encourage repeat visitation, the DET said. The city will also host the 32nd edition of Dubai Shopping Festival from December 4, 2026, to January 17, 2027. Looking ahead, DET said it will continue to work closely with its international network of travel trade, airline and industry partners across key source markets to maintain demand and respond quickly to changing travel patterns.

events.title: Australian inflation hots up in October, core hits two-year high
events.summary: The Reserve Bank of Australia has raised rates by 125 basis points in 2026, more than many other developed economies. Australian inflation rose more than expected in October. Headline CPI hit 4.9% and core inflation reached 3.8%, its fastest pace since 2024. Higher fuel costs drove much of the rise. The Australian Bureau of Statistics said monthly CPI increased 0.5%, above forecasts of 0.4%. The data cooled hopes for early rate cuts. Markets still expect the next move to be down, but the RBA faces a tougher choice as unemployment also rises. SYDNEY – Australian consumer prices climbed by more than expected in October, while core inflation accelerated to its fastest pace since 2024, adding to signs of broad-based price pressures that had markets temper some rate cut enthusiasm. The data sent the Australian dollar up 0.1% to 66.5 US cents, while three-year government bond futures pared earlier gains to be down five ticks at 95.48. Markets are still wagering that the next move in interest rates will be down given weakness in the labour market, but do not fully price a first cut until August. A June cut is now seen as a 75% chance, down from about fully priced before. Data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics on Nov 25 showed its monthly consumer price index rose 0.5% in October from September, above forecasts of 0.4%, as fuel costs jumped 6.3% on higher global oil prices. That took annual inflation to 4.9%, the fastest reading in the short life of the monthly series and well above the central bank’s target band of 2% to 3%. The trimmed mean measure of core inflation, which stripped out fuel costs for the month, increased by 0.5% in the month and pushed the annual pace up to 3.8% from 3.6%, where it had been since June. Luci Ellis, chief economist at Westpac, said there was upside risk to her forecast for fourth-quarter inflation, though she expected October would mark the peak in inflation. “We are still forecasting a negative print for headline CPI (consumer price index) in November because of the large fall in fuel prices. Trimmed mean is expected to moderate next month as well,” she said. “For now, we see nothing to change our view that the RBA (Reserve Bank of Australia) is likely finished hiking rates but will still be considering another move in coming months.” RBA has raised rates by 125 basis points in 2026 , more than many other developed economies, but that has come at the cost of rising unemployment, with the jobless rate hitting a five-year high of 4.9% in September. “We are in for some tough times ahead and the economy is on the knife’s edge with inflation going up and unemployment also rising,” said Russel Chesler, head of investments at VanEck. “The risk is that inflation is becoming truly entrenched into the Australian economy, and how far does the RBA need to go before pushing the economy into a recession.” The report on Nov 25 showed goods inflation jumped 1% in the month, lifting the annual pace to 5.8%, while services inflation was unchanged in October, leaving the annual pace at 4%. New dwelling prices rose 0.8% in October, after a flat September, as home builders in some cities reduced discounts and promotional offers and raised base prices despite reports of subdued demand. “Inflation this persistent may ultimately require policy to become more restrictive before demand cools sufficiently,” said Krishna Bhimavarapu, Asia-Pacific economist at State Street Investment Management. Ramaswami announced his decision on Tuesday and in conversation with The Register said he doesn’t have another job lined up, isn’t sure what he will do next, fancies sitting on boards or advising startups, but will take a break after Nutanix finds its next leader. The CEO moved from VMware to Nutanix in 2020 and characterized his time at the company as writing its “second chapter.” The first, he explained, saw Nutanix focus on hyperconverged infrastructure (HCI) and a limited group of workloads, especially desktop virtualization, while struggling to make a profit. In chapter two, Nutanix redefined HCI as “hybrid cloud infrastructure” by enabling its stack to run on-prem or in public clouds, and by adding support for containers alongside VMs. Ramaswami took credit for stabilizing Nutanix’s finances while leading the expansion of its platform and for keeping net promoter scores high while the company grew. The CEO added that Nutanix’s decision to end its devotion to virtualized storage and start to support external arrays was also part of chapter two. Ramaswami said he hopes to expand the number of storage vendors Nutanix supports beyond Dell, Everpure, and NetApp, until it works with all major array suppliers. Chapter 3, he said, will be making Nutanix an AI platform, “by catering to a whole new set of ecosystems.” Ramaswami told The Register he had been thinking about moving on for some time and raised it with the board in recent weeks. In the letter he wrote to Nutanix staff , the CEO said the company's board has begun the search for a successor and said he will remain at his post until a replacement is found and then “continue to serve as a senior advisor to the company for a period of time.” News of the CEO’s planned departure came on the same day Nutanix announced its Q1 results, which saw 15 percent revenue growth to $772.4 million. The company added 410 customers in the quarter, the slowest growth for several years. Ramaswami said high hardware costs remain “a headwind” for Nutanix, but said the company continues to win customers seeking an alternative to VMware. He also pointed to the largest new customer win for the quarter coming from a financial services outfit that uses Dell external storage, a significant score because two years ago Nutanix could not have competed for that business. Nutanix forecast slightly faster growth for the rest of its financial year, suggesting it is not ready to ride AI’s rocket to riches. Investors knocked about ten percent off the company’s share price in after-hours trading, sending it to around $50, roughly double what it was when Ramaswami took over as CEO, but below $79-plus peaks in late 2025.

events.title: Asian stocks tumble as AI rally fizzles and Trump tariff fears return
events.summary: The region’s chip-heavy markets bore the brunt of the sell-off. Asian stocks fell sharply as fresh US tariff fears returned and the AI rally faded, with South Korea and Taiwan hit hardest. US trade officials are preparing findings from a probe into 16 trading partners, including China and the EU, raising the risk of new tariff measures. Markets also watched US core PCE data and mixed Wall Street trading, while weak AI shares, higher Australian inflation, and falling metals added pressure. TOKYO – Asian stocks tumbled on Nov 25 as fresh US tariff threats hit sentiment and a tech-led rally fizzled, with the region’s chip-heavy markets bearing the brunt of the sell-off. MSCI’s gauge of Asia Pacific equities fell 2.35%, led by a 6.16% slide in South Korea and a 4.8% drop in Taiwan, the region’s two key barometers of the AI trade. Taiwan’s Taiex tumbled 4.8% as AI chipmaker Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co slid 3.59%. Chip designer Mediatek plunged 10%. In South Korea, the Kospi lost 6.16% to 4,697.51 as Samsung Electronics fell 9.87%. SK Hynix declined 10.32%. Japan’s benchmark Nikkei 225 dropped 2.78% to 57,011.62. Shares of OpenAI investor SoftBank Group slumped 14.83%, and semiconductor maker Kioxia plunged 14.18%. In Hong Kong, the Hang Seng fell 1.14% to 21,966.01, while the Shanghai Composite index fell 2.03% to 3,476.47. Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 edged 0.5% lower to 8,683.90. The consumer price index in October rose to 4.9% from a year earlier, topping expectations. That could put pressure on the central bank to raise interest rates. Futures for the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 Index fell 1.4%, pointing to a second straight day of losses for US technology stocks after the underlying gauge rallied from the cusp of a bear market on Nov 23. Contracts for the S&P 500 Index dropped 0.8%, while European equities were set for a tepid open. Risk appetite weakened after media reports the Trump administration was preparing to release findings of a trade investigation that could pave the way for new tariff measures . The US Trade Representative’s (USTR) office is preparing to release the findings of the probe into alleged excess industrial capacity among 16 major US trading partners, including China and the European Union, three people with knowledge of the matter said on Nov 24. “The re-emergence of tariffs from the USTR has been met with a collective sigh from investors,” said Chris Weston, head of research at Pepperstone Group in Melbourne. “Much like the US debt ceiling, which is also making an unwelcome comeback onto the radar, traders appear reluctant to commit significant capital on the headlines alone.” Overnight, stocks on Wall Street were mixed , with the S&P 500 down 0.5% and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite off 1.5%, while the small-cap Russell 2000 gained 0.6% and the Dow Jones Industrial Average rallied 0.9%. “The news of potential new US tariffs is probably mostly baked into market expectations at this point,” said Frederic Neumann, chief Asia economist at HSBC Holdings. “The US administration has been working for a while to replace some of the tariffs struck down by judges earlier (in 2026), and its efforts have been well telegraphed.” Attention now turns to US core PCE (personal consumption expenditure) data due on Nov 25 ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday later in the week. “Wall Street pared its (Nov 23) advance as sobriety returned to the market and a focus returned to fundamentals,” said Kyle Rodda, a senior market analyst at Capital.com in Melbourne. The moves followed data showing US consumer confidence increased by more than expected in November, touching its highest level in nearly two years and better-than-expected earnings from Dell on surging artificial intelligence server demand. The shares rose 4.1% in after-hours trading. Nvidia surrendered some of its gains after Jensen Huang’s return as chief executive earlier this week, falling 5.9%, while Anthropic fell 6.5% to below its initial public offering price. “This is so dizzying day to day,” said Adam Phillips, managing director of portfolio strategy at EP Wealth Advisors, who is not buying the dip in stocks yet. “Nothing has significantly changed from (Nov 23), but we’re not out of the woods yet. There is still a whole lot of fear and uncertainty around the AI trade that needs to be worked through.” Australian shares slid 0.9% and the Australian dollar strengthened 0.2% after the release of data showing consumer prices climbed by more than expected in October as fuel and clothing jumped. The annualised trimmed mean measure of 3.8% means inflation is still running well above target and ramps up pressure on the Reserve Bank of Australia, which has already raised rates by 125 basis points in 2026. In commodities, Brent crude opened 0.5% lower at US$90.97 in Asia after a choppy session on Nov 24, which saw crude prices settle more than 2% higher as new attacks were reported on vessels in and around the Strait of Hormuz.

events.title: Probe finds Chevron knowingly vented huge methane plume over WA's Pilbara
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Regulator says Chevron deliberately vented methane plumes that triggered UN warning Methane plumes were detected by satellite emerging from Chevron's Gorgon project on Barrow Island. ( Supplied: Chevron ) WA's Department of Water and Environmental Regulation says Chevron deliberately vented methane to relieve its carbon capture and storage system at the Gorgon gas project. Environment Minister Matthew Swinbourn found it was not a leak or an "unauthorised emissions source". Critics say the investigation highlights ongoing problems with the gas giant's reliance on CCS technology. Chevron's Gorgon gas project vented massive methane plumes to ease pressure on its troubled carbon capture and storage (CCS) system, investigators say. The finding was prompted by a United Nations alert sent in August, when huge clouds of the greenhouse gas were detected soaring above the $81 billion facility off Western Australia's Pilbara coast. Five consecutive satellite observations between November 2025 and August 2026 estimated methane emissions averaging 4.9 tonnes an hour — nearly five times the reported rate at Gorgon over the past two years. But the WA's Department of Water and Environment Regulation (DWER) says August's emissions event was planned, based on information from Chevron and gathered during a site inspection earlier this month. "DWER concluded that the emissions were associated with venting of reservoir carbon dioxide through approved facility infrastructure during periods where constraints affected operation of the CCS system," Environment Minister Matthew Swinbourn said in a statement. "DWER has found no evidence that the emissions detected on 29 August 2026 were associated with an uncontrolled leak, upset condition, incident, or unauthorised emissions source." Matthew Swinbourn says the emissions were part of the venting of reservoir carbon dioxide. ( ABC News: Lauren Smith ) Mr Swinbourn told a parliamentary committee today that Gorgon's licence may be amended to more closely scrutinise methane. WA regulator actively investigating methane cloud at Chevron The WA government has confirmed it is now investigated the repeated large methane emissions from Chevron's Gorgon gas complex. Located on Barrow Island, about 60 kilometres from the West Australian mainland, the Gorgon complex remains the country's most expensive resources venture. A Chevron spokesperson told the ABC the company had worked "constructively" with DWER and was committed to responsibly managing its emissions, including methane. "Gorgon operates within some of Australia's most rigorous environmental and regulatory frameworks, with extensive requirements governing how emissions are managed, monitored and reported," the spokesperson said. Whistleblower: Emissions 'deliberate' In claims tabled by WA Greens MLC Sophie McNeill before state parliament overnight, a whistleblower working on Barrow Island accused Chevron of "deliberately releasing" the methane rather than slowing down production. The three-point statement made to Ms McNeill reiterated that the emissions had not been a leak and blamed Chevron's CCS. Reporting by Chevron shows its production of liquefied natural gas (LNG) at Gorgon has regularly outstripped its stated 15.6 million tonne per annum design capacity. According to the multinational's own compliance reports to DWER, it has surpassed 15.6 million tonnes by close to 8 per cent each year since 2021. Sophie McNeill tabled the whistleblower statement in parliament. ( ABC News: Courtney Withers ) Global LNG prices sit near multi-year highs following attacks on Qatari suppliers and shipping disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz. Ms McNeill said the emissions amounted to a violation of Gorgon's environmental approvals, which stipulated the project maintain a "no routine venting or flaring policy" except where normal operations were unavailable. The revelations coincide with new data calculating the shortfalls of Gorgon's CCS. Chevron and its joint venture partners are obligated to sequester 80 per cent of the carbon dioxide (CO2) released by Gorgon's particularly carbon-rich gas fields. But engineering issues ensured the CCS system did not operate for the first three years of gas exports, and it has lagged behind the 80 per cent benchmark in the time since. Technicians working on Gorgon's CCS system. events.title: Huang way or another? What leadership succession looks like at Nvidia's peers
events.summary: The Jensen Huang saga took another turn this week, with Nvidia's board surprisingly reinstating its chief executive . That ended an 11-day whirlwind that triggered national security fears and a stock market rout. One issue the drama magnified was the artificial intelligence company's lack of a succession plan. Chief financial officer Colette Kress was named interim chief, but that was more of a stopgap and, as the title implied, temporary. That exposed a weak link in Nvidia's leadership chain, in contrast to some of its peers, which at least have a plan, follow tradition or are experimenting with how they are run. Oracle After 37 years as chief executive, Oracle founder Larry Ellison stepped down in 2014 and the company adopted a co-chief executive model. Mark Hurd and Safra Catz shared the role until Mr Hurd's death in 2019, which left Ms Catz running the company alone until 2025. Clay Magouyrk and Mike Sicilia now lead it. Mr Ellison remains Oracle's chairman and chief technology officer, while Ms Catz has become executive vice chair of the board. The unusual structure, an "experiment", creates ambiguity over who is truly in charge, Fortune noted in 2025. Alphabet Sundar Pichai became chief executive of Google in 2015 and of its parent Alphabet in 2019, succeeding co-founder Larry Page both times. Mr Pichai was reportedly chosen for his leadership and product savvy. Those qualities also drew interest from Microsoft in 2014, before it picked Satya Nadella, and from what was then Twitter, albeit for a less senior role. Alphabet has no public succession plan. Names that stand out include president and chief investment officer Ruth Porat and Google Cloud chief Thomas Kurian . Given AI's influence today, Google DeepMind leaders Demis Hassabis and Koray Kavukcuoglu could also be in the running. Meta Platforms The Facebook parent has no public succession plan. Founder Mark Zuckerberg, who is also chief executive and chairman, has given no sign of when he might retire or who might succeed him. He is only 42 and the youngest person in the top 20 of the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. His top team includes president Dina Powell McCormick and senior executives Joel Kaplan, Susan Li, Javier Olivan, Chris Cox and Andrew Bosworth. Meanwhile, the stock of chief AI officer Alexandr Wang, 29, has risen. Mr Zuckerberg reportedly trusts him to lead the company's AI ambitions and turnaround. Meta may not have a succession plan for Mr Zuckerberg, but Mr Wang could be an example of the company "already creating the conditions for people to speculate about one", said Inna Kuts, founder of Dublin-based executive branding advisory IKCCG. "Mr Wang has capital, organisational authority, direct access to Mr Zuckerberg and responsibility for one of Meta’s most consequential strategic priorities. That is how potential successors often become visible long before anyone uses the word 'succession'." Samsung In South Korea, chaebols are the norm. These are sprawling family-controlled conglomerates, and the word literally means "wealth clan". The Lee family has controlled Samsung Group for 88 years. Its current chairman, Lee Jae-yong, is the son and successor of Lee Kun-hee, who in turn took over from his father, Samsung founder Lee Byung-chul. In 2016, however, Lee Jae-yong was implicated in a corruption, bribery and embezzlement scandal. His father had been incapacitated by a heart attack in 2014, and the case cast serious doubt on the son's expected rise to the top. (His father had legal troubles of his own, which led him to leave the company and later return.) In 2017, Mr Lee was convicted and jailed for his role in the scandal, which also led to the impeachment and conviction of then-president Park Geun-hye. He was paroled in 2021, pardoned in 2022 and named executive chairman that October. Even so, Mr Lee said in 2020 that he did not plan to hand control of the company to his children. It is unclear whether that was down to recent history, political pressure or a genuine attempt to break with chaebol tradition. Separately, Samsung was reported last month to have expanded an affiliate system that draws up shortlists of candidates for chief executive roles across its business units. Apple Apple is arguably the most straightforward case on this list. Since co-founder Steve Jobs returned in 1997, it has changed leaders twice: when Mr Jobs resigned shortly before his death in 2011, and when Tim Cook stepped down this September. Both times, the iPhone maker picked a chief executive who could steer it through a transformational phase in step with the industry. Mr Cook, then Apple's operations chief, had built one of technology's most robust supply chains. Hardware maven John Ternus is expected to strike the right balance in the age of AI. Apple had a strong list of contenders, including Craig Federighi, Greg Joswiak, Eddy Cue and Deirdre O'Brien , and its choice of the low-profile Mr Ternus shows how deep its bench is. Lesson for Nvidia Not having a succession plan at the biggest and most influential companies could prove costly. Having one in place reassures investors and supports business continuity. Nvidia may have learnt this the hard way, especially as Mr Huang's departure was bigger than a succession story, said Mazen Hayek, a Dubai-based media consultant. "It is a stress test of corporate governance, US national security policy, global semiconductor supply chains and the balance of power in the AI race," he told The National . Investors would welcome clearer information about succession plans. Now that Nvidia has seen the risk up close, it should be able to prepare for Mr Huang stepping down again, for whatever reason. "The board’s real test is succession. Those are governance questions because the answers determine what the board can do when it has to make a difficult decision," said Mohammad Fheili, a risk strategist and executive in residence at the American University of Beirut. "Directors who have prepared for a handover can judge a chief executive's conduct on its merits and act on that judgment."

events.title: Japan’s key services inflation gauge hits 36-year high
events.summary: The bank’s Governor Kazuo Ueda has signalled the bank’s readiness to keep raising rates to prevent inflation from deviating above its 2% target. Japan’s services inflation rose 4.2% in October, the fastest since 1990, showing wider price pressure and strengthening the case for a near-term Bank of Japan rate hike. The increase was driven by higher ocean freight, leasing and hotel costs, while the Bank of Japan watches for signs firms are passing on labour costs. Wholesale inflation also stayed high at 7.1% in October. Governor Kazuo Ueda has signalled more rises, and Reuters polls expect a hike in December. TOKYO – A key gauge of Japan’s service-sector inflation jumped 4.2% in October for the fastest annual pace since 1990, data showed on Nov 25 , a sign of broadening price pressures that bolster the case for a near-term interest rate hike by the central bank. The year-on-year rise in the services producer price index, which tracks the prices companies charge each other for services, followed a revised gain of 3.8% in September, data from the Bank of Japan (BOJ) showed. The increase was driven largely by rising costs of ocean freight transport, leasing and higher hotel charges, the data showed. The data is closely watched by the bank for clues to what extent companies are passing on rising labour costs to service-related prices. An index measuring services prices in labour-intensive sectors rose 2.7% in October from a year earlier, accelerating slightly from a 2.6% gain in September , the data showed . “Firms continue to pass on rising labour costs,” though the pace of price rises in labour-intensive sectors is slower than those for overall services prices, said Kenichiro Ahara, an economist at Dai-ichi Life Research Institute. “We need to scrutinise whether the pass-through of labour costs continues in a wide range of sectors, and leads to sustained rises in services prices,” he said. Mounting inflationary pressure for services would add to a steady increase in goods prices. Annual wholesale inflation rose 7.1% in the year to October, data showed in November , as the Middle East conflict and AI-related demand kept pushing up prices for fuel and semiconductor chips. The BOJ raised its policy rate to 1.25% in September after a June hike, for a shorter interval than the roughly twice-a-year hikes of 2024 and 2025. The bank’s Governor Kazuo Ueda has signalled its readiness to keep raising rates to prevent inflation from deviating above its 2% target. A majority of analysts polled by Reuters expect the BOJ to raise rates in December and follow up with another hike by end-March. Many see the terminal rate at around 1.75% or 2% . REUTERS

events.title: Seatrium shares sink more than 7% after group announces job cuts
events.summary: This is Seatrium’s first workforce restructuring exercise since its formation via the merger of Sembcorp Marine and Keppel Offshore & Marine in 2023. Seatrium shares fell more than 7% after it said it will cut about 220 jobs in Singapore, or 2% of staff, as it streamlines global operations. The offshore, marine and energy group is changing systems and processes to fit future needs, and speeding up yard use in Singapore, where it has five yards. Seatrium has cut its global yards from 15 in 2023 to 11 now. Admiralty will be returned to the Government in 2028, while other yards will focus on higher-value work. SINGAPORE – Shares of Seatrium extended their losses on Nov 25, a day after the offshore, marine and energy group announced that it would lay off 2% of its employees in Singapore. The counter fell as much as 7.75%, or 11 cents, to $1.31 in morning trading, before paring some losses to close at $1.36. Nearly 45 million shares changed hands. This followed a 7.19% decline on Nov 24, when the counter closed at $1.42, with about 55 million shares changing hands. OCBC equity analyst Rachel Miu said that the sell-off was driven by concerns over Seatrium’s order book, compounded by its workforce and yard restructuring announcement, which the market interpreted as a sign of weaker demand rather than a move to improve operational efficiency. However , Seatrium had secured a contract from Japanese offshore engineering firm Modec in November to integrate a floating production, storage and offloading vessel for a project in Guyana, South America. This was a positive signal for Seatrium’s project pipeline, although the contract value was not disclosed, she said, adding that it followed the announcement of two new projects worth a combined $700 million in October. Seatrium announced on Nov 24 that it would cut its workforce here by about 220 people as part of a broader effort to streamline its global operations and consolidate its network of yards. This comes as the Singapore-listed group transforms its systems and processes in line with future business needs, which include speeding up the optimisation of facilities in Singapore, where it has five yards. Globally, Seatrium has pared its yards from 15 in 2023 to 11 currently. It has progressively scaled down its yard in Admiralty and will return it to the Singapore Government as planned in 2028. Its yard in Tuas Boulevard will remain its flagship, while the other three in Benoi, Pioneer and Tuas will be refocused on work that supports the group’s global projects, such as higher-value repairs and upgrades. Its global headcount in August 2025 stood at about 24,000.

events.title: Pentagon eyes GM for drone production: WSJ
events.summary: The Pentagon is in discussions with General Motors to turn over some of its auto assembly lines for the mass production of drones , The Wall Street Journal reported, as Washington reckons with persistent munitions shortfalls amid the nine-month conflict with Iran. Even as the US downplays the shortages , it is increasingly turning to automakers — who offer proven industrial supply chains and manufacturing capacity — in efforts to ramp up production of cheaper weapons systems to counter Iran’s mass-produced drones . US efforts echo those of Europe, where lucrative government contracts promise to compensate automakers pressured by Chinese imports: Germany’s Rheinmetall recently converted two auto factories to build ammunition, mirroring similar initiatives in France and Slovakia . — Brendan Ruberry

events.title: Inconsistent laws fuelling assistance dog discrimination, report finds
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Assistance dog refusals and discrimination fuelled by inconsistent laws, report finds Navigating public spaces was difficult and stressful for Ollie Andrews before he got his assistance dog Orla. ( Supplied: Ollie Andrews ) A new report has found the absence of a national definition for what constitutes an assistance dog is fuelling discrimination and undermining their legitimacy. It also found fragmented provider and training standards are contributing to access refusals. Several solutions have been proposed to bolster community trust and educate the public. Ollie Andrews's assistance dog Orla provides the army veteran with support and independence. But she also makes him the target of "infuriating" discrimination in places like an outback cafe they tried to visit recently on a trip to South Australia. "The owner basically said we weren't welcome to stay inside the cafe with her because he didn't want to set a precedent for all his customers that had farm dogs," Mr Andrews said. "I showed him all the documentation that we have, an ID card that has my photo on there, her photo and South Australian legislation on the back of it, but he still wasn't having a bar of it." Ollie Andrews went to great lengths to make sure Orla was properly trained and accredited. ( Supplied: Ollie Andrews ) Getting Orla legally recognised as an assistance animal was a rigorous process that included a medical assessment, getting her properly trained, and then accredited through Assistance Dogs International (ADI). "She can sense if I'm getting nervous. She'll come up and she'll like nudge my thigh with her nose and make eye contact with me. That forces me to stop, slow down, think about what I have to do and she'll keep doing that … until I'm a bit calmer," Mr Andrews said. Thousands of Australians use assistance dogs but there is widespread confusion about the critical role they play. A new report, prepared by research firm Mandala for ADI, has found there is broad scepticism about the use of assistance dogs because there is no national definition of what they are and no requirement for formal accreditation. "[The inconsistency] makes it harder for businesses to understand their legal obligations relating to assistance animals," the report said. "It makes it harder to enforce these obligations to uphold the rights of handlers. And it makes it harder to build public trust in the assistance dog system." 'If they can take a drunk, they can take a guide dog' The ABC has recently heard hundreds of stories from Australians with disability about their experiences with transport across the country. Advocates say systems are failing them. While it is illegal to refuse service to someone with an assistance animal, such incidents are frequent, particularly during taxi and rideshare trips , air travel, and in hospitality venues . Fifty-eight per cent of assistance dog handlers in Australia experienced an access refusal in the past year, according to the report, and almost 60 per cent said they considered avoiding public places altogether, compared with 40 per cent globally. Anyone can train an animal to be a companion, but the process of having it legally considered an assistance animal is different depending on where people live. Some systems require medical checks for handlers, and while some bodies issue their registered animals with ID cards, others do not. The federal Disability Discrimination Act contains three different definitions and state-based legislation also varies. Some states define assistance animals or dogs, while Tasmania only defines a guide dog. States also apply different standards for providers, meaning an assistance dog accredited in one state may not be recognised in another. The report found at least 1,000 dogs were placed with Australians with disability in 2025, but only about 25 per cent came from providers accredited by ADI or the International Guide Dog Federation, which ensures training reflects established global best practice. The remaining 75 per cent, about three in four of all assistance dogs placed in 2025, were trained by other organisations "to varying and often unknown standards". That did not mean those dogs were poorly trained, but it was difficult to immediately verify the level of training they had, the report said. "A handler may have a dog that's had some training, but a venue owner or driver has no way of knowing that," Mandala partner Tom McMahon said. Issue to persist without change, advocates say Ashley De Silva, CEO of Guide Dogs New South Wales/ACT, said handlers should not have to "prove over and over again that [they] belong".

events.title: Foxconn faces India insolvency lawsuit over unpaid vendor dues
events.summary: Vendors in India often initiate insolvency proceedings to recover overdue payments, though these filings rarely push a company into bankruptcy. Foxconn’s India unit faces an insolvency lawsuit from BCD Emprasa over unpaid rent and utilities, with the company claiming “grave financial prejudice” and “substantial commercial harm”. About half a dozen vendors say Foxconn has delayed payments for months, and at least four others are still waiting for dues from work on the Bengaluru facility. The dispute is unlikely to derail Foxconn’s India growth plans, but it adds pressure as it competes with Tata Electronics for a bigger role in Apple’s supply chain. About half a dozen vendors in India are experiencing payment delays by Foxconn Technology Group’s local unit, said sources familiar with the matter, with one even filing an insolvency lawsuit to recover US$15 million (S$19.3 million) in unpaid dues. BCD Emprasa, which leased dormitory housing in southern India for the Foxconn unit’s employees at the Bengaluru facility, has alleged that it did not receive payment for rent and utilities in an Aug 12 petition to the National Company Law Tribunal’s (NCLT) Chennai bench. The company is seeking about 1.43 billion rupees (S$19.8 million) for past dues along with interest, service charges and damages as at July 8 from Foxconn Hon Hai Technology India Mega Development, according to the filing, which was seen by Bloomberg News. While the dispute is not expected to derail Foxconn’s growth plans in India, it adds to the challenges facing the iPhone assembler as it competes with Tata Electronics for a bigger role in Apple’s supply chain. Bloomberg News reported in 2025 that Foxconn recalled hundreds of Chinese workers from India – though the reason was not clear at the time – in a move that saw the company bring in staff from Taiwan and Vietnam to minimise the impact on production. Foxconn did not reply to e-mailed queries seeking comments on BCD’s lawsuit in India. “These defaults have caused grave financial prejudice and substantial commercial harm to the company,” BCD said in an e-mailed response, adding that the matter was sub judice before NCLT. At least four vendors other than BCD have been waiting for several months to over a year for Foxconn to clear their dues, said sources familiar with the matter, who asked not to be identified discussing private information. Several were hired for construction-related work on the Bengaluru facility and were working with Foxconn for the first time. Under an April 2024 agreement with BCD, Foxconn leased 700 residential units for female employees, with rent payable regardless of occupancy and a lock-in through July 2026, according to the NCLT filing. Foxconn defaulted on an invoice due in May 2025, it said. The electronics giant also did not agree to appointing an arbitrator. Departures of some non-Indian staff have slowed payments to local contractors, the people said. BLOOMBERG

events.title: Beyond the bottom line: What financial results reveal and conceal about true value
events.summary: A market that aspires towards better value creation must also aspire towards better value recognition. Singapore is backing market revival with the $6.5 billion Equity Market Development Programme and $30 million Value Unlock Programme, but it must also reward real value creation. Headline profits can mislead. Singtel’s reported NPAT fell 72 per cent to $818 million, but underlying NPAT rose 21 per cent to $831 million after last year’s one-off gains. Investors should look beyond reported profit to recurring earnings, cash flow and capital use. Exceptional items, IFRS 18 and AI help, but judgment still matters. SINGAPORE – S ingapore is investing considerable resources in revitalising its equity market. Improving liquidity, attracting capital and encouraging quality listings are essential. Yet, a more fundamental challenge remains: ensuring that the market recognises and rewards genuine corporate value creation. Reflecting this ambition are the $6.5 billion Equity Market Development Programme and $30 million Value Unlock Programme – both government-backed initiatives spearheaded by the Republic’s financial regulators. Singapore-headquartered multinational corporations like Keppel, Sembcorp Industries and Singtel have pursued strategic transformation and capital recycling to unlock shareholder value. Smaller companies are also exploring new avenues, including Addvalue Technologies’ proposed spin-off of its space connectivity business for a US listing. Yet, corporate transformation is only part of the equation. Whether retail investors can recognise genuine value creation is equally important. Uneven independent research coverage, particularly among small and mid-cap companies, can leave potentially undervalued businesses underappreciated. Every results season, corporate performance is distilled into headlines: profits surged; earnings halved. While accurate, such figures rarely tell the whole story. International Financial Reporting Standard 18 (IFRS 18) – issued by the International Accounting Standards Board and effective from January 2027 – is designed to make financial statements more transparent, including by requiring companies to disclose management-defined performance measures. Meanwhile, artificial intelligence is accelerating financial analysis. Yet, better disclosure and faster analysis do not guarantee better decisions. Technology can accelerate analysis, but it cannot substitute for sound investment judgment. Accounting truth is not operating truth Reported net profit after tax (NPAT) captures profits from recurring operations, asset disposals, impairments and fair-value movements. An asset disposal may boost reported profits without improving recurring earnings. Conversely, an impairment may depress reported earnings even when the underlying business remains resilient. Investors must distinguish between what a company has earned and what it can reasonably be expected to earn again. The income statement records what happened. The investor must determine what is repeatable. Understanding the story behind the numbers Singtel’s first-quarter results for financial year 2027 – for the three months ended June 30, 2026 – illustrate this distinction. Reported NPAT fell 72% to $818 million. The headline suggested a sharp deterioration in performance. Yet, underlying NPAT rose 21% to $831 million, reflecting a stronger operating performance. The divergence was largely attributable to exceptional gains of $2.2 billion recognised a year earlier, arising from a partial stake sale in Airtel and the Intouch-Gulf Energy merger. Following the results announcement on Aug 13, Singtel shares initially fell 0.9%, before rebounding 4.7% the following day. While market movements reflect multiple factors, the reversal illustrates why investors should look beyond headline earnings to understand the underlying business. The lesson extends beyond Singtel. Companies have a responsibility to communicate their performance transparently. Investors, analysts and the media have an equally important role in interpreting the numbers with discernment. Financial reporting provides the information. Sound judgment determines its meaning. Exceptional does not mean irrelevant Exceptional items are often excluded from underlying earnings because they do not reflect a company’s recurring operations. Yet, they can reveal whether past investments and asset disposals have created or eroded shareholder value. Suppose a company acquires a business for $1 billion and subsequently recognises a $500 million impairment. Excluding that impairment may be appropriate when assessing recurring earnings. But the write-down raises legitimate questions about the original investment decision and the returns shareholders can reasonably expect. Conversely, an asset sale may generate a non-recurring gain while unlocking economic value, particularly when it releases capital for more productive uses.

events.title: Saudi crown prince will come to US for G20 summit
events.summary: Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman is planning to travel to the United States in December for the G20 Leaders’ Summit, a US official confirmed to Semafor, a trip that would be his first to the US since the outbreak of the Iran war. The summit, which US President Donald Trump will host on December 14-15 at his Trump National Doral resort in Miami, is expected to bring together leaders from the world’s major economies. MBS’ potential attendance is particularly notable given his limited international travel since the war began. The crown prince also skipped the 2024 and 2025 editions of the summit. If he attends, the gathering could provide an opportunity for Trump and MBS to meet in person for the first time since the outbreak of the conflict. Saudi Arabia has been pressing Washington for assistance in countering Yemen’s Houthis and strengthening the kingdom’s defenses. A face-to-face meeting could provide a forum to discuss those security concerns, particularly given the close relationship between Trump and the Saudi crown prince. The Saudi government did not respond to a request for comment. MBS’ last trip to the US, in November 2025, featured an elaborate White House reception and a series of high-profile announcements, with Washington and Riyadh pledging hundreds of billions of dollars in commercial agreements and investment commitments.

HPE went first, on Monday, when CEO Antonio Neri declared “We are now a fundamentally different company” after acquiring Juniper Networks and creating products “built to capitalize on the next phase of AI.” On Tuesday, Dell’s chief operating officer and vice chairman Jeff Clarke declared “We are now a different company” because the Infrastructure Solutions Group (ISG) has become the source of “the vast majority of our profit and growth.” HPE’s claim to having changed is perhaps more credible on the face of it, given that its acquisition of Juniper means it has become more of a networking player. Dell hasn’t made significant additions to its hardware portfolio, but there’s a big difference in its sources of revenue, which three years ago was just about evenly split between its infrastructure and client devices. In its Tuesday announcement, Dell revealed ISG revenue grew 198 percent year over year to $42 billion, while CSG racked up three percent growth to $12.9 billion – meaning Dell is now predominantly an infrastructure company. Clarke said he’s seen some companies deferring their PC purchases to buy AI hardware instead, and said Dell is re-assigning parts it ordered to build PCs and using them for servers instead. Dell exited its Q3 with a backlog of $32 billion worth of AI servers and is clearly aware that investors might worry that’s not a useful metric because some buyers’ dreams of operating neoclouds have struck financial or regulatory barriers. Clarke assured investors that Dell is “highly selective about the partners we work with” “Every AI order is vetted for access to capital, end customer quality, trade and export compliance, and access to land and power.” HPE also has wrinkles in its AI business, because buyers won’t stand for fat margins and that’s dented the company’s profits a little. Neri was able to point to AI-related revenue also rising sharply, up 68.6 percent year over year to $11.3 billion, while overall revenue climbed 50 percent to reach $14.5 billion. Networking grew at a more relaxed 12 percent. The CEO said HPE expects better growth ahead, because new server purchases create demand for networks and storage. He also pointed to HPE having the opportunity to sell its networking kit to other OEMs who build AMD’s Helios rack-scale systems. events.title: Inflation rises more than expected in 'RBA's worst nightmare'
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Inflation rises more than expected to 4.9pc in year to October The Reserve Bank forecasts inflation to remain outside of its target band for another year. ( ABC Pilbara: Cody Fenner ) The consumer price index lifted more than forecast in October, with inflation and unemployment now above the Reserve Bank's forecasts. Housing was the largest contributor to annual inflation, driven by electricity and new dwelling prices, as builders passed on higher costs. The RBA board next meets in just under a fortnight's time, with its interest rates decision to be handed down on December 8. Inflation has come in hotter than expected in October, leaving Australia grappling with accelerating price rises and increasing unemployment. The consumer price index rose half a per cent in October, in original terms, with the annual rate of inflation lifting to 4.9 per cent, the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) said. It's the highest headline inflation rate in three years. The trimmed mean, a measure of underlying inflation, also picked up pace, rising 3.8 per cent over the year. Economists had expected it to remain steady at 3.6 per cent, which would have still been above the Reserve Bank's target of 2-3 per cent. Rising inflation, unemployment 'RBA's worst nightmare' The RBA had forecast headline inflation to remain elevated for another year, before easing to 2.7 per cent by the end of 2027. However, headline inflation, underlying inflation and unemployment are now all above where the central bank had forecast them to sit at the end of 2026. "Rising inflation and unemployment are the RBA's worst nightmare," Oxford Economics head of economic research Harry Murphy Cruise said. "Both are at odds with its dual mandate of price stability and full employment, but they require opposing policy responses. Taming inflation requires higher rates, but that comes at the expense of employment." Betashares chief economist David Bassanese said the higher-than-expected underlying inflation result highlighted the "tough challenge" facing the economy. "Although economic growth has slowed, the inflation dragon has not yet been slain," Mr Bassanese wrote. Mr Bassanese, who has been forecasting a February rate hike, said it "remain[ed] on the table". "Overall, while the economy is showing signs of slowing, the risk is that it has not slowed enough. If the RBA moves rates in 2027, the risk remains tilted towards a hike." Oxford Economics has maintained its view that rates will remain on hold in December and through 2027. Economists at UBS, on the other hand, still expect the RBA to cut interest rates in August 2027. While they saw the high inflation numbers as raising the risk of an extra rate hike in February, they noted that the split in the central bank board, with "dovish external board members" arguing for rates to remain on hold, would likely mean no hike. AMP economists Diana Mousina and My Bui said the October inflation would likely lead to concerns about a stagflation environment in 2027. Stagflation, where high inflation collides with stagnating economic growth and rising unemployment , would put the RBA in a difficult position, they noted. What contributed to rising inflation in October? The data reflected the continuing cost-of-living pressures facing households, with the cost of essentials rising. Non-discretionary prices were up 6.1 per cent over the year, compared to 3.2 per cent for discretionary. "Since it's hard for households to reduce their spending on non-discretionary goods and services, households cannot mitigate the impact of this latest round of high inflation," Indeed economist Callam Pickering said. Housing was the largest contributor to annual inflation in October, the ABS said. Housing prices rose 6.4 per cent, compared to a rise of 5.2 per cent in the 12 months to September. The economist behind a famous recession indicator says Australia should be wary of rising unemployment. Electricity, which is classified as a housing cost, rose 25.2 per cent over the year to October. "The rise in electricity reflects Commonwealth government rebates, which reduced household electricity costs last year but are no longer in place," ABS head of price statistics Rachael McCririck said. New dwelling prices also increased in pace, up 5.1 per cent annually, driven by builders passing on higher costs for materials and labour. "Builders were reported to be giving less discounts or promotional offers, despite subdued demand," AMP economists noted. New dwelling prices rose as builders passed on higher costs.

events.title: Yale’s Sonnenfeld: Nvidia is a ‘detriment’ to US industrial might — not a champion
events.summary: Investors cheered Jensen Huang’s return as Nvidia’s CEO on Monday, but renowned business academic Jeffrey Sonnenfeld of Yale thinks they’re celebrating a mistake. He sees a company that is largely responsible for putting sophisticated technology in the hands of the country’s adversaries, at a moment when the risks couldn’t be higher . Far from a champion of American industry, he says, Nvidia is “a detriment to U.S. global industrial might.” As evidence, Sonnenfeld points to research suggesting Nvidia’s most advanced chips have reached China despite U.S. export controls and to sinking shares of Anthropic, which he links to the realization that China’s seemingly miraculous open source AI models are, in a sense, copies of top U.S. labs’ work, even as Nvidia has insisted that smuggling is a “non-factor.” Indeed, Huang’s return was greeted with just as much enthusiasm in Asia, The Washington Post reported. “The king is back!” read one headline from China’s state-affiliated Star Market Daily. The reinstatement itself followed heavy pressure from Washington. Nvidia’s chairman had effectively ruled out Huang’s return just last week. Then, in a torrent of private weekend calls led by Vice President JD Vance, top administration officials leaned on the board to welcome Huang back, with President Trump calling the board directly to vouch for him. “ I made the deal ,” Trump told CNBC on Monday. Sonnenfeld says the directors who went along, and who returned Huang to the board even as it investigates whether foreign intelligence efforts targeted him, now face a “historic level of individual liability.” The legal deluge has already begun. As we noted a couple of weeks ago , a potential class-action lawsuit was filed almost immediately. Days later, a shareholder derivative suit followed. Filed on Nvidia’s behalf against the directors themselves, the suit alleges the board ignored red flags about Huang’s relationship with suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang. The class action is very much aimed at making Nvidia and Huang compensate investors for their losses, while the derivative suit puts the directors’ own behavior on trial, with any recovery going to Nvidia. Three more suits followed on November 18, the day after Nvidia’s most recent earnings call; all five were filed in Northern California, where Nvidia is based. Huang and Nvidia are also juggling a Justice Department antitrust investigation, a reported SEC probe into Nvidia’s accounting, a possible FBI review, a California subpoena , an export-control case that landed partner Megaspeed on the U.S. trade blacklist on Monday, and congressional inquiries, including a Senate Banking hearing next week at which Huang has agreed to testify. Here’s more of what Sonnenfeld had to say, in a Q&A that’s been edited for length and clarity. So much has happened since we last talked . Huang was ousted, he’s come back. Do you think the board’s reliance on government assurances here is defensible or an abdication of its own duties? They failed to rely on experts. That’s one of the reasons this board is going to be sued and lose, and these directors are likely to face a historic level of individual liability. They have a very inadequate directors and officers liability policy . They have also just failed in their diligence. They hired the Wachtell [law] firm. The Wachtell firm barely got off the blocks to do an investigation. And then they have already reversed themselves, so they didn’t use the expertise needed. It’s wild that they also put Huang right back on the board of directors. The board showed, in addition to incompetence and collaboration, just cowardice in their capitulation because Trump has nothing to wave over them. If this was SpaceX, where 46% of its business comes from the government [you could maybe see the case for Trump’s involvement]. For Nvidia, it’s not even 1% of its business that comes from the U.S. government, so [the board] didn’t have that threat. [Trump] can call off [federal] investigations, but he can’t call off the shareholder litigation. Some are already filed, and the estimates are there’ll probably be 30 of them, and they’re going to be extremely costly. And this is not, by the way, just a blue or red state issue. We already have 14 GOP senators who’ve already come out against this, and very prominent conservatives, like Pete Ricketts and Josh Hawley and Tom Cotton and John Cornyn. Those are some issues that may help explain why Nvidia’s stock is tumbling today. Might the board say, “We saw the classified intelligence findings, and they assure us Jensen will be absolved of wrongdoing”? They haven’t seen those findings, and we also haven’t seen what will be the result of the Senate Intelligence Committee, the Senate Special Committee on Investigations, the Senate Banking Committee, and all their House counterparts. The board hasn’t seen any of that, and even if they saw it, which they have not yet, that still wouldn’t matter.

events.title: Trump reportedly says pardoning Jensen Huang is ‘an option’
events.summary: During an interview with the New York Post on Tuesday, President Trump said that pardoning Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who has been ensnared in a scandal involving an alleged Chinese spy, is “an option,” albeit one that he doesn’t think he will have to exercise. “It’s always an option, I guess, but I don’t think it’ll be necessary,” the president reportedly told the outlet . Huang, who was ousted from his own company less than two weeks ago, was reinstated Monday. He faces ongoing questions about his relationship with Alice Huang, an executive with alleged ties to Chinese intelligence who previously worked for a company that has been accused of illegally diverting Nvidia chips to China. Huang is scheduled to testify at a public Senate Banking Committee hearing next week. When asked about the hearing, Trump reportedly said: “I think I want him to just tell the truth, and I mean, his lawyers are going to have to advise him, but I’ve always found him to be 100% aboveboard, and you know a very smart person.” At another point in the interview, when asked what he knew about Huang’s other extramarital affairs, Trump reportedly said: “I really didn’t get into that. I got into the business of chips, much more than the business of sex.” TechCrunch has reached out to the White House for comment. events.summary: The BIS supports central banks' pursuit of monetary and financial stability through international cooperation. Our authors publish economic analysis and research on monetary and financial stability issues. The BIS hosts committees engaged in standard setting & the pursuit of financial stability through the Basel Process. Access our statistics in the BIS Data Portal Ethics & conduct, risk management & internal audit Consultative Council for the Americas Historical monetary & financial statistics Regulatory Consistency Assessment Programme (RCAP) Countercyclical capital buffer (CCyB) Global systemically important banks (G-SIB) Basel Committee provides additional information regarding the 2026 G-SIB assessment. Further details include global denominators and individual bank indicators. The release accompanies the Financial Stability Board's updated G-SIB list. The Basel Committee on Banking Supervision today published further information related to its 2026 assessment of global systemically important banks (G-SIBs), with additional details to improve understanding of the scoring methodology. The publication accompanies the Financial Stability Board's release of the updated list of G-SIBs and includes: The denominators of the high-level indicators used to calculate banks' scores. The high-level indicators for each bank in the sample used to calculate these denominators. The cut-off score used to identify the G-SIBs in the updated list and the thresholds used to allocate G-SIBs to buckets for calculating the higher loss-absorbency requirements. The Committee's methodology assesses the systemic importance of global banks using indicators calculated from data for the previous fiscal year-end (2025) supplied by banks and validated by national authorities. The final scores are mapped to corresponding buckets that determine the higher loss-absorbency requirement for each G-SIB. The Basel Committee's G-SIB interactive dashboard has been updated to reflect the latest results. The Basel Committee is the primary global standard setter for the prudential regulation of banks and provides a forum for cooperation on banking supervisory matters. Its mandate is to strengthen the regulation, supervision and practices of banks worldwide with the purpose of enhancing financial stability. The Committee reports to the Group of Central Bank Governors and Heads of Supervision and seeks its endorsement for major decisions. The Committee has no formal supranational authority, and its decisions have no legal force. Rather, the Committee relies on its members’ commitments to achieve its mandate. The Group of Central Bank Governors and Heads of Supervision is chaired by Tiff Macklem, Governor of the Bank of Canada. The Basel Committee is chaired by Erik Thedéen, Governor of Sveriges Riksbank.

events.title: Shein to pay $100 million to settle US shipping, customer service claims
events.summary: Shein was known for selling US$5 dresses and US$10 jeans, but it has been forced to raise its prices as the US and then Europe closed customs duty loopholes. Shein will pay US$100 million (S$128 million) to settle FTC claims it misled US shoppers on shipping times, product reviews and cotton origin. The FTC said customers got late or missing orders. The company agreed not to misstate delivery times or block negative reviews. Shein said it did not admit liability and would improve consumer and compliance practices. The FTC also challenged Shein’s supply chain and “evoluSHEIN” claims. The funds will reimburse customers, while Shein faces wider scrutiny over Xinjiang cotton concerns. Chinese fast-fashion giant Shein will pay US$100 million (S$128 million) to settle with the US Federal Trade Commission (FTC) over claims it misled consumers on shipping times, product reviews and the origin of cotton in some of its goods, according to court documents filed on Nov 24 . Despite marketing fast shipping, Shein knew customers were receiving packages days or months late and, in some instances, not at all, the FTC said in its complaint. The company makes up around half of fast-fashion sales in the US, the agency said. A Shein spokesperson said the company had not admitted liability and that it disagreed with some of the FTC’s claims. Shein agreed to continue strengthening its consumer practices and compliance efforts as part of the settlement, the company said. Shein also agreed not to misrepresent shipping times or block negative reviews, among other changes. The FTC, which protects consumers from unfair business practices, will use the funds to reimburse customers, according to court documents. Review practices and sustainability claims challenged The company also filtered out negative product reviews, the FTC said. Shein internal guidance told employees to exclude “extremely bad comments”, such as that a piece of jewellery would stain the customer’s skin, the FTC said. The FTC also accused Shein of making misrepresentations and unsubstantiated claims about its supply chain. The company claimed products with the “evoluSHEIN” label had come from suppliers with above-average scores on social responsibility audits, but could not produce any independent audits to back the claims, the FTC said. The FTC also questioned Shein’s claims about the origin of cotton used in its US products, saying that the company’s testing was often inaccurate or inconclusive. Shein has long grappled with claims that its clothes contain cotton from the Xinjiang region, where the US and human rights groups say government-sponsored forced labour programmes target Uighur minorities. Shein has previously said it does not use Chinese cotton in products sold in the US, where the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act bans any imports from Xinjiang. Shein, founded in China and headquartered in Singapore, went public in September in Hong Kong. The retailer was known for selling US$5 dresses and US$10 jeans, but it has been forced to raise its prices as the US and then Europe closed customs duty loopholes. REUTERS

events.title: Nvidia option trader scores 1,984% gain after CEO Huang’s return
events.summary: The trader made US$376,900 (S$485,900) in profit on US$19,000 worth of Nvidia call options bought on Nov 20. A Reddit trader made US$376,900 from Nvidia calls, a 1,984% gain, after Jensen Huang returned as chief executive officer and shares jumped 31%. Institutional traders had already bet on a rebound while Nvidia fell 39% in November, using calls, call spreads and sold puts to profit from any recovery. One large January US$160 call trade made US$23.8 million, but another social media claim was unconfirmed, and some traders later hedged against a fresh slide. Reddit user Outrageous-Voice1459 made a lot of money on Nov 23. The trader made US$376,900 (S$485,900) in profit on US$19,000 worth of Nvidia call options bought on Nov 20 . But Outrageous-Voice1459’s winnings pale in comparison to that of institutional traders who had been positioning for a rebound in the chip giant’s shares, even as the stock price kept sinking. With shares dropping 39% in November through Nov 20 , some option traders had moved bullish positions to lower strike prices, paying a premium for the chance to profit more quickly on a recovery. Others bought tens of thousands of calls and call spreads to bet on higher prices by early 2027. Still others sold put options, willing to purchase shares in case of a deeper slide in Nvidia’s stock. The massive spike in shares after Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive on the morning of Nov 23 finally rewarded the traders looking for a rebound. That included a buyer on Nov 20 of January-expiry US$160 calls, who sold half of their position to secure a US$23.8 million gain, with the stock surging 31% to US$165.05. Between irreverent memes and satirical artificial intelligence videos of Nvidia’s Huang, Outrageous-Voice1459 posted screenshots of his brokerage account on the subreddit r/WallStreetBets, saying he had made made “10x my years salary in one trade”. The trade entry details match a real block trade at the same time and price on an electronic options exchange. “Sold At Open. Thank You Jensen,” wrote the Reddit user. Another purported trade caused a stir on social media for being suspiciously well-timed – a block of US$160 calls expiring on Nov 23 supposedly sold at a vast profit. But an examination of the options tape from that day shows no trace of such a trade. “There seems to be no confirmation this trade actually happened,” said Daniel Roos, co-founder of options research provider VolSignals. “Even if it did, this type of order flow is completely typical at extremes when the index or high-interest names are moving like this.” Just as institutional traders started to position for a rebound on the way down, after the spike in shares on Nov 23 some large bets were placed to hedge against a renewed slide. events.title: The Fairphone 6 Plus is modular, repairable, and $100 off right now
events.summary: The Fairphone 6 Plus comes with 12 replaceable parts. | Photo: Dominic Preston / The Verge Unlike most smartphones, the Fairphone 6 Plus is designed for home repair, with easily replaceable parts that could help extend its lifespan well into the future. That makes its midrange price point easier to justify, especially now that it’s dropped to a new low of $552.49 (about $98 off) at Amazon as part of the retailer’s ongoing Black Friday sale. Fairphone 6 Plus Where to Buy: $649.99 $552.49 at Amazon (black) $649.99 $552.49 at Amazon (green) $649.99 $552.49 at Amazon (blue) The 6.3-inch Fairphone 6 Plus features 12 user-replaceable parts, including the battery, screen, USB-C port, and cameras, all of which you can swap out with the included screwdriver. Replacement parts are relatively affordable, too; a new battery costs $39.99, which helps offset its middling battery life and lack of wireless charging. It also comes with a five-year warranty and up to six Android OS upgrades, making it a good option if you want a phone you can keep using for years. Although repairability is its marquee feature, the 6 Plus is also a solid midrange Android device. Fairphone prioritizes ethically sourced materials , making it a strong choice for environmentally conscious buyers who don’t want to sacrifice performance. Its Snapdragon 7s Gen 4 processor handles everyday tasks well, and its cameras take decent photos, though they’re not quite on par with those of pricier phones. What’s more, it offers a clean, bloatware-free Android experience and modular back panels, which you can swap for optional accessories like a card holder or crossbody strap. Our own Allison Johnson particularly liked the phone’s dedicated switch for turning on customizable focus modes called Moments, which can simplify your homescreen and limit access to distracting apps — something we could all use a little less of. events.title: A Startup Tied to Donald Trump Jr. Could Get a Historic $15 Billion Loan From the Pentagon
events.summary: Donald Trump Jr. during the Bitcoin 2025 Expo in Las Vegas Roger Kisby/Redux In what would rank among the largest government loans in U.S. history, the Pentagon is considering extending $15 billion to a California-based startup with financial ties to Donald Trump Jr., according to interviews and records reviewed by ProPublica. The award would be one of the biggest the federal government has given to a firm connected to the Trump family and would go to a defense contractor with a largely untested track record. The startup, Hadrian Automation, has attracted over a billion dollars in private investment in recent months on the promise that it can build factories that use AI and robots to more efficiently produce precision components for defense, aerospace and other industries. If approved, the loan would be almost twice the value of the entire company, based on estimates from a round of financing this summer. Hadrian announced that round of investment included “major participation by 1789 Capital,” the venture capital firm that Trump Jr. joined as a partner after his father was elected in November 2024. 1789 also invested in the company in 2025. A spokesperson for 1789 Capital said it holds a “minority stake” in Hadrian, but the total size of its share has not been disclosed. Do You Have Information We Should Know About Donald Trump Jr.? We’re still reporting. If you know anything about Trump Jr. or his businesses, please get in touch with our reporting team. Robert Faturechi Contact me, by email or securely on Signal, with tips about the federal government and Trump’s businesses. Contact Me The potential loan is 10 times the size of the largest deal the Pentagon has made in a recent lending spree.  According to Pentagon documents, a loan to Hadrian would be used to build a dozen “automated factories” in a partnership with other defense companies and potentially commercial ones to expand production of munitions, drones and other equipment.  The U.S. military has been dealing with a severe shortage of some types of munitions because of the wars in Ukraine and Iran, though it’s unclear if the factories are an attempt to address those particular shortages.  The size and structure of the deal would form an interdependence between the company and the federal government that could run afoul of long-standing guidance on how to protect taxpayer money, former Defense Department officials said. The government would use taxpayer money to vastly expand a fledgling defense contractor, which it would then presumably award contracts to, essentially paying the company money that it could use to repay the loan. Pentagon staff have also raised several concerns about Hadrian, including its ability to expand and hire fast enough, the documents show. The loan is under consideration weeks before Democrats take control of both chambers of Congress. The party’s leaders have vowed to use their new oversight powers to scrutinize the raft of contracts and other actions by the Trump administration that have financially benefited the Trump family and others who work in the administration or have ties to it.   Since the start of President Donald Trump’s second term, firms in which his elder sons hold stakes have won billions of dollars in federal backing. ProPublica recently reported on the Trump administration awarding nearly $40 million to one company to screen for Ebola and other infectious diseases. We also revealed how a White House aide intervened to secure a Pentagon loan of $620 million to Vulcan Elements, a rare earth magnet startup, a few months after 1789 Capital invested in it. Omeed Malik, founder of 1789 Capital, center, signs the guest book on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange in 2025 as Donald Trump Jr. looks on. Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images Responding to a question about whether the White House, Trump Jr. or 1789 lobbied for the loan, the Pentagon said in a statement that no company receives preferential treatment. “Outside affiliations, investors, or political connections play absolutely no role in the Department’s funding decisions.”  A Pentagon spokesperson also cast the loan discussions with Hadrian as being in “early stages” and disputed that the potential deal was for $15 billion. The spokesperson characterized the size of the Hadrian loan that is under discussion as not extraordinary, saying multibillion-dollar deals with other companies had been agreed to but not yet announced.  In a statement, 1789 Capital said it does not get involved in government contracts sought by the companies it invests in but is excited about Hadrian. “Our thesis is to invest in American companies that are rebuilding domestic industrial capacity and reducing dependence on China for critical supply chains that underpin our economy. Hadrian embodies the opportunity we see to strengthen America’s productive capabilities while pursuing compelling returns for our investors.”   Trump Jr.’s lawyer, Alan Garten, said his client played no role in Hadrian being considered for any contract and has no involvement with the company’s operations. “Don is a private citizen who has been building businesses and investing in companies since long before his father first ran for public office. He holds no government position and has never sought to influence government policies, regulations or decisions to advance or benefit his personal business interests,” his lawyer said. Hadrian did not respond to requests for comment. In the past, Trump Jr. and Eric Trump have described themselves as passive investors who aren’t involved in federal award decisions and said it is not a conflict for companies they hold an interest in to win government contracts.  1789 Capital’s first investment in Hadrian was announced in July of last year. That round of investments was co-led by conservative billionaire investor Peter Thiel’s Founders Fund. Hadrian said it would use that money to expand its shipbuilding and naval defense capabilities, and build a sprawling new factory in Arizona.  This March, the company announced a deal to make submarine parts for the Navy, which committed up to $900 million to the effort. And in July, Hadrian’s CEO became a significant donor to Republican groups, contributing nearly a half million dollars, campaign filings show.   1789’s second investment in Hadrian was announced in August in a round of financing that included participation from institutional investment managers. “This is just the beginning,” 1789 wrote in a LinkedIn post about the funding round.  It’s unclear when the Pentagon began considering Hadrian for the loan. But defense documents cite the August funding round that Trump Jr.’s firm was part of.
