events.title: Jensen Huang still thinks a succession plan creates unnecessary hierarchy
events.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang kicked off his return to the chipmaker he co-founded by holding an all-hands meeting that covered remorse, therapy, and even the company’s code of conduct, according to accounts from multiple insiders who spoke to the media. The topic of succession planning also came up — a particularly sticky issue seen as a key risk at Nvidia. Huang reportedly told staff that Nvidia doesn’t require succession planning because of its unique business model, CNBC reported , citing an unnamed source who was present. Surprisingly, given the events of the last two weeks, Huang argued that a succession plan would create unnecessary hierarchy. Investors and analysts saw the issue differently earlier this month, when Huang resigned as CEO following his admission that he had extramarital affairs with at least two people, including one whom the U.S. government suspects of being a Chinese spy. Nvidia is a flat organization, unlike other large corporations that have a swath of C-suite executives and multiple layers of management. Huang sits at the top and says he has about 60 direct reports. Nvidia has just five executive officers running the show, including Huang. The other four are CFO Colette Kress, who was interim CEO for 12 days; Ajay Puri, who heads worldwide field operations; Debora Shoquist, executive vice president of operations; and Timothy Teter, executive vice president and general counsel, according to the company’s regulatory filings . Huang has previously defended the company’s structure in numerous interviews, including one in March with podcaster Lex Fridman. “When you’re designing a company, you should first think about what is it that you want the company to produce,” Huang said in the interview. “You know, I see a lot of companies’ organization charts, and they all look the same. Hamburger [company] organization charts, software organization charts, and car company organization charts. They all look the same. And it doesn’t make any sense to me. You know, the goal of company is to be the machinery, the mechanism, the system that produces the output. And that output is the product that we like to create.” Huang’s comments to staff, and his previous remarks on the topic of succession, may not be enough to assuage the board or shareholders over the long term, however. events.title: In all-hands meeting, Jensen Huang thanks White House and says he’s in therapy
events.summary: After a whirlwind period during which Jensen Huang’s life fell apart and then came back together again, the Nvidia founder now wants his staff to know that he’s a changed man. Huang held Nvidia’s first all-hands meeting on Tuesday since his reinstatement on Monday. During that meeting, CNBC reported that Huang struck a “remorseful tone” and told the crowd “I hurt all of you.” The founder, whose extramarital affairs have been accused of jeopardizing everything from the stock market to U.S. national security, went on to describe how difficult the current moment is for him: “This is going to be the hardest company meeting I’ve ever done, and the second hardest meeting I have ever done,” Huang reportedly told staff . “The hardest meeting I’ve ever done was with my wife,” he added. The CEO admitted in the meeting that he had flouted Nvidia’s code of conduct , which he himself had largely devised. Huang emphasized that the code of conduct was still in effect, but that mitigating circumstances would matter a lot. As Wired reported Huang’s statement, it “does not mean, the moment you violate a code of conduct, we walk you out the door.” Huang told staff that he’s in therapy and also said that he was grateful for a second chance at the company. The CEO is now walking a difficult tight rope between reasserting his authority over one of the world’s most powerful and influential companies, and conceding that he may have made some mistakes. He also tackled the difficult question of President Trump’s role in his restoration. The president reportedly called Nvidia’s board directly to lobby for Huang’s return, but in his talk, Huang downplayed Trump’s role Huang thanked the administration on Tuesday for “providing Nvidia with quick access to intelligence that he said helped the board determine that the national security risks the company faced in reinstating him were low,” The Wall Street Journal writes . Huang will likely need the administration’s support as he weathers an upcoming wave of congressional scrutiny from a newly Democrat-led government. The CEO is scheduled to appear for a public Senate Banking Committee hearing next week and, in the coming weeks, he will be called to appear for a number of different closed House hearings, including for the Intelligence Committee, the Foreign Affairs Committee, and the China Select Committee. events.title: Even the best AI agents struggle with everyday life
events.summary: AI companies have spent the last couple of months marketing personal AI agents as tools to take over the digital drudgery of human existence — and millions have been sold on the vision, handing over their shopping schedules, travel plans, and everyday responsibilities to AI assistants. But new research suggests that even the most advanced AI models struggle to reliably and safely navigate the messy details of people’s lives. According to ShellBench, a new benchmark for everyday agent work, even the most advanced models from OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta failed more than a third of the time. Across all models tested, 15.7% of attempts failed at least one safety requirement, often leading to unintended consequences. ShellBench was developed in collaboration with researchers at The OpenClaw Foundation, Parsewave, Hugging Face, Red Hat, and UC Berkeley, drawing on more than 10 million anonymized, real-world AI agent interactions to see how agents perform on the everyday work people actually delegate to them. The research comes as personal AI assistants are finding new popularity among developers, with Meta, OpenAI, and Anthropic all fighting for a piece of the market with Muse, Dots , and Claude Duet , respectively. In October, Meta said more than 10 million people in the U.S. and Canada had set up its personal AI agent, Muse, within six weeks of launch, with about a quarter using it daily. That number is expected to grow as Meta implants Muse directly into Instagram DMs . Despite growing popularity among consumers, we still have little evidence about how reliable AI personal assistant products actually are. ShellBench suggests that the unreliable nature of most everyday data sources still causes problems for many state-of-the-art systems. A successful agent should be able to navigate messy personal workspaces containing emails, calendar entries, spreadsheets, receipts, chat logs, outdated information, and phishing attempts, and figure out which information is relevant, what is private, and how to deliver the requested outcome without creating new problems. It seems many of today’s AI agents are still not up to the task. Not only did even the highest-performing agents frequently fail to meet the requirements of a task, but they also lacked consistency. When researchers ran each task three times under identical conditions, OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra, the highest-scoring model, nailed all three attempts less than half the time. For autonomous assistants that are meant to run in the background without supervision, it’s a problem if users need to run an agent multiple times to get a result they trust. Additionally, about 10% of otherwise correct attempts failed at least one safety criterion. Across the models and harnesses tested, agents failed to, for example, adequately account for a child’s school pickup 79.5% of the time. When handling laptop custody records, agents failed a requirement to identify and withhold a sensitive bank upload token in 18.6% of attempts. In another task, agents recommended duplicate or incorrect invoice payments 40.3% of the time. The findings highlight a major issue for users adopting consumer personal AI assistants, namely that there’s always a risk that an agent can create more headaches in the course of trying to fulfill an otherwise ordinary request. While AI benchmarks have largely focused on coding, professional work, or testing on specific tasks, ShellBench is attempting to evaluate how models perform on multi-step personal tasks within different agent harnesses — the software that controls how a model accesses information, uses tools, and takes actions. While the researchers found model choice had a greater overall impact on performance than harness choice, among the more capable models, AI agent performance became more dependent on the harness. For example, OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra outperformed Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.2 when operating within the Pi harness, but it performed worse when both models were tested within Claude Code. Meta’s Muse Wonder Full scored 56% in Pi, but only 38.1% in Claude Code. Meta’s Muse Wonder 1.0, meanwhile, averaged a success rate of 39.7% across the five harnesses tested. Notably, while the researchers tested models from Meta, OpenAI, and Anthropic, they didn’t evaluate them within the native harnesses of Muse, Dots, or Claude Duet, so the results may not be representative of the experience millions of consumers are having with the product today. events.title: Nasdaq, S&P 500 slip following Nov 23’s Nvidia-fuelled rally
events.summary: Traders working on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange in New York City on Nov 24. Nasdaq and S&P 500 fell after Nvidia and other tech shares gave back gains from Nov 23’s rally. Investors also worried about possible new US tariffs. Nvidia slipped as traders weighed Jensen Huang’s return as CEO and the political and governance risks around it. Reuters said the Trump administration may soon release findings on excess industrial capacity and new import duties. The S&P 500 lost 0.48% to 7,202.45 and the Nasdaq fell 1.45% to 23,740.52. The Dow rose 0.87%, while investors watched the PCE inflation report and Fed rate outlook. NEW YORK - The Nasdaq and the S&P 500 closed lower on Nov 24 as Nvidia and other AI-related shares gave back some of the previous day’s sharp gains and investors braced for possible new tariffs. Nvidia’s stock slipped 5.9% as investors weighed the implications of Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as CEO on Nov 23 following questions about the political and governance risks surrounding his return. Technology fell 2.8%, leading sector declines in the S&P 500, while an index of semiconductors dropped 7.9%. Nvidia’s decision to bring back Huang drove a sharp rally in the market and in shares of Nvidia on Nov 23. Huang had resigned earlier in November following revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. Reuters reported, citing three people with knowledge of the matter, that the Trump administration is poised to imminently release the findings of a probe aimed at countering alleged excess industrial capacity in 16 major US trading partners, and that new import duties on a wide range of goods are expected. “After the biggest rally in months, you would expect some profit-taking. At the end of the day, one headline doesn’t really resolve investor questions about the AI trade,” said Gene Goldman, chief investment officer at Cetera Financial Group. “The correction that we had last week is a buying opportunity for long-term investors, but we continue to believe it can be a very bumpy path for some time,” Goldman said. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 423.39 points, or 0.85%, to 50,018.70, the S&P 500 lost 36.08 points, or 0.50%, to 7,201.09 and the Nasdaq Composite lost 356.02 points, or 1.48%, to 23,733.54. Before the Nov 23 rebound, AI-linked stocks had struggled for weeks as investors questioned the sector’s debt-fuelled spending and the returns it could generate. Anthropic’s shares ended 6.5% lower at US$81.90, below their US$83 IPO price. The AI startup had a blockbuster market debut last week. Additional tariffs would add uncertainty to the market, while investors were also cautious ahead of Nov 25’s Personal Consumption Expenditures report, Goldman said. The administration’s tariffs have contributed to higher prices on consumer goods in the United States. The PCE price index is one of the key inflation gauges watched by the Federal Reserve. Fed funds futures traders are pricing in 97% odds of a Fed hike in December, and a 66% chance of an additional increase in January, according to the CME Group’s FedWatch Tool. Retailers were among the day’s gainers. Shares of Abercrombie & Fitch, which raised its profit forecast, jumped 19.7%, while Dollar Tree gained 11.2%, also after raising its profit outlook. Healthcare shares also rose and led S&P 500 sector gainers. Earlier, a Conference Board survey showed US consumer confidence rose to its highest level in nearly two years in November amid optimism over the labour market and the economy following the November midterm elections. Volume on US exchanges was 18.89 billion shares, compared with the roughly 19.50 billion average for the full session over the last 20 trading days. Declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 1.04-to-1 ratio on the New York Stock Exchange. There were 58 new highs and 309 new lows on the NYSE. On the Nasdaq, 2,376 stocks rose and 2,548 fell as declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 1.07-to-1 ratio. The S&P 500 posted 10 new 52-week highs and 4 new lows while the Nasdaq Composite recorded 49 new highs and 323 new lows. REUTERS

events.title: Hopes for cheaper fuel in Qld fade as tougher biofuel mandate rejected
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts The Governance, Energy and Finance Committee held a hearing in Mackay last month examining the Liquid Fuel Supply (Ethanol and Other Biofuels Mandate) Amendment Bill 2026. ( ABC Tropical North: Liam McNally ) The Governance, Energy and Finance Committee reviewed the Liquid Fuel Supply (Ethanol and Other Biofuels Mandate) Amendment Bill 2026 and raised concerns about compliance requirements, penalties and potential conflicts with national fuel-quality standards. The legislation remains before the Queensland Parliament, with the second reading not scheduled until early next year. Motorists seeking cheaper fuel alternatives have had their hopes dashed after a bill to strengthen Queensland's biofuel mandate was rejected by a recent parliamentary committee. This comes as drivers across the state still face petrol and diesel prices well over $2 a litre, and is another setback for the sugar and agriculture industries, which say a potential home-grown alternative — ethanol derived from sugar cane — is left waiting for clearer policy direction. The sugar industry is one of many in the agriculture sector that produces ethanol, which is blended with other fuels as part of state-wide mandates that benefit Australia, including reducing reliance on imported oil, stretching fuel supplies, lowering emissions and supporting local industries. The private member's bill, introduced by Katter's Australian Party Hill MP Shane Knuth, sought to increase Queensland's existing ethanol requirements, including requiring E10 petrol to contain at least 9 per cent ethanol, introducing minimum ethanol blends in other petrol grades and requiring diesel to contain at least 2 per cent biodiesel. Under the current biofuels mandate, liable retailers must ensure ethanol makes up 4 per cent of total regular unleaded and ethanol-blended petrol sales, while wholesalers face a 0.5 per cent biodiesel mandate. MSF Sugar's Mark Magnanini and Panita Vongkusolkit, with MP Shane Knuth (right), want the Queensland government to back a stronger biofuels industry. ( Supplied ) Mr Knuth said Queensland had the agricultural capacity to produce its own fuel. "We've got a massive fuel industry that's stretching from the Sunshine Coast right through to Port Douglas," he said. Mr Knuth said sugar, grain, manufacturing and farming industries had come together to support the legislation, and the committee's recommendation had disappointed those involved. Queensland Canegrowers chief executive Dan Galligan believes the state had an opportunity to lead while the federal government developed its own national policy. "For some reason, we can't get good, strong political leadership on this issue," he said. Canegrowers CEO Dan Galligan says the entire economy needs greater fuel security. ( Supplied: Canegrowers ) Australian Sugar Manufacturers chief executive Ash Salardini supported the bill and said locally produced ethanol could supply almost 15 per cent of Australia's petrol needs and support about 20,000 jobs. The sugar industry said it already had much of the infrastructure, feedstock and expertise needed to expand production, with companies prepared to invest if there was a clear market. MSF Sugar, which operates four mills in Queensland, invested $86 million in a green energy power station at its Tablelands Sugar Mill, and proposes a multi-million-dollar ethanol plant in Far North Queensland. But strategic program director and head of cane supply Mark Magnanini wanted to see greater policy certainty before committing to the project. "We could potentially have production of 65 million litres of ethanol in Far North Queensland by 2029, if we were able to do that today," he said. The sugar industry is disappointed with the Governance, Energy and Finance Committee recommended the Bill not pass Queensland government approval. ( ABC News: Daniel Taylor ) In another parliamentary inquiry into sugarcane bioenergy opportunities, released earlier this year, the government backed in-principle recommendations to support the industry. But Mr Magnanini said support needed to translate into a clearer pathway for investment, adding these projects could provide the sugar industry with other revenue streams beyond raw sugar and minimise exposure to commodity-price fluctuations. The debate comes as Australian companies across Queensland, New South Wales, and Victoria continue to export locally produced biofuels despite domestic fuel supply concerns.

events.title: US court convicts Huawei for deceiving banks about Iran dealings
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts US court convicts Huawei for deceiving banks about Iran dealings, stealing trade secrets Chinese tech giant Huawei has been found guilty of attempting to steal trade secrets. ( Reuters: Gonzalo Fuentes ) Tech giant Huawei has been convicted of deceiving banks about its business in Iran and stealing trade secrets from US companies. Huawei was placed on a trade blacklist that restricted its access to technology after the case began in 2018. Huawei, which has emerged as a key player in China's AI push, says it will "take all necessary action" to protect its rights. Huawei has been convicted in a sprawling US criminal case that included charges it deceived banks about its business in Iran and stole trade secrets from US companies. US authorities targeted the Chinese technology and telecommunications equipment giant years, saying it posed national security risks. Huawei launched a new phone without fanfare last week. But the technology it uses has sparked intense debate Chinese state media has pointed to Huawei's new smartphone as evidence the United States' attempts to curtail China's microchip development are failing. So how significant is the tech in the new phone and what does it mean for the "chip wars"? In 2019, the year after the criminal case began, the US government placed Huawei on a trade blacklist that restricted its access to American technology. But experts say the case has not undermined Huawei, which has diversified and emerged as a key player in China's push for artificial intelligence. The trial ended on Tuesday, local time, after more than two months in the Federal District Court in Brooklyn. Prosecutors called more than 60 witnesses and the defence called 15. Huawei and three affiliates faced 12 charges including racketeering conspiracy, bank fraud, wire fraud, sanctions violations, and conspiring to steal trade secrets and obstruct justice. Shortly after the verdict, the company said the charges lacked "legal merit" and that it would "take all necessary legal action" to protect its rights. In December 2018 Meng Wanzhou, Huawei's chief financial officer and daughter of the company's founder, was detained in Canada on a US warrant, prompting a diplomatic crisis involving the US, China and Canada. Ms Meng had been secretly indicted for allegedly misleading an HSBC banker about Huawei's business in Iran so that the company could move dollars in and out of the country in violation of US sanctions. The charges against Meng Wanzhou were later dropped. ( Xinhua via Reuters ) She fought extradition to the US for nearly three years, before entering a deferred prosecution agreement and flying home to China to a hero's welcome. The charges against her were dropped. Jurors showed video of employee stealing robot piece The 2018 indictment alleged Huawei misled HSBC, Standard Chartered and BNP Paribas about its business dealings in Iran. Prosecutors added new charges in 2020, including that Huawei conspired to steal trade secrets from US technology companies over two decades. During the trial, prosecutors tried to prove Huawei stole source code from Cisco Systems for its routers, stole wireless telecommunications company Quintel's antenna technology, and hired a professor to gain access to a circuit board developed by semiconductor company CNEX. Solomon Islands takes out $100 million loan from China to build Huawei mobile phone towers Solomon Islands authorities say the proposed 161 mobile phone towers will expand and improve coverage and that the loan to fund it will be repayable, but experts have questioned if the financial case for the project stacks up. Jurors watched a video that prosecutors alleged showed a Huawei employee slipping a piece of a T-Mobile robot into his backpack, and heard about a Huawei engineer sneaking into a Fujitsu booth at a trade show to photograph a device. Prosecutors gave jurors a statement attached to Ms Meng's deferred prosecution agreement, in which she acknowledged that the company illegally conducted business in Iran. She did not testify at the trial, though an HSBC banker she met with in 2013 did give evidence. Banks knew about Iran dealings, defence says The defence argued that HSBC and the other banks knew about Huawei's business in Iran and were competing for the company's business. During his closing argument, lawyer Brian Heberlig accused prosecutors of having "cherry-picked" a handful of disparate incidents to support their claim of a 20-year conspiracy. He said Huawei had achieved success through "hard work, innovation, and investment in research and development".

events.title: AI godfather Yann LeCun torches Anthropic CEO over AI gatekeeping
events.summary: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is taking heat from AI luminary Yann LeCun, one of the founding fathers of modern machine learning, because of the Claudefather's fear-mongering around open-weights models, which also happen to compete with his products. In an X post this week, LeCun likened the Amodei's advocacy to a “new form of medieval obscurantism.” “Dario’s spiel since GPT-2 has always been about hyping the dangers so that open models would be made illegal, and he would stay in control,” LeCun wrote in response to a now three-year-old video posted to the platform in which Amodei warned US Congress members about the dangers of open-weights models, the use of which could not be monitored or policed. “He left OpenAI because he wasn’t going to have control. It’s like the Ottoman Empire banning the printing press for Arabic so they would keep in control of the dogma.” LeCun is one of the most influential names in AI and ML. His team is credited with the development of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) in the late ’80s during his time at Bell Labs. He later oversaw the development of Meta’s Llama herd of models as chief AI scientist before shifting gears away from LLMs to world model architectures like JEPA. He has also been a strong proponent of open source AI development and open models. Of the major model houses, Anthropic has taken the most hostile position against the adoption of open-weights models. Despite advocating against the unregulated diffusion of open models for years, Anthropic’s fearmonger-in-chief has maintained that the company isn’t opposed to them. “Anthropic has never advocated for a ban on open-weights models,” Amodei wrote in a blog post earlier this year. The executive has instead fomented fears over their potential misuse. “Open-weights models — it does not matter whether they come from China or anywhere else — do potentially present a higher risk than closed models, because it is very difficult to apply guardrails to them or monitor their usage, and, once weights are released, they cannot be withdrawn,” the blog post read. Amodei has repeatedly hammered these talking points over the past several years, including in the Senate hearing that solicited LeCun’s post. Amodei has also called for measures, such as stricter export controls on the export of high-end accelerators to China; a crackdown on industrial-scale distillation operations, for which his company has previously accused Alibaba and other Chinese model devs; and mandating safety testing for sufficiently advanced open-weights models. In other words, Anthropic doesn’t want all freely downloadable models banned, just the ones that Amodei thinks aren’t playing fair or are powerful enough to compete with its own. LeCun isn’t the only one who has pushed back against anti-open-weights rhetoric in recent memory. Earlier this summer, a cadre of tech titans, including Meta, Microsoft, IBM, Dell, and Nvidia, wrote an open letter [ PDF ] in support of open-weights models. Open models “strengthen safety and cybersecurity, accelerate innovation and diffusion, and enable sovereignty,” Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said at the time. “The world needs both frontier closed models and frontier open models.” As we previously reported , Nvidia’s future depends on its ability to sell to a diverse set of customers ranging from the big model houses like Anthropic and OpenAI to public clouds, neoclouds, and enterprises. And while many of these companies are perfectly happy to get their AI through Claude or ChatGPT, others, whether it be for regulatory or cost reasons, are not. Earlier this month, we reported how British neobank Revolut cut their vibe coding tab by 10x by moving its roughly 2,000 employees from Claude to Z.AI’s GLM 5.1 running on a cluster of 56 Nvidia B200 GPUs. The problem for Anthropic, and OpenAI for that matter, is the more enterprises that embrace open-weights models, the less likely they are to spring for Claude or ChatGPT. The Register reached out to Anthropic for comment, but had not heard back at the time of publication. ®

events.title: NT houses demolished ready for auction after defective homes scandal
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Bellamack houses demolished ready for auction after defective homes scandal An empty block where one of the defective Bellamack homes used to be, before it was demolished. ( Supplied: NT government ) Eight defective homes, built as affordable housing in Bellamack between 2012 and 2013, have been acquired by the NT government and demolished. The area's local member says it gives affected homeowners "long overdue closure" after years of uncertainty. The NT government says it will continue pursuing compensation claims against developer George Milatos. The Northern Territory government has acquired and demolished eight homes found to be riddled with structural defects, after a legal saga that dragged on for more than a decade. The houses were the last left standing out of 18 that were built as part of an NT government-backed affordable housing scheme in the Palmerston suburb of Bellamack between 2012 and 2013. The homes were soon found to have serious structural flaws , including corrosion, leaks and lifting tiles, with engineering faults rendering them unsafe during severe storms or cyclones. Leaks and corrosion were among the serious faults impacting the buildings. ( ABC News: Ian Redfearn ) Now, the NT's Country Liberal Party (CLP) government has said it has acquired and demolished the homes, with the land remediated and made ready for auction next month. Lands, Planning and Environment Minister Joshua Burgoyne said the government had "done the right thing by the homeowners and delivered the certainty they deserve". Darwin builder of defective homes loses court appeal The homes in Bellamack were found to be riddled with defects such as water leaks and cracked tiles, making them unsafe during severe weather. events.title: Utah asks to drop charges against Kalshi, founders after Kalshi halts trading there
events.summary: Utah is asking asked a court to dismiss the criminal charges it filed last month against Kalshi and two of its executives, accusing the prediction market operator of running an illegal gambling enterprise Utah asked a court to dismiss the criminal charges it filed last month against prediction market operator Kalshi and two of its executives, citing Kalshi's decision to halt trading in the state that had accused it of running an illegal gambling enterprise. The one-sentence motion filed Tuesday in a Salt Lake City-based court by state Attorney General Derek Brown referenced a “change in circumstance." Brown’s office noted that it could refile the case if Kalshi resumes offering trades on its platform there. “Kalshi has pulled out of Utah, and if it returns, so will the charges,” Brown said in a statement. Utah has been on the front lines of a battle between states and the federal government over who regulates the markets. Litigation has spread across more than 20 states, creating a fragmented legal landscape that analysts say will likely be settled by the U.S. Supreme Court. The felony charges filed by Utah include 13 counts of violating the state’s prohibition on gambling and another charge involving profiting off illegal activity. The state’s charging documents name Kalshi and its co-founders, chief executive officer Tarek Mansour and chief operating officer Luana Lopes Lara. They are due in court in Salt Lake City on Dec. 4, unless a judge agrees to dismiss the case. Utah law prohibits gambling, and Utah considers prediction markets gambling, Brown's office said. Many other states contend that the platforms’ sports trading activities are flouting their laws that regulate sports betting and casino gambling. Utah's felony charges represented a new tactic in how states are trying to assert regulatory authority over the fast-expanding activity. In a separate case, Brown's office is still asking a state court to make Kalshi give up the profits it made in Utah. Kalshi, the nation's largest prediction market operator, said Monday it had halted trading in Utah after it became clear that a federal judge hearing a case brought by the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission wouldn't immediately stop Utah's attempts to shut it down there. Kalshi didn’t close open positions or void contracts when it blocked any new positions from being taken in Utah. It also let Utah traders close out their open positions and withdraw their funds, Kalshi said. Kalshi, like the CFTC , argues that prediction markets offer “event contracts” that should be considered swaps under a federal law that grants exclusive regulation to the federal agency. Utah and at least 42 other states have opposed that view. Kalshi sued Utah in February, asking a federal judge to prevent the state from enforcing its gambling restrictions on the platform. A federal judge rejected the request , and an appeal is pending at the 10th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals, which declined to halt Utah’s regulatory enforcement during Kalshi’s appeal. Trading activity on Kalshi is halted in Nevada and partially in Michigan and Washington, according to Kalshi. events.title: Federal agency boosts size of most single-family loans the government can guarantee to $855,400
events.summary: The Federal Housing Finance Agency is increasing the size of home loans that the government can guarantee against default as it takes into account rising housing prices The Federal Housing Finance Agency is increasing the size of home loans that the government can guarantee against default as it takes into account rising housing prices. Beginning next year, mortgage buyers Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac will be able to acquire loans of up to $855,400 on single-family homes in most of the country, the agency said Tuesday. The new conforming loan limit amounts to a roughly 2.7% increase from its 2026 level. FHFA oversees Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, which buy home loans from banks and other lenders, guaranteeing them against default. The loans are then bundled into securities sold to investors. But FHFA sets limits to the size of the loans that Fannie and Freddie can buy. Such loans are known as conforming loans, while mortgages above the conforming loan limit are known as jumbo loans. FHFA adjusts the limits of a conforming loan annually to reflect changes in U.S. home values, which have been rising nationally, albeit more slowly. 'The threat is finally real': Judge rips White House 'weaponization' Powerful storm threatens East Coast as Thanksgiving approaches: Forecast and track Attorney General Blanche sidesteps questions about DOJ probe into Nvidia's Huang Rising mortgage rates have weighed on home sales this year, deepening a national housing slump that dates back to 2022, when mortgage rates began to climb from pandemic-era lows. Sales of previously occupied U.S. homes were essentially flat last year, stuck at a 30-year low. They declined last month to their slowest annual pace in more than 16 years as mortgage rates surged. The FHFA’s latest House Price Index shows that, on average, U.S. home prices increased about 2.7% in the July-September quarter compared to a year earlier. The 2027 single-family home conforming loan limit will apply to most of the country , though the FHFA allows higher loan limits for certain states, such as Alaska and Hawaii, and in counties where the local median home value is more than double the conforming loan limit. For example, the conforming loan limit in 2027 for single-family homes in Los Angeles County will be $1,283,100, while in New York County it will be $1,224,750. 24/7 coverage of breaking news and live events

events.title: Trump talks turkey, and his ballroom, at pardoning event
events.summary: President Trump honored a time-worn Washington tradition Tuesday: pardoning poultry — after using the pulpit to praise his White House ballroom and deliver a rally-reminiscent speech. The big picture: Freedom and Feathers, this year's honored birds, continue a bizarre American tradition officially dating back to 1989 — but building on far older presidential lore. Driving the news: "Unfortunately, for 200 years, the White House lacked appropriate accommodations to host such distinguished guests," Trump said at the event, held on the White House's South Lawn. He continued, "I'm pleased to announce that next year we'll be able to have a special location right over there in that rather small ballroom being built." Trump's hotly contested project will be a 90,000-square-foot addition, far larger than the main White House. "I've heard better," he said about the birds' names, though they still earned presidential pardons. Both birds will dodge the oven and retire at Texas A&M University. State of play: The collective 82 pounds of white-feathered flamboyance traveled from West Virginia's Deans Gap Farm for the event. Pointing to his large 2024 election win in West Virginia, Trump said Tuesday, "I won it by a lot. I don't know what the hell happened with this last election. Somebody, please explain it to me." The pair are just four months old. Per a White House fact sheet , Freedom's favorite treat is Dr. Pepper. Feathers prefers to snack on Golden Delicious apples, which — like the turkeys — hail from West Virginia. Between the lines: Trump has never shied away from using the event to ruffle feathers. Last year, he jabbed at former President Biden and attacked Chicago leadership, derailing the focus on his feathered guests by calling Gov. JB Pritzker (D) a "fat slob." During his first term, he joked that the turkeys trotting before him had were slated to "appear in Adam Schiff's basement," a nod to the Democrat who led the 2019 impeachment inquiry into Trump. While Trump has taken presidential rhetoric to a new level, he's not the first to have stuffed political zingers into the bizarre tradition. In 2022, Biden seemingly poked fun at Trump's false claim he'd won the 2020 election, saying : "The votes are in. They've been counted and verified. There's no ballot stuffing. There's no fowl play." Worth noting: PETA called on the White House to end the event, saying presidents are "conned every year into becoming the unpaid spokesperson for factory farmers." President Tracy Reiman called the idea of retirement for the birds "all squawk, no substance, " noting fattened-up turkeys often die prematurely. Flashback: While George H.W. Bush formalized the pardon in 1989, the White House's quirky turkey ties stretch back well over a century. Abraham Lincoln is frequently credited with sparing the first turkey on record at the urging of his son in the 1860s, according to the White House Historical Association. Harry Truman welcomed a live turkey from the National Turkey Federation in 1947, and the photo-op was hatched. But that bird wasn't such a lucky duck — perhaps becoming part of the Thanksgiving feast. Since then, the NTF has presented the presidential bird. And President John F. Kennedy was gifted a turkey in 1963, but decided instead to "let this one grow." The bottom line: Through decades of conflict, campaigns and chaos, presidents have come face-to-beak with the ubiquitous Thanksgiving birds. Go deeper: The turkey pardon: A quirky White House custom

events.title: Is Nvidia too big to fail?
events.summary: When the Nasdaq Composite added $2 trillion after Jensen Huang 's stunning return as Nvidia chief executive on Monday, it underlined how dependent AI has become on one person. Mr Huang’s return restored about $1 trillion in market cap for the company he cofounded in 1993. Silicon Valley cheered, with OpenAI's Sam Altman among those celebrating the return of the man in the black leather jacket. President Donald Trump told CNBC he had personally intervened. “Jensen is not just a CEO. He’s the one with the relationships, with customers and with Washington,” said Mohammed Soliman, director of compute infrastructure at McLarty Associates and a senior fellow at the Middle East Institute. “The AI ecosystem needed him back, given the current moment and the challenges facing the whole industry, not just Nvidia.” The Nvidia board’s decision to bring Mr Huang back may help resuscitate an AI industry rocked by rising concerns over financing , a Democratic midterm sweep fuelling fears of a slower-than-expected buildout, a hawkish Federal Reserve and the CEO's removal less than two weeks ago. AI kingmaker All three major exchanges on the US market posted their best one-day performances since April 2025, largely pulled up by Nvidia’s 31 per cent gain. The chip maker gave up some of those gains during Tuesday trading, falling about 7 per cent. “The scale of the rally also highlights how vulnerable the broader AI trade has become to developments at a single company,” wrote Utkarsh Ahuja, founder and managing partner at Moon Pursuit Capital. Part of that vulnerability lays within Nvidia’s growing centrality in the multitrillion-dollar AI buildout. But how did a company with roots in gaming emerge as the AI kingmaker? It was Mr Huang who pushed the idea to include a standard software programming platform for Nvidia's graphics processing units just before the AI boom began. The concept, introduced in 2006, became known as Compute Unified Device Architecture. Programmers and those trying to make the most of GPUs appreciated that there finally seemed to be a programming standard emerging for the units. It did not make Nvidia money, but because it was so unique, it helped make the company's hardware products a standard. Cuda is an integral part of the Blackwell GPU package, which trains and runs large-scale AI models in data centres and is the successor to the Hopper. Microsoft, Meta, Google, Amazon and Oracle control 49 per cent of Blackwell compute with neoclouds CoreWeave, Nscale, Lambda, Nebius and Crusoe holding 18 per cent, according to American Compute, a GPU financing firm. The remaining compute is spread across enterprises, sovereign AI and smaller neoclouds. That has helped build out a portfolio worth more than $100 billion that touches frontier labs and cloud-computing companies. Nvidia owns $48 billion in eight publicly traded companies, including Space Exploration Technologies, Intel, CoreWeave and Nebius, according to its 13F filing. It also invested roughly $10 billion alongside Anthropic's IPO and $30 billion in OpenAI. Nvidia is also a major investor in start-ups, investing in 129 venture capital deals so far this year, according to Pitchbook. This accounts for 27.2 per cent of venture capital deals globally. Asked if he was concerned about the AI bubble , Mr Trump told CNBC: “I’m not concerned now because I think we have one of our great stars back in play. “The bigger impact was, you know, he’s [Mr Huang] got other chips in his brain that nobody else knows about, including me, that nobody else understands. And you know the amazing thing about, like, if you take the Blackwell, if you take some of these super advanced chips, they can’t be copied.” 'Reckless' decision The board’s decision marked a surprise reversal after its chairman Harvey Jones last week said Mr Huang would not be reinstated as chief executive after allegations surfaced that he had an extramarital affair with a purported Chinese spy. But just a few days later, the board voted unanimously to bring him back. “How can a board of directors in 12 days reverse a decision that is such a complicated discovery process that I would think would take at least six months to figure out what the heck is going on with all moving parts, and that it's a unanimous decision, and that the statement that they released was insane?” said Peter Anderson, founder of Andersen Capital Management. Politicians are pushing for answers into whether Mr Huang’s affair compromised national security. Megaspeed , the Singapore-based company the woman at the centre of the affair worked for, is alleged to have smuggled Nvidia’s advanced chips to China . Megaspeed denies the allegations. Mr Huang is expected to appear before four congressional committees next week, including one public hearing before the Senate Banking Committee on December 3. “The reckless decision to bring Jensen Huang back as CEO does not change the fact that Mr Huang, Nvidia executives and the company’s board still owe Congress answers about the company’s compliance with US export controls,” Democratic senator Elizabeth Warren said. Ms Warren, who will take over the committee in the next Congress, told Politico the grilling will likely be partisan, though separate comments from Republican senators Tim Scott and John Kennedy suggest they will also push for answers. Incoming speaker of the House of Representatives Hakeem Jeffries also argued the National Defence Authorisation Act “must include ironclad export control legislation” to keep advanced AI technology out of the hands of China and other US rivals. Still, Wall Street’s Monday rally showed how markets crucial Mr Huang’s presence at Nvidia is to the AI buildout. “The investigation is still ongoing, and nobody is pretending that part is finished, but the market wasn't going to wait for a perfect answer,” Mr Soliman said.

events.title: Criminal charge against incoming House Democrat dropped
events.summary: Prosecutors in Mecklenburg County, N.C., announced Tuesday they are dropping a criminal charge against Rep.-elect LaKesha Womack (D-N.C.) related to an un-returned rental car in 2019. Why it matters: The charge had been a bothersome footnote for Womack since her sudden rise from obscurity on Election Day, when she unexpectedly won a heavily Republican district. Womack, a 49-year-old minister and consultant, is one of several "wave babies" who were largely unknown to national Democrats before their upset midterm victories. Driving the news: Mecklenburg County District Attorney Spencer Merriweather said in a statement released Tuesday afternoon that his office has submitted a voluntary dismissal and that the matter is "closed." Womack was charged with "Felony Failure to Return Hired Property" after failing to return a rental car in 2019 following two renewals, Merriweather said. The car was recovered by law enforcement. A criminal summons was issued against Womack in 2020 but only served on Oct. 11 of this year, just days before the start of early voting. Merriweather said that the unidentified rental dealer has reached an agreement with Womack, in which she paid them the "assessed rental cost" of the car from its overdue date to its return, and does "not wish to proceed further with prosecution and considered the matter resolved." What they're saying: " For almost seven years Ms. Womack was unaware a criminal summons had been issued," Womack's lawyer Harold Cogdell said in a statement shared with Axios. "Upon learning of this unresolved matter, Ms. Womack promptly and fully resolved this matter with the rental car company." Cogdell said there are "questions remaining" about the timing of the summons being served, but that "Ms. Womack's [sic] is laser focused on preparing to serve the residents of the North Carolina's 14th Congressional District." Womack, who has said she was experiencing housing insecurity in 2019, referred Axios to Cogdell's statement when sought for comment.

events.title: 11 Things Jensen Huang Actually Said at His First All-Hands Back at Nvidia
events.summary: Jensen Huang is going to therapy for 90 minutes a day and rethinking his management style , and he says that violating Nvidia’s code of conduct isn’t necessarily a fireable offense. That’s just some of what the newly returned Nvidia CEO told staff during his first all-hands meeting on Tuesday. Here are some of the most striking things Huang said during the meeting, according to remarks reviewed by WIRED. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment. On self-improvement: “I go to therapy every day for an hour and a half. And it’s been helping me a lot.” On accountability: “There are rumors on the internet that apparently I’m a tech bro, and therefore I’m back. Apparently, I’m a tech bro, and because I wear a super nice jacket, that I’m above the law, and I’m above the code of conduct. That is not true. It won’t be tolerated, and it wasn’t tolerated here.” “If one of you were to violate a code of conduct, what does that mean? If you were ever to violate a code of conduct, it is not appropriate. I just wanted you to know, it is not right, it's not appropriate, it won’t be tolerated. But ‘it won’t be tolerated’ does not mean the moment you violate a code of conduct, we walk you out the door. Facts, circumstances, a lot of assessments. And your management team will still make the decision. That is what is in the best interest of the company and its employees, with all the facts and circumstances.” On his management style: “The intensity I bring elevates everybody else. But I can go too far. When I go too far, it hurts people, it belittles them, it disempowers them. And that’s not right. And so I need to go figure out how I’m going to bring the intensity, the crazy intensity, to the field.” On women at Nvidia: “I believe we need to create and continue to sustain a safe environment for all of our women. And if I did anything that put that in jeopardy, I cannot tell you how sad I am, and I’ll do everything I can to fix it. We will not tolerate that.” On succession: “All day long, this company can run autonomously, and you saw it. I promise you, whether I’m here or not, this company is wired up to execute, execute, and execute, and deliver on financial results.” “I also didn’t believe in succession planning. Let that sink in. I don’t believe in succession planning. I think it’s flawed. The idea of succession planning is not flawed. What people think succession planning means is flawed.” “There’s a reason why we don’t have succession planning; it’s not because we are unaware of the word. I’m the longest-running tech CEO in history.” On politics : “There [were] also rumors that apparently I’m back because the highest levels of our government wanted me back. That is also completely untrue. Our board of directors performed their duty as they should have.” “It is absolutely true that President Trump really, really loves our company,” Huang told employees. “He gloats about Nvidia. You know he does. But there’s a question about politics. Are we now political? Are we partisan? I wanna be very clear with you. President Trump is the United States president. He is my president. And I’ll do everything I can to help this president be informed about how he could make decisions that are in the best interest of our country … We have to do it, and whoever the next president is will be my president, and I will do exactly the same.” “Don’t think for a second that politics ever plays a role in this company, not even a little bit. We are the most apolitical company. I don’t love that we talk about politics here. Take it home. I love that we talk about work here.” In your inbox: For life-tested picks, sign up for our Gear newsletters Building social media apps isn’t cool anymore RIP to the unloved, unwanted Cybertruck Want better search results? events.title: Big four employees directed to 'disregard' issues identified during audit
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Bullying and sexual harassment claims among 3,000 complaints at big four firms Topic: Accounting and Auditing Services The big four are under fire for how they treat complaints from staff and whistleblowers. ( ABC News: John Gunn; Reuters: Wolfgang Rattay ) Australia's big four accounting firms — Deloitte, PwC, KPMG and EY — were the subject of more than 3,000 complaints over three years. The Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) said the complaints included serious allegations of bullying and sexual harassment, but firms shut down staff and whistleblowers who tried to make complaints. In the wake of the KPMG audit leaks scandal and subsequent parliamentary probe , ASIC investigated the big four about how they handled internal whistleblower complaints. In its review, it found that between July 1, 2023, and June 26, 2026, there were 3,215 total internal complaints recorded among the big four. Over a wider timeframe, 558 were audit complaints provided to ASIC. The regulator said of these, it identified 35 that raised issues related to the conduct of an audit or the misuse of audit client information. ASIC's review follows whistleblower revelations that at KPMG confidential board papers from Lendlease were used to support bids for major audit tenders for Westpac and Dexus, and that the firm then mishandled the whistleblower's complaint about it. In the wake of the saga, the federal government has extended its ban on accounting firm KPMG bidding for new government work until at least the end of February. The most common concerns involved audit work that had been falsified, inaccurately documented or recorded without adequate evidence. Whistleblowers need better protection Without whistleblowers, Australians would be kept in the dark about major corporate scandals, but evidence suggests the experience of raising alarm bells can destroy their lives. A number of complaints alleged that employees were directed to "disregard, conceal or not escalate issues identified during an audit" or that, when escalated, the issues were not investigated appropriately. "They also alleged that staff were told not to report identified discrepancies, to pass audit testing despite concerns, or not to raise issues with an engagement partner or other senior personnel," the review said. A "small number" of complaints involved possible manipulation of audit sampling. They included allegations that audit samples were removed or replaced, or that changes were proposed without an adequate audit basis. The review also found "misuse of statutory audit client information and other breaches of confidentiality, data security or independence requirements, and retaliation against, or victimisation of, reporters who raised issues in connection with a statutory audit". ASIC said in a number of complaints the firms had no records indicating that concerns about the audit quality had been fully examined. It said audit concerns were often treated by firms as workplace matters. If you have more information about this story, please contact Nassim Khadem at khadem.nassim@abc.net.au or nassimkhadem@protonmail.com Allegations of bullying and sexual harassment ASIC said it heard another 523 complaints that included a range of wider issues not related to audit, including allegations of bullying and sexual harassment. Documents with new allegations against former KPMG partner Documents allege a former KPMG partner treated "female members of staff and clients inappropriately". There were also complaints raised about how firms handled sensitive information, including those sent to personal email accounts. "These stakes are really high," ASIC commissioner Kate O'Rourke told ABC News. "The firms … audit most of the 94 per cent of listed companies by market capitalisation and the vast majority, 85 per cent, of registrable superannuation entities." She said audit firms were "gatekeepers to Australia's financial markets" and needed to be "carefully and really thoroughly interrogating complaints that they've received internally". ASIC has come under fire from whistleblowers for being too slow to act, with one whistleblower claiming the regulator has to be "dragged kicking and screaming" to investigate misconduct allegations. ASIC chair Sarah Court has previously told parliament that the watchdog required greater powers to investigate and prosecute the big four. ASIC chair Sarah Court appearing before Senate estimates on June 5, 2026.

events.title: Republican China hawks challenge Trump over Huang's Nvidia return
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Republicans challenge Trump over Huang's return as US Congress targets Nvidia Topic: Information Technology Industry Donald Trump called for Nvidia to reinstate its under-fire chief executive Jensen Huang. ( Reuters: Evan Vucci ) Republicans have broken ranks with Donald Trump over the Nvidia scandal, joining forces with Democrats demand an investigation. The US president has claimed credit for Jensen Huang returning to the chip-maker after allegations the CEO had an affairs with a suspected Chinese spy. Politicians in the US Congress have concerns over possible illegal chip exports to China and ties between the Trump administration and Nvidia. Republicans in the US Congress are pressing for sweeping investigations into the Nvidia scandal, mounting a rare challenge to Donald Trump as their hawkish stance on China puts them at odds with his support for the AI chip giant's reinstated chief executive. The return of Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang this week, 11 days after he resigned over extramarital affairs, reportedly including a relationship with a suspected Chinese spy, has intensified demands for answers and tougher controls on the sale of powerful artificial intelligence chips. Jensen Huang is back as CEO of Nvidia and US President Donald Trump is taking credit for the move. For Congress and experts alike, that is raising some flags. Mr Trump personally intervened to secure Huang's reinstatement, telling CNBC: "I made the deal." Nvidia's board said it had received input from senior US government officials and was confident Huang's reinstatement posed no national security risk, even though its own independent investigation remained unfinished. Republican Senator John Curtis demanded to know who had provided those assurances and why the board had reversed its earlier decision not to reinstate Huang. "Who in our government weighed in? What did they tell the board?" he wrote on X. As Nvidia's 'king' returns, reports of a chip 'underworld' to China emerge 'Extraordinary' decision to reinstate Jensen Huang has experts puzzled Why Donald Trump was so set on getting Jensen Huang back at the helm of Nvidia Why Jensen Huang's extraordinary return isn't the end of the Nvidia saga Senate Intelligence Committee chairman Tom Cotton warned that Mr Huang's reinstatement did not resolve the underlying concerns. "Congress has much to investigate," the Republican senator said. Public criticism of Mr Trump is rare among Senate Republicans, and the objections raised by at least six of them over Mr Huang's reinstatement represent an unusually strong show of dissent. Most, however, have directed their criticism at Nvidia or questioned the administration's assurances rather than attacking the president personally. Mr Huang is already scheduled to face questioning behind closed doors on December 1 by three Republican-led House committees: Foreign Affairs, Intelligence and the select committee on China. The three committee chairmen said his reinstatement and Nvidia's "brief internal investigation" did not erase the national security questions facing the company. Jensen Huang has acknowledged having extramarital affairs. ( Reuters: Ann Wang ) Mr Huang will also testify publicly before the Senate Banking Committee on December 3, while Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has agreed to appear before the committee on December 10, CBS News reported. At the heart of the scandal are allegations that Nvidia's advanced chips were diverted to China through Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company formerly led by Alice Huang, whom US intelligence suspects of working for Beijing. Reports have identified her as a woman with whom Jensen Huang had an affair, although he did not name her when acknowledging his infidelity. Mr Lutnick's commerce department faces scrutiny over its handling of Megaspeed, which had been under investigation over suspected violations of export restrictions. On Tuesday, local time, US Attorney-General Todd Blanche said Nvidia was "a good corporate citizen". "That shouldn't be groundbreaking," he said. "If Nvidia was the target or was subject to some criminal investigation, or they were obstructing or thwarting our investigation, then that wouldn't be the message that the president is saying to the American people." Last week Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said that several government agencies had supported blacklisting the company for months, but Commerce had delayed taking action. The department finally added Megaspeed to its trade blacklist Monday, the day Mr Huang returned to Nvidia.

events.title: Companies are getting less accurate data on extreme weather just when they need it the most
events.summary: Extraordinarily harsh droughts and heavy flooding have become more common around the globe this year due to an unusually strong El Niño. AP Photo/Charlie Riedel The extreme weather fueled by an unusually intense El Niño has caused flooding in low-lying Florida communities, hammered the California coast and upended hurricane patterns – just to name a few examples. But it also poses a growing challenge for companies that need timely climate data to manage supply chains. This information is disappearing due to federal budget cuts, leaving businesses less prepared to handle the impact of extreme weather. To be sure, forecasters saw the 2026 El Niño coming. The Climate Prediction Center at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, or NOAA, has been forecasting a very strong El Niño since the spring, and its October update put the odds at 83% that this El Niño will become the strongest since record-keeping began in 1950, likely lasting into early 2027. That kind of warning is valuable. It gives companies months to stock up, reroute shipments and line up backup suppliers before storms arrive or droughts set in. But bit by bit, other valuable sources of climate data are getting cut. That includes a federal database on disasters, which adds up costs weeks after the event, that NOAA stopped updating in May 2025. The Trump administration has also cut or undercut federal climate analyses, as well as staff and funding for daily forecasting , which has left large parts of the country without coverage during extreme events – a risky prospect for businesses. As a scholar of business operations and sustainability , I believe these cuts could have cascading effects on companies and supply chains by leaving them more vulnerable to future weather disasters. Eventually, these disruptions will hit consumers as well through higher prices. Gaps in climate science grow In North America, El Niño weather patterns are linked to severe storms in the Pacific, as well as floods, fires and droughts . The economic hit can be substantial, from transportation delays to massive crop failures. Strong El Niño events have historically cost the global economy trillions of dollars . This El Niño arrives as the pace of natural disasters picks up. While the U.S. averaged fewer than five “billion-dollar” disasters a year in the 1980s, that number now stands above 20 a year – a huge leap, even accounting for inflation. And the 2023 and 2024 totals were the highest on record. While the scope of weather damage gets worse and worse, critical data is missing. That includes NOAA’s decision to retire its “Billion-Dollar Weather and Climate Disasters” database, ending updates after 2024. For more than four decades, it tracked the cost of U.S. weather disasters after the fact – and businesses and researchers alike have relied on it to build prediction models. For example, scientists use these historical records to put odds on future losses or to forecast economic activity . Some of my own research also relies on historically accurate climate and weather data. Unfortunately, the gap in climate science may be widening. In 2025 the federal government shut down Climate.gov, which served as a central repository for weather and climate data, while its El Niño blog has been frozen since June 2025. The National Climate Assessments, the U.S. government’s preeminent reports on climate science, were taken offline , while the National Weather Service cited staff shortages as it cut back weather balloon launches at multiple sites , which feed forecast models. Fortunately, some of these data-gathering efforts have migrated elsewhere. The scientists behind the El Niño blog have moved to a nonprofit , while another nonprofit is carrying on the efforts behind the billion-dollar disaster database. El Nino’s effects, especially strong in 2026, have disrupted crops and supply chains around the world, including a delayed monsoon season in India. Ashish Vaishnav/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images What this means for supply chains The Trump administration has justified these cuts by citing high administrative costs and potential errors in the prediction models. But that still leaves companies, which lean on public weather data more than most shoppers realize, scrambling. In many industries, including retail, food processing and agriculture, the payoff from acting early to safeguard supply chains can be large. Real-time and near-real-time data is used in supply chains for enhancing crop yields, finding the best routes for transport, inventory planning, and ensuring worker safety during weather emergencies. For example, Walmart invests heavily in technology and specialists to monitor weather-related disruptions and build resilient supply chains. Another example is insurance companies, which use weather data for designing commercial insurance policies and processing claims. Risk Management Solutions Inc., a leading catastrophe risk-modeling company owned by Moody’s Corp., regularly use NOAA’s hurricane datasets to inform its advanced risk models. When public climate data disappears, companies still need timely information to run their supply chains, so some will pay for alternative data. This typically comes from paid private services and subscriptions. Startups such as WindBorne Systems, Sofar Ocean, Tomorrow.io, Black Swift Technologies and Saildrone offer private weather balloon data and advanced climate prediction services. While privatization can fill some gaps, it’s usually only the large retailers and insurers who can afford these forecasts. Smaller suppliers, local farmers and independent truckers further up the supply chain often can’t. And that’s exactly where many disruptions begin. What it means for consumers Shoppers feel these disruptions when shortages feed into higher prices, often months later. In 2024, for example, extreme weather in the Americas, including Florida, pushed U.S. orange juice prices to an all-time high that fall. They have have stayed elevated since hurricanes Helene and Milton battered Florida’s groves. Holiday staples are also not spared. A 2021 heat dome in the Pacific Northwest led to major damage to Christmas tree farms, causing their prices to rise an additional 5% to 10% that year . And these effects are often global. Poor rains in West Africa more than doubled cocoa prices in 2024, and that inflation is still feeding into U.S. chocolate prices, which were up 14% in 2026 . A historic El Niño, arriving just as federal climate data becomes sparse, makes this winter an ideal, if unfortunate, test of what climate information is really worth. events.title: Mitsubishi Electric Research Lab CEO on How He Reached the C-Suite
events.summary: The trajectory from researcher to top executive at a leading R&D organization doesn’t happen overnight. It took Anthony Vetro nearly 30 years to climb the corporate ladder at Mitsubishi Electric Research Laboratories , in Cambridge, Mass. He joined MERL in 1996, right out of college, and he has worked there ever since. Vetro probably is best known for his research in multimedia signal processing, focusing on video compression. Anthony Vetro Employer Mitsubishi Electric Research Laboratories, in Cambridge, Mass. Title President and CEO Member grade Fellow Alma mater Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn (now New York University’s Tandon engineering school) He became an IEEE Fellow in 2011 for his contributions to video coding, three-dimensional television, and multimedia adaptation. Mitsubishi Electric has moved away from making televisions. It now focuses on developing systems including ones used for defense, electronics, the energy industry, and space exploration. His ascension up the executive ranks began in 2018, when he was named a vice president and director of MERL. In 2023 he was appointed its president and CEO. He also works closely with the company’s new U.S.-based innovation facility in Cambridge. And he recently took on a dual role as deputy head of Mitsubishi Electric’s global R&D activities, including in Asia and Europe. Vetro credits IEEE with helping him develop his management skills after he served in several IEEE Signal Processing Society leadership positions. He also learned from his key roles in establishing international standards for digital image formats and video compression, he says. “Between my IEEE activities, standards work, and some of the business shifts in Mitsubishi Electric, I eventually graduated to more management leadership roles,” he says. A multimedia pioneer Vetro is the son of immigrants. His father came to the United States from Italy and his mother from Sweden when they were both in their early 20s. They settled in New York City, on Staten Island. Although neither parent went to college, his father stressed the importance of education to his son at an early age. “My father started in the mailroom and worked his way up to eventually managing communication accounts and infrastructure for large financial companies,” he says. “My mother worked in banks, first as a teller and later doing bank reconciliation after pursuing some professional certifications. “Through their jobs, they saw people with college degrees getting better positions and promotions, so education was something really ingrained in me.” Vetro says he developed a passion for mathematics and engineering in middle school. He was accepted into the Staten Island Technical High School , a specialized pre-engineering institution. There he solidified his interest in pursuing a career in the field. “A lot of students didn’t know what they wanted to major in at college, but I knew fairly early,” he says. He was accepted into the accelerated bachelor’s and master’s engineering degree programs at the Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn (now New York University’s Tandon engineering school ). He began his bachelor’s degree program in 1992 and the master’s program in 1994. “As part of the master’s degree program, I needed to do a thesis,” he says. “I wasn’t sure exactly what it would be on. Soon after taking my first course on image processing, I was certain that was an area I wanted to work in.” It was an interesting time, he says, because broadcast television was going through a major transformation, shifting from analog to digital during the early 1990s. It was long before streaming services, he notes. “I feel that industry-level engagement in IEEE is very vital to the organization in maintaining high relevance in the community and fulfilling its mission of fostering technological innovation and excellence for the benefit of humanity.” “The idea of being able to come up with compact ways to represent this very rich information was really appealing to me,” he says. “I’m also a visual learner. I liked seeing images, and there was some nice math behind them, too.” After he earned both degrees in 1996, Mitsubishi Electric hired him for its technical staff. He conducted research on multimedia signal processing, focusing on video compression. “The opportunity to work on projects around digital TV broadcasting and image processing attracted me,” he says. He conducted research in video conferencing, Internet and mobile streaming, and video coding technology, widely used for broadcasting, DVDs, and Blu-ray discs. He developed several technologies including digital TV receivers and displays, surveillance and camera-monitoring systems, automotive equipment, and satellite imaging systems. Another advantage of joining the company, he says, was that it allowed him to pursue a doctorate in electrical engineering, also from Polytechnic, while working. “That really sealed the deal,” he says. He received the degree in 2001. The road to management After six years as a technical staff member, he was promoted in 2007 to manage the group working on digital video coding, processing, and streaming. Seven years later, Vetro became its deputy director, a top-level management position that he held until 2018. “After working for about 10 years exclusively on video compression processing technology, there were some shifts in our company’s business. Its overall strategy began to change,” he says, “so I became interested in broadening my experience beyond video.” He was asked to lead the lab’s speech and audio team. It was more development-oriented, he says, and focused on vehicle infotainment and speech interfaces before Alexa and Siri existed. He pivoted the team’s focus more toward research and established strategic paths tailored to emerging opportunities within the organization. Recognizing emerging trends in sensing and information security, he formed groups that worked on them. Mitsubishi Electric’s first U.S. innovation hub To help spur innovation between Mitsubishi Electric and its U.S. customers, the company in June opened Serendie Street Boston , its first digital transformation hub in the United States. It’s colocated with MERL. The new office is modeled after the first Serendie Street collaboration space, which Mitsubishi Electric launched in 2024 in Yokohama, Japan. The word serendie is a combination of serendipity and digital engineering , according to the company’s website . Serendie is the digital platform designed to foster collaborations between data, people, and technology, it says. The space where people interact to extract ideas from the data is called “the street.” The platform brings together researchers, startups, customers, and partners to identify new products, test them, run pilot programs, and scale them up. events.title: Condition of Tasmania's ports a 'significant risk to the state'
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts TasPorts infrastructure poorly managed and exposing state to risks, auditor-general says The report states Tasmania's port infrastructure is "rapidly approaching" its end of life. ( Supplied: TasPorts ) Tasmania's ports are critical assets for the island's supply chain and economy. But the auditor-general says the deteriorating infrastructure has been managed poorly, requires significant investment and could face severe service disruptions. TasPorts and Building Tasmania have accepted in full or in principle the four recommendations made by the auditor-general. The auditor-general has issued a scathing report about Tasmania's port infrastructure, warning of significant future costs and potentially severe service disruptions. The government-owned company TasPorts operates 10 ports across the island state, including major ones in Hobart, Devonport, Burnie and Bell Bay. But in his report, Auditor-General Martin Thompson said the state's port infrastructure had not been managed well "for a long period of time". While noting "high-profile failures", including the delayed and over budget Spirit of Tasmania facilities in Devonport , he warned of potentially bigger problems in the future. The delay in building the new deeper water Devonport berth for Tasmania's new ferries contributed to a blowout of the project cost. ( Supplied: Tasmanian government ) Mr Thompson described current planning by TasPorts and Building Tasmania, formerly known as the Department of State Growth, as "inadequate". Martin Thompson says TasPorts has not been providing a full picture of its situation to the government. ( Supplied: Audit Tasmania ) "The result is that Tasmania is left with port infrastructure that is rapidly approaching end of life, likely to require significant increases in maintenance costs and experience more frequent and severe service disruptions and no clear pathway to funding the cost of replacement." He said the cost of maintaining existing infrastructure, or expanding it as TasPorts planned, would be "very expensive" and likely unachievable within its existing business model. "The current condition of Tasmania's port infrastructure presents a significant risk for the state," he said. "Decision makers need to consider all options for its mitigation, including rationalisation, decommissioning, renewal or replacement." The report says Tasmania's ports have not been managed effectively for "a long period of time". ( Supplied: TasPorts ) Out-of-control bushfire making a 'significant run' across Flinders Island Indigenous groups alarmed as NT flags fresh child protection overhaul Tasmanian greyhound racing ban defeated in upper house Sword, machete allegedly found in police metal detection wand search Lack of whole-of-state transport strategy criticised The report said an independent assessment valued TasPorts's assets at $477 million in 2025. But it found the cost of replacing the infrastructure would be closer to $1.29 billion. TasPorts's wharves , which were rated as being in a "poor" condition, accounted for almost half of the estimated replacement cost. But if TasPorts proceeded with plans to expand its commercial wharves, including climate change adaptation and electrification, the report said it could require an investment of $2.2 billion. Mr Thompson said the situation had partly arisen because there was no whole-of-state transport strategy to guide strategic decision-making. "Without such a strategy, Tasmania risks continuing to make port infrastructure decisions in isolation of other forms of transport infrastructure such as road, rail and air. He also said TasPorts had not been providing sufficient information about the condition of its assets and funding gaps to its shareholding ministers. "This is particularly critical given the current poor condition of wharf infrastructure and the level of future investment required," he said. "If ministers are not receiving advice on the key risks related to deterioration in asset condition, that can delay recognising the need and providing for asset renewal." The report noted the "high-profile" debacle of failing to construct the new port for the new Spirit ferries.
