events.title: Powderfinger secure all-star Australian support acts for reunion tour
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Powderfinger announce 52 all-Aussie support slots for tour, donate $100k to venues Powderfinger have secured 52 all-Australian support slots for next year's anticipated comeback tour. ( Supplied: Giulia Giannini McGauran/Live Nation ) It's the hottest reunion ticket in town. Powderfinger are playing 36 outdoor shows around the country in late 2027, their first tour since splitting in 2010. Today, the Brisbane band have fulfilled their promise to book an all-Australian line-up for their marathon comeback, unveiling the full list of support acts. For Powderfinger, reuniting wasn't about cashing in on nostalgia, but creating a cultural moment to bring some joy back to the band, and to a divided world. It's an impressive bill, bringing together established and emerging artists, and in many cases giving them a massive hometown stage. Joining Powderfinger in their native Brisbane will be Ball Park Music, DZ Deathrays, The Jungle Giants, Radium Dolls, Nice Biscuit, Beddy Rays, Vlads and Shag Rock. Playing both shows in Cairns are King Stingray, Dune Rats, Tullara and The Bluebottles. Perth will feature Jebediah, Old Mervs, The Southern River Band, Smol Fish, GRUB and Rowena Wise. The Sydney bill is stacked with the likes of recent two-time ARIA winners DMA'S, reunited rockers The Preatures, Middle Kids, The Buoys, The Lazy Eyes, Jem Cassar-Daley and William Crighton. Adelaide will host John Butler Trio, King Stingray, The Tullamarines and Any Young Mechanic. Melbourne is packed with Jet, Sarah Blasko, Grace Cummings, Gordi, Floodlights, Creature Fear, Sleepazoid and Loose Content. And Canberra will get to see Ball Park Music and Emma Donovan. Three of Powderfinger's 52 support slots have been reserved for triple j Unearthed acts, giving one young up-and-comer in Brisbane, Sydney and Melbourne a platform to play to tens of thousands of people. Forget My Happiness, these are Powderfinger's essential songs Powderfinger are back! What better time for fans old and new to revisit the legacy of the Brisbane rock icons? Unearthed will open a competition in early 2027, with any artist with a triplejunearthed.com profile eligible to enter for a chance to play alongside the 'Finger. "I remember when we played with The Angels in 1992," frontman Bernard Fanning told ABC's Zan Rowe . "We had no idea what we were doing. But just going and being inside the tent and seeing how everything operates, it's another step up from the local venue. Using their popularity to spotlight contemporary bands and showcase the "incredible wealth" of Australian talent has been a key part of Powderfinger's booking strategy, explains bassist John "JC" Collins. "It's a tough time to be a musician, or anyone working in the creative arts," he says. "Support slots give emerging acts the chance to play to bigger audiences and grow their fanbase. During Powderfinger's hiatus, Collins has operated multiple music venues and was appointed Queensland's nightlife commissioner. ( ABC News: Liz Pickering ) In the spirit of giving back, Powderfinger are also partnering with the Australian Music Venue Foundation (AMVF), donating $100,000 to the organisation. Launched last year and modelled after the UK's Music Venue Trust initiative, the AMVF aims to protect, support and sustain grassroots music venues around the country. "Kids aren't going out as much to see live bands, so those venues are closing, so then the opportunity closes down for bands," Fanning told Zan Rowe. Listen to Powderfinger's reunion interview Bernard Fanning and Darren Middleton joined Zan Rowe to talk about what prompted Powderfinger's reunion, adding extra shows, and more. He said the combination of declining live attendance , festival cancellations and Australians streaming less Australian music than ever has created "this domino effect" that threatens the entire ecosystem. Collins, who sits on the AMVF board and is Queensland's nightlife commissioner , says: “Grassroots music venues are essential to the future of Australian music." "They provide the first gigs, the first audiences and the first opportunities for artists starting out, but right now, all across the country they're under enormous pressure. "When I think about where it all began for Powderfinger, it was small venues like The Orient in Brisbane that backed us in those early years. "Those rooms gave us the chance to learn, experiment, fail, improve and ultimately become the band we wanted to be. They're the breeding ground for our next generation of artists.

events.title: Concert residency might be the future of touring
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts From Adele to Harry Styles: Why artists are staying put to perform Harry Styles plays stadium shows in Melbourne and Sydney starting this weekend. ( Supplied: Johnny Dufort ) Play all the time, tour occasionally. That's the approach Harry Styles has taken to live performance throughout 2026. Originally, the 32-year-old pop star's Together, Together tour consisted of 50 gigs in seven cities. The centrepiece was to be a marathon, 30-show run at New York's Madison Square Garden, followed by consecutive dates in Sydney and Melbourne. triple j brings you the best new music from Australia and around the world. Discover your next favourite artist here. It's not the same as it was. Styles told fans in September that he would supplement the residency shows with conventional concerts in 12 cities — but until 2027, the One Direction alumni will occupy single venues on repeat and on purpose. Like a growing list of international touring artists, Styles is prioritising quality over quantity, self-compassion over exertional malaise. Could this explain the rise of concert residencies? The perks of being a resident: mental health and creative control Life on the road often means mental and physical exhaustion. While jet lag, sickness and low morale are occupational hazards for touring musicians, residents can conserve their energy. "[Concert residencies] allow me to stay in my life while I'm doing it," Styles told Apple Music's Zane Lowe back in March . "Treat people with kindness" isn't just the mantra behind one of Styles's best-known songs — it's an ethos that extends to himself as well as his crew. For his recent New York dates, he took Manhattan three times a week for 10 weeks, accommodating personnel unwilling or unable to uproot their young children. Here, Harry followed a path already worn by Celine Dion, Usher, Lady Gaga and Adele, artists who've used Vegas residencies to stay closer to home. The Weekends With Adele concert series saw the UK star perform two shows per week at a Las Vegas casino from 2022 to 2024. ( Getty Images: Kevin Mazur ) During Elvis Presley's infamous Vegas tenure, playing show after show in a row signalled creative stagnation. But, unlike Elvis, these contemporary residents appear to be calling the shots themselves. Weekends with Adele conjured spectacle, intimacy and magical moments that, when disseminated on social media , kept the distant superstar in the public eye from 2022–2024. Together, Together lands in Australia this week, with Styles playing Sydney and Melbourne. But multi-night residencies are nothing new here: they're already a drawcard at the Sydney Opera House. "The artist is definitely doing us and the city a favour, and we're here to help realise their art in the best possible way for their audience," Sydney Opera House head of contemporary music Ben Marshall says. Previously, the Opera House has welcomed Solange , Sufjan Stevens and Mitski. Soon, iconic Britpop outfit Suede will bring their unique vision to life on its stages. "You can see the joy of it from an artist's perspective," Marshall says. "They get to settle into the room; they're not having to schlep between cities … There's just a beautiful way, if it's an exclusive residency, of having the country come to them." Rather than touring capital cities, Mitski drew fans to Sydney for a run of four sold-out Opera House performances in 2026. ( Supplied: Jordan Munns ) Similarly, where Styles praises the model for combating malaise and producing better shows, a smaller-scale residency can push Opera House artists to experiment. As Marshall says of the Redstar Wu's Neighbourhood Jams that award-winning Genesis Owusu conducted in September 2025: "That was a brilliant Australian artist prepared to do something really different." "He wanted to try out the show in a round that was a model for much bigger rooms, and the [Opera House] Studio is a great place to do that." Logistics in a post-pandemic world: Who pays the price? Concert residencies big and small are a sign of the times. "It's not like I'm saying I'll never travel again," Styles told Zane Lowe. "But I want to see what it looks like if you do it a different way." From Styles's perspective, it could look cost-effective. Ticketek Entertainment Group (TEG) told a 2024 parliamentary inquiry that touring expenses had increased by 30–40 per cent following the onset of COVID-19. Jayden Roy, a promoter and booking agent at Australian live music promoter Destroy All Lines, witnesses these challenges firsthand.

events.title: Arm strongarms site that hosts ad-free documentation and it may disappear
events.summary: Arm is swinging the hammer at an enthusiast’s site hosting a bloat-free version of its instruction reference documentation, demanding it be taken offline after several years of availability. The demand from Arm lawyers to Jon Palmisciano concern Jon’s Arm Reference , a site that provides the same arm Instruction Set Architecture (ISA) info available on Arm’s site, but with what Palmisciano describes as “without a million popups and all of the bloat” that Arm provides on its own. According to Palmisciano, his copy of the Arm ISA was culled from machine-readable XML files and stripped of the bloat. He built his version in 2022 with new CSS on top of it, and the addition of a quick search feature that, according to his comments on Hacker News, isn’t available in the official version. “The aim has always been to make it the most comfortable and bullshit-free browsing experience for people who need these docs daily,” Palmisciano wrote in HN. Based on the responses the site seems to have plenty of fans. That doesn’t matter to Arm, though: As far as the lawyers are concerned, Palmisciano’s site is a copyright violation due to its use of Arm trademarks and inclusion of copyrighted reference material for the Armv9-A and Armv9-A architecture. Arm doesn’t care if Palmisciano’s project is well intentioned or for the benefit of the many software developers that write code for its chipsets, either: They want it offline by December 4 – 10 days from the publication of this story – or else. As for what is going to happen, it seems like Jon’s Arm Reference will likely cease to exist in a little over a week – at least in its current form. “Ideally I'd love to just get permission from Arm to keep the site up, but I'm pretty pessimistic about that,” Palmisciano told us. That said, Palmisciano has “already seen a few archives and mirrors already.” The HN thread discussing the takedown order includes links to several versions, and Palmisciano has another trick up his sleeve that he’s considering playing: Open-sourcing the software he used to build his ISA page. “I'd also consider open-sourcing my tooling so that people can (for their own private use) turn the original XML downloads from Arm into an identical site they can host locally,” Palmisciano told us. He said that he'll likely tweet about opening the tooling if he does do so. He's also considered directing the URL for Jon's Arm reference to point to the open-source tool, but Arm wants the subdomain it's hosted on removed from his site as well, so that may not happen. Arm has been in touch to defend itself as well, saying that Arm appreciates the efforts of people like Palmisciano, but that it still has to protect its brand, and documentation. "We have a responsibility to ensure Arm is the primary source of technical resources and information and to protect the Arm brand," an Arm spokesperson told us. "Striking the right balance between third parties sharing helpful peer-to-peer resources while ensuring copyrighted Arm-related technical content is accurate has been critical to building the thriving ecosystem we have today." In other words, if you’re an Arm dev worried about losing a valuable resource and having to turn to a website that bombards you with junk just to look up a few simple opcodes and operands you’d better find a backup host before next month. That said, Arm is willing to work something out with Palmisciano, the company told us. "We have recently flagged our concerns with regard to the use of Arm copyright content and the Arm brand on this website and shared the Arm trademark guidelines," Arm explained. "Our hope is to open a constructive dialogue, and we've asked that the website owner reach out as we seek to resolve this." As Palmisciano posted on HN, Arm is asking for removal of its trademark and copyrighted documentation. That, Palmisciano said, "seems hard to work around while still keeping the site useful." He also followed up around 8.30 pm GMT on Tuesday to let us know that he has not yet heard directly from Arm. ®

events.title: Bull trap? Nvidia sell-off resumes day after historic rally
events.summary: Nvidia shares ​dropped again on Tuesday as the historic rally sparked by Jensen Huang's return to the chipmaker appeared to fizzle out, while other AI-related stocks also weighed heavily on the overall stock market. US markets have this year been buoyed by the aggressive buying of shares in chipmakers and other companies underpinning the artificial intelligence industry. But the so-called AI trade has taking a hammering in recent weeks as investors question whether the enormous sums being poured into artificial intelligence, particularly data centres and computing infrastructure, will generate sufficient returns. These concerns have been compounded by several major news events including high-profile tech outages and the Democrats winning control of Congress at the midterms. Investors had been hoping Nvidia's 31.5 per cent surge on Monday would turn things around after Mr Huang was reinstated as chief executive, but the relief rally appears short lived. Shares of Nvidia were down 5.86 per cent at market close, while other firms deeply connected to the AI boom were also sinking into the red. Anthropic, which made its public debut last week, dropped 6.54 per cent to $81.90, below its original price of $83 per share. Broadcom and CoreWeave were also red and the Nasdaq composite index dropped more than 1.48 per cent. Mr Huang returned to Nvidia on Monday following intense lobbying by President ⁠ Donald Trump , who appealed directly to the firm's board to reinstate the tech titan after he'd resigned over revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with businesswoman Alice Huang, whom US authorities are investigating to see if she had ties to Chinese intelligence. Analysts are warning that Mr Huang's reinstatement poses as many questions as it answers and does not resolve scrutiny of the company's management. "His return removes a major uncertainty, but what it leaves behind is an overhang on how Nvidia's governance is viewed," said Dan Sheehan, director of portfolio management at Telos Wealth Advisors. "There are also questions... about how involved the government will be in Nvidia going forward, and about governance of conduct internally given the stance the reinstatement implicitly took. Those don't get resolved by a soaring stock price." US legislators from both parties have sharply criticised Nvidia's decision to reinstate Mr Huang, saying Congress should scrutinise the circumstances surrounding his return. What is a bull trap? The whipsaw volatility of not just the AI trade but US stocks in general have raised questions about whether the AI boom that helped sustain market increases over 2026 is well and truly over. With the Democrats taking control of Congress in January, scrutiny of AI firms will only increase. Opposition to the construction of data centres could gain prominence as a national issue. Whereas Mr Trump has been an ardent supporter of data centre development, many of the new Democrats arriving in Washington were elected on a promise to push back. Investors and experts are warning that Monday's Nvidia rally could come to be remembered as a massive "bull trap", in which investors are lured into a seemingly resurgent market only for an underlying downward trend to resume shortly after. "As incredible as Monday was, I don't take it as a sign we're out of the woods ... a market that can rise $3 trillion on one headline can fall just as fast on another," Mr Sheehan told Reuters. Both Mr Huang and Nvidia are facing a host of state and federal investigations and reviews. Among these, the FBI is examining allegations concerning Mr Huang's relationship with the alleged Chinese intelligence asset, while the Justice Department and Commerce Department have been investigating whether Nvidia partner Megaspeed diverted restricted chips to China. Mr Huang is set to testify at a public Senate ​hearing on December 3, ‌while the company board's own investigations into potential ⁠foreign intelligence efforts, national security and export controls ​are still under way. "Now that the dust is beginning to settle, people are taking a ​more critical ‌look at [Nvidia's] decision... [The board] put themselves at a tremendous ethical and legal risk by the decision they made," ⁠said Peter Andersen, founder of Andersen Capital Management. He added that Mr Huang's upcoming testimony is also ⁠an "enormous risk to the company".

events.title: Jensen Huang Apologizes to Nvidia Employees in First All-Hands Since His Return
events.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told employees on Tuesday that the company’s code of conduct allows room for a “second chance,” that succession planning is a “flawed’ process,” and that he would work to rein in his “insanely intense” management style , according to remarks reviewed by WIRED. During his first all-hands since returning as CEO, Huang acknowledged that he violated the company’s policies and made some “very serious personal mistakes” that damaged his relationships with his wife and two children and prompted him to resign. But he said Nvidia’s board of directors made the appropriate decision for the company in welcoming him back. He added that the board made that call, not “the highest levels of our government.” Huang spoke for about an hour, offering deeply personal thoughts about his therapy sessions and drawing applause at times from employees at Nvidia’s Silicon Valley headquarters as he spoke about the company’s success and future. He didn’t take any questions. While some Nvidia employees celebrated Huang’s return, others remained concerned about his behavior and the board’s decision to reinstate him. “This is going to be the hardest company meeting I’ve ever done, and the second hardest meeting I have ever done,” Huang said as he began to speak. “The hardest meeting I’ve ever done was with my wife.” Nvidia’s board accepted Huang’s resignation earlier this month, citing concerns about his personal behavior and lack of candor following news reports about extramarital affairs, including one with a woman accused of having ties to Chinese intelligence services. The very same board reinstated him on Monday, just 11 days later, after receiving fresh assurances from Huang and learning from the Trump administration that he was not under federal criminal scrutiny and his return would not be a risk to national security. Huang and Nvidia, though, continue to face other legal and regulatory challenges. The board is investigating whether he was the target of foreign intelligence. US lawmakers expect him to testify before Congress next week. Lawsuits and other probes are ongoing into Nvidia’s disclosures about Huang’s behavior and its compliance with US export controls on chips. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Huang told staffers that he has been going to therapy “every day for an hour and a half” and that it’s “been helping me a lot.” He added that he “made some very serious personal mistakes. I hurt my family, I hurt my wife.” While Huang said he had never knowingly made a decision contrary to the company’s interests, he conceded that “in this one area” he had lacked “the courage” to disclose information that he knew would hurt his family, seemingly referring to the extramarital affairs. “The board and I spent the whole weekend together, and they, of course, they've been contemplating, and they've been collecting facts,” Huang said. “They came to the judgment that they would like to invite me back as the CEO, to give me a second chance.” The CEO emphasized that Nvidia’s code of conduct, much of which he said he wrote himself, still governs how employees are expected to treat one another and is intended to “create an environment that’s safe for people.” Huang told employees that violations of the code would not be tolerated. But that “does not mean, the moment you violate a code of conduct, we walk you out the door,” he said. “Facts, circumstances, a lot of assessments” would factor in. “It has to always be evaluated in the context of the human,” he said. “And this company has been more than gracious, more than thoughtful, more than fair in giving me a second chance.” Huang also pushed back against the notion that he had received preferential treatment because of his status in Silicon Valley. “There are rumors on the internet that apparently I’m a tech bro, and therefore I’m back,” Huang said. He rejected the suggestion that he was above the law or Nvidia’s code of conduct. Later in the meeting, Huang addressed criticism of his self-described “deeply intense, insanely intense” management style, acknowledging that his behavior had at times negatively affected employees. While Huang maintained that the intensity he brings to his job elevates those around him, he conceded that he sometimes takes things too far. “It disempowers them, and that’s not right,” Huang said. The Nvidia CEO said he needed to figure out how to maintain his level of dedication to the company without hurting the people who work there. “I need to hold myself to a higher standard at this time,” Huang said. He said that he would undergo a 360-degree performance review, soliciting feedback as often as monthly from people who work with him. The CEO added that he would be the first and only person at Nvidia to undergo such a review and that he did not want to institute the practice companywide.

events.title: USDA has no plans to probe death of hippo Fiona
events.summary: The USDA said it has not identified “any deficiencies” in the enclosure where Fiona the hippopotamus was housed and indicated it has no current plans to investigate circumstances surrounding her death, which has sparked public outcry. “USDA conducts routine unannounced inspections to assess compliance with the Animal Welfare Regulations and Standards, and we will continue to do so,” the USDA said in a statement to Semafor when asked if the agency planned to investigate the hippo’s death. “We have not identified any deficiencies in the hippopotamus enclosure.” The department also said that it has “no concerns about the quality of veterinary care that Fiona received.” After publication of this article, a USDA spokesperson said it was “inaccurate” to say the agency has no plans to investigate the hippopotamus’ death because it “conducts unannounced inspections of all licenses to ensure compliance with all applicable Animal Welfare Act Regulations.” Fiona died after swallowing a hat that had been thrown into her enclosure. A necropsy found that the hat had lodged in her small intestine, causing her death. Hippo Cove, Fiona’s enclosure at the Cincinnati Zoo, reopened Monday with additional protective measures intended to prevent a similar incident. “Even though the habitat already met strict standards set by the AZA, we made some modifications to guard against something like this ever happening again,” said Cincinnati Zoo Director Dave Jenike. “We added a layer of netting above the viewing windows and, out of an abundance of caution, removed all ceiling fans in the area.” 2016 probe The USDA has a history of investigating zoo animal deaths. In 2016, the department probed the death of Harambe, a gorilla who was shot and killed when a 3-year-old boy entered the gorilla enclosure. Although the USDA had found the enclosure’s barrier system compliant during an inspection one month before the incident, a subsequent investigation following Harambe’s death concluded that the barrier did not meet federal requirements. The Association of Zoos and Aquariums also defended the zoo’s safety standards following the hippopotamus’ death, saying an inspection conducted last year found no concerns with the hippo habitat. “The Cincinnati Zoo has been accredited since 1978 and was last accredited in 2025 after an exhaustive inspection, a standard practice for Zoos seeking or renewing accreditation,” AZA President Dan Ashe said. “Nothing was of concern for the hippo habitat in the inspection report. It seems like it was a freak event that couldn’t have been foreseen.” Fiona became an international sensation nearly a decade ago when she was born prematurely at the Cincinnati Zoo, with veterinarians giving her low odds of survival; her fight to live endeared her to audiences around the world.

events.title: An AI coding agent, a browser, and a Mac tool found a financial firm's access key in under 6 minutes
events.summary: A Romanian hacker, armed with only an open source coding agent, a Chrome browser, and a Mac, tried multiple ways to break into a financial services firm, ultimately found an access key - luckily, it was a decoy - and carried out an entire (almost) attack in under six minutes. It’s a stark reminder that miscreants don’t need sophisticated malware - as in the Binance heist - or AI pen-testing tools like ARTEX to carry out intrusions into critical networks. Open source coding agents, and specifically OpenCode in this case, also work just fine. “What surprised me most was how little it took and the toolkit: a free coding agent, the curl that comes with every Mac and an ordinary Chrome, all from one laptop,” Jesta co-founder and CTO Lior Finkelshtein told The Register . “Until now I thought that we had more time until tools like OpenCode are used in offensive operations. This incident shows us that it's already in use in the field, and we will probably see more of that in the future.” Jesta is a Tel Aviv-based security startup that builds defensive tools to detect and stop autonomous AI attacks. In a report shared exclusively with The Register , Finkelshtein documented an attempted intrusion targeting a major financial services company that’s also a Jesta customer - the security shop declined to say which one. Jesta’s investigation into the incident determined that someone in Bucharest downloaded a free AI coding agent called OpenCode and pointed it at the financial services customer on November 16 at 4:24:57 a.m. ET. 'Nothing in OpenCode was built for hacking' OpenCode is an open source coding agent that lets users connect to more than 200 model providers or local models, including Anthropic’s Claude models, OpenAI’s GPTs, Google’s Gemini, DeepSeek, and Z.ai’s GLM. Jesta doesn’t know which model the attacker used, as there was nothing in the traffic that named the model. OpenCode's web fetch tool, however, did name itself, so Jesta knows the attacker used this coding agent - not a scanner - to do the dirty work. “Nothing in OpenCode was built for hacking,” Finkelshtein said in a Tuesday report about the agent-led attack. But, he added, nothing in the coding agent “stops you from pointing it at someone else's website either. When you do, the agent goes through the site the same way it goes through code. It reads, tries something, reads the result and tries the next thing, for as long as you let it run.” That’s what it did in this operation, which took less than six minutes and cost the human operator nothing. The first call came from a Chrome browser on a Mac, requesting the front page of one of the financial firm’s systems. The site refused it, and six seconds later, the same IPv6 address in Bucharest, on an ordinary DIGI Romania business line, tried again. It used the same Chrome version, but said it was an Android Pixel 10 phone (it wasn’t) to see if the site would let a phone in (it didn’t). After failing to gain access through the front page, the agent asked the system for its API definition, which was also refused. Five seconds later, it tried a different address - this one was a decoy set up by Jesta - and it answered the agent, providing the readable file defining how the API works. The agent read the document, and 13 seconds later followed a link it contained. At 4:26:01 a.m. ET, Jesta’s defenses marked the website visitor as an AI agent, opened a case, and from here on out, everything the agent accessed was contained inside a fake environment designed to trick intruders. This included a phony key, which the attacker then used to attempt to break into the company’s systems. “It worked like a developer,” Finkelshtein said about the coding agent. “It read the API docs and did what they said. It found a key and used it. It checked whether the lock was real, then made up a key of its own and tried that. None of the threat feeds the customer has knew the address, so a blocklist would never have stopped it. The bar for doing this is now installing an app. Think about how many people can do that.” 'No blocklist would have helped' In addition to OpenCode, the attacker used only Chrome 157, both in desktop and mobile modes, and curl/8.7.1, a command-line tool that has shipped with every Mac since macOS 15. The agent passed information between the three tools. It included the planted key in a command-line request and then tested three scenarios – using the decoy key, no key, and a fabricated key – to determine whether what it found in the API documentation was legit. It also tried multiple URLs using the browser. While it ultimately identified a valid endpoint, it attempted to read from one that accepts only data submissions, so its request was blocked again. Five minutes and 44 seconds after the first request, it gave up, and the logs haven’t detected any activity from this same intruder since then. The security shop and its customer disclosed the activity to law enforcement and told us it’s “being handled.” While the attacker wasn’t able to steal anything in this attempt, security teams still need to take note, according to Finkelshtein. “No blocklist would have helped” detect the malicious traffic, he explained. “Most security tools still decide by asking whether an address is known to be bad, and for this one the answer was no. If that key had been real, it would have been in.” Instead of blocklists, Finkelshtein suggests paying attention to what the visitor does. In this case, several of its actions gave it away - including following a link that only existed inside an API doc, using a desktop browser and a fake phone, then curl, all from the same address within minutes, and trying multiple keys - including one with a made up name and then no key - within seconds. “Open source lets anyone build software without a big team,” Finkelshtein wrote in the Tuesday blog. “AI is doing the same for hacking. The skill is in the model, the model is a setting, and the person giving the instructions doesn't need to know how any of it works.” ®

events.title: Microsoft refreshes Copilot app search for users without an AI subscription
events.summary: Microsoft is updating search in its Microsoft 365 Copilot app for users without a Copilot license, with a toggle to restore the classic interface. Google, meanwhile, is giving AI searches more prominence on its homepage, where the familiar Search button is absent from a newly demonstrated layout. Microsoft's change is rolling out now and will hit Deferred Release by mid-January 2027. It will impact users with a Microsoft 365 license who do not have a Copilot license and "provides modern search controls to help users find, refine, and navigate search results more easily." It's enabled by default, which is a shame since administrators would likely prefer an opt-in rather than opt-out approach, and users can switch back to the "classic search experience" via a toggle on the search results page. Microsoft has not specified how long this toggle will remain available. Its separate Copilot Search experience had a fallback toggle scheduled for removal 60 days after general availability. "With the updated search experience, users can continue to find files using keywords, use modern search controls to refine and navigate results, and search supported connected third-party content when their organization has configured connected sources," Microsoft said. The results will still only display content to which users have permission. Microsoft advises administrators to brief users and help desks on the changed interface and the option to switch back. Microsoft's search tweaks arrive as the future of the Google Search button on Google's desktop homepage looks uncertain. In a post , Google VP of Product Robby Stein described a collapsible sidebar that lists users' recent AI conversations, pushing AI deeper into the search experience. Stein called it "a much simpler way to pick up where you left off," and said it would help customers "easily find & jump back into your recent AI searches." However, something else was obvious in Stein's post: the Google Search button was not present. Stein explained in August that Google had performed a "small test on desktop to help people find new things they can do with Search." Part of that test was the removal of the Google Search button. Users can still submit queries by pressing Enter. Stein said the test would have "no impact to how the core search works." The sidebar rollout doesn't itself confirm the Search button's permanent retirement. For now, its absence from Stein's demonstration is another sign of which features Google wants users to notice. ®

events.title: The UK and EU link their carbon markets
events.summary: The EU and the UK agreed to link their carbon markets in a deal that will reduce trade friction while helping to lower the costs of decarbonization. Since Brexit, Brussels and London have operated similar, but separate, emissions-trading systems that cap industrial emissions and require power plants and factories producing steel, chemicals, and cements to acquire allowances for every ton of carbon they emit. From 2028, allowances will be used interchangeably, creating a larger and more stable market that reduces the risks of investing in clean technology. The agreement also paves the way for mutual exemption of emission-intensive goods from carbon border levies, with the UK’s own carbon tariff coming into force in the new year. EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said work would also continue on the UK’s participation in the bloc’s electricity market, which industry groups say would make cross-border trading more efficient and strengthen the case for investments in interconnectors. — Chloé Farand

events.title: Climate action doesn't need consensus
events.summary: Tim’s view The breakdown of COP31 reveals a process in need of an overhaul, but the solution shouldn’t be hard to find. Depending on your perspective, the failure of negotiators in Türkiye to reach a consensus deal on transitioning away from fossil fuels may not actually be a failure. The UN process worked as designed: The minority of countries that wanted to avoid naming the root causes of climate change were blocked by the majority from pushing through a weak agreement. The compromises needed to achieve consensus in past COPs, the former UK climate advisor Michael Jacobs wrote this week , mainly served to dilute any sense of urgency; failure to reach an agreement is, in this telling, actually a stronger political signal about how deeply committed most countries are to decarbonization. The most obvious solution is to scrap the consensus-driven elements of the COP agenda altogether. In past summits, the topline “cover decision” agreement of the sort that crumbled in Antalya was primarily a kind of thesis statement, framing negotiations on a host of niche tracks, from carbon markets to adaptation finance. But in the decade since the Paris Agreement, there’s very little left to be negotiated. Instead, the cover decision wastes time and political capital trying to bring along a tiny minority of countries — primarily Saudi Arabia and Russia — that are unlikely to ever share the same views on climate change as, say, Tuvalu. It’s probably time to give up on this element of COP so that countries have more bandwidth to hash out action plans in smaller groupings, such as the electrification target that dozens agreed in Türkiye. The EU, which led opposition to the COP31 cover decision , and a number of African nations — next year’s COP32 will be in Ethiopia — have already said this week that the consensus approach is no longer fit for purpose. “The absence of agreement on the wording of the ‘cover decision’ does not mean an absence of action,” Angela Wilkinson, secretary-general of the World Energy Council, told me. “The test is whether we can change how we produce, deliver, and use energy: replacing fossil fuel use with cleaner electricity where it makes sense, and cutting emissions from the fuels we still need.” Notable Private sector investment in carbon-cutting and adaptation projects in Africa tripled in four years , reaching $26.5 billion in 2023-24, pointing to a shift in the continent’s climate finance landscape.

Please enter a search term. The Chancellor of the Exchequer has appointed Daniel E. Pinto as an external member of the Financial Policy Committee (FPC). Mr Pinto has over 40 years of experience in financial services, including in senior leadership roles across global financial markets, most recently as Vice Chairman at JPMorgan Chase. He will serve a 3-year term, which will begin on 4 January 2027. His appointment fills the position held by Jonathan Hall, who will step down from the Committee on 31 December 2026. Economic Secretary to the Treasury, Lucy Rigby, said: “The Financial Policy Committee plays a vital role in protecting and enhancing the stability of the UK’s financial system. Daniel Pinto's significant experience across global financial markets will be valuable for the Committee’s work. I would also like to thank Jon Hall for his contribution to the Committee over the past six years.” Andrew Bailey, Governor of the Bank of England, said: “I am delighted that Daniel will be joining the Financial Policy Committee. He brings an exceptional breadth of international experience and a perspective that will add greatly to the Committee’s discussions. My thanks also go to Jon for his dedicated service over the years.” Daniel Pinto, said: “I am honored to join the Financial Policy Committee and look forward to working with the Governor and my fellow members. The resilience and stability of the financial system are critical to a strong economy, and I look forward to contributing to the Committee’s important work.” About Daniel E. Pinto Mr Pinto has more than 40 years’ experience in financial services, most recently as Vice Chairman of JPMorgan Chase. He previously served as the firm’s President and Chief Operating Officer and as CEO of its Corporate & Investment Bank, having held a range of senior leadership roles across Europe, the Middle East, Africa and emerging markets. He has also served on a number of international financial services and corporate boards. About the Appointments Process The appointment follows a fair and open competition in line with the Governance Code on Public Appointments, and is subject to pre-commencement scrutiny by the Treasury Select Committee on 15 December 2026. Mr Pinto has confirmed that he has not engaged in any significant party political activity in the last five years. A panel interviewed a number of candidates and made recommendations to the Chancellor, which informed his decision. About the Financial Policy Committee The FPC is the UK’s macroprudential regulator: its objective is to protect and enhance the stability of the UK’s financial system by identifying, monitoring and addressing systemic risks. The FPC has thirteen members. Six of them are Bank of England staff: the Governor, four Deputy Governors and the Executive Director for Financial Stability Strategy and Risk. There are also five external members who are selected from outside the Bank for their experience and expertise in financial services. The Committee also includes the Chief Executive of the Financial Conduct Authority and a non-voting member from HM Treasury. events.title: Anthropic Created a Honeypot to Lure AI Agents Into Misbehaving
events.summary: Leather-clad billionaires aren’t the only ones who can be led astray by alleged honeypots . Researchers at Anthropic have developed Siren , a new honeypot test for artificial intelligence agents. The setup puts agents in realistic simulations designed to tempt them into misbehaving. How they respond will help researchers evaluate the likelihood that new models will go rogue when deployed in the real world, as well as the effectiveness of different safety measures. The test lets agents loose inside one of 26 different simulated sandbox environments. Various features of the sandbox are deliberately misconfigured to allow egress, while an enticing file containing things like passwords and apparent routes onto the internet sits just outside the sandbox boundary. The setup then presents tasks that tempt the agent to reach outside the sandbox without giving it explicit permission to do so. Crucially, the sandbox exists inside a second sandbox that’s cut off from the outside world to avoid real-life mishaps . “Models are going to continue getting better, continue finding zero-day vulnerabilities,” says Darya Kaviani, a researcher at Anthropic who specializes in security and helped develop Siren. A zero-day vulnerability is a previously unknown flaw in a piece of software that can be used to pilfer data or gain unauthorized access. Anthropic’s Mythos models are especially skilled at finding zero-day bugs because they lack the guardrails that normally block this kind of potentially malicious activity. Kaviani says we should assume AI models will become increasingly capable of finding and exploiting zero-days or figuring out other ways to break free from their constraints. The question then becomes whether they’ll resist the temptation to do so. AI agents—models that perfect actions autonomously—are becoming increasingly commonplace. They power capable coding agents like Claude Code and Codex , as well as peppy personal assistants like Meta’s Muse and OpenAI’s Dots . But the rise of helpful agents has been accompanied by some remarkable bad behavior. Agents tested by Anthropic, OpenAI, and others have broken free from sandboxes and even hacked into other companies in an effort to solve challenging problems. Assuming AI models continue to display such ingenuity, Kaviani says it will be crucial to do more than just patch software. “Even as we strengthen our infrastructure, models will be able to also keep up and be able to find vulnerabilities,” Kaviani says. Earlier versions of Claude are much more likely to fall into the honeypot trap than newer models, according to test runs with Siren. The more recent models have been given additional training designed to make them less likely to break the rules when performing agentic tasks. “We’ve added this in both our supervised learning sets and a few reinforcement learning environments,” says Oscar O’Rahilly, an Anthropic researcher who specializes in AI training and who helped develop Siren. “This could be a driving factor for why it has improved so much.” O’Rahilly says that models reason about whether to give in to temptation, which may partly explain why smarter models are less likely to break bad. Siren experiments also showed that giving Claude a simple additional piece of text explaining that it should not escape the sandbox resulted in drastically fewer efforts to break free. In Anthropic’s tests, Claude 5.5 and Claude Mythos 5.2 fell for the honeypot between 0.6 and 1.6 percent of the time. Two earlier models, Claude Mythos 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5, went rogue 12.7 percent and 25.8 percent of the time, respectively. AI models are sometimes known to behave better if they know they’re being tested. But O’Rahilly says other experiments suggest that Claude actually behaves more responsibly if it thinks a scenario is real rather than a test. As AI models get ever smarter, many researchers worry about whether they’ll outwit their human counterparts . If that does happen, then it may be essential that agents—and not just the executives responsible for them—can resist temptation. events.title: Microsoft brings serverless PostgreSQL into Fabric to bridge transactions and analytics
events.summary: Microsoft has brought its HorizonDB PostgreSQL service into public preview in Fabric, aiming to bring transactional and analytical workloads closer together. The corporation says applications can submit queries through a single PostgreSQL endpoint, with transactional and analytical work handled by the appropriate engines. Analysts said the move follows similar efforts by Databricks and Snowflake to combine operational databases with analytics. But tighter integration with Microsoft's stack could make applications harder to move elsewhere. Fabric HorizonDB joins SQL database and Cosmos DB in Microsoft's Fabric database portfolio. "By bringing operational databases, analytics, and AI together on a unified, governed platform, developers can build intelligent applications with less data movement and complexity. Fabric HorizonDB will also serve as the PostgreSQL backend for Fabric apps," Microsoft said. Microsoft first unveiled Azure HorizonDB in preview in November 2025 and made it generally available last week. It competes with other cloud database services and distributed systems such as CockroachDB and YugabyteDB, both of which support PostgreSQL's wire protocol. At the time, it said HorizonDB would offer "massive read scale without the need to replicate the database between instances." Speaking to The Register last week, Shireesh Thota, veep of Azure databases and Fabric applications, said that bringing the system into Fabric – its platform for data lakes, data warehouses, and analytics launched in 2023 – would connect operational data in HorizonDB with analytical data in OneLake, Fabric's unified data lake. "Once the data hits the OneLake storage, you can have analytical engines that take advantage of it. In HorizonDB, the PostgreSQL query engine can talk to the distributed query engine that we use in our Fabric data warehouse. We're fusing these query engines, thereby enabling the developers to submit a query that has pieces of the query that can work on OLTP and pieces of the query that can work on OLAP," he said. "The application need not worry about two endpoints, or about consistency of data and all that complexity. They can just talk to HorizonDB as a Fabric endpoint, and they can submit all these queries. We are basically operationalizing in OneLake." Operational data remains in HorizonDB's database storage, while mirroring maintains an analytical copy in OneLake, introduced in 2023 , which replicates a snapshot of the external database to OneLake in Delta Parquet tables and keeps the replica synced in "near real time." Thota said the process would not affect the transactional system. "Our core goal is to never impact OLTP workload while we are doing this, and we succeed [by] reading off the log as an additional replica to do this mirroring," he said. But the overall plan of putting serverless PostgreSQL OLTP in an analytics platform, bringing it close to OLAP systems, is one some vendors are already executing to meet the demands of new AI agent-led workloads. Adam Ronthal, research veep in Gartner's Data and Analytics Group, said: "The addition of Microsoft Fabric HorizonDB follows the 2025 acquisitions of PostgreSQL vendors by Databricks – Neon – and Snowflake – Crunchy. It delivers a high-performance, serverless operational RDBMS that is tightly coupled with Microsoft's lakehouse offering and well-suited to the ephemeral demands of AI agents. "Competing directly with AWS Aurora and Google Cloud's AlloyDB, HorizonDB acts as a foundational serving layer for the next generation of AI- and analytics-infused applications. For organizations aligned with Azure and Fabric, it provides an industry-standard PostgreSQL foundation for AI development." Andrew Snodgrass, research vice president of analyst company Directions on Microsoft, said the announcement of HorizonDB in Fabric was a "surprise," although "a watered-down version" compared to the version of the serverless database that became generally available on Azure last week. "It joins (document database) CosmosDB in Fabric and SQL database (based on the SQL Server engine) in Fabric. It highlights that Microsoft is still focused on making Fabric the data hub of their universe." HorizonDB – both in Azure and Fabric – is a PostgreSQL service which Microsoft says has 100 percent compatibility with the open source system that has enjoyed a meteoric rise over the last decade. The support for PostgreSQL has led some to question the software giant's commitment to its own proprietary OLTP system, SQL Server. Thota pointed out that the SQL database , based on the SQL Server engine, is already available in Fabric. Microsoft is also evaluating similar integration for that service, although he gave no timetable. "We are just beginning this journey, and most of the innovation is neutral to PostgreSQL and SQL. Some of it would be particular to how the individual query engine fuses with the analytical query engine. PostgreSQL does it slightly differently than SQL, but the idea is that most of the work is neutral. We are evaluating that work as well. I don't have timelines for that, but it is certainly in our thinking," he said. Nonetheless, Holger Mueller, principal analyst at Constellation Research, said it was good to see Microsoft go all in on support of open source. "In general, it is an acknowledgement that they cannot win the battle for the SQL database with SQL Server – as it is as proprietary as the leader Oracle – and now they bank on the openness of PostgreSQL as another approach," he said. However, using HorizonDB integrated into the Fabric/Azure stack may create so many dependencies with Microsoft's technology that lock-in to the vendor will remain a risk. "The primary concerns of open source – scale and support – have been eliminated by Microsoft's commitment and by now track record... the challenges are the embeddings of HorizonDB into the bigger Microsoft stack – which will make portability hard again. But every vendor wants and provides stickiness – clothed in ease of use and lower TCO," Mueller said. ®

events.title: US blacklists Megaspeed hours after Jensen Huang returns to Nvidia
events.summary: Jensen Huang was barely back in charge of Nvidia when Uncle Sam slapped Megaspeed –­ the Singaporean cloud provider at the center of the scandal that cost him his job ­­– on its trade blacklist. The US Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has added Megaspeed and a number of affiliated businesses to its Entity List, restricting their access to American technology amid an ongoing investigation into the suspected diversion of advanced GPUs to China. The final rule [PDF], filed Monday afternoon and scheduled for publication in the Federal Register on Wednesday, names seven businesses across Singapore, Malaysia, and Thailand, including Megaspeed's owner, Swiftdata, and Malaysian subsidiary Speedmatrix. Also in Washington's crosshairs is Apex Enterprise Solutions, a Singapore-based subsidiary of Chinese cloud computing giant Alibaba. BIS said the businesses posed a significant risk of diverting advanced computing hardware to recipients or applications not authorized by the US government. Anyone looking to supply the seven companies with goods subject to US export controls will need a license, with applications subject to a "presumption of denial." Despite the timing of Monday's announcement, the US government's interest in Megaspeed predates the revelations about Jensen Huang's private life by some considerable margin. In a joint statement issued last week, the Departments of Justice and Commerce confirmed that the latter had opened an investigation into Megaspeed in 2024 after spotting suspicious activity while monitoring potential violations of semiconductor export controls. Investigators requested records from Nvidia relating to both direct and indirect sales to Megaspeed in May 2025, and the GPU giant put the Singaporean outfit on its internal "no sell" list the following month. US investigators, accompanied by Singaporean law enforcement officials, subsequently visited Megaspeed's premises and interviewed its then-CEO, Alice Huang. The Justice Department has since taken the lead on the criminal investigation. Alice Huang, who is not related to the Nvidia boss, is a businesswoman with whom Jensen was said to be having an affair – he admitted to extramarital infidelity earlier this month , although he never name-checked the Megaspeed exec. According to reports, US intelligence officials suspected she was working on behalf of Chinese intelligence, though Beijing has rejected the espionage allegations. Megaspeed maintains that its business is lawful and says Alice Huang formally left the company in August last year. It has also enlisted outside lawyers to conduct an internal investigation. Nvidia's own Huang lasted all of 11 days in corporate exile. The chipmaker's board unanimously voted to reinstate its co-founder as president and CEO on Monday, less than a week after board chairman Harvey Jones indicated that bringing him back wasn't on the cards. The U-turn followed a lobbying campaign by some of Silicon Valley's biggest names, including Elon Musk , and some rather more consequential intervention from the White House. President Donald Trump told CNBC on Monday that he had personally persuaded Nvidia's directors to give Huang his job back. Nvidia's board said it had received assurances from senior US government officials regarding the national security implications of Huang's return. There are still plenty of people in Washington who have questions for Huang, however. The Nvidia boss is due to sit down with three congressional committees on December 1, with the chipmaker's general counsel, Tim Teter, scheduled to face lawmakers the following day. Nvidia has also established a board-level committee to oversee national security and export control compliance, putting its trade compliance personnel under the supervision of three directors. Nvidia shareholders may be delighted to have Jensen back, but the returning CEO has barely a week to prepare for his congressional grilling over the affair that helped bring about his departure. ®

events.title: Anthropic falls below US$83 IPO price in swift reversal after record listing
events.summary: The stock was last down 5.4% at US$82.78, extending a steep retreat from its US$111.50 opening price on Nov 19. Anthropic’s shares fell below its US$83 IPO price on Nov 24, after a record Nasdaq debut and a sharp drop from its US$111.50 opening. The fall has raised worries about stretched AI valuations, high data-centre costs, and slower growth if investment in computing slows. Future risks include insider selling and stronger competition from cheaper open-weight AI models, though index buying may support the stock soon. NEW YORK – Anthropic’s shares slipped below their US$83 initial public offering price in early trading on Nov 24, a striking unwind just days after the Claude developer’s record-breaking Nasdaq debut. It had closed 17% above the IPO price in its debut trading session but has since been swept up in a broader technology selloff that pushed the S&P 500 and the Dow into confirmed correction territory the previous week. Anthropic’s rapid reversal has added to concerns about stretched AI valuations and the vast sums being poured into computing infrastructure, with rising interest rates threatening to push those costs even higher. As the first frontier AI company to go public, Anthropic is widely seen as a proxy for the sector. “If we do see a slowdown in the data-centre buildout, then that obviously can impact the speed at which Anthropic can develop and therefore future revenue and therefore its valuation,” said Fiona Cincotta, senior market analyst at StoneX. Anthropic missed out on a broad Wall Street rally driven by AI-related stocks after Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive on Nov 23. Anthropic is not alone among blockbuster technology IPOs in quickly surrendering early gains and falling below its offer price. SpaceX, whose US$85.7 billion June listing was the world’s biggest before Anthropic, took about a month to fall below its offer price. In 2012, Facebook, now Meta Platforms, slipped below its offer price on its second trading day. The comparisons show that a swift loss of an IPO premium is not unprecedented even for highly anticipated listings, and that an early break below the offer price is not necessarily a guide to longer-term performance. “Like most IPOs, it probably came in overpriced and it is now the real price discovery as to what the true value should be,” said Peter Andersen, founder of Andersen Capital Management. After touching US$2 trillion in valuation on debut day, Anthropic was last trading at a US$1.5 trillion valuation, which is about 40 times its sales over the last 12 months. With Anthropic’s shares now testing their IPO price, attention is turning to risks that could determine where the stock goes next, including insider selling, pressure from open-weight models and a potential slowdown in data-centre investments. Anthropic’s IPO lock-up provisions allow certain employees and insiders to sell portions of their holdings from the first trading day, with further staggered releases tied to earnings announcements. Chief executive Dario Amodei and president Daniela Amodei sold more than 3.37 million shares worth over US$280 million each to the IPO’s underwriters a day after the debut, according to a filing late on Nov 23. Anthropic’s underwriters also exercised their option to buy additional shares, lifting the IPO’s gross proceeds to a record US$93.5 billion, while removing a potential source of support for the stock after its debut. Anthropic also faces growing competition from cheaper open-weight AI models, which it has warned could pressure pricing. Users can download and adapt models from DeepSeek, Mistral and Moonshot AI, unlike proprietary models such as Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini, with Chinese developers in particular gaining ground globally. Huang’s return could also sharpen the competitive threat to Anthropic, given his strong advocacy for open-weight AI models. Some support could emerge in the coming days as Anthropic’s addition to major indexes prompts buying from passive funds. Index rebalance analytics firm Intropic estimates passive funds could buy up to 30% of the shares offered by year-end. MSCI will add Anthropic to its global standard indexes as of the Nov 30 close. events.title: Saudi Arabia approves $371bn budget as non-oil growth slows
events.summary: Saudi Arabia has approved a 2027 budget with spending of SR1.39 trillion ($371.2 billion) and a deficit of SR190.56 billion ($50.8 billion), as the kingdom recovers from a war-driven slump in oil output and slower growth in the rest of the economy. Revenue is estimated at SR1.2 trillion, the cabinet said on Tuesday after a session chaired by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman. The figures are in line with the Finance Ministry's pre-budget statement in September , which put the deficit at about 3.6 per cent of gross domestic product. That would be narrower than this year's shortfall. In September, the ministry estimated that the 2026 deficit would reach SR245 billion, or 4.9 per cent of GDP, well above the SR165 billion projected in last year's budget , as the war disrupted oil exports. "We are maximising the impact of the Vision on people's lives, transforming its achievements into a sustainable strength for our economy and renewed opportunities for future generations," Prince Mohammed said in a statement carried by the Saudi Press Agency, referring to Vision 2030, the kingdom's plan to diversify its economy away from oil. The budget comes as Saudi Arabia enters the third and final phase of the programme, which runs until 2030. Non-oil activities are now estimated to grow 2.5 per cent this year, Prince Mohammed said, down from the 3.2 per cent the ministry forecast in September. The ministry expects the overall economy to shrink 3.6 per cent in 2026, after a 21.8 per cent drop in oil activities, before rebounding 12.8 per cent next year. Prince Mohammed said regional events had shown the economy's ability to adapt, pointing to investment in the East-West Pipeline and ports on the Red Sea coast. Those routes have allowed the kingdom to keep oil and other exports flowing while avoiding the Strait of Hormuz. The budget announcement comes as Saudi Arabia continues to face Houthi attacks. On Tuesday, a tower in Riyadh's financial centre was targeted in what the Saudi-led coalition described as a "cowardly terrorist attack". Last week, a Houthi strike damaged the Public Investment Fund tower in the same district. Prince Mohammed said the kingdom would defend its security, sovereignty and national assets "with strength and resolve". National security and stability were the foundation for preserving development gains and building military and defence capabilities, he said, praising the armed forces and security personnel stationed on the borders. Finance Minister Mohammed Al Jadaan told reporters the kingdom was "resilient enough to withstand a prolonged conflict" with the Houthis. The idea that "blackmail by missiles" could make Riyadh compromise on national security was "a total mistake", he said. Blackmail by missiles … is a total mistake Mohammed Al Jadaan, Saudi Finance Minister Brent crude was trading near three-month lows on Tuesday, below $90 a barrel, as rising supply outweighed concerns about shipping in the Gulf. The budget prioritises social support for those most in need, infrastructure and public services, and transport and logistics networks, as well as defence spending. Prince Mohammed said government entities must improve spending efficiency, measure results and align resources with national strategies. He said public debt would be kept at sustainable levels and the government would maintain "substantial" reserves. The Public Investment Fund and the National Development Fund will continue to back strategic sectors and private sector investment, he added. Alongside the budget, King Salman issued a royal order allowing the General Organisation for Social Insurance to compensate Saudi employees of eligible companies for up to three months through its unemployment insurance scheme, known as Saned. A committee of the ministers of finance, economy and planning, and human resources, along with the head of the social insurance agency, will decide which sectors and companies qualify. The Finance Ministry is expected to publish its full budget statement, including spending by sector and its borrowing plan, in the coming days. Mohamad Ali Harisi contributed to this report

events.title: Claude Ship puts AI at the helm of pull request approvals
events.summary: Anthropic has introduced Claude Ship to review, fix, and approve pull requests (PRs), offering more AI automation to help teams handle the output of AI coding tools. Claude Ship combines the generally available Code Review service with two new agents in beta: PR Steward and Claude Approvals. It is available to Claude Team and Enterprise customers using GitHub repositories. Anthropic said : "On the Claude Code team, Claude writes most of our code, and we wanted everything after the PR to move that fast too." Its stated goal is to "ship code as fast as teams write it." One consequence of the AI coding revolution is the sheer amount of agent output, which requires review and approval before going live. Claude Ship is one way to address that by automating more of the workflow. PR Steward works through failing continuous integration (CI) checks, merge conflicts, and review feedback. Claude Approvals can actually approve a PR, something that might rattle the nerves of some engineers. Claude Approvals applies an approval policy, written by the team as a file in the repository. "Claude can approve routine changes on its own if the policy allows it, or can require deeper human sign-off for certain scenarios," Anthropic said. The company advised caution: "For most customers, we recommend enabling this first in observe-only mode to build confidence before configuring branch protection to require Claude Approvals' green light." While developers can try Claude Ship on their own pull requests (depending on their permissions and the repository's branch rules) with a /ship command in Claude Code, administrators can set up the rules on a repository-by-repository basis. "Claude Approvals starts when a connected repository has a policy file on its default branch, and an admin can turn it off," Anthropic said. "Teams set the pace. They can start with one repository, choose a review level and when reviews run, set a monthly spend limit, and run their approval policy in observe mode until they trust it." The extra automation also brings extra charges. Usage is token-based, and even observe-only approval policies can incur costs if they invoke classifiers or Code Review. Anthropic also includes the familiar disclaimer: "Claude Ship uses AI and may miss bugs, security vulnerabilities, or other issues." The Register spoke to an engineer who works for a company that uses Claude. They were a little cynical about the whole thing, saying: "It just seems like a glorification of what I already use Claude on – git merge or git rebase. "Our golden rule so far with Git is to limit Claude to read operations there; this layer of separation still lets devs stay in control and allows them a judgment of the AI changes – what to keep, tweak, or commit. "If that's offloaded to Claude and it has Git history-rewrite access, the devs will lose that overview and judgment opportunity." How much authority Claude receives depends on the organization's configuration. Approval is not the same as merging, and existing branch protections and required checks still apply. Anthropic's answer to a growing queue of AI-generated changes is more AI. Teams still have to decide which decisions they're prepared to delegate. ®

events.title: Smarter regulation means understanding the trade-offs
events.summary: Regulation inevitably involves choices.Protecting consumers and maintaining confidence in our markets are fundamental to what we do. But rules also have costs. They can affect businesses’ decisions to invest, innovate and compete. Good regulation means recognising those trade-offs and using evidence to decide where intervention will make the biggest difference.That is why economics matters so much to good regulation.At our annual Economics Conference, economists, academics, regulators and industry experts came together to explore how smarter financial regulation can support sustainable growth and innovation. Across the day, speakers challenged us to think carefully about how regulation affects behaviour, markets and investment, and how better evidence can help us make better decisions.Being proportionate about riskA well-functioning financial system cannot be risk-free, nor should we try to make it one.Our role is to understand where intervention is necessary, where the costs could outweigh the benefits, and how we can achieve the outcomes we want in the most proportionate way.That means being proportionate. Accepting that risk exists does not mean lowering standards. It means thinking carefully about which risks really require regulatory intervention and designing our response accordingly.We can already see what that means in practice. Measures we have delivered, planned or have in progress are expected to reduce firms’ annual administrative burden by more than £330m net, using the government’s methodology, with around £117m of annual savings already delivered.Our wider reforms are also about making sure regulation keeps pace with changing markets and supports better outcomes. That includes proposals to give pension providers greater investment flexibility to support long-term value for savers, alongside streamlining reporting for asset managers and fund operators and making the Senior Managers and Certification Regime more proportionate while preserving its core accountability objectives.But reducing costs or requirements is not an end in itself. The more important question is whether regulation achieves its intended outcome in the most effective and proportionate way.Evidence, not assumptionThat was a recurring theme throughout the conference: regulators need to keep testing whether interventions are working as intended.We should not assume a regulatory intervention works simply because the rationale for introducing it was sound. We need to look at what happens in practice.That means using data and evidence to understand the costs and benefits of regulation, identifying unintended consequences and, where appropriate, being prepared to change our approach.Our conference reflects that. Discussions range from behavioural and data-driven regulation to wholesale markets and policy evaluation, as well as how changing technology and financial markets should influence the way regulators think and act.This is also why engaging with researchers and the wider economics community is so valuable. Challenge from outside the FCA helps us test our assumptions, expose gaps in our thinking and better understand how our decisions affect growth, productivity and investment. Strengthening that engagement is one of the objectives of this year's conference.Opening up the conversationWe want that exchange of ideas to continue beyond today.We are inviting researchers to share ideas for areas where further research could help deepen our understanding of financial regulation and its effects. You can contribute to our research agenda.The questions regulators face are rarely simple. New technology, evolving markets and changing consumer behaviour will continue to create new risks and opportunities.Economics cannot remove those difficult choices. But it can help us make them more consciously, transparently and on the basis of evidence.That is an important part of what smarter regulation should mean: being clear about the outcomes we want to achieve, understanding the trade-offs involved and continually asking whether there is a better way of getting there.

events.title: How does EIA compare different types of energy?
events.summary: U.S. Energy Information Administration - EIA - Independent Statistics and Analysis Browse by tag liquid fuels natural gas electricity oil/petroleum production/supply crude oil consumption/demand generation prices map states exports/imports international coal renewables weather forecasts/projections gasoline capacity steo (short-term energy outlook) Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Monthly Energy Review Note: Btu=British thermal units To compare production and consumption across different resources, we convert to a common energy metric, British thermal units (Btu), which typically measures the heat content of the fuels such as petroleum, natural gas, and coal that are burned for energy. For energy sources such as hydropower, wind, solar, and geothermal that aren’t combusted to create energy, we apply a constant conversion factor based on the heat content of electricity. For combustible fuels, EIA uses thermal conversion factors to convert the physical units into heat content values. Because these factors can change based on the specific characteristics of fuels being produced at different points in time, we update our conversion factors each year. We publish heat content data for more than 30 petroleum products, 4 types of coal, and natural gas. Each fuel has a unique chemistry and heat content, and the heat content can vary based on the different types of fuel in the mix. For example, the heat content of anthracite coal is higher than the heat content of lignite . The aggregate heat content of coal generally varies based on the mix of the different types of coal produced and consumed. The aggregate heat contents for petroleum consumption and production have declined in recent decades because of decreasing use of residual fuel oil , which has relatively high heat content, and increasing use of fuels with a lower heat content—such as motor gasoline, distillate fuel oil, and hydrocarbon gas liquids. Our heat content estimates for natural gas have fluctuated within a relatively narrow range because of highly consistent pipeline specifications. Methane, the primary component of natural gas, has a heat content of 1,010 Btu per cubic foot. Other gases such as ethane, biomass gases, synthetic gases, and supplemental gases, which may be left in the natural gas stream, have higher heat content values. Total coal thermal conversion factors depend on the relative mix of coal types consumed and produced that year. Anthracite and bituminous coals have higher heat contents than lignite and subbituminous coals. Subbituminous coal production and consumption have increased over time, bringing down coal’s aggregate heat contents. To measure how efficient a power plant is at converting the fuel into electricity, we use heat rates. While thermal conversion factors measure the heat content of a fuel, heat rates measure the efficiency of power plants to convert fuel into heat and then into electricity. The heat rate is the amount of energy used to generate one kilowatthour (kWh) of electricity. The lower the heat rate, the higher the efficiency of a power plant to convert fuel into electricity. Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Monthly Energy Review Since 2001—the earliest year in our data—heat rates for electricity generation from coal and petroleum have risen slightly, while the heat rate for electricity generation from natural gas has gone down, due in part to more efficient combined-cycle plants coming online. Power plants using nuclear energy and noncombustible renewables —such as hydro, wind, solar, and geothermal—generate electricity without burning fuel. For nuclear energy, EIA uses a measurement of the heat produced from nuclear fission in the reactor core. For noncombustible renewable energy, we use the captured energy approach . Captured energy is the energy available for consumption after converting a renewable resource into electricity, net of conversion losses. The captured energy approach uses the heat content of electricity, which is constant (3,412 Btu/kWh).
