events.title: Volkswagen starts crunch wage talks as workers carry coffins in protest over cuts
events.summary: Volkswagen works council chief Daniela Cavallo and IG Metall chief negotiator Thorsten Groeger march with workers on Nov 24. Volkswagen began wage talks in Emden as workers protested cuts with black coffins, saying trust and the company’s future were at risk. Management wants pay freezes, fewer benefits and longer hours, while unions warn of strong industrial action if no deal is reached. The carmaker faces pressure from China competition, weak sales and high costs, with 100,000 layoffs planned and German plants under review. EMDEN, Germany – Volkswagen began crunch wage talks with labour representatives on Nov 24 amid mounting worker anger over deep cost cuts, with protesters carrying black coffins to symbolise what they said was the death of trust and the company’s future prospects. Intensifying competition from China, billions of euros in annual tariff costs and rapid technological change have put the world’s No. 2 carmaker under pressure to overhaul its global business, with 100,000 layoffs planned. Volkswagen’s plants in Germany have been a focus of the restructuring, with four identified for possible closure early next decade and management telling the group’s 120,000 German workers that domestic production has become too expensive. The first round of talks takes place in the northern German town of Emden, home to one of the factories fighting for survival, where around 4,000 workers protested before representatives of the IG Metall union and the carmaker’s works council met Volkswagen management. “If necessary, there will also be industrial action of a kind never before seen at Volkswagen,” works council head Daniela Cavallo told workers chanting “strike-ready” and carrying black coffins inscribed with the words “future” and “trust”. “Before we discuss any specific issues, we need to clarify a few basic points first,” she said, adding the cuts proposed by management were no basis for negotiations. Volkswagen has said it wants to freeze German workers’ pay in 2027 and 2028 while cutting a range of benefits. It is also seeking concessions to the union’s hard-won 35-hour week, asking staff to work longer on the same pay when needed. A letter from the company to labour representatives, seen by Reuters, showed a raft of proposed cuts that went further than management had publicly announced when it laid out its position ahead of the talks last week. Volkswagen still hopes to strike an agreement with workers in 2026, the group’s co-chief negotiator Frank Ischner said, adding that while the cuts were painful, they were inevitable. Citing sluggish sales, dwindling cash and weak margins at the group’s core VW brand, management wants to abolish special wage agreements for managerial staff and anniversary bonuses paid to workers in their 25th and 35th years at the company, according to the letter dated Nov 19. Strikes could begin from Jan 1 at Volkswagen after the union said the renewed restructuring push put the carmaker in breach of a late-2024 restructuring deal. “Then, it won’t just be the production lines that come to a standstill,” IG Metall chief negotiator Thorsten Groeger said, adding that investors, most notably the Porsche and Piech families – Volkswagen’s top shareholders – may face dividend cuts, too. The initial 2024 agreement included 35,000 layoffs in return for employment and investment guarantees. Since then, Volkswagen’s China sales, which long helped offset Germany’s high production costs, have fallen further, and the group’s operating margin is expected at no more than 1% in 2026, down from 5.9% in 2024. events.title: Anthropic posts $405,000-a-year job for gas specialist to secure fuel for AI
events.summary: Anthropic is offering a natural gas specialist up to $405,000 annually to secure fuel for its data centres, underscoring how the race for AI computing capacity is turning tech companies into energy buyers. The Claude developer has advertised for a gas supply and transport lead to negotiate fuel contracts and manage pipeline deliveries to its data centres in the US and Canada, The Wall Street Journal reported. “If gas does not arrive, in the volume and at the pressure the plant needs, the compute does not run,” the listing says. The annual salary of $320,000 to $405,000 is about double that offered for comparable roles recently, the newspaper reported. It comes as Anthropic's shares fell below their $83 initial public offering price in premarket trading in New York on Tuesday, dropping 6.5 per cent to $82. The company, which raised $93.5 billion in the world's largest IPO , opened at $111.50 on its Nasdaq debut on November 19 and closed that day at $97.17 . Technology companies are increasingly bypassing electricity grids to power data centres, using gas turbines, reciprocating engines, diesel generators and even repurposed jet engines to avoid lengthy waits for grid connections. Anthropic, which was not pursuing off-grid developments last year, has since emerged as one of the leading developers, according to research company Cleanview . In August, it struck a deal with reciprocating engine supplier ERock. The company has committed about $900 billion in spending, almost entirely on computing and infrastructure, with about half due by the end of 2030. The shift towards off-grid generation comes at an environmental cost. Electricity generated by on-site engines and turbines can produce 63 per cent to 80 per cent more greenhouse gas emissions than grid power, climate scientist Zeke Hausfather estimates. Unlike several of its big technology rivals, Anthropic has no long-standing emissions targets. The company identified changing environmental standards for power generation as a risk in its IPO prospectus and says it aims to adopt pollution-reducing technology and use more low-carbon energy. The scale of off-grid development could also depend on the fate of bipartisan-permitting legislation in the US Congress aimed at accelerating grid connections.

events.title: Jensen Huang's Nvidia comeback leaves him unfireable and indebted to Trump
events.summary: Liz’s view Fine, Jensen Huang can come back. Nvidia’s board cannot. In a truly Keystone Kopsian display of corporate governance, Nvidia’s comically weak board reversed itself in six days . It either caved to a lame-duck US president — who, as Semafor scooped yesterday, called into Nvidia’s board meeting Sunday to lobby for a “national treasure” — or gratefully took the air cover he provided them to bring back a CEO who appears to have lied to them repeatedly. After firing Huang without all the facts, they rehired him still lacking those facts. The interim period encouraged a parade of Jensen School of Management stories , unimportant to the questions at hand but now an unflattering part of Nvidia canon. And Huang is unfireable now, even if the ongoing investigation turns up new bad facts, which it almost certainly will. Law firm Wachtell and its investigator, Joon Kim, might as well withdraw from what is now a no-win assignment. I’ve written before that we should all be a little less puritanical about intraoffice relationships . But CEOs can’t sleep with customers, for no other reason than that it makes other customers mad, and they can’t sleep with spies, for reasons that don’t require elaboration. Set aside the national-security breach: One of the most important people in the business world, on whose every move hang trillions of dollars, has been walking around with a giant “Blackmail Me” sign taped to his back. It’s now been replaced by an explicit debt to President Donald Trump, to whom Huang literally owes his job. His comeback has repaired Nvidia’s stock price, sort of: Even Monday’s restored only about a third of the value lost since the AI trade began wobbling in September. But Huang cannot protect Nvidia, or the bull market that Trump appears determined to prop up, from the laws of gravity starting to assert themselves. Money is getting prohibitively expensive as AI’s let-a-thousand-flowers-bloom era comes to a screeching halt. The data-center buildout is one construction delay or faulty grid hook-up from a calamitous and contagious flu. The AI labs have huge trust gaps with the customers they need to generate the revenue for all the Nvidia chips and GE turbines and Dell servers they’ve signed contracts to buy. The hyperscalers burned through their cash and are now burning through other people’s cash — they’re turning to Canada , one Wall Street executive told me yesterday, with a for-Pete’s-sake eye roll. Democrats are none too happy and Huang’s GOP allies are politically weakened. Having bullied his board into submission, Jensen Huang is now the most powerful corporate executive in the world. He’s still not powerful enough to outrun all of that. The question is whether, when he fails to do so, he retains Trump’s loyalty or becomes his fall guy. Notable “Huang has become the figurehead of the AI boom and one of the few people who can move the dial on sentiment across the sector,” an analyst told Reuters. Huang’s return was pushed by a faction of Silicon Valley’s elite, but small traders piled in and reaped the rewards , Semafor’s Jake Angelo and Ellen DiMauro write.

events.title: FCC proposes 'tit-for-tat' restrictions on foreign satellite operators
events.summary: The US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) will vote in December on proposals [PDF] that would restrict foreign satellite operators in the same way their home countries restrict US providers. The telecoms regulator says the move is to "ensure reciprocity and fair dealing" in the rules governing satellite operators. The main aim appears to be hitting back at European efforts to build up the region's own space communications industries. According to the FCC, the US has so far welcomed satellite systems licensed abroad on a level playing field, but that regulators elsewhere have begun holding US systems to different rules than they apply to their own domestic suppliers. "This has operated to the disadvantage of American satellite providers that are or may be burdened with regulatory and spectrum limitations that their competitors in foreign nations simply do not face," said FCC chairman Brendan Carr. The FCC has singled out the EU's Digital Networks Act , which proposes harmonized connectivity rules across the bloc. A separate proposal would overhaul authorization for mobile satellite services (MSS) in the 2 GHz band after existing rights expire in May 2027. Earlier this year, the FCC laid out some of its concerns, saying that EU-wide authorization of satellite spectrum would replace the national licensing by member states "with which US satellite operators have become accustomed," and could require wholesale relicensing of any US systems operating in Europe. "The FCC voting on foreign satellite companies is consistent with the Digital Networks Act, but is more of a response to the EU's decisions on how it plans to allocate the EU-wide 2 GHz spectrum," CCS Insight analyst Joe Gardiner told The Register . "The EU outlined in its proposal that, for two-thirds of the spectrum, only operators based in the EU with EU ownership and aligned with the EU's strategic goals will be considered for the spectrum. "This has locked out companies like SpaceX and Amazon Leo from attaining access to spectrum that is highly valuable for satellite direct-to-device services. The US government is looking to retaliate, to support the US constellations that would have attempted to win this EU-wide spectrum." Following an initial consultation in March, the FCC will vote in December on opening a rulemaking to reconsider how foreign-licensed satellite operators gain access to the US market. "It is time for this regulatory asymmetry to end," Carr said, adding that the FCC now proposes to mirror any regulations that foreign nations apply to American satellite providers. "If there are limits or restrictions on American providers operating abroad, then the notice proposes to apply those or similar regulatory restraints to satellite providers from those countries that are operating here." Britain is outside the EU, but does not escape the FCC's ire. The agency previously claimed the UK Space Agency allocates a significant portion of its budget, circa 75 percent in 2023/24, to European Space Agency (ESA) procurements, which US companies are not allowed to bid for as America is not a member of ESA. British satellite operators could therefore face restrictions on access to the US market if the FCC adopts reciprocal measures. The UK's space industry generated £18.6 billion in income in 2022/23, according to the UK Space Agency. ®

events.title: Small traders reap the reward from buying Nvidia dip
events.summary: Jensen Huang’s return was pushed by a faction of Silicon Valley’s elite, but small traders piled in and reaped the rewards. Nvidia was the most-traded name across all of Robinhood on Nov. 12, when Huang resigned, and the retail broker’s customers remained net buyers in the days that followed, a spokesman told Semafor. Shares in Nvidia dropped 28% in the seven trading days following Huang’s resignation, only to rev back up and then some on Monday following the news of his return. Robinhood said it saw “record-breaking traffic” yesterday after Nvidia’s pre-market release announcing Huang’s return. “The fundamentals of the company didn’t change, but the company fundamentally changed,” Joe Tigay, portfolio manager at Equity Armor Investments, told Semafor. — Jake Angelo and Ellen DiMauro

events.title: Oil's downward trend is pushing gasoline lower
events.summary: Data: Financial Modeling Prep ; Chart: Ben Geman/Axios Brent crude is trading below $90 per barrel to start the week and briefly dipped to its lowest level since late August. Why it matters: Recent declines should help gasoline prices keep falling. The average U.S. retail price is $3.61 per gallon, down nearly 70 cents over the last month, per AAA data. The big picture: "The prospect of negotiations has eased some immediate concerns over Middle East supply, particularly as crude exports from the Persian Gulf have remained relatively resilient despite continued disruption around the Strait of Hormuz," ING analysts write. Catch up quick: Qatar's prime minister met with Vice President JD Vance at the White House on Monday to discuss talks with Iran, according to Axios' Barak Ravid. Reality check: Major risks remain, with the Strait of Hormuz and the wider region remaining a very dangerous place, so don't assume the downward trend will continue. And nothing is really back to normal. The market intelligence firm Kpler finds tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz was 42% below prewar levels in the seven days through Nov. 21, the WSJ reports. Flashback: The International Energy Agency on Nov. 13 predicted the global oil market will return to a surplus this quarter with supply rising and oil demand lowered by the conflict. The bottom line: "The status quo is growing ever more bearish," Sparta Commodities' Aaron Kildow said in a note Monday. Sign up here for Axios' Future of Energy newsletter.

events.title: Australia set to pass digital duty of care law, fines up to 5% of global revenue
events.summary: Australia is set to create new online safety laws that would make tech giants potentially liable for multibillion dollar fines for failing to prevent foreseeable online harms MELBOURNE, Australia -- The Australian government clinched a political deal on Tuesday to introduce online safety laws that could expose tech giants to multibillion-dollar fines for failing to prevent foreseeable online harms. The United States warned that the legislation would lead to censorship of lawful speech. The Digital Duty of Care Bill would require Big Tech to proactively reduce the risk of harm before it occurs, according to an Australian government statement. The legislation is similar to the European Union’s Digital Services Act, passed in 2022, and the United Kingdom's Online Safety Act passed a year later. The proposed legislation would set minimum safety standards for online services, including games, apps and artificial intelligence chatbots, requiring them to protect Australians from seriously harmful material and conduct, the government said. “We can’t cure the internet, but this is providing some basic safety standards and saying if you build it, you are responsible for its risks,” Communications Minister Anika Wells told reporters at Parliament House in Canberra. Wells announced on Tuesday her center-left Labor Party government had accepted amendments proposed by the minor Greens party to get the legislation through the Senate, where no party holds a majority. Greens leader David Shoebridge confirmed his party had agreed to support the amended bill. “Today we are taking power back from a handful of billionaire-owned, largely U.S. corporations and giving it back to Australians who have been paying too high a price for their profits,” Shoebridge said in a statement. The Senate will likely pass the bill on Wednesday and the House of Representatives, where the government holds a majority, would pass it into law before Parliament rises for the year on Thursday. The Greens' amendments include increasing maximum penalties for breaches from 109 million Australian dollars ($72 million) to 5% of a tech company’s global revenue. U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration expressed “serious concerns” in a submission in September to a parliamentary committee examining the draft law. U.S. concerns included how Australia would designate what constitutes “foreseeable harm.” U.S. Ambassador to Australia David Brat said he had conveyed his government’s objections to the amended legislation to Wells on Tuesday. “Vaguely defined ‘harms,’ backed by penalties of up to 5% of global revenue, will push platforms to censor lawful speech,” Brat posted on social media. 'The threat is finally real': Judge rips White House 'weaponization' Teen fatally struck by gunfire while camping near Florida river: Authorities Pennsylvania teen who died in 2020 could become first Gen Z saint “As Australia’s largest foreign investor, the U.S. is concerned with regulations that impose disproportionate compliance burdens on American companies relative to competitors,” he added. Wells said of their conversation: “There are points of difference and we’re ironing them out.” The conservative opposition Liberal Party shares U.S. concerns that the bill empowers government ministers and the nation's online safety watchdog to judge what was harmful. Opposition lawmakers oppose the legislation. “This bill undermines both the online safety of Australians and our freedom of expression,” senior opposition senator Sarah Henderson told reporters. The Greens' amendments would also give people a legal right to sue social media companies in Australian courts for harms suffered online. It follows Australian mining magnate Andrew Forrest having to go to U.S. courts to sue Meta over scam ads on its platforms that use his likeness without permission. The case is not yet resolved. In October, a U.S. judge ordered Meta to pay New Mexico $25 billion after a jury found the company liable for deceiving users about privacy on Facebook, marking the biggest fine ever against the tech giant. Australia's bill would also let social media users opt out of algorithms that send them content and empower Australia’s online safety watchdog to remove apps and websites that fabricate naked images from genuine images of people. It would also require protections for children against content that promotes eating disorders, hostile ideas about women, pornography, crime or dangerous stunts, or causes serious mental health distress. Lisa Given, an information sciences expert at RMIT University in Melbourne, described the draft legislation as “very good” and largely in line with European laws. “It’ll be very interesting to see what happens now globally,” Given said. “I’ve always been of the view that if countries can band together and put through similar legislation, collectively we have a better chance of actually pushing Big Tech to make real changes in terms of the design of their systems.

events.title: California raised minimum wages for fast-food workers – here’s how it played out 2 years later
events.summary: About half a million Californians were affected by the state's hike in minimum wage for fast-food workers. AP Photo/Jae C. Hong Even before the 2026 midterm elections delivered a clear message about cost-of-living concerns, many states had been raising their minimum wage on their own as one way to increase workers’ purchasing power. And some have taken a more targeted approach, setting wage floors for specific industries. As the example of California shows, however, these initiatives can produce mixed results. In April 2024, California began requiring fast-food chains with at least 60 locations nationwide to pay a minimum wage of US$20 an hour, $4 above the statewide minimum at the time. The governor’s office estimated that more than 500,000 workers would be covered by this mandate. As a researcher of health and labor markets , I joined with economists David Neumark , Gary Wagner and Vitor Melo to run a study measuring the impact on California’s fast-food industry – specifically, whether restaurants employed fewer workers because of the ensuing higher labor costs. We found that the answer depends on which establishments you look at. For the state as a whole, the law didn’t affect employment in any statistically detectable way, we concluded. But smaller chains did take a hit, with employment falling by roughly 20%, while the number of locations dropped by about 10%. New openings fell by 17%-20%, and closures rose by 9%-21%. This employment decline comes almost entirely from fast-food chains ceasing to operate in California, rather than from staffing cuts at the locations that remain. The impact of minimum wage hikes holds importance far beyond the fast-food sector. Their proponents point to the fact that the federal minimum wage of $7.25 an hour has stayed unchanged since 2009 and argue that states and municipalities need to take action on their own. Los Angeles is phasing in a $30 wage for hotel and airport workers, while California’s healthcare workers just received another scheduled increase . Vermont lawmakers have proposed a $20 fast-food wage of their own. In addition, a total of 16 states will raise their minimum wages across the board on Jan. 1, 2027. With the federal minimum wage unchanged since 2009, many states and municipalities have raised the wage floor on their own, including for specific sectors. AP Photo/Andrew Harnik Smaller chains see an impact The question of whether and how minimum wages affect employment still provokes a vigorous debate among economists. In California’s case, some researchers have found that lifting the minimum wage caused small declines in employment compared with other states; others contend that the effect on jobs is essentially zero. More broadly, some researchers have found that minimum wage hikes cost jobs. But the time horizon matters, and effects tend to get larger in the long run . Our study didn’t try to settle that disagreement. Instead, we wanted to find out how employers did adjust, and whether large and small chains responded differently. What happens when higher minimum wages raise one sector’s costs and prices while its closest substitutes – such as sit-down restaurants – keep paying the lower statewide minimum wage? We relied on a database that recorded every business location in the country by name, along with the number of employed workers, each year. That let us directly identify the chains that were subject to California’s law, count each chains’ national footprint to apply the 60-location rule, and track outcomes from 2019 through 2025: total employment, employment at locations that stayed open, the number of locations, and openings and closures. We also compared California with other states and separately compared each chain’s California restaurants with the same chain’s restaurants elsewhere. Finally, we divided the covered chains into two groups: The 20 largest, which account for about 60% of covered jobs, and the 261 smaller ones. For the state as a whole, we found that employment at covered restaurants was basically unchanged, and employment at restaurants that stayed open didn’t change. Among the 20 largest chains, there was no detectable effect at all for any of the measures we tracked over this period. But the smaller chains tell a different story, recording substantial declines in employment, locations and openings, while closures rose. How to reconcile the flat statewide numbers with the sharp effects on smaller chains? The largest chains employ most of the workers affected by the new minimum wage rule, so the statewide total is dominated by them. And the reduced entry and higher exit among smaller chains may have eased competitive pressure on the largest ones. A final point: The biggest chains tend to be the most automated, relying more on equipment such as self-serve kiosks that can reduce the number of workers needed. That may help explain the muted employment response among these larger businesses. Taking the longer view First, we caution that the absence of a clear short-run effect on total employment doesn’t prove that the policy won’t cause bigger job losses over time as companies adapt to the new law. We also can’t answer what happened to the workers at the most affected restaurants or what happened to prices at those establishments, although other research suggests they rose by 3% to 4%. That said, the law was implemented barely 2½ years ago, and some of the larger effects that economists might expect – such as the closure of labor-intensive restaurants or fewer openings – are already apparent among smaller chains. Second, it’s important to remember that California’s fast-food minimum wage applies only to chains with 60 or more locations. So the smaller chains in that range likely lack the scale, automation and pricing power of the national brands and are most sensitive to the new wage floor. Indeed, the law appears to have shifted California’s fast-food market toward its largest chains, a pattern that other researchers documented in a similar study that looked at Germany’s national minimum wage. For the cities and states now weighing wage floors of their own, the California evidence isn’t a slam dunk either way. It shows that the costs, broadly speaking, fall first on the smaller chains covered by the law – but whether it meaningfully impacts the largest chains is unclear. events.title: The Download: AI’s gas power boom and a consciousness reality check
events.summary: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. Data centers are getting their own natural gas power plants One of the biggest obstacles to building a data center is getting approval to connect to the grid, a wait that could last as long as a decade. Some developers won’t wait and are instead building their own off-grid gas power plants to fuel the AI boom. As of October 2026, developers had announced plans for more than 100 such gas power plants at data centers in the US. But bypassing the grid brings its own problems, from worsening climate emissions to potentially higher energy bills for everyone else. Find out how the push for gas power could shape the grid—and the climate—for decades . —Casey Crownhart A legendary philosopher isn’t buying Anthropic’s consciousness argument Before going public last week, Anthropic named the possibility of AI consciousness as a risk factor for investors, warning that it might introduce new rules to protect its models. But that stance came under fire from an inconvenient source: one of the philosophers who helped shape our understanding of consciousness in the first place. Thomas Nagel, best known for his essay about what it’s like to be a bat, was blunt. “Here are some of the smartest people on the planet being completely idiotic,” he said. He argued that producing language isn’t enough to establish consciousness. But other philosophers disagree. events.title: 9/UX brings a classic Mac feel to 9front
events.summary: Bringing a classic MacOS Finder to Linux is all very well, but there's no shortage of Linux desktops… however, bringing one to 9front is even more unexpected – and even more useful. 9/UX is a new project by Jeff " Progrium " Lindsay, who was one of the people behind Docker, Webhooks, and more. When you follow that link, and you should, pay close attention to what looks like a screenshot at the top. It is not an image. It's a real live executing instance of the OS, running inside your web browser, running on top of hyper9 . (That is worth reading too – it's an impressive project in its own right.) As its GitHub repository describes, 9/UX is a "Macintosh-inspired graphical environment for 9front." The README provides more detail: "9/UX brings the classic Mac and A/UX desktop experience (a spatial desktop, a global menu bar, consistent controls and dialogs, icons, and resource-driven presentation) to 9front, built the Plan 9 way: rio and libdraw draw the screen, 9P exposes every application's UI state and commands as files, namespaces define the working environment, the plumber opens documents, and ndb holds human-editable metadata." Lindsay introduced 9/UX earlier this month in a short X thread , saying he "made my own kind of A/UX but on Plan 9." In its creator's own words, "it's slop", but this is kind of interesting, original, creative bot-assisted coding that we enjoy looking at. At the end of last week, he returned to explain more : "9/UX isn’t just a pretty Mac-style UI on Plan 9. It's filesystem inspectable. Shell scriptable. Even the Mac resource file format can be used through the filesystem." Regular readers may have noticed that The Reg FOSS desk is fascinated by Plan 9 and its FOSS continuation 9front. We've written and presented at length about this remarkable OS, and tried to explain its FOSS continuation 9front several times . But even with the best will we can muster, its unique GUI is not an especially friendly or easy one. Its idiosyncratic UI was inspired by the late great Niklaus Wirth 's unbelievably tiny Oberon OS, which we have written about before . It's cryptic, and that's being generous. The research and development effort that led to Unix didn't stop when Unix 7th Edition escaped from the Bell Labs in 1981 and mutated into Unix System III. The industry enthusiastically adopted System III and later System V. A decade after 7th Edition Unix, Linux became a GPL version of something very like that traditional Unix, closely followed by the BSDs – and between them, they have very effectively distracted most of the FOSS world ever since. Even so, Research Unix lived on, saw 8th, 9th, and 10th editions, and then was replaced by Plan 9. In 1996, many of Plan 9's limitations were overcome by Inferno – whose revival as InferNode we covered this week. We always vaguely thought that if 9front were to receive an improved GUI that was slightly more compliant with later GUI design standards, it might be with a version of the Inferno UI … But apparently not. A new, easier, and yet still simple, clean and attractive desktop for 9front is here, and it looks like classic MacOS from the era of Apple's 68030 Unix A/UX. We do not think the chances are high that the 9front community will adopt this with enthusiasm. Even so, there is an AI programming manual for agents , and we've seen some interesting looking LLM-assisted 9front apps of late. Several can be found in the agent9 distributio n , which includes LLM-assisted ports of C++ , Python , and Rust , plus a version of DOSbox , and even a package manager called pac9 .®

events.title: UAE launches AI assistant to track children’s learning
events.summary: The News Starting in March, parents of students in UAE public schools will be able to ask the UAE’s new government AI assistant why their child is falling behind in certain subjects and how to remedy the gaps, Education Minister Sarah Al Amiri said in an interview. The new tool, called Mira, will also allow parents to check grades and attendance and arrange meetings with teachers. It is part of a broader government initiative to streamline services using agentic AI. Mira will draw on data that schools already collect, including classroom observations, project results, and benchmark assessments that parents rarely see, Al Amiri said. It will use those records to flag problems early. A parent whose child is struggling in math, for example, could ask which topics to focus on and get a more focused answer than previous methods of assessment provided. The ministry will roll out the system across more than 530 public schools that serve about 280,000 students, Al Amiri said. The UAE’s total student population is 1.1 million, with the rest in private schools that don’t have to adopt Mira, she said. AI curriculum The agent is being deployed a year after the UAE mandated an AI curriculum, which began in fall 2025 in all public and some private schools, from kindergarten through grade 12. The UAE initially planned around 20 lessons per grade, ranging from discussing robots with younger children to building machine learning algorithms in later years. About a quarter of the first year’s classes focused on ethics, Al Amiri said. Students learned how to write prompts, question AI-generated answers, and recognize when using the tools would be inappropriate. Al Amiri said students now “take a subject called AI and technology from one to three times a week,” depending on their grade. While the ministry is pushing AI adoption among students and teachers, it decided to remove devices from sixth-grade classrooms in four core subjects this year. Al Amiri said students at that age have the greatest chance of closing gaps in reading, writing, and math. In those subjects, “they’re back to books, paper, pen.” Notable The UAE became one of the first countries to mandate AI learning last year, teaching students about concepts such as plagiarism and prompt engineering , Semafor reported.

events.title: CrowdStrike splashes $44B on Zscaler, customers brace for the bill
events.summary: CrowdStrike has agreed to buy Zscaler for $43.9 billion in what would be the biggest cybersecurity acquisition on record, and customers are already bracing for pricier renewals. The all-stock deal, announced on Monday , will see Zscaler shareholders receive 1.135 CrowdStrike shares for every share they own, representing a 34 percent premium on Friday's closing price. The transaction dwarfs even Google's $32 billion acquisition of cloud security upstart Wiz . Buying Zscaler gives CrowdStrike a sizeable foothold in the network security market, where it will be going up against the likes of Palo Alto Networks and Fortinet. The plan is to combine Falcon's endpoint protection capabilities with Zscaler's zero-trust network security technology, giving customers a single platform for securing devices and the connections between them. Naturally, there's an AI angle to the biggest cyber deal in history. CrowdStrike reckons owning both technologies will allow it to keep tabs on what AI agents are doing on corporate devices, where they're connecting, and what data they're getting their hands on. CrowdStrike CEO George Kurtz described the proposed combination as "cybersecurity’s operating system." The acquisition also gives CrowdStrike's salespeople plenty to get excited about. Around 8,000 Zscaler customers don't currently buy CrowdStrike's wares, and the companies already have more than 2,000 customers in common. CrowdStrike reckons it can boost its annualized revenue by around $1 billion within 30 months of closing the deal by selling more products to the two companies' existing customers. Some of those customers, however, don't sound particularly keen on being cross-sold to. Over on Reddit's r/sysadmin subreddit, news of the purchase was met with a familiar set of concerns from IT professionals who've lived through big-ticket enterprise software acquisitions before. "As a zscaler customer, this does worry me. Cost increase, forced move to Falcon, integration issues, etc," wrote one sysadmin. Another, whose organization already uses both vendors' products, added: "I think they're both great products but I imagine they'll jack up the price for our next renewal. Fun." CrowdStrike intends to make Zscaler's products available through its Falcon Flex licensing scheme, which allows customers to commit to a certain level of spending and pick and choose the products they deploy. Monday's acquisition announcement didn't spell out what the deal would mean for customers who want to continue using Zscaler alongside a rival endpoint security product. Others raised concerns about the fate of Red Canary, the managed detection and response specialist snapped up by Zscaler in August 2025. CrowdStrike already operates a competing service in Falcon Complete. There may also be some nervous employees at both companies. CrowdStrike is targeting $500 million in annual cost savings within two years of completing the acquisition, identifying datacenter infrastructure, supplier spending, and wider operations as areas where it can trim the fat. Neither company disclosed whether that would involve job cuts. Then there's the matter of putting more of the world's corporate security infrastructure in the hands of CrowdStrike, whose botched July 2024 software update took down an estimated 8.5 million Windows machines , grounding flights and disrupting hospitals, banks, and businesses worldwide. The incident gave IT departments a rather painful lesson in the risks of relying heavily on a single technology supplier. The deal is expected to close in the second half of CrowdStrike's fiscal 2028, assuming regulators and Zscaler shareholders give it the green light. Zscaler founder and CEO Jay Chaudhry will remain in charge of the business and take a seat on CrowdStrike's board. CrowdStrike reckons the combined business will have more than $10 billion in annual recurring revenue when the deal closes. Judging by the reaction from some customers, they'll be keeping a particularly close eye on how much of that revenue comes from them. ®

events.title: Saudi Arabia asks allies from America to Asia for help restocking missile defenses
events.summary: The Scoop Saudi Arabia made fresh calls to allies for more missile interceptors amid regular Houthi missile attacks as the kingdom prepares for what it expects to be a prolonged conflict in Yemen, according to people familiar with the matter. Saudi authorities, including the defense and foreign ministries, have in the past few weeks reached out to traditional partners like the US, the UK, and France, along with countries from the Americas to Asia, with a specific list of military equipment, according to multiple sources involved in talks with Riyadh on the issue, who asked not to be identified. The Saudi requests include ground-based systems and air-to-air missiles used for drone interceptions made by a variety of manufacturers. The kingdom is looking to either acquire the equipment or structure the deals as a swap, whereby Saudi Arabia will replace any military hardware it borrows when it receives new stock, the sources said. Beyond the US The Saudi request is notable in how widely authorities have reached out beyond their traditional defense partners, according to the sources. In the past, Riyadh has mostly relied on US military equipment and the presence of American forces for its security. It is unclear if the latest request is a signal that Saudi Arabia’s stockpiles of interceptors are running low, or if it is preparation for what is increasingly expected to be a protracted conflict with the Houthis, with the risk of further attacks from Iran in future, the sources said. The Saudi government didn’t respond to requests for comment. The size of Saudi Arabia’s stockpiles of interceptors is a closely guarded secret, but supplies across the Gulf have fallen sharply after months of conflict with Iran and now the Houthis: Saudi Arabia has been dealing with near-daily missile and drone attacks from the Houthis for several weeks. Most of these have been intercepted, but some resulted in damage to the capital’s airport , and the headquarters of Saudi Aramco and Public Investment Fund . That’s combined with a global drawdown of interceptor stocks as a result of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. The US approved a $9 billion sale of missiles for Patriot air defense systems to Saudi Arabia in January. But the supplier, Lockheed Martin, said in June that while it was accelerating production capacity, it could not guarantee what countries would be prioritized for delivery of the in-demand equipment, or when orders might be fulfilled. Saudi Arabia uses a combination of defense systems from different countries, including Germany and South Korea, but mostly relies on US manufacturers. Houthi attacks have intensified since September and the kingdom is preparing for the war in Yemen to last well into 2027 , Reuters reported. The state also appears to be sending messages to prepare the population for months of conflict. “Some have mentioned six months, but Saudi staying power can extend well beyond that ,” Ali Shihabi, a Saudi commentator with close ties to the government, wrote in a recent Arab News column. Notable UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham confirmed that Britain will give military support to Saudi Arabia to fight the Houthis in Yemen , after the kingdom came under drone and missile attack by the Houthis.

events.title: This Hollywood Star Took on Crypto. Now He’s Got a New Target
events.summary: Ben McKenzie promised his wife that he was through with being an activist ; that he’d go back to the acting gigs that had made him famous. At the end of his documentary taking on the cryptocurrency industry, Everyone Is Lying to You for Money ,” the former star of The O.C. and Gotham turned to his spouse and fellow actor Morena Baccarin and swore he was done. Turns out, that scene might need an edit. McKenzie is launching a new nonprofit, The Public Trust and Transparency Project , that not only continues his battle with the crypto business but widens it to fight prediction markets like Polymarket and Kalshi. McKenzie tells WIRED he’s worried about “the gamification of the economy and the notion that we're turning everything into gambling—both investments, in the form of cryptocurrencies, and “prediction markets,” which look an awful lot like online casinos.” “The more gambling gets into our culture, the more people feel like it's somehow a good idea to view these things as legitimate investment strategies,” he says. The prediction markets reject the comparison (although 80 percent of Kalshi’s trades came from sports in September, according to Bloomberg). McKenzie rejects the rejection: “I mean, if your investment strategy is, ‘I'm going to gamble on the Spurs-Knicks,’ like, come on! So there's a real, real problem here.” John Reed Stark, who spent 18 years in the Securities and Exchange Commission’s enforcement division, will serve as an adviser to the Project. American Kleptocracy author Casey Michel and Tonantzin Carmona, who runs economic policy for the left-of-center Century Foundation, will sit on the board. The group is coming together at a time when regulators and law enforcement officials at every level are looking to rein in prediction markets. Federal regulators have launched new probes into both major prediction markets. The GOP-led House Oversight Committee recently released its investigation into US troops and government insiders trading on insider knowledge on Polymarket and Kalshi. The Senate just passed a bill prohibiting prediction markets for military operations and assassinations. Executives at the markets know they’re in for a rough few months; Kalshi even launched an ad campaign, starring Martha Stewart, reminding its users not to trade on confidential information. But insider trading is only one concern among many. There’s also the problem you find in old-school gambling houses too: The vast majority of people who use the markets lose their money. A recent Wall Street Journal report shows that .01 percent of accounts take in two-thirds of all of the profits on Polymarket. On Kalshi, unprofitable accounts outpace profitable ones by almost three to one. Then there’s the corruption angle, which McKenzie says is going to be front-and-center for the Project, especially with it featuring as a top issue in the recent midterm elections . Donald Trump Jr. was, until recently, a paid adviser to Kalshi. Trump Jr.’s venture firm, 1789 Capital, made its latest and biggest in a series of investments in Polymarket over the summer; months earlier, the Trump Justice Department sued the state of Minnesota when it tried to ban the prediction markets in the state. (At a recent conference, Polymarket CEO Shayne Coplan called Trump Jr.’s involvement “ heavily overblown. We have all types of investors .”) Prediction markets have been around for hundreds of years, as a forthcoming book on the subject notes. American academics have been turning to them as teaching tools since the late ’80s . Their advocates note that they can be an effective way to hedge against risk, and a form of trading on sports that’s far more consumer-friendly than the online gambling houses. “I accept that there may be some utility,” McKenzie notes. “I'm not saying these things should not exist. I'm just saying they need to be properly regulated.” McKenzie’s plan will be to push Congress in that direction, sort of the inverse of how the former actor lobbied publicly and privately against the “Clarity Act,” which would’ve brought cryptocurrencies into the financial mainstream. (The bill was rejected in September.) That pressure is only bound to increase when Democrats take control of Congress next year. “In the bold new world starting [on the] first Monday in January,” Representative Frank Lucas, an Oklahoma Republican, told Politico, “ nobody’s untouchable anymore .” In your inbox: For life-tested picks, sign up for our Gear newsletters Building social media apps isn’t cool anymore RIP to the unloved, unwanted Cybertruck Want better search results? events.title: European Commission confirms personal data stolen in AI-assisted cyberattack
events.summary: The European Commission has confirmed that hackers made off with personal data in the AI-assisted cyberattack disclosed last week, but has relied on a website notice rather than contacting affected users directly. Speaking at a press briefing on Monday , Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier confirmed that EU Academy, an online learning platform offering courses on EU policies and initiatives, was among the systems compromised during the cyber campaign targeting the bloc's executive arm. The stolen data includes the names and email addresses of people outside the EU institutions, though the Commission has yet to figure out how many users are affected or whether other personal information was compromised. Public access to the platform has been disabled as a precaution. Despite confirming the theft, the Commission hasn't contacted affected individuals directly. Instead, it has posted a notice on the EU Academy website, a decision Regnier defended when quizzed by reporters on Monday. "There was no reach out to individual users, but rather a general message to all users on the website out of transparency," Regnier said. The notice warns users that they could find themselves on the receiving end of spearphishing attacks, impersonation attempts, and spam as a result of the breach. The Commission is also advising users not to hand over personal information to anyone who contacts them claiming to be involved in EU Academy activities. The trouble with notifying users via the EU Academy website is that they've already been told not to come back until January. A separate notice says the platform will be offline from November 11 through January 14, 2027, while the Commission rebuilds it. When it reopens, users will have to register again, and any record of their previous coursework won't be transferred. The Register has asked the Commission whether the downtime and the requirement to create new accounts are connected to the cyberattack.A spokesperson didn't answer those points. The Commission has informed the European Data Protection Supervisor (EDPS), the watchdog responsible for policing EU institutions' handling of personal data. The EDPS told The Register that the Commission had notified it of the incident in stages, but declined to say whether it considered the Commission's approach to notifying affected users sufficient. "I can confirm that the EDPS has been informed and notified in phases by the European Commission," a spokesperson said. "Our colleagues remain in regular contact with EC services on the cyberattack and its implication. This is an ongoing case, so I cannot tell you more at this stage on the actions the EDPS might take as supervisory authority." The Commission first publicly acknowledged the cyberattack last Thursday , almost a month after suspicious activity was detected on October 22. Several internal applications were temporarily taken offline, and while most had since been restored, some remained unavailable at the time of Thursday's briefing. The Commission has confirmed the attackers used an AI-assisted hacking tool, and the incident comes amid mounting concerns over ARTEX, an AI-powered penetration testing framework that security researchers have linked to large-scale cyber espionage campaigns. More than a month after the Commission first spotted the intrusion, Regnier was unwilling to say on Monday whether its security teams had finally seen off the hackers. "As long as the investigation is ongoing, I will not make any conclusive statements at this stage on where we are," he said. ®

events.title: We’re entering a Chinese world
events.summary: Andy’s view Sooner than anybody thought possible, we’re entering a Chinese world. The signs are everywhere — from great-power pageantry in Shenzhen, to the collapse of multilateralism at the COP31 climate talks, to the political rescue of Nvidia’s Jensen Huang. These may appear to be random data points. Look more carefully, however, and they have something in common: They’re all harbingers of a global system shaped more and more by Chinese values, models, and interests. In Shenzhen, flanked by US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin — and framed by a giant Chinese landscape painting — Chinese leader Xi Jinping convened the Big Three in a meeting designed to signal the birth of a new global order. Ahead of the trilateral, the influential Chinese scholar and think tank leader, Wang Wen, imagined a “Shenzhen International System” running parallel to the UN setup. Afterward, China’s foreign minister hailed “a landmark event that will go down in history.” That may be true, at least insofar as it represented a break from how China traditionally views its role — as leader of the Global South in a multipolar world — and offered a new vision for how the planet should be ordered: by a trio strongmen at the apex of a global hierarchy, wielding power, parading force, and bringing smaller countries to heel. Get used to more gales of empty rhetoric from this new format — and global drift: China will not fill the vacuum as the US retreats. In Türkiye, UN climate talks broke down in part due to the absence of an engaged America. Unlike the Trump White House, China hasn’t recanted its belief in climate science, but neither is the world’s largest carbon emitter ready to assume the responsibilities of pushing a policy agenda to avert climate catastrophe. Beijing’s main message to developing economies threatened by heat waves, droughts, and floods: Buy our green hardware . The US, meanwhile, is adopting its own version of Chinese state capitalism. Huang is back in the saddle at Nvidia — after Trump stepped in, much as Xi gives orders to strategically important private sector companies. (In a way, this was Jack Ma in reverse; we haven’t yet reached the point where a US President can bring down a corporate icon, although boards everywhere are now on notice that the White House gets a vote on personnel issues .) History will likely record that the accelerated advent of the Sinosphere wasn’t so much about China grabbing power than the US giving up, abandoning what’s worked so well for Washington — and, by and large, the rest of the world — since World War II. It’s certainly true that the collapse of what used to be called the US-led “liberal global order” has fed Beijing’s ambitions. In Shenzhen, where Asia-Pacific leaders were holding an annual summit, America’s friends and allies witnessed the astonishing spectacle of a US president relishing a photo-op with two strongmen who chafe at US power and, indeed, represent twin pillars of the “Axis of Autocracy” — also including North Korea and Iran — dedicated to dismantling much of the world Washington created. Xi’s big payoff was playing the host. Putin came away a winner, too, officially treated as an equal to China and the US. What did Trump get out of all this? The economic historian Niall Ferguson portrays him as a latter day Nixon , a realist prepared to do deals with tyrants to further the US national interest. But there’s a crucial difference: Nixon achieved a historic breakthrough from his 1972 meeting with Mao Zedong, sealing a Cold War partnership against the Soviet Union and opening a pathway out of a military quagmire in Vietnam. Trump got nothing — no progress on winding down the war in Ukraine, or ending the conflict with Iran, or cutting nuclear stockpiles. The viral moment came when Trump hailed Putin as “my friend.” That’s what a post-American world, orchestrated by Beijing, looks like. Notable A Council on Foreign Relations expert argued that if Chinese AI models surpassed their US counterparts in terms of popularity, this would mean that the Chinese government could gain a cultural lead on the US by “ imposing its values on the world .”

events.title: "The Axios Show": Bob Woodward's memoir spills 50 years of secrets
events.summary: Bob Woodward — out Tuesday with " Secrets ," his memoir of 55 years of reporting for The Washington Post and 24 cinematic bestsellers, covering 10 presidents — told me in an interview for "The Axios Show" that the book exposes some confidential sources who are now dead because he feels a duty to history. Why it matters: Woodward, 83, is a double Pulitzer winner whose Watergate investigative reporting with Carl Bernstein became a book and movie, "All the President's Men," that inspired generations of would-be reporters, including me. But no journalism school teaches students they can out " secret sources " who are dead, as Woodward does in " Secrets ." "It's history," Woodward told me in the Georgetown home where so many sources have spilled to him, administration after administration, decade after decade. He explained that in many cases, the sources were widely known anyway or appeared in other files and records that have become public. He said some living sources gave him permission to be named in the book. "Look at the histories that come out — the Adams-Jefferson letters , which were very secret. But when they come out, historians rejoice. We now see what they were saying to each other ... I'm for history on occasions like that." Axios: "So you have zero qualms?" Woodward: "Well, you always have qualms, but what's your responsibility to get the history right? ... [For] people who are reading the history and trying to understand it deeper into the story, deeper is naming those sources." More from our interview, which you can watch here: Axios: " Based on your reporting, and your rich understanding of governance, put President Trump's level of corruption in historical perspective. How does President Trump compare to Richard Nixon, the president you helped bring down?" Woodward: "Trump is worse, much worse than Nixon. And the evidence is on two fronts: First of all, how much money he's made — billions of dollars himself as president. I mean, imagine that. It used to be a scandal if the president was getting a free ride on somebody's jet. ... I think what we'll remember and [will] endure from the Trump presidency is the Iran war. ... It's such a mistake. ... We shouldn't start wars. We should prevent wars. ... President Nixon had people who were in his circle who tried to stop wars and prevent wars. In Trump's circle now, there are all these people who are just feeding the beast." Axios: "What is President Trump's strength? What is a quality of his that you admire?" Woodward: "Well, he persists. He doesn't give up." Axios: "You famously did 20 [phone] interviews with President Trump, all during COVID — you were phone pals. And this was when he was not being super-promiscuous with reporters and his phone. ... How did you keep President Trump talking?" Woodward: "Well, I would call and ask, 'What happened? Why? Why did you do that?' ... It's this mental attitude of not looking for a headline, but looking for the relationship. And he would always take my calls. He would call me. " Axios: "You're still an associate editor of The Washington Post, the paper you helped make world-famous, a place where we were colleagues. You've worked there 55 years. This morning's hard copy is sitting right over here on your kitchen table. You've been blunt about your concerns about the ties that the owner, Jeff Bezos, has to President Trump. Did Jeff Bezos put The Washington Post's reputation and future at risk?" Woodward: "Yes, certainly. I mean, he's the owner and to show up at Trump's inaugural, voluntarily, in a very visible way, which is not just: 'Oh, I'm going to the movies.' It's: 'I am blessing and endorsing this man.' And I remember seeing it and just feeling sick to my stomach. I knew Katharine Graham , the owner of the Post during Watergate, would never do anything like that, because she wanted the reporting to be hard and fiery and she didn't want to take sides. ... I literally felt sick to my stomach that that had happened, that he would do that. I've known Bezos for years. He used to have me before he really became rich out to the West Coast to talk to his staff ... And when he bought the Post, I thought: 'This is salvation that's come.' And he has tarnished not only his own reputation, but that of The Washington Post." Axios: "Have you told [Jeff Bezos] that?" Woodward: "I've said it publicly." Axios: "Does he answer your emails?" Woodward: "I don't send emails to him. ... If I'm going to say something that's critical of him, I want to say it publicly. I don't want to hide." Axios: "When I first walked into The Post as a young Metro reporter [in 1997] — I was hired to cover the Alexandria City Council — I walked into that newsroom on 15th Street, and it was like walking onto Lambeau Field. It was The Show. The Post has shriveled since then." Woodward: "Shriveled is the wrong word. I mean, there have been some valleys. There's no question about that. But I still, from my contacts and dealings with Matt Murray, who's the executive editor, I think he ... understands the weaknesses, and wants to make improvements." Axios: "If we're going to be honest, we're going to say that [The Post] is no longer the player, the force, the destination that it was. How did that happen?" Woodward: "Well, you could write not just a book, but volumes on that. And that happens when ownership forgets what the job is. And the job is to [conduct] aggressive, neutral examinations. I conduct those examinations of everyone — all individuals, all ideologies. And I fault myself. Before I said this about Bezos and criticized him, I should have called him and said: 'I'm going to say this, and I think you're making a mistake.' And I didn't do that, and I should have." Axios: What was Joe Biden's fatal flaw? Woodward: "Being president." Axios: "Your long, long-awaited memoir is ' Secrets .' Why did you finally write it?" Woodward: "Because I wanted to take people as close to what has happened in my reporting life and, frankly, my personal life, because that sets the stage. ... I've tried to learn something, but I also have that feeling I haven't learned enough. And of course, how do you learn more in our business? Go to work." Full episode ... Get "Secrets."

events.title: BepiColombo takes the long way around Mercury after software glitch
events.summary: A software fault cut short BepiColombo's Mercury orbit insertion burn, but the European Space Agency (ESA) says the mission remains on track to separate its two science orbiters on December 9. ESA's Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO), still carrying JAXA's Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (Mio), fired its four axial thrusters on November 21 to place the spacecraft in orbit. The burn began at 1824 UTC, when BepiColombo was approximately 635 km above the planet's surface. It was supposed to last for 37 minutes but shut down early . The shutdown , caused by a software issue involving attitude guidance and thruster control, left the spacecraft in safe mode, a protective state in which all non-essential activities cease. Ignacio Tanco, ESA's BepiColombo Flight Operations Director, said: "Upon finding Bepi in safe mode, it was like flipping a switch. Everybody was focused in understanding what had happened." The burn achieved around 77 percent of the planned velocity change, securing an orbit around Mercury but leaving BepiColombo taking 75 hours to circle the planet instead of the intended 58. The good news is that multiple burns were always going to be needed to adjust the orbit ahead of Mio separation and MPO reaching its science orbit. "The remaining MOI [Mercury Orbit Insertion] sequence has already been adapted to the new trajectory, with no additional burns required," ESA said. "After each burn, the Flight Dynamics team determines the achieved orbit to then design the next manoeuvre," said Frank Budnik, ESA's BepiColombo Flight Dynamics Manager. "So, the sequence is not only more propellant-efficient, it also allows Flight Dynamics to adapt each subsequent burn to the spacecraft's actual trajectory. It's a dynamic sequence! Each new manoeuvre is based on the previous ones." Teams at ESA's European Space Operations Centre (ESOC) and Airbus continue to investigate the underlying software fault. ESA has not said whether the revised burn sequence will affect propellant reserves available for a possible mission extension. The separation of Mio and MPO is planned for December 9, and more burns will be needed to guide MPO to its final orbit by March 2027, with science operations starting in April 2027. ®

events.title: Inside the Chinese City Where Furniture Dupes Are Made
events.summary: On the morning of May 31, 2025, Shirley Bekker made an impulsive decision. The then 29-year-old doctor living in London finally pulled the trigger on plane tickets to visit Foshan, in southern China , for a flight later that same day. Two months prior, Bekker had little knowledge of the city of 9 million; she had no idea what hotel to stay at or where to go once she landed. But Bekker was convinced that six days in Foshan to furnish her apartment—and possibly having all of the furniture shipped back to London—would still be cheaper than getting everything at home. With over 100,000 followers on social media , she also later turned her adventure into content , detailing her finds and their cost. Bekker was in the process of buying her dream one-bedroom apartment in East London and spent weeks obsessively watching home renovation videos on TikTok. “When I saw that things like a sofa cost thousands of pounds, I was like, ‘OK, I’m convinced now that I’ll probably do something drastic to not have to pay that much,’” she says. Her social media algorithm was already feeding her a radical solution. “Made in China, shit quality?” a Chinese furniture seller said in videos on Bekker’s TikTok feed. “ Grass sofa ? Our factory has mass-produced it; UFO table ? Our factory has mass-produced it.” Soon, Bekker says, her “entire timeline became Foshan, Foshan, Foshan.” She learned all about China’s furniture capital, which each year exports nearly $10 billion worth of couches and beds and bathroom vanities, and everything else you could possibly need for your home. Bekker is just one of a growing number of people around the world who order furniture directly from factories in Foshan. By either flying to the city—or through WhatsApp, TikTok, AliExpress, or Alibaba—buyers can commission made-to-order pieces. And most importantly, they can purchase dupes. In 2025, Shirley Bekker flew to China to buy furniture, hoping that even with shipping the cost would be lower than shopping in London. Duplicates were once primarily the domain of fashion and beauty, but consumers are now seeking out knockoffs of luxury designer furniture that promise the same quality as the original at a much lower cost—even after international shipping rates and tariffs. During the week of April 13, 2025, the number of videos urging Americans to buy directly from Chinese factories soared 250 percent . Tens of thousands of videos had been posted under hashtags like #ChineseFactory, and many of them were about furniture pieces . Some videos garnered millions of views and included contacts of Chinese sellers in the comments. @gabwithmeg, a working mom in California, claims on TikTok that she saved at least $100,000 by furnishing her entire house directly from China. “It is all Restoration Hardware and Arhaus-style furniture, and I’m going to tell you exactly how I did it,” she promised her followers in January . @gabwithmeg’s post received over 65,000 likes, and the comments are filled with users clamoring to opt out of the traditional furniture market, if not bragging about having already done so. Together, they represent a turning tide in furniture shopping for Westerners. If people can buy a couch that looks exactly like the famous Togo for $200 on AliExpress, why would they pay $4,800 for one from Design Within Reach? Sure, Ligne Roset is a legendary brand, famously crafting all its furniture near the French Alps, made by trained artisans using an almost entirely manual process . But not everyone cares about history, owning an original, or the ethics of intellectual property in design. In fact, some furniture buyers, including Bekker, aren’t even aware that some pieces they covet are copies. Bekker feels that designer furniture is more expensive because of the brand name, not necessarily the quality. “Sorry to say, for me, it’s a bit bullshit,” she says. “I’m really not one to buy into the idea that the name of the brand makes it worth the price.” “We’re seeing the beginnings of a revolt against the brandification of everything,” says Christopher Sprigman, a law professor at New York University who has studied the knockoff economy. As a consumer, Sprigman expects brands to offer good and consistent quality, but there is a perception that “there’s no real quality control, there’s no real integrity, it’s basically just advertising and driving up costs, creating demand, creating desire without any real substantial benefit that the consumer can feel or taste or see,” Sprigman says. The videos Bekker saw never explicitly said how much the furniture in Foshan would cost, but she was confident it would be far less than at the posh showrooms in London. Despite not speaking Chinese, she roamed around the furniture markets in Foshan’s warm and humid air. By the end of the trip, she had furnished her entire apartment for around £7,000 (about $9,200).

events.title: Data centers are getting their own natural gas power plants
events.summary: One of the biggest roadblocks to starting up a data center is getting approval to connect to the electric grid—a wait that could last as long as a decade. Some developers aren’t willing to wait and are instead opting to build their own off-grid, or behind-the-meter, gas power plants to fuel the AI boom.   xAI’s Memphis campus has famously used dozens of natural gas turbines, some of them without permits, as far back as 2024. At the time, that facility was a rarity, and it faced scrutiny from regulators. It remains the subject of ongoing legal battles . But the strategy of going off-grid for power has since become a lot more common. As of October 2026, data center developers have announced plans for more than 100 behind-the-meter gas power plants at facilities in the US, according to data from Cleanview, a market intelligence company. The facilities have a combined planned capacity of over 115 gigawatts, more than double the peak power demand of California. The vast majority of these announcements have come since the beginning of 2025. It’s possible that not all these facilities will be built; only a small fraction are under construction or operating today. But there’s a growing trend of large data centers looking to build their own power supply, and this could shape the grid—and its climate impacts—for decades to come. Building your own power plant is generally more expensive than just hooking up to the grid, but the AI rush has made developers willing to pay a significant premium to get online faster. “The biggest motivator for on-site power right now from data centers is speed,” says Musfika Mishi, an associate at BloombergNEF, an energy consultancy. When developers want to build a new industrial facility—like a data center—that requires a lot of electricity, they need to request a grid connection from a local utility or regional grid operator. That request kicks off a yearslong process in which grid planners study the existing grid to understand what would need to be built to safely deliver power to the facility without compromising reliability. Upgrades might be required, like building new transmission lines or larger transformers, and the developer might be on the hook to help pay for them. Rather than waiting for that process to play out, developers can opt to instead build their own power plants. These facilities are referred to as “behind the meter” because they sit on the customer’s side of a utility meter—supplying the building directly, rather than relying on a utility via a grid hookup. “This shift in the data center developers’ power strategies towards off-grid gas raises some important questions about how data centers will be powered going forward,” says Brendan Pierpont, director of electricity at the think tank Energy Innovation. Behind-the-meter doesn’t always mean being totally disconnected from the grid, however. Some facilities may build such plants as a temporary measure, eventually connecting to the grid and tapping their own power plants only as backup. “It’s really just a very expensive way to bridge that maybe five-to-seven-year timeline gap until these data centers can get a grid connection,” Pierpont says.  Even if gas plants are pitched as a near-term solution, building new fossil fuel infrastructure could lead to longer-term effects, since an operator might choose to continue running plants once they’ve spent money building them. “Even though data centers say that it’s a grid-bridging solution, the probability that it is going to be in use much longer is a real risk, and that leads to fossil fuel lock-in,” Mishi says.  The on-site gas rush could have major implications for greenhouse-gas emissions. Today, the US grid is still reliant on fossil fuels, but nuclear and renewables together make up about 40% of electricity generation. That means making a grid connection is generally a lower-emissions option than relying entirely on an on-site gas plant. (That’s not the case everywhere—India, for example, is expecting to see a data center boom in the next decade, and its grid is largely served by emissions-intensive coal-fired power plants today.)  Utilities are already planning to build more natural gas power plants on the grid to meet rising electricity demand. Equipment manufacturers are struggling to keep up with the surge, and it’s pushing developers of behind-the-meter plants toward less-efficient alternatives.  Today, large natural gas plants generally use combined-cycle turbines. These capture heat to generate additional electricity, making them more efficient than single-cycle turbines, which are generally cheaper to build. Very few of the planned behind-the-meter facilities, however, will use combined-cycle turbines, Mishi says. That means these off-grid plants will likely produce more greenhouse-gas emissions than even other natural gas resources.  BloombergNEF is also tracking on-site natural gas plants at data centers, finding 181 gigawatts’ worth of announced projects globally, with 90% of that capacity designated for the US. If all planned behind-the-meter gas plants for data centers in the US go ahead, they could emit 345 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent each year by 2035, according to a BloombergNEF report . That’s 152 million metric tons more than if those data centers pulled power from the US grid—a difference greater than the total annual emissions of the Netherlands.  And while it might seem logical that data centers bringing their own power could ease communities’ energy bills, those facilities going off-grid doesn’t protect prices for everyone else, says Matthias Fripp, director of global policy research at Energy Innovation. More demand for natural gas could push its price higher, he explains, which could in turn raise rates for the roughly 60% of American households that use natural gas for heating and cooking. That effect may also trickle into electricity prices. There’s still a lot of uncertainty about how much of this gas rush will come to fruition, so this future isn’t set in stone. Today, just 4.9 gigawatts of behind-the-meter gas projects tied to data centers are operating, and 15.8 gigawatts are under construction, according to Cleanview’s data. Creative solutions could also help limit the climate burden of the on-site gas buildout, BloombergNEF’s Mishi says. Building gas alongside on-site renewables or energy storage could help limit how often a gas plant needs to fire up, she says, though the economics of building multiple energy sources can be tricky.  While the grid is struggling to keep up with demand, building more renewables could help, Fripp adds. In a recent study , his team found that building renewables and energy storage to meet rising electricity demand could be reliable and cheaper than relying on fossil fuels. “These data centers want a lot of power, and they want it fast, and the grid is not well equipped to provide that,” Fripp says. “Th
