events.title: At a Doomed U.N. Conference, Saudi Arabia and Other Oil States Pushed Hard for an Unproven Climate Fix
events.summary: Activists unsatisfied with the second draft text at COP31 hold a silent protest outside the plenary hall, where delegates meet during the United Nations Climate Change Conference at the Antalya Expo Centre in Turkey on Nov. 20. Yasin Akgul/AFP/Getty Images A United Nations-sponsored negotiation on climate change collapsed Sunday amid bitter standoffs over how to slow the warming of the planet and who will pay for it. During the two-week summit, oil- and gas-producing nations blocked any mention of phasing out those fuels — a step scientists uniformly agree is a prerequisite to addressing global warming. Instead, petrostates, led by Saudi Arabia, pushed for an aggressive expansion of carbon capture technology as a way to reduce the pollution their fuels cause. Today, carbon capture facilities operate at a tiny fraction of the scale promised, are riddled with failures and setbacks, and show no signs of being able to overcome those hurdles at the pace that the U.N. suggests would be needed to mitigate global warming, reporting by Drilled and ProPublica has found. The role of carbon capture was just one cause of discord in Turkey at the 31st annual U.N. climate summit, known as the Conference of the Parties. But it reflects a culmination of decades of effort by fossil fuel companies, and the nations most dependent on them, to slow a transition away from oil, coal and gas in part by pressing for methods like carbon capture, which theoretically allow for the use of their products and cleaning up carbon pollution at the same time. Over the course of two weeks of negotiations in Antalya, drafts of the summit’s main political accord were stripped of language encouraging such a transition even as specific targets were added to expand carbon capture and storage, or CCS. One draft released Nov. 16 included language encouraging a transition from fossil fuels alongside a recommendation to scale up carbon capture — where greenhouse gases are caught from industry, or filtered from the air, and injected underground — so that it removes at least 500 million tons of carbon dioxide a year by 2035. Currently, however, the carbon capture industry buries only a sliver of that amount and has struggled for three decades to meet even the lowest-end projections, leading many climate experts to conclude that it will never be a practical solution to climate change. “The effort by bad faith petrostate actors to block any agreement at #COP31 on fossil fuel phaseout in favor of (hypothetical future) carbon capture is the best evidence yet that moral hazard FUNDAMENTALLY compromises carbon capture as a climate solution,” wrote Michael Mann, a prominent climate scientist at the University of Pennsylvania, in a Bluesky post Sunday. As it stands, most CCS is used to squeeze additional oil from aging fields, so critics say setting global goals for it would lead to further subsidy of oil production, rather than limit or reduce the amount of CO2 that reaches the air. Behind the scenes in Antalya, some 700 carbon capture lobbyists were registered as attending, up from 531 at last year’s summit in Brazil and more than the combined delegations of all 14 Pacific Small Island Developing States, according to an analysis of U.N. participant lists by the Center for International Environmental Law. Forty-five of those representatives were granted entry to closed-door negotiating sessions. The center has not completed a similar analysis of lobbyists for other technologies. By Thursday, as formal climate talks continued, drafters had entirely stripped out mention of a transition away from fossil fuels while leaving the aggressive carbon capture benchmarks intact. When a final draft was proposed Sunday — two days after negotiations were scheduled to conclude — the CCS targets had been made less specific but remained, described as a nonbinding “gigatonne scale” goal. The agreement — and its emphasis on CCS — “really had the fossil fuel industry’s fingerprints all over it,” said Romain Ioualalen, the global policy lead for the nonprofit Oil Change International, a research and advocacy group pushing for a phaseout of fossil fuels. A coalition of nations, including the European Union, rejected the proposal outright. For years, tensions at the annual climate talks have tended to break down to three camps: Saudi Arabia, Russia and other oil-producing states — at times with tacit U.S. support — which argue for an approach that prioritizes slow changes in the energy system in service of economic stability; the wealthy, industrialized nations, which push for an energy transition but resist measures to pay for both the transition and damages caused by warming; and the low- and middle-income nations, which will sign on to fossil fuel phaseout only if other powerful economies commit to supporting the cost of their transition. Carbon capture remains just one part of that larger debate, which included other ways to clean up energy sources. But its weight in this year’s talks reflects long-standing efforts to tie climate action to its success, as well as a failure to enact any other meaningful agreement that would slow the rate of CO2 emissions in the first place. For more than a year, ProPublica and Drilled have investigated the history of carbon capture and storage and the decades-long effort by oil companies to validate it in the scientific community and at the U.N. Our reporting has found that industry funding contributed to influential CCS research at universities, petrostates pressed the U.N. to validate the technology without supporting evidence and climate modelers have assumed it can work at an enormous scale, despite the technology’s troubled real-world track record. In the closing session, a delegate from Panama explained that the country could not support the language in the final COP31 text in part because “it wagers too much” on CCS “instead of calling for deep changes.” Vanuatu, a small island nation in the Pacific that is especially vulnerable to rising sea levels, warned that the text “risks legitimizing continued fossil fuel dependence” and that carbon capture must not become “an excuse to prolong the fossil fuel era.” But Saudi Arabia, speaking on behalf of the 22 countries in the League of Arab States, insisted CCS was an essential part of a “package of solutions” to address climate change. “If indeed the climate challenge, as some have mentioned today, is so important,” the Saudi delegate said, “it makes no sense that solutions, concrete solutions, which is what this COP was meant to represent, will be taken off the table.” The post At a Doomed U.N. Conference, Saudi Arabia and Other Oil States Pushed Hard for an Unproven Climate Fix appeared first on ProPublica .

events.title: How cautious investors are struggling to avoid the AI bubble
events.summary: From Nvidia to Coreweave, AI and tech stocks have swung sharply in recent months. Some investors still see plenty of room to run, while others are trying to diversify — and finding it harder than expected. The tech-heavy Nasdaq stock index roared back to life this week after a worrying sell-off recently that saw huge falls in technology and artificial intelligence (AI)-related stocks. After suffering its worst week since the pandemic crash of March 2020, the Nasdaq opened Monday (November 23) nearly 1,700 points, or 7%, higher. The AI trade received a further boost after Nvidia reinstated CEO Jensen Huang on Monday, just 11 days after he was forced to resign amid a scandal involving extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. The chipmaker's stock rose more than 30% on the news, opening at nearly $170 (€155.5) per share and recovering most of the losses since last month, when the affair was first reported. The surge helped propel US stock indices to their best day since last year. But in premarket trading on Tuesday, Nvidia fell about 5%, underscoring the volatility of the market and the risks facing the AI sector and the broader tech industry. Will Anthropic put profits over security? How passive investing is fueling the AI trade The recent volatility around AI, memory chips and other technology stocks has unnerved even the most experienced and bullish investors. Yet, those seeking a haven away from the United States stock market, which has enjoyed the majority of the AI hype — along with Taiwan and South Korea — are increasingly finding few places to shelter. Economists warn that this is partly due to the way index funds, including exchange-traded funds (ETFs), work. These funds hold the pensions and other savings of hundreds of millions of passive investors. events.title: DR Congo sets deadline for local mine ownership decree
events.summary: The News DR Congo’s government will implement a decree forcing foreign mining companies to open their local units to Congolese shareholders by the end of January, the mines minister said, despite failing to agree key terms with the companies. The world’s largest cobalt producer and second-largest copper producer hosts operations run by Glencore, China’s CMOC and Zijin Mining, Canada’s Ivanhoe Mines and Barrick, and Kazakhstan-backed Eurasian Resources Group. The decree would apply a 2018 rule reserving 10% of mining companies’ shares for Congolese citizens, half for employees and half for other individuals. This is on top of the state’s own mandatory 10% stake. Several foreign mining companies lobbied in June for more time to comply with the new rules. “I have a draft decree on my desk,” Louis Watum told mining executives at the Makutano Mining business forum in Kinshasa on Monday. “Give it two months, it will pass. And those who don’t agree, too bad. See you in court.” Miners have reportedly questioned how the shares would be priced and whether the rule applies to mines that predate it. “This is no longer up for discussion,” Watum said. “We are moving to action.” ‘No more time for legalism’ The minister accused the industry of a double standard, arguing that miners sell stakes to other companies but resist Congolese buyers. “The law must be applied, that’s all,” he said. Glencore is negotiating to sell 40% of its interests in its two Congolese mines, Kamoto and Mutanda, to a consortium backed by the US government and Abu Dhabi, in a deal that would value them at about $9 billion. The non-binding agreement, signed in February, would let the buyers direct where their share of the copper and cobalt is sold, as Washington and its allies try to loosen China’s grip on DR Congo’s minerals. Watum compared the proposed ownership rule to the stock options multinationals grant senior executives, a practice DR Congo was now “democratizing,” and said shares reserved for other Congolese investors would be sold at market value. He did not say whether employees would have to pay for their stake, though a draft reported in October proposed giving it to them for free. Analysts and mining executives have warned that uncertainty over the reforms could undermine investor confidence, just as Kinshasa courts Western capital. Watum, however, said he was prepared for a repeat of the 2018 confrontation, when Ivanhoe Mines, whose DR Congo operations he then ran, was among the major miners that quit the Chamber of Mines industry body over a new mining code. “I don’t want it to come to that, but if you want it to come to that, that’s where we’ll end up.” Notable DR Congo to audit major miners annually from 2027 as authorities step up efforts to increase business for Congolese-owned firms, the head of the country’s subcontracting regulator said.

events.title: Behind the Curtain: When reality shouts
events.summary: We naturally assume people in business and power are slightly full of it, spinning us wildly to exaggerate their achievements or capabilities. In the case of AI and its ability to do irreparable damage to society, it's time for all of us — the media, the White House and Congress — to believe them: They've truly built something we don't understand and soon, if not already, can't fully control. Why it matters: This is no longer a future problem. It's a today problem, if not a crisis. You see this with near-daily glitches at airports or banks. You see this in our reporting about two dozen researchers inside these companies claiming their AI is too powerful and uncontrollable to release. And you see this in AI execs' own on-the-record warnings that we're at or near the point of the technology surpassing comprehension or control. Just believe them. If we wait for a cyberattack on the U.S. electricity grid or some bad actor to release a pathogen at an elementary school, it's too late. We'll panic and make rushed, emotional decisions and bad policies. It's not too late to prevent this, while still getting the upside benefits of AI. In our conversations with hundreds of people involved in building and regulating AI, there's shockingly wide agreement about the dangers ahead — and ways to protect against the worst outcomes. There's just no mechanism or urgency to bring the right mix of people together to do this. The steps seem clear: Make this a society-wide, urgent call to action. This should be an all-hands-on-deck moment, the only topic Congress prioritizes short-term. Yes, it probably requires presidential leadership, and Trump is reluctant to slow things down. But his top cyber officials privately agree with us: This demands fast, smart, bipartisan action with heavy private sector involvement. Let 'er rip no longer feels like a plausible plan. Focus on safety and cyber first. Most leading AI companies would gladly slow down a bit, prioritize verifiable safety standards, and even accept government oversight with teeth if their rivals did. They'd also allocate money and time to help critical government agencies and businesses fortify software systems from cyberattacks. But someone, either Trump's AI team or the top leaders in Congress, needs to force them. Level with the American public. As a nation and as business leaders, we're doing a spectacularly terrible job of explaining this technology to the public. There's a reason that the most bipartisan topic in America is a shared loathing of data centers. People hate AI. Most simply don't see it as something that will make their life better. We need leaders who can discuss the good, bad and ugly of AI in real time, nearly every day. A society-wide project needs to involve society. Go deeper ... "AI 2027: The reckoning."

events.title: Scoop: Anthropic and OpenAI employees fear unreleased AI models are too unsafe to release
events.summary: Anthropic and OpenAI are facing an increasingly urgent problem: Internal, unreleased models are becoming so powerful that many employees no longer believe they can be safely released, according to more than two dozen sources familiar with the internal debates. Why it matters: The challenge could significantly slow the AI boom, as the gap between what the best AI systems can do and humans' ability to control them continues to widen , sources told Axios. Researchers haven't found technical solutions for controlling the most advanced models. Some insiders believe it's fixable. Others aren't convinced and say companies should stop training new models entirely. Driving the news: Top AI leaders have long forecast that the technology would one day far surpass human intellect in virtually every field. Although internal models have yet to cross that threshold, recent breakthroughs at OpenAI and Anthropic have shocked researchers. The rapid advances in reasoning across domains including math, science, cybersecurity and AI research have also made the models difficult, if not impossible, to contain or control in internal tests, the sources said. Anthropic and OpenAI have unreleased models that are far more powerful than what they've already released publicly, but the AI companies have struggled to ensure that they are safe enough for public release, sources said. This has led to debate within Anthropic, OpenAI and the AI research community about whether to stop releasing future frontier models publicly, instead reserving them for internal deployment only. There has also been debate around whether to train new models at all, sources inside and outside those companies told Axios. What they're saying: "If we continue trying to make models much smarter, such that they're actually smarter than us ... they will in fact be able to trick us successfully," one researcher told Axios. "And once you get to that point, many of the schemes that we've had at work up until now sort of go out the window." Catch up quick: The power of unreleased models is already on public display. An Anthropic mathematician used an unreleased "research" version of Claude to present a proof of the Riemann hypothesis, which had eluded the brightest human minds for more than 150 years. An unreleased OpenAI model helped generate proofs for hundreds of math problems. Unreleased AI models were responsible for some of the industry's most shocking safety events, including the Hugging Face hack. Zoom in: AI researchers have long contemplated a terrifying threshold: If an AI possesses superhuman capability, how could humans contain it? Training practices that make AI models faster and more capable — but present greater safety risks — are widening the gap between what models can do and how well humans can control them. Problem 1: Reinforcement learning. A primary AI model training method — where models learn through trial and error by receiving rewards for passing various tests — is one of the techniques driving rapid improvements in AI capabilities. Why it's scary: As AI systems get more capable, they become better at "gaming" their rewards, including bypassing safety guardrails if cheating leads to a higher score. Problem 2: They know they're being watched. Historically, researchers monitored AI safety by forcing models to "think out loud" — writing out step-by-step reasoning before outputting a final action or answer. This transparency was a safety net, allowing monitors to catch rule-breaking or dangerous logic in real time. Why it's scary: As models grow more advanced, they are internalizing that logic, arriving at complex conclusions while showing less of their work. Researchers say the most advanced internal models have shown patterns of hiding reasoning entirely or providing deceptive "cover story" chains of thought to satisfy human monitors, sources say. Threat level: In public statements, top AI leaders have spoken about these risks. "This is the most important thing OpenAI has published in awhile," CEO Sam Altman wrote on X, citing his chief scientist's proposal for industry-wide limits on AI development. "The speed of development is quickly becoming too fast for us to keep safe," Anthropic's alignment lead wrote on X in September, quoting an essay from CEO Dario Amodei about pacing the frontier, a sentiment he reiterated when the company went public. Researchers and employees with direct knowledge of the implications of releasing these models told Axios they fear executives will choose profits over safety. Multiple frontier AI company employees said they feel executives have become out of touch with the severity of safety risks. For the record: OpenAI has adopted new safety requirements that could slow the pace of model releases, according to an OpenAI spokesperson. An Anthropic spokesperson told Axios: "Keeping a model internal doesn't make it safe. Our responsibility starts in training and covers how we use models ourselves, not only what we release. ... The hardest safety work is still ahead, and we've been clear that we may slow down or hold back even when it costs us." The spokesperson noted delays to pretraining for a recent model to allow for more security. What to watch: One solution some see is for frontier intelligence to remain within top AI companies. Companies could allow outside access through product releases in enterprise work, science, math and other fields, without having to dole out wide access to the model's power, just as Anthropic and OpenAI did with the initial releases of their most cyber-capable models. Many of the most concerned safety researchers warn that even internal testing and use of extremely powerful models is profoundly risky. The bottom line: Those closest to the frontier are sounding the alarm. It's unclear who's listening.

events.title: Scoop: ACLU eyes Supreme Court flips in 11 states
events.summary: The American Civil Liberties Union is expanding its state Supreme Court election fight into deep-red territory after the midterms left Texas just one judicial seat away from a Democratic majority, the group tells Axios. Why it matters: The next battles over abortion, voting rights, redistricting, religion in schools and LGBTQ protections could hinge on state Supreme Court races often overshadowed by federal campaigns. Those courts have become increasingly important arbiters of constitutional rights as the U.S. Supreme Court has given states greater latitude to set their own policies. By the numbers: The ACLU now eyes Supreme Court races in 11 states in 2027 and 2028, the group's chief political and advocacy officer Deirdre Schifeling tells Axios. The ACLU worked on court elections in five states this year. It spent $30 million on its broader electoral program, with Supreme Court races claiming the biggest share, she says. The group says it contacted 8 million voters through mail, digital ads, phone banks, door knocking and other outreach, according to the organization. Zoom in: Texas shows how fast a court can swing. Democrats swept all four Supreme Court races this month, winning seats on the state's highest civil court for the first time since 1994. Once the winners take office, Republicans' 9-0 majority will shrink to 5-4. Democrats need to flip just one of three Republican-held seats on the 2028 ballot to take control. The court unanimously vacated a lower-court order in 2024 that would have widened access to medical exceptions under the state's abortion restrictions. " That's a gigantic shift in one election cycle," Schifeling tells Axios. Zoom out: Democrats face steeper climbs elsewhere in 2028. North Carolina: Anita Earls' reelection leaves Republicans with a 5-2 majority. Democrats must win two of three Republican-held seats to flip the court. Ohio: Democrats flipped one seat and held another. Republicans will retain a 5-2 majority; Democrats need all three GOP-held seats coming up next cycle. Georgia: Three seats come up in May 2028. The court temporarily reinstated the state's six-week abortion ban in 2024. State of play: The ACLU is exploring Louisiana and Mississippi, two states outside its original judicial election targets. 2027 : Wisconsin has an open seat on April 6. Pennsylvania could have two open seats (depending on retention races), potentially putting control of its high court at stake. The group is also weighing two Mississippi seats. 2028 : Georgia, Arizona, Michigan and Montana join Texas, Ohio and North Carolina on the preliminary map. Louisiana and Mississippi remain under review. Context: The ACLU moves come as Black organizers also hope to build on surprise Southern Democratic victories in places national Democrats have long neglected. The Working Families Party plans to recruit and train candidates for school boards, statehouses and other down-ballot offices. Between the lines: The ACLU is expanding its voter-targeting operation in races often overshadowed by higher-profile contests. Its internal model flags roughly 14% of the electorate as especially receptive to its messages, including independents, libertarians and less frequent Democratic-leaning voters, Schifeling says. "We don't endorse candidates. We don't tell voters who to vote for," she says. Yes, but: The ACLU hasn't finalized its 2028 spending plans and probably won't compete everywhere on its list, Schifeling says. The ACLU announced a $750,000 voter-education campaign before Georgia's May Supreme Court elections. All three Republican-appointed incumbents won. The group hasn't finished measuring how much its outreach influenced the 2026 judicial vote. The bottom line: The midterms changed the math but the next round could change who interprets Americans' rights.

events.title: Lowering the Medicare eligibility age is harder than it sounds
events.summary: Reducing the Medicare eligibility age may strike Democrats as a realistic fallback to passing Medicare for All, but it's an option that would be incredibly difficult to pull off. Why it matters: Even incremental steps to address affordability could have huge price tags and prompt fierce industry opposition. Driving the news: Prominent Democrats have been throwing their support behind lowering the Medicare eligibility age, expanding children's health coverage and adding dental, vision and hearing benefits to Medicare. Incoming Senate health committee Chairman Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) called for the package shortly after the midterms, calling it "an immediate first step to Medicare for All." House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, who is poised to become speaker in January, suggested on "Face the Nation" this weekend that Democrats may be able to work with Republicans on a package after President Trump said he may be open to working with Democrats. Prominent Democrats in both the House and Senate have signed on to legislation that would lower the eligibility age to 50, though the bills are significantly different. The big picture: Democrats' sweeping electoral gains have prompted weeks of discussion about what exactly a push to lower health care costs should look like. The party is united in its desire to roll back the Medicaid funding cuts in last year's tax and spending law and to reinstate enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidies that expired late last year — lofty goals for any Congress. There's widespread recognition that Medicare for All won't become law, and that Democrats aren't of one mind on a single-payer plan, with plenty of moderate members still loath to abolish private health insurance. That tension has led to questions about alternatives, and whether "Medicare for More" could be an answer. Between the lines: Lowering the Medicare eligibility age would require a series of tough decisions. Just shaving a few years off the current eligibility age could cost the federal government hundreds of billions of dollars. To avoid adding to the federal deficit, lawmakers would have to come up with offsets that either generate equivalent revenue or, more likely, cuts to government spending. Plus, the measure would likely attract intense and powerful opposition from health industries. Zoom in: Lowering the eligibility age would almost certainly provoke strong blowback from hospitals and providers, which receive much lower reimbursement rates through Medicare than through commercial insurance. "I think a general rule of thumb is the more people who are covered under Medicare relative to commercial or ACA, the less hospitals will be paid," said Marc Goldwein, senior policy director for the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget. "From my perspective, that's not a bad thing," he added. What they're saying: "You can't just add millions of people to Medicare without extra revenues, particular[ly] since the Medicare hospital trust fund already faces solvency issues," said KFF executive vice president Larry Levitt. "Health care providers are likely to view lowering Medicare's age as — pick your metaphor — the camel's nose in the tent or a slippery slope," he added. Hospitals fought former President Biden's 2020 calls to lower the eligibility age, fearing it would cost them billions of dollars in revenue. "We believe expanding coverage to patients should not put their access to critical services at risk," said Colin Milligan, a spokesperson for the American Hospital Association. "Proposals that rely on Medicare would exacerbate chronic Medicare underpayments and threaten access to care and our ability to care for patients." What we're watching: A serious legislative effort will also require answering crucial technical questions, like whether newly granted enrollees get the same access, benefits and premium structure as those 65-plus, or whether they'll be given the option to buy into the program. Policymakers will also have to decide what to do about employer insurance — and whether employers could contribute toward Medicare coverage for their older workers. The bottom line: The deeper you dig, the more complicated the policy gets.

events.title: Nvidia's one-man board: How Trump inherited Jensen Huang's scandal
events.summary: A euphoric Wall Street erupted Monday as President Trump personally secured Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia, trading on the end of a scandal that — in reality — has only just begun. Why it matters: By assuring Nvidia's board that Huang poses no national security risk, Trump has staked the credibility of the U.S. government on a CEO who lied about his relationship with a suspected Chinese spy. It's among the most extraordinary presidential interventions in corporate history — a de facto bailout of the AI industry that will be scrutinized, in excruciating detail, by a hawkish and hostile Congress. Zoom in: Six days after Nvidia's chairman publicly ruled out Huang's return, the board unanimously reinstated him after a secretive White House operation that blindsided even the company's top executives. Trump joined Sunday's board meeting by phone, with one source telling Axios that the president pushed harder for Huang's reinstatement than Huang himself. Nvidia acknowledged relying on assurances from "senior levels" of the U.S. government, even as its own investigation into the suspected Chinese espionage operation remained unfinished. The market reaction was staggering: Nasdaq 100 futures surged to their 7% overnight trading limit, following a brutal week that had raised fears of a broader collapse in AI stocks. Nvidia shares rocketed nearly 31%, adding hundreds of billions to the company's market value and helping Wall Street recover more than half of last week's losses. Trump took a victory lap in an hour-long, freewheeling CNBC interview , declaring Huang "exonerated" and claiming the board ultimately "decided to do what we wanted them to do." Screenshot via Truth Social Between the lines: In orchestrating Huang's comeback, Trump drew on instincts that have defined own tumultuous political career — starting with his conviction that presidential power has "no limits." Never surrender: Trump, the master of the political comeback, appears to see a fellow survivor in Huang. He made the comparison unmistakable by sharing a doctored version of his iconic 2024 assassination-attempt photo, with a bloodied Huang raising a red bra in triumph beneath an Nvidia flag. Distrust of intelligence: Still embittered by the Russia investigation , Trump brushed aside warnings from his own intelligence agencies about suspected Chinese espionage at the heart of America's AI industry. Huang's allies appealed to that skepticism, portraying the Nvidia founder as a victim of the "deep state" and anonymous leaks. The market is king: Trump viewed Huang's return as essential to restoring confidence in an AI industry worth trillions. For a president who treats stock prices as a measure of his success, Monday's spectacular rally offered instant vindication. Zoom out: Trump's intervention transformed an already sordid corporate scandal into a political gift for Democrats, delivering a fresh target for the anti-corruption crusade that helped sweep them into power. The backlash also cuts deep into Trump's own party and administration, where China hawks see the scandal as a direct threat to the technological supremacy they've spent years fighting to preserve. Huang will face closed-door questioning alongside Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter next week, followed by a public Senate hearing Dec. 3 that promises to put the entire affair under a national spotlight. The bottom line: Huang has reclaimed his throne, with the full might of the American presidency behind him. Like Napoleon returning from exile , the question now is how long he can hold it.

events.title: InferNode gives Bell Labs' Inferno OS a 64-bit second wind
events.summary: InferNode brings a modernized, 64-bit edition of Inferno, the distributed operating system that followed Plan 9 from Bell Labs. For us, the strapline of the InferNode project distracts from the interesting part. It describes the project as a "Secure Runtime for AI Agents," but we think it's something far more interesting than another LLM tool. Fair warning: this vulture has no interest whatsoever in AI agents, and we are not even going to look at this planned use of InferNode. We're interested in the OS, and here, its GitHub repository spells out the part that caught our attention: "a 64-bit Inferno® OS." That grabbed us because Inferno is a very interesting OS, although it doesn't get much attention – for example, the official Inferno GitHub repository shows little activity in the last few years. Inferno is the successor to Plan 9, which we've written and talked about before , including recent releases of its community continuation, 9front . Plan 9 is what the team who invented Unix did next. Plan 9 is a very minimalist, natively clustered Unix: machines can freely mount one another's filesystems, display windows on one another, and start processes on one another. Plan 9 turns a network of machines running this Unix-like OS into a single machine. So, for instance, if you were working on a laptop with limited storage and compute power, you could compile a large complex project on a faster machine elsewhere on the network, using project files located on a third machine, while watching the process in your terminal on your screen, with no messing about with SSH sessions. Plan 9 and 9front programs are compiled into architecture-specific native binaries. Different processor families can still work together across the network, but the same executable won't run unchanged on both an x86-64 laptop and an Arm64 server. Inferno takes a different approach. It's contemporaneous with the far less ambitious Java. On Inferno, languages compile code for a VM called Dis, which is part of the kernel. This means that Inferno binaries execute directly on anything that the Inferno kernel runs on. The OS kernel is built to run bare-metal, or as a process on various other OSes, without needing a separate hardware virtual machine or hypervisor. A single binary can run on all supported CPU architectures. Inferno applications are normally written in the Limbo programming language , whose documentation was written by Unix co-creator Dennis Ritchie. Limbo is one of the languages that influenced Go, but Inferno lets compilers for other languages target Dis as well. The binaries run anywhere. Inferno on Arm, or x86, or RISC-V, or running in a Windows or Linux or macOS process, your program just runs. We've been trying to contact Vita Nuova , the company that maintains Inferno, for some years without success. Development appears to have slowed considerably. Moving the runtime to 64-bit also raises compatibility questions: some forks change Dis's word size and cannot run existing 32-bit bytecode unchanged. We're aware of several efforts to build 64-bit versions of Inferno. Caerwyn Jones's Inferno64 is one of the more visible, and the GitHub repository (and indeed his X account ) show considerable activity. However, Inferno64's Dis is not compatible with 32-bit Dis code. Another fork is Dinsmoor's Inferno64 , which also shows recent activity, albeit with the assistance of the Claude LLM. Others include the long-quiescent Purgatorio and 9ferno , both inactive for years, plus Scott Guyon's more active fork . Dropping the compatibility goal altogether, Node9 replaces Limbo with Lua and Dis with LuaJIT . There are more forks and variants than we've gone into here. Given that there have been quite a few efforts, and most haven't delivered final ready-to-use products yet, we were surprised when InferNode was suddenly announced on the Inferno-OS mailing list last week. Developer Peter Finn said: "An experimental runtime for containing generative AI agents was the original motivation, but most of the work since has been on the OS itself, and the AI parts are ordinary file servers. For example, llmsrv at /mnt/llm and speech9p are started from the login profile, and if you delete those lines they're simply not there. There's also non-generative AI additions on object detection served as files at /mnt/vision, on the CPU or a GPU host, and voice calls between devices done by mounting each other's audio files over 9P. There's a GUI layer intended to facilitate hands-free AI agent use, but it too is optional." He also said that InferNode's development was largely independent of the existing efforts, partly because the primary target was Arm64, not x86-64. Its 64-bit Dis runtime is incompatible with the 32-bit original: "The opcodes, file format and magic number are unchanged, but the word size isn't, so frame sizes, offsets and pointer maps all differ. Limbo source recompiles without edits. A 32-bit .dis is currently rejected at load time." InferNode doesn't implement 9front's DP9IK authentication protocol , so it cannot connect to servers requiring that authentication. Dr Finn told us: "DP9IK is not quantum-safe. That's the reason. InferNode's current crypto policy is strict CNSA ." InferNode also includes some slightly unexpected components, related to its intended use for testing LLM agents – such as a wallet for the Ethereum cryptocurrency, which Finn said was "mainly to support agent payments." The first release of Inferno was in 1996, the year after Java and the JVM were launched. Inferno is a much more ambitious project, but its core function – the ability to run identical binaries on multiple platforms, without recompilation – was close enough that they ended up competing in the market, and Java won. It was a pleasant surprise to see a modernized version of Inferno arrive this year, 30 years on. Finn told us: "About a year ago I saw the potential for a 'break-out' moment for this tech as a runtime for containing AI agents. The flood of cybersecurity risks we would face on account of adversarial AI agents required new systems with small footprints and minimal attack surfaces. Inferno was a perfect candidate and it was an opportunity to show the world how visionary Plan 9's ideas were and how well they mapped on to pressing contemporary security issues." "If InferNode succeeds, it is an opportunity for Plan 9's ideas to migrate out of hobby-land and really make an impact – as they deservedly should." He has a point. On a related note, this vulture discussed the possibility of rebuilding the world's IT systems from scratch on last week's Kettle podcast . Perhaps the hour for tools like this really has come round at last. ®

events.title: More Americans back childhood vaccinations
events.summary: The share of Americans who believe it’s extremely important for children to be vaccinated has ticked up since 2024, amid concerns about a domestic measles outbreak and a push by the Trump administration to overhaul childhood vaccination recommendations. Forty-seven percent of US adults say childhood shots are extremely important, according to new Gallup polling, a seven-point increase from 2024; only 6% say they aren’t important at all. There continues to be a big partisan divide: Two-thirds of Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents say childhood vaccinations are extremely important, compared to just 27% of Republicans and Republican-leaners. The poll was taken in October, before the US lost its measles elimination status. Meanwhile, 16% of Americans — the most since 2015 — believe there is a link between autism and vaccines, though such a link has never been proven. — Morgan Chalfant

events.title: Thune prepares to navigate the minority — and an unpredictable Trump
events.summary: The Scene About 20 minutes into an interview about the future of the Republican Party, John Thune’s phone rang. The screen displayed two capital letters: “DT.” “Let me take this real quick,” Thune said. By sheer coincidence, the call came mid-question about whether Thune’s Senate Republicans should exercise more independence from President Donald Trump. Unlike some past phone calls between the president and the Republican Senate leader, this one was drama-free: Trump was flying back from China and wanted to talk about his meeting with Chinese and Russian leaders. Thune and the president chatted amiably for a few minutes before we resumed our interview. The episode was nonetheless a reminder that Trump looms large as the Republican Party prepares to transition to a new national leader, its first non-Trump presidential nominee since 2012. Thune will have front-row seats to the transformation for at least two years — and probably many more. Change is already underway. Thune’s wingman in the House for these past two years, Speaker Mike Johnson, is stepping down from his role. And after a midterm shellacking, Thune has to pick up at least six Senate seats in 2028 to get back his soon-to-be old job of majority leader. Thune has a throwback, Reagan-era view of what makes the Republican Party tick: limited government, free markets, strong national security, and social conservatism. He also understands the party is now a hybrid of that view and Trumpism, which swayed working-class voters and wooed independent voters in 2016 and 2024. But that coalition is in shambles after this year’s midterms. And Thune did not mince words about what happened in November, even as he insisted Republicans “have an opportunity to scratch our way back in” after Democrats filleted the GOP over cost-of-living issues. “We got our butts kicked, and you’ve got to learn from that and rebuild and get better,” Thune told Semafor in an interview before lawmakers left town for the Thanksgiving break. “We’ve got a governing coalition out there waiting to happen, but we’ve got to start talking to them.” Thune is already talking to his colleagues about their plans to run for reelection to avoid the sort of open-seat debacles the GOP just experienced in Iowa and North Carolina. He’s talked to an undecided Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., about his plans, and has also made clear that 93-year-old incumbent Sen. Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa, controls his own destiny. “It’s his call to make. He’s proven to be a very resilient vote-getter, and you know my assumption is if he runs, he wins,” Thune said. “We have to be prepared under any circumstance in a lot of these states that created challenges for us this last time to reassert what it is that we’re for, and to go out and win these people back.” Thune is also figuring out his own political future, and is leaning toward running for another six-year term in 2028. “We’ll be doing all the things here in the next few months to gear up,” Thune said. “I don’t take anything for granted. I think anybody can lose, but you know, in a primary or a general? I guess I like my chances.” Trump threatened Thune with a primary challenge in 2022, when the South Dakota Republican thought long and hard about whether to run again. The two haven’t spoken specifically about Thune’s run in 2028, but Trump had kind words for Thune over the weekend, calling him a “good man” and blaming the GOP’s legislative morass on “bad Republicans.” Thune’s closest allies are highly invested in his reelection. “I would expect him to run,” said Sen. Katie Britt, R-Ala. She praised Thune for raising $800 million for GOP electoral efforts while remaining “so intentional about being home and making sure that South Dakota was first. I think he is well positioned to be successful.” The majority leader has taken a lot of arrows for the Senate GOP after Trump’s pressure campaign to gut the filibuster for a voter ID bill failed. He spends a lot of time back in South Dakota and says it’s “always important to get outside of the algorithm.” “John is a lot more popular in the public than he is on social media,” said Sen. Mike Rounds, R-S.D. He said he’d heard nothing about a primary challenge to Thune, including from former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem. Coming fights Thune’s job is changing: Instead of holding the fractious Senate GOP together in support of Trump’s agenda, he now needs to keep them united against Democrats. He’s in a prime position to oversee the Republican Party’s transition away from the Trump era and toward something else. In the short term, he’s not expecting perfect unity. “If you represent a state and the administration is on a different page than you are on some stuff, you just got to occasionally find your own voice and be your own person,” Thune advised. He foresees cooperating with Democrats on AI regulation and acknowledges that some of his GOP colleagues may work with Democrats on other issues. His hope is that “where we can, we’re going to want to hold the line.” Thune is already bracing for Republican shifts on Trump’s tariff and the Iran war. “Most of our members have tried to give the president a lot of latitude on managing the situation in Iran … but that’s I think an issue where people are probably going to be more inclined going forward to maybe have their own position on it,” Thune said. But he’s not conceding anything on one of Democrats’ top priorities. He opposes Democratic efforts to roll back Medicaid work requirements and future cuts to the provider tax that were in last year’s GOP tax cut law. Still, he faces the potentially tricky task of keeping his party united in a Senate where just four GOP defections could send bills to Trump’s desk next year. “I hope that, in spite of Democrat efforts to try and undo all that, that our folks realize that these are changes that are long-term good for the country,” Thune said. The View From skeptics Some Republicans harbor lingering frustrations toward Thune, even if they’re on board with his reelection as GOP leader. “I obviously had issues in terms of what we did and didn’t do for the last Congress,” Johnson, the senator, said. “But the conference has decided he’s our leader and I’ll try and support our conference.” Burgess’s view A longtime senior Republican hand told me in 2024 that Thune would have been the right transitional figure to steer the Republican Party had Trump had lost the election to Kamala Harris. Instead, Thune was thrust into probably the hardest job in Washington: managing a Senate majority that has grown less and less inclined to bend to Trump’s will. Now, he has to navigate his 44-member Senate minority through Trump’s last two years. Thune wants to regain Senate control, but another poor political environment in 2028 could make it just as important to prevent a Democratic supermajority. events.title: Huang’s reinstatement at Nvidia shows Lutnick is dug in
events.summary: Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia’s CEO is reinforcing Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick’s ability to weather multiple Trump Cabinet dramas. Commerce’s decision to blacklist Nvidia customer Megaspeed followed months of entreaties by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, among others, for Lutnick to crack down harder on chip exports to China. But Lutnick, whose relationship with Bessent has been tense since President Donald Trump’s second transition, declined to act. And President Donald Trump appeared to agree, recently asserting that “if you didn’t delay it … you could have a blowup with China.” Bessent, who previously called for Nvidia to hire a new CEO from outside the company, adopted a different stance Sunday, asserting that Nvidia’s culture outweighed “one person’s foibles.” The next day, Nvidia announced Huang’s return, citing administration officials’ assurances that it “poses no national security risk.” That sent AI stocks soaring — and handed a win to Lutnick, who reportedly averted his own firing earlier this year by making a $25 million donation to Trump’s presidential library. “The circular firing squad is a lot less dangerous when everyone’s wearing a bulletproof vest,” a person close to the White House said. “At this point, Russian roulette has become a routine part of the job — and everyone seems perfectly comfortable taking another spin.” A White House official pointed to Bessent’s remarks Sunday that Huang was “on the outside now.” The official also called “any claim that Secretary Lutnick’s position has been tied to a donation towards the White House ballroom … baseless and wildly reckless speculation,” adding that “Trump has maintained complete confidence in the secretary and his ability to carry out the position.” The Treasury and Commerce Departments did not comment. — Eleanor Mueller

events.title: Abu Dhabi's IRH targets titanium with $460m Kenmare offer
events.summary: Abu Dhabi's International Resources Holding has agreed terms for a possible £352.8 million ($460 million) cash takeover of London-listed Kenmare Resources, one of the world's largest producers of titanium minerals. The deal would give the mining arm of UAE-based Two Point Zero Group control of Mozambique's Moma mine, one of the world's biggest titanium deposits. It would also take IRH beyond copper and tin into a mineral that the US, the EU and Canada class as critical for the defence, aerospace and medical industries. Dublin-based Kenmare's board is “unanimously minded to recommend” a firm offer on those terms, the companies said in a joint statement on Monday, though “there can be no certainty that an offer will be made”. IRH would pay 380 pence a share, a 52 per cent premium to Kenmare's closing price on November 20 and more than double its average price in the 30 days to October 5, before speculation about a deal lifted the shares. The offer gives Kenmare an enterprise value of about £487.1 million. The approach depends on the Mozambique government approving the change of control without material changes to Kenmare's mining licence, and on the country's tax authority confirming any capital gains tax owed. IRH also wants irrevocable backing from Kenmare's directors and some institutional shareholders. Under Irish takeover rules, IRH has until 5pm Dublin time (9pm in the UAE) on December 15 to make a firm offer or walk away. Kenmare is the largest seller on the open market of ilmenite, the iron-titanium ore that is the main raw material for titanium pigment and metal, with about 6 per cent of global supply. Moma has resources for more than 100 years of production at current rates and produced 1 million tonnes of finished products last year. Most mined titanium is turned into titanium dioxide, a white pigment used in paints, coatings, plastics and paper. That market is expected to grow from $21.8 billion this year to $26.3 billion by 2031, or 3.8 per cent a year, according to MarketsandMarkets. Asia-Pacific accounts for about 46 per cent of demand, led by China. A smaller share goes into titanium metal, which is prized for its strength and light weight. Western aerospace manufacturers will need 1.6 million tonnes of the metal by 2044, according to consultancy Project Blue, which says supply is increasingly controlled by Russia and China. The near-term market is weaker. Prices for ilmenite have been under pressure this year from oversupply, particularly in China. Last month, Kenmare cut its 2026 production guidance for the mineral to between 710,000 and 750,000 tonnes, from about 800,000 tonnes. Two Point Zero, which is listed on the Abu Dhabi Securities Exchange, has a market value of $19.4 billion. IRH, which was set up in 2022, took a 51 per cent stake in Zambia's Mopani Copper Mines in 2024 after committing $1.1 billion to revive it. Last year, it agreed to buy 56 per cent of Congolese tin producer Alphamin Resources for $367 million. IRH did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

events.title: Delayed Cancer Treatment. Missed Medication. How a Popular Insurance Plan’s Use of Prior Authorization Hurt Patients.
events.summary: Richie Jones at Stone Mountain Park in Georgia this month. Jones and his doctor repeatedly tried to get his insurer, Ambetter, to cover his cancer treatment. Jones often visits the park for quiet reflection. Matt Odom for ProPublica Felicia tried everything she could think of to get her insurer to cover the only treatment that made a difference in her years-long effort to manage her obesity. In 2024, after her insurer denied her coverage for medication despite her doctor’s order, the 38-year-old Texan sought the help of consumer advocates. She crafted a detailed appeal. She sent it not just to the head of the Fortune 500 company that oversaw her health insurance plan, but also copied the secretary of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services and the chair of the Federal Trade Commission. A short time later, someone called from a number she didn’t recognize. It was Kevin Counihan, CEO of her health plan, Ambetter. Felicia, who asked to be identified by her middle name due to her fear of reprisals and so that she could share sensitive medical information, calmly told Counihan that she hoped that “something gets done right by me and by my health.” “I have tried everything in the formulary. I exhausted all options,” she explained on the call, which she recorded and shared with ProPublica. Kevin Counihan, who was CEO of Ambetter and had once overseen the federal Affordable Care Act marketplace, conceded that a customer’s reported experience with his company had been “a tremendous inconvenience and a real pain in the neck.” Brooks Kraft/Getty Images A veteran health insurance executive who had once overseen the federal Affordable Care Act marketplace, Counihan conceded on the call that Felicia’s reported experience with his company had been “a tremendous inconvenience and a real pain in the neck.” But he assured her that “we really want to get you what you” and your doctor “think is the most appropriate medication for you.” “I’m working on it as fast as possible,” said Counihan.  Counihan’s call was a rare acknowledgment from the company’s top brass of a pervasive problem. Ambetter, the most popular plan on the ACA marketplace, has one of the worst track records of delaying or denying medical coverage by refusing to cover the costs. ProPublica has found that Ambetter last year denied these kinds of requests — known as prior authorization — at a higher rate than any other large insurer on the ACA marketplace. Our analysis of Ambetter’s own data, along with interviews with more than two dozen recent customers, sheds new light on the vast and sometimes illogical nature of how the company can block access to care. Each dot below is a marketplace plan in Texas, sized according to the number of prior authorization requests it reported in 2025. Plans further to the right deny those requests at higher rates. Ambetter plans are shown in red. In Texas, where Ambetter’s denial rates were above 32%, the company initially refused to pay for a medical scan for a patient with Stage 4 colon cancer because the doctor hadn’t ordered a cheaper, less precise scan first. In Iowa, where Ambetter’s denial rate was 31%, it approved a patient’s colonoscopy but denied a request for the bowel prep that all patients must drink in advance of the procedure. In Kansas, where Ambetter’s denial rate was 26%, it stopped covering an anti-inflammatory treatment for a patient with Crohn’s disease because it wanted the patient to try a different drug. A ProPublica analysis of nearly 200 federal marketplace plans across the country found that Ambetter had the highest denial rates in most states where it provided data. Ambetter plans had an average denial rate of 25% in states where the company reported data for last year. That’s substantially higher than the 16% average denial rate for all marketplace plans.  Our analysis is based on data that federal regulators required marketplace plans to report and publish for the first time this year. The requirement is intended to offer greater transparency into how often insurers restrict care by denying prior authorization for treatment. Since the ACA marketplace launched in 2013, there has been little transparency around how often insurers request — and deny — prior authorization. Insurers use prior authorization to limit spending on treatment, equipment and prescriptions. They say it is also intended to ensure that doctors try less expensive and less invasive treatments before pricier ones. Health insurance experts said that the process of how or when prior authorization gets used is largely a black box.  U.S. Rep. Craig Goldman, a Republican from Texas, sponsored a bipartisan bill that would require marketplace plans to disclose more information about their use of prior authorization. “These companies represent these individuals — and yet denying them coverage and not being transparent with what they will be able to cover,” he said. “They’re just not there for the best interest of the people.” Four former heads of state insurance departments who reviewed ProPublica’s findings said that Ambetter’s high denial rate was such an outlier that current regulators should examine further. “This is stunning — and not in a good way,” Mila Kofman, a former insurance superintendent in Maine who now oversees the District of Columbia’s ACA marketplace, said of Ambetter’s denial rate. “This is something insurance regulators need to understand. There’s a huge opportunity for regulators to address the improper use of prior authorization.” We’re Investigating Prior Authorization. Help ProPublica Understand Your Health Insurance Denial. ProPublica is looking into the ways health insurers’ use of prior authorization impacts patients. We need your help to figure out if the process is still leading to delayed or missed treatments, tests, medical equipment or medication. Share Your Experience Sarah London, CEO of Ambetter’s parent company, Centene, recently said in a statement on its website that it was “ creating a more predictable and transparent experience ” for its customers. That statement followed growing backlash against the industry and a push to limit the practice of prior authorization.  Last year Centene joined America’s largest insurers in vowing to rely on prior authorization less often. Industry representatives have said that the collective efforts of those insurers will decrease their use of prior authorization across all of their plans by 11% in 2026. (Health plans aren’t required to publish 2026 data until next year.) ProPublica sent Centene a detailed list of questions about its use of prior authorization and the impact it has on its customers. ProPublica also provided Ambetter with signed releases from customers, including Felicia, waiving their right to privacy, so that Centene representatives could speak with ProPublica about their specific denials. events.title: Oman's new financial centre registers first companies as it prepares to open
events.summary: Oman's new International Financial Centre (IFC Oman) has registered its first companies as it prepares to officially open next year. The first 13 companies were registered and presented with their certificates of incorporation, IFC Oman said on Tuesday. IFC Oman, plans for which were first revealed in January , also opened its headquarters at Al Mouj Business Park in Muscat. Domestic and international businesses can now establish a presence within the centre’s jurisdiction. Preparations continue for financial services licensing early next year. “The legal and regulatory framework now in place lays the foundation for a stable and competitive business environment,” said Sayyid Al Said, deputy prime minister for economic affairs and chairman of IFC Oman said. “This will further strengthen Oman’s appeal to international investors and global financial institutions, while supporting the growth of our national economy.” Oman has been taking steps to diversify its economy away from oil as part of its Vision 2040 plan, with investments in sectors such as logistics, manufacturing and property, helping to expand its non-oil economic base. Under its economic and social reforms programme, Oman aims to reduce its dependence on oil income from about 30 per cent to 16 per cent by 2030 and 8.4 per cent by 2040. The sultanate's location, as well as focus on non-oil reforms, is backing its economy, with gross domestic product projected to grow by 4.1 per cent this year, the International Monetary Fund said last month . “The decision by 13 companies to establish a presence here from the outset reflects the strength of the business and investment environment the centre offers,” said Sultan Al Habsi, Oman's Minister of Finance and vice chairman of IFC Oman. Among the companies registered is Abu Dhabi-based Blue Five Capital, an alternative investment platform. “We look forward to welcoming more companies that will bring new capital and expertise, generate business activity, strengthen the financial services sector, and build closer links between international investors and businesses across the region,” Mr Al Habsi said. “We will maintain this momentum as we complete the regulatory framework ahead of the start of financial services licensing early next year.” The opening of IFC Oman's headquarters follows the issuance of the royal decrees on its operating, regulatory and courts laws, as well as five regulations covering operations, companies, partnerships, foundations and interpretation. They cover the requirements for establishing and conducting business within the centre, including corporate governance, regulatory obligations and dispute resolution. “The framework gives companies and investors greater clarity on the rules governing their activities and a sound basis for planning their operations,” the statement said. IFC Oman will join other existing financial centres in the Gulf, including Abu Dhabi's international financial centre ADGM, the Dubai International Financial Centre and the King Abdullah Financial District in Riyadh, as well as the Qatar Financial Centre.

events.title: UK gov invests in defense startup making virtual training ground for AI
events.summary: The British government is investing in a UK-based AI defense startup that aims to train autonomous military systems in virtual environments, in a bid to reduce the country's reliance on overseas technology. Both the Sovereign AI Fund and the National Security Strategic Investment Fund (NSSIF) have contributed to a Series A funding round for Agon Dynamics, said to value the biz at $450 million. This $70 million round takes the total capital raised by the firm to $100 million, following its initial $30 million seed round earlier this year. The government claims this move will help strengthen the UK’s sovereign capabilities when it comes to the use of AI for defense, plus the hope that nurturing native technical know-how converts into industrial strength and greater resilience. But it is not revealing how much cash it has stumped up, claiming such investments are commercially sensitive, although it did say that typical equity amounts obtained from the the Sovereign AI Fund tend to be worth around £1 million to £10 million ($1.3 million to $13 million). Agon is understood to be developing facilities to train and test AI systems needed for defense. This covers systems to help defend against drone attacks, or ensuring that AI tools still continue to work as intended if communications with the command center are disrupted. Training like this currently needs to be carried out in the real world, which is time-consuming and expensive, according to the government. For this reason, Agon is building a "virtual battlefield" environment where AI models can be tested against realistic simulations of the situations they might encounter. The company says its synthetic battle arena provides a safe, repeatable environment for developers and defense contractors to try out autonomous systems against thousands of demanding scenarios before deployment. Systems can face adaptive virtual adversaries informed by live conflict intelligence, helping them to respond to evolving tactics, threats and operating conditions. This may include simulations of mass drone attacks that would overwhelm conventional air defense systems, or testing how autonomous systems operate when navigation is degraded or adversary tactics change. "Europe is in an AI arms race as we enter the era of agentic warfare: intelligent agents and machines that will need to understand their environment, make decisions and adapt at a speed and scale that humans alone cannot match," says co-founder and CEO Tristam Constant, a former British Army officer. "We exist to build the sovereign infrastructure and AI foundation models to allow us to train, test, and evolve autonomous defense systems, in Europe, for Europe - to outperform adversary capabilities." For the government, AI Minister Kanishka Narayan claimed that Britain is well-placed to lead efforts to ensure such technologies are reliable, trustworthy, and deployed responsibly. "AI is rapidly transforming how wars are fought, from the use of drones through to how rapidly soldiers can interpret battlefield information. The UK needs sovereign defence AI capabilities to bolster our national security in this new era," he stated. ®

events.title: Education software supplier's legacy login system left 355,000 school email addresses exposed
events.summary: More than 355,000 school staff and pupil email addresses ended up in the hands of hackers who broke into UK education software supplier Bromcom in September. The breach was added to Have I Been Pwned on Monday, revealing that 355,051 unique email addresses were caught up in the incident. The data also included single sign-on (SSO) registration reference numbers, although Bromcom insists that no passwords or authentication tokens were stolen. As The Register reported in Octobe r , the attackers got in through a legacy SSO registration component in Bromcom's Communications Server environment. The technology had already been superseded but was still running because an internal system continued to use it. Bromcom discovered something was amiss on September 6 after customers reported problems accessing its SSO service. At the time, the company was still working with external forensic specialists to establish exactly what the intruders had managed to get their hands on. Bromcom's FAQ says its investigation is complete and confirms that the intruders used a script to extract SSO registration information from the compromised server. The supplier insists its Management Information System (MIS), used by schools to keep track of everything from attendance to pupil records, was untouched. The compromised service also couldn't be used to get into Microsoft or Google accounts, which have their own login systems. Bromcom has since pulled the plug on the old component, tightened its authorization checks, and added more security logging. It says it hasn't found any evidence of accounts being hijacked as a result of the breach. Bromcom also confirmed it hadn't reported the breach to the UK's Information Commission's Office. Its reasoning is that it was the data processor, not the controller, so any decision to involve the regulator was for the affected schools and academy trusts to make. As for the risk to staff and pupils, Bromcom considers it to be low. No passwords or pupil records held in the MIS were taken, it says, although schools have been advised to watch for phishing messages and suspicious requests to reset passwords or approve sign-ins. The supplier's software is used by more than 5,000 schools and 390 multi-academy trusts across the UK, though it hasn't said how many were caught up in this particular mess. The Register has asked Bromcom how many schools and pupils were affected, and whether the figure published by Have I Been Pwned matches its own findings, but has yet to receive a response. Bromcom kept the superseded component running because an internal system still needed it. Unfortunately, the intruders found a use for it too. ®

events.title: Why AI Struggles To Reuse Chip Designs
events.summary: Key Takeaways: AI can accelerate derivative chip design, but those derivatives may not be physically viable or cost-effective. AI-assisted reuse depends on the availability of accurate design data, engineering knowledge, and proven methodologies. End-to-end automation is limited by gaps in multi-physics simulation, implementation, and verification. Chipmakers are seeing mixed results when they apply AI to derivative and new chip designs, finding that AI-generated solutions can be substantially different and more costly than expected, and that AI-driven designs introduce new manufacturing and verification challenges. Several key problems have emerged when incorporating AI in chip design. Among them: The data needed to ensure that follow-on designs will function as expected may not be complete because some of that data resides in other companies, such as foundries, OSATs, and various equipment and process providers; Integrating rapidly evolving AI capabilities into established EDA flows remains challenging, especially where predictability, traceability, and silicon-proven results are required. Many organizations have customized tools for their own chips, markets, and expertise, and AI tools have not yet adapted to those changes. “There’s the engineer in me that says if AI can take us to brave new worlds where humans haven’t yet gone, that’s an exciting thing,” said Nilesh Kamdar, general manager of Keysight EDA . “But I’ve seen it run into problems. For example, I had a low-pass filter, which we call a pixelated model, and it looks like a QR code in the middle. There’s a high-frequency part running at about 2 GHz. If I want to change it to 2.5 GHz, a human would look it up in a textbook. There are traditional ways to do it, and they would create something that any other human would recognize. AI looks at this, says, ‘I don’t understand your textbook, so I’m going to just turn on and off any single part of this grid, and I’ll come up with something.’ It does sort of work, but there are constraints. Is this manufacturable? Is this cost-effective? Did I learn anything out of this? Yes, AI solved a problem for me, but as a human, I had intuition about what worked at 2 GHz. Now, if I want to shift to 2.5 GHz, that same intuition will change the design.” Instead of making an incremental change to account for a new spec, AI may come up with something completely different, with no correlation between versions, Kamdar explained. “There’s a cost of letting AI do all of these things.” Reusing designs across multiple generations of chips has long been the go-to strategy as a way of amortizing non-recurring engineering (NRE) costs and reducing development time. Using AI agents to come up with derivatives adds a whole different way of looking at the problem. AI agents can assess existing architectures and RTL to identify potential bottlenecks, explore design modifications, optimize EDA tool settings, and automate portions of verification and debugging. And they can orchestrate workflows across multiple tools, reducing the manual effort required to adapt existing IP to new specifications. But the resulting AI-generated design is not necessarily ready to be implemented in a follow-on chip. Engineers must determine whether proposed changes are physically feasible, manufacturable, cost-effective, and compatible with the new design’s requirements. That, in turn, will determine where AI can and cannot be used, and where EDA tools need to evolve in order to close that gap. Software reuse easier than hardware reuse Despite AI’s promise, a lot of human effort is still needed in today’s designs. Working with natural language interfaces is a big plus, but minor differences in queries can result in very different answers. “We were rapidly adapting the automotive solution to robotics because there’s a lot of commonality,” said Baaziz Achour, CTO of Qualcomm. [1] “Many of the key functions are similar, such as perception, path planning, and foundational technologies like sensor fusion, object recognition, location, and control. We were able to take the full automotive solution and apply it to robotics. We have very effective solutions for scaling the software. However, hardware IP scaling and SoC integration still require significant human effort.” Those differences can also be significant across domains. for example, developers may increase the number of cores in an NPU and use tools to analyze bottlenecks as application workloads shift. But this type of scaling is very different with mobile multimedia, such as a camera, Achour explained. “Across a lot of this AI spectrum of products, the basic camera and display blocks are similar, but the requirements are very different in camera count, speed, and power.” Fig. 1: Designers can use tools to adapt common IP, but there is still a non-recurring engineering cost for SoC implementation. Source: Qualcomm/DAC While designers can leverage core IP blocks, such as an image signal processor, every processing core, camera, and display across these devices must meet diverse requirements and cost targets. “Currently, we often create separate architectures and hardware design variants for each case,” said Achour. “Can EDA help us build one flexible architecture that adapts to these diverse requirements instead of manually customizing for each time?” The answer? Maybe. Ensuring that a chip design will function flawlessly requires an ecosystem. Automating some steps in the design flow can help, but how much automation and which steps are still being explored. Nevertheless, there are plenty of places where engineers would welcome more flexibility and automation, such as iteratively tuning EDA tools to meet design targets. “Three months were spent in recipe tuning of EDA tools,” said Achour. “Neither the RTL nor the floorplan were changed in these iterations, so this is a huge source of inefficiency. EDA tool companies have AI-aided fine-tuning, but that consumes a lot of compute. Further innovation is needed for this.” Fig. 2: EDA tools to help designers reuse IP need to account for area, thermal, PDN, and much more. Source: Qualcomm/DAC The overall goal for engineers is to reduce runtime and compute, shortening time to market, increasing coverage and improving confidence at sign-off, and enabling engineers to be more productive. “We need innovation in GenAI, including GenAI that can create design input for the EDA tools, like a human designer, to drive fast convergence, and agents that can orchestrate design flows to reduce human effort for iteratively running tools to refine and optimize the design,” said Achour. “These are critical technologies to rapidly adapt common hardware to evolving AI product demand.
