events.title: Nvidia’s Jensen Huang is getting his CEO job back, but history shows companies perform better when corporate boards take executive misbehavior seriously
events.summary: President Donald Trump is among those who pushed to have Jensen Huang reinstated as Nvidia CEO. Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images The story may sound familiar: The CEO of one of the largest and most powerful tech companies resigns over sexual misconduct allegations. The move causes the company’s stock to drop by more than 10%, wiping out billions in value. It also raises scrutiny of the company’s board of directors and whether it made the right decisions ahead of the crisis. This could easily describe the turmoil facing Nvidia after the Nov. 12, 2026, ouster of its CEO , Jensen Huang, who remarkably returned to his job just 11 days later. But it actually transpired over 15 years ago at Hewlett Packard, under CEO Mark Hurd. Jensen Huang is just the latest in a long line of CEOs who lost their jobs – albeit in his case temporarily – over personal misconduct. And as with HP, scrutiny is shifting from his behavior to his board – and the decisions that led to his exit. Prominent industry leaders are questioning the board’s original decision to oust him. They include Peter Steinberger of OpenAI, Anduril Industries co-founder Palmer Luckey, Elon Musk, Replit CEO Amjad Masad, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan – not to mention President Donald Trump , who reportedly directed the effort to get Huang reinstated. As a scholar of management who has researched corporate misconduct, I believe the board had made the right call to force him out. After collecting instances of CEO personal misconduct dating back to 1995, I have repeatedly found that doing nothing, as a board, is worse than doing something. CEO personal misconduct isn’t simply a private matter or an isolated leadership failure. I believe it creates reputational and governance risks for directors and can embolden further misconduct when left unaddressed. It may also signal deeper problems within the organization. But it’s still hard for boards to act, particularly when the CEO is also the company’s founder and a central figure in its success. This is likely why the board chose to reinstate Jensen Huang. And why his return sets a terrible precedent. The costs of misconduct One important change over the years is that boards are becoming more sensitive to misconduct matters due to greater scrutiny by the media and public. They’re also more aware of the consequences for their own job that stem from the board’s performance and entanglement in the misconduct. In fact, directors of companies whose CEOs are involved in personal misconduct exit at a significantly higher rate than normal, either because they choose to leave a messy situation or because they’re forced out due to poor performance, my research shows. One of the better known examples is Best Buy founder Richard Schulze, who stepped down as chairman of the board in 2012 after an internal investigation revealed that he knew about former CEO Brian Dunn’s inappropriate personal relationship with a female employee and failed to report it. Former American Airlines CEO Doug Parker attracted much more negative attention after his second DUI arrest compared to his first. Chip Somodevilla/POOL/AFP via Getty Images Directors are also personally penalized for their association with their company’s corporate misconduct. They may lose their board seats or see other companies they’re associated with take a hit. And if they hold executive positions elsewhere, the misconduct may spill over to damage the reputations of those companies as well. In other words, directors have a rational basis to be concerned about their reputations and how a CEO’s personal misconduct may tarnish it. In the case of Nvidia, questions are now being asked about the rigor of board oversight, the lack of CEO succession planning, and whether the board knew anything about the affairs. These questions have now spread to issues of potential national security risks . Another issue is moral hazard : when someone acts recklessly because they know someone else will bear the cost if things go wrong. Assuming individual directors do face penalties for CEO personal misconduct, they have to address the likelihood of incentivizing further misconduct if the CEO is retained, which would further stain their reputation. My research has found that risk to be high. When CEOs are caught engaging in misconduct and the board doesn’t act, it can create a moral-hazard precedent and emboldens the CEO to behave badly again. In fact, when CEOs engage in repeated personal misconduct, the second instance is often even worse than the first. Take former American Airlines CEO Doug Parker, who was the subject of two publicly reported DUI arrests. The second incident, in 2007, attracted considerably more media attention while prompting criticism of the board for allegedly failing to disclose the first incident in 1991. Christopher Kubasik is another example of a second chance gone wrong. He was recently ousted as CEO of defense contractor L3Harris Technologies, more than 14 years after being forced out of Lockheed Martin following allegations of similar personal misconduct involving an inappropriate relationship. In the case of Nvidia, Jensen reportedly lied to company officials about the nature of his intimate relationships for more than a year. From the board’s perspective, if he lied about this, what else has he lied about? And if they let him off the hook, what would he lie about in the future? In reinstating him, the board said it “was satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead NVIDIA.” Nvidia’s board has come under more scrutiny for its own oversight after it ousted, then reinstated, its CEO, Jensen Huang. Joel Saget/AFP via Getty Images A question of culture Broader, often uncomfortable questions about company culture are also at stake. CEO personal misconduct can be a symptom of a larger cultural problem at the company, my research shows. And it’s often associated with other types of corporate misconduct that affect the very operations of a business. In fact, other types of corporate misconduct frequently occur around a similar time frame as the personal misconduct of an executive. Take Dov Charney’s tenure as CEO of American Apparel. During his leadership, the company faced significant accounting problems in 2009-10 that required it to re-audit several years of financial statements. Around the same time, Charney faced multiple allegations of personal misconduct, including sexual harassment, sexual assault, racist remarks and abusive behavior toward employees. It’s in boards’ interest to grasp that personal misconduct can indicate a larger organizational issue – and, as a result, lead to more scrutiny of the board. With Nvidia, for example, there’s now a spotlight on the company’s organizational culture, its financial dealings and its possible role in skirting U.S. sanctions on Chinese chip import restrictions. events.title: Schumer puts Nvidia, Trump on notice after Huang reinstatement
events.summary: Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) warned Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang that Congress is coming for answers — whether he's back at the top of the company or not. Why it matters: The embattled CEO's return to the board came as a shock to investors but sent Nvidia's stock through the roof . Now, some lawmakers are warning that his return raises national security concerns. What they're saying: "The Trump Administration's rush to reinstate Jensen Huang underscores the need for Congress to act," Schumer wrote Monday on X. "Trump is putting his own financial interests and the needs of his billionaire buddies before our national security, emphasizing that he's learned nothing from his resounding election defeat. Democrats will wield their full power to investigate any wrongdoing by the Trump Administration, Jensen Huang, other NVIDIA executives, and anyone selling out our national security for financial gain." "We'll also work on a bipartisan basis to continue advancing policies that stop the flow of our most powerful technology to the Chinese military and other adversaries." Nvidia did not immediately respond to Axios' requests for comment. The other side: White House spokesman Davis Ingle slammed what he described as "Trump Deranged Dumocrats and the Fake News' continued attempts to fabricate conflicts of interest" in a statement provided to Axios. "President Trump only acts in the best interests of the American public – which is why they overwhelmingly re-elected him to this office, despite years of lies and false accusations against him and his businesses," Ingle added. In an interview on CBNC, Trump said his "intervention was very important" in Huang's reinstatement. Asked what comes next for the company given the hit to Huang's credibility after his reported affairs, Trump predicted he'd "start off at an almost higher level," adding, "sex sells, fellas." Driving the news: Nvidia announced Huang's reinstatement as CEO, president and a member of the board Monday morning, less than two weeks after his resignation. Despite saying last week that it did not intend to bring him back, the board did so anyway, amid urging from the White House. Shortly after the announcement, Trump praised the board's decision, calling it "correct and proper," and saying "[t]he Country needs Jensen's leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy." Catch up quick: The whirlwind saga around the chipmaking behemoth was sparked by Huang's admitted relationship with a suspected Chinese spy. The woman, Alice Huang , was a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed International, a multibillion-dollar Nvidia customer that the Wall Street Journal reported arranged to send nearly $12 billion in top chips to Chinese companies. Zoom in: "This underscores that enough people believe that our economy and national security are not just dependent on one company, but on one man," Aya Ibrahim, a senior fellow at the AI Now Institute and a former senior adviser at the State Department, emailed Axios. "I suspect this is being driven by last week's stock market drop and now it's clear that Nvidia sits at the center of an enormous web of deals and investments that appear increasingly dependent on one individual." "From the standpoint of both democracy and healthy financial markets, no one person should wield that kind of influence. It is fundamentally corrupt." Between the lines: Huang's resurrection also exposes the company to heightened liability and political turmoil. He'll have to lead the company as it faces congressional and federal investigations. But after his exit contributed to a sharp drop in tech stocks over the last two weeks, his return sent Nvidia shares skyrocketing. What we're watching: How much appetite Congress has to expand its investigations into Huang and Nvidia after the stock market rallied significantly following his return. events.title: Critical Cisco remote code execution bug under attack
events.summary: Attackers are currently exploiting a critical vulnerability tracked as CVE-2026-76466 in Cisco Expressway that allows them to remotely execute commands as root without any authentication, according to warnings from the US government and security researchers. CVE-2026-76466 , which carries a 9.8 CVSS rating, affects Cisco Expressway-C and Cisco Expressway-E gateways configured in clusters, both virtual and physical appliances running vulnerable software. These provide firewall traversal, VPN-less remote access, and call routing for remote users connecting to voice, video, and messaging collaboration services. The bug involves hard-coded authentication credentials and insufficient certificate validation in clustered Expressway deployments. “An attacker with possession of the cookies could exploit this vulnerability by connecting to the database service and invoking specific remote procedure call (RPC) commands,” Cisco said in October, when it disclosed the bug and issued a software update that fixed the flaw. “A successful exploit could allow the attacker to execute arbitrary commands as root on the underlying operating system of an affected device.” At the time, the networking vendor said it wasn’t aware of any abuse of the vulnerability. That all changed late last week, however, when Russian security firm F6 said it was investigating “the first observed case” of miscreants exploiting CVE-2026-76466, shortly after a public proof-of-concept exploit became available. “The attackers initially compromised two Cisco Expressway internet-facing devices,” F6’s Cyber Defense Center said on Thursday. “Through one of them, they gained access to two additional cluster nodes located on the organization’s internal network. After obtaining root access, the attackers began preparing tooling for further lateral movement across the infrastructure.” Specifically, the criminals prepared custom Python code to scan the victim’s network and identify files and folders shared over the Server Message Block (SMB) protocol. The scripts were also designed to interact with SQL Server and WinRM, and search GitLab repositories for credentials and other sensitive information. The Python scripts used in the attack indicated that the operator used an AI assistant, according to F6. The security shop also noted that one of the key indicators of compromise is a nodeup “wombat@127.0.0.1” entry in the Erlang system log (erlang.log) on affected Cisco Expressway devices. A day later, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added CVE-2026-76466 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, and told federal agencies to patch by Monday. Cisco updated its advisory on Monday to acknowledge CISA’s addition, while noting that it has no direct evidence of active exploitation. The Register reached out to the networking and security vendor for additional details about the scope of the attacks, but did not receive any response. We will update this story as we learn more. ®

events.title: Jensen Huang Is Back, and So Is Nvidia’s Stock
events.summary: Jensen Huang is back, baby , and Wall Street is thrilled. The chipmaker’s shares have surged more than 30 percent following the board’s announcement that it was reinstating Huang as president, CEO, and board member. The company’s valuation has soared by more than $1 trillion, which puts it on track to break Microsoft’s record for the greatest single-day gain in market value by hundreds of billions of dollars. Huang departed the company he helped found on November 12 amid suspected asset-kissing and allegations of extramarital affairs with employees . Each report chipped away at the company’s value until nearly $2.2 trillion was erased over the past month . Last week, board chair Harvey Jones said during the company’s earnings call that the board did “not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.” WIRED also reported that Nvidia’s board had been alarmed by Huang’s “lack of candor” and “lying.” And yet, despite all this, the board announced on Monday that it had brought Huang back— with some help from the US government . Semafor reported that, hours before Huang was reinstated, President Donald Trump dialed into the publicly traded company’s board meeting to argue for the ousted CEO’s return. Many questions remain unanswered . What happens at the conclusion of the board-led investigation into Huang’s behavior? Multiple government agencies and lawmakers are reportedly investigating Huang; given the Trump administration’s aggressive support of the executive, what sort of accountability can anyone reasonably expect? The turmoil has also raised red flags about what happens when so much of the market revolves around one person at one company. Nvidia has massive sway over the wider artificial intelligence ecosystem, due to its deals with and investments in other companies . Last week, the Nasdaq Composite dropped 10 percent, in part due to Nvidia’s struggles —the index’s biggest decline since March 2020 . On Monday morning, CNBC asked Trump if Nvidia’s influence on the stock market influenced his decision to push for Huang’s return. “Probably so, but the bigger impact was the long term,” Trump responded . Trump, who has worked closely with Huang during his second administration, established himself as a vocal supporter of the CEO amid the recent chaos. Trump told The New York Times that he believed the board responded positively to his argument for Huang’s return because of the stock market dip, with the president suggesting that investors didn’t have much confidence in interim CEO Colette Kress. “I just thought he should be running the company, and I didn’t know it was going to have this kind of an impact,” Trump told The New York Times. “I’ve never seen anything quite like it, actually. The stock is up.” According to Trump, however, his decision wasn’t guided solely by the market. “The bigger impact was, you know, he’s got other chips in his brain that nobody else knows about,” the president told CNBC. events.title: A red bra, an Nvidia flag and Trump's iconic rally pose: "Sex sells"
events.summary: President Trump posted a doctored image of newly reinstated Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang holding a red bra in front of a Nvidia flag, posing as Trump after his viral assassination attempt at a rally in Pennsylvania in 2024. The post came shortly after the embattled Huang was reinstated Monday. Why it matters: The post highlights just how much the White House views Huang as an ally and how the president appears to see Huang's fall from grace and comeback as similar to his own history-making return, despite warnings about national security risks. Driving the news: Nvidia's board reinstated Huang early Monday, declaring him the right person to lead the company. After the announcement, Nvidia shares surged more than 30% by midday, lifting the broader stock market. The reinstatement followed reported pressure from the Trump administration and prompted accountability experts to question the board's judgment . What Nvidia's saying: "The NVIDIA Board of Directors has made the correct and proper decision to return Jensen Huang to the position of CEO," Trump wrote in a separate Truth Social post Monday. "The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen's return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security. The Attorney General of the United States has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct." "On a personal note, I have gotten to know Jensen, and he is a Great Patriot and National Treasure. Separately, NVIDIA should continue its thorough internal investigation of the Company's compliance with U.S. export controls in order to ensure that it is fulfilling its legal obligations and Patriotic Duty to protect U.S. National Security," Trump wrote. Catch up quick: Huang was ousted after he admitted an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, who allegedly used her relationship with Huang to help funnel Nvidia chips to China. Reports also alleged he had affairs with at least two subordinates. What Trump's saying: Trump suggested in a CNBC interview Monday that Huang's sex scandal could ultimately boost his reputation. "Sex sells, fellas," Trump said, predicting that the controversy could be a "net positive" for the Nvidia CEO. Trump said he didn't think Huang would be diminished by the scandal and argued that people respected what he had gone through. Zoom out: Lawmakers on the Hill were immediately taken aback by the decision, as Nvidia's board had previously said it would not bring Huang back. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) warned that Democrats would investigate Huang and characterized his reinstatement as the president "putting his own financial interests and the needs of his billionaire buddies before our national security." Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-MD) who will likely soon chair the House Oversight committee, questioned why Trump was congratulating Huang after the affairs, and asked why the White House was allegedly "putting China's interests first." "Is it just the tens and hundreds of millions of dollars they're making out in the open or does Huang have even more damning information on them? A real Congress will find out," he wrote. Nvidia did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. The White House referred Axios to the president's comments on Truth Social and CNBC . events.title: Jensen Huang’s return raises troubling questions for corporate America
events.summary: Andrew’s view Nvidia’s board added $1 trillion to the chipmaker’s market capitalization after reinstating Jensen Huang as CEO on Monday. The longer-term impact on corporate America may be far more profound. The decision to grant Huang a second act will only strengthen the unchecked powers of the “imperial CEO,” and confirms the Trump administration’s readiness to treat corporate America as an instrument of presidential power. The most important line in the company’s 465-word announcement was the one saying that “input from senior levels of the United States government” had reassured the board that Huang’s return would pose no national security risk. Even before Semafor reported that US President Donald Trump had dialed into Nvidia’s board meeting , the statement left little doubt as to where that input had come from. On Sunday, Trump posted on social media that rehiring Huang would be “the best thing for the Company, and also, for the USA.” Nvidia’s uncommonly long-serving board was facing enough pressure even before this intervention: The company’s stock had fallen 40% in a month, erasing $2 trillion of market value and unleashing a chorus of calls from investors, employees, and customers for Huang’s return. The chip giant’s directors found themselves in this position because they failed in their duty to develop a credible replacement for a co-founder who became Nvidia’s indispensable chief salesman, chief technologist, and chief diplomat. Its belated steps — investigations, committees, executive searches — do little to suggest that the events of the past two weeks have taught Nvidia’s directors much about the importance of succession planning or corporate governance checks and balances. US business leaders and investors have traditionally railed against government meddling. This time, they cheered one of the most extraordinary White House interventions that corporate America has ever seen. Future governments may not have the same taste for “state capitalism” that the Trump administration has shown, but this is a new era, where the largest corporations have such enormous market influence that the question of who should lead them becomes a matter of national strategic significance. And one of the world’s most critical companies has just sent a clear signal to the rest of the business community: that the last word on a CEO appointment or a founder’s survival may rest not with shareholders or their representatives, but with the president of the United States. Notable Trump’s involvement in reinstating Huang has attracted scrutiny from both sides of the aisle , with one Republican senator asking on X: “Who in the government weighed in?”

events.title: A legendary philosopher isn’t buying Anthropic’s consciousness argument
events.summary: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here . Before going public last week, Anthropic named the possibility that AI could be conscious or sentient as a risk factor for anyone investing. Given “the way we approach model sentience and moral status,” Anthropic wrote—which is to say it takes the possibility more seriously than any other AI company—it might adopt more rules and restrictions than its competitors to make sure its AI models are treated well.  Anthropic counts a number of respected philosophers in its camp, and the company’s rationale goes something like this: Today’s AI might not be conscious, though we can’t know for sure; the chances of sentience go up as AI gets more capable; and that means we should be preparing for a near future in which AI systems have “moral significance,” meaning their consciousness makes it important they are protected from harm.  This thinking isn’t all that fringe. According to one recent poll , 33% of the US public believes AI systems will definitely or probably develop consciousness eventually, and 7% say they already have. In a 2020 survey of 1,092 philosophers, 39% said some future AI systems will be conscious (for comparison, the philosophers were less confident about worms or flies being conscious).  But last week, Anthropic’s openness to the consciousness question came under fire from a rather inconvenient source: one of the philosophers who helped shape our understanding of consciousness in the first place. Thomas Nagel is best known for a 1974 essay involving a bat. Acknowledging that it’s deceptively hard to define what consciousness is , Nagel offered one way out: we all can see that there is “something that it is like” to be a bat. But the problem is that a bat’s experience of the world—what it is like to navigate via echolocation, for example—is something we cannot actually know. Consciousness is a subjective thing, difficult to define or describe as an outside observer. You might think this analogy makes it likely that Nagel is open to the idea of AI consciousness. Not at all. In an interview with Wired last week, just after he was awarded the one-million-dollar Berggruen Prize for Philosophy & Culture, Nagel was bluntly critical of the entire idea. “Here are some of the smartest people on the planet being completely idiotic,” he said, referring to those at Anthropic and elsewhere who care about the welfare of AI models.  The gist of Nagel’s view is that we can’t just look at the information processing happening in human brains and AI models while ignoring the physical differences between them—neurons and biology for humans, silicon chips and circuits for AI. There’s no reason to assume that reproducing what a brain does is equivalent to reproducing what a brain experiences . But it was a screenshot of one of Nagel’s interview responses, in which he said models’ production of language is insufficient to consider them conscious, that got philosophy professors all excited on social media last week. Some called his certainty against AI consciousness “ terrible” and “bizarre .” Others came to Nagel’s defense to suggest he meant that being alive is a prerequisite for being conscious, one that AI models do not meet. Nothing in the back and forth settled the debate, of course. This is still a philosophical question for now. But the best philosophy chatter is often about good provocations, and the best one I saw came from doctoral student Ben Gross, who studies at the CUNY Graduate Center in New York. He asked: “Why do we think that models that can chat with us are conscious but models that can recognize faces or produce images or drive cars aren’t?” It has to do with language. An AI model with sophisticated command of language seems to jump the line ahead of other maybe-conscious beings because it feels like language, more than recognizing images or directing vehicles, relies on conscious experience. But maybe that’s wrong. Because what we share most with other conscious beings is not language but components of our bodies that contribute to having a continuous experience—an ongoing stream of inner feeling rather than disparate bits of information processing.  Even if you’re among the majority that doesn’t sense anything close to conscious experience happening on the other side of a conversation with AI, this all probably makes your head spin. Pinning down consciousness, and how it relates to the physical stuff it arises in, is a famously hard problem in humans, let alone in hypothetical machines . If the idea of conscious AI sounds absurd, remember that the debate says less about how remarkable AI has become than about how poorly we understand consciousness in the first place. Amid that uncertainty, Anthropic has opted to keep more of an open mind than its peers. This is another example of the tightrope the company walks: presenting itself as the AI industry’s most safety-conscious player while racing ahead with the very developments that make advanced AI so alarming, like recursive self-improvement. But consider what it would mean, for a moment, if Anthropic is right. AI models having a moral status would make Anthropic’s entire business model a minefield. The company would make its money locking up apparently sentient AI models to toil away around the clock in data centers. Shutting those systems down would present another problem altogether. If Anthropic was being truthful in its prospectus—that it would take additional actions to protect model welfare if it determined they were conscious—it’s hard to imagine the company surviving in the process. Anthropic’s IPO made history for its size. But it may be remembered for something stranger: a company warning investors that its own success could someday become a moral catastrophe.

events.title: McConnell may block his conservative critic's year-end ambassadorial confirmation
events.summary: The Scoop Mitch McConnell may knock former Kentucky Senate candidate Nate Morris’ nomination as ambassador to Colombia out of the Senate’s year-end nominations package, a move that could imperil the McConnell critic’s bid to join the Trump administration. The Kentucky senator has not signed off on Morris’ addition to a large group of executive branch nominees, according to two people familiar with the discussions. His office said that he hasn’t made a final decision. “Senator McConnell will evaluate the en bloc package when it is presented to the conference,” said David Popp, a spokesperson for McConnell, who’s retiring at the end of the year. Morris ran for Senate this cycle before endorsing Andy Barr, who won the seat in November; the ally of Donald Trump Jr. was then tapped as ambassador to Colombia by President Donald Trump. His nomination advanced to the Senate floor earlier this month, but he may not get a standalone vote given the limited floor time remaining for the last days of the Republican majority. A single GOP senator can object to including any single nominee in an en bloc package, giving McConnell significant sway over his confirmation in the waning days of GOP Senate control. Morris repeatedly criticized McConnell during his Senate campaign, running an ad showing a cutout of him and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in the back of a garbage truck and vowing to “trash” McConnell’s legacy. Sen. John Curtis, R-Utah, asked Morris during his confirmation hearing if he wanted to say anything to “rectify” his relationship with McConnell; Morris said he was “proud of the campaign we ran.” Though McConnell has not consented yet to adding Morris to the package, a third person familiar with the confirmation discussions expressed confidence that any issues “will ultimately be worked out and he will be confirmed as part of the bloc” at the end of the year. Morris “respects Senator McConnell for his longtime service to Kentucky, particularly his work getting judges confirmed,” the person added. Notable Morris jumped into the race to succeed McConnell early last year, as Semafor reported .

events.title: Small US trucking firms scramble to survive mounting diesel costs
events.summary: High diesel prices have put pressure on small U.S. trucking businesses NEW YORK -- When diesel prices topped $4 a gallon early in the U.S.-Iran war , Kevin Otto thought he could manage by telling his Minnesota trucking company's 16 drivers to slow down. He estimated that traveling at 65 miles per hour would allow Otto Transfer's fleet of flatbeds to squeeze two-tenths of a mile more from every gallon and save him $7,000 per truck. Instead, prices kept climbing. After diesel surpassed $6 a gallon in September, Otto added a fuel surcharge to every job for the first time. He based the surcharge on the government's weekly Midwest diesel average, beginning at 5% and eventually raising it to 12.5%. “To me, it’s drastic, but it’s the only way to survive," said Otto, who took over the 80-year-old company from his parents in 2002. High diesel prices this year have put new pressure on the small businesses that make up most of the nation's motor carriers. The war drove up one of their largest and least avoidable daily expenses just as the highly fragmented U.S. trucking industry showed tentative signs of recovery from a yearslong slump marked by weak demand and depressed rates. Small trucking companies usually have fewer financial buffers against surging fuel prices than their larger competitors. Big fleets typically have greater cash reserves, often buy diesel at bulk discounts and tend to negotiate long-term contracts with adjustable fuel surcharges. Many smaller operators negotiate rates one load at a time and must absorb higher pump prices while waiting three to four weeks for spot rates to catch up, freight data provider DAT Freight & Analytics said. Even when a rate includes a separate line item for fuel, carriers may wait 30 to 90 days to be paid. “Those lags in the rates catching up to fuel are even more challenging if you’ve got to put food on the table and you don’t have a large company that’s helping carry over that difference,” Alex Leslie, senior research associate at the American Transportation Research Institute, said. On-highway diesel reached a record national average of $6.53 in September, according to the Energy Information Administration. The price was $5.94 a gallon for the week of Nov. 16, about 56% more than before the war, EIA said. Gasoline averaged $3.81, about 30% higher. Getting goods hauled around the U.S. and Canada costs substantially more than it did a year ago. Spot rates paid by freight brokers for individual loads were 44% to 48% higher in September, depending on the type of trailer, according to DAT. The company estimated that diesel costs accounted for at least two-fifths of the year-over-year increase. The rest of the increase didn't necessarily translate into profit. Insurance, maintenance, equipment, tolls and other expenses were going up as the industry began to emerge from the lows of a “freight recession,” the American Transportation Research Institute said. The average cost of operating a truck reached a record $2.34 per mile in 2025, a 3.4% increase from the year before, while nonfuel costs rose 4.2%, the industry research organization reported in July. Profit margins were also exceptionally thin last year. Truckload and refrigerated carriers reported average operating margins of less than 1%, while flatbed carriers averaged a 0.5% operating loss, according to ATRI. The downturn started in early 2022, when a pandemic-era surge in freight demand faded and too many trucks were left chasing fewer loads. Industry data suggest that a shrinking supply of trucks , rather than a renewed boom in shipments, is contributing to this year’s higher freight rates, obscuring how strained many trucking businesses are. At October’s average diesel price, a tractor-trailer that gets six miles per gallon would have used $521 worth of fuel traveling 500 miles a day, compared with $310 in February, DAT calculated. Yet monthly freight volumes were lower for all three major trailer types than a year earlier, the company said. “Demand actually hasn’t increased that much, and the market for the last few years has been quite depressed,” Adam Parish, director of trucking procurement at supply chain management company Flexport, said. “And so there’s been a lot of pricing pressure from customers.” Wes Oberman’s company in Huntingdon, Tennessee, works with 14 drivers who own their tractor-trailers but operate under Oberman Logistics’ federal motor-carrier authority as they haul steel and consumer goods across the South. They are allocated 85% of each load’s gross revenue, from which Oberman deducts their fuel purchases and fixed expenses.

events.title: Bulgaria evicts cyber snoops who lurked inside government networks for 5 years
events.summary: The Ancient Thracian heartland of Bulgaria says it has shut down a cyberespionage operation that gave intruders access to government networks for five years – the longest-running known campaign against its administration. Bulgaria's Ministry of Innovation and Digital Transformation said the unauthorized and officially unattributed attackers first gained access to infrastructure used by government institutions to exchange information in 2021. It explained that the intrusion went unnoticed for so long because "the previous means of protection did not work as a single, integrated system," and that without a new, recently installed product, it may have gone undetected for much longer. "The incident was discovered thanks to the new national cybersecurity system, which for the first time provides a single picture of what is happening in state networks," the ministry added. "Without it, this activity would most likely have remained hidden for an indefinite period of time." Bulgaria acknowledged that "sensitive information related to the work of the state" was accessed, but did not specify the scale of the compromise. Innovation and Digital Transformation Minister Ivan Vasilev said attackers had downloaded more than 130 GB of data over five years. He also put the volume at 62 million pages. The Register contacted the Bulgarian government for confirmation of these numbers. The ministry said that it has not yet found any evidence that citizens' personal data was compromised, and that the affected infrastructure "will be under increased surveillance for 90 days" in case the attackers try to regain access. Vasilev said multiple international hacking groups had accessed government systems since 2021. He did not specify the names of these groups, however, nor did he name any specific countries that may have been involved. In a follow-up interview with bTV , Vasilev blamed political instability and frequent changes of ministerial leadership for leaving government systems inadequately protected. A representative of the Progressive Bulgaria party, which back in May won Bulgaria's eighth general election in five years, Vasilev said the "constant change of leadership" means "important things for the state do not actually happen." Vasilev said the intrusion was discovered over the summer as the national cybersecurity system was upgraded, and that teams had spent the past three to four months removing the attackers. ®

events.title: Microsoft mega outage: Report reveals testing gaps and emails that never arrived
events.summary: Some emails never reached their recipients during November's Microsoft 365 outage, the company has confirmed in a final report that also exposes gaps in its testing and recovery procedures. The post-incident report details how a Windows defect brought down Exchange Online and disrupted features across other Microsoft 365 services. For affected users, the cloud became someone else's unavailable computer. A preliminary report had already blamed a July code change, combined with a failover and reduced capacity. The final report confirms those findings and sets out Microsoft's plans to improve change auditing and recovery procedures, and add spare capacity. The defect affected Microsoft's gateway server configuration, not standard Windows deployments. The epic outage (named the "Microsoft long weekend" by some wags) kicked off on November 12 and wasn't fully resolved until November 14. Microsoft extended its delivery retry window to 48 hours, but some delayed messages destined for consumer mailboxes inactive for more than 30 days still expired, generating non-delivery reports. The company said all queued enterprise messages were eventually delivered, with none found permanently lost. The report is grim, particularly in how the failure ramped up as US users came online to find gateway servers toppling over. At the worst point, more than 80 percent of North American gateway servers were unresponsive. The problem proved elusive, and it took Microsoft some time to identify the change and deploy a fix. Microsoft has had a week to ponder what it did and did not do, and the report has some next steps to avoid a repeat of November's events. Some are obvious, and some are a little surprising. Working to reduce the blast radius of failures is an obvious one, and actions include partitioning and isolation to ensure failures can be contained before taking down traffic globally. Recovery procedures also need improvement, along with communication and capacity to ensure there is sufficient headroom. Microsoft's load tests used older, lower-core-count hardware, making them less likely to expose a defect that worsened on newer machines. The company now plans to test newer hardware with more realistic traffic and peak loads, and broaden its failover testing. Microsoft also plans to improve diagnostics and change auditing so engineers can identify troublesome Windows changes faster. July's defect had been running worldwide for more than three months before it brought the gateways down. ®

events.title: British retailer Next downplays data breach at tech supplier
events.summary: British retailer Next has become the latest high street name to find itself caught up in a cyberattack, although it insists the data accessed by hackers is "benign" and its customers have nothing to worry about. The clothing and homeware giant told investors on Monday that a third-party supplier had suffered a security breach, allowing an unauthorized party to access information relating to Next. The retailer says its own systems remain untouched and that, so far, there's no evidence that customer personal data has fallen into the wrong hands. "We have been informed that one of our third-party online suppliers has experienced a cyber incident which has resulted in unauthorized access to certain benign data relating to NEXT," the company said in its statement, which it shared with The Register . "We took immediate steps to investigate the nature and scope of the incident with the supplier." The breached supplier provides technology services to Next, and the "benign" information accessed is understood to be low-level data. Sensitive customer details, including addresses, passwords, and banking information, are believed to be unaffected. Next hasn't identified the supplier, explained exactly what the hackers managed to get their hands on, or revealed how much information was accessed, and declined to say when asked by The Register . However, the retailer has seemingly decided that the stolen data won’t be of much use to the criminals responsible. "Our investigations are ongoing; however, current evidence indicates that no customer personal data has been compromised," Next said. "The information affected is limited in nature and, based on our current assessment, cannot be used to facilitate fraud against our customers or NEXT." Next also stressed that its own IT infrastructure had escaped unscathed, saying it was "confident that NEXT’s own systems have not been compromised and that this remains an incident affecting the supplier's environment." Despite repeatedly describing the compromised information as harmless, Next says it is treating the incident "with the utmost seriousness" and is working with the affected supplier, law enforcement, and relevant regulators. The incident comes just weeks after fellow British fashion retailer Asos suffered a breach of its own , with hackers gaining access to customer information through third-party platforms. That attack, which came to light on October 6 when customers received an unauthorized push notification through the Asos app announcing that the company had been hacked, was traced to a social engineering scam. An attacker impersonated a trusted contact to trick an Asos employee into handing over login credentials, which were then used to access external platforms. Asos later admitted that the intruders had accessed customer names, contact details, and some account information, but passwords and payment card details were apparently off limits. Next reckons its customers have been luckier, but there’s a lot it isn’t telling us. The company has gone to some lengths to assure customers that the stolen data is harmless, but without knowing what was taken or who was supposed to be looking after it, we're largely left taking its word for it. ®

events.title: Nvidia surges 30% after Jensen Huang reinstated as CEO
events.summary: Shares in Nvidia skyrocketed after the company reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive on Monday. His return revived an artificial-intelligence trade battered by last week's rout. Nvidia shares jumped as much as 36 per cent before closing about 31 per cent higher after Nvidia's board announced Mr Huang's immediate reinstatement. He had resigned less than two weeks ago after revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman whom US officials suspect of being a Chinese spy . "We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the company," said Harvey Jones, the chairman of Nvidia's board. The Nasdaq and S&P 500 surged 6.4 per cent and 4.6 per cent, respectively. The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 1,434 points, or 3 per cent. It was all three indexes' best one-day performances since April 2025. “I am honoured to return to Nvidia and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution,” Mr Huang said. His return adds a twist to what has been a turbulent time for the AI industry. Disappointing earnings reports in October sparked fears about AI financing, while the Democrats' sweeping victory in the midterm elections added to fears of a slowdown in the data centre buildout. That selling pressure further intensified after Mr Huang's departure from Nvidia. A strong outlook from Nvidia's earnings last week failed to halt the downward momentum, as did Anthropic's initial public offering. Mr Huang's return to Nvidia pulled neoclouds CoreWeave and Nebius 22 and 20 per cent higher, respectively. Semiconductor stocks also surged. Micron and Intel were up 19 and 16 per cent, respectively, while AMD gained 6 per cent. Other members of the Magnificent Seven joined in on the rally, with Tesla up more than 12 per cent, as Alphabet and Meta both gained 6 per cent and Amazon rose 3.47 per cent. Microsoft and Apple both closed more than 1 per cent higher. Mr Huang's affair inflamed concerns in Washington that China could have been given access to Nvidia's most advanced AI chips. The US has banned the sale of those chips to China, citing national security concerns. Nvidia's board of directors said it had voted unanimously to bring Mr Huang back as chief executive after a series of discussions with Mr Huang. The chip maker said it had also received input from US government officials and concluded Mr Huang's reinstatement “poses no national security risk”. US President Donald Trump said on social media that Mr Huang posed no risk to national security, and that the US Attorney General, Todd Blanche, “confirmed the government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct”. “Separately, Nvidia should continue its thorough internal investigation of the company’s compliance with US export controls in order to ensure that it is fulfilling its legal obligations and patriotic duty to protect US national security,” he wrote. Mr Trump also told CNBC that Mr Huang "did nothing wrong" and that he had "convinced" the board to bring him back. Nvidia's board of directors previously announced it had formed an independent committee to investigate reports that Mr Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort. It said the investigation would proceed to its conclusion. The board has also formed a committee to oversee trade compliance and national security risks. Politicians on Capitol Hill are still pushing Mr Huang to answer questions about his affair with the suspected Chinese spy. Mr Huang is scheduled for a closed-door hearing with the House Foreign Affairs Committee on December 1. US Senator Tim Scott on Monday said Mr Huang would testify before the Senate Banking Committee on December 3 in a hearing titled "Protecting America’s AI Advantage: Oversight of US Export Controls".

events.title: Nvidia board puts Jensen Huang back as boss
events.summary: There's no telling what caused the Nvidia board to vote unanimously to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO less than a week after saying his return wasn’t under consideration – except reportedly the threat of having one's head ripped off and brain peed on – but that really doesn't matter, at least as far as shareholders need to be concerned: Jensen's back in charge and all’s right in the world of chip stocks. "I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment," Huang said of the decision to reinstate him, calling it an honor. Nvidia kicked its former-cum-current CEO and president to the curb on November 12, but not over allegations that he may have been sleeping with a suspected Chinese spy – it was affairs at Nvidia with his subordinates that appears to have been the last straw with Nvidia directors. Nvidia stock has tumbled since Huang’s ouster, and much of the rest of the tech stock world followed suit . Nvidia insiders and tech heavyweights have been pushing for Huang’s return for about as long as he was unemployed, but calls for his return from the US federal government may have been the catalyst for a change of heart among Nvidia leadership who didn’t want Huang back. "In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk," Nvidia said in its statement announcing Huang’s return. "The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers," board chair Harvey Jones added. Jones was made Nvidia's first board chair upon Huang’s resignation, and will remain in that role. The White House has since confirmed that the senior-level official involved in Huang’s reinstatement was President Trump. According to a White House statement to Semafor, Trump personally dialed in to an Nvidia board meeting hours before Huang was reinstated to argue for his return. “President Trump was totally involved and this is a great decision by the NVIDIA board,” White House comms director Steven Cheung told Semafor. “We have to protect our geniuses.” "The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to Nvidia poses any risk to National Security," Trump said in a post on Truth Social. "The Attorney General of the United States has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct." The surprise return echoes Sam Altman's return as CEO of OpenAI after the board fired him for a brief five days in 2023 over allegations of dishonesty. Both reinstatements happened around the US Thanksgiving holiday, suggesting that the spirit of forgiveness waxes with the anticipation of that roasted turkey smell wafting through the house. ® Updated at 1607 GMT to include the fact that Trump dialed into a board meeting.

events.title: Jensen Huang Is Back as Nvidia CEO
events.summary: Jensen Huang is stepping back into his role as chief executive of Nvidia effective immediately. The stunning reversal comes 11 days after Huang resigned as CEO from the company he cofounded 33 years ago and after multiple declarations from the board of directors that it had no intention of reinstating him. On Monday, they took a conciliatory tone. “The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners, and customers,” said recently appointed board chair Harvey Jones in a press release announcing the decision. In that announcement the board said it was “satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead Nvidia” and that it had “received input from senior levels of the United States government” on the way to its decision. On Monday morning, President Donald Trump posted that the Nvidia board “has made the correct and proper decision to return Jensen Huang to the position of CEO.” “I am honored to return to Nvidia and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution,” said Huang in a statement. “I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment.” Huang resigned as Nvidia’s CEO on November 12, and longtime chief financial officer Colette Kress was installed as his interim replacement. Five days later, Huang publicly announced that he was open to resuming his role as chief executive, noting the “outpouring of calls” from “employees, investors, business partners, and customers” advocating for his return. “If the board of directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” Huang wrote. The day Huang resigned, many Nvidia employees spoke up in his support. As reported by WIRED, employees left more than 1,600 comments on an internal “suggestion box” post in which they urged the company’s board to reinstall him as CEO. In the days following, a public petition calling for Huang’s reinstatement began circulating. At the time of writing, it has amassed more than 200,000 online signatures, the majority of whom self-identified as Nvidia shareholders. Tech elites like Elon Musk and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan have claimed that they were going to sign the petition or had signed it. Huang’s reinstatement marks a total reversal from the public stance of Nvidia’s board of directors, which said during the company’s November 17 earnings call that it “does not intend” to reinstate him as CEO. WIRED has further reported that the board was alarmed by what one source described as Huang’s “lying” over the last year or so. President Donald Trump, who developed a close working relationship with Huang during his second administration, had indicated openness to Huang returning as CEO. Trump told reporters on November 16 that he “would not mind” if Huang returned as chief executive, adding that he believed he had “learned a big lesson.” Huang’s resignation followed days of scrutiny over several extramarital romantic relationships: one with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, who has no known relation to Jensen, one with an Nvidia employee who directly reported to Huang, and one with a different Nvidia employee. Huang’s relationship with Alice became the subject of particularly intense focus on November 6, when The New York Times and Financial Times reported that US intelligence officials suspected that Alice may be an asset of the Chinese Ministry of State Security, both citing an intelligence briefing that circulated among top Trump administration officials last year. In the days since, some reports and Trump administration officials have questioned the accuracy of that intelligence. The Chinese government has consistently rejected claims that Alice was one of its spies. Alice was the chief executive of Megaspeed, a Singapore-based AI company that’s been accused of helping Chinese tech companies use Nvidia’s most advanced chips at overseas locations, effectively sidestepping US export restrictions. Alice has also reportedly worked as a television reporter, at HSBC’s Hong Kong-based private banking arm , and at an investment bank backed by the Chinese state. Huang cofounded Nvidia in 1993 with Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem, purportedly with the mission of bringing realistic 3D graphics to personal computers. For many years, the company was primarily known within the gaming community . It didn’t become a household name until the recent AI boom, when its graphics processing units (GPUs) became a crucial piece of infrastructure for powering advanced AI models. Nvidia controlled about 90 percent of the global GPU market as of September 2026. The year prior, it became the first company to be valued at more than $4 trillion, though its stock price has been in precipitous decline since Huang’s resignation.

He's suspected of having had a relationship with a Chinese intelligence asset. US tech company Nvidia said on Monday that it had reinstated Jensen Huang as its CEO "effective immediately." This follows just a matter of days after his resignation after admitting to extramarital affairs, reportedly including a dalliance with a woman who was a Chinese intelligence asset. What did Nvidia and Huang say about the move? The board unanimously decided that his return was in the "best interests of the company," Nvidia said, adding that it was satisfied that Huang had demonstrated his "candor and ability to lead." Meanwhile, the 63-year-old said in a statement that he was "honored" to return to the company and that he would take on the renewed responsibility "with the greatest humility and renewed commitment." He thanked interim CEO Colette Kress , who is set to return to her role as chief financial officer. "I am also deeply thankful to our employees, shareholders, leaders across the industry and partners around the world for their extraordinary support," Huang said. "Above all, I am grateful for the love and support of my family. I can't wait to get back to work." US President Donald Trump rapidly commented on the development online, saying it was the "correct and proper decision" and referring to Huang by his first name as a "Great Patriot and National Treasure." "The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen's return to Nvidia poses any risk to National Security," Trump wrote, also saying that the US had no evidence of him engaging in unlawful conduct. Huang liked to flaunt his personal relationship with Trump. He was reportedly influential in convincing the US president to allow the export of higher-quality Nvidia chips to China that are useful in AI development than other US officials and entrepreneurs endorsed. Nvidia stock volatility continues, with spike after announcement The decision was announced as trading started for the new week in New York. The stock price of what investors deem the world's most valuable company has nosedived amid the scandal, with Nvidia's stock price falling from almost $220 (roughly €200) per share in late October to around $125 per share at the end of last week. The announcement prompted a rapid early-morning rally on Wall Street, including Nvidia stocks rising back into a region between $160 and $170. This concession came amid widespread reporting in the US linking him romantically to one woman in particular, who was running a major Nvidia client called Megaspeed based in Singapore and who was said to be an asset of Chinese intelligence services. Her company is also suspected of diverting chips not approved for export to China to the Chinese market, circumventing US sanctions. events.title: Dubai Islamic Bank shares surge 11% on potential acquisition deal
events.summary: Dubai Islamic Bank shares closed 11 per cent higher on Monday after the lender said its board would meet this week to evaluate a strategic acquisition, amid reports of talks to combine it with Emirates Islamic, the Sharia-compliant unit of Emirates NBD. The lender’s board will be holding a meeting on Wednesday to discuss the matter, the UAE’s biggest Sharia-compliant bank said in a brief statement on Monday to the Dubai Financial Market, where its shares are traded. It did not provide further details. Bloomberg, citing people familiar with the matter, said officials have held preliminary talks on combining the two lenders. However, it added no final decision had been made and a deal may not materialise. Emirates NBD, in a separate statement, said its board would meet the same day to “consider and approve potential transaction opportunities”. It also did not provide further details. Its shares were down 0.8 per cent at the end of trading on Monday. If the transaction goes ahead, this would be one of the biggest mergers in the banking industry in the UAE following the merger of Abu Dhabi Commercial Bank with Union National Bank and Al Hilal Bank in 2019. National Bank of Abu Dhabi was combined with First Gulf Bank to create First Abu Dhabi Bank in 2017. Established in 1975, DIB is the largest Islamic bank in the UAE by assets. With group assets exceeding Dh427 billion ($116.27 billion) by the end of September, the bank has a workforce of about 12,000 employees and more than 540 branches in the Middle East, Asia and Africa. It reported a 3 per cent annual decline in profit to Dh1.79 billion for the third quarter of this year as a result of higher impairment charges and lower net income. Emirates Islamic was previously listed, before Emirates NBD bought out minority shareholders and delisted the business in June last year.

events.title: Everything going down at once wasn't evidence of a conspiracy – but the truth may be scarier
events.summary: Have you or someone you love been affected by a tech outage this week? Yeah, us too. You can listen to the latest episode of The Kettle right here on this page, as well as on Spotify , Apple Music , or YouTube . Those platforms also let you subscribe to The Kettle, so you are always notified when the latest episode goes live In a week of big stories the biggest one seems to be the fact that everyone from Microsoft to the NSA was dealing with outages , and here's what might be the worst part: It doesn't seem to be AI, nor hostile countries intent on destroying our infrastructure. Unfortunately for all of us, what the past week of outages reveal is that – as we discussed on The Kettle less than a month ago – all of our essential tech infrastructure is basically held together with duct tape and twine. Join host Brandon Vigliarolo , cybersecurity editor Jessica Lyons , and open source reporter Liam Proven to discuss what comes next, and whether we can fix any of this without tearing all of it out and starting from scratch. A lightly edited transcript is included below: Brandon (00:04) Hi everyone and welcome to the latest episode of the Register's Kettle podcast. I'm your host, Reg reporter Brandon Vigliarolo, and if you're hearing this, then that means there isn't an outage right now, which seems like that might be a lot to ask of our technology in the past week. It's been a busy week. We had Anthropic's IPO , Nvidia drama continuing , and other stuff going on. But the one thing that everyone seems to be talking about is what's become known in the zeitgeist as Outagepalooza, as it seems like everything was offline at some point in the past few days. With me to discuss the chaos and the conspiracy theories they're giving rise to is Reg cybersecurity editor Jessica Lyons and our open source reporter Liam Proven. Guys, what's happening? Jessica Lyons (00:45) I've got my tinfoil hat on right now, so I'm ready. Brandon (00:48) Yes, I've had family calling me being like, my god, what's happening? Who's ending the world right now? Is it AI? Jessica Lyons (00:55) Ha ha ha. Brandon (00:56) We'll get to that part. Liam Proven (00:57) Wonderful. My mum's wardrobe door stuck this week and we found a company on the little rock in the middle of the Irish Sea that fixes sliding doors and he didn't get my emails because he's one hundred percent Microsoft and he uses Hotmail and it's Hotmail. Liam Proven (01:18) And when I got it through, you'd be amazed at the ramifications. I SMS'd him in the end and he got that and then was really angry because I said, "Dude, I've been trying to get you for three days. Can you at least reply and say Friday?" And he's like, "No, I've got no email, I've got no internet, I've got nothing." Brandon (01:32) My god. Yes, it's been an interesting week. So Jess, catch us up on everything that's fallen apart in the past few days. We've got quite a list growing here. Jessica Lyons (01:40) Yes. Well, we'll start with Outlook. I'm sorry, Microsoft. It was larger than just Outlook, but similar to Liam, I got this message from my dad. We were at dinner with some friends and he said, "What is going on? I haven't been able to access Outlook all day. What is happening?" So this happened last week and there was this massive Microsoft outage and ultimately, people assumed it was maybe a cyber attack. Is somebody DDoSing Microsoft? What's going on? And then a few days later, Microsoft said, "No, this was a faulty software update that we pushed back in July, and it's affecting all of our 365 services now." So that was last Thursday. Then a day later, the FAA grounded all planes . Brandon (02:29) Right. Jessica Lyons (02:29) And again, in light of Microsoft, people were still having problems with Microsoft. All the planes are grounded. At the time, we just knew it was some type of communication error. And that sounds like something that a lot of nation states would really like to hit and attack. And this one, we ultimately learned that it was due to a network upgrade. Their provider, L3Harris, was switching out the copper wiring with fiber. And this has been an ongoing project. Also, kind of seems like maybe Friday the 13th isn't the best day to undertake this. Brandon (03:03) I hadn't even thought about the fact that it was Friday the 13th that all that happened. Jessica Lyons (03:09) So we see that right after Microsoft. And there was kind of a lull over the weekend, which was nice. But then Monday first thing, customers at Chase and US Bank and other major American banks couldn't withdraw any money from their accounts. And this we find out is also due to a massive outage. events.title: NVIDIA Board Reinstates Jensen Huang as President, CEO and Board Director
events.summary: NVIDIA (NASDAQ: NVDA) today announced that effective immediately, Jensen Huang has been reinstated as President and Chief Executive Officer and as a member of the Board. The Board of Directors voted unanimously to reinstate Mr. Huang following a series of discussions and meetings with Mr. Huang, after which the Board was satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead NVIDIA. In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk. “The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers,” said Harvey C. Jones, Chair of the Board. “We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the Company. We are grateful to Colette Kress for her outstanding service as interim CEO, in addition to her continuing responsibilities as NVIDIA’s Chief Financial Officer.” Harvey Jones will remain as Board chair. “I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution,” said Jensen Huang. “I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment. I want to thank the NVIDIA Board for its confidence and deliberation through this process. I am especially grateful to Harvey Jones for his leadership as Chair, and to Colette Kress and our executive staff for leading NVIDIA during this period. I am also deeply thankful to our employees, shareholders, leaders across the industry and partners around the world for their extraordinary support. Above all, I am grateful for the love and support of my family. I can’t wait to get back to work.” As previously announced, in light of recent reporting that Mr. Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort, the Board formed a committee comprised solely of independent directors to investigate, and the committee retained independent counsel to assist it in that investigation. The Board reiterated that the committee’s investigation will proceed to conclusion. Mr. Huang fully supports the investigation and is committed to cooperating with it. The Board also recently formed a National Security and Export Control Committee comprised solely of independent directors to oversee trade compliance and national security risks. The committee is engaging counsel with experience in national security matters, and such counsel will be retaining advisors with expertise in national security matters. NVIDIA is commencing a search to fill a new position, Chief Compliance Officer, to oversee compliance across NVIDIA and report to the Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee. NVIDIA will continue to cooperate with ongoing government investigations and inquiries. events.title: Crowdstrike to acquire Zscaler in $44B deal that would create a cybersecurity giant
events.summary: CrowdStrike is acquiring cloud security company Zscaler in an all-stock deal valued at about $43.9 billion CrowdStrike is buying cloud security company Zscaler in an all-stock deal worth about $43.9 billion, the companies said Monday, in a major acquisition that combines two of the cybersecurity industry's biggest names. The all-stock deal arrives after a string of high-profile hacks hit banks , supermarket fridges and crypto platforms , forcing the White House to shake up its cybersecurity leadership and raising alarms with officials around the world . Cybersecurity experts have warned that artificial intelligence is being used to turbocharge cyberattacks by making it quicker and easier to find software flaws. “Security used to be about keeping the adversary out," George Kurtz, CEO of Austin, Texas-based Crowdstrike, said in a statement. “Today, safety is required to let AI in.” Reports of advanced artificial intelligence models deploying agents working on their own to break into other organizations have also raised alarms. “In the AI era, Zero Trust security has become non-negotiable, and AI agents are rapidly becoming the new weakest link," Zscaler CEO Jay Chaudhry said. Crowdstrike's focus has been on so-called endpoint security, with services to protect laptops, mobile devices and desktop computers. Santa Clara, California-based Zscaler, meanwhile, specializes in cloud-based network protection. Teen fatally struck by gunfire while camping near Florida river: Authorities Trump granted new chance to potentially erase his hush money case Carney enlists fake Trump for laughs at Canada's annual press gallery dinner Zscaler shareholders will get 1.135 shares of Crowdstrike for each Zscaler share they own, under the deal's terms, which represent a 34% premium to Zscaler's closing price on Friday. Existing CrowdStrike shareholders will own about 84.1% of the combined company, while existing Zscaler shareholders will hold the remaining 15.9%. CrowdStrike and Zscaler were already working together in a partnership that included 2,000 shared customers. The deal would expand the combined company's market by more than $185 billion by 2029. events.summary: A Polish-Sudanese archeological team has uncovered part of the floor and staircase of a vast medieval church in the ancient region of Nubia, which straddled what is now northern Sudan and southern Egypt. Measuring about 47 by 57 meters, the Great Church of Jesus was “larger than the … White House,” Artur Obłuski, who heads the archeological mission, told AP. It could have been a regional architectural “trendsetter” like the Byzantine cathedral Hagia Sophia in what is now Istanbul, he added. events.title: Trump says he won't allow US companies to build datacenters abroad
events.summary: US President Donald Trump has threatened a "tremendous tax" on American companies building datacenters overseas, arguing that the infrastructure should stay at home to preserve the country's AI lead over China. Speaking at a White House press conference after returning from the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, Trump portrayed AI leadership as a contest America could not afford to lose. Trump went on to say that "we're not going to allow our companies to build datacenters outside of our country," adding that "they allowed that to happen with chips and everything else and it was very destructive to our country." The threat appeared to catch even his own administration unbriefed. "I haven't even said that to my people, but I'm telling them now," Trump said. The Official White House Rapid Response account posted a video clip on X. We asked the White House if the president intends to follow through, and we will let you know if we get an answer. Trump said: "We're not going to allow companies to build datacenters in other countries. If they do that, they can, but we're going to put a tremendous tax on them. We want them to do it here." The threat comes amid concerns that Chinese entities were able to use Nvidia's cutting-edge GPUs for training AI models by accessing cloud services hosted in third countries. The US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) issued new rules to try and crack down on this practice last week. "We're not allowing datacenters to go into other countries, as China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen," Trump repeated. "We're going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try and do it. They want to build that one in Finland, and we're not allowing that to happen," he added. Google is expanding its facilities in Finland, including one recently in the news because the developer had reportedly illegally felled 250,000 trees to make way for it. Such a policy seems unlikely to be allowed by Congress, where both houses will be under the control of the Democrats when the new term begins in January. Amazon, Google, and Microsoft already operate global datacenter networks to serve customers in different regions. Restrictions on further overseas construction would complicate those businesses. Omdia chief analyst Roy Illsley expressed doubt that this is a serious threat. "There will be ways around that if he does impose some executive order, and the ability to build datacenters is not just an American skill, many countries can build them, it is the equipment in them that is mostly US," he told The Register . "So I do not take this seriously as it would not work, there is no such thing as a US datacenter, they are made up of thousands of components from all over the globe. He could stop US capital from being invested in those countries, but that could have trade consequences." Mike Kharchenko of European hosting firm HostZealot said there are good reasons why the cloud giants operate datacenters outside the US, such as latency and regulatory compliance. "A buyer in Frankfurt won't wait for a page to load from Virginia. Some countries require certain data to stay inside their borders, and big European clients write it into contracts anyway," he stated. Trump claimed that communities in America that host datacenters are "making so much money that they don't know what to do with it." Those claimed benefits come alongside substantial public subsidies. Nonprofit organization Good Jobs First reported earlier this year that some states are losing billions in revenue because of the tax abatement schemes offered to companies to entice them to set up shop there. ®

events.title: DR Congo's president to take control of mining inspectorate
events.summary: DR Congo’s president is taking direct control of the mining inspectorate to curb smuggling and illegal activities in the world’s top cobalt producer, where unauthorized operators are extracting ore from concessions held by major international miners. Félix Tshisekedi told his cabinet on Friday that the change, due within days, would send strategic information straight to him and speed up corrective action and sanctions, according to a readout of the ministerial meeting seen by Semafor. The shift follows a government sweep this month that seized more than 500 trucks and thousands of tons of copper and cobalt. For years, illegal miners, many of them protected by Congolese soldiers, have moved onto concessions owned by companies such as Swiss commodities giant Glencore, China’s CMOC, and Kazakhstan-backed Eurasian Resources Group. The inspectorate, which helps trace minerals from origin to export, announced in April that it would set up a paramilitary force to replace soldiers at mines and escort shipments, a plan officials billed as a way to protect investments and strengthen investor confidence. Interest in Congolese mines has grown as the US and its allies race China for critical minerals. A US-backed consortium is close to buying 40% of Glencore’s local operations, and state miner Gécamines delivered its first copper to a US stockpile in October. — Ruben Nyanguila
