events.title: Goodbye, World: The End of Programmers
events.summary: Becoming a programmer was, for me, a compromise. Midway through my junior year of college, it became clear that, as an international student from Korea, I likely wouldn’t be able to stay long after graduation unless I changed my major from philosophy to a STEM field that made me eligible for a visa extension. The obvious choice was computer science, which was already my minor. The switch came with a sense of shame, which in retrospect had a whiff of melodrama. I suppose I was afflicted by what Ian McEwan once called “modern forms of snobbery” in describing a character who, after her bookish college education, came to consider “a man with a degree in chemistry incomplete as a human being.” Chemistry, computer science—same diff. It’s safe to say I did not have many friends in the CS department. But I don’t think my squeamishness was entirely misplaced. In the post-Facebook-IPO ferment of the 2010s, this country’s computer science departments were newly flush with a certain breed of striver who in another era would’ve gone to Wall Street. My theory is that many in America who acquired a hostility toward technology acquired it by way of a hostility toward these upstarts. That is to say, they aren’t so much anti- technology as anti- technologist . In any event, I half-assed my way through a good many CS assignments, which meant I was never in danger of going to grad school for AI. But by virtue of a robust public math education in Korea, my entry into the subject was, mercifully, not too bumpy. If anything, theoretical computer science and distributed systems seemed like a continuation of philosophy. But I could not dispel the sense that programming was a frivolous waste of energy. Every line of code I had to read, every line of code I had to write, was a theft of the time I could’ve spent reading something I cared about. Perhaps it didn’t help that my first two languages were Java (hideous and tedious) and C (admirable but unforgiving). To this day, Java code is like a poisoned madeleine that brings back unwelcome memories. After college, my visa dictated that I take a job directly tied to my major, and I found a tech company willing to sponsor my green card. The issue was, it could be any number of years until I got the green card—four, it’d turn out—so I figured I might as well find a way to make programming pleasurable. The first couple of months on the job were joyless. I worked at a health care startup, which I thought gave me a serviceable sense of moral cover against the ongoing techlash and a way to indemnify myself later as a writer. But I liked my coworkers, some of whom also harbored artistic ambitions, and after work we’d regularly adjourn to literary events at the McNally Jackson, a block from our office. Then, one day, I discovered a language called Haskell . I was tasked with rewriting a code base using a library that borrowed concepts from it. My vague impression of Haskell had been that it was a difficult language involving a branch of mathematics called category theory. There was something seductive about the intimidating aura around it, and when I tried my hand at writing basic programs, the language was indeed challenging, but appealingly so. I started lurking in Haskell forums where researchers in the field of programming languages—“PL,” as it’s known—flaunted their lavish command of the language. PL researchers might as well be the poets of computer science: a small community of attentive monomaniacs who engaged in a largely unprofitable enterprise—a rarity in computer science—with all the attendant beef and infighting. The unprofitability meant that, unlike AI, the field had an incorruptible dignity to it. Soon, to my surprise, I found myself programming outside work. After months of tinkering with Haskell, I discovered a book titled Writing a Compiler in Go . Turns out you could even invent a language yourself. I made a few toy languages, useless in practice but invaluable for demystifying how programming languages work. There was also an oblique way coding could help writing. In Draft No. 4 , John McPhee, the journalist’s journalist, says that he still uses an ancient text editor called Kedit, recommended to him in 1984 by a programmer at Princeton. (“I have never used a word processor,” he writes.) When I switched to a text editor myself, I could see why he’d stuck with it. With open source code, I could add silly but useful features, such as highlighting “TK”—a common shorthand in journalism for placeholder text—in a conspicuous color so that it was easy to locate later. If nothing else, I came to appreciate that programming was a reliable way to enter that elusive mode called flow, a state in which we’re somehow forgetful and alert at once. In the industry, there’s a general impression that fussing over programming languages is juvenile. If a job candidate expresses enthusiasm for languages, it could very well be a red flag.

events.title: If They Call 911 About Domestic Abuse, Will They Be Deported?
events.summary: A tres leches cake is cut and served during a support group in Kent County, Michigan, for immigrant women who have experienced domestic abuse. Jamie Kelter Davis for ProPublica About a dozen women chitchatted in Spanish between forkfuls of a tres leches cake. They spoke about their hopes and dreams — learning to drive, speaking English, visiting a son who had been deported. Some brought their young children, who scurried around them, circling the tables and tugging at their shirts, before the older kids nudged them into a nearby playroom, giving the women space to talk. The women were from Mexico and Guatemala, the Dominican Republic and El Salvador. Some settled here in west Michigan decades ago and had already become U.S. citizens or permanent residents. Others were more recent arrivals, with pending asylum cases. All of them said they had been abused by their current or former partners. And they had gathered at this informal support group, hosted by a local nonprofit, to talk. I’m a ProPublica reporter in Detroit, and my colleague Melissa Sanchez is in Chicago. We each drove over 100 miles last summer to be in this room because we were working on a story. It published in mid-October, and it’s about how the immigration policies of President Donald Trump’s administration have made life more perilous for victims of domestic abuse . While reporting, we had heard about the pervasive presence of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents in west Michigan, and we wanted to hear from immigrant women there who were living through domestic abuse. How did they weigh whether it was safer to stay with an abusive partner or to seek help from law enforcement, knowing they might be detained — and even deported? That night, a young woman with a toddler told us that she called 911 about a year earlier, after her boyfriend slapped her when he was drunk. If he hit her today, she said, she wouldn’t dial that number again. With arrests by federal immigration officers constantly in the news, she said, the risk is too great. None of the others in the room said they were currently living with an abusive partner. Those women were out there, the group’s facilitators told us. But they were too afraid to even leave their homes. Children play while their relatives take part in the support group. Jamie Kelter Davis for ProPublica After the meeting, as empty paper plates were cleared from the tables, the facilitators told us about E. She was once a regular at the meetings, they said, but hadn’t been around in a while. They worried about her. We asked if E. might be open to talking with us and, after a few texts, we learned that she was — if we could be ready to talk in about 20 minutes. We hurried back to our nearby lodgings, dialed E.’s number and put her on speakerphone. In Spanish, Melissa explained what we were reporting on, why it was so important to hear from somebody like her and the kinds of questions we wanted to ask. Then we began the interview. E., who asked not to be fully identified, told us that she avoids going out unless it’s absolutely necessary. She’d heard harrowing stories about women at the immigration detention center in Michigan where other women we’d interviewed were locked up. As we described in our story, several had been arrested here in Kent County when local police responded to domestic violence calls. E. doesn’t want to end up in ICE custody herself or, worse, deported. For the sake of her kids, E. said, she tolerates her husband’s abuse in silence. When he tells her she’s “nobody here” and to “go back to your country,” she said she puts her head down. When he pulls her hair in bed and says she belongs to him, she said she pretends it’s a joke. When he asks for the money she makes from selling food at a local factory, she said she hands it over. A filing in E.’s immigration case says her husband is a U.S. citizen who has been “verbally and financially abusive” and has threatened to take away the child they share. E. said that, except for the hair pulling, he isn’t physically abusive.  For help in English or Spanish , call the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 800-799-7233 or text “start” to 88788. (Like the other women we interviewed, E. asked that ProPublica not interview her alleged abuser because she’s afraid he will retaliate against her, take away her children or call ICE. To report these women’s stories, we interviewed attorneys, advocates, family and others who interacted with them. When available, we also reviewed text messages, and records from law enforcement and immigration court.) E. said her husband doesn’t overtly threaten her with calling ICE. But she said she found a hotline number for the agency written in his journal, alongside a description of his ideal woman: obedient and submissive. That reminded us of what a local immigration attorney, Catherine Villanueva, had told us: “We have this idea that we’re deporting these really bad people,” she said. “What we’re doing is we’re empowering the bad people who are already here.”  We asked E. if she had ever called the police to report her husband’s abuse. Her answer came quickly: No. Her husband is frail. She worries police officers will look at both of them and decide that he’s the victim. “They won’t see me as the abused one,” she said. “If I called the police, the one who would wind up losing is me.” When we reached out to federal officials for our story, White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said in a statement that ICE is targeting the “worst of the worst.” The real story, she added, is the “American women whose lives have been taken by illegal alien criminals.” A spokesperson for the U.S. Department of Homeland Security said in a statement that “we will never apologize for deporting illegal aliens, because that’s how we save lives.” As part of our reporting, we examined the backgrounds of the women we interviewed. Most had no criminal records we could find.   Angelica Ferrer, a victim witness coordinator for Kent County Prosecutor’s Office Jamie Kelter Davis for ProPublica People in law enforcement and the prosecutor’s office in Kent County told us that they wanted everybody to feel safe reaching out to report crimes, regardless of their immigration status. Kent County Prosecutor Chris Becker said that he and a Spanish-speaking assistant prosecutor met with local advocates for immigrants who are victims of domestic violence “to try and lower that barrier, to make people understand that we see them as victims and want to serve them as victims.” “But,” he added, “we can talk all we want, and still, I think it’s still difficult.” Indeed, Angelica Ferrer, the victim witness coordinator in Becker’s office, said she used to be able to tell victims that if they came to court, “we’re not going to have ICE here.” She doesn’t say that to them anymore. “That is a choice that you have to make,” she said. “I can’t guarantee that you won’t be stopped on the

events.title: What Capricor’s denial says about the FDA
events.summary: The denial of Capricor Therapeutics’ Duchenne muscular dystrophy cell therapy is a sign that there are limits to how flexible the FDA will be toward rare disease applicants even after the departure of former Commissioner Marty Makary. The company had hoped data on the effect of the therapy, called deramiocel, on the upper limb function of boys and young men with this severe progressive genetic disorder would convince regulators to greenlight the treatment — but questions surrounding the data integrity of the trial led the FDA to conclude that “the underlying data cannot serve as a reliable foundation for a marketing approval determination.” “FDA approaches rare disease applications with every intention of finding a path forward; however, flexibility in regulatory approach cannot come at the cost of the foundational requirement that the data underlying an approval decision be reliable,” the agency said in an unusual statement defending the decision. Capricor CEO Linda Marbán told Semafor she stands by the data behind the drug, insisting the FDA’s decision “is leading to hundreds of people losing their jobs.” The company — which said as of Sept. 30 it had $198.5 million to fund planned operations for at least the next 12 months — is “still evaluating” whether to move forward with a new clinical study requested by the FDA, which Marbán said would take four years to complete. “I just don’t have the capital to do it,” Marbán said. — David Lim

events.title: Inside the DCCC’s recruitment win
events.summary: The House Democratic campaign arm is trumpeting its role in the party’s big wins this cycle by encouraging top recruits to run, as House Democrats prepare to take their biggest majority in decades. “I think you know the reality is that the committee is often the first call or typically the most convincing to get most of these folks to run. And I was happy to be a lot of their first conversations about … running and what that looked like,” said DCCC National Political Director Brooke Butler. She pointed to recruitment successes, like incoming Reps. Christina Hines of Michigan and Paige Cognetti of Pennsylvania, both of whom ran in districts that were top DCCC targets this cycle. Butler said before Hines launched, she listened to the Michigan Democrat’s “questions, hesitancies, and things like that, and encouraged her to go for it.” Party leaders also encouraged the campaigns of some repeat candidates who came up narrowly short in previous cycles, like incoming Reps. Christina Bohannan of Iowa and Janelle Stelson of Pennsylvania, Butler said. Despite some intraparty drama over the DCCC’s backing of certain candidates in contested primaries this cycle, Butler said, the committee felt that all of the candidates they backed could win. It was “not the case that the DCCC was ever going to give up on or not get behind anybody,” she said. She also pointed to Rep.-elect Johnny Garcia, D-Texas, as an example of a successful party-backed first-time candidate. The DCCC and party leaders intervened in that primary to ward off a candidate accused of making antisemitic statements. Democrats face an expansive map to defend next cycle, including some incoming lawmakers who weren’t even on party leaders’ radar. But the broader House battleground has shifted, with Maine’s 2nd Congressional District, set to be the bluest state held by Republicans when Rep.-elect Paul LePage takes office. The future House battleground was “a lot of getting a sense of the opportunities come 2028, and then obviously we have a lot of defense we have to do as well. So [we’re] making sure we can reelect a lot of the people that we were able to get here,” Butler said. And with runoff elections still to come in Louisiana, “I never could write anything off, given what we saw, come Tuesday,” she said.

events.title: Merkley irks colleagues amid push to change rules
events.summary: Oregon Democratic Sen. Jeff Merkley isn’t making it easy on himself as he pitches Democratic colleagues on his proposal to alter the Senate rules. That’s because many of them are perturbed by his decision to block a vote on a manager’s amendment to the bipartisan permitting reform bill that just passed the Senate. “The irony was not missed,” said Sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., one of the bill’s Democratic authors. Without commenting on the specifics of Merkley’s rules reform proposal, Sen. Angus King, I-Maine, said he “did not like it” when Merkley objected to the bipartisan amendment, after other senators prevented a vote on banning data centers from public land. “I couldn’t understand what the rationale was. The bill was going to pass. So why not make it better? It didn’t compute for me,” King said. Merkley’s rules reform proposal, with Sen. Steve Daines, R-Mont., would fast-track popular bills out of committee to the floor; his proposed fix wouldn’t have applied to the permitting bill because it didn’t go through the regular committee process, according to a Merkley spokesperson. “The proposal is premised on the idea that bills receive special fast-track status only if there is robust, bipartisan support from members of the committee,” the spokesperson said. ‘Dirty’ or fair play? The Democratic anger at Merkley is real. Sen. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., called it “dirty” and said that Merkley blocked “a largely Dem amendment that would have improved the bill significantly in the hopes that [the] bill is so unpopular that it will die in the House.” One Democratic senator who opposed the permitting bill told Semafor that the failure to attach the manager’s amendment would ultimately tamp down support for the bill among progressives, making it trickier in the House. But not all Democrats feel that way. “People fight by the rules that we have. I don’t think there’s ever an element where people are unilaterally disarming,” said Sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., who has expressed interest in Merkley’s rules reform. So has Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., who is challenging Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., for the job of Democratic leader and has endorsed Merkley’s package. Of course, Schumer is highly likely to win the leader race — and Merkley has endorsed Van Hollen, which won’t build goodwill with next year’s probable majority leader. GOP support Current Senate Majority Leader John Thune said he “really” likes the idea of getting rid of time-wasting procedures and making it easier for bipartisan bills to reach the floor. But he’s bearish on getting a deal with Schumer to vote on that before the next Congress, citing the dwindling calendar. “It’s getting impossible to do anything around here,” Thune said in an interview. “I agree with Daines that if you don’t do something to modify the rules around here, one side or the other at some point is going to blow up the filibuster.” Asked if Merkley endorsing Van Hollen hurts the effort, Thune demurred: “You observed that.”

events.title: AI is disrupting entry-level work, report finds
events.summary: AI is already reshaping the US economy, staunching job growth in white-collar industries and making it harder for young Americans to find entry-level jobs, according to a new report shared first with Semafor. The report — prepared by the group RAISE US, led by former Commerce Secretary Gina Raimondo, and the Burning Glass Institute, a labor research think tank — found that, overall, white-collar industries have 1.5 million fewer jobs than they would have had under pre-pandemic trajectories. In industries that use AI widely, the number of early-career opportunities shrank 3-8% on average between 2021 and 2026. Middle-skilled jobs that involve office and administrative work fell by 780,000 between 2023 and 2025, according to the report. “This analysis should be a wakeup call to leaders from Washington to Silicon Valley that we need to act now to prepare our workers for the transition to an AI economy,” Raimondo said. She launched her group with former GOP Indiana Gov. Eric Holcomb to help the US workforce adapt to the AI economy.

events.title: State Department bypasses Democrats on Africa health aid
events.summary: The State Department plans to bypass objections from leading Democrats to move forward with distributing more than $170 million in health assistance to three countries in Africa, Semafor has learned. The decision comes after the State Department sent a notification to Congress about the planned funding, which is being sent to Kenya, Malawi, and Uganda, at the end of August. Days later, Democrats on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee and House Foreign Affairs Committee placed holds on distributing the funds. The State Department says that the Bureau of Global Health Security and Diplomacy provided briefings for relevant congressional staffers on the topic, and it ultimately requested the committees lift their holds by October 31. Now, the department says it will push past the holds and begin obligating the funds anyway. “The Trump administration is determined to follow through on its commitment to these bilateral health agreements,” State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott said in a statement to Semafor, criticizing what he described as an attempt by Democrats to “block” the funds and arguing that it will go to “critical health efforts” like HIV treatment and malaria prevention. Health aid shifts The State Department has been negotiating bilateral agreements with African countries to provide health aid after drastically cutting back foreign assistance with the closure of the US Agency for International Development. Democrats have criticized the Trump administration for cutting back traditional health assistance and not releasing details about its bilateral deals with other countries. The hold on the funding stems from concerns from Democratic lawmakers about the way the State Department was handling government-to-government financing and was meant to ensure the department is meeting requirements laid out in appropriations legislation, said a Democratic aide. “Instead of funding the corrupt NGO industrial complex that wasted taxpayer money with no end in sight, we have reformed foreign assistance to focus on partnerships,” Pigott said. “We are encouraging burden sharing and capacity building so that countries can take control of their own health infrastructure.” In September, Emily Bass, a writer focused on global health policy, argued on Substack that the department’s congressional notification was overly “brief,” adding that it “effectively asks appropriating lawmakers to take it on faith that USD$176 million will be well spent in Malawi, Kenya and Uganda, which failed a 2026 US government assessment of ‘control of corruption and accountability.’” The State Department’s move overrides the committees’ normal oversight process, though it’s not a first for the Trump administration. In September, the State Department redirected $52 million in military aid to Latin American countries despite objections from top Democrats on both foreign affairs committees.

events.title: Germany's Early Start Pension: Can child investment accounts help?
events.summary: Germany plans to pay €10 a month into investment accounts for children to encourage long-term retirement saving. Economists say the measure may help build wealth but won't solve the country's pension funding challenge. Germany's pension system is under growing strain as demographic change leaves a shrinking workforce funding the pensions of an increasing number of retirees. In the 1960s, for instance, six workers contributed to the pay-as-you-go public retirement system for each pensioner. Today, that figure has fallen to just two contributors per retiree. According to the Federal Statistical Office, Germany's fertility rate is currently 1.32 children per woman, and has remained below the 2.1 needed to maintain a stable population since the 1970s. As a large cohort of baby boomers reaches retirement age, fewer young people are entering the workforce. Germany's working-age population is shrinking by around 1% each year due to demographic change alone, according to the German bank LBBW. To keep up, nearly a quarter of the federal budget, over €123 billion ($135 billion), is transferred to the statutory pension system each year to help finance pension payments. Now to help ease the pressure on the pension system , Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government plans to implement a raft of reforms, including a supplementary, capital-funded savings scheme known as the Frühstartrente , or Early Start Pension. How does the Early Start Pension work? Under the plan, the state would pay €10 per month into an investment account for every child and teenager aged six to 18. Beneficiaries would not be able to access the money until they reach retirement age, though current plans would allow the funds to be transferred into private retirement accounts. Investment returns would be tax-free during the accumulation phase and taxed only when funds are withdrawn. Assuming an average annual return of 7%, the €1,440 contributed by the government over 12 years would grow to around €53,000 by retirement, according to government projections. Parents and relatives would be able to make additional contributions. If they invest an extra €50 per month, the account could grow to as much as €300,000 by retirement. Starting to save early makes sense because of the power of compound interest, Axel Börsch-Supan, a professor of economics at the Technical University of Munich, told DW. "But it will not solve Germany's pension problems , which stem from the pay-as-you-go system and costly policies such as the pension level guarantee and retirement at 63," he added, referring to a provision that allows workers with at least 45 years of pension contributions to retire at age 63 with a full pension. What are the German government's pension, labor reforms? Börsch-Supan argues that government subsidies under the program are likely to benefit higher-income families more than lower-income households. "That's a waste of taxpayer money, because higher-income individuals are already well-positioned to provide for their own retirement and that of their children," he said. The Ifo Institute, one of Germany's leading economic think tanks, shares a similar assessment. It argues that the scheme effectively means "the government hands out money indiscriminately, only to reclaim it through taxes from the same citizens." The government, however, argues that the plan gives every child a head start in the capital markets regardless of their family's financial circumstances and helps them build retirement savings and long-term wealth. Similar capital market-based savings and investment accounts for children exist in several countries, including the United Kingdom, Israel, Canada and Singapore. Many of these programs include government contributions, matching payments or tax incentives designed to encourage long-term saving and asset accumulation from an early age. But Germany's plan differs slightly as it links state-funded childhood investment accounts directly to retirement provision. The government also hopes the program will boost financial literacy among children and young adults by familiarizing them with investing, saving and capital markets. What Germans young and old think about the pension system Can the scheme encourage long-term investing? Johannes Geyer, deputy head of the department of public economics at the German Institute for Economic Research (DIW Berlin), says there is little evidence the Early Start Pension will fundamentally change how people engage with financial markets. "The idea is that people will develop a connection to the capital markets through their experiences with their investment portfolios," he told DW. "But this is not very convincing. We neither know what experiences the future will bring nor what conclusions people will draw from them." Geyer stresses that the program's impact will not be visible for decades because participants cannot access the funds until retirement.

events.title: Copper sinks below $12,000 for the first time since March amid AI demand uncertainty
events.summary: Copper prices fell briefly below $12,000 a tonne on the London Metal Exchange on Monday, amid uncertainty over demand for the metal in the artificial intelligence sector and possible interest rate rises next month. The red metal, which is used widely in the construction of data centres and energy infrastructure, fell below the $12,000 mark for the first time since March, before paring losses. It rebounded to $12,160 a tonne at about 9.18am UAE time. This came after the metal tumbled 9 per cent last week, copper's third biggest decline in a decade, amid a broader sell-off in AI-related stocks, even as Anthropic made a strong debut on Nasdaq following a blockbuster initial public offering that helped the company raise $81.3 billion, the largest in history. Major US indexes, including S&P 500, Dow Jones Industrial Average and Nasdaq Composite ended the week lower, as investors cast doubts regarding sustainability of AI spending. Copper hit a record high of $14,694 per tonne in September, surpassing the previous record of $14,527.50 set in January. “Copper fell sharply from September highs amid growing doubts about the scale and returns of AI-related spending, prompting investors to unwind earlier bullish positions that linked the metal to data-centre growth,” Tony Sage, chief executive of Critical Metals, an Australia-based mining development company focused on critical metals and minerals, told The National . “A stronger US dollar and rising expectations of further Federal Reserve rate increases have added pressure by raising the cost of holding the metal and weighing on broader risk sentiment.” Higher interest rates would strengthen the US dollar, making metal priced in the greenback more expensive for buyers using other currencies. There are also concerns that the pace of future AI and data-centre investment may slow down, as Democrats swept the midterm elections in the US. Analysts expect tighter AI regulations and more scrutiny over the building of data centres following the Democrats' victory. “Growing public resistance to the electricity requirements, environmental impact and costs associated with large-scale data-centre expansion has increased uncertainty around a sector that has become an important pillar of copper's demand outlook,” said Ole Hansen, head of commodity strategy at Saxo Bank. The economic outlook for China – a major producer of refined copper – also remains challenging, particularly in traditional copper-consuming sectors such as property and construction, he added. The International Monetary Fund has trimmed its projection for China’s economic growth this year by 0.1 percentage point to 4.5 per cent. China is by far the largest consumer of refined copper, accounting for well over half of global use. “Near-term prices are likely to remain sensitive to shifts in AI investment sentiment, the dollar and Federal Reserve policy signals,” Mr Sage said. However, once current macro and positioning pressures ease, “the underlying supply-demand balance should reassert itself, supporting a firmer tone over the medium term”, he added. Copper is increasingly regarded as an essential component for AI building, electrification, electric vehicles and grid expansion. The US Geological Survey added it to its critical minerals list last year.

events.title: Bereaved families need support, not a battle with paperwork
events.summary: Investment firms must do more to help people dealing with the death of a loved one, after a review found confusing communications, delays and gaps in support. The FCA reviewed how financial advisers, wealth managers and investment platforms support bereaved families and those handling someone’s estate.Some firms provided thoughtful, personal support. Others had processes that risked adding to people’s distress and financial pressure.Some firms left people unclear about what to do next or offered limited ways to get in touch. In some cases, advice fees were still being taken until an original death certificate was provided.Kate Tuckley, head of department, consumer investments at the FCA, said, 'Dealing with someone’s finances after a death should not mean a battle with paperwork. Firms should ease the burden, not add to it.'Families need clear information and help without needless delays, not fees for advice they no longer receive. Some firms get this right and do it really well, now others must follow their lead.'The review identified useful steps firms can take, such as:Explain what happens next in plain English and give people options about how they can report a death, such as by phone, email or online to suit needs. Keep paperwork requirements proportionate and avoid unreasonable delays in access to money.Explain which charges stop or continue and stop ongoing advice fees where the related service is no longer being provided.Check whether people are getting the support they need, rather than relying on low complaint numbers as proof that everything is working.Notes to editorsThe review examined bereavement data, processes and 36 case summaries from firms that advise on, manage or administer investments. Firms were selected to reflect different sizes and business models.The FCA considered case and complaints data covering 1 May 2025 to 30 April 2026.The findings echo earlier FCA reviews of banks and insurers.The Consumer Duty requires firms to deliver good outcomes for retail customers, including providing support that meets their needs.

events.title: Saudi Arabia tightens rules to boost employment of citizens in finance jobs by May
events.summary: Saudi Arabia has announced that private sector companies must ensure 50 per cent of certain financial professions are held by Saudi citizens by May 23 next year. The decision applies to companies that employ two or more staff in 17 targeted roles, the Ministry of Human Resources and Social Development said on Sunday. The initiative is being implemented by the ministry in partnership with the Saudi Organisation for Chartered and Professional Accountants. The aim is to provide "quality job opportunities for citizens and increase their participation in the labour market", the ministry said. The roles covered are: financial analyst; financial consultant; investment manager; financial control specialist; investment specialist; financial planning specialist; financial product development specialist; treasury specialist; credit manager; financial services control manager; financial investigator; government revenue specialist; financial brokerage manager; investment adviser; investment expert; financial adviser; and financial expert. The decision gives the companies a six-month grace period from the date of its launch, allowing them to prepare and meet the requirements, the statement said. The ministry said it also offered incentives to help companies follow the rule, including nominating national talent, training and qualification, and support for employment and job stability. It urged companies to understand how the Saudisation rate is calculated to avoid penalties for non-compliance. The kingdom has been carrying out its Saudisation programme aggressively across sectors to boost the local employment rate under its Vision 2030 economic diversification agenda. Its Vision 2030 website says the kingdom has managed to reduce the Saudi unemployment rate to 6.4 per cent as of the first quarter of this year, down from 12.3 per cent in 2016. Engineering, project management and tourism The ministry, in partnership with Ministry of Municipalities and Housing, this month also raised the Saudisation rate for 94 technical engineering professions to 35 per cent. The decision, which takes effect from May 9, 2027, applies to all private sector companies with five or more employees. The roles targeted include civil, electrical, mechanical, and electronic engineering technicians, as well as surveying technicians, mechanical maintenance technicians and architectural draftsmen. Meanwhile, starting from February 14, 2027, the kingdom is also set to increase the Saudisation rate for project management roles to 70 per cent from 40 per cent. It applies to private sector organisations with three or more employees in roles such as project management director, project management engineer and project management specialist. In October last year, the Ministry of Tourism also said it aims to raise its localisation policy to 50 per cent by 2028 in all licensed tourism facilities. It said the move will be implemented in phases, with 40 per cent localisation by April 2026, 45 per cent by January 2027 and 50 per cent by 2028. The ministry's policy also prohibits the outsourcing of jobs that are eligible for Saudisation to establishments or employees outside the kingdom.

events.title: Poll shows media ripples of midterm blue wave — and Rogan’s lasting appeal
events.summary: Two years out from the “manosphere election,” Joe Rogan remains American men’s most trusted voice in media, even as their electoral sympathies have swung back towards the Democratic Party. That’s according to a sweeping post-midterms report conducted by Precision Strategies and data firm Tunnl — titled — that found an American populace riven by economic anxiety and split across race and gender lines. Meanwhile, the survey found, there’s no equivalent consensus voice for female audiences: Forty-nine percent of men (including 41% of Democratic men) said they trust Rogan, a greater share than any other figure polled, while no one person earned more than 22% of women’s trust. One possible reason why: Sixty-three percent of men said they had no male role models to turn to in their lives, and the potent parasocial relationships Rogan’s intimate longform chats can foster have inspired imitators from Theo Von to the US military . “The landscape of influence is changing, and understanding who people trust — and why — is becoming just as important as understanding what they believe,” said Tunnl’s Brent Seaborn. Another data point from Precision’s survey may disquiet journalists: Half of Republicans (51% of men, 50% of women) say the US government should be able to restrict media access for outlets that it believes to be biased, while a slight majority of the overall population say press access takes precedence. On partisan politics, the report broadly tracked with other midterms polling: Americans, particularly Gen Z, shifted towards Democrats without developing an abiding loyalty to the Democratic Party as their fears about job losses and financial difficulties continued to mount. Forty-five percent of men under age 30 reported identifying as independents, despite that group’s noted Democratic swing. But some findings underscored a growing weariness with some of MAGA’s cultural agenda: Only 16% of men and 11% of women said the Trump administration’s crusade against DEI had helped them in some way, while most reported no difference. And just 13% of women and 19% of men want more women to be full-time homemakers, something the Trump administration has sought to incentivize . Americans also report varying attitudes towards AI usage: A fifth of respondents said they’d used AI chatbots for companionship, with higher rates among younger Americans. Asian, Black, and Hispanic Americans also said they used AI more often than white Americans. — Graph Massara

events.title: High-profile events businesses can strain media companies’ trust and credibility
events.summary: The News Semafor is facing scrutiny for hiring high-profile Washington consultants to assist with event bookings, a revelation that underscores the murkiness embedded into a high-level convening business that’s become a vital and growing revenue source for some global media companies. As online web traffic and the associated advertising dollars have diminished across the industry, publishers have leaned into sponsored in-person events to support their newsrooms. The growing importance of these events has raised thorny standards and ethics questions regarding sponsors who pay to be onstage at places like Fortune, The Wall Street Journal and The Atlantic — even if their sessions are clearly labeled as sponsored — or regarding media CEOs who strike deals with advertisers while interviewing those same CEOs. Of the last decade’s crop of digital media outlets, none have leaned further into the events-driven business than Semafor, which has hosted hundreds of high-profile gatherings since launching in late 2022. While Semafor primarily relies on an in-house events team to secure bookings of business, political and government leaders, for its flagship April gathering, Semafor World Economy, the Washington Post reported on Thursday that the company enlisted a handful of external consultants to recruit politicians for onstage interviews. Among the consultants were former Trump advisers Jason Miller and Kellyanne Conway, as well as former Kamala Harris and Joe Biden adviser Adrienne Elrod. Miller is no longer on contract, but Conway and Elrod remain consultants at Semafor. The contracts were intended to help secure the best guests for its flagship Washington event, a multimillion-dollar revenue-driver for the four-year old company. A spokesperson for Semafor said in a statement that “we don’t pay speakers and both our speakers and guests come for tough, fair, and independent interviews,” noting that “many other media companies” employ consultants from across the political spectrum to recruit high-profile guests to attend their events. But others saw it as a potential conflict of interest. “Bad look all around,” one anonymous media executive told Puck’s media analyst, Dylan Byers. “We shouldn’t have to learn from court documents in a child support case that Semafor paid Jason Miller $100,000 because Semafor should have disclosed that,” the editor-in-chief of the left-leaning publication MeidasTouch posted . On Friday, the publication updated 11 stories disclosing the company’s financial relationship with Miller, Conway, and Elrod. Max’s view The death of the previous generation of digital media startups like BuzzFeed News and Vice taught many in the news media a lesson: the free, ad-supported model of digital startup journalism is unsustainable. In this environment, Semafor’s success has aroused some suspicion. At a moment when many media companies have struggled to stay afloat, Semafor has built a profitable news outlet that’s still free for online users, prompting some skeptics to wonder what the real reason is for the business’ growth. As a four-year veteran of the company, I can say Semafor’s viability is the result of a hardworking and creative commercial team, fairly shrewd financial planning, and talented journalists producing an editorial product readers find to be important. In my time here, I’ve never been asked by any editor — explicitly or implicitly — to lay off a guest or subject for commercial reasons. I’ve watched our editors defend our critical coverage and skeptical questions at events from subjects that aren’t always pleased with the content, and, when our offices were much smaller, I occasionally caught a glimpse of our revenue team navigating skittish sponsors who weren’t always comfortable with sensitive topics in the news cycle. At Semafor World Economy earlier this year, which occurred weeks after the Iran war began, a number of high-profile guests dropped out after asking us if our journalists could avoid asking about the war. They were told no. But media organizations are built on trust, and few institutions are less trusted in 2026 than the news media. America is cynical about the real and perceived coziness between politicians, lobbyists and the media companies that cover them. Compensating well-known political hands to ask important players to appear at events deepens that perception, even if they had zero influence on questions that the journalists asked once they got there. Semafor is not wrong that the use of external firms to help with high-profile events isn’t unusual. Many Washington organizations hire strategic public affairs firms for events that require executive wrangling. Two people familiar with the arrangement told me that former Harris adviser Shari Yost Gold had been enlisted for the White House Correspondents’ Association dinner and Politico’s major Sunday brunch (though unlike Conway, Yost Gold has not worked in the federal government). Bloomberg has enlisted FGS’ Capricia Marshall, a veteran of the Clinton and Obama White Houses, for its events. “Every public affairs firm offers this,” one industry insider told me. But even if you accept the premise that it is a routine practice, Miller was not just a normal lobbyist; at the time that he was an adviser for Semafor, he was also working for Paramount to help secure its bid for Warner Bros. Discovery, and get the resulting Skydance megamerger approved by federal regulators. The Semafor reporters and editors covering the deal considered Miller a part of that story, and were completely unaware that he was simultaneously being paid by the commercial side of the business. Miller has also been so close to the White House at times that it’s hard to consider him an outside actor. He’s been looped into key moments with the Trump administration, such as when he was asked to pull short-lived White House press secretary Katie Zacharia from an interview with The Wall Street Journal before she was pushed out of the job. Semafor was founded with principles of transparency at the forefront, positioning itself as a more honest and straightforward media company than its competitors. Our format, which separates reporters’ opinions from the facts, is in the service of hoping to rebuild some trust between a skeptical public and honest journalists. Hiring consultants did not build trust; instead, it resulted in a flurry of conspiracy theories that undermined the publication’s hard-hitting journalism and undercut its message. events.title: Directors push back on ‘You Can See Everything’ reporting
events.summary: The directors of are pushing back against new reporting about the film’s controversial subject. At the end of the documentary, which follows disgraced pharmaceutical entrepreneur Elizabeth Holmes’ final days before going to prison, it is revealed that her husband, Billy Evans, negotiated — and later relinquished — the rights to payment for the family’s role in the film. Last week, The Hollywood Reporter published a story saying the film had omitted key details that made Evans look slightly better — principally, that he “did retain rights to the payout on after all.” “The payout still went out; it was just redirected to a charity, in a move that puts Evans in a slightly warmer light,” the outlet reported. But during a Q&A Saturday night at the Darryl F. Zanuck Theater on the Fox studio lot, Lance Oppenheim and Nathan Fielder said that the THR story’s framing and wording was inaccurate, and that none of the documentary’s subjects were paid, according to one person in attendance. An A24 spokesperson declined to comment. But a studio source said that after Evans negotiated a profit participation deal, he ultimately relinquished his right to it. He and A24 mutually agreed to donate the proceeds to charity; as a part of the deal, the source said, Evans gave up his right to participate in the film’s profits. Oppenheim told the audience he was surprised by the story because The Hollywood Reporter is a “great publication.” “It is?” Fielder replied. In an email, THR’s editor-in-chief, Maer Roshan, said that the organization stood by its reporting, and that A24’s view “seems like a pretty semantic argument.” Further, he noted that THR’s Julian Sancton raised the story with Oppenheim during THR’s yet-to-be-released director’s roundtable yesterday featuring the director, plus Alex Gibney, Ron Howard, and Ava Duvernay, among others.

events.title: ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’ marks a turning point for the series
events.summary: The highest-grossing film of all time, , grossed $2.9 billion during its theatrical run. , the long-awaited next installment of the video game franchise, recorded $3.8 billion in sales on its first day. In a rave review, The New York Times called it “a game about love and relationships, their joy and heartache, and the work required to make them successful,” while The Washington Post gushed that the game was “an astonishing American epic.” The Miami Heat released special-edition Vice City jerseys. The record-setting release represents the cultural acceptance of a franchise that was once the center of a backlash to violent video games. During a press conference in 2005, then-Sen. Hillary Clinton said that the “disturbing material in and other games like it is stealing the innocence of our children,” and The House of Representatives passed a resolution (by a bipartisan 355-21 vote) asking the FTC to investigate Rockstar, the studio that makes. The late Sen. Joe Lieberman (who some GTA fans suspect is parodied by the weedy in-universe character “Chaz Lieberman”) denounced GTA for years. The franchise outlasted and outgrew the backlash. The game added layers of narrative tenderness in between some of the brutal and comic setpieces, and expanded its range of playable tasks into the comically mundane, like painting your character’s house and picking up groceries for his girlfriend. Years of research also tamped down some fears about links between video games and real violence. Beyond some segments in conservative media, the criticism this time around has been fairly muted; in some corners of the incel right, the game has been criticized as, if anything, too respectful to women. The mainstream acceptance of GTA has even reached Fox News, where a former police captain, brought on to warn parents about GTA’s influence on children, admitted : “It’s probably a really fun game.” — Manny Fidel

events.title: Trump's top intelligence official is also taking charge of cyber policy
events.summary: Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton will also serve as acting national cyber director while Kirsten Davies awaits Senate confirmation to lead the office, Axios has learned. A White House official said the strong support Davies received convinced Trump to nominate her to lead the office permanently rather than keep her in an acting capacity. Why it matters: Clayton, the nation's top intelligence official, will now coordinate cybersecurity policy as outages and reported cyberattacks expose vulnerabilities in America's digital infrastructure. Catch up quick: President Trump announced Thursday he was tapping Davies, the Pentagon's chief information officer, to replace Sean Cairncross as national cyber director. Davies will assist Clayton as a senior adviser in the Office of the National Cyber Director until she is confirmed. Trump has increasingly turned to Clayton. He became director of national intelligence in August, and then Trump named him AI czar coordinating the government's approach to AI. Now he will temporarily lead the office responsible for coordinating cybersecurity policy. What they're saying: "I'm excited to work more with Kirsten, who has the experience and capabilities needed to help America navigate our increasingly complex and powerful digital infrastructure as our next National Cyber Director," Clayton said in a statement to Axios. "I look forward to working with the ONCD team to ensure Kirsten has a seamless transition into the role upon her confirmation by the Senate." The big picture: Two critical national security roles will temporarily fall under one official as President Trump shakes up his cybersecurity team amid the growing threat of AI-powered attacks. The disruptions have raised concerns about the vulnerability of the nation's digital infrastructure, although administration officials say there is no evidence they were caused by coordinated cyberattacks. Clayton himself has played a prominent role in the administration's response, telling lawmakers Wednesday that the outages appeared to stem from unrelated technical problems and system upgrades. Driving the news: Clayton spent Sunday morning on CNN's "State of the Union," ABC's "This Week" and "Fox News Sunday," explaining recent technology disruptions and national security concerns. On CNN, he warned that Americans should expect more "glitches, gaps, interruptions in service" as government agencies and businesses modernize their systems. On ABC, Clayton maintained that recent widespread outages were neither coordinated nor state-sponsored, but declined to discuss reported cyberattacks on the FBI and Department of Agriculture. On Fox News, he said AI is giving malicious actors more powerful tools and warned that critical infrastructure will need upgrades. Zoom in: Davies oversees the Pentagon's information technology and cybersecurity strategy, including efforts to modernize aging systems and protect military networks. She has nearly two decades of technology experience, including senior roles at Unilever, Estée Lauder, Barclays Africa, Hewlett Packard Enterprise and Siemens. Behind the scenes: Clayton has already worked closely with the Office of the National Cyber Director, National Security Council, National Security Agency and other agencies through his AI leadership role, according to the White House official.

events.title: How bitter rivals Buttigieg and Klobuchar went from enemies to friends
events.summary: To the surprise of many Democrats and even some of their former aides, Pete Buttigieg and Amy Klobuchar now consider themselves friends after their bitter clashes during their campaigns for president in 2020. Their journey from snarky tension to "real respect and friendship," as Klobuchar describes it, is a story of how two ambitious Democrats came to appreciate each other once the heat of a presidential primary had subsided. Why it matters: It's also a reflection of how Buttigieg — who's weighing another run for president — has become a well-regarded Democratic stalwart after many in the party viewed him as a presumptuous lightweight when he ran six years ago as a little-known 37-year-old former mayor of South Bend, Ind. "I'm sincerely grateful for Amy's friendship," Buttigieg, who was President Biden's transportation secretary, told Axios. "My appreciation has continually grown for her substantive leadership and sense of humor alike." "I know there are people that run against each other for president and literally hate each other," Klobuchar, who's in her fourth term in the Senate but will leave in January to become Minnesota's governor, told Axios. "That was far from the case for us." Flashback: A casual observer might see that as a bit of revisionist history. The Buttigieg-Klobuchar spats during the 2020 Democratic primary were some of the most vicious of that campaign. Aides from both sides can still quote the barbs, word for word. "I wish everyone was as perfect as you, Pete," Klobuchar sniped at one debate in Las Vegas before saying "You've memorized a bunch of talking points and a bunch of things." She added after the debate that Buttigieg was "haughty" and that "given the guy [Trump] we have in the White House, maybe you need someone who's a little more humble." Buttigieg repeatedly mocked Klobuchar for not remembering the name of the president of Mexico in an interview. He said Klobuchar was "not able to speak to literally the first thing about the politics of the country to our south." She shot back: "Are you trying to say that I'm dumb?" Asked today about those mutual attacks, Klobuchar says simply: "We both wanted to win." Many Democrats laughed that their feud appeared to continue into 2021, when the two wrote books with opposite titles — "Trust" by Buttigieg, and "Anti-Trust" by Klobuchar. When Buttigieg announced recently that he has a book coming out in January titled "Next," he texted Klobuchar: "Please tell me you're not putting out a book called 'Last.'" Zoom in: Klobuchar said their relationship has become increasingly warm through the years. "We kept consistently in touch, and not just over work. We had lunch when he first got into Washington. I remember I saw their apartment at the time," she said. "I also worked with him extensively on transportation issues." She added that she came to appreciate "how smart and even-keeled he is" at a time when "'hair on fire' is kind of cool to be." Buttigieg, who campaigned with Klobuchar during the 2026 midterms, said he's "looking forward to seeing all that she accomplishes as governor, and also to my next opportunity to join her at the Minnesota State Fair." What they're saying: A former Klobuchar aide told Axios that it's a "very Midwestern friendship story." "You meet someone new with a healthy dose of competition, skepticism, and a little frostiness. And along the way, you find out you genuinely like each other. That's Amy and Pete." What's next: Klobuchar, who has said she's not running for president, didn't want to weigh in on 2028 because she knows many people who are likely to run. As for what she thinks of Buttigieg's potential candidacy: "He has always been impressive."

events.title: Scoop: DeSantis' secret book project fuels 2028 speculation
events.summary: Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis is quietly working on a book, two sources tell Axios — a project likely to fuel speculation about his making another run for the White House. Why it matters: DeSantis hasn't publicly acknowledged the book project or disclosed what it will be about. But writing a book is often the first step toward a presidential campaign, and it could give the term-limited governor a platform to lay out his vision for the Republican Party's future. DeSantis' state was a rare bright spot for Republicans in this month's midterms, as Democrats made historic gains across the nation. Driving the news: Word of DeSantis' book comes as he's become increasingly outspoken on a range of policy issues, particularly the economic and social impact of artificial intelligence — potentially offering clues about what the book might address. DeSantis has become a vocal critic of the potential dangers of AI, warning that it could eliminate jobs, threaten children's safety and privacy, and drive up electricity bills as data centers expand. DeSantis has pushed for an "AI Bill of Rights" and signed state legislation aimed at preventing tech companies from passing the costs of data centers on to residential consumers. His stance has put him at odds with the Trump administration's efforts to limit states' ability to regulate AI. DeSantis has emphasized affordability, immigration and education — issues likely to remain central to national politics long after he leaves office. Zoom out: DeSantis has made other moves that could keep him in the national spotlight after he leaves office in January. NBC News recently reported that DeSantis is preparing to launch a conservative think tank, which could enable him to retain a political and donor infrastructure. After the midterms, DeSantis embarked on a flurry of media appearances that resembled a victory tour, highlighting how Florida Republicans had largely escaped the Democratic wave. Yes, but: Some DeSantis allies are highly skeptical that he'll mount another presidential campaign after his unsuccessful 2024 bid. DeSantis has sent mixed signals about his political future. He downplayed the prospect of another presidential bid last year and, after the midterms, questioned how much a Republican president could accomplish with Democrats controlling Congress. He also disputed a report that he was building a campaign operation. But he hasn't ruled out a 2028 run, saying he'll assess the political landscape after leaving office. What they're saying: DeSantis' spokespeople did not respond to requests for comment about the book.

events.title: Scoop: The Pentagon's case for Canada to "get serious" on defense
events.summary: The Pentagon accused Canada of failing to become a "credible partner" due to its faltering military readiness and low defense spending, according to a sharply worded fact sheet issued by the Pentagon to justify new restrictions on America's northern neighbor. Why it matters: The restrictions deepen tensions between the U.S. and Canada over trade and defense, as Ottawa reconsiders billions of dollars in purchases of American weapons. The new restraints — which do not affect defense or intelligence sharing— limit U.S. military personnel from fraternizing with their Canadian counterparts at official events without prior authorization from the Pentagon, an official told Axios. The Pentagon fact sheet has not been reported. But the Washington Post first reported the restrictions, followed by the New York Times . Zoom in: At the heart of the dispute are NATO defense spending goals and military readiness under the bilateral North American Aerospace Defense Command where, the memo says, Canada falls short in three ways: 🛩️ Air: Only 41.9% of the Royal Canadian Air Force fleet "was serviceable from 2025-2026, largely due to ageing equipment and personnel shortages," the Pentagon fact sheet says. The shortfall limits Canada's "ability to meaningfully contribute to air defense commitments … to defend our North American airspace against all threats." Canada relies on the U.S. and NATO for airborne early-warning aircraft but is negotiating to buy its own from Sweden's Saab. ⚓️ Sea: Just 53.9% of Canada's naval fleet was "serviceable" from 2025-2026, limiting its "ability to monitor maritime approaches to North America," the fact sheet says. Only one of Canada's "four ageing Victoria-class submarines" is "seaworthy at any given time." Canada has a new fleet of conventional submarines, manufactured by ThyssenKrupp Marine Systems, coming on line, but until then, its undersea "capability will be limited." 🪖 Land: The Canadian Army had an operational readiness rate of 48% from 2025-2026. The other side: Canada's own defense department reported the same equipment shortages while finding that 61% of its military units were ready for operations. "Canada continues to engage constructively and professionally with our American counterparts and would not speculate on media reports of this nature," Canada's Department of National Defence said in a written statement concerning the new U.S. military restrictions. "Canada and the United States have a long history of defence cooperation built on a shared commitment to continental defence and protecting our collective security around the globe. This collaborative work continues," the statement said, noting the "deeply interconnected" relationship between the countries and their "enduring partnership." Friction point : NATO defense spending has been a constant sore spot for President Trump. Canada first agreed to spend 2% of GDP on defense spending in 2006, but it was only at 1.5% until 2025, according to the Pentagon. Canada announced in March that it had achieved 2% GDP-defense spending, but now the target is 5% by 2035 and U.S. policy makers say Ottawa "has yet to articulate a resourced path to reach this target. "Canada must get serious and focused," the fact sheet said. The big picture: More defense spending by NATO allies is a revenue generator for the U.S., which has the globe's largest military-industrial complex. "Since March 2025," the Pentagon fact sheet noted, "Ottawa has been reviewing its decision to procure 88 F-35s to replace its ageing fighters and is considering a mixed fleet that will compound existing personnel shortfalls." Canada is increasingly looking to European manufacturers for its military buildup. Context: Relations between the two countries soured when Trump scrapped a free-trade agreement he insisted on in his first term, began a tariff war and threatened to annex Canada as the 51st state. At a Friday news conference, Trump complained about Canada and trade imbalances between the two countries. The bottom line: The two nations remain allies and work closely together on defense issues. Canada has an office in the Pentagon next to the joint staff. The limited restrictions imposed by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on official interactions between U.S. and Canadian personnel are a "shot across the bow," a U.S. official said. "Unfortunately," the Pentagon fact sheet said, "Canada has yet to make the hard decisions and tradeoffs needed to put it on track to fulfill its NATO Defense Investment Pledge and become a credible partner in the defense of our shared continent. Canada's defense shortfalls speak for themselves." Editor ' s note: This story has been updated with comment from Canada's defense department.
